Antimavatthuajjhāpannassāpi attheva āpatti. Vuṭṭhānadesanāhi pana asujjhanato “payoge payoge āpatti pārājikassā”ti na vuttaṃ. Gaṇanapayojanābhāvato kiñcāpi na vuttaṃ, atha kho padabhājane (pārā. 58) “āpatti pārājikassā”ti vacanenāyamattho siddhoti yuttiñca vadanti.

'The sexual act' is a name obtained through common usage. If one should engage, by one's own effort or by another's effort, by way of consenting to any one of the acts of insertion, having been inserted, remaining, or withdrawal of one's own organ into one's own orifice or another's orifice, or of another's organ into one's own orifice, he is defeated, no longer in communion. Some, however, say: 'If he engages in four, three, two, or one of these acts, beginning with insertion, he is defeated. For it is said: "If he consents to insertion, consents to having been inserted, consents to remaining, consents to withdrawal, it is a pārājika offense," and so on' (Pārā. 58). According to their view, one incurs four pārājika offenses in all four acts. They themselves say thus: 'Let him incur the pārājika offense for the sexual act. Because a person—who, having incurred pārājika offenses in his own transgressions that are of the same class as the pārājika for the sexual act, as well as a saṅghādisesa offense, then gives up the training, and while a householder commits a pārājika act such as sexual intercourse, and then goes forth and receives higher ordination again—becomes free of offense only after having made amends for one or many saṅghādisesa offenses, therefore he was an offender while a householder.' Even for one who has committed the final offense, there is indeed an offense. But since there is no purification through rehabilitation or confession, it is not said, 'in each attempt, there is a pārājika offense.' Although it is not said because there is no purpose in counting, they state as their reasoning that this meaning is established by the statement 'it is a pārājika offense' in the analysis of the terms (Pārā. 58).

Yadi [V 0.0018] evaṃ mātikāyampi “yo pana bhikkhu methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭiseveyya, pārājika”nti vattabbaṃ bhaveyya, pārājikassa anavasesavacanampi na yujjeyya. Sabbepi hi āpattikkhandhe, bhikkhugaṇanañca anavasesetvā tiṭṭhatīti anavasesavacananti katvā paveseva āpatti, na paviṭṭhādīsu. Tamevekaṃ sandhāya “yassa siyā āpattī”ti (mahāva. 134) pārājikāpattimpi anto katvā nidānuddesavacanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tasmā mātikāyaṃ “pārājika”nti avatvā “pārājiko hotī”ti (pārā. 42, 44) puggalaniddesavacanaṃ tena sarīrabandhanena upasampadāya abhabbabhāvadīpanatthaṃ. “Āpatti pārājikassā”ti padabhājane vacanaṃ antimavatthuṃ ajjhāpannassāpi [M 0.0019] pārājikassa asaṃvāsassa sato puggalassa atheyyasaṃvāsakabhāvadīpanatthaṃ. Na hi so saṃvāsaṃ sādiyantopi theyyasaṃvāsako hoti, tasmā upasampanno “bhikkhū”tveva vuccati. Tenevāha “asuddho hoti puggalo aññataraṃ pārājikaṃ dhammaṃ ajjhāpanno, tañce suddhadiṭṭhi samāno anokāsaṃ kārāpetvā akkosādhippāyo vadati, āpatti omasavādena dukkaṭassā”ti (pārā. 389) anupasampannassa tadabhāvato siddho so upasampanno “bhikkhū”tveva vuccatīti, tena padasodhammaṃ, sahaseyyañca janeti, bhikkhupesuññādiñca janetīti veditabbaṃ (vajira. ṭī. pārājika 39).

If it were to be stated thus in the mātikā: 'Whatever bhikkhu engages in sexual intercourse is pārājika,' then the expression 'without remainder' for a pārājika would not be fitting. For, with regard to all the aggregates of offenses and the counting of bhikkhus, it stands without remainder, and is thus called 'the expression without remainder'; the offense is in the entering, not in what has been entered, and so on. With reference to that very one, the introductory statement, 'For whom there may be an offense,' should be understood as including the pārājika offense. Therefore, in the mātikā, instead of saying 'pārājika,' the phrase 'he is pārājika' is used as a designation of the person, to indicate the state of being unfit for higher ordination due to that bodily connection. The phrase 'an offense of pārājika' in the word-analysis is to show the state of not being one who partakes in communion by theft for a person who, having committed the final offense, is pārājika and not in communion. For even if he assents to communion, he is not one who partakes in communion by theft; therefore, the ordained one is still called a 'bhikkhu.' For that reason, it is said: 'A person is impure, having committed one of the pārājika offenses, and if one of pure view, without granting an opportunity and with the intent to revile, speaks, there is a dukkaṭa offense for abusive speech.' Since that is not the case for the unordained, it is established that the ordained one is still called a 'bhikkhu.' By that, it should be understood, he gives rise to the padasodhamma, co-residence, slander among bhikkhus, and so on.

Nidānā mātikābhedo, vibhaṅgo tanniyāmako;

Tato āpattiyā bhedo, anāpatti tadaññathāti. (vajira. ṭī. pārājika 43-44) –

From the origin comes the distinction of the mātikā; the analysis is its determinant. From that comes the distinction of the offense; non-offense is otherwise.

Ayaṃ nayo veditabbo. Tattha sudinnavatthu (pārā. 24 ādayo)-makkaṭivatthu (pārā. 40 ādayo)-vajjiputtakavatthu (pārā. 43) cāti tippabhedavatthu imassa sikkhāpadassa nidānaṃ nāma. Tato nidānā “yo pana bhikkhu bhikkhūnaṃ…pe… asaṃvāso”ti (pārā. 44) imissā mātikāya bhedo jāto. Tattha hi “antamaso tiracchānagatāyā”ti (pārā. 44) itthiliṅgavasena “saccaṃ, āvuso, bhagavatā sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ, tañca kho itthiyā, no purise, no paṇḍake, no ubhatobyañjanake cā”ti makkaṭipārājiko viya aññopi lesaṃ oḍḍetuṃ sakkoti, tasmā tādisassa alesokāsassa dassanatthaṃ idaṃ vuccati, makkaṭisaṅkhātā nidānā “antamaso tiracchānagatāyapī”ti mātikāya vacanabhedo, na itthiyā eva methunasiddhidassanato. Tasmā vibhaṅgo tanniyāmako tassā mātikāya adhippetatthaniyāmako vibhaṅgoti. Vibhaṅge hi “tisso itthiyo, tayo ubhatobyañjanakā, tayo paṇḍakā, tayo purisā. Manussitthiyā tayo magge, tiracchānagatapurisassa dve magge”tiādinā (pārā. 56) nayena [V 0.0019] sabbalesokāsaṃ pidahitvā niyamo kato. Etthāha – yadi evaṃ sādhāraṇasikkhāpadavasena vā liṅgaparivattanavasena vā na kevalaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ, bhikkhunīnampi “sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno”ti vibhaṅge vattabbaṃ siyā. Tadavacanena hi bhikkhunī purisaliṅgapātubhāvena bhikkhubhāve [M 0.0020] ṭhitā evaṃ vadeyya “nāhaṃ upasampadākaraṇakāle bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāsājīvasamāpannā, tasmā na apaccakkhātasikkhāpi methunadhammena pārājikā homī”ti. Vuccate – yathā vuttaṃ, tathā na vattabbaṃ aniṭṭhappasaṅgato. Tathā vutte bhikkhunīnampi sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ atthīti āpajjati. Tañcāniṭṭhaṃ. Idamaparamaniṭṭhaṃ “sabbasikkhāpadāni sādhāraṇāneva nāsādhāraṇānī”ti. Apicāyaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāsājīvasamāpannāva hotīti dassanatthaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, taṃyeva upajjhaṃ tameva upasampadaṃ tāni vassāni bhikkhūhi saṅgamitu”ntiādi (pārā. 69) vuttaṃ. Tato āpattiyā bhedoti tato vibhaṅgato “akkhayite sarīre pārājikaṃ, yebhuyyena khayite thullaccaya”ntiādi (pārā. 73, pari. 157) āpattiyā bhedo hoti. Anāpatti tadaññathāti tato eva vibhaṅgato yena ākārena āpatti vuttā, tato aññenākārena anāpattibhedova hoti. “Sādiyati, āpatti pārājikassa, na sādiyati, anāpattī”ti hi vibhaṅge asati na paññāyati. Ettāvatā “nidānā mātikābhedo”ti ayaṃ gāthā samāsato vuttatthā hoti. Visesakāraṇaṃ pana tasmiṃ tasmiṃ sikkhāpade āvibhavissati.

This method is to be understood. Herein, the origin (nidāna) of this training rule is of three kinds: the story of Sudinna, the story of the monkey, and the story of the Vajjiputtaka bhikkhu. From that origin, a distinction in this mātikā arose: 'Whatever bhikkhu...pe... is not in communion.' For here, regarding 'even with a female animal,' because of the feminine gender, another, like the bhikkhu who committed pārājika with a monkey, might find a loophole, saying: 'Truly, friends, the training rule was laid down by the Blessed One, but that was for a woman, not for a man, not for a paṇḍaka, and not for a hermaphrodite.' Therefore, to show there is no room for such a loophole, this is said: from the origin known as the monkey story, the distinction in the wording of the mātikā is 'even with a female animal,' not because the accomplishment of sexual intercourse is seen only with a woman. Therefore, the analysis is its determinant; the analysis is the determinant of the intended meaning of that mātikā. For in the analysis, by the method beginning, 'There are three kinds of women, three kinds of hermaphrodites, three kinds of paṇḍakas, three kinds of men. For a human woman, there are three orifices; for a male animal, there are two orifices,' every opportunity for a loophole is closed off and a determination is made. Here it is said: If so, then by way of a shared training rule or by way of a change of gender, it should be stated in the analysis not only for bhikkhus but also for bhikkhunīs, 'having undertaken the training and livelihood.' For without that statement, a bhikkhunī who has become a bhikkhu through the appearance of male characteristics could say: 'At the time of my higher ordination, I had not undertaken the training and livelihood of bhikkhus; therefore, even without having renounced the training, I am not pārājikā through the act of sexual intercourse.' It is said: It should not be stated as was suggested, because of the undesirable consequence. If it were so stated, it would follow that bhikkhunīs also have the renunciation of the training. And that is undesirable. This is another undesirable consequence: 'All training rules are shared, not unshared.' Moreover, to show that she has indeed undertaken the training and livelihood of bhikkhus, it was said: 'I allow, bhikkhus, that same preceptor, that same higher ordination, those same years to be counted among the bhikkhus,' and so on. Then, 'the distinction of the offense': from that analysis, the distinction of the offense occurs, as in 'When the organ is intact, it is a pārājika; when mostly destroyed, it is a thullaccaya,' and so on. 'Non-offense is otherwise': from that very analysis, in whatever way an offense is stated, in a way other than that, there is a distinction of non-offense. For if the analysis were absent, it would not be known that 'If one consents, it is an offense of pārājika; if one does not consent, it is not an offense.' To this extent, the meaning of this verse, 'From the origin, the distinction of the mātikā,' has been stated in brief. The specific reason, however, will become apparent in each respective training rule.

Paṭhamapaññatti tāva paṭhamabodhiṃ atikkamitvā paññattattā, āyasmato sudinnassa aṭṭhavassikakāle paññattattā ca rattaññumahattaṃ pattakāle paññattā, dutiyapaññatti bāhusaccamahattaṃ pattakāle. So hi āyasmā makkaṭipārājiko yathā mātugāmappaṭisaṃyuttesu sikkhāpadesu tiracchānagatitthī na adhippetā, tathā idhāpīti saññāya “saccaṃ, āvuso…pe… tañca kho manussitthiyā, no tiracchānagatāyā”ti (pārā. 41) āha. Tatiyapaññatti lābhaggamahattaṃ pattakāle uppannā “yāvadatthaṃ bhuñjitvā”tiādi (pārā. 43) vacanato, vepullamahattampi ettheva labbhatīti imaṃ paṭhamapārājikasikkhāpadaṃ tividhampi vatthuṃ upādāya catubbidhampi taṃ kālaṃ patvā paññattanti veditabbaṃ.

The first laying down of the rule, having been laid down after passing the first period of enlightenment, and also because it was laid down when the venerable Sudinna was in his eighth year, was laid down at a time when greatness of seniority had been attained. The second laying down of the rule was at a time when greatness of great learning had been attained. For that venerable one who committed pārājika with a monkey, with the perception that 'just as in the training rules connected with womenfolk a female animal is not intended, so too here,' said: 'Truly, friends...pe... but that was with a human woman, not with a female animal.' The third laying down of the rule arose at a time when greatness of the highest gain had been attained, on account of the words, 'having eaten as much as he wished,' and so on. The greatness of abundance is also obtained here. Thus, this first pārājika training rule should be understood as having been laid down in dependence on three kinds of stories and having reached four kinds of time.

Tattha yo panāti anavasesapariyādānapadaṃ. Bhikkhūti tassa atippasaṅganiyamapadaṃ. Bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāsājīvasamāpannoti tassa visesanavacanaṃ. Na hi sabbopi bhikkhunāmako, yā bhagavatā yāya kāyaci upasampadāya upasampannabhikkhūnaṃ heṭṭhimaparicchedena sikkhitabbā sikkhā vihitā[M 0.0021], “ettha saha jīvantī”ti yo ca sājīvo vutto, taṃ ubhayaṃ samāpannova hoti. Kadā pana samāpanno hoti? Yāya kāyaci upasampadāya upasampannasamanantarameva tadubhayaṃ [V 0.0020] jānantopi ajānantopi tadajjhupagatattā samāpannova nāma hoti. Saha jīvantīti yāva sikkhaṃ na paccakkhāti, pārājikabhāvaṃ vā na pāpuṇāti. Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “sikkhaṃ paripūrento sikkhāsamāpanno sājīvaṃ avītikkamanto sājīvasamāpanno”ti, taṃ ukkaṭṭhaparicchedavasena vuttaṃ. Na hi sikkhaṃ aparipūrento, kāmavitakkādibahulo vā ekaccaṃ sāvasesaṃ sājīvaṃ vītikkamanto vā sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno nāma na hoti.

Here, 'whoever' (yo pana) is a term of exhaustive inclusion. 'Bhikkhu' is a term that restricts its over-extension. 'One who has entered upon the training and livelihood of bhikkhus' (bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno) is its qualifying phrase. For not every one who is merely called a bhikkhu is included; rather, only one who has received higher ordination by the Blessed One through any valid ordination procedure, and who, by the lowest standard, is to train in the training prescribed, and who is also described as 'living together thereby' (sājīva), is one who has entered upon both. But when is one considered to have entered upon it? Immediately upon receiving higher ordination by any valid ordination procedure, whether knowing it or not, by virtue of having undertaken it, one is considered to have entered upon both. 'Living together thereby' means until one renounces the training or incurs a pārājika offense. However, what is stated in the Andhakaṭṭhakathā—'one who fulfills the training has entered upon the training; one who does not transgress the livelihood has entered upon the livelihood'—is said from the perspective of the highest standard. For it is not that one who does not fulfill the training, or who is much given to sensual thoughts, or who transgresses some remaining part of the livelihood, is not called one who has entered upon the training and livelihood.

Ukkaṭṭhaparicchedena pana catukkaṃ labbhati – “atthi bhikkhu sikkhāsamāpanno sīlāni paccavekkhanto na sājīvasamāpanno acittakaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ vītikkamanto, atthi na sikkhāsamāpanno kāmavitakkādibahulo sājīvasamāpanno nirāpattiko, atthi na sikkhāsamāpanno na ca sājīvasamāpanno anavasesaṃ āpattiṃ āpanno, atthi ubhayasamāpanno sikkhaṃ paripūrento sājīvañca avītikkamanto”ti. Ayamettha catuttho bhikkhu ukkaṭṭho idha adhippeto siyā. Na hi bhagavā anukkaṭṭhaṃ vattuṃ yuttoti ce? Na, “tatra yāyaṃ adhisīlasikkhā, ayaṃ imasmiṃ atthe adhippetā sikkhā”ti vacanavirodhato, ukkaṭṭhaggahaṇādhippāye sati “sikkhāti tisso sikkhā”ti ettakameva vattabbanti adhippāyo. Sikkhattayasamāpanno hi sabbukkaṭṭho. “Methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭiseveyyā”ti parato vacanaṃ apekkhitvā adhisīlasikkhāva vuttāti ce? Na, tassāpi abhabbattā. Na hi adhisīlasikkhaṃ paripūrento, sājīvañca avītikkamanto methunadhammaṃ paṭisevituṃ bhabbo, taṃ sikkhaṃ aparipūrento, sājīvañca vītikkamantoyeva hi paṭiseveyyāti adhippāyā. Tasmā evamettha attho gahetabbo. Yasmā sikkhāpadasaṅkhāto sājīvo adhisīlasikkhameva saṅgaṇhāti, na itarasikkhādvayaṃ, tasmā “tatra yāyaṃ adhisīlasikkhā, ayaṃ imasmiṃ atthe adhippetā sikkhā”ti vuttaṃ. Tasmā adhisīlasikkhāya saṅgāhako sājīvo sikkhāsājīvoti vutto. Iti sājīvavisesanatthaṃ sikkhāggahaṇaṃ kataṃ. Tadatthadīpanatthameva vibhaṅge sikkhaṃ aparāmasitvā “tasmiṃ sikkhati, tena vuccati sājīvasamāpanno”ti (pārā. 45) vuttaṃ. Tena [M 0.0022] ekamevidaṃ atthapadanti dīpitaṃ hoti. Tañca upasampadūpagamanantarato paṭṭhāya sikkhanādhikārattā “sikkhatī”ti ca “samāpanno”ti ca vuccati. Yo evaṃ “sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno”ti saṅkhaṃ gato, tādisaṃ paccayaṃ paṭicca aparabhāge sājīvasaṅkhātameva sikkhaṃ apaccakkhāya tasmiṃyeva dubbalyaṃ anāvikatvā methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭiseveyyāti ayamattho yujjati.

However, by the highest standard, a tetrad is obtained: 'There is a bhikkhu who has entered upon the training, reflecting on the precepts, but has not entered upon the livelihood, having transgressed a training rule unintentionally; there is one who has not entered upon the training, being much given to sensual thoughts, etc., but has entered upon the livelihood, being free from offense; there is one who has neither entered upon the training nor the livelihood, having committed an offense without remainder; there is one who has entered upon both, fulfilling the training and not transgressing the livelihood.' Here, this fourth bhikkhu might be the one intended as the most excellent. If it be said: 'Is it not appropriate for the Blessed One to speak of the less excellent?' No, because it contradicts the statement, 'Here, the higher virtue training is the training intended in this context.' If the intention were to grasp the most excellent, the meaning is that it would suffice to say only, 'the training means the threefold training.' For one who has entered upon the threefold training is indeed the most excellent of all. If it be said: 'Is it that only the higher virtue training is spoken of, considering the phrase

Kintu aṭṭhakathānayo paṭikkhitto hoti, so ca na paṭikkhepāraho hoti, adhippāyo panettha [V 0.0021] pariyesitabbo. Sabbesu sikkhāpadesu idameva bhikkhulakkhaṇaṃ sādhāraṇaṃ yadidaṃ “bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno”ti. Khīṇāsavopi sāvako āpattiṃ āpajjati acittakaṃ, tathā sekkho, puthujjano pana sacittakampi, tasmā sekkhāsekkhaputhujjanānaṃ sāmaññamidaṃ bhikkhulakkhaṇanti katvā kevalaṃ sikkhāsamāpanno, kevalaṃ sājīvasamāpanno, ubhayasamāpanno cāti sarūpekadesaekasesanayena “sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno”tveva sampiṇḍetvā ukkaṭṭhaggahaṇena anukkaṭṭhānaṃ gahaṇasiddhito aṭṭhakathāyaṃ ukkaṭṭhova vutto. Tameva sampādetuṃ “tasmiṃ sikkhati, tena vuccati sājīvasamāpanno”ti ettha sikkhāsaddassa avacane parihāraṃ vatvā yasmā pana so sikkhampi samāpanno, tasmā sikkhāsamāpannotipi atthato veditabboti ca vatvā “yaṃ sikkhaṃ samāpanno, taṃ apaccakkhāya, yañca sājīvaṃ samāpanno, tattha dubbalyaṃ anāvikatvā”ti vuttanti ayamaṭṭhakathāya adhippāyo veditabbo. Etasmiṃ pana adhippāye adhisīlasikkhāya eva gahaṇaṃ sabbatthikattā, sīlādhikārato ca vinayassāti veditabbaṃ. Yathā ca sikkhāpadaṃ samādiyanto sīlaṃ samādiyatīti vuccati, evaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paccakkhanto sīlaṃ paccakkhātīti vattuṃ yujjati, tasmā tattha vuttaṃ “yaṃ sikkhaṃ samāpanno, taṃ apaccakkhāyā”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. sikkhāpaccakkhānavibhaṅgavaṇṇanā). Ettāvatā samāsato “sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno”ti ettha vattabbavinicchayo niṭṭhito hoti.

However, the commentary's method is rejected, but it is not worthy of rejection; the intended meaning here must be sought. In all the training rules, this is the common characteristic of a bhikkhu, namely, 'one who has entered upon the training and livelihood of bhikkhus.' Even a disciple whose defilements are destroyed may commit an unintentional offense, as may a trainee, whereas an ordinary person may commit one intentionally. Therefore, considering this as the common characteristic of trainees, non-trainees, and ordinary persons, it is succinctly stated as 'one who has entered upon the training and livelihood' by the method of combining these aspects—some parts similar, others distinct, others single—and because the inclusion of the inferior is established through the inclusion of the superior, in the commentary, only the superior is mentioned. To accomplish this, a justification is given for the omission of the word 'training' in the phrase 'he trains in that, therefore he is called one who has entered upon the livelihood.' And since he has also entered upon the training, it should be understood that he is, in meaning, 'one who has entered upon the training.' Therefore, the commentary's intention should be understood as this: that it is said, 'without renouncing the training he has entered upon, and without revealing any weakness in the livelihood he has entered upon.' In this context, it should be understood that the inclusion is of the higher virtue training alone, because it is universally applicable and because the Vinaya pertains to virtue. Just as one who undertakes a training rule is said to undertake virtue, so too one who renounces a training rule can be said to renounce virtue. Therefore, it is stated there, 'without renouncing the training he has entered upon' (Pārā. Aṭṭha. Sikkha-paccakkhāna-vibhaṅga-vaṇṇanā). Thus, in summary, the analysis of what is to be said regarding 'one who has entered upon the training and livelihood' is concluded.

Kiṃ iminā visesavacanena payojanaṃ, nanu “yo pana bhikkhu sikkhaṃ apaccakkhāya dubbalyaṃ anāvikatvā…pe… asaṃvāso”ti ettakameva vattabbanti ce? Na vattabbaṃ aniṭṭhappasaṅgato. “Yo pana sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno theyyasaṃvāsādiko kevalena samaññāmattena, paṭiññāmattena [M 0.0023] vā bhikkhu, tassāpi sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ atthi, sikkhaṃ apaccakkhāya ca methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevantassa pārājikāpatti. Yo vā pacchā pārājikaṃ āpattiṃ āpajjitvā na sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno, tassa ca, yo vā pakkhapaṇḍakattā paṇḍakabhāvūpagamanena na sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno, tassa ca tadubhayaṃ atthīti āpajjati. Paṇḍakabhāvapakkhe ca paṇḍako upasampadāya na vatthū”ti vuttaṃ. Tasmā itarasmiṃ pakkhe vatthūti siddhaṃ. Tasmiṃ pakkhe upasampanno paṇḍakabhāvapakkhe paṇḍakattā na sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno, so pariccajitabbāya sikkhāya abhāvena sikkhaṃ apaccakkhāya mukhena parassa aṅgajātaggahaṇanayena methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭiseveyya, tassa kuto pārājikāpattīti adhippāyo. Ayaṃ nayo apaṇḍakapakkhaṃ alabhamānasseva parato yujjati, labhantassa pana arūpasattānaṃ kusalādisamāpattikkhaṇe bhavaṅgavicchede satipi amaraṇaṃ viya paṇḍakabhāvapakkhepi bhikkhubhāvo atthi. Saṃvāsaṃ vā sādiyantassa na theyyasaṃvāsakabhāvo atthi antimavatthuajjhāpannassa viya. Na ca sahaseyyādiṃ janeti[V 0.0022]. Gaṇapūrako pana na hoti antimavatthuṃ ajjhāpanno viya. Na so sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno. Itarasmiṃ pana pakkhe hoti, ayaṃ imassa tato viseso. Kimayaṃ sahetuko, udāhu ahetukoti? Na ahetuko. Yato upasampadā tassa apaṇḍakapakkhe anuññātā sahetukappaṭisandhikattā. Paṇḍakabhāvapakkhepi kissa nānuññātāti ce? Paṇḍakabhūtattā opakkamikapaṇḍakassa viya.

What is the purpose of this specific statement? If it is said: 'Is it not enough to say, "Whatever bhikkhu, without having renounced the training and without having revealed his weakness... is not in communion"?' It should not be said, because of an undesirable consequence. For it would follow that for one who is a thief-in-communion and so on, who is a bhikkhu merely by designation or by claim, there is also the renouncing of the training, and for him, engaging in sexual intercourse without having renounced the training would be a pārājika offense. And it would also apply to one who, having later committed a pārājika offense, is not one who has undertaken the training and livelihood; and to one who, being a fortnightly eunuch or having become a eunuch, is not one who has undertaken the training and livelihood. And in the case of a eunuch, it is said, 'A eunuch is not a basis for higher ordination.' Therefore, it is established that in the other case, he is a basis. In that case, one ordained in the non-eunuch state who, in the eunuch state, being a eunuch, is not one who has undertaken the training and livelihood—if he, due to the absence of a training to be renounced, were to engage in sexual intercourse in the manner of taking another's sexual organ with his mouth without having renounced the training, whence would there be a pārājika offense for him? This is the intention. This method is applicable only to one who does not subsequently attain the non-eunuch state. But for one who does attain it, just as for formless beings there is no death even when the life-continuum is interrupted at the moment of attaining wholesome states and so on, so too for him, the status of a bhikkhu exists even in the eunuch state. Or, for one consenting to communion, there is no state of being a thief-in-communion, as for one who has committed an ultimate offense. Nor does it give rise to sharing a bed and so on. He does not, however, complete a quorum, like one who has committed an ultimate offense. He is not one who has undertaken the training and livelihood. But in the other state, he is; this is the difference between this one and that one. Is this with a cause, or without a cause? It is not without a cause. Since his higher ordination is permitted in the non-eunuch state, it is because of having a rebirth-linking with a root-cause. If it is asked, 'Why is it not permitted even in the eunuch state?' Because of having become a eunuch, like one made a eunuch by an external act.

Apica “sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno”ti iminā tassa sikkhāsamādānaṃ dīpetvā taṃ samādinnaṃ sikkhaṃ apaccakkhāya, tattha ca dubbalyaṃ anāvikatvāti vattuṃ yujjati, na aññathāti iminā kāraṇena yathāvuttāniṭṭhappasaṅgato “yo pana bhikkhu bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno sikkhaṃ apaccakkhāyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yathā cettha, evaṃ “yo pana bhikkhu bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno sikkhaṃ apaccakkhāya dubbalyaṃ anāvikatvā gāmā vā araññā vā adinnaṃ…pe… yo pana bhikkhu bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno sikkhaṃ apaccakkhāya dubbalyaṃ anāvikatvā sugatacīvarappamāṇaṃ cīvaraṃ kārāpeyyā”ti sabbattha yojetabbaṃ.

Furthermore, by “one who has undertaken the training and livelihood,” his undertaking of the training is shown. Without renouncing that undertaken training, and without declaring his weakness in that respect, it is proper to speak of a transgression, not otherwise. For this reason, to avoid the undesirable consequence as stated, “Should any bhikkhu, having undertaken the training and livelihood of the bhikkhus, without renouncing the training…” and so on, was stated. Just as here, so too it should be applied in all cases: “Should any bhikkhu, having undertaken the training and livelihood of the bhikkhus, without renouncing the training and without declaring his weakness, take what is not given from a village or wilderness…” and so on. Similarly: “Should any bhikkhu, having undertaken the training and livelihood of the bhikkhus, without renouncing the training and without declaring his weakness, have a robe made to the Sugata’s standard…” — this should be applied in all such cases.

“Antamaso tiracchānagatāyapī”ti manussitthiṃ upādāya vuttaṃ. Na hi pageva paṇḍake, purise vāti vattuṃ yujjati. Sesaṃ tattha tattha vuttanayameva[M 0.0024]. Ayaṃ tāva mātikāya vinicchayo aññatthāpi yathāsambhavaṃ yojetvā dīpetabbo.

'Even with a female animal': this is said with reference to a human female. For it is certainly not fitting to speak thus of a eunuch, let alone a male. The rest is according to the method stated in each respective case. This, for now, is the analysis of the matrix; it should be applied and explained elsewhere as is suitable.

Sāriputtabelaṭṭhasīsānandādayopi sikkhāpadapaññattikāraṇattā ca āpattiāpajjanato ca kasmā mahāvibhaṅge ñatticatutthaupasampadāyeva āgatāti? Paṭikkhittāya saraṇagamanūpasampadāya anuññātappasaṅgabhayāti upatissatthero. Āpattiyā bhabbataṃ sandhāya tasmimpi vutte pubbe paṭikkhittāpi bhagavatā puna anuññātāti bhikkhūnaṃ micchāgāho vā vimati vā uppajjati, tasmā na vuttāti vuttaṃ hoti.

Why is only the ñatticatuttha upasampadā mentioned in the Mahāvibhaṅga, despite the involvement of Sāriputta, Belaṭṭhasīsa, Ānanda, and others in establishing the training rules and in committing offenses? The Elder Upatissa said it was because of the fear of the rejected going-for-refuge ordination being permitted as a consequence. Because if the possibility of an offense were implied, even if that were stated there, the bhikkhus would have a wrong understanding or doubt that what the Blessed One had previously rejected he had later approved; therefore, it was not stated—this is what is meant.

“Adhammakammaṃ vaggakamma”ti (mahāva. 387) vacanato kuppakammampi katthaci “kamma”nti vuccati, tasmā “akuppenā”ti vuttaṃ. Yasmā akuppakammampi ekaccaṃ na ṭhānārahaṃ, yena apatto osāraṇaṃ suosāritoti vuccati, tasmā “ṭhānārahenā”ti vuttaṃ. Yadi evaṃ “ṭhānārahenā”ti idameva vattabbaṃ iminā akuppasiddhitoti ce? Na, aṭṭhānārahena akuppena upasampanno imasmiṃ atthe na adhippeto aniṭṭhappasaṅgato. Dvīhi panetehi ekato vuttehi [V 0.0023] ayamattho paññāyati – kevalaṃ tena akuppena upasampanno ayampi imasmiṃ atthe adhippeto bhikkhūti, ṭhānārahena ca akuppena ca upasampanno ayampi imasmiṃ atthe adhippeto bhikkhūti, kuppena upasampanno nādhippetoti.

According to the saying, 'An unlawful act is a factional act,' even an invalid act is sometimes called an 'act'; therefore, it is said 'by a valid one.' Since even some valid acts are not fit to stand, whereby one undeserving of rehabilitation is said to be 'well-rehabilitated,' therefore it is said 'by one fit to stand.' If so, should only 'by one fit to stand' be stated, since this would establish its validity? No, because one ordained by a valid but unfit act is not intended in this sense, due to an undesirable consequence. When these two are stated together, however, this meaning is understood: one ordained merely by a valid act is also intended as a bhikkhu in this sense; and one ordained by an act that is both fit to stand and valid is also intended as a bhikkhu in this sense; but one ordained by an invalid act is not intended.

“Paṭisandhiggahaṇato paṭṭhāya aparipuṇṇavīsativasso”ti vuttattā opapātikañcāti soḷasavassuddesikā opapātikā paṭisandhito paṭṭhāya aparipuṇṇavīsativassāti vadanti. ‘Soḷasavassuddesikā hontī’ti vuttattā puna cattāri vassāni icchitabbāni, ‘paṭisandhiggahaṇato paṭṭhāyā’ti idaṃ gabbhaseyyakānaṃ vasena vutta”nti eke. “Keci vadantī”ti yattha yattha likhīyati, tattha tattha vicāretvā atthaṃ suṭṭhu upalakkhaye. Opakkamike paṇḍakabhāvo āruḷhanayena veditabbo. “Pakkhapaṇḍako apaṇḍakapakkhe pabbājetvā paṇḍakapakkhe nāsetabbo”ti (vajira. ṭī. mahāvagga 109) likhitaṃ.

Because it is said, 'From the moment of rebirth-linking, one who is not yet twenty years old,' and because they are spontaneously born, some say that sixteen-year-old novices who are spontaneously born are 'not yet twenty years old from the moment of rebirth-linking.' Others say: 'Because it is said, "They are sixteen-year-old novices," four more years are required; the phrase "from the moment of rebirth-linking" is said with reference to those born from the womb.' Wherever it is written, 'Some say,' one should investigate and thoroughly grasp the meaning in each case. The state of being a eunuch through an external act should be understood by the established method. It is written: 'A fortnightly eunuch, having been given the going-forth in his non-eunuch phase, should be expelled in his eunuch phase.'

“Binduṃ adatvā ce nivāseti, theyyasaṃvāsako na hotī”ti vadanti, vīmaṃsitabbaṃ. Liṅgānurūpassāti sāmaṇerārahassa saṃvāsassa sāditattāti adhippāyo.

'If one wears a robe without applying the determination mark, one is not a thief-in-communion,' they say; this should be investigated. The intention is that this is because communion appropriate for a novice, which is in accordance with his outward sign, has been consented to.

Rājabhayādīhi [M 0.0025] gahitaliṅgānaṃ “gihī maṃ ‘samaṇo’ti jānantū”ti vañcanacitte satipi bhikkhūnaṃ vañcetukāmatāya ca tehi saṃvasitukāmatāya ca abhāvā doso na jātoti. “Yo evaṃ pabbajati, so theyyasaṃvāsako nāma hotī”ti vā “evaṃ kātuṃ na labbhatī”ti vā “evaṃ pabbajito sāmaṇero na hotī”ti vā na jānāti, vaṭṭati. “Jānāti, na vaṭṭatī”ti ca likhitaṃ. “Rājadubbhikkhādiatthāya cīvaraṃ pārupitvā saṃvāsaṃ sādiyanto theyyasaṃvāsako hoti. Kasmā? Asuddhacittattā. Puna so ‘suddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ karissāmi, kiṃ etenāti vippaṭisārena vā paccayādisulabhatāya vā karissāmī’ti suddhamānaso hutvā yāva so saṃvāsaṃ nādhivāseti, tāva theyyasaṃvāsako na hoti. Evaṃ suddhacittuppattito paṭṭhāya saṃvāsaṃ sādiyati ce, theyyasaṃvāsako hotīti adhippeto. Itarathā sabbaṃ virujjhatī”ti eke.

For those who adopt the outward signs due to fear of the king and so on, thinking, 'Let laypeople know me as a recluse,' even with such deceitful intent, no fault arises, because there is no desire to deceive the bhikkhus, nor any wish to live in communion with them. If he does not know that 'One who goes forth in this way is called a thief-in-communion,' or 'It is not permissible to do so,' or 'One thus gone forth is not a novice,' it is valid. It is also written: 'He knows, so it is not valid.' Some say: 'One who, for the sake of escaping the king, famine, and so on, dons the robe and consents to communion, becomes a thief-in-communion. Why? Because his mind is impure. But if later, with a purified mind, he thinks, "I will practice the pure holy life; what is the use of this?"—either out of remorse or because requisites are easily obtained—then as long as he does not consent to communion, he is not a thief-in-communion. It is intended that from the moment a pure mind arises, if he consents to communion, he becomes a thief-in-communion. Otherwise, everything would be contradictory.'

“Nābhiparāmāsādinā jāto tathārūpaṃ pitaraṃ ghāteti ce, pitughātako hotī”ti vadanti.

'If one who is born without the touching of the navel and so on (i.e., without sexual intercourse) kills such a father, he is a parricide,' they say.

Yo pana kāyasaṃsaggena sīlavināsaṃ pāpeti, na so bhikkhunidūsako “tiṇṇaṃ maggāna”nti [V 0.0024] vacanato. Bhikkhuniṃ pana ekatoupasampannaṃ dūsetvāpi bhikkhunidūsako hoti, sopi pārājiko hotīti vinicchayo. Bhikkhunī pana theyyasaṃvāsikā, mātupituarahantaghātikā, lohituppādikā, titthiyapakkantikā ca hoti, aṭṭhakathāsu anāgataṃ vinayadharā sampaṭicchanti.

Whoever causes the destruction of virtue through bodily contact is not a 'defiler of bhikkhunīs' according to the statement 'of the three paths.' However, one who defiles even a bhikkhunī ordained by one party is a defiler of bhikkhunīs, and he too is subject to a pārājika offense—this is the decision. Furthermore, if a bhikkhunī is one who co-resides by theft, a killer of her mother, father, or an arahant, a shedder of a Buddha's blood, or one who has gone over to the heretics, the Vinaya-holders accept what is not found in the commentaries.

“Sampajānamusāvāde pācittiya”nti (pāci. 2) vuttaṃ mariyādaṃ avītikkamanto tasmiñca sikkhāpade sikkhatīti vuccati. Sikkhāpadanti asabhāvadhammo saṅketova, idha paññatti adhippetā. “Methunasaṃvarassetaṃ adhivacana”nti samantapāsādikāyaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ panatthaṃ sandhāyāti likhitaṃ. Sikkhāti taṃ taṃ sikkhāpadaṃ, sikkhanabhāvena pavattacittuppādo. Sājīvanti paññatti. Tadatthadassanatthaṃ pubbe “methunasaṃvarassetaṃ adhivacana”nti vuttaṃ. Yasmā sikkhāya guṇasammatāya puññasammatāya tantiyā abhāvato lokassa dubbalyāvikammaṃ tattha na sambhavati. Patthanīyā hi sā, tasmā “yañca sājīvaṃ [M 0.0026] samāpanno, tasmiṃ dubbalabhāvaṃ appakāsetvā”ti vuttaṃ. Āṇāya hi dubbalyaṃ sambhavatīti upatisso. Dubbalyāvikammapadaṃ sikkhāpaccakkhānapadassa byañjanasiliṭṭhatāya vā parivārakabhāvena vā veditabbaṃ. Atha vā yasmā sikkhāpaccakkhānassa ekaccaṃ dubbalyāvikammaṃ akataṃ hoti, tasmā taṃ sandhāya “sikkhaṃ apaccakkhāyā”ti padassa atthaṃ vivaranto “dubbalyaṃ anāvikatvā”ti āha. Tattha siyā yasmā na sabbaṃ dubbalyāvikammaṃ sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ, tasmā “dubbalyaṃ anāvikatvā”ti paṭhamaṃ vatvā tassa atthaniyamatthaṃ “sikkhaṃ apaccakkhāyā”ti vattabbanti? Taṃ na, kasmā? Atthānukkamābhāvato. “Sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno”ti hi vuttattā “yaṃ sikkhaṃ samāpanno, taṃ apaccakkhāya, yañca sājīvaṃ samāpanno, tattha dubbalyaṃ anāvikatvā”ti vuccamāne anukkameneva attho vutto hoti, na aññathā, tasmā idameva paṭhamaṃ vuttanti. Tesaṃyevāti cuddasannaṃ.

“In a deliberate lie, there is a pācittiya,” it is said (Pāci. 2). Not transgressing this boundary, one is said to be training in that training rule. A training rule is a conventional designation, not an inherent phenomenon; here, a regulation is intended. “This is a term for restraint regarding sexual intercourse,” as stated in the Samantapāsādikā; it is written with reference to that meaning. Training is that particular training rule, the arising of a mental state proceeding in the manner of training. The livelihood is a regulation. To show its meaning, it was previously said, “This is a term for restraint regarding sexual intercourse.” Since the training is esteemed as virtuous and meritorious, a worldly declaration of weakness does not apply to it, for it is desirable. Therefore, it is said, “And having undertaken the livelihood, without revealing a state of weakness in it.” For weakness arises from a command—this is Upatissa's view. The term 'declaration of weakness' should be understood either due to its verbal connection with the term 'renunciation of the training' or as serving as an ancillary matter. Or else, since some declaration of weakness is not a renunciation of the training, therefore, with reference to that, explaining the meaning of the phrase, “without renouncing the training,” it says, “without revealing weakness.” Here, it might be asked: Since not every declaration of weakness is a renunciation of the training, should “without revealing weakness” not be stated first, and then “without renouncing the training” be stated to establish its meaning? That is not so. Why? Because there is no sequence of meaning. For since it is said, “one who has undertaken the training and livelihood,” when it is said, “without renouncing the training which one has undertaken, and, having undertaken the livelihood, without revealing weakness therein,” the meaning is stated in due order, and not otherwise. Therefore, this was stated first. “Of those very” means of the fourteen.

“Sikkhaṃ apaccakkhāyā”ti sabbasikkhāpadānaṃ sādhāraṇatthaṃ “ayamettha anupaññattī”ti vuttaṃ.

The phrase “Without renouncing the training” was stated as “this is a supplementary regulation here” because it is a matter common to all training rules.

Pavesanaṃ nāma aṅgajātaṃ pavesentassa aṅgajātena samphusanaṃ. Paviṭṭhaṃ nāma yāva mūlaṃ pavesentassa vippakatakālo vāyāmakālo. Sukkavisaṭṭhisamaye aṅgajātaṃ ṭhitaṃ nāma. Uddharaṇaṃ nāma nīharaṇakālo. Vinayagaṇṭhipade pana “vāyāmato oramitvā ṭhānaṃ ṭhitaṃ nāmā”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ [V 0.0025] asaṅkarato dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Pavesanapaviṭṭhauddharaṇakālesupi sukkavisaṭṭhi hotiyeva. Sādiyanaṃ nāma sevanacittassa adhivāsanacittassa uppādanaṃ.

Entering means the contact of the sexual organ with the sexual organ when one is inserting. Inserted means the time of the unfinished act or the time of effort when one is inserting as far as the root. The sexual organ is said to be stationary at the time of semen emission. Withdrawal is the time of drawing out. However, in the Vinayagaṇṭhipada, it is said, “Having ceased from effort, the state is called stationary.” This was stated to show it without confusion. Emission of semen occurs even during the times of entering, being inserted, and withdrawing. Consenting is the arising of a mind of indulgence or a mind of endurance.

Ubhatovibhaṅge eva paññattāni sandhāya “idañhi sabbasikkhāpadānaṃ nidāna”nti vuttaṃ. “Vinayadharapañcamena gaṇena upasampadā”ti (mahāva. 259) vuttattā idha tatiyā sahayogena vuttā. Tasmā vīsatipi bhikkhū ce nisinnā, pañcamo vinayadharova icchitabbo, evaṃ sati pārājiko ce vinayadharo, upasampadākammaṃ kopetīti ce? Na, parivārāvasāne kammavagge (pari. 482 ādayo) yaṃ kammavipattilakkhaṇaṃ vuttaṃ, tassa tasmiṃ natthitāya. “Kathaṃ vatthuto vā ñattito vā anussāvanato vā sīmato vā parisato vā”ti ettakaṃ vuttaṃ, nanu ayaṃ “parisato vā”ti vacanena saṅgahitoti ce? Na, “dvādasahi ākārehi parisato kammāni vipajjantī”ti (pari. 487) suttassa [M 0.0027] hi vibhaṅge tassa anāmaṭṭhattāti ayamattho yasmā tattha tattha sarūpena vuttapāḷivaseneva sakkā jānituṃ, tasmā nayamukhaṃ dassetvā saṃkhittoti likhitaṃ. “Aṅga”nti padaṃ uddharitvā “sabbasikkhāpadesu āpattīnaṃ aṅgānaṅgaṃ veditabba”nti vuttaṃ, idha pana “aṅga”nti vuttaṃ, kasmā? Samuṭṭhanādīnaṃ parivārādīsu saṅkhepena āgatattā tattha gahetvā idhāpi niddiṭṭhānaṃ anaṅgānaṃ vavatthānābhāvato, sabbattha saṅkhepato ca vitthārato ca anaṅgatte vuccamāne ativitthāratāya tasmiṃ tasmiṃ sikkhāpade anūnaṃ vattabbato cāti veditabbo, sabbāpattīnaṃ saṅgāhakavasenāti attho.

With reference to the regulations established in the Ubhatovibhaṅga alone, it was said, “This is indeed the origin of all training rules.” Because it is stated, “Ordination is by a chapter with a Vinaya-holder as the fifth” (Mahāva. 259), here the instrumental case is used to mean 'in association with.' Therefore, even if twenty bhikkhus are seated, a Vinaya-holder is required as the fifth. This being so, if the Vinaya-holder has committed a pārājika offense, does he invalidate the ordination act? No, because at the end of the Parivāra, in the Kammavagga (Pari. 482 ff.), whatever characteristic of a failed act was stated, that is absent in his case. “How? From the object, or the motion, or the proclamation, or the boundary, or the assembly?”—this much was stated. But is this not included by the words “or the assembly”? No, because in the Vibhaṅga of the sutta “Acts fail in twelve ways due to the assembly” (Pari. 487), this is not touched upon. Since this meaning can be known from the Pāli text itself as it is stated in its own form in various places, it is written concisely after showing the method. Having extracted the word “aṅga” (factor), it was said, “In all training rules, the factors and non-factors of offenses should be understood.” But here “aṅga” is stated. Why? Because the origins, etc., are given concisely in the Parivāra, etc., and because there is no determination here of the non-factors that are not specified, and because if the state of being a non-factor were stated everywhere, both concisely and in detail, it would be excessively elaborate, and in each and every training rule, it would have to be stated completely; this is to be understood by way of encompassing all offenses.

Yāni sikkhāpadāni “kiriyānī”ti vuccanti, tesaṃ vasena kāyavācā saha viññattiyā veditabbā, akiriyānaṃ vasena vinā viññattiyā veditabbā. Cittaṃ panettha appamāṇaṃ bhūtārocanasamuṭṭhānassa kiriyattā, acittakattā ca. Tattha kiriyā āpattiyā anaṅgantaracittasamuṭṭhānā veditabbā. Aviññattijanakampi ekaccaṃ bāhullanayena “kiriya”nti vuccati yatheva paṭhamapārājikaṃ. Viññattiyā abhāvepi “so ce sādiyati, āpatti pārājikassa, na sādiyati, anāpattī”ti hi vuttaṃ, viññattisaṅkhātāpi kiriyā vinā sevanacittena na hoti vuttacittajattā, vikārarūpattā, cittānuparivattikattā ca. Tasmā kiriyāsaṅkhātamidaṃ viññattirūpaṃ, itaraṃ cittajarūpaṃ viya janakacittena vinā na tiṭṭhati, itaraṃ saddāyatanaṃ tiṭṭhati, tasmā kiriyāya sati ekantato tajjanakaṃ sevanacittaṃ atthi evāti katvā na sādiyati, anāpattīti na yujjatīti. Yasmā viññattijanakampi samānaṃ sevanacittaṃ na sabbakālaṃ viññattiṃ janeti, tasmā vināpi viññattiyā sayaṃ uppajjatīti katvā “sādiyati, āpatti pārājikassā”ti vuttaṃ. Nuppajjati ce, na sādiyati nāma, tassa [V 0.0026] anāpatti. Teneva bhagavā “kiṃcitto tvaṃ bhikkhū”ti (pārā. 135) citteneva āpattiṃ paricchindati, na kiriyāyāti veditabbaṃ.

Regarding those training rules that are called 'actions,' body and speech are to be understood as being together with intimation; regarding those called 'non-actions,' they are to be understood as being without intimation. Herein, the mind is not the measure, because the origin of a true declaration is an action, and because it is unintentional. Therein, actions leading to an offense should be understood as arising from a mind that is not an intervening factor. Even something that does not generate intimation is, by way of general usage, called an 'action,' just like the first pārājika offense. For even in the absence of intimation, it is said: 'If one consents, it is a pārājika offense; if one does not consent, it is no offense.' An action, even one reckoned as intimation, does not occur without a mind of indulgence, because it is mind-born, is a form of alteration, and follows upon the mind. Therefore this form of intimation, reckoned as an action, does not endure without the generating mind, just like other mind-born matter, whereas the sound-base does endure. Therefore, on the grounds that when an action exists, the mind of indulgence that generates it definitely exists, the statement 'if one does not consent, it is no offense' is not logical. Because the mind of indulgence, although it generates intimation, does not always generate it, it was said, 'if one consents, it is a pārājika offense,' on the grounds that it arises by itself even without intimation. If it does not arise, that is called 'not consenting,' and for that person there is no offense. For that very reason, the Blessed One determines the offense by the mind alone, asking, 'With what mind, bhikkhu?' (Pārā. 135), and not by the action; so it should be understood.

Ettha samuṭṭhānaggahaṇaṃ kattabbato vā akattabbato vā kāyādibhedāpekkhameva āpattiṃ āpajjati, na aññathāti dassanappayojanaṃ. Tesu kiriyāggahaṇaṃ kāyādīnaṃ saviññattikāviññattikabhedadassanappayojanaṃ. Saññāggahaṇaṃ āpattiyā aṅgānaṅgacittavisesadassanappayojanaṃ. Tena [M 0.0028] yaṃ cittaṃ kiriyalakkhaṇe vā akiriyalakkhaṇe vā sannihitaṃ, yato vā kiriyā vā akiriyā vā hoti, na taṃ avisesena āpattiyā aṅgaṃ vā anaṅgaṃ vā hoti. Kintu yāya saññāya “saññāvimokkha”nti vuccati, tāya sampayuttaṃ cittaṃ aṅgaṃ, itaraṃ anaṅganti dassitaṃ hoti. Idāni yena cittena sikkhāpadaṃ sacittakaṃ hoti, tadabhāvā acittakaṃ, tena tassa avisesena sāvajjatāya “lokavajjamevā”ti vuttaṃ. Kintu sāvajjaṃyeva samānaṃ ekaccaṃ lokavajjaṃ, ekaccaṃ paṇṇattivajjanti dassanappayojanaṃ cittalokavajjaggahaṇaṃ. Cittameva yasmā “lokavajja”nti vuccati, tasmā manokammampi siyā āpattīti aniṭṭhappasaṅganivāraṇappayojanaṃ kammaggahaṇaṃ.

Here, the inclusion of 'origination' serves the purpose of showing that one incurs an offense only in dependence on the distinction of body, etc., as to whether something is to be done or not to be done, and not otherwise. Among these, the inclusion of 'action' serves the purpose of showing the distinction of body, etc., as being with or without intimation. The inclusion of 'perception' serves the purpose of showing the distinction of factors and non-factors of an offense, and specific states of mind. Therefore, whatever mind is present in the characteristic of action or inaction, or from which action or inaction arises, is not indiscriminately a factor or a non-factor of an offense. Rather, it is shown that the mind associated with the perception by which one is 'released through perception' is a factor, while another is a non-factor. Now, it is by a certain mind that a training rule becomes intentional, and in its absence, unintentional. Therefore, because of its general blameworthiness, it is said to be 'merely blameworthy in the world.' However, while being blameworthy, some things are blameworthy in the world, and some are blameworthy by regulation; the inclusion of 'mind' and 'blameworthy in the world' serves the purpose of showing this. Since the mind itself is called 'blameworthy in the world,' mental action could also be an offense; the inclusion of 'action' serves the purpose of preventing this undesirable implication.

Yaṃ panettha akiriyalakkhaṇaṃ kammaṃ, taṃ kusalattikavinimuttaṃ siyāti aniṭṭhappasaṅganivāraṇappayojanaṃ kusalattikaggahaṇaṃ. Yā panettha abyākatāpatti, taṃ ekaccaṃ avedanampi nirodhaṃ samāpanno āpajjatīti vedanāttikaṃ ettha na labbhatīti aniṭṭhappasaṅganivāraṇatthaṃ vedanāttikaggahaṇaṃ. Sikkhāpadañhi sacittakapuggalavasena “ticittaṃ tivedana”nti laddhavohāraṃ acittakenāpannampi “ticittaṃ tivedana”miceva vuccati. Tatridaṃ sādhakasuttaṃ – “atthāpatti acittako āpajjati acittako vuṭṭhāti (pari. 324), atthāpatti kusalacitto āpajjati kusalacitto vuṭṭhātī”tiādi (pari. 470). “Sacittakaṃ āpattidīpanaṃ, saññāvimokkhaṃ anāpattidīpanaṃ, acittakaṃ vatthuajānanaṃ, nosaññāvimokkhaṃ vītikkamanājānanaṃ. Idameva tesaṃ nānātta”nti (vajira. ṭī. pārājika 61-66 pakiṇṇakakathāvaṇṇanā) likhitaṃ.

Lest the action here which has the characteristic of non-action be excluded from the wholesome triad, the inclusion of the wholesome triad serves to prevent this undesirable implication. As for whatever indeterminate offense is here, one who has attained cessation may incur it even without feeling; lest it be said that the feeling triad is therefore not obtained here, the inclusion of the feeling triad serves to prevent this undesirable implication. For a training rule, in relation to a person with consciousness, has received the designation 'threefold in consciousness, threefold in feeling'; even when incurred by one without consciousness, it is still called 'threefold in consciousness, threefold in feeling.' Here is the corroborating text: 'There is an offense that one without consciousness incurs and from which one without consciousness emerges' (Pari. 324); 'There is an offense that one with a wholesome mind incurs and from which one with a wholesome mind emerges,' and so on (Pari. 470). It is written: 'Intentionality is the elucidation of an offense; release through perception is the elucidation of non-offense. Unintentionality is not knowing the object; not being released through perception is not knowing the transgression. This alone is the difference between them' (Vajirabuddhiṭīkā, Pārājika 61-66, Commentary on the Miscellaneous Section).

Sacittakapakkheti ettha ayaṃ tāva gaṇṭhipadanayo – sacittakapakkheti surāpānādiacittake sandhāya vuttaṃ. Sacittakesu pana yaṃ ekantamakusaleneva samuṭṭhāti, tañca ubhayaṃ lokavajjaṃ nāma. Surāpānasmiñhi “surā”ti vā “pātuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti vā jānitvā pivane akusalamevāti. Tattha “na vaṭṭatīti jānitvā”ti vuttavacanaṃ na yujjati paṇṇattivajjassapi [V 0.0027] lokavajjatāpasaṅgato. Imaṃ aniṭṭhappasaṅgaṃ pariharitukāmatāya ca vajirabuddhittherena likhitaṃ – “idha ‘sacittaka’nti ca ‘acittaka’nti ca vicāraṇā vatthuvijānane eva hoti, na paññattivijānane. Yadi paññattivijānane hoti[M 0.0029], sabbasikkhāpadāni lokavajjāneva siyuṃ, na ca sabbasikkhāpadāni lokavajjāni. Tasmā vatthuvijānane eva hotīti idaṃ yujjati. Kasmā? Yasmā sekhiyesu paññattivijānanameva pamāṇaṃ, na vatthumattavijānana”nti. Ayaṃ panettha attho sikkhāpadasīsena āpattiṃ gahetvā yassa sikkhāpadassa sacittakassa cittaṃ akusalameva hoti, taṃ lokavajjaṃ, sacittakācittakasaṅkhātassa acittakassa ca sacittakapakkhe cittaṃ akusalameva hoti, tampi surāpānādilokavajjanti imamatthaṃ sandhāya “yassā sacittakapakkhe cittaṃ akusalameva hoti, ayaṃ lokavajjā nāmā”ti vuttaṃ. “Sacittakapakkhe”ti hi idaṃ vacanaṃ acittakaṃ sandhāyāha. Na hi ekaṃsato sacittakāya “sacittakapakkhe”ti visesane payojanaṃ atthīti, evaṃ santepi aniyamena vuttañca niyamavasena eva gahetabbanti attho.

Regarding 'in the intentional category' (sacittakapakkhe), this is the exegesis of the difficult phrase: 'in the intentional category' is stated with reference to unintentional offenses such as drinking liquor. However, among intentional offenses, that which arises entirely from the unwholesome, and both of these, are called worldly offenses. For in the case of drinking liquor, when one drinks knowing it is 'liquor' or 'it is not proper to drink,' it is entirely unwholesome. Here, the statement 'knowing it is not proper to drink' is not tenable, because of the undesirable implication that even an offense by regulation would become a worldly offense. And wishing to avoid this undesirable implication, the Elder Vajirabuddhi wrote: 'Here, the investigation into "intentional" and "unintentional" concerns only the knowing of the object, not the knowing of the regulation. If it concerned the knowing of the regulation, all training rules would be worldly offenses, but not all training rules are worldly offenses. Therefore, it is tenable that this concerns only the knowing of the object. Why? Because in the Sekhiya rules, the knowing of the regulation is the standard, not the mere knowing of the object.' The meaning here is this: Taking an offense by way of the training rule, for whichever intentional training rule the mind is entirely unwholesome, that is a worldly offense. And for an unintentional offense, designated as intentional-and-unintentional, if the mind in its intentional aspect is entirely unwholesome, that too is a worldly offense, like drinking liquor. It is with reference to this meaning that it was said: 'That for which the mind in the intentional category is entirely unwholesome is called a worldly offense.' For the phrase 'in the intentional category' refers to the unintentional. There is no purpose in qualifying something that is exclusively intentional with 'in the intentional category.' Even so, the meaning is that what is stated indefinitely should be understood definitively.

Tiracchānānaṃ panāti pana-saddena thullaccayādikāraṃ nivatteti. Kiriyāti ettha “ṭhitaṃ sādiyatī”ti (pārā. 58) vuttattā taṃ kathanti ce? “Sādiyatī”ti vuttattā kiriyā eva. Evaṃ sante “kāyakammaṃ manokamma”nti vattabbanti ce? Na, pacuravohāravasena “kāyakamma”nti vuttattā. Ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalikāya labbhati evāti likhitaṃ. Pubbe vuttanayena saṃsandetvā gahetabbaṃ. “Dunnikkhittassa, bhikkhave, padabyañjanassa atthopi dunnayo hotī”ti (a. ni. 2.20) vadantenāpi atthassa sukhaggahaṇatthameva padabyañjanassa sunikkhittabhāvo icchito, na akkharavacanāya, tasmā āha “atthañhi nātho saraṇaṃ avocā”tiādi.

Regarding 'of animals,' the word 'pana' excludes the case of a grave offense, etc. Regarding 'action,' if it is asked, 'How is this so, since it is said, "he consents to one who is standing" (Pārā. 58)?' Because 'consents' is said, it is indeed an action. If that is so, should it not be stated as 'bodily action and mental action?' No, because it is stated as 'bodily action' according to common usage. It is written that it is incurred even by one sitting with knees drawn up. This should be understood by connecting it with the method previously stated. Even when it was said, 'Bhikkhus, when words and phrases are badly placed, the meaning is also difficult to grasp' (A.N. 2.20), the well-placed state of words and phrases was desired only for the easy grasping of the meaning, not for the sake of the syllables. Therefore, it is said: 'For the Protector declared the meaning to be the refuge,' and so on.

Paṭhamapārājikavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the First Pārājika is concluded.

2. Dutiyapārājikavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Second Pārājika.

Gāmā vā araññā vāti lakkhaṇānupaññattikattā ādimhi vuttā. Sabbasmiñhi vinayapiṭake gāmo, gāmūpacāro, gāmakkhettaṃ, gāmasīmā, gāmasīmūpacāroti pañcavidho gāmabhedo veditabbo. Tathā āraññakasīmāya ekaṃ agāmakaṃ araññaṃ, saṃvidhānasikkhāpadānaṃ (pāci. 180 ādayo) ekaṃ, sagāmakaṃ ekaṃ[M 0.0030], avippavāsasīmāya ekaṃ, gaṇamhāohīyanakassa (pāci. 691) ekanti pañcavidho araññabhedo veditabbo. Tattha atthi [V 0.0028] gāmo na gāmaparihāraṃ katthaci labhati, atthi gāmo na gāmakiccaṃ karoti, tathā atthi araññaṃ na araññaparihāraṃ katthaci labhati, atthi araññaṃ na araññakiccaṃ karotīti ayampi bhedo veditabbo.

'From a village or from a wilderness' was stated at the beginning because it is a regulation subsequent to a characteristic. Indeed, in the entire Vinaya Piṭaka, the distinction of 'village' should be understood as fivefold: the village, the village vicinity, the village field, the village boundary, and the village boundary vicinity. Likewise, the distinction of 'wilderness' should be understood as fivefold: one is a wilderness without a village for the purpose of a forest-dweller's boundary; one is for the training rules on arrangements; one is a wilderness with a village; one is for the boundary of non-separation; and one is for a monk who falls away from the community. Herein, this distinction should also be understood: there is a village that nowhere receives the privileges of a village, and there is a village that does not perform the functions of a village; likewise, there is a wilderness that nowhere receives the privileges of a wilderness, and there is a wilderness that does not perform the functions of a wilderness.

Tattha avippavāsasīmāsammannanakammavācāya ṭhapetvā “gāmañca gāmūpacārañcā”ti (mahāva. 144) ettha gāmo nāma parikkhitto ce, parikkhepassa anto, aparikkhitto ce, parikkhepokāsato anto veditabbo. Ayaṃ udositasikkhāpade “antogāmo”ti (pārā. 478) āgato. Sāsaṅkasikkhāpade “antaraghara”nti (pārā. 654) āgato anāsaṅkato. Yathāha “antaraghare nikkhipeyyāti samantā gocaragāme nikkhipeyyā”ti (pārā. 654). Tathā antaragharappaṭisaṃyuttānaṃ sekhiyānaṃ ayameva paricchedo veditabbo. “Yā pana bhikkhunī ekā gāmantaraṃ gaccheyyā”ti (pāci. 687) etthāpi ayameva paricchedo adhippeto “parikkhittassa gāmassa parikkhepaṃ atikkamantiyā, aparikkhittassa gāmassa upacāraṃ atikkamantiyā”ti vuttattā.

Herein, setting aside the formal act of announcing the boundary of non-separation, in the passage 'the village and the village vicinity' (Mahāvagga 144), 'village' is to be understood as inside the enclosure, if it is enclosed; if it is unenclosed, it is to be understood as the inside from the place of an enclosure. This appears as 'inside the village' in the Udosita training rule (Pārā. 478). In the Sāsaṅka training rule, it appears as 'inside a house' in the section on what is not grounds for suspicion (Pārā. 654). As it is said: '“One should deposit it inside a house” means one should deposit it in the surrounding alms-resort village' (Pārā. 654). Likewise, for the Sekhiya rules connected with being inside a house, this same definition should be understood. In the rule, 'Whatever bhikkhunī should go to another village alone' (Pācittiya 687), this same definition is also intended, because it is said: 'when she crosses the enclosure of an enclosed village, or when she crosses the vicinity of an unenclosed village.'

Yesu purāṇapotthakesu “upacāraṃ okkamantiyā”ti likhitaṃ, taṃ vikāle gāmappavesanasikkhāpadesu āciṇṇaṃ nayaṃ gahetvā pamādena likhīyati, na pamāṇaṃ. Yesu ca potthakesu vikāle gāmappavesanasikkhāpadassa vibhaṅge (pāci. 513) “gāmaṃ paviseyyāti parikkhittassa gāmassa parikkhepaṃ atikkamantassa, aparikkhittassa gāmassa upacāraṃ atikkamantassā”ti likhīyati, sā pamādalekhā. Upacāraṃ okkamantassāti tattha pāṭho. Vuttañhi samantapāsādikāyaṃ “aparikkhittassa gāmassa upacāro adinnādāne vuttanayeneva veditabbo”ti (pāci. aṭṭha. 512). Idha kaṅkhāvitaraṇiyampi vuttaṃ “santaṃ bhikkhuṃ anāpucchitvāti…pe… upacāraṃ okkamantassā”tiādi (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. vikālagāmappavesanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā).

In some ancient books, it is written as 'upacāraṃ okkamantiyā'; this is written through carelessness, having adopted the method customary in the training rule on entering a village at the wrong time, and it is not authoritative. In some books, in the analysis of the training rule on entering a village at the wrong time (Pāc. 513), it is written: '‘Should enter a village’ means for one crossing the enclosure of an enclosed village, or for one crossing the vicinity of an unenclosed village.' This is a careless writing. The reading there should be 'upacāraṃ okkamantassa' (for one stepping into the vicinity). For it is stated in the Samantapāsādikā: 'The vicinity of an unenclosed village should be understood in the same way as explained in the case of theft.' (Pāci. Aṭṭha. 512). Here, in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī, it is also stated: '‘Without informing an available bhikkhu’… and so on… ‘for one stepping into the vicinity’' etc. (Kaṅkhā. Aṭṭha. Commentary on the training rule on entering a village at the wrong time).

Yaṃ pana katthaci potthake “bhikkhuniyā gāmantarādhikāre ekena pādena itarassa gāmassa parikkhepaṃ vā atikkamante, upacāraṃ vā okkante thullaccayaṃ, dutiyena atikkantamatte, okkantamatte ca saṅghādiseso”ti pāṭho dissati. Tattha “okkante, okkantamatte”ti etāni padāni adhikāni[M 0.0031], kevalaṃ likhitakehi aññehi likhitāni. Katthaci potthake “okkantamatte cā”ti padaṃ na dissati, itaraṃ dissati. Tāni dve padāni pāḷiyā virujjhanti. “Aparikkhittassa gāmassa upacāraṃ atikkāmentiyā”ti (pāci. 692) hi pāḷi[V 0.0029]. Tathā samantapāsādikāya (pāci. aṭṭha. 692) virujjhanti. “Parikkhepārahaṭṭhānaṃ ekena pādena atikkamati, thullaccayaṃ, dutiyena atikkamati, saṅghādiseso. Apicettha sakagāmato…pe… ekena pādena itarassa gāmassa parikkhepe vā upacāre vā atikkante thullaccayaṃ, dutiyena atikkantamatte saṅghādiseso”ti (pāci. aṭṭha. 692) hi vuttaṃ.

However, in a certain book this reading is found: 'In the matter of a bhikkhunī going to another village, when crossing the enclosure of the other village with one foot, or when stepping into its vicinity, it is a thullaccaya offense; upon crossing with the second foot, and upon fully stepping in, it is a saṅghādisesa offense.' There, the words 'when stepping into' and 'upon fully stepping in' are superfluous, merely written by other scribes. In some books, the phrase 'and upon fully stepping in' is not found, but the other is. Those two words contradict the Pāḷi. For the Pāḷi is: 'For one crossing the vicinity of an unenclosed village' (Pāc. 692). They are also contradicted by the Samantapāsādikā (Pāc. Aṭṭha. 692). For it is said: 'If she crosses a place fit for an enclosure with one foot, it is a thullaccaya offense; if she crosses with the second foot, it is a saṅghādisesa offense. Moreover, in this case, from her own village… when crossing the enclosure or vicinity of another village with one foot, it is a thullaccaya offense; upon crossing with the second foot, it is a saṅghādisesa offense' (Pāc. Aṭṭha. 692).

Gaṇṭhipade cassa “parikkhepaṃ atikkāmentiyā”ti vatvā “upacārepi eseva nayo”ti vuttaṃ. Anugaṇṭhipade ca “aparikkhittassa gāmassa upacāraṃ ‘okkamantiyā’tipi potthakesu ekaccesu dissati, taṃ na gahetabba”nti vuttaṃ. Aparampi vuttaṃ “aparikkhittassa gāmassa upacāraṃ ‘atikkāmentiyā’ti vacanenāpi evaṃ veditabbaṃ – vikāle gāmappavesane dvinnaṃ leḍḍupātānaṃ eva vasena upacāro paricchinditabbo, itarathā yathā ettha parikkhepārahaṭṭhānaṃ parikkhepaṃ viya katvā ‘atikkāmentiyā’ti vuttaṃ, evaṃ tatthāpi ‘aparikkhittassa gāmassa upacāraṃ atikkāmentassā’ti vadeyya. Yasmā pana tattha parikkhepārahaṭṭhānato uttarimeko leḍḍupāto upacāroti adhippeto. Tasmā tadatthadīpanatthaṃ ‘aparikkhittassa gāmassa upacāraṃ okkamantassā’ti vutta”nti.

And in its Gaṇṭhipada, having said 'for one crossing the enclosure,' it is stated, 'this same method applies also to the vicinity.' And in the Anugaṇṭhipada it is said: 'In some books, the reading "for one stepping into the vicinity of an unenclosed village" is also seen; that should not be accepted.' Furthermore, it is said: 'By the statement "for one crossing the vicinity of an unenclosed village," it should also be understood thus: in the case of entering a village at the wrong time, the vicinity is to be determined by means of two clod-throws; otherwise, just as here, having treated a place fit for an enclosure as an enclosure, it is said "for one crossing," so also there one would say "for one crossing the vicinity of an unenclosed village." But since there the vicinity is intended as one clod-throw beyond the place fit for an enclosure, therefore, to clarify that meaning, it is said "for one stepping into the vicinity of an unenclosed village."

Yaṃ pana andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ parikkhepārahaṭṭhānaṃyeva upacāranti sallakkhetvā “parikkhepapaakkhepārahaṭṭhānānaṃ ninnānākaraṇadīpanatthaṃ upacāraṃ okkamantassā”ti vuttaṃ, pāḷivisesamasallakkhetvā “aparikkhittassa gāmassa upacāraṃ atikkamantassa idha upacāro parikkhepo yathā bhaveyya, taṃ upacāraṃ paṭhamaṃ pādaṃ atikkāmentassa āpatti dukkaṭassa, dutiyaṃ pādaṃ atikkāmentassa āpatti pācittiyassā”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ na gahetabbameva pāḷiyā visesasambhavatoti. Porāṇagaṇṭhipade “upacāraṃ atikkāmentiyā bhikkhuniyā gāmantarāpattī”ti vuttaṃ. Tasmā idha kaṅkhāvitaraṇiyā “ekena pādena itarassa…pe… atikkantamatte saṅghādiseso”ti ayameva pāṭho veditabbo. Ettāvatā imesu yathāvuttesu ṭhānesu yathāvuttaparicchedova gāmoti veditabbo. Imassa [M 0.0032] atthassa dīpanatthaṃ “gāmo nāma ekakuṭikopī”tiādi (pārā. 92) vuttaṃ. Imassa vasena asatipi parikkhepātikkame, upacārokkamane vā antarārāmato vā bhikkhunupassayato vā titthiyaseyyato vā paṭikkamanato vā taṃ gāmaṃ pavisantassa antarārāmaparikkhepassa, upacārassa vā atikkamanavasena gāmapaccayā āpattiyo veditabbā.

But what is said in the Andhakaṭṭhakathā—having noted that the vicinity is just the place fit for an enclosure: 'To explain the non-difference between a place fit for an enclosure and a place not fit for an enclosure, it is said "for one stepping into the vicinity"'; and, not having noted a distinction in the Pāḷi: 'For one crossing the vicinity of an unenclosed village, here the vicinity should be like the enclosure. For one crossing that vicinity with the first foot, there is a dukkaṭa offense; for one crossing with the second foot, there is a pācittiya offense'—that should not be accepted at all, because of the possibility of a distinction in the Pāḷi. In the ancient Gaṇṭhipada it is said: 'For a bhikkhunī crossing the vicinity, there is a gāmantara offense.' Therefore, here this very reading from the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī should be understood: 'with one foot over the other… upon the moment of crossing, it is a saṅghādisesa.' To this extent, in these places as described, a village should be understood as having the definition previously stated. To clarify this meaning, it is said: 'A village is even a single hut,' etc. (Pārā. 92). By this means, even when there is no crossing of an enclosure or stepping into a vicinity, for one entering that village from within a monastery, or from a bhikkhunī's residence, or from a heretic's lodging, or from a place of return, offenses dependent on the village should be understood by way of crossing the monastery's enclosure or its vicinity.

Gāmūpacāro pana “ṭhapetvā gāmañca gāmūpacārañcā”ti (mahāva. 144) ettha parikkhittassa [V 0.0030] gāmassa parikkhepova, aparikkhittassa gāmassa parikkhepokāsova. Vuttañhetaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “gāmūpacāroti parikkhittassa gāmassa parikkhepo, aparikkhittassa gāmassa parikkhepokāso. Tesu adhiṭṭhitatecīvariko bhikkhu parihāraṃ na labhatī”ti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 144). Kiṃ panettha kāraṇaṃ, yena ayaṃ gāmo, gāmūpacāro ca idha aññathā, aññattha tathāti? Aṭṭhuppattito “tena kho pana samayena bhikkhū ‘bhagavatā ticīvarena avippavāsasammuti anuññātā’ti antaraghare cīvarāni nikkhipantī”ti (mahāva. 143) imissā hi aṭṭhuppattiyā “ṭhapetvā gāmañca gāmūpacārañcā”ti (mahāva. 144) vuttaṃ. Tasmā yattha antaragharasaññā, tattha avippavāsasīmā na gacchatīti veditabbā. Tena ca udositasikkhāpade “antogāme cīvaraṃ nikkhipitvā antogāme vatthabba”nti (pārā. 478) ca “sabhāye vā dvāramūle vā, hatthapāsā vā na vijahitabba”nti ca vuttaṃ. Kappiyabhūmiyaṃ vasantoyeva hi kappiyabhūmiyaṃ nikkhittacīvaraṃ rakkhati. Sāsaṅkasikkhāpade pana “yasmā yattha gāme cīvaraṃ nikkhittaṃ, tena gāmena vippavasanto cīvarena vippavasatīti vuccati, tasmā puna gāmasīmaṃ okkamitvā vasitvā pakkamatī”ti vuttaṃ. Tasmiñhi sikkhāpade gāmasīmā gāmo nāmāti adhippeto. Tattha vikāle gāmappavesanasikkhāpadavibhaṅge “parikkhittassa gāmassa parikkhepaṃ atikkamantassa āpatti pācittiyassā”ti (pāci. 513) vacanato parikkhepo na gāmo. Kintu gāmūpacāroti lesena dassitaṃ hoti. Imasmiṃ pana sikkhāpadavibhaṅge “gāmūpacāro nāmā”ti ārabhitvā “aparikkhittassa gāmassa gharūpacāre ṭhitassa majjhimassa purisassa leḍḍupāto”ti iminā aparikkhittassa parikkhepokāso gāmūpacāroti siddhaṃ. Tadatthasambhavato tasmiṃ gharūpacāre ṭhitassa leḍḍupāto gāmūpacāroti kurundaṭṭhakathāyaṃ, mahāpaccariyampi vuttaṃ[M 0.0033]. Upacāro hi “gāmo ekūpacāro nānūpacāro”tiādīsu dvāraṃ, “ajjhokāso ekūpacāro”ti ettha samantā sattabbhantarasaṅkhātaṃ pamāṇaṃ, tasmā “gāmūpacāroti parikkhittassa gāmassa parikkhepo, aparikkhittassa gāmassa parikkhepokāso”ti andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Tathā kurundiyaṃ, mahāpaccariyañca. Tathā pāḷiyampi “ajjhārāmo nāma parikkhittassa ārāmassa anto ārāmo, aparikkhittassa upacāro. Ajjhāvasatho nāma parikkhittassa āvasathassa anto āvasatho, aparikkhittassa upacāro”tiādīsu dissati. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “gāmūpacāro”tiādīsu dissati. Tasmā dutiyo leḍḍupāto upacāroti adhippeto.

The vicinity of a village (gāmūpacāra), however, in the passage “excluding the village and its vicinity” (Mv. 144), is the enclosure itself for an enclosed village, and the space for an enclosure for an unenclosed village. This is stated in the Commentary: “The vicinity of a village means the enclosure of an enclosed village or the space for an enclosure of an unenclosed village. A bhikkhu who has determined his three robes in these areas does not receive the exemption” (Mv.A. 144). What, then, is the reason that this village and its vicinity are defined one way here, and another way elsewhere? It arises from the origin story: “At that time, bhikkhus, thinking, ‘The Blessed One has permitted the agreement of non-separation from the three robes,’ left robes inside houses” (Mv. 143). It is with reference to this origin story that it is stated, “excluding the village and its vicinity” (Mv. 144). Therefore, it should be understood that where there is the perception of being inside a house, the boundary of non-separation does not extend. And in the Udosita training-rule, it is said, “Having left a robe inside the village, one must stay inside the village,” and “It must not be abandoned in an assembly hall, at a doorway, or beyond arm’s reach” (Pārā. 478). For one dwelling in allowable territory indeed protects a robe left in allowable territory. However, in the training-rule on a matter of doubt, it is said, “Because wherever a robe is left in a village, by departing from that village one is said to depart from the robe, therefore, one must re-enter the village boundary, stay, and then depart.” In that training-rule, the village boundary is intended to mean the village itself. There, in the analysis of the training-rule on entering a village at the wrong time, it is said, “For one who crosses the enclosure of an enclosed village, there is an offence of expiation” (Pāci. 513), from which it is subtly indicated that the enclosure is not the village, but the village vicinity. In the analysis of this training-rule, however, beginning with “What is called the vicinity of a village,” it is established by the words, “the clod-throw of a man of average height standing in the vicinity of the houses of an unenclosed village,” that the space for an enclosure of an unenclosed village is the village vicinity. Because this meaning is possible, it is stated in the Kurundī Commentary and also in the Mahāpaccarī that the clod-throw of one standing in the vicinity of the houses is the village vicinity. For ‘vicinity’ (upacāra), in passages such as “a village with one vicinity, not many,” means a gate; and in “an open space with one vicinity,” it means a measure known as seven abbhantaras all around. Therefore, it should be understood that it is stated in the Andhaka Commentary, “The vicinity of a village means the enclosure of an enclosed village, or the space for an enclosure of an unenclosed village.” Likewise in the Kurundī and the Mahāpaccarī. Similarly, in the Pāli Canon itself, it is seen in passages such as, “The inner monastery (ajjhārāma) means the interior of an enclosed monastery or the vicinity of an unenclosed one. The inner dwelling (ajjhāvasatha) means the interior of an enclosed dwelling or the vicinity of an unenclosed one.” In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, however, it is seen in passages such as “the vicinity of a village.” Therefore, the second clod-throw is intended as the vicinity.

“Aparikkhittassa gāmassa upacāraṃ okkamantassa āpatti pācittiyassā”ti pāḷivisesasambhavato ca paṭhamo leḍḍupāto gāmo eva, dutiyo gāmūpacāroti vuttaṃ. Parikkhittassa [V 0.0031] pana gāmassa indakhīle ṭhitassa majjhimassa purisassa leḍḍupāto gāmūpacāroti vuttanti ettha bhedo natthi. Ettāvatā parikkhittassa duvidho upacāro, aparikkhittassa catubbidho upacāro yattha sambhavati, yattha ca na sambhavati, taṃ sabbaṃ dassitaṃ hoti.

And because of the specific Pāli text, “For one entering the vicinity of an unenclosed village, there is an offence of expiation,” it is said that the first clod-throw is the village itself, and the second is the village vicinity. However, regarding the statement that for an enclosed village, the village vicinity is the clod-throw of a man of average height standing at the boundary post (indakhīla), there is no disagreement. By this much, the two kinds of vicinity for an enclosed village and the four kinds for an unenclosed village, where they are possible and where they are not, have all been shown.

Gāmakhettassa ca gāmasīmāya ca lakkhaṇaṃ aṭṭhakathāyameva vuttaṃ. Ubhayañhi atthato ekaṃ. Tattha gāmasīmāya gāmabhāvo sāsaṅkasikkhāpadavasena veditabbo.

The characteristics of village land and the village boundary are stated in the Commentary itself. For both are indeed one in meaning. Therein, that the village boundary has the status of a village should be understood by way of the training-rule on a matter of doubt.

Gāmasīmūpacāro nāma manussānaṃ kaṭṭhatiṇapupphaphalādiatthikānaṃ vanacarakānaṃ valañjanaṭṭhānaṃ. Imassa gāmasīmūpacārabhāvo udositasikkhāpade, “agāmake araññe samantā sattabbhantarā”ti (pārā. 494) āgataṭṭhāne khandhake (mahāva. 147) ca veditabbo. Ettha hi bhagavā gāmantavāsīnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ sīmaṃ dassento “yaṃ gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā upanissāya viharatī”ti (mahāva. 147) vatvā dasseti. Tadanantarameva “agāmake”tiādinā sattabbhantarasīmaṃ dasseti. Tasmā yo bhikkhu gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā upanissāya na viharati, kevalaṃ nāvāyaṃ vā thalamaggena vā addhānamaggappaṭipanno hoti, tassa tattha tattha sattabbhantarasīmā labbhatīti veditabbo. Vuttañhi “ekakulassa sattho hoti[M 0.0034], satthe cīvaraṃ nikkhipitvā purato vā pacchato vā sattabbhantarā na vijahitabba”ntiādi (pārā. 489). Idameva araññaṃ sandhāya “āraññakasīmāya ekaṃ agāmakaṃ arañña”nti vuttaṃ.

The vicinity of a village boundary (gāmasīmūpacāra) is a place frequented by people seeking wood, grass, flowers, fruit, and so on, and by forest-dwellers. That this is the vicinity of a village boundary should be understood from the Udosita training-rule, in the passage beginning, “in a village-less wilderness, seven abbhantaras all around” (Pārā. 494), and in the Khandhaka (Mv. 147). For here the Blessed One, when indicating the boundary for bhikkhus dwelling near a village, indicates it after saying, “depending on whatever village or town one dwells” (Mv. 147). Immediately after that, he indicates the seven-abbhantara boundary with the words “in a village-less area,” and so on. Therefore, it should be understood that for a bhikkhu who does not dwell depending on a village or town, but is simply journeying on a long road by boat or by land, a seven-abbhantara boundary is obtained for him in each place. For it is said: “If there is a caravan of a single family, having placed the robe in the caravan, one should not go beyond seven abbhantaras ahead or behind,” and so on (Pārā. 489). It is with reference to this same wilderness that it is said, concerning the wilderness boundary, “a single village-less wilderness.”

Yaṃ sandhāya “agāmake araññe addhayojane addhayojane āpatti pācittiyassā”ti (pāci. 414) pāḷiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Idaṃ saṃvidhānasikkhāpadānaṃ ekaṃ agāmakaṃ araññaṃ nāma.

It is with reference to this that it is stated in the Pāli Canon: “In a village-less wilderness, for every half-yojana, there is an offence of expiation” (Pāci. 414). This is called the single village-less wilderness for the training-rules on making arrangements.

Purimena pana sagharaṃ saṅgahitaṃ, iminā tamasaṅgahitanti. Yaṃ sandhāya gaṇamhā ohīyanādhikāre aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (pāci. aṭṭha. 692) “agāmake araññeti ettha ‘nikkhamitvā bahi indakhīlā sabbametaṃ arañña’nti evaṃ vuttaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ araññaṃ. Taṃ paneta kevalaṃ gāmābhāvena ‘agāmaka’nti vuttaṃ, na viñjhāṭavisadisatāyā”ti vuttaṃ. Yaṃ sandhāya “āraññakaṃ nāma senāsanaṃ pañcadhanusatikaṃ pacchima”nti (pārā. 654; pāci. 573) vuttaṃ. Idaṃ āraññakasenāsanaṃ nāma parikkhittassa parikkhepato bahi, aparikkhittassa pana parikkhepokāsato bahi sarukkhaṃ vā arukkhaṃ vā vihāre kunnadisamākiṇṇampi araññaṃ nāma. Tathā “gaṇamhā ohīyanakassa eka”nti vuttaṃ. Idaṃ araññaṃva. Idaṃ pana pubbe agāmakabhāvena āgataṭṭhāne vuttalakkhaṇameva hutvā nikkhamitvā bahi indakhīlā dassanūpacāravijahane [V 0.0032] ekameva āpattiṃ karoti, tato uddhaṃ anāpatti. “Saṃvidhānasikkhāpadānaṃ eka”nti vuttaṃ pana addhayojane addhayojane ekekaṃ āpattiṃ karoti, na tato oraṃ. Itarāni tīṇi yathāvuttaparicchedato orameva tattha vuttavidhiṃ na sampādenti, paraṃ sampādenti. Evametesaṃ aññamaññanānattaṃ veditabbaṃ.

By the former, a place with houses is included; by this, such a place is not included. With reference to this, in the Commentary on the section about leaving the group (Pāci.A. 692), it is said: “Regarding ‘in a village-less wilderness,’ here the characteristic of wilderness is stated thus: ‘having gone out beyond the boundary post (indakhīla), all this is wilderness.’ But this is called ‘village-less’ merely due to the absence of a village, not because it resembles the Viñjhāṭavi forest.” With reference to this, it is said: “A wilderness dwelling is a lodging at a minimum distance of five hundred bow-lengths” (Pārā. 654; Pāci. 573). This so-called wilderness dwelling is outside the enclosure of an enclosed area, or outside the space for an enclosure of an unenclosed area; whether wooded or treeless, even if it is a monastery strewn with small streams, it is called wilderness. Similarly, it is stated: “It is a single area for one who leaves the group.” This is indeed wilderness. This wilderness, having the characteristic stated in the passage that came before regarding its village-less state, incurs a single offence for abandoning sight and proximity upon going out beyond the boundary post; beyond that, there is no offence. However, what is stated as “a single area” for the training-rules on making arrangements incurs an offence for every half-yojana, but not for less than that. The other three, within their aforementioned limits, do not fulfill the stated procedure, but beyond them, they do. Thus, their mutual differences should be understood.

Tattha pañcavidhe gāme yo “parikkhittassa gāmassa indakhīle ṭhitassa leḍḍupāto”ti (pārā. 92) vutto, so na katthaci vinayapiṭake upayogaṃ gato, kevalaṃ aparikkhittassa parikkhepokāsato aparo eko leḍḍupāto gāmūpacāro nāmāti dīpanatthaṃ vutto. Parikkhittassapi ce gāmassa eko leḍḍupāto kappiyabhūmisamāno upacāroti vutto, pageva aparikkhittassa parikkhepokāsato eko. So pana pākaṭattā ca ajjhokāsattā ca okkamantassa āpattiṃ karoti ṭhapetvā [M 0.0035] bhikkhuniyā gāmantarāpattiṃ. Bhikkhuniyo hi tasmiṃ dutiyaleḍḍupātasaṅkhāte gāmūpacāre vasantī āpattiñca āpajjanti, gāmaṃ pavisantī gāmantarāpattiñca. Tāsañhi ṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ araññasaṅkhyaṃ gacchati “tāvadeva chāyā metabbā…pe… tassā tayo ca nissaye, aṭṭha ca akaraṇīyāni ācikkheyyāthā”ti (cūḷava. 430) vacanato. Araññappaṭisaṃyuttānaṃ sikkhāpadānaṃ, vikālegāmappavesanasikkhāpadassa (pāci. 508) ca bhikkhunīnaṃ asādhāraṇattā ca antarārāmabhikkhunupassayappaṭikkamanādīnaṃ kappiyabhūmibhāvavacanato ca “ekā gaṇamhā ohīyeyyāti agāmake araññe dutiyikāya bhikkhuniyā dassanūpacāraṃ vā savanūpacāraṃ vā vijahantiyā āpatti thullaccayassā”tiādisikkhāpadapaññattito (pāci. 692) ca bhikkhunikkhandhakanayaena vā yasmā parikkhittassa gāmassa indakhīlato paṭṭhāya aparikkhittassa upacārato paṭṭhāya nīyati, tattha antaraghare nikkhittacīvare sati caturaṅgasamodhānena bhikkhū vasanti, tasmā sagāmakaṃ nāma hoti.

In the five kinds of villages, the one called 'a clod's throw from the boundary post of a fenced village' (Pārā. 92) is not used anywhere in the Vinaya Piṭaka. It is mentioned only to show that another clod's throw from the place for an enclosure of an unfenced village is called the village vicinity. Even for a fenced village, one clod's throw is said to be the vicinity, like suitable ground; how much more so for an unfenced village, one clod's throw from the place for an enclosure.
