However, because it is manifest and in the open, it incurs an offense for one who enters, except for a bhikkhunī's offense of going between villages. For bhikkhunīs dwelling in this second clod's throw, which is called the village vicinity, incur an offense, and when entering the village, they incur the offense of going between villages. Their standing place is considered wilderness according to the statement: 'Just so, the shade should be measured...and for her, the three supports and the eight things not to be done should be explained' (Cūḷava. 430). Because the training rules connected with the wilderness, and the training rule on entering a village at the wrong time (Pāc. 508), are not common to bhikkhunīs; and because the designation of suitable ground for returning to a bhikkhunī monastery within a park, etc., is stated; and because the training rule beginning with 'If a bhikkhunī, in a wilderness without a village, strays from the group, abandoning the range of sight or sound of a second bhikkhunī, she incurs a grave offense' (Pāc. 692) was laid down; or because, according to the method of the Bhikkhunī Khandhaka, it is measured from the boundary post of a fenced village, and from the vicinity of an unfenced village; and because bhikkhus dwell there with the four factors combined when their robes are left inside a house, therefore it is called 'with a village'.

Avippavāsasīmāya ekaṃ nāma “na, bhikkhave, bhikkhuniyā araññe vatthabbaṃ, yā vaseyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 431) vacanato bhikkhunīnaṃ araññavāso nāma natthīti siddhaṃ. Tāya hi araññe bhikkhunupassaye sati antoāvāsepi dutiyikāya dassanasavanūpacāraṃ vijahantiyā āpatti. Tasmā avippavāsasīmādhikāre “ṭhapetvā gāmañca gāmūpacārañcā”ti (mahāva. 144) ettha yaṃ ṭhānaṃ ṭhapitaṃ, tattheva bhikkhunupassayopi kappati, na tato paraṃ.

Regarding the boundary of non-separation, it is established that: 'Bhikkhus, a bhikkhunī should not dwell in the wilderness. Whichever should dwell, there is an offense of wrong-doing' (Cūḷava. 431). Therefore, it is established that there is no dwelling in the wilderness for bhikkhunīs. For if there is a bhikkhunī monastery in the wilderness, even within the residence, a bhikkhunī who abandons the range of sight or sound of a second bhikkhunī incurs an offense. Therefore, in the section on the boundary of non-separation, the place that is excluded by 'except for the village and the village vicinity' (Mahāva. 144) is also suitable for a bhikkhunī monastery, but not beyond that.

Tāsañca [V 0.0033] avippavāsasīmākammavācāyaṃ “ṭhapetvā gāmañca gāmūpacārañcā”ti vacanaṃ natthīti katvā tesveva gāmagāmūpacāresu pharati. Tato paraṃ dutiyesu leḍḍupātādīsu tāsaṃ akappiyabhūmikattā na samānasaṃvāsakasīmā araññe pharati bhikkhūnaṃ gāmagāmūpacāraṃ viya. Tasmā vuttaṃ “bhikkhuniyā ṭhapetvā gāmantarāpatti”nti.

And because the phrase 'except for the village and the village vicinity' is not present in the formal act for their boundary of non-separation, it extends only to those villages and village vicinities. Beyond that, in the second areas, such as the clod's throw, because those places are unsuitable ground for them, the boundary of common residence does not extend into the wilderness as the village and village vicinity do for bhikkhus. Therefore, it is said, 'except for a bhikkhunī's offense of going between villages'.

Evaṃ tāva pañcavidhaṃ gāmabhedaṃ, araññabhedañca ñatvā idāni “atthi gāmo na gāmaparihāraṃ katthaci labhatī”tiādibhedo veditabbo. Tattha yo aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “amanusso nāma yo sabbaso vā manussānaṃ abhāvena yakkhapariggahabhūto”ti vutto, so gāmo na gāmaparihāraṃ katthaci sikkhāpade labhati. Yañhi sandhāya aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “taṃ panetaṃ buddhakāle, cakkavattikāle [M 0.0036] ca nagaraṃ hoti, sesakāle suññaṃ hoti yakkhapariggahita”nti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.84; dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.150) vuttaṃ. Yo pana paṭirājacorādīhi viluttattā, kevalaṃ bhayena vā chaḍḍito sagharova antarahitagāmabhūto, so “gāmantare gāmantare āpatti pācittiyassā”ti (pāci. 183) vuttapācittiyaṃ janeti, vikāle gāmappavesanaṃ, sekhiye cattāri janetīti veditabbā. Yo pana gāmo yato vā manussā kenacideva karaṇīyena punapi āgantukāmā eva apakkantāti vutto, amanusso so pakatigāmasadisova.

Thus, having understood the five kinds of villages and the kinds of wilderness, now the distinctions such as 'there is a village that does not obtain the village precinct anywhere,' etc., should be understood. Herein, the village that is stated in the commentary as 'a non-human place is one entirely devoid of humans, being occupied by spirits,' does not obtain the village precinct in any training rule. For it is with reference to this that it is stated in the commentary: 'That was a city in the time of the Buddha and the wheel-turning monarch, but in other times it was empty, occupied by spirits' (Pārā. aṭṭha. 1.84; Dī. Ni. aṭṭha. 1.150). But a village that has been plundered by hostile kings or thieves, or simply abandoned out of fear, though still having houses, has become a disappeared village; it gives rise to the pācittiya offense stated as: 'Between villages, there is a pācittiya offense' (Pāc. 183); it also gives rise to the offense of entering a village at the wrong time, and the four sekhiya rules—this should be understood. But a village from which people have departed for some reason, intending to return again, that non-human village is just like an ordinary village.

Atthi araññaṃ na araññaparihāraṃ katthaci labhatīti ettha “ajjhokāso ekūpacāro nāma agāmake araññe samantā sattabbhantarā ekūpacāro, tato paraṃ nānūpacāro”ti (pārā. 494) ettha yvāyaṃ nānūpacāroti vutto, taṃ veditabbaṃ. Yo pana parikkhittassa ekaleḍḍupātasaṅkhāto gāmūpacāranāmako gāmo, yo vā sattho nātirekacātumāsaniviṭṭho, so atthi gāmo na gāmakiccaṃ karoti. Na hi taṃ ṭhānaṃ okkamanto gāmappavesanāpattiṃ āpajjati. Yaṃ pana gāmasīmāya pariyāpannaṃ manussānaṃ valañjanaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ araññaṃ, taṃ atthi araññaṃ na araññakiccaṃ karoti nāma. Na hi tattha āraññakasīmā labbhatīti. Ettāvatā “gāmā vā araññā vā”ti imissā anupaññattiyā lakkhaṇānupaññattibhāvo dassito hoti.

Regarding 'there is wilderness that does not obtain the wilderness precinct anywhere': here, what is called 'various vicinities' in the statement, 'Open space, a single vicinity, means in a wilderness without villages, a single vicinity extends seven abbhantaras around; beyond that is various vicinities' (Pārā. 494), should be understood as such. But a village that is called the village vicinity, defined as a single clod's throw from a fenced village, or a caravan that has not settled for more than four months, is a village that does not perform the function of a village. For one who enters that place does not incur the offense of entering a village. However, wilderness included within the village boundary, serving as a place for human use, is called wilderness that does not perform the function of wilderness. For there, the wilderness boundary is not obtained. To this extent, the nature of the supplementary rule 'from a village or from a wilderness' as a characteristic-defining supplementary rule has been shown.

“Gonisādiniviṭṭhopi gāmo”ti ettha sace tassa gāmassa gāmakhettaparicchedo atthi, sabbopi eko gāmo. No ce, upacārena vā parikkhepena vā paricchinditabbo. Sace gāmakhette sati kānici tāni gharāni aññamaññaupacārappahonakaṃ ṭhānaṃ atikkamitvā dūre dūre katāni honti, vikāle gāmappavese upacārova pamāṇaṃ. Antaragharappaṭisaṃyuttesu sekhiyesu, [V 0.0034] bhikkhuniyā gāmantarāpattīsu ca gharānaṃ parikkhepārahaṭṭhānaṃ pamāṇaṃ, uposathādikammānaṃ gāmakhettaṃ pamāṇaṃ, āraññakasenāsanassa āsannagharassa dutiyaleḍḍupātato paṭṭhāya pañcadhanusatantaratā pamāṇanti evaṃ no paṭibhānanti ācariyā.

Regarding 'a village settled where a cow lies down,' if that village has a defined village field, then the entire area is one village. If not, it should be demarcated by vicinity or enclosure. If, within the village field, some houses are built far apart from each other, exceeding the place sufficient for mutual vicinity, then for entering a village at the wrong time, the vicinity is the measure. For the Sekhiya rules connected with being inside an inhabited area, and for a bhikkhunī's offense of going between villages, the measure is the place suitable for an enclosure of the houses. For Uposatha and other formal acts, the village field is the measure; for a wilderness dwelling, the measure is a distance of five hundred bow-lengths starting from the second clod's throw from the nearest house. Thus the teachers explain.

“Yampi ekasmiṃyeva gāmakhette ekaṃ padesaṃ ‘ayampi visuṃgāmo hotū’ti paricchinditvā rājā kassaci deti, sopi visuṃgāmasīmā hotiyevā”ti [M 0.0037] (mahāva. aṭṭha. 147) aṭṭhakathāvacanato taṃ pavisantiyā bhikkhuniyā gāmantarāpatti hoti eva. Sace tattha vihāro vā devakulaṃ vā sabhā vā gehaṃ vā natthi, kevalaṃ vatthumattakameva hoti, gāmoti vinayakammaṃ sabbaṃ tattha kappati. “Amanusso gāmo”ti hi vuttaṃ. Tañca ṭhānaṃ itarassa gāmassa parikkhepabbhantare vā upacārabbhantare vā hoti, vikāle gāmappavesanaṃ āpucchitvāva gantabbaṃ. No ce, araññaṃ viya yathāsukhaṃ gantabbaṃ. Tattha ce ārāmo vā titthiyaseyyādīsu aññatarovā hoti, laddhakappameva. Bhikkhunupassayo ce hoti, gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisantiyā bhikkhuniyā gāmantarāpatti pariharitabbā. “Araññaṃ nāma ṭhapetvā gāmañca gāmūpacārañca avasesaṃ araññaṃ nāmā”ti (pārā. 92) ettha parikkhepe sati yathāvuttaparicchedaṃ gāmameva ṭhapetvā avasesaṃ tassa upacāraṃ, tato parañca araññaṃ nāma, parikkhepe asati yathāvuttaparicchedaṃ gāmūpacārameva ṭhapetvā tato paraṃ avasesaṃ araññaṃ nāmāti adhippāyo. Evaṃ sati “nikkhamitvā bahi indakhīlā sabbametaṃ arañña”nti (vibha. 529) vuttalakkhaṇe agāmake araññe gaṇamhāohīyanāpatti, tattha avippavāsasīmāya pharaṇaṃ vikāle gāmappavesanāpattiyā anāpattīti evamādivinayavidhi sameti, aññathā na sameti.

According to the commentary's statement: 'Even if, in a single village field, the king demarcates a portion and gives it to someone, saying, "Let this also be a separate village," it indeed becomes the boundary of a separate village' (Mahāva. aṭṭha. 147). For a bhikkhunī entering it, the offense of going to another village certainly occurs. If there is no monastery, shrine, hall, or house there, but only bare ground, it is considered a village, and all Vinaya acts are permissible there. For it has been stated, 'An uninhabited village.' If that place is within the enclosure or the vicinity of another village, one must go only after asking permission to enter a village at the wrong time. If not, one may go as one pleases, as into the wilderness. If there is a monastery or one of the sectarian dwellings, etc., there, it is certainly permissible. If it is a bhikkhunī's dwelling, a bhikkhunī entering the village for alms must avoid the offense of going to another village. Regarding 'wilderness is that which remains when the village and the village vicinity are excluded' (Pārā. 92), the meaning is this: if there is an enclosure, having excluded the village itself as defined above, its remaining vicinity and what is beyond that is called wilderness; if there is no enclosure, having excluded only the village vicinity as defined above, the remainder beyond that is called wilderness. This being the case, the Vinaya procedures—such as the offense of separating from the group in a wilderness without a village, which has the characteristic stated as: 'Having gone out beyond the boundary post, all this is wilderness' (Vibha. 529); the extension of the non-separation boundary there; and the non-offense for entering a village at the wrong time—are reconciled; otherwise, they are not reconciled.

“Ṭhapetvā gāmūpacāraṃ avasesaṃ araññaṃ nāmā”ti (mahāva. 144) vutte gāmūpacārato paro araññanti siddhe “ṭhapetvā gāma”nti visesattho na dissati, gāmassa pana araññabhāvappasaṅgabhayā vuttanti ce? Na, gāmūpacārassa abhāvappasaṅgato. Sati hi gāme gāmūpacāro hoti, so ca tava matena araññabhūto. Kuto dāni gāmūpacāro. Gāmūpacāropi ce araññasaṅkhyaṃ gacchati, parova gāmoti katvā na yuttaṃ gāmassa araññabhāvappasaṅgato ca. Tasmā “gāmā vā araññā vā”ti ettha gāmūpacāropi “gāmo” tveva saṅgahito. Tasmā gāmassa araññabhāvappasaṅgo na yujjati. Yadi evaṃ “ṭhapetvā gāmaṃ avasesaṃ araññaṃ nāmā”ti ettakaṃ vattabbanti ce? Na, araññassa paricchedajānanappasaṅgato. Tathā hi vutto “araññaparicchedo na paññāyatī”ti no laddhi. Gāmūpacārapariyanto hi idha gāmo nāma. Yadi evaṃ “gāmassa ca araññassa ca paricchedadassanatthaṃ vutta”nti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vattabbaṃ, “araññassa [V 0.0035] paricchedadassanatthaṃ vutta”nti kimatthaṃ [M 0.0038] vuttanti ce? Vuccate – aṭṭhakathācariyena paṭhamagāmūpacāraṃyeva sandhāya vuttaṃ “araññaparicchedadassanattha”nti sabbasikkhāpade hi bāhiraindakhīlato paṭṭhāya gāmūpacāraṃ araññaṃ nāma. Gāmaparicchedavacane payojanaṃ panettha natthi parikkhepeneva pākaṭabhūtattā. Dutiyagāmūpacārova gāmassa paricchedadassanatthaṃ vutto parikkhepabhāvena apākaṭattā. Tattha paṭhamagāmūpacāro ce araññaparicchedadassanatthaṃ vutto, tattha na vattabbo. “Nikkhamitvā indakhīlā sabbametaṃ arañña”nti vattabbaṃ. Evaṃ sante subyattataraṃ araññaparicchedo dassito hoti, micchāgāho ca na hoti.

“Excluding the village vicinity, the remainder is called wilderness” (Mahāva. 144)—when this is said, it is established that beyond the village vicinity is wilderness, but the specific meaning of “excluding the village” is not apparent. Is it said out of fear that the village itself might be considered wilderness? No, because of the implication that the village vicinity would not exist. For when a village exists, its village vicinity also exists, but according to your view, that vicinity would be wilderness. How then could a village vicinity exist? If even the village vicinity is counted as wilderness, it would not be proper to consider what is beyond as the village, and there would also be the implication that the village itself is wilderness. Therefore, in the phrase “from a village or from the wilderness,” the village vicinity is included simply as “village.” Hence, the implication that the village itself is wilderness is not justified. If so, should it not simply be said, “Excluding the village, the remainder is called wilderness”? No, because of the implication that the boundary of the wilderness would not be known. For if it were stated thus, our view that “the boundary of the wilderness is not discerned” would not be obtained. Here, the area up to the village vicinity is what is called a village. If that is the case, then the commentary should say, “It is said to show the boundaries of both the village and the wilderness,” but why does it say, “It is said to show the boundary of the wilderness”? It is said: The commentary teacher referred only to the first definition of the village vicinity when saying, “to show the boundary of the wilderness,” because in all training rules, starting from beyond the outer boundary post, the village vicinity is called wilderness. There is no purpose here in defining the village’s boundary, as it is already evident by its enclosure. The second definition of the village vicinity is mentioned to show the boundary of the village because it is not evident by its enclosure. If the first definition of the village vicinity is said to show the boundary of the wilderness, then it should not be mentioned there. Instead, it should be said, “Having gone beyond the boundary post, all this is wilderness.” In this way, the boundary of the wilderness is more clearly shown, and there is no misunderstanding.

“Majjhimassa purisassa leḍḍupāto”ti hi vutte ayaṃ gāmūpacārova araññaṃ gāmūpacārassa vibhaṅgattā. Yadi araññaparicchedadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, avuttakameva, araññato paranti ca micchāgāho hotīti ce, nanu vuttaṃ “paṭhamameva idaṃ parikkhittassa gāmassa upacāraniyamanatthaṃ vutta”nti? Araññaparicchedadassanatthaṃ kiñcāpi “gāmūpacāro”tiādi āraddhaṃ, indakhīle ṭhitassa majjhimassa purisassa leḍḍupātoti pana evaṃ vacanappayojanaṃ. Aparikkhittassa ca gāmassa yvāyaṃ leḍḍupāto upacāro”ti mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vutto, tassa niyamananti vuttaṃ hoti. Kathaṃ paññāyatīti ce? “Araññaṃ nāmā”ti padaṃ anuddharitvā “gāmūpacāro nāmā”ti uddharaṇassa katattā. Tattha “gāmūpacāro nāmā”ti mātikāyaṃ avijjamānaṃ padaṃ uddharanto tayo atthavase dasseti. Seyyathidaṃ – araññaparicchedadassanameko attho, aparikkhittassa gāmassa upacārena saddhiṃ paricchedadassanameko, na kevalaṃ aparikkhittassayeva upacāro vinayādhikāre sappayojano dassitabbo, nippayojanopi parikkhittassa upacāro iminā pariyāyena labbhatīti anusaṅgappayojanameko atthopi veditabbo.

When it is said, “the throw of a clod by a man of average stature,” this very village vicinity is distinguished from the wilderness, because it is a division of the village vicinity. If it were said to show the boundary of the wilderness, it would be as if unsaid, and there would be the misunderstanding that there is something beyond the wilderness. But was it not stated, “This was first said to define the extent of the vicinity of an enclosed village”? Although the phrase “the village vicinity” and so on was introduced to show the boundary of the wilderness, the purpose of saying “the throw of a clod by a man of average stature standing at the boundary post” is this. And in the Great Commentary, it is said, “For an unenclosed village, this throw of a clod marks the vicinity,” meaning it defines the limit. How is this known? By not extracting the word “wilderness” but instead extracting the phrase “the village vicinity,” which is not found in the original text. Here, in extracting the phrase “the village vicinity,” which is absent in the original text, the author indicates three purposes. Namely: one purpose is to show the boundary of the wilderness; another is to show the boundary of an unenclosed village along with its vicinity; and it should also be understood that there is an additional purpose, that not only is the vicinity of an unenclosed village shown to be relevant in Vinaya matters, but also that the vicinity of an enclosed village, though without direct purpose, can be determined by this method.

“Aparikkhittassa gāmassa gharūpacāre ṭhitassa majjhimassa purisassa leḍḍupāto”ti idaṃ bhagavā tayo atthavase paṭicca abhāsi. Seyyathidaṃ – aparikkhittassa gāmassa paricchedadassanameko, avippavāsasīmādhikāre ayameva gāmūpacāroti dassanameko, tattha ṭhitassa dutiyo leḍḍupāto sabbattha gāmappaṭisaṃyuttesu sikkhāpadesu sakiccako upacāroti dassanamekoti evaṃ bhagavā attano desanāvilāsappattiyā ekekapaduddhāraṇena tayo atthavase dassetīti veditabbaṃ.

“The throwing of a clod by a man of average stature standing in the vicinity of a house of an unenclosed village”—this the Blessed One spoke with reference to three purposes. Namely: one purpose is to show the delimited area of an unenclosed village; another is to show that this very village vicinity is the boundary for non-separation; and another is to show that a second clod’s throw, when standing there, is the relevant vicinity in all training rules connected with the village. Thus, it should be understood that the Blessed One, through the grace of his exposition, reveals three purposes by the extraction of each single term.

Tathā [M 0.0039] avippavāsasīmākammavācāya “ṭhapetvā gāmañca gāmūpacārañcā”ti (mahāva. 144) etthāpi [V 0.0036] parikkhepe sati gāmaṃ ṭhapetvā, asati gāmūpacāraṃ ṭhapetvāti attho. Parikkhittassa, aparikkhittassa ca majjhe ārāme avippavāsasīmāsammannanakāle ayaṃ nayo ativiya yujjati. Ubhayaparivajjanato pubbe vuttanayena vā ubhayattha ubhayaṃ labbhateva. “Antarārāmesu pana āciṇṇakappā bhikkhū avippavāsasīmaṃ sammannantī”ti gaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ. “Antaragharappaṭisaṃyuttānaṃ sekhiyānaṃ antarārāmesu asambhavato antarārāmo na gāmasaṅkhaṃ gacchati, tasmā tatthapi avippavāsasīmā ruhatevā”ti eke. Te bhikkhū dutiyassa gāmūpacārassa gāmasaṅkhāsabhāvato tāsaṃ imāya dutiyāya avippavāsakammavācāya abhāvaṃ dassetvā paṭikkhipitabbā. Ajjhārāmo pana gāmopi samāno titthiyaseyyādi viya kappiyabhūmīti veditabbo.

Similarly, in the formal act for the boundary of non-separation, the phrase “excluding the village and the village vicinity” (Mahāvagga 144) means that when there is an enclosure, the village is excluded, and when there is no enclosure, the village vicinity is excluded. This principle is especially applicable when establishing the boundary for non-separation in a monastery located between an enclosed and an unenclosed area. By avoiding both, or by the previously stated method, in both cases both are indeed obtainable. It is stated in the Gaṇṭhipada that “monks accustomed to the practice establish the boundary for non-separation in intermediate monasteries.” Some argue that since the Sekhiya rules connected with inhabited areas are not possible in intermediate monasteries, an intermediate monastery does not count as a village; therefore, a boundary of non-separation is indeed permissible there. Those monks should be refuted by pointing out the absence of this second formal act for non-separation, because the second village vicinity does not have the designation of a village. An inner monastery, however, even if it is a village, should be understood as permissible ground, like the dwellings of sectarians.

Āpattiyā paricchedaṃ, tathānāpattiyāpi ca;

Dassetuṃ gāmasambandha-sikkhāpadavibhāvane.

To show the definition of an offense, and likewise of a non-offense, in the explanation of the training rule connected with a village.

Gāmagāmūpacārā dve, dassitā idha tādinā;

Sīmā sīmūpacārā tu, anekantāti nuddhaṭā.

Village and village vicinity, these two are shown here by the Such-a-one; boundary and boundary vicinity, however, are not presented, as they are indeterminate.

Upacārā ca dve honti, bāhirabbhantarabbasā;

Parikkhittāparikkhitta-bhedā ce caturo siyuṃ.

And vicinities are of two kinds, external and internal; and if distinguished as enclosed and unenclosed, they would be four.

Ayañhi upacārasaddo vinayapiṭake “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, agilānenapi ārāme ārāmūpacāre chattaṃ dhāretu”nti (cūḷava. 270) evamādīsu bāhire upacāre dissati. Bāhiro upacāro nāma parikkhepato, parikkhepārahaṭṭhānato vā eko leḍḍupāto. “Ajjhārāmo nāma parikkhittassa ārāmassa antoārāmo, aparikkhittassa upacāro. Ajjhāvasatho nāma parikkhittassa āvasathassa antoāvasatho, aparikkhittassa upacāro”tiādīsu (pāci. 506) pana upacārasaddo abbhantare upacāre dissati. Abbhantaro upacāro ca nāma parikkhepo, parikkhepārahaṭṭhānañca hoti. Idha pana parikkhepo “ajjhārāmo, ajjhāvasatho”ti vā na vuccati, anto eva ārāmo, āvasathoti vā. Tesu bāhirabbhantarabhedabhinnesu dvīsu upacāresu avippavāsasīmādhikāre “ṭhapetvā gāmañca gāmūpacārañcā”ti (mahāva. 144) ettha gāmūpacāro nāma abbhantarūpacāro [M 0.0040] adhippeto, na bāhiro. Bhikkhuniyā araññasaññitatāya tassa bāhirassa, tassā gāmantarāpattiyā ṭhānabhūtattā ca abbhantaraupacārassāti [V 0.0037] idamettha kāraṇadvayaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tattha idha adinnādānapārājikavibhaṅgeyeva paṭhamo gāmūpacāro dassito, so bāhiro, dutiyo abbhantaroti veditabbo. Paṭhamena ca aparikkhittassa gāmassa dutiyaleḍḍupātasaṅkhāto bāhiro upacāro, dutiyena ca parikkhittassa gāmassa parikkhepato bāhirasaṅkhāto abbhantaro upacāro lesena dassitoti veditabbo. Evaṃ cattāropi upacārā idha bhagavatā desanāvilāsappattena desanālīlāya dassitā hontīti ayaṃ nayo suṭṭhu lakkhetvā ācariyehi sammantayitvā yathānurūpaṃ tattha yojetabbo. Itarathā –

For this term “vicinity” (upacāra) is seen in the Vinaya Piṭaka in external contexts, such as: “I allow, monks, even for one who is not ill to carry an umbrella in the monastery and its vicinity” (Cūḷavagga 270), and similar instances. External vicinity means a single clod-throw from an enclosure, or from a place suitable for an enclosure. However, in passages like: “An inner monastery means the area within an enclosed monastery; for an unenclosed one, it is the vicinity. An inner dwelling means the area within an enclosed dwelling; for an unenclosed one, it is the vicinity” (Pācittiya 506), the term “vicinity” is seen in an internal context. And internal vicinity means the enclosure and the place suitable for an enclosure. Here, however, the enclosure is not called an “inner monastery” or “inner dwelling,” but simply the monastery within or the dwelling within. Regarding these two kinds of vicinity, distinguished as external and internal, in the section on the boundary of non-separation, the “village vicinity” in “excluding the village and the village vicinity” (Mahāvagga 144) is intended as the internal vicinity, not the external. For a bhikkhunī, this is because the external vicinity is associated with her perception of a wilderness, and the internal vicinity is the basis for her offense of going between villages; these two reasons should be understood here. Here, in the analysis of the Pārājika offense of taking what is not given, the first village vicinity shown is external, and the second should be understood as internal. By the first, the external vicinity of an unenclosed village, designated as the second clod-throw, is shown by implication; and by the second, the internal vicinity of an enclosed village, which is designated as external from the enclosure, is shown by implication. Thus, all four kinds of vicinity are shown here by the Blessed One, who has attained grace in exposition, with the elegance of his instruction. This method should be carefully noted, discussed with the teachers, and applied appropriately in each case. Otherwise—

Asambudhaṃ buddhamahānubhāvaṃ;

Dhammassa gambhīranayattatañca;

Yo vaṇṇaye naṃ vinayaṃ aviññū;

So duddaso sāsananāsahetu.

Not understanding the great power of the Buddha and the profound nature of the Dhamma's method, whoever, being ignorant, expounds the Vinaya, he, of wrong view, is a cause for the Dispensation's ruin.

Pāḷiṃ tadatthañca asambudhañhi;

Nāseti yo aṭṭhakathānayañca;

Anicchayaṃ nicchayato parehi;

Gāmoti teyeva purakkhato so.

Indeed, he who, not understanding the Pāli text and its meaning, also destroys the method of the commentary; being without his own conviction, he is led to a conviction by others; he is put forward by those very people as a 'villager'.

Anukkameneva mahājanena;

Purakkhato paṇḍitamāni bhikkhu;

Apaṇḍitānaṃ vimatiṃ akatvā;

Ācariyalīlaṃ purato karoti.

A monk who fancies himself wise, gradually honored by the great populace, not having resolved the doubts of the unwise, performs the teacher's role before them.

Tattha hi pāḷiyaṃ “gāmassa upacāro gāmūpacāro, gāmasaṅkhāto upacāro gāmūpacāro nāmā”ti uddharitvā gāmassa upacāraṃ dassento “indakhīle ṭhitassa majjhimassa purisassa leḍḍupāto”ti (pārā. 92) vatvā puna gāmasaṅkhātaṃ upacāraṃ dassento “gharūpacāre ṭhitassa majjhimassa purisassa leḍḍupāto”ti vuttaṃ. Imamatthaṃ sandhāya vikāle gāmappavesanagāmantaraaappavāsasammutiādīsu parikkhepārahaṭṭhānameva gāmūpacāranti vuttanti likhitaṃ.

Therein, in the Pāli text, having quoted, “‘The vicinity of a village is the village-vicinity; the vicinity designated as a village is called the village-vicinity,’” to show the vicinity of a village, it is said, “A clod’s throw by a man of average height standing at the boundary pillar” (Pārājika 92). Then, to show the vicinity designated as a village, it is said, “A clod’s throw by a man of average height standing in the vicinity of a house.” With reference to this meaning, it is written that in cases such as entering a village at the wrong time, the agreement for non-separation between villages, and so on, the place suitable for an enclosure itself is called the village-vicinity.

Atthato [M 0.0041] ekanti ettha saṅkhāsaddaṃ saṅkhātasaddena samānayati. “Ādiyeyyā”ti idaṃ pañcavīsatiyā avahārānaṃ sādhāraṇapadaṃ. Ṭhānācāvanavasena ca khīlādīni saṅkāmetvā khettādiggahaṇavasena [V 0.0038] cāti attho. Ṭhānācāvane yathā sāmikassa dhuranikkhepādiṃ anoloketvāva āpatti, tathā ihāpīti gahetabbā.

Regarding the phrase 'one in meaning', here the word 'saṅkhā' is equated with the word 'saṅkhāta'. 'Ādiyeyya' (he would take)—this is a term common to the twenty-five types of theft. The meaning is: by way of moving from the place by transferring boundary markers and so on, and by way of taking possession by seizing fields and so on. Just as in moving from the place an offense occurs without even considering the owner's laying down of the burden, so too it should be understood here.

“Asukaṃ nāma bhaṇḍaṃ avaharissāmī”ti sabbesaṃ ekāsayattā “ekenāpī”ti vuttaṃ. Yadi āṇatti icchitabbā, saṃvidhāvahāro nāma eko avahāro parihāyitabbo.

“I will steal such-and-such an item”—since all have the same intention, it is said, “even by one.” If a command is intended, one type of theft, called “theft by prearrangement,” must be omitted.

Okāsaparikappe ṭhānācāvanāya gahitampi okāsaparikappitattā rakkhati. Okāsātikkamova pamāṇaṃ pubbe asuddhacittena gahitattā. Idāni suddhacittena gahitepi hoti evāti vadanti, taṃ na sundaraṃ. Ettha pana vinicchayo samantapāsādikaṃ oloketvā gahetabbo.

In the case of determining a space, even if an item is taken for the purpose of moving it from its place, it is protected because it has been determined as a space. Exceeding the space is the measure, because it was previously taken with an impure mind. Some say that it is the same even if it is now taken with a pure mind, but that is not sound. Here, however, the decision should be made after consulting the Samantapāsādikā.

Uddhāro natthīti ṭhānācāvanaṃ natthīti attho.

“There is no lifting” means there is no moving from the place.

Uddhatamatte avahāro sakalassa payogassa niṭṭhāpitattā, na atthasādhakavasena. Uddhāreyeva rakkhatīti ettha eva-saddena pātane na rakkhatīti atthe siddhepi atthasādhakavasena atthaṃ dassetuṃ “taṃ uddharitvā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

The theft occurs at the very moment of lifting, because the entire effort is completed, not by way of achieving the purpose. “It is protected only at the lifting”—here, although the meaning that it is not protected at the falling is established by the word 'eva' (only), the phrase “having lifted it,” etc., is stated to show the meaning by way of achieving the purpose.

“Pathabyārājapadesarājādayo bahū, tesaṃ saṅgaṇhanatthaṃ ‘rājāno’ti bahuvacanaṃ vutta”nti likhitaṃ. Kiñcāpi bahuvacanaṃ kataṃ, idaṃ pana ekaṃ bimbisāramevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Rājānoti kiñci aniddisitvā sādhāraṇavasena kiñcāpi vuttaṃ, idaṃ pana bimbisāramevāti.

It is written: “There are many, such as kings of the earth, regional kings, and so on; to include them, the plural ‘kings’ is stated.” Although the plural is used, this should be understood as referring only to Bimbisāra. Though ‘kings’ is stated in a general way without specifying anyone, this refers only to Bimbisāra.

Pubbappayogeti ettha gamanakāle maggasodhanādhikaraṇe apācittiyakhette dukkaṭaṃ, latācchedanādīsu pācittiyameva. Gantvā pana kumbhimatthake jātalatādicchedane sahapayogattā dukkaṭaṃ. “Ekabhaṇḍe evaṃ bhāriyamidaṃ, ‘tvampi ekapassaṃ gaṇha, ahampi ekapassaṃ gaṇhāmī’ti saṃvidahitvā ubhayesaṃ payogena ṭhānācāvane kate kāyavācācittehi samuṭṭhāti. Aññathā sāhatthikaṃ vā āṇattikassa aṅgaṃ na hoti[M 0.0042], āṇattikaṃ vā sāhatthikassāti vuttalakkhaṇena virujjhatī”ti vinayagaṇṭhipade likhitaṃ. Pi-saddo panettha tattheva likhito.

Here, regarding 'preliminary effort': while traveling, in the context of clearing the path, a dukkaṭa offense occurs in an area where there is no pācittiya offense; in cutting vines and the like, it is a pācittiya offense itself. But, having gone and cutting vines and so on growing on the top of a pot, because of the simultaneous effort, it is a dukkaṭa offense. It is written in the Vinayagaṇṭhipada: “In the case of a single item so heavy that, having made an agreement, ‘You take one side, and I will take one side,’ it is moved from its place through the effort of both, the offense originates from body, speech, and mind. Otherwise, the act done by one's own hand is not a factor for the one who commanded, or what was commanded is not a factor for the one acting with his own hand; thus, it contradicts the stated characteristic.” The word 'pi' is written here in that very place.

Kāyavācāsamuṭṭhānaṃ, yassā āpattiyā siyā;

Tatra vācaṅgaṃ cittaṃva, kammaṃ nassā vidhīyati.

For whichever offense that may arise from body or speech, therein the action is not determined by the speech-factor or the mind-factor.

Kiriyākiriyādikaṃ [V 0.0039] yañce, yampi kammattayaṃ bhave;

Na yuttaṃ taṃ viruddhattā, kammamekaṃva yujjatīti. (vajira. ṭī. pārājika 131 pakiṇṇakakathāvaṇṇanā);

Whatever action, non-action, and so forth, and whatever threefold kamma there may be; that is not fitting due to contradiction; only one kamma is appropriate. (Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā, Pārājika 131, Pakiṇṇakakathāvaṇṇanā).

Dutiyapārājikavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Second Pārājika is concluded.

3. Tatiyapārājikavaṇṇanā

3. The Explanation of the Third Pārājika

Yathā ñātapariññā dhammānaṃ sabhāvajānanameva “idaṃ rūpaṃ, ayaṃ vedanā”ti, tīraṇapariññā pana dhammasabhāvena saddhiṃ aniccādivasena pavattamānaṃ “rūpaṃ aniccanti vā”tiādi, evamidha saddhiṃ cetetvā ekattenāpi pāṇātipātābhāvā “jīvitā voropeyyā”ti vuttaṃ. “Manussaviggaha”nti vuttattā gabbhaseyyakānaṃ vasena sabbasukhumaattabhāvato paṭṭhāya dassetuṃ “kalalato paṭṭhāyā”ti āha. Ettha jīvitā voropento paccuppannato viyojeti. Tattha khaṇapaccuppannaṃ na sakkā voropetuṃ, santatipaccuppannaṃ vā addhāpaccuppannaṃ vā sakkā. Kathaṃ? Tasmiñhi upakkame kate laddhūpakkamaṃ jīvitadasakaṃ nirujjhamānaṃ dubbalassa parihīnavegassa paccayo hoti. Santatipaccuppannaṃ yathā dve tayo javanavāre javitvā nirujjhati, addhāpaccuppannañca tadanurūpaṃ katvā nirujjhati, tathā paccayo hoti. Tato santatipaccuppannaṃ vā addhāpaccuppannaṃ vā yathāparicchinnakālaṃ apatvā antarāva nirujjhati. Evaṃ tadubhayampi voropetuṃ sakkā. Tasmā paccuppannaṃ viyojeti.

Just as the full understanding of the known is merely knowing the inherent nature of phenomena—'this is form, this is feeling'—the full understanding by investigation, however, is that which proceeds along with the inherent nature of phenomena in terms of impermanence, and so on, such as 'form is impermanent.' Thus here, having intended it together, because there is no killing of a living being by a single unified act, it is said, 'one would deprive of life.' Since 'human form' is stated, to show this from the most subtle state of being, from the state of being in the womb, it is said, 'starting from the embryo.' Here, one who deprives of life separates it from the present. In that case, the momentary present cannot be deprived, but the continuous present or the durational present can be. How? For when that effort is made, the life-decade that has been subjected to the effort, while ceasing, becomes a condition for that which is weakened and of diminished force. The continuous present is such that it ceases after running for two or three apperceptive moments, and the durational present is made to cease accordingly—thus it becomes a condition. Then, the continuous present or the durational present ceases in the interim, without reaching its determined time. In this way, both of these can be deprived. Therefore, it separates from the present.

“Imassa panatthassā”ti vohāravasena vuttamatthaṃ paramatthavasena āvibhāvatthaṃ “pāṇo veditabbo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Kāyaviññattisahitāya cetanāya payujjatīti payogo, ko so? Sarīre satthādīnaṃ gamanaṃ paharaṇanti kāyavacīviññattisahitāya cetanāya parasarīre satthapātanaṃ. Dūre ṭhitanti dūre vā tiṭṭhatu, samīpe vā. Hatthato [M 0.0043] muttena pahāro nissaggiyo. Tatthāti nissaggiyappayoge. Yo koci maratūti ettha mahājanasamūhe na sakkā. Yassūpari saro patati, tasseva jīvitamaraṇaṃ kātuṃ, na yassa kassaci jīvitamaraṇaṃ. Āṇāpananti vacīviññattisahitāya cetanāya adhippetatthasādhanaṃ. Teneva “sāvetukāmo na sāvetī”ti (pārā. 54) vuttaṃ. Āṇattiniyāmakāti āṇattikappayogasādhikā. Etesu hi avirajjhitesu eva āṇattipayogo hoti, na aññathā.

Regarding 'the meaning of this': to clarify the meaning stated conventionally in its ultimate sense, the passage beginning 'life should be understood' was stated. Effort is that which is applied with intention accompanied by bodily intimation. What is that? The movement of weapons and so on towards a body, a strike—that is, the casting of a weapon into another's body with intention accompanied by bodily and verbal intimation. 'Standing at a distance' means whether one stands far away or nearby. A blow from that which is released from the hand is a relinquished one. 'Therein' means in the application of relinquishment. Regarding 'Let whoever die,' here, in a large crowd, it is not possible to cause the life and death of just anyone. Life and death can be caused only for the one upon whom the arrow falls, not for just anyone. 'Commanding' is the accomplishment of the intended purpose with intention accompanied by verbal intimation. For that reason it is said, 'wishing to inform, one does not inform' (Pārā. 54). 'Regulators of a command' means that which accomplishes the application of a command. For the application of a command occurs only when these are not violated, not otherwise.

Rūpūpahāroti [V 0.0040] ettha –

Here, regarding 'offering of form':

“Mamālābhena esitthī, maratū”ti samīpago;

Duṭṭhacitto sace yāti, hoti so itthimārako.

'May this woman die from not getting me!' If, thinking thus, he goes near with a corrupt mind, he becomes the killer of that woman.

Bhikkhatthāya sace yāti, jānantopi na mārako;

Anatthiko hi so tassā, maraṇena upekkhako.

If he goes for the sake of alms, even while knowing, he is not a killer; for he is not seeking her harm, being indifferent to her death.

Viyogena ca me jāyā, jananī ca na jīvati;

Iti jānaṃ viyuñjanto, tadatthiko hoti mārako.

'My wife and my mother cannot live separated from me.' Knowing this, if he separates from them, desiring that outcome, he becomes a killer.

Pabbajjādinimittañce, yāti jānaṃ na mārako;

Anatthiko hi so tassā, maraṇena upekkhako.

If he goes for a reason such as ordination, even while knowing, he is not a killer; for he is not seeking her harm, being indifferent to her death.

Hārakasaddassa bhedato atthaṃ vitthāretvā ubhayampi ekamevāti dassetuṃ “satthañca taṃ hārakañcā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Etena thāvarappayogaṃ dasseti sāhatthikādīsu payogesu. “Iti cittamano”ti uddharitvāpi itisaddassa attho na tāva vutto. Kiñcāpi na vutto, adhikāravasena pana āgataṃ itisaddaṃ yojetvā iti cittasaṅkappoti ettha “maraṇasaññī maraṇacetano maraṇādhippāyo”ti vuttattā maraṇaṃyeva vakkhatīti veditabbo. Vuttanayenāti chappayogavasena. Sāhatthikanissaggiyappayogesu sanniṭṭhāpakacetanāya sattamāya saha uppannakāyaviññattiyā sāhatthikatā veditabbā. Āṇattike pana sattahipi cetanāhi saha vacīviññattisambhavato satta satta saddā ekato hutvā ekekakkharabhāvaṃ gantvā yattakehi akkharehi [M 0.0044] attano adhippāyaṃ viññāpenti, tadavasānakkharasamuṭṭhāpikāya sattamacetanāya sahajātavacīviññattiyā āṇattikatā veditabbā.

Having elaborated the meaning by distinguishing the term 'remover' (hāraka), to show that both are one and the same, the phrase beginning 'the weapon and that remover' was stated. By this, it shows the application of a fixed device in the context of applications such as direct action. Even after quoting 'thus with mind,' the meaning of the word 'iti' has not yet been stated. Although it has not been stated, by connecting the word 'iti' which has come up here by virtue of the topic, with 'thus with mental resolve,' it should be understood that because it is said, 'perceiving death, intending death, having the aim of death,' death itself will be spoken of. 'According to the method stated' means by way of the six applications. In the applications of direct action and relinquishment, direct action should be understood as the bodily intimation arisen together with the seventh, finalizing volition. In the case of a command, however, since vocal intimation can arise with all seven volitions, various sounds, having come together and become single syllables, by as many syllables as they convey one's intention, command should be understood as the vocal intimation co-arisen with the seventh volition which originates the final syllable.

Tatiyapārājikavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Third Pārājika is concluded.

4. Catutthapārājikavaṇṇanā

4. The Explanation of the Fourth Pārājika

Idheva saṅgahanti “iti jānāmi, iti passāmī”ti pade kathanti ce, “iti jānāmī”tiādimāha[V 0.0041]. Kevalaṃ “pāpicchatāyā”ti (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. catutthapārājikavaṇṇanā) vacanato mandattā momūhattā samudācarantassa anāpattīti dīpitaṃ. “Atītakāle sotāpannomhī”ti vadanto pariyāyena vadati, “yo te vihāre vasati, so bhikkhu arahā”tiādīsu (pari. 165) viya sikkhāpadepi “iti jānāmī”ti (pārā. 195, 197) paccuppannameva vuttaṃ.

They are included right here. If it is asked how, he states the phrase beginning 'I know thus.' It is shown that, based on the words 'merely due to evil desire' (Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī-aṭṭhakathā, Catutthapārājikavaṇṇanā), there is no offense for one who acts out of dullness and delusion. One who says, 'I was a stream-enterer in the past,' speaks indirectly, just as in cases like, 'The bhikkhu who dwells in your monastery is an Arahant' (Parivāra 165). In the training rule itself, 'I know thus' (Pārājika 195, 197) is stated only with reference to the present.

Catutthapārājikavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Fourth Pārājika is concluded.

Mātughātakapitughātakaarahantaghātakā tatiyapārājikaṃ āpannā, bhikkhunidūsako, lambīādayo ca cattāro paṭhamapārājikaṃ āpannā evāti katvā kuto catuvīsatīti ce? Na, adhippāyājānanato. Mātughātakādayo hi cattāro idhānupasampannā eva adhippetā, lambīādayo cattāro kiñcāpi paṭhamapārājikena saṅgahitā, yasmā pana ekena pariyāyena methunadhammaṃ paṭisevino honti, tasmā visuṃ vuttā. Na labhati bhikkhūhīti ettha “uposathādibhedaṃ saṃvāsa”nti ettakaṃ vuttaṃ. Vinayaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “uposathappavāraṇāpātimokkhuddesasaṅghakammappabheda”nti vuttaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ “saṃvāso nāma ekakammaṃ ekuddeso samasikkhatā”ti (pārā. 55, 92, 172, 198) vuttaṃ. Tividhenāpi saṅghakammaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭatīti paṭikkhittaṃ. “Na, bhikkhave, gahaṭṭhena nisinnaparisāya pātimokkhaṃ uddisitabba”ntiādi (mahāva. 154) pātimokkhappavāraṇāsu eva āgataṃ, aññesu ca evarūpesu ṭhānesu sesaṃ kammaṃ kātuṃ natthi paṭikkhepo. Ācariyāpi “sesaṃ kammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati, natthi āpattī”ti vadanti. “Antimavatthu ajjhāpannaṃ amūlakena pārājikena codentassa saṅghādiseso, saṅghādisesena [M 0.0045] codentassa pācittiyanti bhikkhuno viya vuttaṃ, na anupasampannassa viya dukkaṭaṃ. Tasmā tena sahaseyyā, tassa paṭiggahaṇañca bhikkhussa vaṭṭatīti ācariyā vadantī”ti likhitaṃ. “Yathā pure tathā pacchāti ‘ekakammaṃ ekuddeso samasikkhatā’ti evaṃ vuttasaṃvāsassa abhabbatāmattaṃ sandhāya vutta”nti vadanti, vīmaṃsitabbaṃ.

If it is asked, 'Since a mother-killer, a father-killer, and an Arahant-killer have incurred the third Pārājika, and a defiler of a bhikkhunī, Lambī, and the other three have incurred the first Pārājika, whence the twenty-four?' The answer is: No, this is from not understanding the intention. For here, the four beginning with the mother-killer are intended as being unordained. As for the four beginning with Lambī, although they are included under the first Pārājika, they are stated separately because they engage in sexual intercourse in a certain way. Regarding 'does not have communion with bhikkhus,' this much is stated: 'communion of the kind of Uposatha and so forth.' In the Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā, it is said: 'of the kind of Saṅgha acts such as Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, and the recitation of the Pātimokkha.' In the Pāḷi, it is said: 'Communion means one act, one recitation, and common training' (Pārājika 55, 92, 172, 198). It is prohibited to perform a Saṅgha act in any of the three ways. The passage beginning 'Bhikkhus, the Pātimokkha should not be recited in an assembly where a householder is seated' (Mahāvagga 154) pertains only to the Pātimokkha and Pavāraṇā; in other such cases, there is no prohibition against performing the remaining acts. The teachers also say, 'It is permissible to perform the remaining acts; there is no offense.' It is written: 'The teachers say: "For one who accuses another who has committed a final offense with a groundless Pārājika, there is a Saṅghādisesa; for one who accuses of a Saṅghādisesa, there is a Pācittiya"—this is stated as for a bhikkhu, not as a Dukkaṭa as it would be for an unordained person. Therefore, it is permissible for a bhikkhu to share a lodging with him and to accept from him.' They say: 'The phrase "As before, so after" is stated with reference to the mere unsuitability for the communion thus defined as "one act, one recitation, common training."' This should be investigated.

Idāni catunnampi sādhāraṇaṃ pakiṇṇakaṃ – methunadhammaṃ paṭisevanto atthi koci pārājiko hoti asaṃvāso, atthi koci na pārājiko hoti asaṃvāso, atthi koci na pārājiko saṃvāso dukkaṭavatthusmiṃ vā thullaccayavatthusmiṃ vā paṭisevanto, atthi koci na pārājiko pakkhapaṇḍako apaṇḍakapakkhe upasampanno paṇḍakapakkhe methunadhammaṃ paṭisevanto. So āpattiṃ nāpajjatīti na pārājiko nāma. Na hi abhikkhussa āpatti nāma atthi. So [V 0.0042] anāpattikattā apaṇḍakapakkhe āgato kiṃ asaṃvāso hoti, na hotīti? Hoti. “Abhabbo tena sarīrabandhanenā”ti (mahāva. 129) hi vuttaṃ. “Yo pana bhikkhu bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno…pe… asaṃvāso”ti (pārā. 44) vuttattā yo bhikkhubhāvena methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevati, so eva abhabbo. Nāyaṃ apārājikattāti ce? Na, “byattena bhikkhunā paṭibalena saṅgho ñāpetabbo”ti (mahāva. 126) vuttaṭṭhāne yathā abhikkhunā kammavācāya sāvitāyapi kammaṃ ruhati kammavipattiyā asambhavato, evaṃsampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ viseso – upasampannapubbo evaṃ ce kammavācaṃ sāveti, saṅgho ca tasmiṃ upasampannasaññī eva ce, kammaṃ ruhati, nāññathāti no khantīti ācariyo.

Now, regarding the common miscellany for all four offenses: concerning one who engages in sexual intercourse, there is one who becomes pārājika and is not in communion; there is one who does not become pārājika but is not in communion; there is one who does not become pārājika and is in communion, engaging in a matter of a dukkaṭa or thullaccaya offense; and there is one who does not become pārājika—a pakkhapaṇḍaka who was ordained in the group of non-paṇḍakas, engaging in sexual intercourse in the group of paṇḍakas. He does not incur an offense, hence he is not called a pārājika. For there is no offense for one who is not a bhikkhu. Since he is free from offense, having come into the group of non-paṇḍakas, is he not in communion, or is he? He is. For it is said, 'He is incapable by that bodily constitution' (Mahāvagga 129). Because it is stated, 'Whatever bhikkhu, having undertaken the training and livelihood of bhikkhus... and so forth... is not in communion' (Pārājika 44), one who engages in sexual intercourse in the state of a bhikkhu, he alone is incapable. If it is said that this is because he is not a pārājika, (the answer is) no. For in the passage where it is said, 'A competent and capable bhikkhu should inform the Saṅgha,' just as when a formal act is recited by a non-bhikkhu, the act is not valid, since a procedural defect is impossible, so this should be understood as a case of accomplishment. Here is the distinction: if one who was formerly ordained were to recite such a formal act, and if the Saṅgha perceives him as ordained, the act is valid; otherwise, it is not acceptable—so says the teacher.

Gahaṭṭho vā titthiyo vā paṇḍako vā kammavācaṃ sāveti, saṅghena kammavācā na vuttā hoti. “Saṅgho upasampādeyya saṅgho upasampādeti, upasampanno saṅghenā”ti (mahāva. 127) hi vacanato saṅghena kammavācāya vattabbatāya saṅghapariyāpannena, saṅghapariyāpannasaññitena vā ekena vuttāya saṅghena vuttā hotīti veditabbo, na gahaṭṭhatitthiyapaṇḍakādīsu aññatarena. Ayameva sabbakammesu yutti daṭṭhabbā.

If a householder, a sectarian, or a paṇḍaka recites the formal act, the Saṅgha has not recited the formal act. For it is said, 'The Saṅgha should confer the higher ordination, the Saṅgha confers the higher ordination, he is given higher ordination by the Saṅgha' (Mahāvagga 127). Therefore, since the formal act must be uttered by the Saṅgha, it should be understood that it is recited by the Saṅgha when it is uttered by one who is included in the Saṅgha or is perceived as included in the Saṅgha, not when it is uttered by a householder, sectarian, paṇḍaka, or any other such person. This very principle should be seen in all formal acts.

Tathā atthi methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevanto koci nāsetabbo, “yo bhikkhunidūsako, ayaṃ nāsetabbo”ti (mahāva. 114-115 atthato samānaṃ) vuttattā tena eva so anupasampannova [M 0.0046] sahaseyyāpattiṃ vā aññaṃ vā tādisaṃ janeti, tassa omasane ca dukkaṭaṃ hoti. Abhikkhuniyā methunadhammaṃ paṭisevanto na nāsetabbo, “antimavatthuṃ ajjhāpanno, bhikkhave, anupasampanno na upasampādetabbo”ti pāḷiyā abhāvato, teneva so upasampannasaṅkhaṃ gacchati, sahaseyyāpattiādiṃ na janeti, kevalaṃ asaṃvāsoti katvā gaṇapūrako na hoti. Ekakammaekuddeso hi saṃvāsoti vutto, samasikkhatāpi saṃvāsoti katvā so tena saddhiṃ natthīti. Padasodhammāpattiṃ pana janetīti kāraṇacchāyā dissatīti. Yathā bhikkhuniyā saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghassa ekakammādino saṃvāsassa abhāvā bhikkhunī asaṃvāsā bhikkhussa, tathā bhikkhu ca bhikkhuniyā, padasodhammāpattiṃ pana na janeti. Tathā antimavatthuṃ ajjhāpannopi ekecco “yo nāsetabboti vutto”ti iminā nidassanena sakāraṇacchāyā ajjhupekkhitā hotīti na gahaṇaṃ gacchati. Apica “ubho nāsetabbā, dūsako nāsetabbo”ti (pārā. 66) vacanato, “mettiyaṃ bhikkhuniṃ nāsethā”ti (pārā. 384) vacanato ca yo saṅghamajjhaṃ pavisitvā anuvijjakena anuvijjiyamāno parājito, sopi anupasampannova, na omasavādapācittiyaṃ janetīti veditabbo.

Similarly, there is someone who should be expelled for engaging in sexual intercourse, since it is said, 'The one who violates a bhikkhunī, he should be expelled' (Mahāvagga 114-115, same in meaning). By that very fact, he is unordained, and he incurs an offense of sharing a bed or another such offense, and for touching him, there is a Dukkaṭa. One who engages in sexual intercourse with a non-bhikkhunī should not be expelled, due to the absence of a Pāḷi text (to that effect), unlike the text: 'One who has committed the final offense, O bhikkhus, being unordained, is not to be ordained.' By that very fact, he is counted among the ordained, does not incur the offense of sharing a bed, and so forth; being merely not in communion, he does not complete the quorum. For communion is said to be one formal act and one recitation, and since having the same training is also communion, he has no such communion with them. However, a semblance of a reason is seen for his incurring a padasodhamma offense. Just as, due to the absence of communion through a single formal act and so forth between the bhikkhu-saṅgha and a bhikkhunī, a bhikkhunī is not in communion with the bhikkhu, and likewise the bhikkhu with the bhikkhunī, yet he does not incur a padasodhamma offense. Similarly, even one who has committed the final offense, when it is said, 'The one who should be expelled is stated thus'—by this indication, the semblance of its reason is overlooked, and thus it is not accepted. Furthermore, based on the statements, 'Both should be expelled,' 'The violator should be expelled' (Pārājika 66), and 'Expel the bhikkhunī Mettiyā' (Pārājika 384), it should be understood that one who enters the midst of the Saṅgha and, being investigated by an investigator, is defeated—he too is unordained and does not incur the pācittiya offense for insulting speech.

Apicettha [V 0.0043] sikkhāpaccakkhātakacatukkaṃ veditabbaṃ. Atthi hi puggalo sikkhāpaccakkhātako na sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno, atthi puggalo na sikkhāpaccakkhātako sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno, atthi puggalo sikkhāpaccakkhātako ceva sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno ca, atthi puggalo neva sikkhāpaccakkhātako na sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno. Tattha tatiyo bhikkhunī sikkhāpaccakkhātakā veditabbā. Sā hi yāva na liṅgaṃ pariccajati, kāsāvesu saussāhāva samānā sāmaññā cavitukāmā sikkhaṃ paccakkhantīpi bhikkhunī eva sikkhāsājīvasamāpannāva. Vuttañhi bhagavatā “natthi, bhikkhave, bhikkhuniyā sikkhāpaccakkhāna”nti. Kadā pana sā abhikkhunī hotīti? Yadā sā vibbhantāti saṅkhaṃ gacchati. Vuttañhi bhagavatā “yadeva sā vibbhantā, tadeva sā abhikkhunī”ti (cūḷava. 434). Kittāvatā pana vibbhantā hotīti? Sāmaññā cavitukāmā kāsāvesu anālayā kāsāvaṃ vā apaneti, naggā vā gacchati, tiṇapaṇṇādinā vā paṭicchādetvā gacchati, kāsāvaṃyeva [M 0.0047] vā gihinivāsanākārena nivāseti, odātaṃ vā vatthaṃ nivāseti, liṅgeneva vā saddhiṃ titthiyesu pavisitvā kesaluñcanādivataṃ samādiyati, titthiyaliṅgaṃ vā samādiyati, tadā vibbhantā nāma hoti. Tattha yā saliṅge ṭhitāva titthiyavataṃ samādiyati, sā titthiyapakkantabhikkhu viya pacchā pabbajjampi na labhati. Sesā pabbajjameva labhati, na upasampadaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ kiñcāpi “yā, bhikkhave, bhikkhunī sakāvāsā titthāyatanaṃ saṅkantā, sā āgatā na upasampādetabbā”ti (cūḷava. 434) vacanato yā paṭhamaṃ vibbhamitvā pacchā titthāyatanaṃ saṅkantā, sā āgatā upasampādetabbāti anuññātaṃ viya dissati. Saṅgītiācariyehi pana “catuvīsati pārājikānī”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.233) vuttattā na puna sā upasampādetabbā. Tasmā eva sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ nānuññātaṃ bhagavatā. Antimavatthuṃ ajjhāpannā pana bhikkhunī eva. Pakkhapaṇḍakīpi bhikkhunī eva. Imaṃ nayaṃ catūsupi yojetvā yathārahaṃ kathetabbaṃ.

Furthermore, the fourfold classification of one who renounces the training should be understood. For there is a person who has renounced the training but has not undertaken the training and livelihood; there is a person who has not renounced the training but has undertaken the training and livelihood; there is a person who has both renounced the training and undertaken the training and livelihood; and there is a person who has neither renounced the training nor undertaken the training and livelihood. Among these, the third is to be understood as a bhikkhunī who has renounced the training. For as long as she does not abandon the monastic insignia, even if she renounces the training while still wearing the ochre robes and desiring to abandon the monastic state, she is still a bhikkhunī who has undertaken the training and livelihood. For the Blessed One has said: “Monks, there is no renunciation of the training for a bhikkhunī.” But when does she become a non-bhikkhunī? When she is considered to have fallen away. For the Blessed One has said: “Only when she has fallen away is she a non-bhikkhunī” (Cūḷavagga 434). And by how much is she considered to have fallen away? When, desiring to abandon the monastic state, she discards the ochre robes without attachment, or goes naked, or covers herself with grass or leaves, or wears the ochre robes in the manner of a laywoman, or wears white cloth, or, while still bearing the monastic insignia, joins the followers of another religion and adopts their practices such as pulling out hair, or adopts the insignia of another religion—then she is called one who has fallen away. Here, one who, while still bearing the monastic insignia, adopts the practices of another religion, is like a monk who has gone over to another religion and therefore cannot later receive the going forth. The others can receive the going forth, but not the higher ordination. Although in the Pāḷi it seems permitted, as stated in the words: “Monks, a bhikkhunī who has gone from her own residence to the abode of another religion, if she returns, should not be given higher ordination” (Cūḷavagga 434), suggesting that one who first falls away and later goes to the abode of another religion, if she returns, should be given higher ordination. However, the teachers of the Saṅgīti have said: “There are twenty-four pārājikas” (Pārājika Aṭṭhakathā 2.233), so she should not be given higher ordination again. Therefore, the renunciation of the training was not permitted by the Blessed One. A bhikkhunī who has committed the final offense is still a bhikkhunī. A pakkhapaṇḍakī is also a bhikkhunī. This principle should be applied to all four cases and explained accordingly.

Pārājikavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Pārājika is concluded.

Saṅghādisesakaṇḍaṃ

The Chapter on Saṅghādisesa Offenses

1. Sukkavissaṭṭhisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Training Rule on Intentional Emission of Semen

Aññatra [M 0.0048][V 0.0044] supinantāti svāyaṃ dubbalavatthukattā cetanāya paṭisandhiṃ ākaḍḍhituṃ asamatthā, supine upaṭṭhitaṃ nimittañhi dubbalaṃ. Pavatte pana aññehi kusalākusalehi upatthambhitā vipākaṃ deti. Kiñcāpi vipākaṃ deti, atha kho avisaye uppannattā abbohārikāva supinantacetanāti likhitaṃ. Yaṃ panettha “supine upaṭṭhitaṃ nimittañhi dubbala”nti vuttaṃ, taṃ anekantaṃ, na ca ārammaṇadubbalatāya cittappavatti dubbalā atītānāgatārammaṇāya, paññattārammaṇāya vā adubbalattā. Tasmā dubbalavatthukattāti dubbalahadayavatthukattāti no takkoti (vajira. ṭī. pārājika 236-237) ācariyo. Avatthukatāya dubbalabhāvo yujjatīti ce? Na, avatthukāya bhāvanāpabhavāya atirekabalavasambhavato. Bhāvanābalasamappitañhi cittaṃ arūpampi samānaṃ atibhārampi karajakāyaṃ gahetvā ekacittakkhaṇeneva brahmalokampi pāpetvā ṭhapeti, tappaṭibhāgaṃ anappitampi kāmāvacaracittaṃ karajakāyaṃ ākāse laṅghanasamatthaṃ karoti. Kiṃ panettha taṃ anumānakaraṇaṃ? Yena cittasseva ānubhāvoti paññāyeyya cittānubhāvena ṭhapanalaṅghanādikiriyāvisesanibbattidassanato. Pakaticittasamuṭṭhānarūpaṃ viya asaṃsaṭṭhattā, nikkhamanattā ca vatthisīsaṃ, kaṭi, kāyoti tidhā sukkassa ṭhānaṃ pakappenti ācariyā. Sappavisaṃ viya taṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, na ca vise ṭhānaniyamo, kodhavasena passantassa hoti. Evamassa na ṭhānaniyamo, rāgavasena upakkamantassa hotīti no takkoti ācariyo.

Except in a dream, this volition, due to the weakness of its basis, is unable to draw forth rebirth-linking. For the sign that appears in a dream is indeed weak. However, in the course of existence, supported by other wholesome or unwholesome factors, it yields its result. Although it yields a result, it is written that since it arises outside its proper domain, volition in a dream is non-binding. However, the statement here that 'the sign appearing in a dream is weak' is not absolute, for the process of consciousness is not weak due to the weakness of the object, since it is not weak when its object is past, future, or a concept. Therefore, the teacher (Vajirabuddhi, Pārājika-ṭīkā 236-237) states that 'due to the weakness of its basis' means 'due to the weakness of the heart-basis,' and says, 'this is not my reasoning.' If it is said that its weakness is justified by its lack of a physical basis, this is not so, because extraordinary strength can arise from meditation, which itself is without a physical basis. For a mind fortified by the power of meditation, though formless, can take hold of even a heavy physical body and in a single moment of consciousness convey it and place it in the Brahma-world. Similarly, even a sense-sphere mind that has not reached absorption can make the physical body leap into the air. What then is the inference here? It should be understood as the influence of the mind itself, evident from observing the mind’s power in actions like placing, leaping, and other extraordinary feats. Because of its being unmixed, like matter originated by normal consciousness, and because of its emission, the teachers posit three locations for semen: the head of the bladder, the waist, and the body. It should be seen as being like snake venom, for which there is no fixed location; it happens for one who sees with anger. Thus for this there is no fixed location; it happens for one who strives with lust. The teacher says, 'This is not my reasoning.'

“Dakasotaṃ anotiṇṇepī”ti idaṃ “otiṇṇamatte”ti iminā virujjhatīti ce, taṃ dassetuṃ “ṭhānato pana cuta”ntiādimāha. Tassattho – nimitte upakkamaṃ katvā sukkaṃ ṭhānā cāvetvā puna vippaṭisāravasena dakasotorohaṇaṃ nivāretuṃ na sakkā, tathāpi adhivāsādhippāyena [V 0.0045] adhivāsetvā antarā dakasotato uddhaṃ nivāretuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya “bahi nikkhante vā”ti vuttaṃ, tasmā ṭhānā cutañhi avassaṃ [M 0.0049] dakasotaṃ otaratīti aṭṭhakathāya adhippāyo. Tasmā ubhayaṃ sametīti gahetabbo.

If it is asked whether the phrase 'even if one has not entered the water-stream' contradicts the phrase 'merely by entering,' to explain this, the text says, 'but if it has been dislodged from its place,' and so forth. Its meaning is this: having made an effort regarding the sign and caused the semen to be dislodged from its place, it is not possible to prevent its descent into the water-stream again through remorse. Nevertheless, having endured with the intention of acceptance, because of the impossibility of preventing it from going out from the water-stream midway, it is said, 'or when it has gone outside.' Therefore, the commentary's intention is that what has been dislodged from its place inevitably descends into the water-stream. Thus, both should be understood as consistent.

Etthāha – kasmā imasmiṃ sikkhāpade “yo pana bhikkhū”tiādinā kārako na niddiṭṭhoti? Vuccate – adhippāyāpekkhāya bhāvato kārako na niddiṭṭho tassa sāpekkhabhāvadassanatthaṃ. Kathaṃ? Kaṇḍuvanādiadhippāyacetanāvasena cetentassa kaṇḍuvanādiupakkamena upakkamantassa methunarāgavasena ūruādīsu dukkaṭavatthūsu, vaṇādīsu thullaccayavatthūsu ca upakkamantassa sukkavisaṭṭhiyā satipi na saṅghādiseso “anāpatti bhikkhu na mocanādhippāyassā”ti (pārā. 263) vacanato. Tasmā tadatthadassanatthaṃ idha kārako na niddiṭṭho. Aññathā “yo pana bhikkhu sañcetanikaṃ sukkavisaṭṭhiṃ āpajjeyya, saṅghādiseso”ti niddiṭṭhe kārake “ceteti na upakkamati muccati, anāpattī”ti (pārā. 262) vuttavacanavirodho. Tathā “sañcetanikāya sukkavisaṭṭhiyā aññatra supinantā saṅghādiseso”ti bhumme niddiṭṭhepi so eva virodho hetvatthaniyamasiddhito. Tasmā tadubhayampi vacanakkamaṃ avatvā “sañcetanikā sukkavisaṭṭhi aññatra supinantā saṅghādiseso”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha nimittatthe bhummavacanābhāvato hetvatthaniyamo na kato hoti. Tasmiṃ akate sañcetanikā sukkavisaṭṭhi aññatra supinantā saṅghādisesoti, upakkame asati anāpattīti ayamattho dīpito hotīti veditabbaṃ.

Here it is asked: Why in this training rule is the agent not specified with 'But if any bhikkhu...' and so forth? It is said: The agent is not specified because the matter is dependent on intention, in order to show its dependent nature. How so? Even if there is an emission of semen for one who intends with the intention of scratching and so forth, who strives with the action of scratching and so forth, or for one who strives with sexual lust regarding the thighs and so forth, which are grounds for a dukkaṭa offense, or regarding wounds and so forth, which are grounds for a thullaccaya offense, there is no saṅghādisesa offense, because of the statement: 'O bhikkhu, there is no offense for one who does not have the intention to emit' (Pārā. 263). Therefore, to show that meaning, the agent is not specified here. Otherwise, if the agent were specified as 'Whatever bhikkhu should intentionally bring about an emission of semen, it is a saṅghādisesa,' it would contradict the statement: 'He intends, he does not strive, it is emitted; there is no offense' (Pārā. 262). Similarly, if it were stated in the locative case as 'In the case of an intentional emission of semen, except in a dream, it is a saṅghādisesa,' the same contradiction would arise from the establishment of a fixed meaning of cause. Therefore, without stating either of these phrasing methods, it is said: 'An intentional emission of semen, except in a dream, is a saṅghādisesa.' There, because there is no locative expression in the sense of a cause, a fixed meaning of cause is not made. When that is not made, it should be understood that this meaning is clarified: 'An intentional emission of semen, except in a dream, is a saṅghādisesa,' and 'if there is no striving, there is no offense.'

Imasmiṃ sikkhāpade dve āpattisahassāni honti. Kathaṃ? Attano hatthādibhede ajjhattarūpe rāgūpatthambhanavasena aṅgajāte kammaniyappatte ārogyatthāya nīlaṃ mocentassa ekā āpatti, ajjhattarūpe eva rāgūpatthambhe pītakādīnaṃ mocanavasena navāti dasa. Evaṃ “sukhatthāyā”tiādīnaṃ navannaṃ vasenāti rāgūpatthambhe ajjhattarūpavasena sataṃ. Evamevaṃ vaccappassāvavātauccāliṅgapāṇakadaṭṭhūpatthambhesu ca sataṃ sataṃ katvā sabbaṃ pañcasataṃ. Yathā ajjhattarūpe pañcasataṃ, evaṃ bahiddhārūpe vā ajjhattabahiddhārūpe vā ākāse vā kaṭiṃ kampentoti dve sahassāni āpattiyo hontīti.

In this training rule, there are two thousand offenses. How? For one who, due to the instigation of lust, causes the emission of dark semen for the sake of health, on his own internal body parts such as the hand, on a limb fit for work, there is one offense. For the instigation of lust in the same internal form, causing the emission of yellow and so forth, there are nine, making ten. Thus, for 'for the sake of pleasure,' and so forth, in nine categories, due to the instigation of lust regarding internal form, there are one hundred. Just so, in the instigations regarding feces, urine, wind, high seats, insects, and bites, there are one hundred each, making a total of five hundred. Just as there are five hundred regarding internal form, so too regarding external form, or both internal and external form, or in space, by shaking the hips—thus there are two thousand offenses.

Sukkavissaṭṭhisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on the emission of semen is concluded.

2. Kāyasaṃsaggasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. The Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Bodily Contact

“Otiṇṇo”ti [M 0.0050][V 0.0046] imināssa sevanādhippāyatā dassitā. Teneva “kāyasaṃsaggarāgasamaṅgissetaṃ adhivacana”nti vuttaṃ. “Vipariṇatena…pe… saddhi”nti imināssa vāyāmo dassito. “Saddhi”nti hi padaṃ saṃyogaṃ dīpeti, so ca saṃyogo samāgamo. Kena cittena? Vipariṇatena cittena, na pattappaṭiggahaṇādhippāyādināti adhippāyo. “Kāyasaṃsaggaṃ samāpajjeyyā”ti imināssa vāyamato phassappaṭivijānanā dassitā hoti. Vāyamitvā phassaṃ paṭivijānanto hi samāpajjati nāma. Evamassa tivaṅgasampatti dassitā hoti. Atha vā otiṇṇo vipariṇatena cittena yakkhādinā satto viya. Upayogatthe vā etaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ, otiṇṇo vipariṇataṃ cittaṃ kūpādiṃ viya satto. Atha vā “rāgato uttiṇṇo bhavissāmī”ti bhikkhubhāvaṃ upagatopi yo pana bhikkhu tato uttiṇṇādhippāyato vipariṇatena cittena hetubhūtena tameva rāgaṃ otiṇṇo. Mātugāmena attano samīpaṃ vā āgatena, attanā upagatena vā. Etena mātugāmassa sārattatā vā hotu, virattatā vā, sā idha appamāṇaṃ.

'Overcome'—by this, his intention to indulge is shown. Therefore, it is said: 'This is a designation for one endowed with lust for bodily contact.' 'With a corrupted mind... with'—by this, his effort is shown. For the word 'with' indicates connection, and that connection is coming together. With what mind? With a corrupted mind—not with the intention of receiving a bowl or the like—this is the meaning. 'Would engage in bodily contact'—by this, his recognition of the contact resulting from the effort is shown. For one who, having striven, recognizes the contact is indeed said to engage. Thus, his fulfillment of the three factors is shown. Alternatively, 'overcome by a corrupted mind' is like a being possessed by a yakkha or the like. Or, in the sense of application, this is an instrumental expression: 'overcome by a corrupted mind' is like a being fallen into a well or the like. Or, though having entered the state of a monk with the thought, 'I shall emerge from lust,' yet a monk who, having deviated from that intention to emerge, is overcome by that very lust, with a corrupted mind as the cause. With a woman who has come near him or whom he has approached. By this, whether the woman is impassioned or dispassionate is immaterial here.

Hatthaggāhaṃ vāti ettha hatthena sabbopi upādinnako kāyo saṅgahito, na bhinnasantāno tappaṭibaddho vatthālaṅkārādi. Veṇiggahaṇena anupādinnako abhinnasantāno kesalomanakhaggadantaggādiko kammapaccayautusamuṭṭhāno gahitoti veditabbaṃ. Tenevāha “antamaso lomena lomaṃ phusantassāpī”ti. Tena aññatarassa vā…pe… parāmasananti ettha anupādinnakānampi sesalomādīnaṃ aṅgabhāvo veditabbo. Evaṃ sante “phassaṃ paṭijānantassa saṅghādiseso”ti iminā virujjhatīti ce? Na, tadatthajānanato. Phuṭṭhabhāvaṃ paṭivijānantopi phassaṃ paṭijānāti nāma, na kāyaviññāṇuppattiyā eva. Anekantikañhettha kāyaviññāṇaṃ. Tasmā eva idha phassappaṭivijānanaṃ aṅgantveva na vuttaṃ. Tasmiñhi vutte ṭhānametaṃ vijjati “na ca me lomaghaṭṭanena kāyaviññāṇaṃ uppannaṃ, tasmiṃ ‘na phassaṃ paṭijānāmī’ti anāpannasaññī siyā”ti. “Veṇī nāma kahāpaṇamālādisampayuttaṃ, tattha ‘veṇiṃ gaṇhissāmī’ti kahāpaṇamālādiṃ eva gaṇhāti, na lomaṃ, natthi saṅghādiseso”ti vadanti. Vīmaṃsitabbaṃ.

In the phrase 'Hatthaggāhaṃ vā,' here, the entire appropriated body is grasped by the hand—not something with a separate continuity, nor objects connected to it such as ornaments. By 'Veṇiggahaṇena' (grasping a braid), it should be understood that what is grasped is the unappropriated, with unbroken continuity, such as hair, body hair, nails, teeth, and so on, produced by kamma and temperature. Therefore, it is said, 'even if one touches hair with hair.' Then, in the phrase 'aññatarassa vā…pe… parāmasananti,' here, the remaining unappropriated things, such as hair, should also be understood as part of the body. If this is so, does this not contradict the statement, 'for one who admits to contact, there is a Saṅghādisesa offense'? No, because of knowing its meaning. Even one who recognizes the state of being touched is said to admit to contact—not merely by the arising of body-consciousness. For here, body-consciousness is not definite. Therefore, in this case, the recognition of contact is not stated as a factor. If it were so stated, this situation could arise: 'Since body-consciousness did not arise for me from the brushing of hair,' thinking, 'I do not admit to contact,' he might perceive it as no offense. Some say, 'A "veṇī" is something connected with a string of coins, a garland, etc. There, if one thinks, "I will grasp the veṇī," but grasps only the string of coins or garland, not the hair, there is no Saṅghādisesa offense.' This should be examined.

Kāyasaṃsaggasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning physical contact is concluded.

3. Duṭṭhullavācāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Training Rule on Offensive Speech

“Kadā [M 0.0051][V 0.0047] te mātā pasīdissatī”ti āyācanaṃ duṭṭhullavācāya sikhāpattalakkhaṇadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, na methunupasaṃhiteyeva duṭṭhullavācāti dassanatthaṃ. “Ubhatobyañjanakāsī”ti vacanaṃ pana purisanimittena asaṅghādisesavatthunā missavacanaṃ, purisaubhatobyañjanakassa ca itthinimittaṃ paṭicchannaṃ, itaraṃ pākaṭaṃ. Yadi tampi janeti, kathaṃ ‘animittāsī’tiādīni padāni na saṅghādisesaṃ janentī”ti eke, taṃ na yuttaṃ purisassāpi nimittādhivacanattā. “Methunupasaṃhitāhi saṅghādiseso”ti (pārā. 248) mātikāyaṃ lakkhaṇassa vuttattā ca methunupasaṃhitāhi obhāsane paṭivijānantiyā saṅghādiseso, appaṭivijānantiyā thullaccayaṃ, itarehi obhāsane paṭivijānantiyā thullaccayaṃ, appaṭivijānantiyā dukkaṭanti eke, vicāretvā gahetabbaṃ. Etthāha – “sikharaṇī”tiādīhi akkosantassa paṭighacittaṃ uppajjati, kasmā “tivedana”nti avatvā “dvivedana”nti vuttanti? Rāgavasena ayaṃ āpatti, na paṭighavasena. Tasmā rāgavaseneva pavatto akkoso idha adhippeto. Tasmā “dvivedana”nti vacanaṃ suvuttameva.

The request, 'When will your mother be pleased?' was stated to show the characteristic of a full offense of offensive speech, and to show that offensive speech is not only that which is connected with sexual intercourse. The statement 'you are a hermaphrodite' is mixed speech, with the male sign being a non-Saṅghādisesa object. For a male hermaphrodite, the female sign is concealed, while the other is manifest. Some say: 'If that also produces an offense, how is it that phrases such as "you are without a sign" do not produce a Saṅghādisesa offense?' That is not correct, because 'sign' is also a designation for a man. Because the characteristic is stated in the matrix as 'Connected with sexual intercourse, it is a Saṅghādisesa offense' (Pārā. 248), for alluding speech connected with sexual intercourse, if she understands, it is a Saṅghādisesa; if she does not understand, it is a Thullaccaya. For other alluding speech, if she understands, it is a Thullaccaya; if she does not understand, it is a Dukkaṭa—this is the view of some; it should be investigated and then accepted. Here it is said: When one abuses with terms like 'sikharaṇī,' a mind of aversion arises, so why is it said to be 'of two feelings' and not 'of three feelings'? This offense is by way of lust, not by way of aversion. Therefore, the abuse intended here is that which proceeds by way of lust. Hence, the statement 'of two feelings' is well-stated.

Duṭṭhullavācāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning offensive speech is concluded.

4. Attakāmasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Self-Gratification

Duṭṭhullobhāsane vuttappakārāyāti duṭṭhullāduṭṭhullajānanasamatthāya. Parassa bhikkhuno attakāmapāricariyāya vaṇṇabhaṇane dukkaṭaṃ, “yo te vihāre vasati, tassa aggadānaṃ methunaṃ dhammaṃ dehī”ti pariyāyavacanepi dukkaṭaṃ, “attakāmapāricariyāya vaṇṇaṃ bhāseyya, yā mādisaṃ sīlavanta”nti ca vuttattāti eke. Pañcasu aṅgesu sabbhāvā saṅghādisesovāti eke, vicāretvā gahetabbaṃ. “Imasmiṃ sikkhāpadadvaye kāyasaṃsagge viya yakkhipetīsupi duṭṭhullattakaāmavacane thullaccayanti vadanti. Aṭṭhakathāsu pana nāgata”nti (vajira. ṭī. pārājika 295) likhitaṃ. Ubhatobyañjanako pana paṇḍakagatikova.

'To one of the kind mentioned in the rule on obscene speech' means to one who is capable of knowing what is obscene and not obscene. In praising service for the gratification of another monk, there is a dukkaṭa. Even in indirect speech, such as saying, 'Give the supreme gift, sexual intercourse, to the one who dwells in your monastery,' there is a dukkaṭa. Some say this is because it is stated, 'He would praise service for his own gratification, to one such as a virtuous one like me.' Some say that when the five factors are present, it is a saṅghādisesa; this should be investigated and then accepted. It is written: 'Regarding these two training rules, some say that just as in the case of physical contact with yakkhīs and petīs, so too in speaking obscene and lustful words, there is a thullaccaya. However, this has not come down in the commentaries.' As for the hermaphrodite, he is in the category of a paṇḍaka.

Attakāmasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning self-gratification is concluded.

5. Sañcarittasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

5. Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Acting as a Go-Between

Alaṃvacanīyāti [M 0.0052][V 0.0048] na vacanīyā, nivāraṇe alaṃ-saddo, na alaṃvacanīyā nālaṃvacanīyā. “Paṭiggaṇhāti vīmaṃsati paccāharati, āpatti saṅghādisesassā”ti (pārā. 305) vuttattā yassa ekantena saṅghādiseso hoti, tassa paṭiggaṇhanavīmaṃsanapayogā ete dukkaṭathullaccayā natthīti vadantīti likhitaṃ. Kiñcāpi ettha “itthī nāma manussitthī, na yakkhī na petī na tiracchānagatā. Puriso nāma manussapuriso, na yakkho na peto na tiracchānagato”ti pāḷi natthi, tathāpi kāyasaṃsaggādīsu “mātugāmo nāma manussitthī”ti (pārā. 285) itthivavatthānassa katattā idhāpi manussitthī evāti paññāyati. Methunapubbabhāgasāmaññato itthivavatthānena purisavavatthānaṃ katameva hoti. Tenevāha “yesu sañcarittaṃ samāpajjati, tesaṃ manussajātikatā”ti (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. sañcarittasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā). Kāyasaṃsaggādīsu ca paṇḍakayakkhipetiyo thullaccayavatthukāva vuttā, tathā idhāpi, paṇḍakasabhāvattā manussaubhatobyañjanako ca thullaccayavatthukova hoti. Sesā manussapurisaamanussapaṇḍakaubhatobyañjanakatiracchānagatapurisādayo dukkaṭavatthukāva micchācāradassanasabhāvatoti veditabbaṃ.

The term 'alaṃvacanīyā' means 'not to be spoken to'; the word 'alaṃ' here signifies prevention, thus 'na alaṃvacanīyā' becomes 'nālaṃvacanīyā'. It is written that some say that since it is stated (Pārā. 305), 'If one accepts, investigates, or reports back, it is a Saṅghādisesa offense,' for one for whom it is definitively a Saṅghādisesa, these preliminary acts of accepting and investigating do not entail dukkaṭa or thullaccaya offenses. Although in this context, the Pāli does not explicitly state, 'A woman means a human female, not a female yakkhī, petī, or animal. A man means a human male, not a male yakkha, peta, or animal,' nevertheless, in cases of physical contact and so on, because the definition of a woman has been made as 'a female means a human woman' (Pārā. 285), here too it is understood that a woman refers to a human female. By the commonality with the preliminary acts of sexual intercourse, the definition of a man is indeed established by the definition of a woman. Hence, it is said, 'Those among whom acting as a go-between occurs must be of human birth' (Kaṅkhā. Aṭṭha. Sañcarittasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā). In cases of physical contact and so on, paṇḍakas, yakkhīs, and petīs are stated as grounds for thullaccaya offenses. Similarly here, due to having the nature of a paṇḍaka, a human hermaphrodite is also grounds for a thullaccaya offense. The rest—human males, non-human paṇḍakas, hermaphrodites, and male animals, etc.—are grounds for dukkaṭa offenses, as they are by nature seen as wrong conduct. This should be understood.

Sañcarittasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning acting as a go-between is concluded.

6. Kuṭikārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. Explanation of the Training Rule on Making a Hut

Kiṃ bhanteti ettakepi vutte. Pucchito yadatthāya paviṭṭho, taṃ kathetuṃ labhati pucchitapaññattā bhikkhācāravatteti likhitaṃ. Hatthakammaṃ yācito “upakaraṇaṃ, mūlaṃ vā dassatī”ti yācati, vaṭṭati, na vaṭṭatīti? Vaṭṭati senāsane obhāsaparikathādīnaṃ laddhattāti eke. Tihatthā vāti ettha vaḍḍhakihatthena tihatthā. “Pamāṇayutto mañcoti pakatividatthiyā navavidatthippamāṇamañco, so tattha ito ca na sañcarati, tasmā catuhatthavitthārā na hotī”tiādi likhitaṃ. Akuṭiyā pana vatthudesanākiccaṃ natthi ullittāvalittaṃ kātuṃ vuttattā. “Ullittādibhāvo…pe… ‘chadanameva sandhāya vutto’ti yuttamidaṃ. Kasmāti ce? Yasmā mattikāmayabhittiṃ [M 0.0053] uṭṭhāpetvā upari ullittaṃ vā avalittaṃ vā ubhayaṃ vā bhittiyā ghaṭitaṃ karontassa āpatti eva vināpi bhittilepenā”ti likhitaṃ. Evamettha thambhatulāpiṭṭhasaṅghāṭādi niratthakaṃ siyā. Tasmā vicāretvāva gahetabbaṃ. “Uposathāgārampi bhavissati, ahampi vasissāmī”ti vā “bhikkhūhi vā sāmaṇerehi vā ekato vasissāmī”ti vā karontassa vaṭṭati eva. Kasmā? “Attuddesa”nti vuttattāti likhitaṃ.

Even when only this much is said: 'What, venerable sir?' It is written that when asked, having entered for some purpose, he is allowed to speak about it, because of the allowance for one who is asked, in accordance with the conduct for alms-going. When asked for manual labor, if one asks, 'Will you give a tool or the payment?', is it allowable or not? Some say it is allowable, because an opportunity for discussion about the lodging has been obtained. The phrase 'three hands' here means three hands by the carpenter's measure. It is written: 'A bed of proper size is a bed of nine spans according to the natural span; it does not move from there, therefore it is not four hands wide,' and so on. However, for a hut that is not one's own, there is no duty of indicating the site, since it is said that it is to be plastered and coated. 'The state of being plastered, etc. … is said with reference to the roofing only'—this is appropriate. Why? Because it is written that for one who raises a clay wall and then makes it plastered or coated or both, joined to the wall, there is an offense even without plastering the wall. In that case, pillars, beams, lintels, and so on would be meaningless. Therefore, this should be investigated before being accepted. If one builds thinking, 'It will be an Uposatha hall, and I too will live in it,' or 'I will live together with the monks or novices,' it is allowable. Why? Because it is written that it is said to be 'for one's own purpose'.
