Just as the Saṅgha for whom the Kathina has been spread enjoys the benefits regarding the triple robe from the day it is spread until its withdrawal, but not after, so too one obtains the allowance from the day it is spread until its withdrawal, but once the Kathina is withdrawn, one does not obtain it even for a single day. Here it is asked: Does one obtain another ten days starting from the day of withdrawal? No. Why? Because it is said, 'I allow, O monks, an extra robe to be kept for a maximum of ten days.' It would follow that even within the Kathina period, it becomes subject to forfeiture at the rising of the dawn on the eleventh day. But to prevent that over-extension, the words 'when the robe-work is finished,' etc., were stated, not for the purpose of showing that the Kathina days are not counted as days. This meaning will become clear in various places. Alternatively, the rains-residence robe, of a size that is not extra, should be determined for the four months of the rains in the manner stated, and after that, it should be rescinded and assigned to another. Here, by the word 'having rescinded,' it is meant that it has been rescinded on the Uposatha day, assigned to another, and set aside; after that, from the first day of the cold season onward, there is no rescinding. In this way, a robe that has arisen during the Kathina period should also be understood—so it is written.

Kathinasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Kathina training rule is concluded.

2. Udositasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. The Explanation of the Udosita Training Rule

“Atthatakathinassa [V 0.0066] pañca māse baddhasīmāyaṃ yattha katthaci cīvaraṃ nikkhipitvā pakkamantassa anāpattī”ti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. “Abaddhasīmāyapi vaṭṭatī”ti idaṃ abaddhasīmāyaṃ kathinatthārañca āraññakasikkhāpadañca sādhetīti likhitaṃ. Idāni –

“For one who has spread the Kathina, for five months within a bounded area, if, having deposited his robe anywhere, he departs, there is no offense,” as stated in the commentary. “It is also permissible in an unbounded area”—this is written to establish the spreading of the Kathina in an unbounded area and the wilderness-dweller's training rule. Now –

“Chinnaṃ dhutaṅgaṃ sāsaṅka-sammato santaruttaraṃ;

Acīvarassānāpatti, paccuddhārādisiddhito”ti. (vajira. ṭī. pārājika 479) –

“A broken ascetic practice is considered doubtful concerning the inner and outer robe; there is no offense for one without a robe, as established by the revocation and other such reasons.” (Vajira. Ṭī. Pārājika 479) –

Idaṃ pakiṇṇakaṃ veditabbaṃ.

This should be understood as miscellaneous.

Tatrāyaṃ [M 0.0072] codanāpubbaṅgamavinicchayo – keci “diguṇaṃ saṅghāṭi”nti (mahāva. 348) vacanato “ekaccikā saṅghāṭi nādhiṭṭhātabbā. Sace adhiṭṭhāti, na ruhatī”ti vatvā upasampadāpekkhānampi diguṇaṃyeva saṅghāṭiṃ datvā upasampādenti, te iminā suttalesena saññāpetabbā. Bhagavatā hi “chinnakaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ, chinnakaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ, chinnakaṃ antaravāsaka”nti paṭhamaṃ anuññātaṃ. Tato “aññatarassa bhikkhuno ticīvare kariyamāne sabbaṃ chinnakaṃ nappahoti. Dve chinnakāni ekaṃ achinnakaṃ nappahoti, dve achinnakāni ekaṃ chinnakaṃ nappahotī”ti imasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, anvādhikampi āropetu”nti (mahāva. 360) anuññātaṃ, tasmā ekaccikāpi saṅghāṭi vaṭṭatīti siddhaṃ. Yā chijjamānāpi nappahoti, tassā kuto diguṇatāti? Aṭṭhakathāyampissa vuttaṃ “anvādhikampi āropetunti āgantukapattampi dātuṃ, idaṃ pana appahonake āropetabbaṃ. Sace pahoti, āgantukapattaṃ na vaṭṭati, chinditabbamevā”ti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 360). Kathinaṃ pana chinnakameva vaṭṭati, āveṇikalakkhaṇattā, “chinnakaṃ diguṇaṃ nappahotī”ti vacanābhāvato cāti sanniṭṭhānamettha gantabbanti.

Herein is the analysis preceded by the objection: Some, citing the phrase “a double-layered outer robe” (Mahāva. 348), say, “A single-layered outer robe should not be determined. If one determines it, it is not valid.” Thus, they give only a double-layered outer robe even to those seeking ordination and ordain them. These should be instructed by this scriptural passage. For the Blessed One first allowed, “a patched outer robe, a patched upper robe, a patched lower robe.” Then, in the case where a certain monk’s three robes were being made, but all patched ones were insufficient, or two patched ones and one unpatched one were insufficient, or two unpatched ones and one patched one were insufficient, it was allowed: “I allow, monks, to add even an extra piece.” (Mahāva. 360). Therefore, it is established that even a single-layered outer robe is permissible. If even when being cut up, it is insufficient, how could it be double-layered? In the commentary it is also said: “‘To add even an extra piece’ means to give even an extra piece of cloth, but this should be added only if it is insufficient. If it is sufficient, an extra piece of cloth is not permissible; it must be cut.” (Mahāva. Aṭṭha. 360). However, for the Kathina, only a patched robe is permissible, due to its special characteristic, and because there is no statement that “a patched double-layered robe is insufficient.” Thus, the conclusion here should be reached.

Dhutaṅganti anupasampannānaṃ tecīvarikadhutaṅgābhāvato ticīvareneva tecīvarikoti, tesaṃ adhiṭṭhānābhāvato “adhiṭṭhitenevā”ti vattabbaṃ hotūti ce? Na, dhutaṅgabhedena virodhappasaṅgato. Catutthacīvarasādiyanena hi dhutaṅgabhedo, na ticīvaravippavāsena, nāpi atirekacīvarasādiyanena, nāpi atirekacīvaradhāraṇena. Yasmā pana bhikkhūnaṃ eva bhagavatā adhiṭṭhānavasena nava cīvarāni [V 0.0067] anuññātāni, jātivasena ca vuttāni, na evaṃ anupasampannānaṃ, tasmā nesaṃ cīvaraniyamābhāvā na taṃ dhutaṅgaṃ anuññātaṃ gahaṭṭhānaṃ viya. Tasmā tassa samādānavidhāne avacanato ca sanniṭṭhānamettha gantabbanti.

Regarding the ascetic practice: since the unordained do not have the ascetic practice of wearing only three robes, if it is asked whether one becomes a ‘three-robed one’ merely by possessing three robes, and whether, since they cannot make a formal determination, the rule should be ‘only by what is determined,’ the answer is: No, because this would lead to a contradiction regarding the breaking of the ascetic practice. For the breaking of the ascetic practice occurs by accepting a fourth robe, not by being separated from the three robes, nor by accepting an extra robe, nor by wearing an extra robe. Since the Blessed One has allowed nine kinds of robes for monks by way of determination, and they are spoken of according to their type, but this is not so for the unordained, therefore, as they have no regulation regarding robes, that ascetic practice is not permitted for them, just as it is not for householders. Therefore, since there is no statement regarding the procedure for undertaking it, a conclusion should be reached here accordingly.

Sāsaṅkasammatoti kaṅkhāvitaraṇiyaṃ (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. sāsaṅkasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) sāsaṅkasikkhāpade visuṃ aṅgāni na vuttāni, “sesamettha cīvaravaggassa dutiyasikkhāpade vuttanayeneva veditabba”nti vuttaṃ, na ca panetaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha rattivippavāso catutthamaṅgaṃ, idha chārattavippavāso, ayamettha visesoti. Tasmā aṅgasāmaññato ca sammutisāmaññato ca sāsaṅkasikkhāpadamevidanti idaṃ [M 0.0073] nippadesaṃ, taṃ sappadesaṃ māsaparamattā. Tattha bahigāmepi gāmasīmaṃ okkamitvā vasitvā pakkamantassa anāpatti, idha na tathā. Idha anantare anantare aruṇuggamane nissaggiyaṃ, tattha sattameti ayaṃ imesaṃ dvinnaṃ viseso. Aṅgāni pana cīvaranikkhepanaṅgasampattito vipariyāyena, idha vuttanayena ca siddhattā na vuttāni. Tāni kāmaṃ na vuttāni, tathāpi catutthamaṅgaṃ visesitabbaṃ, na pana visesitaṃ. Kiṃ kāraṇaṃ? Idha vuttanissajjanakkamena nissajjitvā āpattidesanato, tatthāpannāpattivimokkhadīpanatthaṃ. Saṃvaccharavippavutthampi rattivippavutthameva, pageva chārattavippavutthaṃ. Evaṃ santepi tattha yathāvuttaaṅgasampattiyā sati tattha vuttanayeneva nissajjitabbaṃ. Hemante, gimhe vā nissajjati ce? Idha vuttanayenāpi nissajjituṃ vaṭṭatīti ñāpanatthaṃ catutthamaṅgaṃ na visesitanti no takkoti ācariyo. Māsātikkantaṃ, dasāhātikkantampi cīvaraṃ “dasāhātikkanta”nti vatvā nissaṭṭhameva, na ūnamāsaṃ hutvā “dasāhātikkanta”nti vatvā, māsātikkanta”nti vatvāti eke. Tathāpi sace paccāsācīvaraṃ hoti, nissaggiyaṃ. “Dasāhātikkanta”nti vatvā mūlacīvaraṃ pana “māsātikkanta”nti vatvā nissajjitabbaṃ.

Regarding ‘considered doubtful’: in the Sāsaṅka training rule in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī (Kaṅkhā. Aṭṭha. Sāsaṅkasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā), the individual factors are not stated separately; it is said, “the rest here should be understood in the same way as stated in the second training rule of the Robe Chapter,” but this is not actually stated. There, being separated for a night is the fourth factor; here, it is being separated for six nights—this is the difference. Therefore, due to the commonality of factors and the commonality of agreement, this rule is the Sāsaṅka training rule itself. This one is general, while that one is specific, with a limit of one month. There, even if one goes outside the village, enters the village boundary, stays, and then departs, there is no offense; here it is not so. Here, it becomes an offense requiring forfeiture at each successive sunrise; there, it becomes so on the seventh—this is the difference between these two. The factors, however, are not stated because they are established by the opposite of the fulfillment of the factor of depositing the robe, and by the method stated here. Although they are not stated, the fourth factor should still be specified, yet it is not. Why? For the purpose of confessing the offense by forfeiting according to the procedure of forfeiture stated here, and for clarifying the release from an incurred offense there. Even being separated for a year is just being separated for a night, how much more so being separated for six nights. Even so, if the factors stated there are fulfilled, it should be forfeited in the way stated there. If one forfeits in winter or summer? The teacher thinks that the fourth factor is not specified in order to make it known that it is permissible to forfeit also in the way stated here. Some say that a robe kept beyond a month or beyond ten days is to be forfeited simply by saying ‘kept beyond ten days,’ not, when it is less than a month, by saying ‘kept beyond ten days’ and ‘kept beyond a month.’ Nevertheless, if it is a robe that is expected, it requires forfeiture. The original robe, however, should be forfeited by saying ‘kept beyond a month,’ whereas the other is forfeited by saying ‘kept beyond ten days.’

“Santaruttara”nti vā “saṅghāṭi”nti vā “cīvara”nti vā kiṃ ticīvaraṃ, udāhu aññampīti? Kiñcettha – yadi ticīvarameva paṭisiddhaṃ, pariyāpannavasena acchinnacīvaraaachandanadhovāpanaviññattiādivirodho. Atha aññampi “niṭṭhitacīvarasmi”nti evamādinā virodhoti? Vuccate – na niyamato veditabbaṃ yathāsambhavaṃ gahetabbato. Tathā hi “cīvaraṃ nikkhipitvā santaruttarena janapadacārikaṃ pakkamantī”ti (pārā. 471) evamādīsu ticīvarameva, “na, bhikkhave, santaruttarena gāmo pavisitabbo (mahāva. 362), santaruttaraparamaṃ tato cīvaraṃ sāditabba”nti (pārā. 523-524) evamādīsu yaṃ kiñci, tathā “saguṇaṃ katvā saṅghāṭiyo dātabbā, nivāsanaṃ dātabbaṃ, saṅghāṭi dātabbā, handa te, āvuso[V 0.0068], saṅghāṭi, dehi me paṭa”nti evamādīsu. Vuttañhetaṃ “sabbañhi cīvaraṃ saṅghaṭitaṭṭhena ‘saṅghāṭī’ti vuccatī”ti (pāci. aṭṭha. 898). Tathā “niṭṭhitacīvarasmi”nti etthāpīti eke. Antosamaye yāvadatthaṃ cīvaraṃ anuññātaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ kariyamānaṃ kadā niṭṭhānaṃ gacchissati, tasmā ticīvaramevāti eke.

Do the terms ‘inner and outer robe,’ ‘outer robe,’ or ‘robe’ refer to the three robes, or to something else as well? And what is the issue here? If only the three robes are prohibited, then by way of inclusion, there would be a contradiction with the rules concerning uncut robes, undyed cloth, requesting the washing of robes, and so forth. If it refers to something else as well, would there be a contradiction with statements such as ‘when the robe is completed’? It is said: this should not be understood according to a fixed rule, but should be taken as is appropriate to the context. For instance, in passages such as, “having laid aside the outer robe, one may depart on a journey through the country with the inner and upper robe” (Pārā. 471), it refers only to the three robes. However, in statements like, “Monks, a village should not be entered with only the inner and upper robe” (Mahāva. 362), and, “a maximum of an inner and upper robe; beyond that, a robe may be accepted” (Pārā. 523–524), it refers to any robe. Similarly, it is used broadly in phrases such as, “having folded them well, outer robes should be given,” “a lower garment should be given,” “an outer robe should be given,” and, “Here, friend, is an outer robe for you; give me the cloth.” For it has been said: “All robe-cloth is called ‘saṅghāṭī’ in the sense of being joined together” (Pāci. Aṭṭha. 898). Likewise, some say that it is also used in this way in the phrase ‘when the robe is completed.’ During the robe season, as much robe-cloth as is needed is permitted; if all of that is being made, when will it ever be completed? Therefore, some hold that it refers only to the three robes.

Acīvarassānāpatti [M 0.0074] paccuddhārādisiddhitoti kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti – udositasikkhāpadassa nippayojanabhāvappasaṅgato ticīvaravippavāse tecīvarassa āpattīti eke. Tatthetaṃ vuccati na hoti āpatti paccuddhārādisiddhito. “Anāpatti antoaruṇe paccuddharati vissajjetī”ti (pārā. 496) hi vuttaṃ. Aññathā paccuddharantassa, antoaruṇe vissajjentassa ca yāva añño nādhiṭṭhāti, tāva āpattiṃ āpajjati yathāvuttanayeneva. Aññathā sattabbhantarena vippavāsassāti vippavāsato yathārutaṃyeva sati vippavāse vippavāsato, avippavāse sati avippavāsatoti.

What is meant by ‘there is no offense for one without a robe, as proven by restoration and so forth’? Some say that, due to the consequence of the Udosita training rule becoming purposeless, an offense is incurred by one with three robes in the case of separation from the three robes. Herein, it is said: there is no offense, as proven by restoration and so forth. For it is said, “There is no offense when one restores it or relinquishes it before dawn” (Pārā. 496). Otherwise, for one restoring or relinquishing it before dawn, one incurs an offense according to the method already stated until another determines it. Otherwise, concerning separation within seven days, it is just as it is heard: when there is separation, it is due to separation; when there is no separation, it is due to no separation.

Udositasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Udosita training rule is concluded.

3. Akālacīvarasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Out-of-Season Robes.

Aparikkhittassa parikkhepārahaṭṭhānassa dubbijānattā taṃ dassetuṃ “apica bhikkhūna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Vihārapariyante niviṭṭhadhuvasannipātaṭṭhānato vā pariyante ṭhitabhojanasālato vā nibaddhavasanakaāvāsato vāti evaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Sace vihāre sannipatitabhikkhūhi saddhiṃ ekābaddhā hutvā yojanasatampi pūretvā nisīdanti, yojanasatampi upacārasīmā hotīti attho. “Samānasaṃvāsakasīmāyā”ti vutte khaṇḍasīmādīsu ṭhitānaṃ na pāpuṇāti, tāsaṃ visuṃ samānasaṃvāsakasīmattāti ca samānasaṃvāsakaavippavāsasīmānaṃ idaṃ nānattaṃ. “Avippavāsasīmāya dammī”ti dinnaṃ pana gāme ṭhitānaṃ na pāpuṇāti. Kasmā? “Ṭhapetvā gāmañca gāmūpacārañcā”ti (mahāva. 144) vacanato. “Samānasaṃvāsakasīmāyā”ti dinnaṃ pana yasmiṃ ṭhāne avippavāsasīmā atthi, tattha ṭhitānampi. “Tatra ṭhitānañca pāpuṇātī”ti ca, “khaṇḍasīmāyaṃ ṭhatvā ‘sīmaṭṭhakasaṅgho gaṇhātū’ti vutte upacārasīmāya eva paricchinditvā dātabba”nti ca, “tesaṃ bahisīmaṭṭhānampi pāpuṇāti yāva kathinassubbhārāti attho”ti ca, “anatthate pana kathine antohemante sace vihāraṃ pavisitvā ‘vassaṃvuṭṭhasaṅghassa dammī’ti vadati, ye tattha vassacchedaṃ akatvā pacchimavassaṃvuṭṭhā, tesaṃ bahisīmaṭṭhānampi pāpuṇātī”ti vinayadharā [V 0.0069] paricchindanti, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana anāgataṃ. Tasmā samantapāsādikāyaṃ “lakkhaṇaññū vadantī”ti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 379) vuttanti ca, “‘cīvaramāsato paṭṭhāya yāva [M 0.0075] hemantassa pacchimo divaso, tāva vassāvāsikaṃ demā’ti vutte kathinaṃ atthataṃ vā hotu, anatthataṃ vāti yaṃ samantapāsādikāvacanaṃ (mahāva. aṭṭha. 379), etthāpi yadi atthataṃ, purimavassaṃvuṭṭhā pañca māse. Yadi anatthataṃ, pacchimavassaṃvuṭṭhā cattāro māse labhantīti vinicchayo”ti ca likhitaṃ.

Because of the difficulty in determining the boundary for a place suitable for delimitation that has not been delimited, to clarify this, it is stated: “Moreover, for the bhikkhus…” and so on. It should be understood as follows: from the established permanent assembly site at the monastery’s boundary, or from the dining hall standing at the boundary, or from a residence with fixed dwelling places. If the bhikkhus, having gathered in the monastery, sit together, being bound as one, filling even a hundred yojanas, then the proximity boundary is a hundred yojanas—this is the meaning. When it is said, “Within the boundary of common residence,” it does not reach those standing in fragmented boundaries and so forth, because these have their own separate boundaries of common residence; thus, this is the distinction between the boundaries of common residence and non-separation. If one says, “I give within the boundary of non-separation,” what is given does not reach those standing in the village. Why? Because of the statement: “Excluding the village and its vicinity” (Mahāva. 144). However, if one says, “I give within the boundary of common residence,” it reaches even those standing in a place where there is a boundary of non-separation. Further, it is said: “It reaches those standing there as well,” and “If, while standing in a fragmented boundary, one says, ‘Let the Saṅgha of the boundary area accept,’ it should be given after having defined it by the proximity boundary.” Moreover, “It reaches even those standing outside the boundary until the Kathina is uplifted”—this is the meaning. But if the Kathina is not spread, then during the winter, if one enters the monastery and says, “I give to the Saṅgha that has completed the rains-residence,” it reaches even those standing outside the boundary who have not broken the rains-residence but have completed the later rains-residence—thus the Vinaya experts determine. However, this has not come up in the commentary. Therefore, in the Samantapāsādikā, it is said: “Those who know the characteristics say so” (Mahāva. Aṭṭha. 379). And it is written: “If one says, ‘From the robe month onward until the last day of winter, we give to the rains-resident,’ whether the Kathina is spread or not—this is the statement of the Samantapāsādikā (Mahāva. Aṭṭha. 379). Here too, if it is spread, those who completed the earlier rains-residence receive it for five months. If not spread, those who completed the later rains-residence receive it for four months—this is the determination.”

“Yehi mayhaṃ yāgu pītāti yehi nimantitehi mayhaṃ yāgu pītāti adhippāyo. Tasmā yehi nimantitehi yāgu pītā, tesaṃyeva pāpuṇātīti vuttaṃ. Aññathā ‘yehi mayhaṃ yāgu pītā’ti vutte nimantitā vā hontu, animantitā vā, yehi pītā, tesaṃ pāpuṇitabbānī”ti vadanti. Ettha “niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ bhikkhunā ubbhatasmiṃ kathine”ti vadanto ñāpeti etthantare tiṇṇampi akālacīvarānaṃ uppattiabhāvanti. Kasmā pana padabhājane vitthāritānīti? Vuccate – idaṃ pana sikkhāpadaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ sandhāya na vuttaṃ kintu paṭhamasikkhāpade dasāhaparamaṃ anujānitvā tasmiṃ appahonte sace paccāsā atthi, tameva vaḍḍhetvā māsamanujānanto imampi atthavisesaṃ dīpeti. Akālacīvaraṃ nāma sammukhībhūtena bhājetabbaṃ. Taṃ pana “ākaṅkhamānena bhikkhunā paṭiggahetabba”nti iminā sikkhāpadena vaḍḍhetvā vuttanti. Tasmā tīṇipi padabhājane vitthāritānīti.

“Those by whom my gruel was drunk”—the intention is, ‘those invited ones by whom my gruel was drunk.’ Therefore, it is said that it accrues only to those invited ones by whom the gruel was drunk. Otherwise, they say, if it were said, ‘those by whom my gruel was drunk,’ whether they were invited or not, it should accrue to those by whom it was drunk. Here, by stating, “When the Kathina is uplifted by a bhikkhu whose robe-making is finished,” he indicates that during this interval there is no arising of any of the three kinds of out-of-season robes. But why are these elaborated in the word-analysis? It is said: this training rule was not spoken with reference to determination, but rather, by allowing a maximum of ten days in the first training rule, and if that is not sufficient and there is still expectation, extending that very period and allowing a month, this also reveals a special meaning. An out-of-season robe, indeed, must be distributed in the presence of the Saṅgha. But this is extended and stated by this training rule: “It should be received by a bhikkhu who desires it.” Therefore, all three are elaborated in the word-analysis.

“Khippameva kāretabbanti sīghaṃ antodasāheyeva kāretabba”nti idaṃ pana pahonakabhāve purimasikkhāpadalakkhaṇenāti dīpetuṃ vuttaṃ. Tasmā evaṃ “sīgha”nti vā “lahu”nti vā ādinā avatvāpi “dasāhā”ti vuttanti. Atthatakathinassa evaṃ hotu, anatthate pana kathine kathanti vutte anatthatassa paṭikkhepataṃ dassetīti vutto apassanto vighātaṃ āpajjatīti (vajira. ṭī. pārājika 499-500) likhitaṃ.

“It should be made quickly, meaning it should be made within ten days.” This is stated to clarify that, in the case of being able, this is in accordance with the characteristic of the previous training rule. Therefore, even without stating “quickly” or “swiftly,” and so on, “within ten days” is said. Let it be so for one for whom the Kathina has been spread; but when it is asked, “What of one for whom the Kathina has not been spread?” it is said to show the rejection of that which is not spread. Not seeing this, one falls into distress—so it is written (Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā, Pārājika 499-500).

Akālacīvarasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Out-of-Season Robes is concluded.

4. Purāṇacīvarasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Old Robes.

“Sākiyāniyo viya suddhabhikkhusaṅghe vā”ti idaṃ “bhikkhunī nāma ubhatosaṅghe upasampannā”ti [V 0.0070] (pārā. 505) iminā virujjhatīti ce? Na, adhippāyājānanato[M 0.0076]. Bhikkhūnaṃ santike upasampadāya paṭikkhittattā tadanuppasaṅgabhayā evaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

“Like Sakyan women in the pure Bhikkhu Saṅgha”—if it is asked whether this is contradicted by the statement “a bhikkhunī is one who has received the full ordination in both Saṅghas” (Pārā. 505), the answer is: No, because of not understanding the intention. It should be understood that it was said thus because ordination in the presence of bhikkhus was rejected, due to fear of that consequence.

Ekena vatthunāti yena kenaci paṭhamena. Avuttā vā dhovatīti avuttā dhovati, rajati ākoṭetīti attho. “‘Avuttā’ti vacanato avādāpetvā dhovanādīsu anāpattī”ti likhitaṃ. Idha cīvaraṃ nāma nivāsanapārupanūpagameva. Yadi evaṃ “nivāsanapārupanūpagameva vattabba”nti ce? Taṃ na vattabbaṃ “purāṇacīvara”nti imināva siddhattā. Vuttañhetaṃ “purāṇacīvaraṃ nāma sakiṃ nivatthampi sakiṃ pārutampī”ti (pārā. 505).

“By one instance” means by any first one. “Or uninstructed, she washes” means uninstructed, she washes, dyes, or beats it—this is the meaning. It is written: “Because of the word ‘uninstructed,’ there is no offense in washing and so forth without having been instructed.” Here, the term ‘robe’ refers only to what is used as the lower robe and the upper robe. If it is asked, “Should it only refer to what is used as the lower robe and the upper robe?” That should not be said, because it is already established by the term ‘old robe.’ For it has been said: “An old robe is one that has been worn once as a lower robe or once as an upper robe” (Pārā. 505).

Purāṇacīvarasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Old Robes is concluded.

5. Cīvarappaṭiggahaṇasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Acceptance of Robes.

Upacāro dvādasahattho. Acittakattā kathaṃ paṃsukūlaṃ vaṭṭatīti ce? Tāya tassa bhikkhuno adinnattā, bhikkhunā ca tato bhikkhunito aggahitattā ca.

The proximity is twelve cubits. If it is asked, “How is a rag-robe allowable without intention?” it is because it was not given to that bhikkhu by her, and because the bhikkhu did not take it from that bhikkhunī.

Cīvarappaṭiggahaṇasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Acceptance of Robes is concluded.

6. Aññātakaviññattisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Requesting from an Unrelated Person.

Ñātakappavārite vā viññāpentassāti ettha ca saṅghavasena pavāritesu pamāṇameva vaṭṭati. Puggalikappavāraṇāya yaṃ yaṃ pavāreti, taṃ taṃyeva viññāpetabbanti likhitaṃ.

Or for one requesting from a relative who has made an invitation: here, in the case of invitations made on behalf of the Saṅgha, only the specified amount is allowable. For an individual invitation, it is written that whatever one is invited for, that very thing should be requested.

Aññātakaviññattisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Requesting from an Unrelated Person is concluded.

7. Tatuttarisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Subsequent Training Rule.

Pakatiyā santaruttarena carati kathinapalibodhavasena vā sāsaṅkasikkhāpadavasena vā. Ettha siyā – “na mattaṃ jānitvā bahuṃ cīvaraṃ viññāpessanti, dussavāṇijjaṃ vā”tiādinā (pārā. 522) ujjhāyantānaṃ sutvā bhagavāpi chabbaggiye bhikkhū [M 0.0077] “kathañhi nāma tumhe moghapurisā [V 0.0071] na mattaṃ jānitvā bahuṃ cīvaraṃ viññāpessathā”ti (pārā. 522) vatvā sikkhāpadassa paññattattā ca imissaṃ kaṅkhāvitaraṇiyaṃ “bahucīvaraviññāpanavatthusmiṃ paññatta”nti vuttattā, samantapāsādikāyaṃ “na hi anacchinnacīvarā attano atthāya sākhāpalāsaṃ bhañjituṃ labhanti, acchinnacīvarānaṃ pana atthāya labhantī”ti vuttattā ca aññassatthāya pamāṇaṃ viññāpetuṃ vaṭṭatīti ce? Na, kasmā? Aññātakaviññattisikkhāpadassa aṭṭhuppattiyā eva aññātakaviññatti vāritā. Tassa sikkhāpadassa anāpatti. Pāḷiyaṃ (pārā. 521) “aññassatthāyā”ti imissā anāpattipāḷiyā aññassatthāya viññāpento tassa ñātakappavārite eva viññāpeti, na aññeti vacanato ca vāritā. Tasmā bhagavāpi “bahuṃ cīvaraṃ viññāpessathā”ti (pārā. 522) vigarahitvā sikkhāpadaṃ paññāpento “abhihaṭṭhuṃ pavāreyyā”ti vuttanayeneva pamāṇato gahaṇaṃ anujāni, na aññassatthāya pamāṇato viññāpanaṃ. Yasmā panimaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ aññassatthāya viññāpanavatthusmiṃyeva paññattaṃ, tasmā idha “aññassatthāyā”ti na vuttaṃ, na na labbhatīti katvā.

By nature, he goes about with an inner and outer robe, either on account of the Kathina impediment or on account of a training rule involving doubt. Here, it might be argued: Since the Blessed One, upon hearing those who were complaining, “Without knowing the measure, they will request much robe-cloth, or engage in the cloth trade,” and so on (Pārā. 522), rebuked the group-of-six bhikkhus, saying, “How can you, foolish men, request much robe-cloth without knowing the measure?” (Pārā. 522), and then laid down the training rule; and since in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī it is stated, “It was laid down in the case of requesting much robe-cloth;” and since in the Samantapāsādikā it is stated, “Indeed, those whose robes have not been stolen are not allowed to break off branches and leaves for their own sake, but they are allowed to for the sake of those whose robes have been stolen;” is it therefore permissible to request the proper measure for the sake of another? No. Why? A request from an unrelated person is prohibited by the very origin story of the training rule on requesting from an unrelated person. The no-offense clause of that training rule is in the Pāḷi (Pārā. 521). By the statement in this no-offense clause, “‘For the sake of another,’” it is prohibited, since one requesting for the sake of another may request only from his invited relatives, not from others. Therefore, the Blessed One, after censuring them with, “you will request much robe-cloth” (Pārā. 522), and laying down the training rule, permitted the taking of a measured amount only in the way stated, “he might be invited to take,” not the requesting of a measured amount for the sake of another. But since this training rule was laid down precisely in the case of requesting for the sake of another, the words “for the sake of another” are not stated here, not with the thought that it is not allowable.

Aṭṭhakathāsu “aññātakappavāritaṭṭhāne pakatiyā bahumpi vaṭṭati, acchinnakāraṇā pamāṇameva vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ “anāpatti ñātakānaṃ pavāritāna”nti (pārā. 526) vuttaanāpattipāḷiyā na sametīti samantapāsādikāyaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.526) vuttattā idhāpi vuttanayeneva ñātakappavārite viññāpentassa attano dhanena gaṇhantassa anāpattīti likhitaṃ. “Aññassatthāyā”ti nidānavirodhato na vuttaṃ, tathāpi anantare vuttanayeneva labbhati evāti vadanti.

In the commentaries, it is said: “In a place where one has been invited by an unrelated person, even a large amount is naturally allowable; for the reason of one's robe having been stolen, only the proper measure is allowable.” Since it is stated in the Samantapāsādikā (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.526) that this does not agree with the Pāḷi of the no-offense clause which states, “There is no offense for relatives who have invited” (Pārā. 526), here too it is written that, in the manner stated, there is no offense for one who requests from invited relatives and takes it with his own funds. The words “For the sake of another” are not stated due to contradicting the origin story; nevertheless, they say that it is indeed allowable in the same manner as stated immediately before.

Tatuttarisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Subsequent Training Rules is Concluded.

8. Upakkhaṭasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning What Has Been Prepared.

Paṭhamaupakkhaṭe “pubbe appavārito”ti (pārā. 528) vacanato tasmiṃ khaṇe pavāritopi appavāritova hotīti veditabbaṃ.

In the first training rule concerning what has been prepared, from the statement “previously uninvited” (Pārā. 528), it should be understood that even if one is invited at that moment, one is still considered as uninvited.

Upakkhaṭasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning What Has Been Prepared is Concluded.

9. Dutiyaupakkhaṭasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Second Training Rule Concerning What Has Been Prepared.

Dutiyaupakkhaṭena [M 0.0078][V 0.0072] kiṃ payojananti ce? Natthi payojanaṃ, kevalaṃ aṭṭhuppattivasena pana paññattaṃ bhikkhuniyā rahonisajjasikkhāpadaṃ viya. Evaṃ sante saṅgītikārakehi saṅgītiṃ anāropetabbaṃ bhaveyya vināpi tena tadatthasiddhito, anissarattā, anāropetuṃ anuññātattā ca. Vuttañhetaṃ “ākaṅkhamāno, ānanda, saṅgho…pe… samūhaneyyā”ti (dī. ni. 2.216; cūḷava. 441). Idaṃ sabbamakāraṇaṃ. Na hi buddhā appayojanaṃ vacanaṃ nicchārenti, pageva sikkhāpadaṃ. Tenevāha aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “imināva nayena attho veditabbo. Idañhi purimassa anupaññattisadisa”ntiādi. Anupaññatti ca nippayojanaṃ natthi. Taṃsadisañcetaṃ, na nippayojananti dassitaṃ hoti. Evaṃ sante ko panettha atthavisesoti? Tato āha “kevalaṃ tattha ekassa pīḷā katā, idha dvinnaṃ, ayamettha viseso”ti. Iminā atthavisesena ko panañño atirekattho dassitoti? Porāṇagaṇṭhipade tāva vuttaṃ “ekasmimpi vatthusmiṃ ubhinnampi pīḷā kātuṃ na vaṭṭatīti ayamatirekattho dassito”ti. Tenetaṃ dīpeti “na kevalaṃ paṭiladdhacīvaragaṇanāya eva āpattigaṇanā, pīḷitapuggalasaṅkhātavatthugaṇanāyapī”ti.

If it is asked, what is the purpose of the second training rule concerning what has been prepared? There is no purpose; it was merely laid down based on its origin story, like the training rule for a bhikkhunī on sitting in a secluded place. If that were so, it should not have been included in the recitation by the compilers of the council, since its purpose would have been achieved even without it, due to its lack of sovereignty and because permission was given not to include it. For it has been said: “If it wishes, Ānanda, the Saṅgha… may abolish…” (Dī. Ni. 2.216; Cūḷava. 441). All this is not the reason. For Buddhas do not utter a purposeless word, let alone lay down a training rule. Therefore, it is said in the commentary: “The meaning should be understood in this very way. For this is similar to a supplementary regulation to the previous one,” and so on. And a supplementary regulation is not without purpose. And this is similar to that; thus it is shown that it is not without purpose. This being so, what is the special meaning here? To this, it is said: “Simply, there harassment was done to one, here to two; this is the distinction here.” By this special meaning, what other additional meaning is shown? In the ancient sub-commentary, it is first stated: “It is not proper to harass both even in a single case—this additional meaning is shown.” By this, it explains: “The counting of offenses is not only by the count of the robe-cloth received, but also by the count of the cases reckoned by the persons harassed.”

Honti cettha –

And here there are these verses:

“Vatthuto gaṇanāyapi, siyā āpatti nekatā;

Iti sandassanatthañca, dutiyūpakkhaṭaṃ idha.

“Even when reckoning by the case, there can be a multiplicity of offenses; and for the purpose of showing this, the second rule on what has been prepared is here.

“Kāyasaṃsaggasikkhāya, vibhaṅge viya kintetaṃ;

Ekitthiyāpi nekatā, āpattīnaṃ payogato”ti. (vajira. ṭī. pārājika 532);

“As in the Vibhaṅga to the training rule on bodily contact, what is this? Even with one woman, there is a multiplicity of offenses due to the application.” (Vajira. Ṭī. Pārājika 532)

Apicetaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ taṃjātikesu sikkhāpadesu sabbesupi gahetabbavinicchayassa dassanappayojananti veditabbaṃ. Āha ca –

Moreover, this training rule should be understood as having the purpose of showing the decision that should be adopted in all training rules of that kind. And it is said:

“Aññātikāya bahutāya vimissatāya;

Āpattiyāpi bahutā ca vimissatā ca;

Iccevamādividhisambhavadassanatthaṃ[V 0.0073];

Satthā upakkhaṭamidaṃ dutiyaṃ avocā”ti. (vajira. ṭī. pārājika 532);

“With a multitude of unrelated women and with a mixture; and with a multitude and mixture of offenses too; for the purpose of showing the arising of methods such as these, the Teacher declared this second rule on what has been prepared.” (Vajira. Ṭī. Pārājika 532)

Tassāyaṃ [M 0.0079] saṅkhepato adhippāyapubbaṅgamā vicāraṇā – purāṇacīvaraṃ ekameva bhikkhu bhikkhunīhi dvīhi, bahūhi vā dhovāpeti, bhikkhunigaṇanāya pācittiyagaṇanā. Tathā dvinnaṃ, bahūnaṃ vā sādhāraṇaṃ ekameva cīvaraṃ aññatra pārivattakā paṭiggaṇhāti, idhāpi tathā dvinnaṃ, bahūnaṃ vā sādhāraṇamekaṃ viññāpeti, viññattapuggalagaṇanāya āpattigaṇanā. Tathā aññesupi evarūpesu sikkhāpadesu nayo netabbo. Ayaṃ tāva bahutāya nayo.

The following is a brief examination of this, beginning with the intended meaning: A bhikkhu has a single old robe washed by two or by many bhikkhunīs; the counting of pācittiya offenses is by the count of the bhikkhunīs. Similarly, regarding accepting a single robe that is the common property of two or many, except in an exchange; here too, similarly, regarding requesting a single item that is the common property of two or many, the counting of offenses is by the count of the persons from whom he requested. A similar method should be applied in other training rules of this type. This, first, is the method concerning multiplicity.

Vimissatāya pana ñātikāya, aññātikāya ca ekaṃ dhovāpeti, ekato niṭṭhāpane ekaṃ pācittiyaṃ. Atha ñātikā paṭhamaṃ thokaṃ dhovitvā ṭhitā, puna aññātikā sudhotaṃ karoti, nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. Atha aññātikā paṭhamaṃ dhovati, pacchā ñātikā sudhotaṃ karoti, aññātikāya payogavasena bhikkhuno dukkaṭameva. Aññātikāya, ñātikāya ca aññātikasaññī, vematiko, ñātikasaññī vā dhovāpeti, yathāvuttanayena nissaggiyadukkaṭādiāpattibhedagaṇanā veditabbā. Tathā aññātikāya, ñātikāya ca santakaṃ cīvaraṃ ubhohi ekato diyyamānaṃ paṭiggaṇhāti, nissaggiyameva. Atha aññātikāya eva hatthato paṭiggaṇhāti, nissaggiyameva. Atha ñātikāya hatthato paṭiggaṇhāti, anāpatti. Atha ubhosu aññātikādisaññī, vuttanayeneva nissaggiyadukkaṭādiāpattibhedagaṇanā veditabbā. Tathā aññātikaviññattiādīsupi yathāsambhavaṃ nayo netabbo. Ayaṃ vimissatāya nayo.

But as to the mixed category: he has a single robe washed by a relative and an unrelated person; if they finish it together, there is one pācittiya. If the relative first washes a little and stops, and then the unrelated person washes it thoroughly, it is a nissaggiya pācittiya. If the unrelated person washes first, and afterwards the relative washes it thoroughly, on account of the application by the unrelated person, for the bhikkhu there is only a dukkaṭa. If he has it washed by an unrelated person and a relative, while perceiving her as unrelated, being uncertain, or perceiving her as a relative, the reckoning of the different offenses—nissaggiya, dukkaṭa, etc.—should be understood according to the method stated. Similarly, when he accepts a robe belonging to both an unrelated person and a relative that is being given by both together, it is a nissaggiya. If he accepts it from the hand of the unrelated person, it is a nissaggiya. If he accepts it from the hand of the relative, there is no offense. Then, if regarding both he has the perception of them as unrelated, etc., the reckoning of the different offenses—nissaggiya, dukkaṭa, etc.—should be understood according to the method stated. A similar method should be applied as appropriate in cases of requesting from an unrelated person and so on. This is the method concerning the mixed category.

Ādisaddena pana aneke aññātikā viññattā, viññattapuggalagaṇanāya dukkaṭaṃ. Eko deti, eko na deti, nissaggiyaṃ. Atha aviññatto deti, na nisaggiyaṃ. Atha viññattāviññattānaṃ sādhāraṇaṃ viññatto deti, nissaggiyaṃ. Ubho denti, nissaggiyameva. Aviññatto deti, nissaggiyena anāpatti. Viññattassa vacanena aviññatto deti, anāpatti eva. Tathā upakkhaṭādīsupi yathāsambhavaṃ nayo netabbo.

By the word “etc.,” if many unrelated persons are requested, there is an offense of wrong-doing for each individual requested. If one gives and another does not give, it is an item to be forfeited. If an unrequested person gives, it is not an item to be forfeited. If something is jointly owned by a requested and an unrequested person and the requested one gives it, it is an item to be forfeited. If both give, it is an item to be forfeited. If an unrequested person gives, there is no offense of forfeiture. If an unrequested person gives in accordance with the request of a requested person, there is no offense. The same method should be applied, as appropriate, to cases involving what has been prepared and so on.

Ettāvatā saṅkhepato aññātikāyādigāthā vuttādhippāyā hoti. Yaṃ panettha bhikkhuniyā rahonisajjasikkhāpadaṃ nippayojanatāya nidassanaṃ [M 0.0080] vuttaṃ, tassa payojanaviseso tasmiṃyeva āvibhavissatīti[V 0.0074]. Evameva aññatthapi vacanena, visesaaṭṭhuppattivasena ca sikkhāpadesu ñātabbaṃ visesappayojananti.

Thus, in brief, the intended meaning of the verses beginning with “aññātikāya” has been stated. As for the training rule concerning a bhikkhunī sitting in private, which was mentioned as an example due to its lack of purpose, its particular purpose will become clear in that very context. Similarly, elsewhere too, the specific purpose in the training rules should be understood through the phrasing and the specific circumstances of their arising.

Dutiyaupakkhaṭasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the second training rule concerning what has been prepared is concluded.

10. Rājasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Kings

“Ṭhānaṃ bhañjati, āgatakāraṇaṃ vināsetī”ti vuttattā puna codanaṃ na labhatīti eke. Āgamanassa sātthakaṃ na hoti, cīvaraṃ na labhissati paṭisanthārassa katattāti eke. Codanālakkhaṇaṃ na hotīti katvā vuttanti eke. “Dhammadesanādhippāyādinā na paṭisanthāro kātabbo”ti upatissatthero “‘āgatakāraṇaṃ vināsetī’ti codanāṭhānāni bhañjati, codetukāmo akattabbamakāsi, tappaccayā vattabhede dukkaṭa”nti ca vadati. Dhammasiritthero pana “āsane ce nisīdati, ekāya nisajjāya dve ṭhānāni bhañjati. Āmisaṃ ce paṭiggaṇhāti, ekena paṭiggahaṇena dve ṭhānāni bhañjati. Dhammaṃ ce bhāsati, dhammadesanāsikkhāpade vuttaparicchedāya ekāya vācāya dve ṭhānāni bhañjati. Taṃ sandhāya ‘āgatakāraṇaṃ vināsetī’ti vutta”nti vadati. “Eso kho”ti vuttena saññatto eko, “ayaṃ veyyāvaccakaroti…pe… avuttepi codetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vutto dutiyo, sace pana dūto gacchantova “ahaṃ tassa hatthe dassāmī”tiādinā vutto tatiyo, “aññaṃ vā pesetvā ārocāpetī”ti vutto catutthoti yathā bhikkhunā niddiṭṭhā cattāro, tatheva dūtena niddiṭṭhā cattāro. Mukhavevaṭikakappiyakārako, parammukhakappiyakārako ceti etesu aññātakaappavāritesu viya paṭipajjitabbanti likhitaṃ.

“He breaks the ground, he destroys the reason for coming”—some say that because of this statement, a further accusation cannot be made. Some say that his coming is not fruitful, and he will not obtain a robe because hospitality has been shown. Some say it is stated because it does not have the characteristic of an accusation. The elder Upatissa says, “Hospitality should not be shown with the intention of teaching the Dhamma and so forth,” and also states, “‘He destroys the reason for coming’ breaks the grounds for accusation; one who wishes to accuse did what should not be done, and on that account, there is an offense of wrong-doing due to a breach of duty.” But the elder Dhammasiri says, “If one sits on a seat, by one sitting, two grounds are broken. If one receives a material offering, by one act of receiving, two grounds are broken. If one speaks the Dhamma, by one speech, two grounds are broken, in accordance with the limit stated in the training rule on teaching the Dhamma. It is with reference to this that it is said, ‘he destroys the reason for coming.’” When it is said, “This is the one,” one person is informed. When it is said, “This one is a steward,” and so forth, or even if nothing is said, it is permissible to accuse—this is the second. But if, while a messenger is going, it is said, “I will give it into his hand,” and so forth, this is the third. If it is said, “Having sent another, he has it announced,” this is the fourth. Just as four are specified by a bhikkhu, so too four are specified by a messenger. The one who makes things allowable by word of mouth, and the one who makes things allowable in one's absence—concerning these, one should act as toward unacquainted, uninvited persons—thus it is written.

Rājasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning kings is concluded.

Cīvaravaggo paṭhamo.

The First Chapter on Robes.

2. Eḷakalomavaggo

2. The Chapter on Wool

1. Kosiyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Kosiya Training Rule

Kārāpeyyāti [M 0.0081][V 0.0075] attano ca parassa ca ubhinnañca kosiyaṃ ekato gaṇhitvā vuttaṃ, ubho vā ekato karontīti atthato veditabbaṃ. Tattha attanā kataṃ ce, “nissajjanakāle sayaṃ kataṃ nissaggiya”nti vattabbaṃ. Ubhohi ce kataṃ, yathāpāḷimeva.

“One should have it made” is stated taking together one’s own kosiya, another’s, and both. Or it should be understood in meaning that both do it together. In this regard, if it is made by oneself, it should be said, “At the time of forfeiture, what was made by oneself is to be forfeited.” If it is made by both, it is just as in the Pāli text.

Kosiyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Kosiya training rule is concluded.

2. Suddhakāḷakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Pure Black

Yathā paṭhame “ekenapi kosiyaṃsunā”ti (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. kosiyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) vuttaṃ, tathā idha “ekenapi aññena amissitāna”nti vacanābhāvato aññena missabhāve satipi apaññāyamānarūpakaṃ ce, “suddhakāḷaka”micceva vuccatīti vadanti.

Just as it was said in the first instance, “even by a single thread of kosiya” (Kaṅkhā. Aṭṭha. Kosiyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā), so here, due to the absence of the statement “unmixed with any other,” even if there is a state of being mixed with another, if its form is unapparent, it is simply called “pure black,” they say.

Suddhakāḷakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning pure black is concluded.

3. Dvebhāgasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Two Parts

“Tulayitvā”ti vacanato yathā tulādhāraṇāya kāḷakādhikā na honti, tathā kāḷakānaṃ dve bhāgā gahetabbā ukkaṭṭhaparicchedena. “Ekassāpi kāḷakalomassa atirekabhāve nissaggiyanti vacanaṃ tulādhāraṇāya kiñcāpi na sameti, acittakattā pana sikkhāpadassa pubbe tulāya dhārayitvā ṭhapitesu ekampi lomaṃ tattha pateyya, nissaggiyanti ayamadhippāyoti no takko”ti ācariyo. Vuttaparicchedena aggahaṇaṃ akiriyā, santhatakaraṇaṃ kiriyā.

According to the word “having weighed,” just as the black wool is not in excess for the purpose of balancing the scales, so two parts of the black wool should be taken according to the highest limit. “The statement that ‘it is to be forfeited in the case of an excess of even a single black hair’—although it may not accord with balancing the scales, but because the training rule is unintentional—means that if even one hair were to fall there among those previously weighed and set aside by the scales, it is to be forfeited—this is the intention, not mere reasoning,” said the teacher. Not taking according to the stated limit is inaction; making the felt cloth is action.

Dvebhāgasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning two parts is concluded.

4. Chabbassasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Six-Year Training Rule

“Orena [M 0.0082][V 0.0076] ce channaṃ vassāna”nti vuttattā chabbasse paripuṇṇe kātuṃ vaṭṭatīti niṭṭhānadivasato paṭṭhāya channaṃ vassānaṃ paricchedo veditabbo. Yāni panettha atirekachabbassavasena vā sammutivasena vā katāni, sabbāni tāni ekato paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭantīti. Gilānassa ca ekaṃ nappahotīti anekampi vaṭṭati. Yato paṭṭhāya rogassa mandatāya santhataṃ ādāya gantuṃ sakkoti, tato paṭṭhāya sammuti vā rogo vā na rakkhatīti eke. Apica chavassabuddhanimmalaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ vicāretuṃ gambhīrattā. Tasmā chavasse kammaṃ katanti.

Since it is said, “Before six years,” it is proper to make it when six full years have passed. The limit of six years should be understood as reckoned from the day of completion. Whatever things are made here by way of exceeding six years, or by way of consent, all those are allowable to be used together. And for a sick person, since one is not sufficient, even many are allowable. From when the illness becomes weaker and one is able to take up a felt cloth and go, from that time onwards, neither consent nor the illness protects—so say some. Moreover, the training rule, made pure by the Buddha over six years, is profound to examine. Therefore, the action is done in six years.

Chabbassasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the six-year training rule is concluded.

5. Nisīdanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Sitting Cloth

Kasmā panettha “santhataṃ pana bhikkhunā”ti sikkhāpadaṃ apaññapetvā “nisīdanasanthata”nti paññattaṃ, nanu ettha kāraṇena bhavitabbanti? Atthi kāraṇaṃ, cīvarasaññitāya santhatānaṃ ujjhitattā tesaṃ acīvarabhāvadassanatthaṃ tathā paññattaṃ bhagavatāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tasmā te bhikkhū tecīvarikadhutaṅgabhedabhayā santhate catutthacīvarasaññitāya santhatāni ujjhitvā terasa dhutaṅgāni samādayiṃsu, bhagavā ca tesaṃ santhataṃ anujāni. Tato tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ evaṃ hoti “nisīdanacīvarasaṇṭhānampetaṃ nisīdanasanthataṃ no bhagavatā anuññātaṃ catutthacīvarabhāvena, pageva katasanthataṃ vā”ti. Tato “santhate tesaṃ cīvarasaññitā na bhavissatī”ti tadatthaṃ bhagavatā “santhata”nti apaññapetvā “nisīdanasanthata”nti paññattanti adhippāyo. Imesu pana pañcasu santhatesu purimāni tīṇi vinayakammaṃ katvā paṭilabhitvāpi paribhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭanti akappiyattā, pacchimāni dve vaṭṭantīti (vajira. ṭī. pārājika 566-567) likhitaṃ. Kathaṃ paññāyatīti ce? “Anāpatti aññena kataṃ paṭilabhitvā paribhuñjatī”ti (pārā. 570) vacanatoti veditabbaṃ.

Why was the training rule not laid down here as “a felt cloth, however, for a bhikkhu,” but instead as “a sitting-cloth felt”? Surely there must be a reason for this? There is a reason. Because felt cloths were regarded as robes and were discarded, to show that they are not robes, the Blessed One laid it down in that way, it is said. Therefore, those bhikkhus, fearing they would break the three-robe ascetic practice, discarded the felt cloths, which they had regarded as a fourth robe, and undertook the thirteen ascetic practices. The Blessed One then permitted them the felt cloth. Then those bhikkhus thought: “This sitting-cloth felt, which is shaped like a sitting-robe, was not permitted by the Blessed One as a fourth robe; how much less a felt cloth that has already been made?” Thus, to ensure that they would not regard the felt cloth as a robe, for that purpose the Blessed One did not lay down the rule as “felt cloth” but instead as “sitting-cloth felt”—this is the meaning. But among these five felt cloths, the first three cannot be used even if obtained after performing a disciplinary action, because they are improper. The latter two, however, are permissible, as written in the Vajirabuddhi commentary (Pārājika 566–567). How is this known? It should be understood from the statement: “There is no offense if one uses what was made by another after obtaining it” (Pārā. 570).

Nisīdanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning the sitting cloth is concluded.

6. Eḷakalomasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Sheep's Wool

“Addhānamaggappaṭipannassā”ti [M 0.0083][V 0.0077] iminā pakatiyā dīghamaggaṃ paṭipannassa uppannānipi tiyojanaparamameva haritabbāni, pageva appaṭipannassāti dasseti. Paṭipannassa ce, addhānaṃ nāma paṭipannassa akāmā vassaṃvuṭṭhabhikkhuniyā maggappaṭipatti viyāti dasseti. Addhānamaggappaṭipannassa nissaggiyanti vā sambandho. Teneva vāsādhippāyassa paṭippassaddhagamanussāhattā “appaṭipanno”ti saṅkhaṃ gatassa anāpattīti siddhaṃ. Imasmiṃ pana atthavikappe “bhikkhuno paneva eḷakalomāni uppajjeyyuṃ…pe… asantepi hārake addhānamaggappaṭipannassa nissaggiyaṃ pācittiya”nti yojanā veditabbā. Yasmā vā eḷakalomānaṃ uppattiṭṭhānato paṭṭhāya tiyojanaparamatā adhippetā, maggaṃ appaṭipannassa ca tiyojanaparamatā natthi, tasmā “addhānamaggappaṭipannassa uppajjeyyu”nti vuttaṃ. Tena acchinnaṃ paṭilabhitvā harato ca anāpattīti siddhaṃ. Paṭilābho hi tesaṃ uppatti nāmāti.

By ‘for one who has set out on a long journey,’ it is shown that even for one who has naturally set out on a long journey, if wool arises, it is to be carried for a maximum of three yojanas, let alone for one who has not set out. And for one who has set out, it shows that ‘a journey’ is like the path of a bhikkhunī who, having completed the rains-residence, must travel against her will. Or the connection is: ‘for one who has set out on a long journey, it is an offense of forfeiture.’ Therefore, because the intention to reside has been calmed by the enthusiasm for travel, it is established that there is no offense for one who is reckoned as ‘not having set out.’ In this alternative interpretation, however, the construction should be understood as: ‘If goat’s-hair wool should arise for a bhikkhu … even if there is no carrier, for one who has set out on a long journey it is an offense of forfeiture entailing expiation.’ Or, because the maximum of three yojanas is intended from the place where the goat’s-hair wool arose, and for one who has not set out on a journey there is no maximum of three yojanas, it is therefore said, ‘if it should arise for one who has set out on a long journey.’ Thus it is established that there is no offense for one who carries it after having regained what was taken away. For regaining it is what is called its ‘arising.’

“Ākaṅkhamānena bhikkhunā paṭiggahetabbānī”ti iminā attanā paṭiggahitānaṃyeva tiyojanātikkame āpattīti dasseti. Tena anākaṅkhamānena parasantakāni paṭiggahitāni harantassa anāpattīti siddhaṃ.

By ‘They are to be accepted by a bhikkhu who is desirous,’ it is shown that an offense is incurred only when one exceeds three yojanas with what has been accepted by oneself. Therefore it is established that there is no offense for one who, not being desirous, carries what has been accepted that belongs to another.

Aṅgesu “attano santakatā”ti natthi, ayamattho “bhikkhuno uppajjeyyu”nti iminā, “acchinnaṃ paṭilabhitvā”ti iminā ca dīpito hotīti veditabbo. Porāṇagaṇṭhipade ca “aññaṃ bhikkhuṃ harāpento gacchati ce, dvinnampi anāpattī”ti vuttaṃ. Tasmā dve bhikkhū tiyojanaparamaṃ patvā aññamaññassa bhaṇḍaṃ parivattetvā ce haranti, anāpattīti siddhaṃ.

Among the factors of the offense, ‘being one’s own property’ is not stated. This meaning should be understood as being clarified by ‘if they should arise for a bhikkhu’ and by ‘having regained what was taken away.’ And in the ancient gloss it is said: ‘If one goes while having another bhikkhu carry it, there is no offense for either of them.’ Therefore, if two bhikkhus, having reached the maximum of three yojanas, exchange their belongings and carry them, it is established that there is no offense.

Tiyojanaparamaṃ sahatthā haritabbānīti tiyojanaparamameva attanā haritabbāni, taṃ kimatthanti? Sīmāya etaparamato. Vuttañhetaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, tiyojanaparamaṃ sīmaṃ sammannitu”nti (mahāva. 140). Vāsādhippāyena, paccāgamanādhippāyena vā gacchato etaparamatā ca. Vuttañhetaṃ “chabbaggiyā bhikkhū atimahatiyo sīmāyo sammannanti…pe… bhikkhū uposathaṃ āgacchantā uddissamānepi pātimokkhe āgacchanti, uddiṭṭhamattepi āgacchanti, antarāpi parivasantī”ti (mahāva. 140).

‘They are to be carried with one’s own hand for a maximum of three yojanas’ means they are to be carried by oneself for a maximum of three yojanas only. For what reason? Because this is the maximum for a boundary. For it has been said: ‘I allow, bhikkhus, to designate a boundary of a maximum of three yojanas’ (Mahāvagga 140). And this is the maximum for one going with the intention of residing or with the intention of returning. For it has been said: ‘The group-of-six bhikkhus designated excessively large boundaries … bhikkhus coming for the Uposatha arrive while the Pātimokkha is being recited, they arrive just after it has been recited, and they reside on the way’ (Mahāvagga 140).

Asante [M 0.0084] hāraketi āṇattiyā hārake asati. Kambalassa upari nisīditvā gacchantassa [V 0.0078] sace ekampi lomaṃ cīvare laggaṃ hoti, tiyojanātikkame āpatti eva kambalato vijaṭitattāti likhitaṃ. Taṃ kambalassa paṭiggahitattā attano atthāya paṭiggahitameva hotīti yuttaṃ.

‘When there is no carrier’ means when there is no carrier who can be commanded. It is written: If a bhikkhu is traveling while sitting on a woolen blanket and even one strand of wool gets attached to his robe, upon exceeding three yojanas there is an offense because it has become separated from the blanket. This is proper, for since the blanket was accepted, it is considered to have been accepted for his own benefit.

Eḷakalomasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Goat's-Hair Wool is concluded.

8. Jātarūpasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Gold and Silver

“Nibbattarukkhacchāyāpi rukkhaparicchedaṃ anatikkantā”ti likhitaṃ.

It is written: ‘Even the shade of a grown tree does not go beyond the tree’s perimeter.’

Jātarūpasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Gold and Silver is concluded.

9. Rūpiyasaṃvohārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Monetary Transactions

Jātarūparajataparivattananti ukkaṭṭhaparicchedena vuttaṃ.

‘The exchange of gold and silver’ is stated by way of the strictest definition.

Rūpiyasaṃvohārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Monetary Transactions is concluded.

10. Kayavikkayasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Trading

Asante pācittiyaṃ desetabbamevāti ettha kiṃ suddhikaṃ pācittiyaṃ, udāhu nissaggiyanti? Nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyameva.

Herein, regarding the statement ‘In the absence [of a steward], the pācittiya offense must be confessed,’ is this a simple pācittiya or a nissaggiya? It is indeed a nissaggiya pācittiya.

Kayavikkayasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Trading is concluded.

Tatridaṃ pakiṇṇakaṃ

Herein, this is the miscellaneous section.

Aṭṭhamasikkhāpadaṃ parena attano atthāya diyyamānassa vā pārivattakabhāvena diyyamānassa vā paṃsukūlassa vā rūpiyassa uggaṇhanauggaṇhāpanasādiyanāni paṭikkhipati.

The eighth training rule prohibits accepting, causing to be accepted, or consenting to a dust-heap robe or money being given by another for one’s own benefit or being given as an exchange.

Navamaṃ parassa vā attano vā rūpiyaparivattanaṃ paṭikkhipati.

The ninth rule prohibits monetary exchange, whether for another or for oneself.

Dasamaṃ [M 0.0085][V 0.0079] arūpiyaparivattanaṃ. “Arūpiye arūpiyasaññī pañcannaṃ saha anāpattī”ti (pārā. 591; vi. vi. ṭī. 1.591; vajira. ṭī. pārājika 587) ca vacanaṃ itarehi saha āpattīti dīpeti. Arūpiyañca dukkaṭavatthu. Tasmā tassa parivattane sati nissaggiyanti ekantena vuttaṃ. Pañcannaṃ saha dukkaṭavatthūnaṃ parivattane anāpattippasaṅgato anāpatti evāti porāṇāti ce? Na, kappiyavatthūnaṃyeva tattha āgatattā. Yadi kappiyavatthu nissaggiyaṃ, pageva dukkaṭavatthūti ce? Na, āpattigarukalahukabhāvena vatthugarukalahukaniyamābhāvato.

The tenth rule concerns exchange not involving money. The statement, ‘For one who perceives what is not money as not money, there is no offense in regard to the five,’ indicates that with other items there is an offense. And an item that is not money can be an object entailing a dukkaṭa offense. Therefore, when there is an exchange of it, it is unequivocally stated to be an offense of forfeiture. If it is asked: ‘Since there is an occasion of no offense in the exchange of the five kinds of objects entailing a dukkaṭa offense, is it simply no offense, according to the ancients?’ No, because only allowable items are included there. If it is asked: ‘If an allowable item is subject to forfeiture, how much more so an object entailing a dukkaṭa offense?’ No, because there is no rule that the gravity or lightness of the object is determined by the gravity or lightness of the offense.

Nissaggiyavatthuto hi muttāmaṇiveḷuriyādi mahagghappahonakampi dukkaṭavatthūti katvā nissaggiyavatthuto muttādi lahukaṃ hoti. Lahukepi vatthusmiṃ yatheva dukkaṭavatthuno paṭiggahaṇe dukkaṭaṃ, tatheva tassa vā tena vā cetāpanepi dukkaṭaṃ yuttanti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.589) aṭṭhakathācariyā.

For, compared to an item entailing forfeiture, even a valuable gift such as pearls, gems, and lapis lazuli is considered an object entailing a dukkaṭa offense; thus, compared to an item entailing forfeiture, pearls and so on are minor. The commentary masters state: ‘Even in the case of a minor item, just as there is a dukkaṭa offense for accepting an object that entails a dukkaṭa, so too it is proper that there is a dukkaṭa for causing it to be purchased or for purchasing with it’ (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.589).

Atha vā yaṃ vuttaṃ “kappiyavatthūnaṃyeva tattha āgatattā”ti, tattha kiñcāpi dukkaṭavatthūnipi adhippetāni, na pana pāḷiyaṃ vuttāni anāpattivārappasaṅgabhayāti vuttaṃ hoti. Muttādīsupi vuttesu anāpattiyaṃ kappiyakārakassa ācikkhati, “idaṃ muttādi amhākaṃ atthi, amhākañca iminā ca iminā ca veḷuriyādinā attho”ti bhaṇati, dasamena āpajjatīti adhippāyo siyā. Yasmā ca idaṃ kappiyakārakassa ācikkhanādisaṃvohāro ca, tasmā taṃ navamena vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Kiñcāpi kayavikkayeva hoti kappiyavatthūhi anuññātaṃ, imināva nayena kiñcāpi dukkaṭavatthupi dasame adhippetaṃ āpajjati, aṭṭhakathāvirodhato pana nādhippetamicceva gahetabbo.

Alternatively, regarding the statement, ‘because only allowable items are included there,’ it is said that although unallowable items are also intended, they are not mentioned in the Pāḷi text for fear of implying an occasion of no offense. Even when no offense is stated regarding pearls and so on, if a bhikkhu informs a steward, saying, ‘We have these pearls, etc., and we have need of this and that, such as lapis lazuli,’ the intention may be that he incurs an offense under the tenth rule. And because this is a transaction involving informing a steward and so on, it should be understood as being stated under the ninth rule. Although trading is permitted with allowable items, by this same method, even if an unallowable item is intended under the tenth rule, one incurs an offense; however, due to contradiction with the commentary, it should be taken as not intended at all.

Kā panettha kāraṇacchāyāti, pañcannaṃ saha tattha anāpattippasaṅgato anāpatti evāti ce? Na, tattha anāgatattā. Anāgatakāraṇā vuttanti ce? Na, pañcannaṃ saha āpattivatthukassa anāpattivāralābhe visesakāraṇābhāvā, akappiyattā pañcannaṃ sahāpi āpattiyā bhavitabbanti siddho aṭṭhakathāvādo.

What is the semblance of a reason here? If it is argued: ‘Because of the implication of no offense there in connection with the five, it is simply no offense’? No, because those items are not included there. If it is said: ‘The reason is stated for what is not included’? No, because when there is an object that is the basis for an offense in connection with the five, there is no special reason for obtaining an exception; due to being unallowable, an offense should be incurred even in connection with the five. Thus the argument of the commentary is established.

Aparo nayo – yadi dukkaṭavatthunā kayavikkaye nissaggiyaṃ, kappiyavatthumhi vuttapariyāyo tattha labbheyya, na pana labbhatīti navame eva tāni vattabbāni. Tasmā saṃvohāro nāma kayavikkayopi aññathā parivattanaṃ [M 0.0086] pariyādiyitvā pavatto, kayavikkayañca mocetvā [V 0.0080] “iminā imaṃ dehī’ti cetāpeti, vaṭṭatī”ti avatvā dasamassa anāpattivāre vuttanayeneva tesaṃ parivattane nissaggiyānumativirodhato aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttanayeneva dukkaṭavatthunā cetāpane dukkaṭameva. Nesaṃ kayavikkayena nissaggiyanti ce? Na, sabbassapi kayavikkayattā. Teneva vuttaṃ “andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana ‘sace kayavikkayaṃ samāpajjeyya, nissaggiyaṃ pācittiya’nti bhāsitaṃ, taṃ dubbhāsitaṃ. Kasmā? Na hi dānaggahaṇato añño kayavikkayo nāma atthī”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.589), attano matiyā kayavikkayalakkhaṇasammate dasamassa anāpattivāre vuttanayeneva tesaṃ parivattane nissaggiyānumativirodhato ca. Bhavatu vā attano paṭisiddhamidaṃ kāraṇaṃ, dasame avassameva jānitabbānīti tāni kayavikkayānevāti tesaṃ nissaggiyabhāvañca gatānīti evampi siddho aṭṭhakathāvādo.

Another line of reasoning: If in buying and selling with an item involving a dukkaṭa offense there is an offense of forfeiture, then in the case of an allowable item the stated procedure would be applicable, but it is not; therefore, those cases should be dealt with only under the ninth rule. Therefore, a transaction, which is also buying and selling, proceeds by encompassing exchange in another way. Having set aside buying and selling, one has something exchanged by saying, ‘Give this for that,’ without saying, ‘It is allowable.’ Because, according to the method stated in the ‘no offense’ section of the tenth rule, their exchange contradicts the allowance regarding forfeiture, and as stated in the commentary, in having something exchanged with an item involving a dukkaṭa offense, there is only a dukkaṭa offense. If it is asked, ‘Is their buying and selling an offense of forfeiture?’ No, because all of it is buying and selling. For this reason it is said: ‘But in the Andhaka commentary it is stated, “If one engages in buying and selling, it is an offense of forfeiture entailing expiation.” That is poorly stated. Why? Because there is no buying and selling other than giving and taking’ (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.589). And this is because, when, according to one’s own opinion, the characteristics of buying and selling are met, their exchange, according to the method stated in the ‘no offense’ section of the tenth rule, contradicts the allowance regarding forfeiture. Or let this reason, which is self-refuted, be. In the tenth rule, these must necessarily be known as just buying and selling, and thus they have acquired the nature of being subject to forfeiture. In this way, too, the argument of the commentary is established.

Etthāhu porāṇā – “attano santakaṃ rūpiyaṃ parahatthagataṃ karoti ajjhācarati, dukkaṭaṃ. Parassa rūpiyaṃ attano hatthagataṃ karoti, aṭṭhamena nissaggiyaṃ. Uggahitavatthuparivattane kathaṃ jātaṃ? Abbohārikaṃ jātaṃ. Atha parassa rūpiyaṃ attano hatthagataṃ paṭhamaṃ karoti, rūpiyappaṭiggahaṇassa katattā aṭṭhamena nissaggiyaṃ. Attano santakaṃ rūpiyaṃ parassa hatthagataṃ pacchā karoti, saṃvohārena nissaggiya”nti. “Rūpiyassa gahaṇamattena aṭṭhamena āpatti, pacchā parivattane navamenā”ti hi tattha vuttaṃ, taṃ pana yuttaṃ. “Ajjhācarati, dukkaṭa”nti duvuttaṃ. Dukkaṭassa aniyamappasaṅgato nissajjanavidhānesu dassitova. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yadi dvīhi nissaggiyehi bhavitabbaṃ, nissajjanavidhāne “ahaṃ, bhante, rūpiyaṃ paṭiggahesiṃ, nānāppakārakañca rūpiyasaṃvohāraṃ samāpajji”nti vattabbaṃ bhaveyya “rūpiyaṃ cetāpetī”ti sabbattha pāḷiyaṃ rūpiyappaṭiggahaṇassa vuttattā.

Here the ancients said: ‘When one makes one’s own money pass into another’s hand, one transgresses; it is a dukkaṭa offense. When one makes another’s money pass into one’s own hand, it is an offense of forfeiture under the eighth rule. In the exchange of an accepted item, what happens? It becomes an invalid transaction. Then, if one first makes another’s money pass into one’s own hand, because the act of receiving money has been done, it is an offense of forfeiture under the eighth rule. If one afterwards makes one’s own money pass into another’s hand, it is an offense of forfeiture through the transaction.’ It is said there: ‘By the mere receiving of money there is an offense under the eighth rule, and afterwards, in the exchange, under the ninth.’ This, however, is correct. The statement ‘one transgresses; it is a dukkaṭa offense’ is poorly stated, as the consequence of the dukkaṭa being indefinite has already been shown in the procedures for forfeiture. What is meant is this: If there were to be two offenses of forfeiture, then in the procedure for forfeiture one would have to say, ‘Venerable sir, I have received money and I have engaged in various kinds of monetary transactions,’ because the receiving of money is mentioned everywhere in the Pāli text, even in the rule that says ‘one has money exchanged’.

Ettāvatā yaṃ porāṇagaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ “dukkaṭavatthunā kayavikkayaṃ pariharantena catūsu nissaggiyavatthūsu ekekasmiṃ gahite aṭṭhamena nissaggiyaṃ hoti. Dukkaṭavatthunā dukkaṭavatthunti “iminā idaṃ dehī”ti gahite teneva nissaggiyaṃ hoti. “Kayavikkayampi nīharitvā gahite dukkaṭaṃ, cetāpitarūpiyaggahaṇe aṭṭhamena, parivattane navamenātiādinā attanā anuggahetvā kappiyavasena nīharitvā pañcahi sahadhammikehi saddhiṃ parivattetuṃ [M 0.0087] vaṭṭatī”ti, taṃ visodhitaṃ hoti. Aparampi tattha vuttaṃ “nissajjitabbe asati kathaṃ pācittiyaṃ, dunnissaṭṭharūpiyampi ‘na chaḍḍetī’ti vadantassa vissaṭṭho upāsako taṃ gahetvā aññaṃ ce bhikkhuno deti, kappatī”ti, tañca duvuttaṃ. Na hi gahitattā tato aññaṃ vatthu hoti. Puna aparañca tattha vuttaṃ “imaṃ ‘gaṇhāhī’ti [V 0.0081] vadantassa saddhādeyyavinipātadukkaṭaṃ, ‘etaṃ dehī’ti vadantassa viññattidukkaṭa”nti, tañca duvuttaṃ. Tattha hi payogadukkaṭaṃ yuttaṃ viya paññāyati.

By this much, what was stated in the ancient glossaries is refuted: ‘For one avoiding buying and selling, when any one of the four items entailing forfeiture is taken by means of an item involving a dukkaṭa offense, it becomes an offense of forfeiture under the eighth rule. When an item involving a dukkaṭa offense is taken for another item involving a dukkaṭa offense by saying, “Give me this for that,” it becomes an offense of forfeiture by that very act. Even having set aside buying and selling, when one takes something, it is a dukkaṭa offense; in receiving money to be exchanged, it is an offense under the eighth rule; in exchanging it, under the ninth, and so on. Not having accepted it for oneself, having had it removed by a permissible means, it is allowable to exchange it with five fellow practitioners.’ Furthermore, it is stated there: ‘When there is nothing to be forfeited, how can there be a pācittiya offense? Even with improperly relinquished money, if a commissioned lay follower, being told “Do not abandon it,” takes it and gives something else to the bhikkhu, it is allowable.’ This, too, is poorly stated. For it does not become a different object merely because it has been taken. Again, it is further stated there: ‘For one who says, “Take this,” there is a dukkaṭa offense for squandering a gift of faith; for one who says, “Give me that,” there is a dukkaṭa offense for soliciting.’ This, too, is poorly stated. For in that case, a dukkaṭa offense in the effort seems more appropriate.

Pakiṇṇakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Miscellaneous Section is finished.

Eḷakalomavaggo dutiyo.

The Chapter on Goat's Wool, the Second.

3. Pattavaggo

3. The Chapter on the Bowl

1. Pattasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Training Rule concerning the Bowl

Dve apattā, tasmā ete bhājanaparibhogena paribhuñjitabbā, naadhiṭṭhānūpagānavikappanūpagatāti atthoti ca. Samaṇasāruppena pakkanti ayopatto pañcahi pākehi pakko hoti, mattikāpatto dvīhi. “Bhikkhuniyā pattasanniccayassa vāritattā (vajira. ṭī. pārājika 602) bhikkhussapi taṃ ‘ananurūpa’nti katvā ‘purāṇapattaṃ paccuddharitvā’ti vutta”nti ca likhitaṃ, taṃ na yuttaṃ pāḷiyaṃ “sanniccayaṃ kareyyāti anadhiṭṭhito avikappito”ti (pāci. 735) vuttattā. So hi kathinakkhandhake (mahāva. 306 ādayo) niccayasannidhi viya ekopi punadivase “sanniccayo”ti vuccati. Anantarasikkhāpade pana “dutiyo vārito”ti adhiṭṭhānaṃ niyataṃ. Tasmā dve patte adhiṭṭhātuṃ na labhati. Sace ekato adhiṭṭhāti, dvepi anadhiṭṭhitā honti. Visuṃ visuṃ adhiṭṭhāti, dutiyo anadhiṭṭhito. Vikappetuṃ pana bahūpi labhati. Kākaṇikamattampīti ettha pi-kāro “ekapākampi janetī”ti pākaṃ sampiṇḍeti. Atha vā sace ekapākeneva sāruppo, vaṭṭatīti pākaparimāṇaṃ na vuttanti gahetabbaṃ. Apattattā adhiṭṭhānūpago [M 0.0088] na hoti. Apaccuddharantena vikappetabboti purāṇapattaṃ apaccuddharantena so patto vikappetabboti atthoti likhitaṃ.

Two are not proper bowls; therefore, they should be used as mere containers, not being subject to determination or assignment for sharing—this is the meaning. An iron bowl is fired so as to be suitable for a recluse when it has been fired five times; an earthen bowl, when fired twice. It is also written: ‘Because a bhikkhunī is prohibited from storing up bowls, and since this is also “unsuitable” for a bhikkhu, it is said, “having relinquished the old bowl.”’ But this is not correct, for it is said in the Pāli text: ‘He may make a store of it, it being undetermined and unassigned for sharing.’ For in the Kathina section, like a stored-up requisite, even a single item kept for the next day is called a ‘store.’ In the immediately following training rule, however, ‘a second one is prohibited,’ so the determination is fixed. Therefore, one cannot determine two bowls. If one determines them together, both become undetermined. If one determines them separately, the second is undetermined. But one may assign many for sharing. Regarding ‘as much as a kākaṇika’: here the particle ‘pi’ includes the firing, meaning ‘it produces even one firing.’ Or else, if it is suitable with only one firing, it is allowable; it should be understood that the measure of firing is not stated. Because it is not a proper bowl, it is not subject to determination. ‘It should be assigned for sharing by one who is not relinquishing’ means that the bowl should be assigned for sharing by one who is not relinquishing the old bowl—this is the meaning as it is written.

Pattasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule concerning the Bowl is finished.

2. Ūnapañcabandhanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Less Than Five Fastenings

Pavāriteti [V 0.0082] ettha saṅghavasena pavāritaṭṭhāne pañcabandhaneneva vaṭṭati, puggalikavasena pavāritaṭṭhāne ūnapañcabandhanenāpi vaṭṭatīti likhitaṃ.

Regarding ‘when invited’: here it is written that in a place where one has been invited by the Saṅgha, it is allowable only with five fastenings, but in a place where one has been invited by an individual, it is also allowable with fewer than five fastenings.

Yo ūnapañcabandhanatthaṃ, vuttampi cetaṃ karo so;

Ūnapañcabandhanatthaṃ, patvāna santike.

Whoever, for the sake of release from the five fetters, does what has been stated; having attained release from the five fetters, he has drawn near.

Ūnapañcabandhanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Less Than Five Fastenings is finished.

3. Bhesajjasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Medicine

“Paṭisāyanīyāni paṭiggahetvā”ti vadantena pādamakkhanādīnaṃ atthāya paṭiggahetvā ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭatīti dīpitanti likhitaṃ. “Yesaṃ maṃsaṃ kappatī”ti vacanena yesaṃ maṃsaṃ na kappati, tesaṃ sappiādi na kappatīti vadantā ajānitvā vadanti. Yesañhi maṃsaṃ kappati, tesaṃ sappītiādi sattāhakālikanissaggiyavatthuparicchedadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tathā paṇītabhojanasikkhāpade yesaṃ maṃsaṃ kappati, tesaṃyeva khīrādi paṇītabhojanaṃ, netaranti dassetuṃ vuttanti. Madhu nāma madhukaribhamaramakkhikānaṃ āsayesu niyyāsasadisaṃ mahāmadhu hoti, taṃ yāvajīvikanti ca likhitaṃ.

By the words, ‘Having received things to be stored,’ it is explained in writing that it is permissible to receive them for the purpose of anointing the feet and so on, and then to set them aside. By the statement, ‘Of those for whom meat is allowable,’ those who say that ghee and so on are not allowable for those for whom meat is not allowable, speak without knowing. For it is said in order to show the delimitation of items, such as ghee, that are to be forfeited after seven days, for those for whom meat is allowable. Similarly, in the training rule on choice foods, it is said in order to show that choice foods such as milk are only for those for whom meat is allowable, not for others. Honey refers to the ‘great honey,’ which is similar to resin found in the hives of bees, bumblebees, and flies; and it is written that this is a lifetime requisite.

Bhesajjasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Medicine is finished.

Pattavaggo tatiyo.

The Chapter on the Bowl, the Third.

Nissaggiyapācittiyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Rules of Expiation with Forfeiture is finished.

Pācittiyakaṇḍaṃ

The Section on Expiation

4. Bhojanavaggo

4. The Chapter on Meals

2. Gaṇabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Training Rule on Group Meals

Devadatto [M 0.0089][V 0.0083] kāle viññāpetvā bhuñjati, tappaccayā bhagavatā “gaṇabhojane pācittiya”nti (pāci. 209) sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ. Padabhājane pana “nimantitā bhuñjantī”ti (pāci. 218) nimantanameva gahetvā vibhattaṃ. Andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana vatthuvasena viññattiyā yācanampi vuttanti likhitaṃ. Kasmā? Parivāre eva “gaṇabhojanaṃ dvīhākārehi pasavati viññattito vā nimantanato vā”ti (pari. 322) vuttattā. Tasmā aṭṭhuppattiyaṃyeva pākaṭattā padabhājane na vuttanti veditabbaṃ. “‘Ekato gaṇhantī’ti ca gahitabhattāpi aññe yāva gaṇhanti, tāva ce tiṭṭhanti, ekato gaṇhanti eva nāmā”ti ca, “yo koci pabbajitoti sahadhammikesu, titthiyesu vāti attho”ti ca, “samayābhāvoti sattannaṃ anāpattisamayānaṃ abhāvo”ti ca, “samayaladdhakena saha cattāro hontī”ti ca, “samayaladdhako sayameva muccati, sesānaṃ gaṇapūrakattā āpattikaro hotī”ti ca likhitaṃ.

Devadatta eats after having food requested at the proper time; on account of that, the Blessed One laid down the training rule: 'In the case of a group meal, there is an offense of expiation.' In the word-analysis, however, it is analyzed taking only the phrase 'being invited, they eat.' But in the Andhaka Commentary, it is written that asking by way of a request is also mentioned based on the story. Why? Because in the Parivāra it is said: 'A group meal comes about in two ways: from a request or from an invitation.' Therefore, it should be understood that this is not mentioned in the word-analysis because it is already clear in the origin story itself. It is also written: '“They receive together”: even those who have received their meal, if they stand by while others receive, they are indeed called “those who receive together.”' And: '“Any kind of one gone forth”: this means among co-religionists or among sectarians.' And: '“Absence of an occasion”: this means the absence of the seven occasions for exemption from the offense.' And: '“With one who has obtained an occasion, they are four.”' And: '“The one who has obtained an occasion is himself released, but for the others, he causes an offense because he completes the group.”'

Etthāha – “paṭiggahaṇameva hettha pamāṇa”nti vuttaṃ, atha kasmā pāḷiyaṃ “gaṇabhojanaṃ nāma yattha cattāro…pe… bhuñjantī”ti (pāci. 218) vuttanti? Vuccate – tattha “bhuñjantī”ti paṭiggahaṇaniyamavacanaṃ. Na hi appaṭiggahitakaṃ bhikkhū bhuñjantīti.

Here it is said: 'Receiving alone is the standard here.' Then why is it stated in the Pāli text: 'A group meal is one where four …pe… bhikkhus eat'? The reply is: There, the word 'eat' is a statement defining the receiving. For bhikkhus do not eat what has not been received.

Gaṇabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on group meals is finished.

3. Paramparabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Training Rule on Successive Meals

Aññatra [V 0.0084] samayāti pana nimantanato pasavanato bhojanāpekkhaṃ pācittiyanti eke. Eko bhikkhu piṇḍāya caranto bhattaṃ labhati, tamañño cūpāsako nimantetvā ghare nisīdāpesi, na ca tāva bhattaṃ sampajjati[M 0.0090]. Sace so bhikkhu piṇḍāya caritvā laddhabhattaṃ bhuñjati, āpatti. Kasmāti ce? “Paramparabhojanaṃ nāma pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ aññatarena bhojanena nimantito taṃ ṭhapetvā aññaṃ pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ aññataraṃ bhojanaṃ bhuñjati, etaṃ paramparabhojanaṃ nāmā”ti (pāci. 227) vuttattā. Paṭhamakathinasadisāni, idaṃ pana kiriyākiriya”nti pāṭho.

Regarding 'Except on an occasion': some say it is an offense of expiation with respect to an expected meal that arises from an invitation. A bhikkhu going for alms receives a meal. Another lay follower invites him and has him sit down in his house, but the meal is not yet ready. If that bhikkhu eats the meal he obtained from his almsround, there is an offense. If it is asked why, it is because it is said: '“Successive eating” means that, having been invited to one of the five kinds of meals, setting that aside, one eats another of the five kinds of meals; this is called “successive eating.”' The reading is: 'It is similar to the first kaṭhina matters, but this is a matter of action and non-action.'

Paramparabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on successive meals is finished.

4. Kāṇamātāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. Explanation of the Training Rule concerning Kāṇamātā

Dvattipattapūrā paṭiggahetabbāti tathānītapūvehi atthikena ukkaṭṭhapattappamāṇavasena gahetabbā. “Mā kho tvaṃ ettha paṭiggaṇhī”ti apātheyyādiatthāya sajjitasaññāya atirekappaṭiggahaṇena ārocane, asaṃvibhāge ca na muccati acittakattā sikkhāpadassa. Atha uggahitakaṃ gaṇhāti, na muccati eva. Asaṃvibhāge pana anāpatti akappiyattā. Acittakatā paṇṇattijānanābhāveneva, na vatthujānanābhāvenāti eke. “Na pātheyyādiatthāya sajjitabhāvajānana”nti aṅgesu avuttattā sace sañcicca na vadati, pācittiyanti porāṇā vadanti. Atirekappaṭiggahaṇanti tattha pañcamaṃva aṅgaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmā appaṭiggahitattā na pācittiyaṃ, kattabbākaraṇato pana dukkaṭaṃ. Aññathā kiriyākiriyaṃ idaṃ āpajjati. Anivāraṇaṃ, anārocanaṃ vā chaṭṭhamaṅgaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā.
