Ekādasame chandaṃ avissajjetvāti “yathāsukha”nti avatvā. Ettha pana ayaṃ vinicchayo – “pārivāsikachandadānenā”ti idaṃ uddharitvā “vuṭṭhitāya parisāyā”ti (pāci. 1168) padabhājanaṃ vuttaṃ. Etassa pana samantapāsādikāyaṃ “vuṭṭhitāya parisāyāti chandaṃ vissajjetvā kāyena vā vācāya vā chandavissajjanamattena vā vuṭṭhitāyā”ti (pāci. aṭṭha. 1167) vuttaṃ. Idha chandassa pana avissaṭṭhattā kammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatīti vuttaṃ. Tasmā chandaṃ avissajjetvāva dvādasahatthapāse viharitvā puna sannipātakaraṇañca vaṭṭatīti likhitaṃ.

In the eleventh, “without having relinquished consent” means “without saying ‘as you please.’” Here, the determination is this: having extracted the phrase “by the giving of consent for probation,” the word-analysis for “for an assembly that has risen” (Pāc. 1168) is stated. Regarding this, in the Samantapāsādikā it is said, “‘For an assembly that has risen’ means: an assembly that has risen having relinquished consent by body, by speech, or merely by the act of relinquishing consent” (Pāc. Aṭṭha. 1167). Here, however, because the consent has not been relinquished, it is said that it is allowable to perform the formal act. Therefore, it is written that without having relinquished consent, it is allowable to dwell within a twelve-cubit range and then to reconvene the assembly.

Aṭṭhamavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the eighth section is concluded.

9. Navamavaggavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Ninth Section

Tatiye [V 0.0113] “sesaṃ vuttanayena veditabbaṃ, idaṃ pana akusalacitta”nti pāṭho.

In the third, the reading is, “The remainder should be understood according to the method stated, but this is an unwholesome state of mind.”

Catutthe vuttanayenāti tatiye vuttanayena.

In the fourth, “according to the method stated” means according to the method stated in the third.

Ekādasame “samuṭṭhānādīni kathinasadisāni, idaṃ pana kiriyākiriya”nti pāṭho.

In the eleventh, the reading is, “The arising, etc., are similar to the Kathina, but this is action and non-action.”

Dvādasame “samuṭṭhānādīni padasodhammasadisāni, idaṃ pana kiriyākiriya”nti pāṭho.

In the twelfth, the reading is, “The arising, etc., are similar to the Padasodhamma, but this is action and non-action.”

Terasame “saṃkaccikaṃ nāma adhakkhakaṃ ubbhanābhi, tassā paṭicchādanatthāyā”ti (pāci. 1226) pāḷiyaṃ vuttattā idhāpi “adhakkhakaubbhanābhisaṅkhātassa sarīrassa paṭicchādanattha”nti [M 0.0117] pāṭho. Aparikkhepe āpattiparicchedaṃ samantapāsādikavasena aggahetvā idha vuttanayena gahetabbanti likhitaṃ.

In the thirteenth, because it is stated in the Pāli, “The saṃkaccika is for the purpose of concealing that which is below the collarbone and above the navel” (Pāc. 1226), here too the reading is, “for the purpose of concealing that part of the body designated as below the collarbone and above the navel.” Regarding the non-delimitation, the delimitation of the offense should be understood according to the method stated here, not according to the Samantapāsādikā—so it is written.

Navamavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the ninth section is concluded.

Suddhapācittiyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Suddhapācittiya is concluded.

Samuṭṭhānavinicchayavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Analysis of Origination

Samuṭṭhānānaṃ vinicchaye pana giraggasamajjādīni “acittakāni lokavajjānī”ti vuttattā “nacca”nti vā “gandha”nti vā ajānitvāpi dassanena, vilimpanena vā āpajjanato vatthuajānanacittena acittakāni. “Nacca”nti vā “gandha”nti vā jānitvā passantiyā, vilimpantiyā vā akusalattā eva lokavajjāni. Corivuṭṭhāpanādīni “corī”tiādinā vatthuṃ jānitvā karaṇeyeva āpajjanattā sacittakāni. Upasampadādīnaṃ ekantākusalacitteneva akattabbattā paṇṇattivajjāni. “Idha sacittakācittakatā paṇṇattijānanājānanatāya aggahetvā vatthujānanājānanatāya gahetabba”nti likhitaṃ. Adhippetattā saṅkhepato dassanābhāvā –

Regarding the determination of origins, things like hill-summit gatherings are called “mindless worldly offenses” because, as one incurs an offense by seeing or anointing even without knowing it is “dancing” or “perfume,” they are mindless due to a mind that is ignorant of the object. If one sees or anoints oneself knowing it as “dancing” or “perfume,” then, due to their unwholesome nature, they are worldly offenses. Reinstating a thief, and so forth, are offenses with mind because an offense is incurred only by performing the act knowing the object as “a thief,” etc. Ordination and so forth are conventional offenses, as they are not to be performed with an entirely unwholesome mind. It is written: “Here, the state of being with or without mind should be understood based on knowing or not knowing the object, not based on knowing or not knowing the convention.” Because this is intended, and because a brief explanation is lacking—

Acittakattaṃ [V 0.0114] dvidhā mataṃ, vatthupaṇṇattiaññāṇā;

Vuttaṃ ñāṇaṃ dvidhā idha, sakanāmena aññātaṃ.

The state of being without mind is considered twofold, due to ignorance of the object and the rule; knowledge is said to be twofold here, known by its own name and known by another.

Paranāmañca jānanaṃ, vatthussekaṃ balakkāre;

Ekadhā samacārike, tasmiṃ tappaṭibandhoti.

And knowing by another name, one object by force; in one way, in even practice, therein is its connection.

Paranāmena jānanaṃ, dvidhā muttādike ekaṃ;

Ekaṃ lomādike matanti, ayaṃ bhedo veditabbo.

Knowing by another name is twofold: one in the case of pearls and the like; one is considered in the case of hair and the like—this distinction should be understood.

Sesamettha uttānaṃ, anuttānatthe vuttavinicchayattā na uddhaṭanti;

The rest here is clear; regarding matters where the meaning is unclear, they are not extracted because a determination has already been stated.

Samuṭṭhānavinicchayavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the determination of origination is concluded.

Bhikkhunīpātimokkhavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha is concluded.

Kaṅkhāvitaraṇīpurāṇaṭīkā niṭṭhitā.

The Old Subcommentary on the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī is concluded.

Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī-abhinavaṭīkā

The New Subcommentary on the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī

Ganthārambhakathā

Introduction to the Text

Tilokatilakaṃ [M 0.0119][V 0.0115] buddhaṃ, vande suddhaguṇākaraṃ;

Karuṇāsītalībhūta-hadayaṃ mahitodayaṃ.

I pay homage to the Buddha, the ornament of the three worlds, the source of pure virtues, whose heart is cooled by compassion, the greatly honored one.

Tenāpi dhammarājena, lokekācariyena yo;

Pūjito tañca saddhammaṃ, vande gambhīramuttamaṃ.

And that True Dhamma, which was honored by that very King of Dhamma, the unique teacher of the world—to that profound and supreme Dhamma I pay homage.

Munindacandasaddhamma-raṃsīhi vimalehi yo;

Bodhitohaṃ sadā vande, taṃ saṅghaṃ kumudākaraṃ.

I, who have been awakened by the pure rays of the true Dhamma from the Moon of Sages, always pay homage to that Saṅgha, the pond of water lilies.

Vinaye [V 0.0116] nayagambhīre, sabbathā pāradassinā;

Vādinā duttarāgādha-sabbasatthamahaṇṇave.

He was profound in method in the Vinaya, master of all aspects; a debater in the great ocean of all doctrines, which is hard to cross and unfathomable.

Yā katā buddhaghosena, therena thiracetasā;

Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī nāma, mātikaṭṭhakathā subhā.

That beautiful commentary on the Mātikā, named Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī, which was made by Buddhaghosa, the elder of steadfast mind.

Thirānekaguṇoghena, therena vinayaññunā;

Kalyāṇācārayuttena, dhīmatā munisūnunā;

Vinayaṭṭhitikāmena, sumedhenābhiyācito.

He was entreated by the wise Sumedha, an elder skilled in the Vinaya, endowed with a multitude of firm qualities, possessing good conduct, an intelligent son of the sage, who desired the stability of the Vinaya.

Tamahaṃ vaṇṇayissāmi, suvisuddhamanākulaṃ;

Sādhavo taṃ nisāmetha, sakkaccaṃ mama bhāsatoti.

I shall explain that which is perfectly pure and unconfused; let the virtuous listen carefully to my words.

Ganthārambhakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Introduction

Sabbakusaladhammappamukhassa vipuloḷāraguṇavisesāvahassa paramagambhīrassa pātimokkhassa atthasaṃvaṇṇanaṃ kattukāmoyamācariyo paṭhamaṃ tāva “buddhaṃ dhamma”ntiādinā ratanattayappaṇāmakaraṇena attano cittasantānaṃ punāti. Visuddhacittasantānanissayā hi paññā tikkhavisadabhāvappattiyā yathādhippetasaṃvaṇṇanāya pariyosānagamanasamatthā hotīti[M 0.0120]. Apica ratanattayappaṇāmena vidhutasabbakibbise cittasantāne bhavantarūpacitānipi antarāyikakammāni paccayavekallato yathādhippetāya atthasaṃvaṇṇanāya nālamantarāyakaraṇāyātipi ācariyassa ratanattayavandanā.

This teacher, desiring to compose an exposition on the meaning of the Pātimokkha—which is foremost among all wholesome states, brings vast and excellent special qualities, and is supremely profound—first purifies his own mental continuum by paying homage to the Triple Gem, beginning with 'Buddhaṃ Dhammaṃ' and so forth. For wisdom, relying on a purified mental continuum, by attaining a state of sharpness and clarity, becomes capable of bringing the exposition to its intended conclusion. Moreover, when the mental continuum is cleansed of all defilements by paying homage to the Triple Gem, even obstructive kamma accumulated in other existences, due to the lack of requisite conditions, becomes incapable of obstructing the intended exposition. This is also why the teacher venerates the Triple Gem.

Tattha buddhasaddassa tāva “bujjhitā saccānīti buddho, bodhetā pajāyāti buddho”tiādinā (mahāni. 192; cūḷani. pārāyanatthutigāthāniddesa 97; paṭi. ma. 1.162) niddesanayena attho veditabbo. Atha vā savāsanāya aññāṇaniddāya accantavigamato, buddhiyā vā vikasitabhāvato buddhavāti buddho jāgaraṇavikasanatthavasena. Atha vā kassacipi ñeyyadhammassa anavabuddhassa abhāvena, ñeyyavisesassa ca kammabhāvena aggahaṇato [V 0.0117] kammavacanicchāya abhāvena avagamanatthavaseneva kattuniddeso labbhatīti buddhavāti buddho yathā “dikkhito na dadātī”ti. Atthato pana pāramitāparibhāvitena sayambhuñāṇena sahavāsanāya vigataviddhastaniravasesupakkileso mahākaruṇāsabbaññutaññāṇādiaparimeyyaguṇagaṇādhārova khandhasantāno buddho. Yathāha –

Here, the meaning of the word “Buddha” should first be understood through the explanation given in such passages as: “He has understood the truths, thus he is a Buddha; he awakens beings, thus he is a Buddha” (Mahāniddesa 192; Cūḷaniddesa, Pārāyanatthutigāthāniddesa 97; Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.162). Alternatively, from the complete cessation of the sleep of ignorance together with its latent tendencies, or from the state of wisdom having blossomed, he is called “Buddha,” with the meaning of awakening and blossoming. Or, because of the absence of even one knowable phenomenon not understood by him, and due to the non-apprehension of knowable distinctions as objects of knowledge, there is no possibility of a passive verbal expression—thus, the agent is indicated with 'Buddha,' as in the phrase 'the initiated one does not give.' In essence, the continuum of aggregates—which, through self-arisen knowledge developed by the perfections, is without remainder free from all defilements along with their latent tendencies, and is the foundation of immeasurable qualities such as great compassion, omniscience, and knowledge—is the Buddha. As it is said:

“Buddhoti yo so bhagavā sayambhū anācariyako pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu sāmaṃ saccāni abhisambujjhi, tattha ca sabbaññutaṃ patto, balesu ca vasībhāva”nti (mahāni. 192; cūḷani. pārāyanatthutigāthāniddesa 97; paṭi. ma. 1.161),

"He is called 'Buddha,' the Blessed One, the Self-Existent One, the One without a Teacher, who in previously unheard-of teachings awakened to the truths by himself, attained omniscience therein, and gained mastery over the powers" (Mahāniddesa 192; Cūḷaniddesa, Pārāyanatthutigāthāniddesa 97; Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.161).

Taṃ buddhaṃ.

That Buddha.

Dhāretīti dhammo. Ayañhi yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjamāne apāyadukkhe, saṃsāradukkhe ca apatamāne dhāretīti, tannibbattakakilesaviddhaṃsanañcettha dhāraṇaṃ. Evañca katvā ariyamaggo, tassa tadatthasiddhihetutāya nibbānañcāti ubhayameva nippariyāyato dhāreti. Ariyaphalañca pana taṃsamucchinnakilesapaṭippassambhanena tadanukūlatāya, pariyattidhammo ca tadadhigamahetutāyāti ubhayampi pariyāyato dhāretīti veditabbaṃ, taṃ dhammaṃ. Ca-saddo samuccayattho. Tena yathāvuttaṃ buddhaṃ, imañca dhammaṃ vanditvāti buddharatanena saha vandanakiriyāya dhammaratanaṃ samuccinoti.

It sustains, thus it is Dhamma. For it sustains those who practice according to the instructions, preventing them from falling into the suffering of the lower realms and the suffering of saṃsāra. Here, 'sustaining' refers to the destruction of the defilements that give rise to those sufferings. In this way, the Noble Path and Nibbāna both sustain in a direct manner, as they are the cause for the attainment of that goal. The Noble Fruit, through the pacification of the defilements eradicated by it, and the scriptural Dhamma, as the cause for its attainment, should both be understood to sustain in an indirect sense. That Dhamma. The word 'ca' has a conjunctive meaning. Therefore, having paid homage to the Buddha as described and to this Dhamma, the act of veneration conjoins the Dhamma Jewel with the Buddha Jewel.

Na kevalaṃ idaṃ dvayamevāti āha “saṅghañcā”ti. Ariyena diṭṭhisīlasāmaññena saṃhato ghaṭitoti saṅgho, aṭṭhaariyapuggalasamūho. Tehi [M 0.0121] tehi vā maggaphalehi kilesadarathānaṃ samucchedapaṭippassambhanavasena sammadeva ghātitattā saṅgho, pothujjanikasaṅghassāpi pubbabhāgappaṭipadāya ṭhitattā purimacetanāya viya dāne ettheva saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Sopi hi kiñcāpi ariyena diṭṭhisīlasāmaññena asaṃhato, niyyānikapakkhiyena pana pothujjanikena saṃhatattā dakkhiṇeyyapaṇipātāraho saṅghoyevāti, taṃ saṅghaṃ. Ca-saddassattho etthāpi vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

It is not only these two; thus, he said, 'and the Saṅgha.' The Saṅgha is the assembly of the eight Noble Individuals, united by a commonality of noble view and virtue. Or, because defilements and distresses are rightly struck down by them through the respective paths and fruits—by way of eradication and pacification—it is a Saṅgha. The inclusion of the conventional Saṅgha should also be understood here, as they stand in the preliminary stage of the practice, similar to the prior intention in an act of giving. For although they are not united by a commonality of noble view and virtue, they are united as worldlings who are aligned with the path to liberation, and are thus a Saṅgha worthy of offerings and reverence. That Saṅgha. The meaning of the word 'ca' here should also be understood in the way previously explained.

Kiṃvisiṭṭhaṃ buddhaṃ, dhammaṃ, saṅghañcāti āha “vandanāmānapūjāsakkārabhājana”nti. Idañca visesanaṃ paccekaṃ yojetabbaṃ “vandanāmānapūjāsakkārabhājanaṃ. Buddhaṃ…pe… vandanāmānapūjāsakkārabhājanaṃ saṅghañcā”ti. Tattha sadevakena lokena arahatādīhi guṇehi seṭṭhabhāvena kariyamāno paṇāmo vandanā, sammāno māno, gandhapupphādīhi upahāro pūjā, abhisaṅkhatapaccayadānaṃ [V 0.0118] sakkāro, vandanā ca māno ca pūjā ca sakkāro ca vandanāmānapūjāsakkārā, tesaṃ mahapphalabhāvakaraṇena bhājanattā ādhārattā vandanāmānapūjāsakkārabhājanaṃ. Iminā ratanattayassa arahatādīhi guṇehi asamabhāvaṃ dasseti. Tandassanampi takkatassa nipaccakārassa sasantānapavanādivasena yathādhippetāya atthasaṃvaṇṇanāya nipphādanasamatthabhāvadīpanatthanti veditabbaṃ.

What distinguishes the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha? It is said: 'a recipient of veneration, honor, offerings, and reverential support.' This qualification should be applied individually: 'a recipient of veneration, honor, offerings, and reverential support—the Buddha… the Dhamma… the Saṅgha.' Here, prostration, which is done by the world with its deities due to the superiority of qualities such as arahantship, is 'vandanā'; high regard is 'māna'; presenting offerings such as fragrances and flowers is 'pūjā'; and the giving of prepared requisites is 'sakkāra.' Veneration, honor, offerings, and reverential support are 'vandanāmānapūjāsakkārā,' and because they are vessels, being supports for the production of great fruit, they are 'vandanāmānapūjāsakkārabhājanaṃ.' By this, it shows the incomparable nature of the Triple Gem due to qualities such as arahantship. This showing should also be understood as being for the purpose of demonstrating the ability to accomplish the exposition of meaning as intended, by way of purifying one's own continuum through such an act of reverence and prostration.

Vippasannena cetasā vanditvāti arahatādianekappakāraguṇavisesānussaraṇavasena vividhena, visesena vā pasannena manasā saddhiṃ kāyavācāhi karaṇabhūtāhi abhivandiyāti attho, tīhi dvārehi namassitvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tividhā cāyaṃ vandanā kāyavacīmanovandanānaṃ vasena. Tattha buddhādiguṇārammaṇā kāmāvacarakusalakiriyānaṃ aññataracetanā kāyavacīviññattiyo samuṭṭhāpetvā kāyavacīdvāravasena uppannā kāyavacīvandanāti vuccati, ubhayaviññattiyo pana asamuṭṭhāpetvā manodvāravasena uppannā manovandanāti. Imassa padassa “vaṇṇanaṃ vaṇṇayissāmī”ti iminā sambandho.

With a clear and serene mind, having paid homage—this means paying homage with body and speech, which are the instruments of action, accompanied by a mind that is clear in various ways, or especially clear, through the recollection of the many kinds of special qualities, such as arahantship and so on. This is to say that homage is paid through the three doors. This homage is threefold: bodily, verbal, and mental. Herein, a certain volition that is a wholesome sense-sphere action, having the qualities of the Buddha and others as its object, which generates bodily and verbal intimation and thus arises through the doors of body and speech, is called bodily and verbal homage. However, that which arises through the mind-door without generating both intimations is called mental homage. The connection of this phrase is with the statement, 'I shall explain the explanation.'

Evaṃ ratanattayassa paṇāmaṃ dassetvā idāni attano nissayabhūtānaṃ aṭṭhakathācariyānañca paṇāmaṃ dassento “theravaṃsappadīpāna”ntiādimāha. Tattha katañjalī pubbācariyasīhānaṃ namo katvāti sambandho. Kato añjali karapuṭo etenāti katañjalī. Chandānurakkhaṇatthañhettha dīgho[M 0.0122], katañjalī hutvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Pubbācariyā porāṇaṭṭhakathākārā tambapaṇṇiyā mahātherā, te eva parissayasahanato, paṭipakkhabhūtakilesahananato, paravādimigehi apadhaṃsanīyato ca sīhasadisattā sīhāti pubbācariyasīhā, tesaṃ pubbācariyasīhānaṃ. Kīdisā te pubbācariyasīhā, yesaṃ tayā namo karīyatīti āha “theravaṃsappadīpāna”ntiādi. Tattha theravaṃsappadīpānanti thirehi sīlakkhandhādīhi samannāgatāti therā, mahākassapādayo, tesaṃ vaṃso anvayoti theravaṃso. Etena bhinnaladdhikānaṃ sattarasabhedānaṃ mahāsaṅghikādīnaṃ vaṃsaṃ paṭikkhipati, theravaṃsapariyāpannā hutvā pana āgamādhigamasampannattā paññāpajjotena tassa theravaṃsassa dīpanato theravaṃsappadīpā, pubbācariyasīhā, tesaṃ theravaṃsappadīpānaṃ. Asaṃhīrattā thirānaṃ. Vinayakkameti ārambhānurūpavacanametaṃ, te pana suttābhidhammesupi thirā eva.

Having thus shown homage to the Triple Gem, now, showing reverence to the commentary teachers who are his own reliance, he speaks the verse beginning with 'theravaṃsappadīpānaṃ.' Herein, the connection is: 'katañjalī pubbācariyasīhānaṃ namo katvā.' 'Katañjalī' means one who has made a gesture of reverence with joined hands. Herein, for the sake of preserving the meter, the vowel is lengthened: 'katañjalī hutvā' is said, meaning 'having become one with joined hands.' The 'pubbācariyā' are the ancient commentary writers, the great elders of Tambapaṇṇī. They are called 'sīhā' (lions) because they are like lions in enduring hardships, in subduing defilements which are their enemies, and in being unassailable by the deer that are proponents of other views. Thus, they are 'pubbācariyasīhā.' To them, the ancient teachers who are lions. What kind are these ancient lion-like teachers to whom you pay homage? He says, beginning with 'theravaṃsappadīpānaṃ.' Herein, 'theravaṃsappadīpānaṃ' means: those endowed with the firm aggregates of virtue, etc., are 'therā' (elders), like Mahākassapa and others. Their lineage is the succession, hence 'theravaṃso' (the lineage of elders). By this, he rejects the lineage of the seventeen sects, such as the Mahāsaṅghikas, who held divergent views. But being included in the lineage of the elders, they were accomplished in scripture and realization, illuminating that lineage of elders with the light of wisdom—hence 'theravaṃsappadīpā' (the lamps of the elders' lineage). To them, the ancient teachers who are lions, the lamps of the elders' lineage. Because they are unshakeable, they are firm. This statement is suitable for the beginning of a treatise on the Vinaya. They were, moreover, firm in the Suttas and Abhidhamma as well.

Evaṃ aṭṭhakathācariyānampi paṇāmaṃ dassetvā idāni saṃvaṇṇetabbadhammavisesassa abhidhānānisaṃsaṃ, desakasampattiyo ca dassento “pāmokkha”ntiādimāha. Tattha mahesinā yaṃ pātimokkhaṃ pakāsitanti sambandho. Tattha mahesināti mahante sīlādike pañca dhammakkhandhe esī [V 0.0119] gavesīti mahesi. Mahantehi esitoti vā puthujjanasekhāsekhaisīhi visiṭṭhattā mahanto isīti vā mahesi, sammāsambuddho, tena mahesinā. Pātimokkhanti sattāpattikkhandhasaṃvarabhūtaṃ sikkhāpadasīlaṃ, taddīpanato ubhatovibhaṅgasuttasaṅkhātaṃ ganthapātimokkhameva vā. Kimbhūtanti āha “pāmokkha”ntiādi. Pamukhe sādhūti pamokkhaṃ, pamokkhameva pāmokkhaṃ, vajjapaṭipakkhattā anavajjānaṃ samādhipaññāsaṅkhātānaṃ parittamahaggatalokuttarānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ādi patiṭṭhābhūtanti attho. “Sīle patiṭṭhāya naro sapañño, cittaṃ paññañca bhāvaya”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.23, 192; peṭako. 22; mi. pa. 2.1.9) hi vuttaṃ. Mukhamivāti mukhaṃ, dvāraṃ. Yathā hi sattānaṃ khajjabhojjaleyyapeyyavasena catubbidhopi āhāro mukhena pavisitvā aṅgapaccaṅgāni pharati, evaṃ yoginopi cātubhūmakakusalaṃ sīlamukhena pavisitvā atthasiddhiṃ sampādeti. Tena vuttaṃ “mukhamivāti mukha”nti. Atha vā mukhaṃ dvāraṃ mokkhappavesāya nibbānasacchikiriyāyāti attho. Vuttañhi –

Having thus paid homage to the commentary teachers, he now, in order to show the benefit of the designation of the special Dhamma to be expounded and the excellences of the expounder, speaks the verse beginning with 'pāmokkhaṃ.' Herein, the connection is: 'that Pātimokkha which was proclaimed by the Great Seer.' Herein, 'by the Great Seer' (mahesinā) means 'Great Seer' because he sought (esī, gavesī) the five great aggregates of Dhamma, such as virtue. Or, because he was sought by great ones, or because he was a great seer (isī) due to his distinction from ordinary people, trainees, and non-trainees, he is the Great Seer, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One; by that Great Seer. 'Pātimokkha' refers to the virtue of the training precepts, which constitutes the restraint over the seven groups of offenses. Or, it is the text of the Pātimokkha itself, known as the Ubhatovibhaṅga, because it illuminates that. What is its nature? He says, beginning with 'pāmokkhaṃ.' 'Pamokkha' means 'good in the forefront.' 'Pāmokkha' is indeed 'pamokkha,' meaning it is the beginning and foundation of blameless wholesome states—namely, concentration and wisdom—which are limited, exalted, and supramundane, being the opposite of what is faulty. The meaning is as stated: 'Established in virtue, a wise person develops both mind and wisdom.' 'Like a mouth' means a mouth, a door. Just as the four kinds of food—hard food, soft food, lickable, and drinkable—enter through the mouth of beings and pervade their limbs, so too for the yogi, the wholesome states of the four planes enter through the door of virtue and bring about the accomplishment of the goal. Therefore, it is said, 'like a mouth' means a mouth. Alternatively, 'mouth' means a door for entering liberation, for the realization of Nibbāna. For it has been said:

“Avippaṭisāratthāni [M 0.0123] kho, ānanda, kusalāni sīlānī”ti (a. ni. 11.1).

'Wholesome virtues, Ānanda, have non-regret as their purpose' (AN 11.1).

Tathā –

Likewise:

“Avippaṭisāro pāmojjatthāya, pāmojjaṃ pītatthāya, pīti passaddhatthāya, passaddhi sukhatthāya, sukhaṃ samādhatthāya, samādhi yathābhūtañāṇadassanatthāya, yathābhūtañāṇadassanaṃ nibbidatthāya, nibbidā virāgatthāya, virāgo vimuttatthāya, vimutti vimuttiñāṇadassanatthāya, vimuttiñāṇadassanaṃ anupādāparinibbānatthāyā”ti (pari. 366) ca.

'Non-remorse is for the purpose of joy; joy, for the purpose of rapture; rapture, for the purpose of tranquility; tranquility, for the purpose of happiness; happiness, for the purpose of concentration; concentration, for the purpose of knowledge and vision of things as they actually are; knowledge and vision of things as they actually are, for the purpose of disenchantment; disenchantment, for the purpose of dispassion; dispassion, for the purpose of liberation; liberation, for the purpose of knowledge and vision of liberation; knowledge and vision of liberation, for the purpose of final Nibbāna without clinging' (Pari. 366).

Evaṃ saṃvaṇṇetabbadhammassa abhidhānādiṃ dassetvā idāni saṃvaṇṇanāya nimittaṃ dassetuṃ “sūratenā”tiādinā catutthagāthamāha. Tattha sūratenāti sobhane ratoti sūrato u-kārassa dīghaṃ katvā, tena sūratena, sobhane kāyikavācasikakamme ratenāti attho, vinītenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Nivātenāti nīcavuttinā. Sucisallekhavuttināti sucibhūtā kilesasallikhanasamatthā vutti paṭipatti etassāti sucisallekhavutti, tena sucisallekhavuttinā, parisuddhāya appicchavuttiyā samannāgatenāti attho. Vinayācārayuttenāti vārittacārittasīlasampannena. Atha vā vinayoti cettha pātimokkhasaṃvarādibhedo saṃvaravinayo. Ācāroti ācāragocaraniddese āgatasamaṇasāruppācāro[V 0.0120]. Soṇattherenāti ettha soṇoti tassa nāmaṃ. Thirehi sīlakkhandhādīhi samannāgatattā thero. Yācitoti abhiyācito. Thero hi pātimokkhassa gambhīratāya duravagāhataṃ, ācariyassa ca taṃsaṃvaṇṇanāya sāmatthiyaṃ ñatvā “pātimokkhassa tayā atthasaṃvaṇṇanā kātabbā. Evañhi sāsanassa suciraṭṭhitikatā hotī”ti sānisaṃsagāravena yācanaṃ akāsi. Tadassa yācanaṃ attano saṃvaṇṇanāya nidānabhūtaṃ dassento “yācito”ti āha.

Having thus shown the designation and so forth of the Dhamma to be expounded, he now speaks the fourth verse, beginning with 'sūratena,' in order to show the occasion for the exposition. Herein, 'by the gentle one' (sūratena) is from 'sūrato,' meaning 'he delights in what is beautiful' (sobhaṇe rato), with the 'u' vowel lengthened; thus, 'by the gentle one' means 'by one who delights in beautiful bodily and verbal actions,' which is to say, 'by one who is disciplined.' 'By the humble one' (nivātena) means 'by one of lowly conduct.' 'By one of pure and austere conduct' (sucisallekhavuttinā) means 'one whose conduct (vutti), whose practice (paṭipatti), is pure (sucibhūtā) and capable of eradicating defilements (kilesasallikhanasamatthā)'; thus, 'by one of pure and austere conduct' means 'by one endowed with purified, contented conduct.' 'By one endowed with discipline and proper conduct' (vinayācārayuttena) means 'by one endowed with the virtue of restraint and proper conduct.' Alternatively, here 'discipline' (vinaya) refers to the Vinaya of restraint, such as the Pātimokkha restraint. 'Proper conduct' (ācāra) refers to the proper conduct suitable for a monk, as presented in the exposition of conduct and resort. 'By the Elder Soṇa' (Soṇattherena): here, 'Soṇa' is his name. He is an 'elder' (thera) because he was endowed with the firm aggregates of virtue and so forth. 'Requested' (yācito) means 'implored.' For the Elder, knowing the profundity and inaccessibility of the Pātimokkha, and the teacher's ability to expound it, made a respectful request with its benefits in mind, saying: 'You should undertake the exposition of the meaning of the Pātimokkha. For thus the Dispensation will endure long.' To show that this request was the cause for his own exposition, he says 'requested.'

Ettha ca “sūratenā”ti imināssa soraccaṃ vuccati. “Nivātenā”ti iminā nīcamanatā nivātavuttitā, yāya nivātavuttitāya samannāgato puggalo nihatamāno, nihatadappo, pādapuñchanacoḷakasamo, bhinnavisāṇūsabhasamo, uddhaṭadāṭhasappasamo ca hutvā saṇho sakhilo sukhasambhāso [M 0.0124] hoti. “Sucisallekhavuttinā”ti iminā indriyasaṃvarapaccayasannissitaājīvapārisuddhisīlaṃ. “Vinayācārayuttenā”ti iminā pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Evamanekaguṇehi tassa abhitthavanaṃ yathāvuttaguṇasamannāgatassa sabrahmacārino ajjhesanaṃ na sakkā paṭibāhitunti paramagambhīrassāpi pātimokkhassa atthasaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ pavattāti dassanatthaṃ. Kiñca – tādisassa ajjhesanaṃ nissāya kariyamānā atthasaṃvaṇṇanā tassa ajjhesanādhipaccena, mamañca ussāhasampattiyā na cirena pariyosānaṃ gacchatīti katanti veditabbaṃ.

Herein, by 'by the gentle one' (sūratena) is meant his mildness (soracca). By 'by the humble one' (nivātena) is meant lowliness of mind and humble conduct, by which a person endowed with such humble conduct becomes one who has subdued pride and arrogance, like a foot-wiping cloth, like a bull with broken horns, and like a snake with extracted fangs—gentle, friendly, and pleasant in conversation. By 'by one of pure and austere conduct' (sucisallekhavuttinā) is meant the virtue of purity of livelihood dependent on sense-restraint and requisites. By 'by one endowed with discipline and proper conduct' (vinayācārayuttena) is meant the virtue of Pātimokkha restraint. This should be understood. Thus, this praise of him with manifold virtues is for the purpose of showing that the request of a fellow monastic endowed with the aforementioned qualities cannot be refused, and that the exposition of the meaning of the Pātimokkha, profound as it is, proceeds. Furthermore, it should be understood that this exposition of the meaning, undertaken in reliance on such a request, is made so that it may reach its conclusion without delay, by the eminence of that request and by my own diligent effort.

Evaṃ saṃvaṇṇanāya nimittaṃ dassetvā idāni tassavane sotujanassādaraṃ janetuṃ tappayojanakaraṇappakāranissayābhidhānādiṃ dassento “tatthā”tiādigāthādvayamāha. Tattha tatthāti “yaṃ mahesinā pātimokkhaṃ pakāsita”nti vuttaṃ, tasmiṃ pātimokkhe. Sañjātakaṅkhānanti padapadatthavinicchayavasena sañjātakaṅkhānaṃ, samuppannasaṃsayānanti attho. Kaṅkhāvitaraṇatthāyāti yathāvuttasaṃsayassa atikkamanatthāya. Tassāti pātimokkhassa. Vaṇṇīyati attho kathīyati etāyāti vaṇṇanā, aṭṭhakathā, taṃ vaṇṇanaṃ. Imassa ca “vaṇṇayissāmī”ti iminā sambandho. Kiṃbhūtanti āha “paripuṇṇavinicchaya”ntiādi. Paripuṇṇavinicchayanti khandhakaparivārapadabhājanādivasena asādhāraṇavinicchayassa ca nidānādivasena sattarasappabhedassa ca sabbasikkhāpadasādhāraṇavinicchayassa pakāsanato sampuṇṇavinicchayaṃ.

Having thus shown the occasion for the exposition, he now speaks the two verses beginning with 'therein,' in order to generate reverence in the listening folk for its hearing and to show its purpose, manner of undertaking, basis, designation, and so forth. Herein, 'therein' (tatthā) refers to 'in that Pātimokkha which was proclaimed by the Great Seer,' that is, in the Pātimokkha. 'For those in whom doubts have arisen' (sañjātakaṅkhānaṃ) means 'for those in whom doubts have arisen by way of determining the meaning of each word,' that is, 'for those in whom uncertainties have arisen.' 'For the purpose of dispelling doubts' (kaṅkhāvitaraṇatthāya) means 'for the purpose of overcoming the aforementioned uncertainties.' 'Of that' (tassa) refers to the Pātimokkha. 'Vaṇṇanā' (exposition) is that by which the meaning is expounded (vaṇṇīyati) and explained (kathīyati); it is the commentary (aṭṭhakathā). That exposition is connected with 'I shall expound' (vaṇṇayissāmī). 'What kind?' He says, 'with complete discernment' and so on. 'With complete discernment' (paripuṇṇavinicchaya) means 'with complete discernment' because it proclaims the uncommon discernment by way of the Khandhaka, Parivāra, word-analysis, and so forth, the seventeenfold classification by way of the origins and so forth, and the discernment common to all training rules.

Mahāvihāravāsīnanti mahāmeghavanuyyānabhūmibhāge patiṭṭhito vihāro mahāvihāro, yo satthuno mahābodhinā vibhūsito, tattha vasanti sīlenāti mahāvihāravāsino, tesaṃ mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ[V 0.0121]. Vācanāmagganissitanti kathāmagganissitaṃ, aṭṭhakathānissitanti attho, mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ sīhaḷaṭṭhakathānayaṃ idha nissāyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Vaṇṇayissāmīti pavattayissāmi. Nāmenāti attano guṇanāmena. Kaṅkhāvitaranti etāyāti kaṅkhāvitaraṇī, taṃ kaṅkhāvitaraṇiṃ. Subhanti atthabyañjanasampannattā sundaraṃ, saddalakkhaṇasubhato, vinicchayasubhato, viññeyyasubhato ca subhaṃ parisuddhaṃ. Ettha ca “kaṅkhāvitaraṇatthāyā”ti iminā payojanaṃ dasseti, puripuṇṇavinicchaya”nti iminā [M 0.0125] saṃvaṇṇanāppakāraṃ, “mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ vācanāmagganissita”nti iminā saṃvaṇṇanāya nissayavisuddhiṃ nikāyantaraladdhisaṅkaradosavivajjanato, “vaṇṇayissāmī”ti iminā attano ajjhāsayaṃ dassetīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Vattayissāmī”tipi pāṭho.

The 'dwellers of the Great Monastery' (Mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ) refers to the Great Monastery, which is the monastery established in the area of the Mahāmeghavana park, adorned by the Great Bodhi Tree of the Teacher; those who dwell there by virtue are called the dwellers of the Great Monastery; of those dwellers of the Great Monastery. 'Dependent on the path of recitation' (vācanāmagganissitaṃ) means 'dependent on the path of discourse,' that is, 'dependent on the commentary.' Here, it is said that the method of the Sinhala commentaries of the dwellers of the Great Monastery is relied upon. 'I shall expound' (vaṇṇayissāmi) means 'I shall set forth.' 'By name' (nāmena) refers to the name of its own qualities. 'The dispeller of doubt' (kaṅkhāvitaraṇī) is that by which doubts are dispelled; that Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī. 'Excellent' (subhaṃ) means beautiful because it is endowed with meaning and expression, beautiful in terms of phonetic characteristics, beautiful in terms of discernment, and beautiful in terms of what is to be understood—pure. Herein, by 'for the purpose of dispelling doubt' (kaṅkhāvitaraṇatthāya) the purpose is shown; by 'with complete discernment' (paripuṇṇavinicchaya) the manner of exposition; by 'dependent on the path of recitation of the dwellers of the Great Monastery' (mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ vācanāmagganissitaṃ) the purity of its basis, by avoiding the fault of mixing with the doctrines of other schools; and by 'I shall expound' (vaṇṇayissāmi) his own intention is shown. This should be understood. The reading 'I shall set forth' (vattayissāmī) is also found.

Ganthārambhakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the discourse on the beginning of the text is concluded.

Nidānavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Origin

Evaṃ ratanattayapaṇāmādisahitaṃ saññādikaṃ dassetvā idāni “pātimokkhassa vaṇṇanaṃ vaṇṇayissāmī”ti vuttattā pātimokkhaṃ tāva vacanatthato, sarūpabhedato, ganthabhedato, uddesavibhāgato, uddesaparicchedato ca vavatthapetvā taduddesakkamenāyaṃ vaṇṇanā bhavissatīti dassetuṃ “tattha pātimokkha”ntiādi āraddhaṃ.

Having thus shown the preliminary matters, including the homage to the Triple Gem and so on, now, since it was said, “I shall expound the exposition of the Pātimokkha,” the Pātimokkha is first to be established in terms of its verbal meaning, its nature and divisions, its textual divisions, its recitation sections, and its recitation boundaries. Then, to indicate that this exposition will proceed according to the sequence of its recitation, the passage beginning with “Therein, the Pātimokkha” is commenced.

Tattha tatthāti tasmiṃ gāthāpade. Paatimokkhanti pakārato ativiya sīlesu mukhabhūtaṃ. Atipamokkhanti tameva padaṃ upasaggabyattayena vadati. Atha vā pa ati mokkhanti padacchedo, tassa upasaggabyattayenatthamāha “atipamokkha”nti. Evaṃ pabhedato padavaṇṇanaṃ katvā saddatthato vadati “atiseṭṭhaṃ atiuttamanti attho”ti. Ettha ca sīlapātimokkhaṃ sabbaguṇānaṃ mūlabhāvato seṭṭhaṃ, ganthapātimokkhaṃ pana seṭṭhaguṇasahacaraṇato seṭṭhanti veditabbaṃ. Uttamanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Itīti evaṃ. Iminā yathāvuttavacanatthaṃ nidasseti. Nidassanattho hi ayaṃ iti-saddo “sabbamatthīti kho, kaccāna, ayameko anto, sabbaṃ natthīti kho, kaccāna, ayaṃ dutiyo anto”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 2.15; 3.90) viya. Imināti āsannapaccakkhavacanaṃ iti-saddena anantaranidassitassa, paṭiggāhakehi ca sotaviññāṇādivīthiyā [V 0.0122] paṭipannassa vacanatthassa vacanato. Atha vā imināti āsannapaccakkhabhāvakaraṇavacanaṃ yathāvuttassa vacanatthassa abhimukhīkaraṇato. Vacanatthenāti “atiseṭṭha”nti saddatthena. Ekavidhampīti ekakoṭṭhāsampi. Sīlaganthabhedato duvidhaṃ hotīti puna sīlaganthasaṅkhātena pabhedena duvidhaṃ hoti, sīlapātimokkhaṃ, ganthapātimokkhañcāti duvidhaṃ hotīti attho.

Herein, 'tattha' means 'in that verse line.' 'Pātimokkha' means that which is exceedingly foremost among virtues by its nature. 'Atipamokkha' expresses the same term by a reversal of prefixes. Alternatively, the word is divided as 'pa ati mokkha,' and its meaning is given by a reversal of prefixes as 'atipamokkha.' Having thus given an explanation of the word by way of its components, its literal meaning is given as 'most excellent, supreme.' Here, it should be understood that the Pātimokkha of virtue is supreme because it is the root of all good qualities, while the textual Pātimokkha is supreme because it accompanies those excellent qualities. The same principle applies to 'supreme.' 'Iti' means 'thus.' By this, it indicates the verbal meaning as stated. For the word 'iti' here has the meaning of pointing out, as in such passages as: '“Everything exists,” Kaccāna, this is one extreme; “Everything does not exist,” Kaccāna, this is the second extreme.' 'By this' (iminā) is a term of immediate reference to what has just been indicated by the word 'iti' and to the verbal meaning that has entered the stream of ear-consciousness and so on of the recipients. Alternatively, 'by this' (iminā) is a term that makes the matter immediately present, by bringing the stated verbal meaning into focus. 'By its verbal meaning' (vacanatthena) means by its literal meaning, 'most excellent.' 'Even of one kind' (ekavidhampi) means even as a single part. 'It is twofold by the distinction of virtue and text' means that it is again twofold by the division designated as virtue and text; that is, it is twofold as the Pātimokkha of virtue and the textual Pātimokkha.

Idāni [M 0.0126] tadubhayassāpi sutte āgatabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “tathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha pāti rakkhatīti pāti, taṃ mokkheti moceti āpāyikādīhi dukkhehīti pātimokkhaṃ, saṃvaraṇaṃ saṃvaro, kāyavācāhi avītikkamo, pātimokkhameva saṃvaro pātimokkhasaṃvaro, pātimokkhasaṃvarena saṃvuto samannāgato pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto. Viharatīti vattati.

Now, to show that both of these are found in the Suttas, the passage beginning with 'Tathā hi' is stated. Herein, 'pāti' means it protects; it liberates (mokkheti) the one it protects from the sufferings of the woeful states and so on, hence 'Pātimokkha.' Restraint (saṃvaraṇaṃ) is restraint (saṃvaro), that is, non-transgression by body and speech. 'Pātimokkhasaṃvaro' is the restraint that is the Pātimokkha itself. 'Pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto' means one who is restrained by, endowed with, the restraint of the Pātimokkha. 'Viharati' (he abides) means 'he carries on' (vattati).

Ādimetanti etaṃ sikkhāpadasīlaṃ pubbuppattiatthena ādi. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

'Ādim etaṃ' (this is the beginning) means this virtue of the training rules is the beginning because of its prior arising. And this has been said:

“Tasmātiha tvaṃ, uttiya, ādimeva visodhehi kusalesu dhammesu. Ko cādi kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ? Sīlañca suvisuddhaṃ, diṭṭhi ca ujukā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.382).

“Therefore, Uttiya, here you should first of all purify the very beginning in regard to wholesome qualities. And what is the beginning of wholesome qualities? Virtue that is well-purified and a view that is straight.”

Yathā hi nagaravaḍḍhakī nagaraṃ māpetukāmo paṭhamaṃ nagaraṭṭhānaṃ sodheti, tato aparabhāge vīthicatukkasiṅghāṭakādiparicchedena vibhajitvā nagaraṃ māpeti, yathā vā pana rajako paṭhamaṃ tīhi khārehi vatthaṃ dhovitvā parisuddhe vatthe yadicchakaṃ raṅgajātaṃ upaneti, yathā vā pana cheko cittakāro rūpaṃ likhitukāmo āditova bhittiparikammaṃ karoti, tato aparabhāge rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, evameva yogāvacaro āditova sīlaṃ visodhetvā aparabhāge samathavipassanādayo dhamme sacchikaroti. Tasmā sīlaṃ “ādī”ti vuttaṃ. “Mukhameta”ntiādīni vuttatthāneva. Ādisaddena “pātimokkhe ca saṃvaro”tiādipāḷiṃ (dī. ni. 2.90; dha. pa. 185) saṅgaṇhāti.

Just as a city architect, wishing to build a city, first clears the city site, then, after dividing it into sections with streets, squares, crossroads, and so on, builds the city; or as a dyer first washes a cloth with three kinds of alkali, and only when the cloth is pure does he apply whatever kind of dye he wishes; or as a skilled painter, wishing to paint a figure, first prepares the surface of the wall, and only then produces the figure—so too, a practitioner of meditation first purifies his virtue and afterwards realizes the states of serenity, insight, and so on. Therefore, virtue is called 'the beginning.' The terms 'the face,' etc., have the same meaning as stated. By the word 'beginning,' it includes the Pali passage 'and restraint in accordance with the Pātimokkha,' and so on.

Sīlanti cārittavārittavasena duvidhaṃ vinayapiṭakapariyāpannaṃ sikkhāpadasīlaṃ, dhammato pana sīlaṃ nāma pāṇātipātādīhi vā viramantassa, vattapaṭipattiṃ vā pūrentassa cetanādayo dhammā veditabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ paṭisambhidāyaṃ “kiṃ sīlanti cetanā sīlaṃ cetasikaṃ sīlaṃ saṃvaro sīlaṃ avītikkamo sīla”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.39) “ubhayāni kho panassa pātimokkhānī”ti bhikkhubhikkhunīpātimokkhavasena ubhayāni pātimokkhāni, dve mātikāti attho. Assāti bhikkhunovādakassa[V 0.0123]. Vitthārenāti ubhatovibhaṅgena saddhiṃ. Svāgatānīti suṭṭhu āgatāni. Ādisaddena “pātimokkhaṃ uddiseyyā”tiādipāḷiṃ (mahāva. 134) saṅgaṇhāti. Tatthāti tesu sīlaganthapātimokkhesu. Yoti [M 0.0127] aniyamaniddeso, yo koci puggalo. Nanti vinayapariyāpannasīlaṃ. Rakkhatīti samādiyitvā avikopento pāleti. Taṃ “pātī”ti laddhanāmaṃ pātimokkhasīle ṭhitaṃ. Mocetīti sahakārikāraṇabhāvato mokkheti. Apāye jātaṃ āpāyikaṃ, dukkhaṃ, taṃ ādi yesaṃ tāni āpāyikādīni. Ādisaddena tadaññaṃ sabbaṃ saṃsāradukkhaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Attānuvādādīhīti attānaṃ anuvādo attānuvādo, so ādi yesaṃ tāni attānuvādādīni, tehi attānuvādādīhi. Ādisaddena parānuvādadaṇḍaduggatibhayāni saṅgaṇhāti. Tassa pātimokkhassa jotakattāti tassa sīlapātimokkhassa dīpanattā. Ādimhi pana vutto vacanatthoti “atiseṭṭha”ntiādinā ādimhi vutto vacanattho. Ubhinnampi sādhāraṇo hoti sīlapātimokkhaṃ sabbaguṇānaṃ mūlabhāvato seṭṭhaṃ, ganthapātimokkhaṃ seṭṭhaguṇasahacaraṇato seṭṭhanti.

Virtue is twofold, by way of performance and avoidance, comprising the virtue of the training rules included in the Vinaya Piṭaka. From the perspective of the Dhamma, however, virtue should be understood as the states, such as volition, of one who refrains from killing living beings and so on, or of one who fulfills observances and duties. This is stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: 'What is virtue? Volition is virtue, the associated mental state is virtue, restraint is virtue, non-transgression is virtue.' 'Both his Pātimokkhas': this means the two Pātimokkhas, for bhikkhus and for bhikkhunīs; the meaning is the two matrices. 'His': refers to the advisor of the bhikkhunīs. 'In detail': means together with both Vibhaṅgas. 'Well-mastered': means well-grasped. By the word 'etc.', it includes the Pāḷi passage beginning 'one should recite the Pātimokkha.' 'Therein': in those, the Pātimokkha of virtue and the Pātimokkha of the text. 'Whoever': this is an indefinite reference to any person. 'It': refers to the virtue comprised in the Vinaya. 'Protects': means one guards it, having undertaken it, without corrupting it. It protects (pāti) him who is established in the virtue of the Pātimokkha; hence its name. 'Liberates': means it frees by being a cooperative cause. 'Āpāyika' means born in a plane of misery, that is, suffering; this is the first among those things [called āpāyikādīni]. By 'and so on,' it includes all other suffering of the cycle of rebirths. 'By self-reproach, etc.': self-reproach is reproaching oneself; this is the first among such things. By 'and so on,' it includes reproach from others, punishment, and fear of an unhappy destination. 'Because it illuminates that Pātimokkha': means because it clarifies that Pātimokkha of virtue. 'The verbal meaning stated at the beginning': refers to the verbal meaning stated at the beginning with 'supreme,' etc. It is common to both: the Pātimokkha of virtue is supreme as the root of all good qualities, and the textual Pātimokkha is supreme because it accompanies excellent qualities.

Tatthāti tesu sīlapātimokkhaganthapātimokkhesu. “Ayaṃ vaṇṇanā”ti vakkhamānavaṇṇanamāha. Ganthapātimokkhassa tāva yujjatu, kathaṃ sīlapātimokkhassa yujjatīti āha “ganthe hī”tiādi. Hīti kāraṇatthe nipāto. Tassāti ganthassa. Atthoti sīlaṃ. Vaṇṇitova hotīti ganthavaṇṇanāmukhena atthasseva vaṇṇanato. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yasmā ganthe vaṇṇite tadavinābhāvato tassattho vaṇṇito hoti, tasmā sīlapātimokkhassapi yujjatīti.

'Therein': in those, the Pātimokkha of virtue and the Pātimokkha of the text. 'This exposition': he refers to the exposition that is about to be given. It may be appropriate for the textual Pātimokkha, but how is it appropriate for the Pātimokkha of virtue? To this he says, 'For in the text,' and so on. 'For' is a particle in the sense of a reason. 'Its': of the text. 'Meaning': virtue. 'Is indeed explained': because by means of the exposition of the text, the meaning itself is explained. This is what is said: since, when the text is explained, its meaning is also explained due to its inseparability from it, it is therefore appropriate for the Pātimokkha of virtue as well.

Evaṃ sarūpabhedato vavatthapetvā idāni ganthabhedato vavatthapetuṃ “taṃ paneta”ntiādimāha. Tatthāti tesu bhikkhupātimokkhabhikkhunīpātimokkhesu dvīsu. Uddesā paricchijjanti yehi vakkhamānavacanappabandhehi, te uddesaparicchedā, tehi. Vavatthitanti asaṅkarato ṭhitaṃ.

Having thus established the distinction by way of nature and division, now, to establish the distinction by way of textual division, he says, 'Taṃ pan' etaṃ,' and so on. 'Therein': in those two, the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha and the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha. Those connected passages to be spoken by which the recitations are delimited are the recitation-delimiters; by these. 'Established': means standing without confusion.

Evaṃ ganthabhedato vavatthapetvā idāni uddesavibhāgato vavatthapetuṃ “tatthā”tiādimāha. Uddisīyati sarūpena kathīyati ettha, etenāti vā uddeso, nidānassa uddesoti nidānuddeso. Evaṃ sesesupi. Vitthārova uddeso vitthāruddeso.

Having thus established the distinction by way of textual division, now, to establish the distinction by way of recitation-division, he says, 'Tatthā,' and so on. A recitation (uddesa) is that wherein or whereby something is pointed out, spoken of in its own nature. The recitation of the introduction is the introductory recitation. Similarly for the rest. The recitation in detail is the detailed recitation.

Idāni nidānuddesādīnaṃ paricchedadassanatthaṃ “tattha nidānuddeso”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tesu pañcasu uddesesu. Nidānuddeso uddiṭṭho [M 0.0128] hotīti sambandho. Yaṃ panettha nidānuddesaparicchedaṃ dassentena “suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho…pe… āvikatā hissa phāsu hotī”ti [V 0.0124] idhāgatanidānapāḷiṃ dassetvā tadanantaraṃ uddesakāle vattabbassāpi “uddiṭṭhaṃ kho āyasmanto nidāna”nti imassa pāṭhassa yojanaṃ akatvā “tatthāyasmante pucchāmī”tiādinā anusāvanādikameva yojetvā dassitaṃ, taṃ pana aparipuṇṇanidānapāḷidassanapubbakanidānuddesaparicchedadassanatthaṃ, khuddakapeyyālavasena vā pākaṭattā tassa ayojanaṃ katanti veditabbaṃ, uddesakāle pana yojetvāva vattabbaṃ. Vakkhati hi “taṃ panetaṃ pārājikādīnaṃ avasāne dissati, na nidānāvasāne. Kiñcāpi na dissati, atha kho uddesakāle ‘āvikatā hissa phāsu hotī’ti vatvā ‘uddiṭṭhaṃ kho āyasmanto nidānaṃ, tatthāyasmante pucchāmī’tiādinā nayena vattabbamevā”tiādi. Avasese sutena sāviteti avasiṭṭhaṃ pārājikuddesādicatukkaṃ “sutā kho panāyasmantehi cattāro pārājikā dhammā…pe… avivadamānehi sikkhitabba”nti evaṃ sutavasena sāvite.

Now, to show the divisions of the introductory recitation and others, the text beginning, 'Therein, the introductory recitation,' and so on, is taken up. Therein, 'therein' refers to those five recitations. The connection is: 'The introductory recitation has been recited.' But here, when showing the division of the introductory recitation, after showing the introductory Pāḷi text that has come here—'Let the Sangha listen to me, venerable sirs… for one who has confessed it is comfortable'—and immediately after, without connecting the text, 'Venerable sirs, the introduction has been recited,' which should also be stated at the time of the recitation, with the text beginning, 'Therein I ask the venerable ones,' only the announcement and so on was connected and shown. This, however, was for the purpose of showing the division of the introductory recitation, which is preceded by showing the incomplete introductory Pāḷi text; or it should be understood that it was not connected because it is evident by way of the minor abbreviation. But at the time of the recitation, it must be connected and stated. For it will be said: 'But this is seen at the end of the Pārājikas, etc., not at the end of the introduction. Although it is not seen, still at the time of the recitation, after saying, "for one who has confessed it is comfortable," it must be stated in the manner of: "Venerable sirs, the introduction has been recited; therein I ask the venerable ones," and so on.' As to 'the remainder is announced by what is heard,' the remaining four recitations, beginning with the Pārājika recitation, are announced by what is heard thus: 'Venerable sirs, the four Pārājika rules have been heard by you… one should train without disputing.'

Eteneva nayena sesā tayo pātimokkhuddesaparicchedā veditabbāti dassetuṃ “pārājikuddesādīna”ntiādimāha. Pārājikuddesādīnaṃ paricchedā yojetabbāti sambandho. Nidānassa ādito paṭṭhāya pārājikādīni osāpetvāti nidānaṃ, pārājikañca, tadubhayaṃ saṅghādisesañca, taṃtikaṃ aniyatañcāti evaṃ yathākkamaṃ uddisitvā pārājikādīni pariyosāpetvā. Yojetabbāti “avasese sutena sāvite uddiṭṭho hoti pārājikuddeso”tiādinā yojetabbā. Avasesaṃ sutena sāvetabbanti vacanatoti uposathakkhandhake –

To show that in the same way the remaining three divisions of the Pātimokkha recitation should be understood, he says, 'of the Pārājika recitation, etc.' and so on. The connection is: 'The divisions of the Pārājika recitation, etc., should be connected.' 'Having brought the Pārājika, etc., to a conclusion starting from the beginning of the Nidāna' means: having recited in sequence the Nidāna; then the Pārājika; then both of those and the Saṅghādisesa; then that group of three and the Aniyata; and thus having brought the Pārājika, etc., to a conclusion. 'Should be connected' means they should be connected with the text beginning: 'When the remainder has been announced by what is heard, the Pārājika recitation has been recited.' Because of the statement in the Uposathakkhandhaka: 'The remainder should be announced by what is heard'—

“Pañcime, bhikkhave, pātimokkhuddesā nidānaṃ uddisitvā avasesaṃ sutena sāvetabbaṃ, ayaṃ paṭhamo pātimokkhuddeso. Nidānaṃ uddisitvā cattāri pārājikāni uddisitvā avasesaṃ sutena sāvetabbaṃ, ayaṃ dutiyo pātimokkhuddeso”tiādīsu (mahāva. 150) –

'Bhikkhus, there are these five recitations of the Pātimokkha. Having recited the introduction, the remainder should be announced by what is heard: this is the first recitation of the Pātimokkha. Having recited the introduction and the four Pārājikas, the remainder should be announced by what is heard: this is the second recitation of the Pātimokkha,' and so on (Mahāvagga 150).

Evaṃ vuttattā. Yasmiṃ vippakateti yasmiṃ uddese apariyosite. Antarāyo uppajjatīti dasasu antarāyesu yo koci antarāyo uppajjati[M 0.0129]. Dasa antarāyā nāma – rājantarāyo, corantarāyo, agyantarāyo, udakantarāyo, manussantarāyo, amanussantarāyo, vāḷantarāyo, sarīsapantarāyo, jīvitantarāyo, brahmacariyantarāyoti. Tattha sace bhikkhūsu “uposathaṃ karissāmā”ti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 150) nisinnesu rājā āgacchati, ayaṃ rājantarāyo. Corā āgacchanti, ayaṃ corantarāyo. Davadāho vā āgacchati, āvāse vā aggi uṭṭhahati, ayaṃ [V 0.0125] agyantarāyo. Megho vā uṭṭhahati, ogho vā āgacchati, ayaṃ udakantarāyo. Bahū manussā āgacchanti, ayaṃ manussantarāyo. Bhikkhuṃ yakkho gaṇhāti, ayaṃ amanussantarāyo. Byagghādayo caṇḍamigā āgacchanti, ayaṃ vāḷantarāyo. Bhikkhuṃ sappādayo ḍaṃsanti, ayaṃ sarīsapantarāyo. Bhikkhu gilāno vā hoti, kālaṃ vā karoti, verino vā taṃ māretukāmā gaṇhanti, ayaṃ jīvitantarāyo. Manussā ekaṃ vā bahū vā bhikkhū brahmacariyā cāvetukāmā gaṇhanti, ayaṃ brahmacariyantarāyo. Iti yaṃ vuttaṃ “antarāyo uppajjatīti dasasu antarāyesu yo koci antarāyo uppajjatī”ti, tassattho pakāsito hotīti.

Because it is said thus. 'In which unfinished' means: in which recitation is not completed. 'An obstacle arises' means: any one of the ten obstacles arises. The ten obstacles are: an obstacle from a king, an obstacle from thieves, an obstacle from fire, an obstacle from water, an obstacle from human beings, an obstacle from non-human beings, an obstacle from beasts of prey, an obstacle from reptiles, an obstacle to life, and an obstacle to the holy life. Therein, if a king arrives while the bhikkhus are seated intending, 'We will perform the Uposatha,' this is an obstacle from a king. If thieves arrive, this is an obstacle from thieves. If a forest fire approaches or a fire breaks out in the dwelling, this is an obstacle from fire. If a storm cloud arises or a flood comes, this is an obstacle from water. If many human beings arrive, this is an obstacle from human beings. If a yakkha seizes a bhikkhu, this is an obstacle from a non-human being. If tigers or other fierce beasts come, this is an obstacle from beasts of prey. If snakes or other reptiles bite a bhikkhu, this is an obstacle from reptiles. If a bhikkhu is ill, or is dying, or enemies seize him intending to kill him, this is an obstacle to life. If people seize one or many bhikkhus intending to make them fall away from the holy life, this is an obstacle to the holy life. Thus the meaning of what was said—'An obstacle arises' means: any one of the ten obstacles arises—is clarified.

Tena saddhinti vippakatuddesena saddhiṃ. Avasesaṃ sutena sāvetabbaṃ uddiṭṭhauddesāpekkhattā avasesavacanassa. Yathāha “nidānaṃ uddisitvā”tiādi (mahāva. 150). Tenāha “nidānuddese panā”tiādi. Sutena sāvetabbaṃ nāma natthi uposathassa antarāyova hotīti adhippāyo. Aniyatuddeso parihāyatīti bhikkhunīnaṃ aniyatasikkhāpadapaññattiyā abhāvato. Tadabhāvo ca “idameva lakkhaṇaṃ tatthāpi anugata”nti katvāti veditabbaṃ. Sesanti avasesuddesaparicchedadassanaṃ. Etesaṃ dvinnaṃ pātimokkhānanti sambandho. Tāvāti paṭhamaṃ. Idanti idāni vattabbaṃ buddhiyaṃ viparivattamānaṃ sāmaññena dasseti, idaṃ akkharapadaniyamitaganthitaṃ vacanaṃ vuccati kathīyatīti attho. Kiṃ tanti āha, “suṇātu metiādīna”ntiādi.

'Together with that' means: together with that unfinished recitation. 'The remainder should be announced by what is heard' is said because the statement 'the remainder' is dependent on the recitation that has been recited. As it is said: 'Having recited the introduction,' etc. Therefore he says: 'But in the case of the introductory recitation,' etc. The meaning of 'to be announced by what is heard' is that there is no obstacle whatsoever to the Uposatha. 'The Aniyata recitation is omitted': this is because of the absence of a prescription of the Aniyata training rules for bhikkhunīs. And it should be understood that its absence is because 'this same characteristic is followed there also.' 'The rest' means the showing of the division of the remaining recitation. The connection is: 'of these two Pātimokkhas.' 'So far' means: at first. 'This' shows in general what is now to be said, which is revolving in the mind. The meaning is: this statement, composed and bound by the rules of letters and words, is said, is spoken. 'What is that?' he says, 'Of "Let it be heard by me," etc.' and so on.

Tattha suṇātu metiādīnanti “suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho ajjuposatho”tiādīnaṃ bhikkhupātimokkhe āgatānaṃ suttapadānaṃ. Atthanicchayanti [M 0.0130] abhidheyyatthassa ceva adhippāyatthassa ca nicchayanaṃ, vavatthāpananti attho. Imāya hi aṭṭhakathāya tesaṃ abhidheyyattho ceva adhippāyattho ca anekadhā vavatthāpīyati. Atha vā nicchinnoti nicchayo. Gaṇṭhiṭṭhānesu khīlamaddanākārena pavattā vimaticchedakathā, attho ca nicchayo ca atthanicchayo, taṃ atthanicchayaṃ, mayā vuccamānaṃ atthañca vinicchayañcāti vuttaṃ hoti. Sīlasampannāti samantato pannaṃ pattaṃ puṇṇanti sampannaṃ, sīlaṃ sampannametesanti sīlasampannā, paripuṇṇasīlāti attho. Atha vā sammadeva pannā gatā upāgatāti sampannā, sīlena sampannā sīlasampannā, pātimokkhasaṃvarena upetāti attho. Adhisīlaadhicittaadhipaññāsaṅkhātā tissopi sikkhitabbaṭṭhena sikkhā, taṃ kāmentīti sikkhākāmā. Suṇantu meti te sabbepi bhikkhavo mama santikā nisāmentu. Iminā attano saṃvaṇṇanāya sakkaccaṃ savane niyojeti. Sakkaccasavanapaṭibaddhā hi sabbāpi sāsanasampattīti. Ettha ca sīlasampannānaṃ sikkhākāmānaṃyeva bhikkhūnaṃ gahaṇaṃ tadaññesaṃ [V 0.0126] imissā saṃvaṇṇanāya abhājanabhāvato. Na hi te vinayaṃ sotabbaṃ, paṭipajjitabbañca maññissanti.

Therein, 'of "Let it be heard by me," etc.' refers to the Sutta phrases that have come in the Bhikkhupātimokkha, such as 'Let the Sangha listen to me, venerable sirs, today is the Uposatha.' 'The determination of meaning' means the ascertainment of both the expressed meaning and the intended meaning; that is, the establishment. For by this commentary, their expressed meaning and intended meaning are established in many ways. Or alternatively, `nicchayo` (determination) is from `nicchinoti` (he determines). A talk that cuts off perplexity, proceeding in the manner of crushing a stake in knotty points, is `attho ca nicchayo ca` (meaning and determination), hence `atthanicchayo`. 'That determination of meaning' means 'the meaning and the decision being spoken by me.' 'Accomplished in virtue': `sampannaṃ` means completely (`samantato`) gone (`pannaṃ`), attained, fulfilled. Those for whom virtue (`sīlaṃ`) is accomplished (`sampannaṃ`) are 'accomplished in virtue' (`sīlasampannā`); the meaning is 'perfect in virtue.' Or alternatively, `sampannā` means rightly (`sammā`) gone (`pannā`), approached. 'Accomplished in virtue' (`sīlena sampannā`) are `sīlasampannā`; the meaning is 'endowed with the Pātimokkha restraint.' The three trainings—namely, the higher virtue, the higher mind, and the higher wisdom—are 'training' (`sikkhā`) because they are to be trained in. Those who desire that are 'desirous of training' (`sikkhākāmā`). 'Let them listen to me' means: let all those bhikkhus listen from me. By this, through praise of his own work, he enjoins them to listen carefully. For all accomplishment in the Teaching is bound up with careful listening. And here, only those bhikkhus who are accomplished in virtue and desirous of training are included, because others are not fit vessels for this exposition. For they will not consider the Vinaya as something to be heard and practiced.

Etthāti etasmiṃ gāthāpade, etesaṃ vā gāthāya saṅgahitānaṃ “suṇātu me”tiādīnaṃ padānamantare. Savane āṇattivacanaṃ savanāṇattivacanaṃ. Kiñcāpi savanāṇattivacanaṃ, tathāpi pātimokkhuddesakena evaṃ vattabbanti bhagavatā vuttattā bhagavato āṇatti, na uddesakassāti navakatarenāpi idaṃ vattuṃ vaṭṭati saṅghagāravena, saṅghabahumānena ca sahitattā sagāravasappatissavacanaṃ. Saṅgho hi suppaṭipannatādiguṇavisesayuttattā uttamaṃ gāravappatissavaṭṭhānaṃ. Idañca sabbaṃ kena kattha kadā vuttanti āha “sabbameva ceta”ntiādi. Pātimokkhuddesaṃ anujānantenāti –

'Here' means: in this verse-line, or among these words included in the verse, such as 'Let it be heard by me,' etc. A statement enjoining listening is a 'listening-injunction.' Although it is a listening-injunction, still, because it was said by the Blessed One that it should be spoken thus by the one reciting the Pātimokkha, it is the Blessed One's injunction, not the reciter's. Therefore, it is proper for even a junior bhikkhu to say this. Because it is accompanied by reverence for the Sangha and great respect for the Sangha, it is a statement with reverence and deference. For the Sangha, being endowed with special qualities such as good conduct, is the supreme basis for reverence and deference. And as to by whom, where, and when all this was said, he says, 'And all this,' etc. 'By the one authorizing the recitation of the Pātimokkha' means:

“Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pātimokkhaṃ uddisituṃ, evañca pana, bhikkhave, uddisitabbaṃ, byattena bhikkhunā paṭibalena saṅgho ñāpetabbo ‘suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho’”ti (mahāva. 133-134) –

'Bhikkhus, I authorize the recitation of the Pātimokkha. And, bhikkhus, it should be recited thus: the Sangha should be informed by an experienced and capable bhikkhu, saying: "Let the Sangha listen to me, venerable sirs."' (Mahāvagga 133-134)

Evamādinā [M 0.0131] anujānantena. Rājagaheti evaṃnāmake nagare. Tañhi mandhātumahāgovindādīhi pariggahitattā “rājagaha”nti vuccati. Taṃ panetaṃ buddhakāle, cakkavattikāle ca nagaraṃ hoti, sesakāle suññaṃ hoti yakkhapariggahitaṃ, tesaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ hutvā tiṭṭhati. Tasmāti yasmā idaṃ pātimokkhuddesakena vattabbavacanaṃ, tasmā. Kiṃ te ubhopi pātimokkhaṃ uddisanti, yenevaṃ vattabbanti āha “saṅghatthero vā hī”tiādi. Therādhikanti therādhīnaṃ, therāyattaṃ bhavitunti attho. “Therādheyya”nti vā pāṭho, soyevattho. Tatthāti tissaṃ parisāyaṃ. Byattoti paññāveyyattiyena samannāgato, paguṇamātikoti attho. Paṭibaloti vattuṃ samattho, abhītoti vuttaṃ hoti. Ettha ca kiñcāpi daharassāpi byattassa pātimokkho anuññāto, atha kho etthāyaṃ adhippāyo – sace therassa pañca vā cattāro vā tayo vā pātimokkhuddesā nāgacchanti, dve pana akkhaṇḍā suvisadā vācuggatā honti, therāyattova pātimokkho. Sace pana ettakampi visadaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti, byattassa bhikkhuno āyattoti.

By one who permits thus, etc. In Rājagaha: in the city so named. For, because it was occupied by Mandhātu, Mahāgovinda, and others, it is called ‘Rājagaha.’ This becomes a city in the time of a Buddha and in the time of a wheel-turning monarch, but at other times it is empty, possessed by yakkhas, and stands as their dwelling place. Therefore: because this is the statement to be spoken by the one who recites the Pātimokkha, therefore. Do both recite the Pātimokkha, that it is said thus? He said, ‘Either the elder of the Saṅgha or…,’ etc. Under the authority of the elder: it means it should be dependent on the elder, subject to the elder. Or the reading is therādheyya, which has the same meaning. There: in that assembly. Skillful: endowed with the skill of wisdom; it means well-versed in the matrix. Competent: able to speak; it is said to mean fearless. And here, although the Pātimokkha is permitted even for a young but skillful bhikkhu, yet this is the intention here: if the elder does not know five, four, or three recitations of the Pātimokkha, but two are unbroken, very clear, and learned by heart, the Pātimokkha is still subject to the elder. But if he is unable to make even that much clear, it is subject to a skillful bhikkhu.

Idāni “saṅgho”ti avisesena vuttattā idhādhippetasaṅghaṃ visesetvā dassetuṃ “saṅghoti iminā pana padenā”tiādimāha kiñcāpīti anuggahatthe nipāto, tassa yadi nāmāti attho veditabbo. Dakkhanti etāya sattā yathādhippetāhi sampattīhi vaḍḍhantīti dakkhiṇā, paralokaṃ saddahitvā [V 0.0127] dātabbaṃ dānaṃ, taṃ dakkhiṇaṃ arahati, dakkhiṇāya vā hito, yasmā naṃ mahapphalakāritāya visodhetīti dakkhiṇeyyo, diṭṭhisīlasaṅghātena saṃhatoti saṅgho, dakkhiṇeyyo ca so saṅgho cāti dakkhiṇeyyasaṅgho. Sammutiyā catuvaggādivinayapaññattiyā siddho saṅgho sammutisaṅgho. Avisesenāti “ariyā”ti vā “puthujjanā”ti vā avisesetvā sāmaññena. Soti sammutisaṅgho. Idhāti imissaṃ uposathañattiyaṃ. Adhippeto uposathañattiyā avisesattā. Nanu ca sopi pañcavidho hoti, tattha katamo idhādhippetoti anuyogaṃ sandhāyāha “so panesā”tiādi. Kammavasenāti vinayakammavasena. Pañca vidhā pakārā assa sammutisaṅghassāti pañcavidho. Tathā hi vidhayuttagatappakārasadde samānatthe vaṇṇayanti. Catunnaṃ [M 0.0132] vaggo samūhoti catuvaggo, catuparimāṇayutto vā vaggo catuvaggo. Evaṃ pañcavaggādi.

Now, since ‘Saṅgha’ has been stated without specification, in order to specify and show the Saṅgha intended here, he says, ‘Saṅghoti iminā pana padenā,’ etc. The particle kiñcāpi is in the sense of concession; its meaning should be understood as ‘if indeed.’ Beings prosper (dakkhanti) by means of this with their desired attainments, thus it is dakkhiṇā (an offering). A gift to be given with faith in the next world is a dakkhiṇa. He is worthy of that dakkhiṇa, or he is beneficial to the dakkhiṇa because he purifies it, making it of great fruit; thus he is dakkhiṇeyyo (worthy of offerings). They are bound together (saṃhato) by a commonality (saṅghātena) of view and virtue, thus they are a saṅgha. He is worthy of offerings and he is a saṅgha, thus a dakkhiṇeyyasaṅgha. The Saṅgha established by a Vinaya designation, such as a quorum of four, by convention is a sammutisaṅgha (conventional Saṅgha). Without specification: generally, without specifying ‘noble ones’ or ‘worldlings.’ That is the conventional Saṅgha. Here: in this motion for the Uposatha. It is intended because of the non-specification in the motion for the Uposatha. But is not that Saṅgha also of five kinds? With reference to the question, ‘In that case, which one is intended here?’ he says, ‘So panesa,’ etc. By way of kamma: by way of a Vinaya formal act. Of five kinds: this conventional Saṅgha has five types, thus it is fivefold. For they explain the words vidha, yutta, gata, and pakāra as having the same meaning. A group of four is a catuvaggo (quorum of four); or a group endowed with the measure of four is a catuvaggo. Similarly for pañcavaggo (quorum of five), etc.

Idāni yesaṃ kammānaṃ vasenāyaṃ pañcavidho hoti, taṃ visesetvā dassetuṃ “tatthā”tiādimāha. Tattha tatthāti pañcavidhe saṅghe. Majjhimesu janapadesu upasampadakammassa dasavaggakaraṇīyattā vuttaṃ “ṭhapetvā…pe… upasampadañcā”ti. “Tathā”ti iminā “na kiñci saṅghakammaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti imamatthaṃ atidisati. Yadi evaṃ kimatthaṃ atirekavīsativaggo vuttoti āha “so panā”tiādi. Atirekatarenāti catuvaggādikaraṇīyaṃ pañcavaggādinā atirekatarena, dasavaggakaraṇīyañca ekādasavaggādinā atirekatarena. Dassanatthanti ñāpanatthaṃ. Idameva cānena kattabbaṃ kammanti “kammavasena pañcavidho”ti vuttaṃ. Kammassāniyame kathametaṃ yujjeyyāti īdisī codanā anavakāsāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Imasmiṃ panattheti uposathe.

Now, in order to specify and show by way of which formal acts this Saṅgha is fivefold, he says, ‘Tattha,’ etc. There: among the fivefold Saṅgha. Because in the middle countries the formal act of higher ordination must be done by a quorum of ten, it is said, ‘excluding… and higher ordination.’ By tathā (similarly) he applies by extension the meaning, ‘it is not allowable to perform any formal act of the Saṅgha.’ If so, for what reason was the quorum of more than twenty mentioned? He says, ‘So panā,’ etc. With a larger number: a formal act to be done by a quorum of four or more with a larger number such as a quorum of five or more; and a formal act to be done by a quorum of ten with a larger number such as a quorum of eleven or more. For the purpose of showing: for the purpose of making known. And it was said, ‘fivefold by way of formal act,’ because this very formal act should be done by this Saṅgha. It should be seen that such an objection as, ‘If the formal act is not fixed, how could this be appropriate?’ is without basis. But in this matter: in the matter of the Uposatha.

Uposathasaddo panāyaṃ pātimokkhuddesasīlaupavāsapaññattidivasesu vattati. Tathā hesa “āyāmāvuso kappina, uposathaṃ gamissāmā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.150; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 3.85) timokkhuddese āgato, “evaṃ aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgato kho, visākhe, uposatho upavuttho”tiādīsu (a. ni. 8.43) sīle, “suddhassa ve sadā phaggu, suddhassuposatho sadā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.79) upavāse, “uposatho nāma nāgarājā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.246) paññattiyaṃ, “na, bhikkhave, tadahuposathe sabhikkhukā āvāsā”tiādīsu (mahāva. 181) divase, idhāpi divaseyeva vattamāno adhippetoti āha “ajja uposathadivaso”tiādi. Upavasanti etthāti uposatho. Upavasantīti sīlena vā sabbaso āhārassa abhuñjanasaṅkhātena anasanena vā khīrapānamadhupānādimattena vā upetā hutvā vasantīti attho.

Now, this word uposatha is used for the recitation of the Pātimokkha, for virtue, for fasting, for a designation, and for the day. Thus it is used for the recitation of the Pātimokkha in such passages as, ‘Come, friend Kappina, let us go to the Uposatha’; for virtue in, ‘Thus, Visākhā, is the Uposatha observed when it is endowed with eight factors’; for fasting in, ‘For one who is pure it is always festival; for one who is pure it is always Uposatha’; for a designation in, ‘Uposatha is the name of a nāga king’; and for the day in, ‘Bhikkhus, on the Uposatha day, a residence should not be without bhikkhus.’ Here too, being used for the day itself, it is intended, so he says, ‘Today is the Uposatha day,’ etc. They observe (upavasanti) on this, thus it is an uposatha. ‘They observe’ means they dwell endowed with virtue, or with fasting—reckoned as the complete non-consumption of food—or with just the partaking of milk, honey-drinks, and the like.

Sabbesampi [V 0.0128] vākyānaṃ eva-kāratthasahitattā “uposatho”ti etassa “uposatho evā”ti ayamattho labbhatīti āha “etena anuposathadivasaṃ paṭikkhipatī”ti. Iminā avadhāraṇena nirākataṃ dasseti, atha vā saddantaratthāpohanavasena saddo atthaṃ vadatīti “uposatho”ti etassa “anuposatho na hotī”ti ayamatthoti vuttaṃ “etena anuposathadivasaṃ paṭikkhipatī”ti. “Esa nayo pannaraso”ti iminā aññaṃ uposathadivasaṃ [M 0.0133] paṭikkhipatīti etthāpi. Etenāti “uposatho”ti etena saddena. Pañcadasannaṃ tithīnaṃ pūraṇavasena pannaraso. Pannarasoti iminā aññaṃ uposathadivasaṃ paṭikkhipatī”ti saṃkhittena vuttamatthaṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ “divasavasena hī”tiādimāha. Catuddasiyaṃ niyutto cātuddasiko. Evaṃ pannarasiko. Sāmaggiuposatho nāma saṅghasāmaggikatadivase kātabbauposatho. Hemantagimhavassānānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ utūnanti ettha hemantautu nāma aparakattikassa kāḷapakkhapāṭipadato paṭṭhāya phaggunapuṇṇamapariyosānā cattāro māsā, gimhautu nāma phaggunassa kālapakkhapāṭipadato paṭṭhāya āsāḷhapuṇṇamapariyosānā cattāro māsā, vassānautu nāma āsāḷhassa kāḷapakkhapāṭipadato paṭṭhāya aparakattikapuṇṇamapariyosānā cattāro māsā. Tatiyasattamapakkhesu dve dve katvā cha cātuddasikāti hemantassa utuno tatiye ca sattame ca pakkhe dve cātuddasikā, evamitaresaṃ utūnanti cha cātuddasikā. Sesā pannarasikāti sesā aṭṭhārasa pannarasikā. Honti cettha –

Because all the statements are accompanied by the meaning of the particle eva, for the word uposatho the meaning ‘it is the Uposatha itself’ is obtained. Thus he says, ‘By this he rejects a non-Uposatha day.’ He shows what is rejected by this emphasis. Or, because a word expresses its meaning by way of excluding the meaning of other words, for uposatho the meaning is ‘it is not a non-Uposatha’; thus it is said, ‘By this he rejects a non-Uposatha day.’ This also applies to the statement, ‘By pannaraso (the fifteenth), he rejects another Uposatha day.’ By this: by this word uposatho. Pannaraso (the fifteenth) is so called by way of completing fifteen lunar days. In order to show in detail the meaning stated concisely as, ‘By pannaraso he rejects another Uposatha day,’ he says, ‘For by way of the day…,’ etc. One connected with the fourteenth is a cātuddasiko. Similarly, a pannarasiko. The Harmony Uposatha is the Uposatha to be done on the day of the Saṅgha’s harmony. Of the three seasons—winter, summer, and the rains: here, the winter season is the four months from the first day of the dark fortnight of the later Kattika up to the full moon of Phagguna; the summer season is the four months from the first day of the dark fortnight of Phagguna up to the full moon of Āsāḷha; the rainy season is the four months from the first day of the dark fortnight of Āsāḷha up to the full moon of the later Kattika. ‘Six fourteenth-day Uposathas, being two in the third and seventh fortnights’: in the winter season, in the third and seventh fortnights there are two fourteenth-day Uposathas; similarly for the other seasons, making six fourteenth-day Uposathas. ‘The rest are fifteenth-day Uposathas’: the remaining eighteen are fifteenth-day Uposathas. And here they are:

“Kattikassa ca kāḷamhā, yāva phaggunapuṇṇamā;

‘Hemantakālo’ti viññeyyo, aṭṭha honti uposathā.

From the dark fortnight of Kattika up to the full moon of Phagguna, should be known the winter season; there are eight Uposathas.

“Phaggunassa ca kāḷamhā, yāva āsāḷhapuṇṇamā;

‘Gimhakālo’ti viññeyyo, aṭṭha honti uposathā.

From the dark fortnight of Phagguna up to the full moon of Āsāḷha, should be known the summer season; there are eight Uposathas.

“Āsāḷhassa ca kāḷamhā, yāva kattikapuṇṇamā;

‘Vassakālo’ti viññeyyo, aṭṭha honti uposathā.

From the dark fortnight of Āsāḷha up to the full moon of Kattika, should be known the rainy season; there are eight Uposathas.

“Utūnaṃ pana tiṇṇannaṃ, pakkhe tatiyasattame;

‘Cātuddaso’ti pātimokkhaṃ, uddisanti nayaññuno”ti.

But in the three seasons, in the third and seventh fortnight, those who know the method recite the Pātimokkha as ‘the fourteenth.’

Pakatiyā nabahutarāvāsikādipaccayena kātabbaṃ pakaticārittaṃ. Bahutarāvāsikādipaccaye pana sati aññasmiṃ cātuddasepi kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Tenāha “saki”ntiādi. Sakinti ekasmiṃ vāre[V 0.0129]. Āvāsikānaṃ anuvattitabbanti āvāsikehi “ajjuposatho cātuddaso”ti pubbakicce kariyamāne anuvattitabbaṃ, na paṭikkositabbaṃ. Ādisaddena “āvāsikehi āgantukānaṃ anuvattitabba”nti (mahāva. 178) vacanaṃ, “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, tehi [M 0.0134] bhikkhūhi dve tayo uposathe cātuddasike kātuṃ, kathaṃ mayaṃ tehi bhikkhūhi paṭhamataraṃ pavāreyyāmā”ti (mahāva. 240) vacanañca saṅgaṇhāti. Ettha ca paṭhamasuttassa ekekassa utuno tatiyasattamapakkhassa cātuddase vā avasesassa pannarase vā sakiṃ pātimokkhaṃ uddisitabbanti pakaticārittavasenapi atthasambhavato “āgantukehī”tiādīni suttāni dassitānīti veditabbaṃ. Tathārūpapaccaye satīti aññasmimpi cātuddasike uposathaṃ kātuṃ anurūpe “āvāsikā bahutarā hontī”ti evamādike paccaye sati. Aññasmimpi cātuddaseti tiṇṇaṃ utūnaṃ tatiyasattamapakkhacātuddasato aññasmiṃ cātuddase.

The customary observance is that which should be performed in the normal course of things, not due to a reason such as there being many residents. But when there is a reason such as there being many residents, it is permissible to perform it on another fourteenth day as well. Hence it is said, 'once,' and so on. 'Once' means on one occasion. 'One should follow the residents' means that when the residents are performing the preliminary duties, saying, 'Today is the Uposatha, the fourteenth,' one should follow them and not object. The word 'etcetera' includes the statement, 'The incoming monks should follow the residents' (Mahāvagga 178), and the statement, 'I allow, monks, for those monks to hold two or three Uposathas on the fourteenth, thinking: “How might we perform the Pavāraṇā with those monks earlier?”' (Mahāvagga 240). Here, it should be understood that since the meaning of the first rule—that the Pātimokkha should be recited once for each season on the fourteenth of the third or seventh fortnight, or on the fifteenth for the remainder—is possible even by way of the customary observance, the rules such as 'by the incoming monks' are shown. 'When such a condition exists' means: when a suitable condition for performing the Uposatha on another fourteenth day exists, such as 'the residents are more numerous.' 'On another fourteenth day' means on a fourteenth day other than the fourteenth of the third or seventh fortnight of the three seasons.

Na kevalaṃ uposathadivasāva hontīti āha “purimavassaṃvuṭṭhānaṃ panā”tiādi. Mā iti cando vuccati tassa gatiyā divasassa minitabbato, so ettha sabbakalāpāripūriyā puṇṇoti puṇṇamā, pubbakattikāya puṇṇamā pubbakattikapuṇṇamā, assayujapuṇṇamā. Sā hi pacchimakattikaṃ nivattetuṃ evaṃ vuttā. Tesaṃyevāti purimavassaṃvuṭṭhānaṃyeva. Bhaṇḍanakārakehīti kalahakārakehi. Paccukkaḍḍhantīti ukkaḍḍhanti. Bhaṇḍanakārakehi anuvādavasena assayujapuṇṇamādiṃ pariccajantā pavāraṇaṃ kāḷapakkhaṃ, juṇhapakkhanti uddhaṃ kaḍḍhantīti attho. “Suṇantu me āyasmanto āvāsikā, yadāyasmantānaṃ pattakallaṃ, idāni uposathaṃ kareyyāma, pātimokkhaṃ uddiseyyāma, āgame kāḷe pavāreyyāmā”ti (mahāva. 240) “suṇantu me āyasmanto āvāsikā, yadāyasmantānaṃ pattakallaṃ, idāni uposathaṃ kareyyāma, pātimokkhaṃ uddiseyyāma, āgame juṇhe pavāreyyāmā”ti ca evaṃ ñattiyā pavāraṇaṃ ukkaḍḍhantīti vuttaṃ hoti.

To show that they are not only Uposatha days, he says: 'the completion of the earlier rains-residence, etc.' The moon is called 'mā' because the day is measured by its movement; here, it is full (puṇṇo) with all its digits, thus it is a 'full moon' (puṇṇamā). The full moon of the earlier Kattikā is the Pubbakattikapuṇṇamā, that is, the Assayuja full moon. It is so called to distinguish it from the later Kattikā. 'Of those very ones' means: only of the completion of the earlier rains-residence. 'By quarrelmakers' means: by those who cause disputes. 'They postpone' means: they delay. The meaning is that, abandoning the Assayuja full moon and so on by way of the accusations of quarrelmakers, they postpone the Pavāraṇā to the dark fortnight or the bright fortnight. It is said that they postpone the Pavāraṇā by means of a motion thus: 'Venerable residents, let the venerable ones listen to me. If it is the proper time for the venerable ones, we should now perform the Uposatha and recite the Pātimokkha, and we should perform the Pavāraṇā in the coming dark fortnight' (Mahāvagga 240), and 'Venerable residents, let the venerable ones listen to me. If it is the proper time for the venerable ones, we should now perform the Uposatha and recite the Pātimokkha, and we should perform the Pavāraṇā in the coming bright fortnight.'

Athāti anantaratthe nipāto. Catuddasannaṃ pūraṇo cātuddaso, divaso. Yaṃ sandhāya “āgame juṇhe pavāreyyāmā”ti ñattiṃ ṭhapayiṃsu, tasmiṃ pana āgame juṇhe komudiyā cātumāsiniyā avassaṃ pavāretabbaṃ. Na hi taṃ atikkamitvā pavāretuṃ labbhati. Vuttañhetaṃ –

'Atha' is a particle in the sense of 'immediately after.' 'Cātuddaso' is the completion of fourteen, a day. With reference to which they established the motion, 'We should perform the Pavāraṇā in the coming bright fortnight,' on that coming bright fortnight, the Komudī at the end of the four months, the Pavāraṇā must certainly be performed. For it is not permissible to perform the Pavāraṇā after transgressing that time. For this has been said:

“Te ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhū bhaṇḍanakārakā kalahakārakā vivādakārakā bhassakārakā saṅghe adhikaraṇakārakā tampi juṇhaṃ anuvaseyyuṃ, tehi, bhikkhave, bhikkhūhi sabbeheva [V 0.0130] āgame [M 0.0135] juṇhe komudiyā cātumāsiniyā akāmā pavāretabba”nti (mahāva. 240).

‘If, monks, those monks—quarrelsome, contentious, disputatious, given to idle chatter, raising legal issues in the Saṅgha—should dwell through that bright fortnight too, then, monks, all those monks, even though unwilling, must perform the Pavāraṇā on the coming bright day, the Komudī at the end of the four months.’ (Mahāvagga 240).

Tenevāha “pacchimavassaṃvuṭṭhānañca pacchimakattikapuṇṇamā evā”ti. Yadi hi taṃ atikkamitvā pavāreyya, dukkaṭāpattiṃ āpajjeyya. Vuttañhetaṃ “na ca, bhikkhave, apavāraṇāya pavāretabbaṃ aññatra saṅghasāmaggiyā”ti (mahāva. 233). Visuddhipavāraṇāyogato pavāraṇādivasā. Pisaddena na kevalaṃ pavāraṇādivasāyeva, atha kho uposathadivasāpi hontīti dasseti. Idāni yo so sāmaggiuposathadivaso vutto, tañca tappasaṅgena sāmaggipavāraṇādivasañca dassento “yadā panā”tiādimāha.
