Osārite tasmiṃ bhikkhusminti ukkhittake bhikkhusmiṃ osārite, taṃ gahetvā sīmaṃ gantvā āpattiṃ desāpetvā kammavācāya kammappaṭippassaddhivasena pavesiteti vuttaṃ hoti. Tassa vatthussāti tassa adhikaraṇassa. Tadā ṭhapetvā…pe… uposathadivaso nāma hotīti sambandho. Kiṃ kāraṇanti āha “tāvadevā”tiādi. Tattha tāvadevāti taṃ divasameva. Vacanatoti kosambakakkhandhake (mahāva. 475) vuttattā. Yattha pana pattacīvarādīnaṃ atthāya appamattakena kāraṇena vivadantā uposathaṃ vā pavāraṇaṃ vā ṭhapenti, tattha tasmiṃ adhikaraṇe vinicchite “samaggā jātamhā”ti antarā sāmaggiuposathaṃ kātuṃ na labhanti. Karontehi anuposathe uposatho kato nāma hoti. Kattikamāsabbhantareti ettha kattikamāso nāma pubbakattikamāsassa kāḷapakkhapāṭipadato paṭṭhāya yāva aparakattikapuṇṇamā, tāva ekūnatiṃsarattidivo, tassabbhantare, tato pacchā vā pana pure vā na vaṭṭati. Ayameva yo koci divasoyeva. Idhāpi kosambakakkhandhake sāmaggiyā sadisāva sāmaggī veditabbā. Ye pana kismiñcideva appamattake pavāraṇaṃ ṭhapetvā samaggā honti, tehi pavāraṇāyameva pavāraṇā kātabbā, tāvadeva na kātabbā. Karontehi appavāraṇāya pavāraṇā katā hoti. Na kātabboyevāti niyamena yadi karoti, dukkaṭanti dasseti. Tattha hi uposathakaraṇe dukkaṭaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ “na, bhikkhave, anuposathe uposatho kātabbo aññatra saṅghasāmaggiyā”ti (mahāva. 183).

Therefore he said: 'The completion of the later rains-residence is indeed the full moon of the later Kattikā.' For if one were to perform the Pavāraṇā after transgressing that time, one would incur an offense of wrong-doing. For this has been said: 'Monks, the Pavāraṇā should not be performed on a non-Pavāraṇā day, except for the sake of the Saṅgha's harmony' (Mahāvagga 233). The Pavāraṇā days are so called due to their connection with the Pavāraṇā of purity. By the word 'also,' he shows that they are not only Pavāraṇā days, but also Uposatha days. Now, to show that Uposatha day of harmony which was mentioned, and in connection with it, the Pavāraṇā day of harmony, he says: 'But when…' and so on. 'When that monk has been reinstated' means: when the suspended monk has been reinstated, that is, it is said that he has been admitted by way of the revocation of the act through a formal procedure, after taking him, going to the boundary, and having him confess his offense. 'Of that matter' means: of that legal issue. The connection is: 'Then, having set aside… there is what is called an Uposatha day.' 'What is the reason?' He says: 'On that very day…' and so on. Therein, 'on that very day' means on that same day. 'Because of the statement' means: because it is stated in the Kosambaka Khandhaka (Mahāvagga 475). But where they suspend the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā while disputing over some trivial matter concerning bowls, robes, and so on, there, when that legal issue has been settled, they are not permitted to perform a Uposatha of harmony in the interim, saying, 'We have become harmonious.' If they do so, it is called a Uposatha performed on a non-Uposatha day. 'Within the month of Kattikā': here, the month of Kattikā is the twenty-nine days and nights from the first day of the dark fortnight of the earlier Kattikā month up to the full moon of the later Kattikā; it must be within that period, for it is not proper before or after. This means any day whatsoever within that period. Here too, the harmony should be understood as similar to the harmony in the Kosambaka Khandhaka. But those who become harmonious after suspending the Pavāraṇā over some trivial matter should perform the Pavāraṇā only on the Pavāraṇā day itself; it should not be done at that very time. If they do so, it is a Pavāraṇā performed on a non-Pavāraṇā day. The phrase 'It should absolutely not be done' shows that if one does it as a fixed rule, it is an offense of wrong-doing. For in that case, performing the Uposatha is an offense of wrong-doing. For this has been said: 'Monks, the Uposatha should not be performed on a non-Uposatha day, except for the sake of the Saṅgha's harmony' (Mahāvagga 183).

“Pattakālameva [M 0.0136] pattakalla”nti iminā sakatthe bhāvappaccayoti dasseti. Nāsatīti anvayato vuttameva byatirekato daḷhaṃ karoti.

By the phrase 'pattakallaṃ is just pattakālaṃ (the time has arrived),' he shows that the suffix indicating state is used in its own sense. 'It does not perish': by this negative statement, he reinforces what was already stated affirmatively.

Anurūpāti arahā anucchavikā, sāminoti vuttaṃ hoti. Sabbantimenāti sabbaheṭṭhimena cattāro, na tehi vinā taṃ uposathakammaṃ karīyati, na tesaṃ chando vā pārisuddhi vā eti. Avasesā [V 0.0131] pana sacepi sahassamattā honti, sace samānasaṃvāsakā, sabbe chandārahāva honti, chandapārisuddhiṃ datvā āgacchantu vā, mā vā, kammaṃ na kuppati. Pakatattāti anukkhittā, pārājikaṃ anajjhāpannā ca. Hatthapāso nāma diyaḍḍhahatthappamāṇo.

'Anurūpā' means worthy, suitable; it is said to mean 'master.' 'By all the last ones' means by the minimum of four. Without them that Uposatha act is not performed, nor does their consent or purity come. But as for the rest, even if they are a thousand, if they are in communion, they are all eligible to give their consent. Whether they come or not after giving their consent and purity, the act is not invalidated. 'Of normal status' means not suspended and not having committed a pārājika offense. 'Hatthapāsa' is the measure of one and a half cubits.

Sīmā ca nāmesā katamā, yattha hatthapāsaṃ avijahitvā ṭhitā kammappattā nāma hontīti anuyogaṃ sandhāya sīmaṃ dassento vibhāgavantānaṃ sabhāvavibhāvanaṃ vibhāgadassanamukheneva hotīti “sīmā ca nāmesā”tiādimāha. Sambhindantenāti missīkarontena. Ajjhottharantenāti maddantena, anto karontenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Imā vipattisīmāyo nāmāti sambandho. Kasmā vipattisīmāyo nāmāti āha “ekādasahī”tiādi. Ākārehīti kāraṇehi. Vacanatoti kammavagge (pari. 482 ādayo) kathitattā. Saṅghakammaṃ nāmetaṃ vīsativaggakaraṇīyaparamanti āha “yattha ekavīsati bhikkhū nisīdituṃ na sakkontī”ti. Yassaṃ sīmāyaṃ heṭṭhimaparicchedena kammārahena saddhiṃ ekavīsati bhikkhū parimaṇḍalākārena nisīdituṃ na sakkonti, ayaṃ atikhuddakā nāmāti attho. Evarūpā ca sīmā sammatāpi asammatā, gāmakhettasadisāva hoti, tattha kataṃ kammaṃ kuppati. Esa nayo sesasīmāsupi.

To show the boundary, with reference to the question, 'And what is this thing called a boundary, wherein those who are present for the act stand without leaving the hand's reach?'; and because the explanation of the nature of things for those who make distinctions occurs by way of showing the distinctions, he says: 'And what is this thing called a boundary?' etc. 'By combining' means by mixing. 'By overlapping' means by covering over; it is said to mean making it internal. The connection is: 'These are called invalid boundaries.' Why are they called invalid boundaries? He says: 'By eleven…' and so on. 'Modes' means reasons. 'Because of the statement' means because it is stated in the Kammavagga (Parivāra 482ff.). To show that this Saṅgha act has a maximum of twenty who can perform it, he says: 'where twenty-one monks cannot sit.' The meaning is: a boundary in which, as a minimum requirement, twenty-one monks eligible for the act cannot sit in a circle, is called 'too small.' Such a boundary, even if it has been agreed upon, is not properly agreed upon; it is just like a village field, and an act performed there is invalid. This is the method for the remaining boundaries as well.

Sammatāti baddhā, vācitakammavācāti attho. Kammavācāya vācanameva hi bandhanaṃ nāma. Nimittaṃ na upagacchatīti animittupago, taṃ animittupagaṃ, animittārahanti vuttaṃ hoti. Tacasārarukkho nāma tālanāḷikerādikā. Paṃsupuñjavālukāpuñjānanti paṃsurāsivālukārāsīnaṃ majjhe. Niddhāraṇe cetaṃ sāmivacanaṃ. Potthakesu pana katthaci “paṃsupuñjaṃ vā vālukāpuñjaṃ vā aññatara”nti pāṭho dissati, so pana apāṭho. Na hi so “aññatara”nti iminā yujjatīti. Antarāti nimittupaganimittānamantarā. Ettha [M 0.0137] ca yā tīhi nimittehi bajjhamānā animittupagesu tacasārarukkhādīsu aññataraṃ antarā ekaṃ nimittaṃ katvā sammatā, sā khaṇḍanimittā nāma hoti. Yā pana catupañcanimittādīhi bajjhamānā imesu tacasārarukkhādīsu aññataraṃ antarā ekaṃ nimittaṃ katvā sammatā, sā khaṇḍanimittā nāma na hotīti viññāyati nimittupagānaṃ nimittānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ sabbhāvato. Aṭṭhakathāsu pana avisesena vuttaṃ, tasmā upaparikkhitvā gahetabbaṃ. Sabbena sabbanti sabbappakārena. Nimittānaṃ bahi ṭhitena sammatāti tesaṃ bahi ṭhitena vācitakammavācā. Nimittāni pana anto ca bahi ca ṭhatvā kittetuṃ vaṭṭanti.

“Agreed upon” means bound; the meaning is by a recited formal act. For the very recitation of the formal act is what is called binding. One that does not serve as a sign is a non-sign-object; it is said to be suitable as a non-sign. A tree with its substance in the bark means such as a palmyra or coconut tree. “Of heaps of dust and heaps of sand” means in the middle of piles of dust and piles of sand; this is a genitive of specification. However, in some books the reading “a heap of dust or a heap of sand, one or the other” is seen, but this is not a correct reading, for it does not fit with “one or the other.” “Between” means between the objects suitable for signs and the signs themselves. Here, a boundary that is bound by three signs, having made one sign in between on one of the non-sign-objects such as a tree with its substance in the bark, and is then agreed upon, is called a boundary with a broken sign. But a boundary that is bound by four, five, or more signs, having made one sign in between on one of these non-sign-objects, and is then agreed upon, is not called a boundary with a broken sign. This is to be understood from the existence of three suitable signs. In the commentaries, however, this is stated without distinction; therefore, it should be accepted only after investigation. “In every respect” means in every way. “Agreed upon by one standing outside the signs” means by a formal act recited by one standing outside them. The signs, however, may be proclaimed while standing either inside or outside.

Evaṃ sammatāpīti nimittāni kittetvā kammavācāya sammatāpi. Imassa “asammatāva hotī”ti [V 0.0132] iminā sambandho. Sabbā, bhikkhave, nadī asīmāti yā kāci nadīlakkhaṇappattā nadī nimittāni kittetvā “etaṃ baddhasīmaṃ karomā”ti katāpi asīmā, baddhasīmā na hotīti attho. Attano sabhāvena pana sā baddhasīmāsadisā. Sabbattha saṅghakammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Samuddajātassaresupi eseva nayo. “Saṃsaṭṭhaviṭapā”ti iminā aññamaññassa āsannataṃ dīpeti. Baddhā hotīti pacchimadisābhāge sīmaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tassā padesanti tassā ekadesaṃ. Yattha ṭhatvā bhikkhūhi kammaṃ kātuṃ sakkā hoti, tādisaṃ ekadesanti vuttaṃ hoti. Yattha pana ṭhitehi kammaṃ kātuṃ na sakkā, tādisaṃ padesaṃ anto karitvā bandhantā sīmāya sīmaṃ sambhindanti nāma, na tu ajjhottharanti nāmāti gahetabbaṃ. Gaṇṭhipadesu pana “sambhindanaṃ paresaṃ sīmāya ekaṃ vā dve vā nimitte kittetvā lekhāmattaṃ gahetvā bandhanaṃ. Ajjhottharaṇaṃ nāma paresaṃ sīmāya nimitte kittetvā taṃ sakalaṃ vā tassekadesaṃ vā anto karontena tassā bahi ekissaṃ dvīsu vā disāsu nimitte kittetvā bandhana”nti vuttaṃ.

“Even when thus agreed upon” means: even when agreed upon by a formal act after proclaiming the signs. This is connected with the phrase “it is not agreed upon.” “Monks, every river is without a boundary” means: any river that has the characteristics of a river, even if it is made into a boundary by proclaiming signs and saying, “Let us make this a bound sīmā,” is without a boundary; the meaning is that it does not become a bound sīmā. By its own nature, however, it is like a bound sīmā. It is permissible to perform a formal act of the Sangha anywhere on it. The same principle applies to lakes originating from the ocean. “With intertwined branches” indicates their nearness to one another. “It is bound” is said with reference to the sīmā in the western direction. “A region of it” means a part of it. It is said to be such a part where it is possible for monks to stand and perform a formal act. But when, in binding a sīmā, they include a region where it is not possible to stand and perform a formal act, they are said to be “interfering with” a sīmā, not “overlapping” it; this is how it should be understood. In the Gaṇṭhipadas, however, it is said: “Interfering is the binding of a sīmā after proclaiming one or two signs of another’s sīmā and taking just a line’s measure. Overlapping is the binding of a sīmā by one who, having proclaimed the signs of another’s sīmā and included all of it or a part of it, proclaims signs in one or two directions outside it.”

Pabbatādīnaṃ nimittānaṃ sampadā nimittasampatti. Pabbatova nimittaṃ pabbatanimittaṃ. Evaṃ sesesupi. Evaṃ vuttesūti uposathakkhandhake (mahāva. 138 ādayo) sīmāsammutiyaṃ vuttesu. Imehi ca pana aṭṭhahi nimittehi asammissehipi aññamaññamissehipi sīmaṃ sammannituṃ vaṭṭati. Tenāha “tasmiṃ tasmiṃ disābhāge yathāladdhāni nimittupagāni nimittānī”ti. Ekena, pana dvīhi vā nimittehi sammannituṃ [M 0.0138] na vaṭṭati, tīṇi pana ādiṃ katvā vuttappakārānaṃ nimittānaṃ satenāpi vaṭṭati. “Puratthimāya disāya kiṃ nimitta”nti vinayadharena pucchitabbaṃ, “pabbato, bhante”ti vutte puna vinayadhareneva “eso pabbato nimitta”nti evaṃ nimittaṃ kittetabbaṃ. “Etaṃ pabbataṃ nimittaṃ karoma, nimittaṃ karissāma, nimittaṃ kato, nimittaṃ hotu, hoti bhavissatī”ti evaṃ pana kittetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Pāsāṇādīsupi eseva nayo. Tenāha “puratthimāya disāya kiṃ nimitta”ntiādi. “Pabbato, bhante, udakaṃ, bhante”ti evaṃ pana upasampanno vā ācikkhatu, anupasampanno vā, vaṭṭatiyeva. Ādisaddena “puratthimāya anudisāya kiṃ nimittaṃ? Pāsāṇo, bhante, eso pāsāṇo nimittaṃ. Dakkhiṇāya disāya, dakkhiṇāya anudisāya, pacchimāya disāya, pacchimāya anudisāya, uttarāya disāya, uttarāya anudisāya kiṃ nimittaṃ? Udakaṃ, bhante, etaṃ udakaṃ nimitta”nti idaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Ettha pana aṭṭhatvā puna “puratthimāya disāya kiṃ nimittaṃ? Pabbato, bhante, eso pabbato nimitta”nti evaṃ paṭhamaṃ kittitanimittaṃ kittetvāva ṭhapetabbaṃ. Evañhi nimittena nimittaṃ ghaṭitaṃ hoti. Sammā kittetvāti aññamaññanāmavipariyāyena, animittānaṃ nāmena ca akittetvā yathāvutteneva nayena kittetvā. Sammatāti “suṇātu me, bhante”tiādinā nayena uposathakkhandhake (mahāva. 139 ādayo) [V 0.0133] vuttāya parisuddhāya ñattidutiyakammavācāya baddhā. Tattha nimittāni sakiṃ kittitānipi kittitāneva honti. Andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana tikkhattuṃ sīmamaṇḍalaṃ sambandhantena nimittaṃ kittetabba”nti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 138) vuttaṃ.

The excellence of signs such as a mountain is the perfection of signs. A mountain itself as a sign is a mountain-sign. So too for the others. “When it is said thus” refers to what is said in the Uposatha Chapter about the authorization of a sīmā. It is permissible to authorize a sīmā with these eight signs, either unmixed or mixed with one another. Therefore he said: “In each respective direction, whatever suitable objects for signs are found are the signs.” However, it is not permissible to authorize a sīmā with one or two signs, but beginning with three, it is permissible even with a hundred signs of the kinds mentioned. The Vinaya expert should ask: “What is the sign in the eastern direction?” When it is said, “A mountain, venerable sir,” the Vinaya expert himself should again proclaim the sign thus: “This mountain is the sign.” But it is not permissible to proclaim it thus: “We make this mountain the sign,” “We will make it the sign,” “The sign has been made,” “Let it be the sign,” “It is the sign,” “It will be the sign.” The same principle applies to rocks and so on. Therefore it is said: “What is the sign in the eastern direction?” and so on. But it is permissible for either an ordained person or an unordained person to point it out, saying, “A mountain, venerable sir,” “Water, venerable sir.” By the word “etc.” is included: “What is the sign in the southeastern intermediate direction? A rock, venerable sir. This rock is the sign. What is the sign in the southern direction, the southwestern intermediate direction, the western direction, the northwestern intermediate direction, the northern direction, the northeastern intermediate direction? Water, venerable sir. This water is the sign.” Here, having proclaimed the eight, one must establish the boundary only after proclaiming the first-proclaimed sign again, thus: “What is the sign in the eastern direction? A mountain, venerable sir. This mountain is the sign.” For in this way a sign is connected with a sign. “Having proclaimed correctly” means having proclaimed in the way stated, without reversing their respective names and without proclaiming them by the name of non-signs. “Agreed upon” means bound by a pure formal act consisting of a motion and one announcement, stated in the Uposatha Chapter in the way beginning, “Venerable sirs, let the Sangha listen to me….” There, the signs, though proclaimed only once, are indeed proclaimed. In the Andhaka Commentary, however, it is said: “The sign should be proclaimed by one connecting the sīmā-circle three times.”

Tatrāti tesu aṭṭhasu nimittesu. Nimittupagatāti nimittayogyatā. “Hatthippamāṇato paṭṭhāyā”ti vacanato hatthippamāṇopi nimittupagoyeva. Hatthī pana sattaratano vā aḍḍhaṭṭharatano (sārattha. ṭī. mahāvagga 3.138) vā. Tato omakataroti tato hatthippamāṇato khuddakataro. Sace catūsu disāsu cattāro vā tīsu vā tayo pabbatā honti, catūhi, tīhi vā pabbatanimitteheva sammannitumpi vaṭṭati, dvīhi pana nimittehi, ekena vā sammannituṃ na vaṭṭati. Ito paresu pāsāṇanimittādīsupi eseva nayo. Tasmā pabbatanimittaṃ karontena pucchitabbaṃ “ekābaddho, na ekābaddho”ti. Sace [M 0.0139] ekābaddho hoti, na kātabbo. Tañhi catūsu vā aṭṭhasu vā disāsu kittentenāpi ekameva nimittaṃ kittitaṃ hoti. Tasmā yo evaṃ cakkasaṇṭhānena vihāraṃ parikkhipitvā ṭhito pabbato, taṃ ekadisāya kittetvā aññāsu disāsu taṃ bahiddhā katvā anto aññāni nimittāni kittetabbāni. Sace pabbatassa tatiyabhāgaṃ vā upaḍḍhaṃ vā antosīmāya kattukāmā honti, pabbataṃ akittetvā yattakaṃ padesaṃ anto kattukāmā, tassa parato tasmiṃyeva pabbate jātarukkhavammikādīsu aññataraṃ nimittaṃ kittetabbaṃ. Sace yojanadviyojanappamāṇaṃ sabbaṃ pabbataṃ anto kattukāmā honti, pabbatassa parato bhūmiyaṃ jātarukkhavammikādīni nimittāni kittetabbāni (mahāva. aṭṭha. 138; vi. saṅga. aṭṭha. 158).

“There” means among those eight signs. “Suitability as a sign” means fitness for a sign. According to the statement “beginning from the size of an elephant,” even an object the size of an elephant is suitable as a sign. An elephant, however, is seven or seven and a half ratanas. “Smaller than that” means smaller than the size of an elephant. If there are four mountains in the four directions or three in three directions, it is permissible to authorize the sīmā with four or three mountain-signs; but it is not permissible to authorize it with two signs or with one. This same principle applies to the other signs that follow, such as a stone-sign. Therefore, one making a mountain-sign should ask: “Is it a single continuous one or not a single continuous one?” If it is a single continuous one, it should not be made a sign. For then, even when proclaiming it in four or eight directions, only one sign has been proclaimed. Therefore, with a mountain that stands surrounding a monastery in the shape of a wheel, one should proclaim it in one direction, and in the other directions one should proclaim other signs inside, having placed that mountain outside. If they wish to make a third part or half of the mountain fall within the sīmā, without proclaiming the mountain, they should proclaim as a sign one of the things growing on that same mountain beyond the region they wish to include, such as a tree or an anthill. If they wish to include the entire mountain of one or two yojanas in extent, they should proclaim as signs things such as trees and anthills growing on the ground beyond the mountain.

Saṅkhaṃ gacchatīti gaṇanaṃ vohāraṃ gacchatīti attho. Dvattiṃsapalaguḷapiṇḍaparimāṇoti thūlatāya, na tulagaṇanāya. Tattha “ekapalaṃ nāma dasakalañja”nti vadanti. Iṭṭhakā mahantāpi na vaṭṭati. Tathā animittupagapāsāṇānaṃ rāsi, pageva paṃsuvālukārāsi. Bhūmisamo khalamaṇḍalasadiso piṭṭhipāsāṇo vā bhūmito khāṇuko viya uṭṭhitapāsāṇo vā hoti, sopi pamāṇūpago ce, vaṭṭati. “Piṭṭhipāsāṇo pana atimahantopi pāsāṇasaṅkhameva gacchatīti āha “piṭṭhipāsāṇo panā”tiādi. Tasmā sace mahato piṭṭhipāsāṇassa ekaṃ padesaṃ antosīmāyaṃ kattukāmā honti, taṃ akittetvā tassupari añño pāsāṇo kittetabbo. Sace piṭṭhipāsāṇupari vihāraṃ karonti, vihāramajjhena ca piṭṭhipāsāṇo vinivijjhitvā gacchati, evarūpo piṭṭhipāsāṇo na vaṭṭati. Sace hi taṃ kittenti, nimittassupari vihāro hoti, nimittañca [V 0.0134] nāma bahisīmāyaṃ hoti, vihāropi bahisīmāyaṃ āpajjati. Vihāraṃ parikkhipitvā ṭhitapiṭṭhipāsāṇo pana ekattha kittetvā aññattha na kittetabbo.

“It comes to be reckoned” means it comes to be counted, it enters into common usage. “The size of a lump of molasses of thirty-two palas” refers to its bulk, not to a calculation by weight. There, they say, “One pala is ten kalañjas.” Even a large brick is not allowable. Likewise a heap of stones not suitable for a boundary marker, and even more so a heap of soil or sand. A flat rock level with the ground like a threshing floor, or a rock that rises from the ground like a tree stump, is allowable if it is of a suitable size. It is said, “But a flat rock…,” etc., because even a very large flat rock is still reckoned as a rock. Therefore, if they wish to make one part of a large flat rock fall within the boundary, they should not designate that rock itself but should designate another rock placed on top of it. If they build a monastery on top of a flat rock, and the flat rock passes right through the middle of the monastery, such a flat rock is not allowable. For if they designate it, the monastery would be on top of the boundary marker, and the marker would be outside the boundary; thus the monastery too would fall outside the boundary. However, a flat rock that stands enclosing a monastery should be designated at one point and not designated elsewhere.

Vananimitte tiṇavanaṃ vā tacasārarukkhavanaṃ vā na vaṭṭatīti āha “antosārehī”tiādi. Antosārā nāma ambajambupanasādayo. Antosāramissakehīti anto sāro yesaṃ te antosārā, tehi missakā antosāramissakā, tehi. Catupañcarukkhamattampīti heṭṭhimaparicchedanāha[M 0.0140]. Ukkaṃsato pana yojanasatikampi vanaṃ vaṭṭati. Ettha pana caturukkhamattañce, tayo sārato, eko asārato. Pañcarukkhamattañce, tayo sārato, dve asāratoti gahetabbaṃ. Sace pana vanamajjhe vihāraṃ karonti, taṃ vanaṃ na kittetabbaṃ. Ekadesaṃ antosīmāyaṃ kattukāmehipi vanaṃ akittetvā tattha rukkhapāsāṇādayo kittetabbā, vihāraṃ parikkhipitvā ṭhitavanaṃ ekattha kittetvā aññattha na kittetabbaṃ (mahāva. aṭṭha. 138).

Regarding a forest as a boundary marker, it is said, “with heartwood…,” etc., because a forest of grass or a forest of trees with only bark and sapwood is not allowable. “Heartwood” trees are mango, rose-apple, jackfruit, and so on. “Mixed with those having heartwood” means: those whose core is heartwood are trees with heartwood; “mixed with those having heartwood” are those mixed with them. “As few as four or five trees” states the lower limit. As an upper limit, however, even a forest of a hundred yojanas is allowable. Here, if there are just four trees, it should be understood that three have heartwood and one is without heartwood. If there are five trees, three have heartwood and two are without heartwood. But if they build a monastery in the middle of a forest, that forest should not be designated. Even by those who wish to make a part of it fall within the boundary, the forest should not be designated; instead, trees, rocks, and so on in that place should be designated. A forest that stands enclosing a monastery should be designated at one point and not designated elsewhere.

Rukkhanimittepi tacasārarukkho na vaṭṭatīti āha “antosāro”ti. “Bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhito”ti iminā kuṭasarāvādīsu ṭhitaṃ paṭikkhipati. Tato apanetvā pana taṅkhaṇampi bhūmiyaṃ ropetvā koṭṭhakaṃ katvā udakaṃ āsiñcitvā kittetuṃ vaṭṭati, navamūlasākhāniggamanaṃ akāraṇaṃ. Khandhaṃ chinditvā ropite pana etaṃ yujjati. Sūcidaṇḍakappamāṇoti “sīhaḷadīpe lekhanadaṇḍappamāṇo”ti vadanti (sārattha. ṭī. mahāvagga 3.138), so ca kaniṭṭhaṅguliparimāṇoti daṭṭhabbo. Idaṃ pana rukkhanimittaṃ kittentena “rukkho”tipi, “sākarukkho, sālarukkho”tipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Ekābaddhaṃ pana suppatiṭṭhitanigrodhasadisaṃ rukkhaṃ ekattha kittetvā aññattha kittetuṃ na vaṭṭati.

Regarding a tree as a boundary marker, it is said “with heartwood” because a tree with only bark and sapwood is not allowable. By “established in the ground,” it rejects one standing in a pot, bowl, or the like. However, after removing it from there, it is allowable to plant it in the ground at that very moment, make an enclosure, water it, and designate it; the emergence of new roots and branches is not a prerequisite. But this is suitable when one plants it after cutting the trunk. “The size of a needle-stick”: they say, “It is the size of a writing stylus in the island of Sri Lanka,” and this should be understood as the size of the little finger. When designating this tree marker, it is allowable to say “a tree,” or “a teak tree,” “a sāl tree.” However, a single, connected, well-established tree like a banyan tree, having been designated in one place, is not to be designated in another.

Magganimitte araññakhettanadītaḷākamaggādayo na vaṭṭantīti āha “jaṅghamaggo vā hotū”tiādi. Yo pana jaṅghamaggo sakaṭamaggato okkamitvā puna sakaṭamaggameva otarati, ye vā jaṅghamaggasakaṭamaggā avalañjitā, te na vaṭṭanti. Tenāha “jaṅghasatthasakaṭasatthehī”tiādi. Ettha ca sace sakaṭamaggassa antimacakkamaggaṃ nimittaṃ karonti, maggo bahisīmāya hoti. Sace bāhiracakkamaggaṃ nimittaṃ karonti, bāhiracakkamaggova bahisīmāya hoti, sesaṃ antosīmaṃ bhajatīti veditabbaṃ. Sacepi dve maggā nikkhamitvā pacchā sakaṭadhuramiva ekībhavanti, dvidhā bhinnaṭṭhāne vā sambandhaṭṭhāne vā sakiṃ kittetvā puna na kittetabbā. Ekābaddhanimittañhetaṃ hoti.

Regarding a path as a boundary marker, it is said, “whether it be a footpath…,” etc., because paths through forests, fields, rivers, lakes, and so on are not allowable. However, a footpath that branches off from a cart track and then rejoins that same cart track, or footpaths and cart tracks that are disused, are not allowable. Therefore it is said, “by foot-travelers and by cart-caravans…,” etc. Here, if they make the inner wheel-rut of the cart track the boundary marker, the path is outside the boundary. If they make the outer wheel-rut the boundary marker, only the outer wheel-rut is outside the boundary; it should be understood that the rest belongs within the boundary. Even if two paths branch off and later become one like a cart's yoke, they should be designated once, either at the place where they split in two or at the place where they join, and not designated again. For this is a single connected boundary marker.

Sace [V 0.0135] vihāraṃ parikkhipitvā cattāro maggā catūsu disāsu gacchanti, majjhe ekaṃ kittetvā aparaṃ kittetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Ekābaddhanimittañhetaṃ. Koṇaṃ vinivijjhitvā gataṃ pana parabhāge kittetuṃ vaṭṭati. Vihāramajjhena [M 0.0141] vinivijjhitvā gatamaggo pana na kittetabbo. Kittite pana nimittassa upari vihāro hoti. Imañca maggaṃ kittentena “maggo pajjo patho”tiādinā (cūḷani. pārāyanatthutigāthāniddesa 101) vuttesu dasasu nāmesu yena kenaci nāmena kittetuṃ vaṭṭati. Parikhāsaṇṭhānena vihāraṃ parikkhipitvā gatamaggo ekattha kittetvā aññattha kittetuṃ na vaṭṭati.

If four paths go in the four directions enclosing a monastery, having designated one in the middle, it is not allowable to designate another. This is a single connected boundary marker. However, one that passes through a corner is allowable to be designated on the other side. But a path that passes right through the middle of the monastery should not be designated. If it is designated, the monastery would be on top of the boundary marker. When designating this path, it is allowable to designate it by any of the ten names mentioned, such as “maggo, pajjo, patho,” and so on. A path that goes enclosing a monastery in the shape of a moat, having been designated in one place, is not to be designated elsewhere.

Yaṃ pana abaddhasīmālakkhaṇe nadiṃ vakkhāmāti “yassā dhammikānaṃ rājūnaṃ kāle”tiādinā (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. nidānavaṇṇanā) udakukkhepasīmāyaṃ nadiyā vakkhamānattā vuttaṃ. Yā pana nadī maggo viya sakaṭadhurasaṇṭhānena vā parikhāsaṇṭhānena vā vihāraṃ parikkhipitvā gatā, naṃ ekattha kittetvā aññattha kittetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Vihārassa catūsu disāsu aññamaññaṃ vinivijjhitvā gate nadīcatukkepi eseva nayo. Asammissanadiyo pana catassopi kittetuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace vatiṃ karonto viya rukkhapāde nikhaṇitvā vallipalālādīhi nadīsotaṃ rumbhanti, udakampi ajjhottharitvā āvaraṇaṃ pavattatiyeva, nimittaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Yathā pana udakaṃ nappavattati, evaṃ setumhi kate appavattamānā nadī nimittaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Pavattanaṭṭhāne nadīnimittaṃ, appavattanaṭṭhāne udakanimittaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati.

What was said, 'We will speak of a river in the characteristic of an unfixed boundary,' was said because a river is spoken of in the context of a water-throwing boundary with the words, 'at the time of righteous kings,' and so on (Kkh.A. Nidānavaṇṇanā). However, a river that has gone enclosing a monastery in the shape of a cart-yoke or a moat, having been designated in one place, is not to be designated elsewhere. This same principle applies also to a set of four rivers that pass through one another in the four directions of the monastery. But four unmixed rivers are all allowable to be designated. If, as if making a dike, they dig at the foot of trees and block the river's current with creepers, straw, and so on, and the water, having overflowed it, the barrier still remains, it is allowable to make it a boundary marker. When a dam has been built, a non-flowing river is not allowable to be made a boundary marker. It is allowable to make a river-marker at a place where it flows, and a water-marker at a place where it does not flow.

Yā pana dubbuṭṭhikāle vā gimhe vā nirudakabhāvena nappavattati, sā vaṭṭati. Mahānadito udakamātikaṃ nīharanti, sā kunnadīsadisā hutvā tīṇi sassāni sampādentī niccaṃ pavattati. Kiñcāpi pavattati, nimittaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Yā pana mūle mahānadito niggatāpi kālantarena teneva niggatamaggena nadiṃ bhinditvā sayameva gacchati, gacchantī ca parato susumārādisamākiṇṇā nāvādīhi sañcaritabbā nadī hoti, taṃ nimittaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati.

But a river that does not flow during a time of poor rain or in the summer due to being without water, is allowable. They lead a water channel from a great river; becoming like a small river and producing three crops, it flows constantly. Although it flows, it is not allowable to make it a boundary marker. But a channel that, though originally having gone out from a great river, after some time breaks through to the river by that same outlet-path and goes on its own, and in its course further on becomes a river to be traveled by boats and so on, teeming with crocodiles and so on, that is allowable to be made a boundary marker.

Asandamānanti appavattamānaṃ. Sandamānaṃ nāma oghanadīudakavāhakamātikāsu udakaṃ. Vuttaparicchedakālaṃ atiṭṭhantanti “yāva kammavācāpariyosānā saṇṭhamānaka”nti vuttaparicchedakālaṃ atiṭṭhantaṃ. Bhājanagatanti nāvācāṭiādīsu bhājanesu gataṃ. Yaṃ pana andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “gambhīresu āvāṭādīsu ukkhepimaṃ udakaṃ nimittaṃ na kātabba”nti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 138; vi. saṅga. aṭṭha. 158) vuttaṃ, taṃ duvuttaṃ[M 0.0142], attano matimattameva. Ṭhitaṃ pana antamaso sūkarakhatāyapi gāmadārakānaṃ kīḷanavāpiyampi sace yāva kammavācāpariyosānaṃ tiṭṭhati, appaṃ vā [V 0.0136] hotu, bahu vā, vaṭṭatiyeva. Tasmiṃ pana ṭhāne nimittasaññākaraṇatthaṃ pāsāṇavālikāpaṃsuādirāsi vā pāsāṇatthambho vā dārutthambho vā kātabbo.

'Not flowing' means not moving. 'Flowing' is water in floods, rivers, and water-carrying channels. 'Not remaining for the specified period of time' means not remaining for the specified period, which is stated as 'remaining until the conclusion of the formal act.' 'Contained in a vessel' means contained in vessels such as a boat, a jar, or the like. However, what is said in the Andhaka Commentary, 'Water drawn up into deep pits and the like should not be made a boundary marker' (Mhv.A. 138; Vism.A. 158), is wrongly said; it is merely their own opinion. But standing water, even in a pig's wallow or a village children's play-pond, if it remains until the conclusion of the formal act, whether it is a little or a lot, is indeed allowable. But at that spot, for the purpose of making a sign for the boundary marker, a heap of stones, sand, soil, or the like, or a stone pillar or a wooden pillar should be made.

Evaṃ nimittasampattiyuttataṃ dassetvā idāni yehi ākārehi baddhā parisāsampattiyuttā nāma hoti, taṃ dassetuṃ “parisāsampattiyā yuttā nāmā”tiādimāha. Imassa pana kammassa catuvaggakaraṇīyattā “catūhi bhikkhūhī”ti vuttaṃ. Imañca sīmaṃ bandhitukāmehi sāmantavihāresu bhikkhū tassa tassa vihārassa sīmāparicchedaṃ pucchitvā baddhasīmavihārānaṃ sīmāya sīmantarikaṃ, abaddhasīmavihārānaṃ sīmāya upacāraṃ ṭhapetvā disācārikabhikkhūnaṃ nissañcārasamaye sace ekasmiṃ gāmakhette sīmaṃ bandhitukāmā, ye tattha baddhasīmavihārā, tesu bhikkhūnaṃ “mayaṃ ajja sīmaṃ bandhissāma, tumhe sakasakasīmāparicchedato mā nikkhamitthā”ti pesetabbaṃ. Ye abaddhasīmavihārā, tesu bhikkhū ekajjhaṃ sannipātāpetabbā, chandārahānaṃ chando āharāpetabbo. Tena vuttaṃ “yāvatikā tasmiṃ gāmakhette”tiādi. Tasmiṃ gāmakhetteti yasmiṃ gāmakhette ṭhatvā kammavācaṃ vācenti, tasmiṃ gāmakhette. “Sace aññānipi gāmakhettāni anto kattukāmā, tesu gāmesu ye bhikkhū vasanti, tehipi āgantabbaṃ, anāgacchantānaṃ chando āharitabbo”ti mahāsumatthero āha. Mahāpadumatthero panāha “nānāgāmakhettāni nāma pāṭiyekkaṃ baddhasīmāsadisāni, na tato chandapārisuddhi āgacchati. Antonimittagatehi pana bhikkhūhi āgantabba”nti vatvā puna āha “samānasaṃvāsakasīmāsammannanakāle āgamanampi anāgamanampi vaṭṭati, avippavāsasīmāsammannanakāle pana antonimittagatehi āgantabbaṃ. Anāgacchantānaṃ chando āharitabbo”ti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 138).

Having thus shown its connection with the accomplishment of the markers, now, to show the ways in which an established boundary is connected with the accomplishment of the assembly, he says: “Connected with the accomplishment of the assembly, it is called,” and so on. Further, because this act is to be performed by a group of four, it is said: “by four bhikkhus.” Those who wish to establish this boundary should ask the bhikkhus in the surrounding monasteries about the boundary limits of each monastery. For monasteries with established boundaries, an intermediate space (sīmantarikā) should be left at their boundary; for monasteries without established boundaries, their precincts (upacāra) should be set aside. At a time when wandering bhikkhus are not traveling, if they wish to establish a boundary in a single village-field, a message should be sent to the bhikkhus in the monasteries with established boundaries there, saying: “Today we will establish a boundary. Do not go beyond the limits of your own boundaries.” The bhikkhus in monasteries without established boundaries should be assembled together, and the consent of those eligible to give it should be obtained. Hence it is said: “As many as are in that village-field,” and so on. “In that village-field” means in the village-field where they stand while reciting the formal act. The Elder Mahāsuma said: “If they wish to include other village-fields within, the bhikkhus who reside in those villages must also come; the consent of those not coming must be obtained.” But the Elder Mahāpaduma said: “Different village-fields are like individually established boundaries; purity of consent does not come from there. But the bhikkhus who have gone within the markers must come.” And he said further: “At the time of authorizing a boundary for common communion (samānasaṃvāsakasīmā), it is permissible to come or not to come. But at the time of authorizing a boundary for non-separation (avippavāsasīmā), those who have gone within the markers must come. The consent of those not coming must be obtained” (Mahāva. Aṭṭha. 138).

Idāni yehi ākārehi sammatā kammavācāsampattiyuttā nāma hoti, taṃ dassetuṃ “kammavācāsampattiyā yuttā nāmā”tiādimāha. Ādisaddena. “Yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, saṅgho etehi nimittehi sīmaṃ sammanneyya samānasaṃvāsaṃ ekūposathaṃ, esā ñatti. Suṇātu [M 0.0143] me, bhante, saṅgho, yāvatā samantā nimittā kittitā, saṅgho etehi nimittehi sīmaṃ sammannati samānasaṃvāsaṃ ekūposathaṃ, yassāyasmato khamati etehi nimittehi sīmāya sammuti samānasaṃvāsāya ekūposathāya, so tuṇhassa. Yassa nakkhamati, so bhāseyya. Sammatā sīmā saṅghena etehi nimittehi samānasaṃvāsā ekūposathā, khamati saṅghassa, tasmā tuṇhī, evametaṃ dhārayāmī”ti (mahāva. 139) imaṃ pāḷisesaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Vuttāyāti uposathakkhandhake vuttāya. Ñattidosaanussāvanadosehi virahitattā parisuddhāya.

Now, to show the ways in which an authorized boundary is connected with the accomplishment of the formal act, he says: “Connected with the accomplishment of the formal act, it is called,” and so on. By the word “and so on,” this remaining portion of the Pāli text is included: “If it is the proper time for the Sangha, the Sangha should authorize a boundary with these markers for common communion and a single Uposatha observance. This is the motion. Venerable sirs, let the Sangha hear me. The markers all around have been proclaimed. The Sangha authorizes a boundary with these markers for common communion and a single Uposatha observance. If the authorization of the boundary with these markers for common communion and a single Uposatha observance is agreeable to any venerable one, he should be silent. If it is not agreeable to anyone, he should speak. This boundary has been authorized by the Sangha with these markers for common communion and a single Uposatha observance. It is agreeable to the Sangha, therefore it is silent. Thus do I hold it” (Mahāva. 139). “As stated” means as stated in the Chapter on the Uposatha. Because it is free from defects in the motion and the proclamations, it is pure.

Khaṇḍasīmā (mahāva. aṭṭha. 138; sārattha. ṭī. mahāvagga 3.138; vajira. ṭī. mahāvagga 138) [V 0.0137] nāma khuddakasīmā. Samānasaṃvāsakatthaṃ sammatā sīmā samānasaṃvāsakasīmā. Avippavāsatthaṃ sammatā sīmā avippavāsasīmā. Imāsu pana tīsu sīmaṃ sammannantehi pabbajjupasampadādīnaṃ saṅghakammānaṃ sukhakaraṇatthaṃ paṭhamaṃ khaṇḍasīmā bandhitabbā. Taṃ pana bandhantehi vattaṃ jānitabbaṃ. Sace hi bodhicetiyabhattasālādīni sabbavatthūni patiṭṭhāpetvā katavihāre bandhanti, vihāramajjhe bahūnaṃ samosaraṇaṭṭhāne abandhitvā vihārapaccante vivittokāse bandhitabbā. Akatavihāre bandhantehi bodhicetiyādīnaṃ sabbavatthūnaṃ ṭhānaṃ sallakkhetvā yathā patiṭṭhitesu vatthūsu vihārapaccante vivittokāse hoti, evaṃ bandhitabbā. Sā heṭṭhimaparicchedena sace ekavīsatibhikkhū gaṇhāti, vaṭṭati. Tato oraṃ na vaṭṭati. Paraṃ bhikkhusahassaṃ gaṇhantīpi vaṭṭati. Taṃ bandhantehi sīmāmāḷakassa samantā nimittupagā pāsāṇā ṭhapetabbā, na khaṇḍasīmāya ṭhitehi mahāsīmā bandhitabbā, na mahāsīmāya ṭhitehi khaṇḍasīmā. Khaṇḍasīmāyameva pana ṭhatvā khaṇḍasīmā bandhitabbā, mahāsīmāyameva ṭhatvā mahāsīmā.

A partial boundary (khaṇḍasīmā) (Mahāva. Aṭṭha. 138; Sārattha. Ṭī. Mahāvagga 3.138; Vajira. Ṭī. Mahāvagga 138) is a small boundary. A boundary authorized for the purpose of common communion is a boundary for common communion (samānasaṃvāsakasīmā). A boundary authorized for the purpose of non-separation is a boundary for non-separation (avippavāsasīmā). Among these three, when authorizing a boundary, a partial boundary should first be established for the convenient performance of formal acts of the Sangha such as the going forth and the higher ordination. But when establishing it, the procedure should be known. If they are establishing it in a monastery where all the structures such as the Bodhi-tree shrine and the meal hall have already been erected, it should not be established in the middle of the monastery in a place where many assemble, but in a secluded place on the outskirts of the monastery. When establishing it in a monastery that has not yet been built, having determined the location of all the structures such as the Bodhi-tree shrine, it should be established so that when the structures are erected, it will be in a secluded place on the outskirts of the monastery. If, at its minimum extent, it can hold twenty-one bhikkhus, it is valid. Less than that is not valid. It is valid even if it can hold up to a thousand bhikkhus. When establishing it, stones that serve as markers should be placed all around the boundary hall (sīmāmāḷaka). A great boundary should not be established by those standing in a partial boundary, nor a partial boundary by those standing in a great boundary. Rather, a partial boundary should be established only by standing in a partial boundary, and a great boundary only by standing in a great boundary.

Tatrāyaṃ bandhanavidhi – samantā “eso pāsāṇo nimitta”nti evaṃ nimittāni kittetvā kammavācāya sīmā sammannitabbā. Atha tassā eva daḷhīkammatthaṃ avippavāsakammavācā kātabbā. Evañhi “sīmaṃ samūhanissāmā”ti āgatā samūhanituṃ na sakkhissanti. Sīmaṃ sammannitvā bahi sīmantarikapāsāṇā ṭhapetabbā, sīmantarikā pacchimakoṭiyā caturaṅgulappamāṇāpi (mahāva. aṭṭha. 138; vi. saṅga. aṭṭha. 163) vaṭṭati. Sace pana vihāro mahā hoti, dvepi tissopi tatuttaripi khaṇḍasīmāyo bandhitabbā.

Herein, this is the method of establishing it: having proclaimed the markers all around, saying, “This stone is a marker,” the boundary should be authorized by a formal act. Then, for the sake of strengthening it, a formal act of non-separation should be performed. For in this way, those who come intending, “We will remove the boundary,” will not be able to remove it. Having authorized the boundary, stones for the intermediate boundary should be placed outside. An intermediate boundary (sīmantarikā) of the measure of four finger-breadths at its final edge is permissible (Mahāva. Aṭṭha. 138; Vi. Saṅga. Aṭṭha. 163). If, however, the monastery is large, two, three, or even more partial boundaries may be established.

Evaṃ [M 0.0144] khaṇḍasīmaṃ sammannitvā mahāsīmāsammutikāle khaṇḍasīmato nikkhamitvā mahāsīmāyaṃ ṭhatvā samantā anupariyāyantehi sīmantarikapāsāṇā kittetabbā. Tato avasesanimitte kittetvā hatthapāsaṃ avijahantehi kammavācāya samānasaṃvāsakasīmaṃ sammannitvā tassā daḷhīkammatthaṃ avippavāsakammavācāpi kātabbā. Evañhi “sīmaṃ samūhanissāmā”ti āgatā samūhanituṃ na sakkhissanti. Sace pana khaṇḍasīmāya nimittāni kittetvā tato sīmantarikāya nimittāni kittetvā mahāsīmāya nimittāni kittenti, evaṃ tīsu ṭhānesu nimittāni kittetvā yaṃ sīmaṃ icchanti, taṃ paṭhamaṃ bandhituṃ vaṭṭati. Evaṃ santepi yathāvuttanayena khaṇḍasīmatova paṭṭhāya bandhitabbā. Evaṃ baddhāsu pana sīmāsu khaṇḍasīmāyaṃ ṭhitā bhikkhū mahāsīmāyaṃ kammaṃ karontānaṃ na kopenti, mahāsīmāyaṃ vā ṭhitā khaṇḍasīmāyaṃ karontānaṃ. Sīmantarikāya pana ṭhitā ubhinnampi na kopanti. Gāmakhette ṭhatvā kammaṃ karontānaṃ [V 0.0138] pana sīmantarikāya ṭhitā kopenti. Sīmantarikā hi gāmakhettaṃ bhajati. Avippavāsasīmāsammannane kate sati sā ca avippavāsasīmā nāma hoti. Tenāha “tassāyeva pabhedo”ti. Tassāyevāti baddhasīmāya eva.

Having thus authorized a partial boundary, at the time of authorizing the great boundary, one should leave the partial boundary, stand in the great boundary, and the stones of the intermediate boundary should be proclaimed by those going around it on all sides. Then, having proclaimed the remaining markers, without leaving hand’s-reach, one should authorize the boundary for common communion by a formal act, and to strengthen it, a formal act of non-separation should also be performed. For in this way, those who come intending, “We will remove the boundary,” will not be able to remove it. If, however, having proclaimed the markers of the partial boundary, then the markers of the intermediate boundary, they then proclaim the markers of the great boundary—having thus proclaimed the markers in three places—it is permissible to establish first whichever boundary they wish. Even so, in the way described, they should be established beginning from the partial boundary. When the boundaries have been thus established, bhikkhus standing in the partial boundary do not invalidate the act of those performing an act in the great boundary, nor do those standing in the great boundary invalidate the act of those in the partial boundary. Those standing in the intermediate boundary do not invalidate the act of either. However, those standing in the intermediate boundary do invalidate the act of those performing an act while standing in a village-field, for the intermediate boundary is included in the village-field. When the authorization of the boundary for non-separation has been done, that is called a boundary for non-separation. Therefore he said: “It is a subdivision of that same one.” “Of that same one” means of the established boundary itself.

Ayaṃ pana viseso – “ṭhapetvā gāmañca gāmūpacārañcā”ti (mahāva. 144) vacanato avippavāsasīmā gāmañca gāmūpacārañca na otarati, samānasaṃvāsakasīmā pana tatthāpi otarati. Samānasaṃvāsakasīmā cettha attano dhammatāya gacchati, avippavāsasīmā pana yattha samānasaṃvāsakasīmā, tattheva gacchati. Na hi tassā visuṃ nimittakittanaṃ atthi. Tattha sace avippavāsāya sammutikāle gāmo atthi, taṃ sā na otarati. Sace pana sammatāya sīmāya pacchā gāmo nivisati, sopi sīmāsaṅkhameva gacchati. Yathā ca pacchā niviṭṭho, evaṃ paṭhamaṃ niviṭṭhassa pacchā vaḍḍhitappadesopi sīmāsaṅkhameva gacchati. Sacepi sīmāsammutikāle gehāni katāni, “pavisissāmā”ti ālayopi atthi, manussā pana appaviṭṭhā, porāṇagāmaṃ vā sagehameva chaḍḍetvā aññattha gatā, agāmoyeva esa, sīmā otarati. Sace pana ekampi kulaṃ paviṭṭhaṃ vā agataṃ vā atthi, gāmoyeva, sīmā na otarati.

This, however, is the difference: in accordance with the text “excluding the village and the village precincts” (Mahāva. 144), the boundary for non-separation does not extend over the village and the village precincts, but the boundary for common communion does extend over them. Herein, the boundary for common communion proceeds according to its own principle, but the boundary for non-separation extends only as far as the boundary for common communion. For it has no separate proclamation of markers. In this regard, if a village exists at the time of the authorization of the boundary for non-separation, the boundary does not extend over it. But if a village is settled after the boundary has been authorized, it too is reckoned as boundary. And just as a later settlement, so too a region added later to an original settlement is reckoned as boundary. Even if houses have been built at the time of the authorization of the boundary, and there is an attachment with the thought, “We will enter,” but humans have not yet entered, or they have abandoned an old village with its houses and gone elsewhere, it is a non-village, and the boundary extends over it. But if even one family has entered or has not left, it is a village, and the boundary does not extend over it.

Evaṃ [M 0.0145] baddhasīmaṃ dassetvā idāni abaddhasīmaṃ dassento “abaddhasīmā panā”tiādimāha. Gāmo eva sīmā gāmasīmā. Gāmaggahaṇena cettha nigamanagarānampi saṅgaho veditabbo. Yattake padese tassa gāmassa gāmabhojakā baliṃ labhanti, so padeso appo vā hotu, mahanto vā, ekaṃ gāmakhettaṃ nāma. Yampi ekasmiṃyeva gāmakhette ekaṃ padesaṃ “ayaṃ visuṃ gāmo hotū”ti paricchinditvā rājā kassaci deti, sopi visuṃgāmasīmā hotiyeva. Tasmā sā ca itarā ca pakatigāmasīmā baddhasīmāsadisāva hoti. Kevalaṃ pana ticīvaravippavāsaparihāraṃ na labhatīti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 147).

Having thus shown the fixed boundary, now, to show the unfixed boundary, he says, “But an unfixed boundary…,” and so on. The village itself is the boundary; this is a village-boundary. And here, by the taking up of “village,” the inclusion of towns and cities should be understood. Whatever is the region in which the headmen of that village receive tribute, whether that region is small or large, it is called a single village-field. Even if, within a single village-field, the king demarcates a certain region, saying, “Let this be a separate village,” and gives it to someone, that too becomes a separate village-boundary. Therefore, both that and the other, the natural village-boundary, are similar to a fixed boundary. However, it does not obtain the exemption from being separated from the three robes (Mahāva. Aṭṭha. 147).

Agāmake araññeti viñjhāṭavisadise araññe. Tenāha “agāmakaṃ nāmā”tiādi. Ayaṃ pana sīmā ticīvaravippavāsaparihārampi labhati. Macchabandhānanti kevaṭṭānaṃ. Agamanapathesūti gantuṃ asakkuṇeyyapathesu. Yattha tadaheva gantvā tadaheva paccāgantuṃ na sakkā hoti, tādisesūti vuttaṃ hoti. Tesaṃ gamanapariyantassa orato pana gāmasīmāsaṅkhaṃ gacchati. Tattha gāmasīmaṃ asodhetvā kammaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Majjhe ṭhitānaṃ sabbadisāsu sattabbhantarāti majjhe ṭhitānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ṭhitokāsato sabbadisāsu sattabbhantarā. Tatthāti tesu abbhantaresu. Tasmāti yasmā parisavasena vaḍḍhati, tasmā. Upacāratthāyāti sīmopacāratthāya. Sīmābhāvaṃ paṭikkhipitvāti [V 0.0139] baddhasīmābhāvaṃ paṭikkhipitvā. Samāno saṃvāso etthāti samānasaṃvāsā. Eko uposatho etthāti ekūposathā. Ettha ca uposathassa visuṃ gahitattā avasesakammavasena samānasaṃvāsatā veditabbā. Vuttāti abaddhasīmāparicchedaṃ dassetuṃ uposathakkhandhake (mahāva. 149) vuttā. Anu anu aḍḍhamāsaṃ anvaḍḍhamāsaṃ, aḍḍhamāse aḍḍhamāseti attho. Evaṃ “anudasāha”ntiādīsupi. Deveti meghe. Valāhakesu vigatamattesūti bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇe bhummaṃ. Sotanti udakappavāho vuccati. Titthena vā atitthena vā otaritvāti pāṭhaseso. Timaṇḍalaṃ paṭicchādetvāti yathā timaṇḍalapaṭicchādanaṃ hoti, evaṃ nivāsetvā. Uttarantiyāti yattha katthaci uttarantiyā. Bhikkhunīvibhaṅge (pāci. 692) bhikkhuniyā vasena nadīlakkhaṇassa pāḷiyaṃ āgatattā “bhikkhuniyā”ti vuttaṃ, na pana visesasabbhāvato.

“In a villageless wilderness” means in a wilderness like the Viñjhāṭavi forest. Hence he says, “A villageless place is…” and so on. This boundary, however, also obtains the exemption from being separated from the three robes. “Of fishermen” means of fishermen. “On impassable paths” means on paths where one cannot go. It is said to mean such places where one cannot go and return on the very same day. But within the limit of their travel, it is reckoned as a village-boundary. There, it is not allowable to perform a formal act without having cleared the village-boundary. “Seven abbhantaras in all directions for those standing in the middle” means seven abbhantaras in all directions from the place where the bhikkhus standing in the middle are. “There” means within those abbhantaras. “Therefore” means: because it increases according to the assembly, therefore. “For the sake of the approach” means for the sake of the boundary’s approach. “Having rejected the state of being a boundary” means having rejected the state of being a fixed boundary. “Those with a common communion” means those for whom there is a common communion here. “Those with a single Uposatha” means those for whom there is one Uposatha here. And here, since the Uposatha is taken up separately, common communion should be understood in regard to the remaining formal acts. “Said” means said in the Uposatha Chapter (Mahāva. 149) to show the delimitation of an unfixed boundary. `Anvaḍḍhamāsaṃ` means every half-month; the meaning is “every half-month.” Similarly also for “every ten days,” and so on. “When it rains” means when there are clouds. “As soon as the thunderclouds have dispersed” is a locative absolute expressing a condition. “A stream” means a current of water. “Having descended by a ford or not by a ford” is the rest of the text. “Covering the three circles” means having dressed in such a way that there is covering of the three circles. “Of one crossing” means of one crossing anywhere. In the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga (Pāc. 692), because the characteristic of a river has come down in the Pāḷi text in connection with a bhikkhunī, it is said “of a bhikkhunī,” not because of the existence of a special case.

Kenaci [M 0.0146] khaṇitvā akatoti antamaso tiracchānenapi khaṇitvā akato. Nadiṃ vā samuddaṃ vā bhinditvāti nadīkūlaṃ vā samuddavelaṃ vā bhinditvā. Etaṃ lakkhaṇanti “yattha nadiyaṃ vuttappakāre vassakāle udakaṃ santiṭṭhatī”ti (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. nidānavaṇṇanā) vuttappakāralakkhaṇaṃ. Loṇīpi jātassarasaṅkhameva gacchati. Yattha pana vuttappakāre vassakāle vasse pacchinnamatte pivituṃ vā hatthapāde dhovituṃ vā udakaṃ na hoti sukkhati, ayaṃ jātassaro gāmakhettasaṅkhameva gacchati.

“Not made by being dug by someone” means not made by being dug even by an animal. “Having breached a river or the sea” means having breached a riverbank or the seashore. “This is the characteristic” means the characteristic of the aforesaid kind, as stated: “where water remains in the river during the rainy season in the aforesaid manner” (Kaṅkhā. Aṭṭha. Nidānavaṇṇanā). A salt-pan also is reckoned as a natural lake. But where, in the aforesaid manner, during the rainy season, as soon as the rain has ceased, there is no water for drinking or for washing hands and feet, and it dries up, this natural lake is reckoned as a village-field.

Udakukkhepāti karaṇatthe nissakkavacananti āha “udakukkhepenā”ti. Kathaṃ pana udakaṃ khipitabbanti āha “tatthā”tiādi. Majjhimena purisenāti thāmamajjhimena purisena. Ayaṃ udakukkhepo nāmāti ayaṃ udakukkhepena paricchinnā sīmā nāmāti attho. Yāva parisā vaḍḍhati, tāva ayaṃ sīmāpi vaḍḍhati, parisapariyantato udakukkhepoyeva pamāṇaṃ. Sace pana nadī nātidīghā hoti, pabhavato paṭṭhāya yāva mukhadvāraṃ sabbattha saṅgho nisīdati, udakukkhepasīmākammaṃ natthi. Sakalāpi nadī etesaṃyeva bhikkhūnaṃ pahoti.

“A water-throw” (`udakukkhepa`): he says “by a water-throw” (`udakukkhepena`) because this is a statement in the instrumental sense. But how should the water be thrown? He says, “There…,” and so on. “By a man of middle stature” means by a man of medium strength. “This is called a water-throw” means: this is the boundary defined by a water-throw. As the assembly increases, so this boundary also increases; the water-throw itself is the measure from the limit of the assembly. But if the river is not very long, and the Saṅgha sits everywhere from its source up to its mouth, there is no formal act of a water-throw boundary. The entire river is sufficient for just these bhikkhus.

Pakativassakāleti pubbe vuttappakāre pakativassakāle. Catūsu māsesūti vassānassa catūsu māsesu. Ativuṭṭhikāle oghena otthatokāso na gahetabbo. So hi gāmasīmāsaṅkhameva gacchati. Antonadiyaṃ jātassare jātapiṭṭhipāsāṇadīpakesupi ayameva vinicchayo veditabbo. Sace pana nadī paripuṇṇā hoti samatitthikā, udakasāṭikaṃ nivāsetvāpi antonadiyaṃyeva kammaṃ kātabbaṃ. Sace na sakkonti, nāvāyapi ṭhatvā kātabbaṃ. Gacchantiyā pana nāvāya kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Kasmā? Udakukkhepamattameva hi sīmā, taṃ [V 0.0140] nāvā sīghameva atikkāmeti. Evaṃ sati aññissā sīmāya ñatti, aññissā anussāvanā hoti, tasmā nāvaṃ arittena vā ṭhapetvā, pāsāṇe vā lambitvā, antonadiyaṃ jātarukkhe vā bandhitvā kammaṃ kātabbaṃ. Antonadiyaṃ baddhaaṭṭakepi antonadiyaṃ jātarukkhepi ṭhitehi kammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati.

“During the normal rainy season” means during the normal rainy season of the aforesaid kind. “In the four months” means in the four months of the rains-residence. At a time of excessive rain, a place submerged by a flood should not be taken, for it is reckoned only as a village-boundary. This same decision should be understood also for a natural lake, a naturally formed sandbank, a rock, and an islet within a river. But if the river is full and has even fords, having put on a bathing cloth, the formal act should be done right within the river. If they are unable, it should be done while standing on a boat. But it is not allowable to do it from a moving boat. Why? Because the boundary is only the measure of a water-throw, and the boat quickly passes beyond it. This being so, the motion would be in one boundary and the proclamation in another. Therefore, the formal act should be done after having stopped the boat with an oar, or having moored it to a rock, or having tied it to a tree that has grown within the river. It is allowable to perform the formal act while standing on a platform constructed within the river or on a tree that has grown within the river.

Sace pana rukkhassa sākhā vā tato nikkhantapāroho vā bahinadītīre vihārasīmāya vā gāmasīmāya vā patiṭṭhito, sīmaṃ vā sodhetvā, sākhaṃ [M 0.0147] vā chinditvā kammaṃ kātabbaṃ. Bahinadītīre jātarukkhassa antonadiyaṃ paviṭṭhasākhāya vā pārohe vā nāvaṃ bandhitvā kammaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Karontehi sīmā vā sodhetabbā, sākhaṃ chinditvā vā tassa bahipatiṭṭhitabhāgo nāsetabbo. Nadītīre pana khāṇukaṃ koṭṭetvā tattha bandhanāvāya na vaṭṭatiyeva.

But if a branch of the tree or a shoot coming from it is established on the bank outside the river, within a monastery-boundary or a village-boundary, the formal act should be done after having either cleared the boundary or cut the branch. It is not allowable to perform the formal act by tying a boat to a branch or a shoot that has entered into the river from a tree that has grown on the bank outside the river. Those who do so should either clear the boundary, or they should cut the branch and destroy the part of it that is established outside. But on the riverbank, it is absolutely not allowable to tie a boat there after having driven in a stake.

Nadiyaṃ setuṃ karonti, sace antonadiyaṃyeva setu vā setupādā vā, setumhi ṭhitehi kammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace pana setu vā setupādā vā bahitīre patiṭṭhitā, kammaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati, sīmaṃ sodhetvā kammaṃ kātabbaṃ. Atha setupādā anto, setu pana ubhinnampi tīrānaṃ upariākāse ṭhito, vaṭṭati. Jātassarepi eseva nayo.

They build a bridge over a river. If the bridge or the bridge-posts are right within the river, it is allowable to perform a formal act while standing on the bridge. But if the bridge or the bridge-posts are established on the bank outside, it is not allowable to perform the formal act; the formal act should be done after having cleared the boundary. Now, if the bridge-posts are inside, but the bridge stands in the space above both banks, it is allowable. This is the same method for a natural lake.

“Yasmiṃ padese pakativīciyo ottharitvā saṇṭhahantī”ti etena yaṃ padesaṃ uddhaṃ vaḍḍhanakaudakaṃ vā pakativīciyo vā vegena āgantvā ottharanti, tattha kammaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭatīti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 147) dasseti. Sace ūmivego bādhati, nāvāya vā aṭṭake vā ṭhatvā kātabbaṃ. Tesu vinicchayo nadiyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Sace pana samuddo gāmasīmaṃ vā nigamasīmaṃ vā ottharitvā tiṭṭhati, samuddova hoti. Tattha kammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Tato paṭṭhāya kappiyabhūmīti ottharitvā saṇṭhitaudakantato paṭṭhāya anto nadījātassarasamuddo nāmāti attho. Dubbuṭṭhikāleti vassānahemante sandhāya vuttaṃ. Sukkhesupīti nirudakesupi. Yathā ca vāpikhaṇane, evaṃ āvāṭapokkharaṇīādīnaṃ khaṇanepi gāmakhettaṃ hotiyevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Vappaṃ vā karontīti lābutipusakādivappaṃ vā karonti. Taṃ ṭhānanti yattha vāpiādikaṃ kataṃ, taṃ ṭhānaṃ. Aññaṃ pana kappiyabhūmi. Sace pana jātassaraṃ pūretvā thalaṃ karonti, ekasmiṃ disābhāge pāḷiṃ bandhitvā sabbameva naṃ mahātaḷākaṃ vā karonti, sabbopi ajātassaro hoti. Gāmasīmāsaṅkhameva gacchati.

By the phrase, “In which region the normal waves spread and settle,” he shows that it is not allowable to perform a formal act in a region that rising floodwaters or normal waves, coming with force, spread over (Mahāva. Aṭṭha. 147). If the force of the waves is an obstacle, it should be done while standing on a boat or a platform. The decision in these cases should be understood in the same way as stated for a river. But if the sea spreads over a village-boundary or a town-boundary and remains, it becomes the sea itself. It is allowable to perform a formal act there. “From that point on it is allowable ground” means: from the limit of the water that has spread and settled, the inside is called river, natural lake, or sea. “At a time of poor rain” is said in reference to the rainy season and winter. “Even when dry” means even when without water. And just as in the digging of a reservoir, so too in the digging of pits, ponds, and so on, it should be seen that it is still a village-field. “Or they make a sown field” means they make a field sown with gourds, cucumbers, and so on. “That place” means the place where the reservoir, etc., has been made. But the other is allowable ground. But if they fill up a natural lake and make it dry land, or if they build an embankment in one part and make the whole thing into a large tank, the whole of it becomes a non-natural lake. It is reckoned only as a village-boundary.

Sace [V 0.0141] nadimpi vināsetvā taḷākaṃ karonti, heṭṭhā pāḷi baddhā, udakaṃ āgantvā taḷākaṃ pūretvā tiṭṭhati, ettha kammaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Upari pavattanaṭṭhāne chaḍḍitaṃ udakaṃ nadiṃ ottharitvā sandanaṭṭhānato paṭṭhāya vaṭṭati. Kāci nadī kālantarena uppatitvā gāmanigamasīmaṃ ottharitvā pavattati, nadīyeva [M 0.0148] hoti, kammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace vihārasīmaṃ ottharati “vihārasīmā”tveva saṅkhaṃ gacchati. Tasmāti yasmā anto gacchati, tasmā. Samantā udakukkhepaparicchedo kātabboti pahonakaṭṭhānaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Yattha pana kunnadīādīsu nappahoti, tattha pahonakaṭṭhānato udakukkhepaparicchedo kātabbo. Upacāratthāyāti sīmopacāratthāya.

If, having destroyed a river, they make a pond, and a bank is built downstream, and water comes and fills the pond and remains there, it is not permissible to perform a legal act there. It is permissible from the point of flowing, where water thrown at the upstream flowing place has overflowed the river. If some river, after a time, arises and flows, overflowing the boundary of villages and towns, it is still a river, and it is permissible to perform a legal act there. If it overflows the monastery boundary, it is reckoned as 'monastery boundary' itself. The word 'therefore' (tasmā) is used because it enters within. 'The measurement of a water-throw should be made all around' is said with reference to a place where it is sufficient. But where it is not sufficient, such as in small streams and so forth, the measurement of a water-throw should be made from a sufficient place. 'For the purpose of proximity' (upacāratthāya) means 'for the purpose of the boundary's proximity' (sīmopacāratthāya).

Kasmā pana aññamekaṃ sattabbhantaraṃ, añño eko udakukkhepo ca upacāratthāya ṭhapetabboti āha “ayaṃ hī”tiādi. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti (sārattha. ṭī. mahāvagga 3.147; vi. vi. ṭī. mahāvagga 2.147) – yasmā ayaṃ sattabbhantarasīmā ca udakukkhepasīmā ca bhikkhūnaṃ ṭhitokāsato paṭṭhāya labbhati, te ca bhikkhū na sabbadā ekasadisā, kadāci vaḍḍhanti, kadāci parihāyanti. Yadā ca vaḍḍhanti, tadā sīmāsaṅkaro hoti. Tasmā aññamekaṃ sattabbhantaraṃ, añño eko udakukkhepo ca upacāratthāya ṭhapetabboti. Yaṃ pana mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “tato adhikaṃ vaṭṭatiyeva, ūnakaṃ pana na vaṭṭatī”ti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 147) vuttaṃ, tampi etadatthameva, na pana tattha katassa kammassa kuppattāti gahetabbaṃ. Paricchedato bahi aññaṃ tattakaṃyeva paricchedaṃ anatikkamitvā ṭhitopīti attano sattabbhantarena, udakukkhepena vā yo tesaṃ sattabbhantarassa, udakukkhepassa vā paricchedo, tato bahi aññaṃ tattakaṃyeva paricchedaṃ anatikkamitvā ṭhitopīti attho. Kathametaṃ viññāyatīti āha “idaṃ sabbaaṭṭhakathāsu sanniṭṭhāna”nti, idaṃ “kammaṃ kopetī”ti mahāaṭṭhakathādīsu vavatthānanti attho. “Iti ima”ntiādi yathāvuttassa nigamanaṃ. Hoti cettha –

But why should another single sattabbhantara and another single udakukkhepa be established for the purpose of upacāra? It is said, “This is because…” and so on. This is what is meant (Sārattha. Ṭī. Mahāvagga 3.147; Vi. Vi. Ṭī. Mahāvagga 2.147): Because this sattabbhantara boundary and udakukkhepa boundary are obtained starting from the place where the monks are staying, and those monks are not always the same in number—sometimes they increase, sometimes they decrease. And when they increase, there is a confusion of boundaries. Therefore, another single sattabbhantara and another single udakukkhepa should be established for the purpose of upacāra. Now, what is stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā—“Beyond that, it is still valid, but less than that is not valid” (Mahāva. Aṭṭha. 147)—that too has this same meaning. However, it should not be taken to mean that the act performed there is thereby invalidated. The phrase 'even if one stands outside the boundary, without exceeding another boundary of that same measure' means this: standing outside the boundary determined by one's own sattabbhantara or udakukkhepa, without exceeding another boundary of that same measure. How is this understood? It is said, “This is the conclusion in all the commentaries,” meaning, this is the determination in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā and others concerning the statement, 'it invalidates the act.' “Thus, this…” and so on is the conclusion of what has been stated. Herein is this:

“Baddhābaddhavasenedha, sīmā nāma dvidhā tahiṃ;

Tisampattiyuttā vajji-tekādasa vipattikā;

Baddhasīmā tidhā khaṇḍā-dito gāmādito parā”ti.

Herein, by way of bound and unbound, the boundary is twofold; endowed with three accomplishments, it should be free from thirteen faults; the bound boundary is threefold: beginning with the fragmented, beginning with the village, and the other.

Sabhāgāpatti ca nāmesā duvidhā vatthusabhāgā, āpattisabhāgāti. Tattha idha vatthusabhāgā adhippetā, netarāti dassetuṃ “yaṃ sabbo saṅgho vikālabhojanādinā”tiādimāha. Lahukāpattinti lahukena vinayakammena visujjhanato lahukā thullaccayapācittiyapāṭidesanīyadukkaṭadubbhāsitasaṅkhātā pañcāpattiyo. Vatthusabhāgāya saṅghādisesāpattiyāpi sati uposathakammaṃ pattakallaṃ [V 0.0142] na hotiyeva. Yathāha [M 0.0149] “sabhāgasaṅghādisesaṃ āpannassa pana santike āvi kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Sace āvi karoti, āpatti āvikatā hoti, dukkaṭā pana na muccatī”ti (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 102). Tassā pana adesanāgāminito evaṃ vuttaṃ. Vatthusabhāgāti vatthuvasena samānabhāgā, ekakoṭṭhāsāti vuttaṃ hoti. Imameva vatthusabhāgaṃ desetuṃ na vaṭṭati “na, bhikkhave, sabhāgā āpatti desetabbā, yo deseyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 169) vuttattā, na pana āpattisabhāgaṃ. Tenāha “vikālabhojanapaccayā āpannaṃ panā”tiādi. Āpattisabhāganti āpattiyā samānabhāgaṃ.

An offense of the same kind (sabhāgāpatti) is of two kinds: sharing the same basis (vatthusabhāga) and sharing the same offense (āpattisabhāga). Here, sharing the same basis is intended, not the other, as shown by the statement, “Whatever the entire Saṅgha has committed, such as eating at the wrong time, etc.” A light offense refers to the five offenses—thullaccaya, pācittiya, pāṭidesanīya, dukkaṭa, and dubbhāsita—which are purified by a light disciplinary action. Even if there is a saṅghādisesa offense sharing the same basis, the Uposatha ceremony is not properly performed. As it is said, “For one who has committed a saṅghādisesa offense sharing the same basis, it is not permissible to reveal it in the presence of the Saṅgha. If he does reveal it, the offense is considered revealed, but he is not freed from the dukkaṭa offense” (Cūḷavagga, Aṭṭhakathā 102). However, since it leads to non-confession, it is stated thus. “Sharing the same basis” means sharing the same ground, or being in the same category, in terms of the object (vatthu). It is not permissible to confess this very offense sharing the same basis, as it is said, “Monks, an offense sharing the same basis should not be confessed. Whoever confesses it commits a dukkaṭa offense” (Mahāvagga 169). But this does not apply to sharing the same offense. Hence, it is said, “But if one has committed an offense due to the condition of eating at the wrong time, etc.” “Sharing the same offense” means sharing the same type of offense.

Sāmantā āvāsāti sāmantaāvāsaṃ, samīpavihāranti attho. Sajjukanti tadahevāgamanatthāya. Pāhetabboti pesetabbo. Iccetaṃ kusalanti iti etaṃ sundaraṃ bhaddakaṃ, laddhakappanti vuttaṃ hoti. No ce labhethāti vihārānaṃ dūratāya vā magge paripanthādinā vā yadi na labhetha. “Tassa santike paṭikarissatī”ti iminā vacanena sabhāgāpatti āvi kātumpi na labbhatīti dīpitaṃ hoti. Yadi labheyya, āvi katvāpi uposathaṃ kareyya. Yadi pana sabbo saṅgho sabhāgaṃ saṅghādisesaṃ āpanno hoti, ñattiṃ ṭhapetvā uposathaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati, uposathassa antarāyova hoti. Ubhopi dukkaṭaṃ āpajjanti “na, bhikkhave, sabhāgā āpatti desetabbā, yo deseyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Na, bhikkhave, sabhāgā āpatti paṭiggahetabbā, yo paṭiggaṇheyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 169) vuttattā. Vimati saṃsayo, tattha niyutto vematiko. “Puna nibbematiko hutvā desetabbamevā”ti neva pāḷiyaṃ, na ca aṭṭhakathāyaṃ atthi, desite pana doso natthi. Vuttanayenevāti “pārisuddhiṃ āyasmanto ārocethā”tiādinā nayena sāpattikassa uposathakaraṇe paññattaṃ dukkaṭaṃ āpajjantīti vuttanayeneva. Kasmā sabhāgāpattiyeva vuttāti āha “etāsu hī”tiādi. Visabhāgāpattīsu vijjamānāsupi pattakallaṃ hotiyevāti visabhāgāsu pana vijjamānāsu tesaṃyeva puggalānaṃ āpatti, na saṅghassāti saṅghassa pattakallaṃ hotiyeva.

'A neighboring residence' means a residence nearby; the meaning is a dwelling in close proximity. 'Immediately' means for the purpose of arriving on the very same day. 'Should be sent' means to be dispatched. 'This is skillful' means this is good and excellent; 'having obtained what is fitting,' is what is said. 'If he does not obtain it' means if he does not succeed due to the distance of the residences or obstacles on the path, etc. By the statement, 'Let him make amends in his presence,' it is shown that it is not possible even to reveal a shared offense. If he were to succeed, he should reveal it and then perform the Uposatha. However, if the entire Saṅgha has committed a shared Saṅghādisesa offense, it is not permissible to perform the Uposatha after proposing the motion; it becomes an obstacle to the Uposatha. Both commit a dukkaṭa offense, because it is said: 'Monks, a shared offense should not be confessed. Whoever confesses it commits a dukkaṭa offense. Monks, a shared offense should not be accepted. Whoever accepts it commits a dukkaṭa offense' (Mahāvagga 169). 'Doubt' means uncertainty; one who is bound by it is 'one with doubt.' The statement, 'Then, having become free from doubt, it should indeed be confessed,' is found neither in the Pāli Canon nor in the commentaries, but there is no fault in confessing. 'In the same way as stated' means: in the same way as it has been stated that they incur the dukkaṭa offense prescribed for one with an offense performing the Uposatha according to the method beginning with 'Venerables, declare your purity.' Why is only a shared offense mentioned? It is said, 'For in these cases...' Even if dissimilar offenses are present, it is still proper to perform the Uposatha; for when dissimilar offenses exist, they are the offenses of those individuals only, not of the Saṅgha, and therefore it is still proper for the Saṅgha.

Antimavatthuajjhāpannako nāma catunnaṃ pārājikānaṃ aññataraṃ ajjhāpannako. Paṇḍakādīnaṃ vinicchayo parato pārājikuddese āvi bhavissati[M 0.0150]. Tiracchānagatoti antamaso sakkaṃ devarājānaṃ upādāya yo koci nāgamāṇavakādiko amanussajātiko veditabbo, na assagoṇādayo. Tenāha “ettha cā”tiādi. Tattha etthāti etissaṃ vajjanīyapuggalakathāyaṃ. Yassa upasampadā paṭikkhittāti “tiracchānagato, bhikkhave, anupasampanno, na upasampādetabbo”ti (mahāva. 111) yassa nāgasupaṇṇādino tiracchānagatassa upasampadā paṭikkhittā[V 0.0143], so idhāpi tiracchānagato nāmāti attho. Tattha hi antamaso deve upādāya nāgamāṇavakādiko yo koci amanussajātiko “tiracchānagato”ti adhippeto. Vuttañhi samantapāsādikāyaṃ “tiracchānagato, bhikkhaveti ettha nāgo vā hotu supaṇṇamāṇavakādīnaṃ vā aññataro, antamaso sakkaṃ devarājānaṃ upādāya yo koci amanussajātiyo, so sabbova imasmiṃ atthe ‘tiracchānagato’ti veditabbo”ti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 111). Titthaṃ vuccati laddhi, taṃ etesaṃ atthīti titthikā, titthikā eva titthiyā, ito aññaladdhikāti attho.

The one who has committed the ultimate offense is one who has committed any of the four pārājikas. The decision on eunuchs and others will become clear later in the exposition of the pārājikas. 'One of animal birth' should be understood as any non-human being, up to and including Sakka, king of the devas, such as a nāga youth or the like, but not horses, cattle, and so on. Therefore it is said, 'And here,' etc. Therein, 'here' means in this discussion on individuals who are to be rejected. 'One whose higher ordination is prohibited' means: 'Monks, one of animal birth is without higher ordination; he should not be given the higher ordination' (Mahāvagga 111). One whose higher ordination is prohibited, such as a nāga, a supaṇṇa, or another of animal birth, is here also called 'one of animal birth'; this is the meaning. For here, 'one of animal birth' is intended to mean any non-human being, such as a nāga youth, up to and including the devas. For it is said in the Samantapāsādikā: '“Monks, one of animal birth”—here, whether it be a nāga or one of the supaṇṇa youths and so on, up to and including Sakka, king of the devas, any non-human being should be understood in this sense as “one of animal birth”' (Mahāvagga Aṭṭha. 111). 'Tittha' is a term for a doctrine; those who have this are 'titthikas.' 'Titthikas' are the same as 'titthiyas,' meaning those of another doctrine than this.

Suttassa uddeso suttuddeso. Pārisuddhi eva uposatho pārisuddhiuposatho. Eseva nayo adhiṭṭhānuposathoti etthāpi. Soti pātimokkhuddeso. Ovādova pātimokkhaṃ, tassa uddeso sarūpena kathanaṃ ovādapātimokkhuddeso. “Imasmiṃ vītikkame ayaṃ nāma āpattī”ti evaṃ āpattivasena āṇāpanaṃ paññāpanaṃ āṇā, sesaṃ anantarasadisameva.

The recitation of the Sutta is the Sutta-recitation. Purity itself is the Uposatha, the purity-Uposatha. This same method applies also to the determination-Uposatha. That is the Pātimokkha-recitation. The exhortation itself is the Pātimokkha; its recitation, which is the teaching in its own form, is the exhortation-Pātimokkha-recitation. 'In this transgression, this is the name of the offense'—thus, the command is the announcement and declaration by way of the offense; the rest is just like what immediately precedes it.

Khantī paramaṃ tapo titikkhā…pe… vuttā tisso gāthāyo nāma –

Patience, forbearance, is the supreme austerity… and so on… the three verses spoken are as follows:

“Khantī paramaṃ tapo titikkhā;

Nibbānaṃ paramaṃ vadanti buddhā;

Na hi pabbajito parūpaghātī;

Na samaṇo hoti paraṃ viheṭhayanto.

Patience, forbearance, is the supreme austerity; the Buddhas declare Nibbāna to be supreme. One who harms others is not a renunciate; one who harasses another is not an ascetic.

“Sabbapāpassa akaraṇaṃ, kusalassa upasampadā;

Sacittapariyodapanaṃ, etaṃ buddhāna sāsanaṃ.

The non-doing of any evil, the undertaking of what is wholesome, the purification of one's own mind—this is the teaching of the Buddhas.

“Anūpavādo [M 0.0151] anūpaghāto, pātimokkhe ca saṃvaro;

Mattaññutā ca bhattasmiṃ, pantañca sayanāsanaṃ;

Adhicitte ca āyogo, etaṃ buddhāna sāsana”nti.(dī. ni. 2.90; dha. pa. 183-185) –

Not reviling, not harming, and restraint in the Pātimokkha; and moderation in food, and a secluded lodging; and application to the higher mind—this is the teaching of the Buddhas.

Imā tisso gāthāyo.

These are the three verses.

Tattha khantī paramaṃ tapoti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.90; dha. pa. aṭṭha. 2.185) adhivāsanakhanti [V 0.0144] nāma paramaṃ tapo. Titikkhāti khantiyā eva vevacanaṃ, titikkhāsaṅkhātā adhivāsanakhanti uttamaṃ tapoti attho. Nibbānaṃ paramaṃ vadantīti sabbākārena pana nibbānaṃ “parama”nti vadanti buddhā. Na hi pabbajito parūpaghātīti yo adhivāsanakhantivirahitattā paraṃ upaghāteti bādhati vihiṃsati, so pabbajito nāma na hoti. Catutthapādo pana tasseva vevacanaṃ. “Na hi pabbajito”ti etassa hi “nasamaṇo hotī”ti vevacanaṃ. “Parūpaghātī”ti etassa “paraṃ viheṭhayanto”ti vevacanaṃ. Atha vā parūpaghātīti sīlūpaghātī. Sīlañhi uttamaṭṭhena “para”nti vuccati. Yo ca samaṇo paraṃ yaṃ kañci sattaṃ viheṭhayanto parūpaghātī hoti, attano sīlavināsako, so pabbajito nāma na hotīti attho. Atha vā yo adhivāsanakhantiyā abhāvā parūpaghātī hoti, paraṃ antamaso ḍaṃsamakasampi sañcicca jīvitā voropeti, so na hi pabbajito. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Malassa apabbājitattā. “Pabbājayamattano malaṃ, tasmā ‘pabbajito’ti vuccatī”ti (dha. pa. 388) idañhi pabbajitalakkhaṇaṃ. Yopi na heva kho upaghāteti na māreti, apica daṇḍādīhi viheṭheti, so paraṃ viheṭhayanto samaṇo na hoti. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Vihesāya asamitattā. “Samitattā hi pāpānaṃ, ‘samaṇo’ti pavuccatī”ti (dha. pa. 265) idañhi samaṇalakkhaṇaṃ.

Therein, 'patience is the supreme austerity' (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.90; Dhp. Aṭṭha. 2.185) means that enduring patience is the supreme austerity. 'Forbearance' is a synonym for patience; the meaning is that enduring patience, known as forbearance, is the supreme austerity. 'The Buddhas declare Nibbāna to be supreme' means that the Buddhas declare Nibbāna to be 'supreme' in every way. 'One who harms others is not a renunciate' means that whoever, being devoid of enduring patience, harms, injures, or hurts another, is not called a renunciate. The fourth line is a synonym for this. For 'is not a renunciate' is a synonym for 'is not an ascetic.' 'One who harms others' is a synonym for 'one who harasses another.' Alternatively, 'one who harms others' means one who harms virtue. For virtue, in the ultimate sense, is called 'para' (other/supreme). And any ascetic who, while harassing any being whatsoever, harms others and destroys his own virtue, is not a renunciate; this is the meaning. Or, whoever, due to the absence of enduring patience, harms others—intentionally depriving even a gadfly or a mosquito of life—is not a renunciate. For what reason? Because his defilements have not been driven out. For 'He drives out his own defilements, therefore he is called a “renunciate”' (Dhp 388): this is the characteristic of a renunciate. And one who does not kill, but harasses with sticks and the like, such a one who harasses another is not an ascetic. For what reason? Because his vexation has not been pacified. For 'Through the pacification of evils, one is called an “ascetic”' (Dhp 265): this is the characteristic of an ascetic.

Dutiyagāthāya sabbapāpassāti sabbākusalassa. Akaraṇanti anuppādanaṃ. Kusalassāti catubhūmakakusalassa. Upasampadāti upasampādanaṃ paṭilābho. Sacittapariyodapananti attano cittassa vodāpanaṃ pabhassarabhāvakaraṇaṃ sabbaso parisodhanaṃ, taṃ pana arahattena hoti. Iti sīlasaṃvarena sabbapāpaṃ pahāya lokiyalokuttarāhi samathavipassanāhi kusalaṃ sampādetvā arahattaphalena cittaṃ pariyodāpetabbanti etaṃ buddhānaṃ sāsanaṃ ovādo anusiṭṭhi.

In the second verse, 'of all evil' means of all that is unwholesome. 'The non-doing' means its non-arising. 'Of the wholesome' refers to the wholesome of the four planes. 'The undertaking' means its acquisition and attainment. 'The purification of one's own mind' is the cleansing of one's own mind, making it radiant, its thorough purification; this is achieved through Arahantship. Thus, by abandoning all evil through restraint in virtue, accomplishing what is wholesome through mundane and supramundane serenity and insight, and purifying the mind with the fruit of Arahantship—this is the teaching, the exhortation, the instruction of the Buddhas.

Tatiyagāthāya [M 0.0152] anūpavādoti vācāya kassaci anupavadanaṃ. Anūpaghātoti kāyena kassaci upaghātassa akaraṇaṃ. Pātimokkheti yaṃ taṃ pātimokkhaṃ paatimokkhaṃ atipamokkhaṃ uttamaṃ sīlaṃ, pāti vā agativisesehi, mokkheti duggatibhayehi. Yo vā naṃ pāti, taṃ mokkhetīti “pātimokkha”nti vuccati, tasmiṃ pātimokkhe ca. Saṃvaroti sattannaṃ āpattikkhandhānaṃ avītikkamalakkhaṇo saṃvaro. Mattaññutāti paṭiggahaṇaparibhogavasena pamāṇaññutā. Pantañca sayanāsananti janasaṅghaṭṭanavirahitaṃ nijjanasambādhaṃ vivittaṃ, senāsanañca. Ettha ca dvihiyeva paccayehi catupaccayasantoso dīpitoti veditabbo paccayasantosasāmaññena itaradvayassāpi lakkhaṇahāranayena jotitattā.
