Sace pana kassaci rājā kuddho hoti, so “evaṃ me sotthi bhavissatī”ti sayameva liṅgaṃ gahetvā palāyati. Taṃ disvā rañño ārocenti. Rājā “sace pabbajito, na taṃ labbhā kiñci kātu”nti tasmiṃ kodhaṃ paṭivineti. So “vūpasantaṃ me rājabhaya”nti saṅghamajjhaṃ anosaritvāva [M 0.0170] gihiliṅgaṃ gahetvā āgato pabbājetabbo. Athāpi “sāsanaṃ nissāya mayā jīvitaṃ laddhaṃ, handa dāni ahaṃ pabbajāmī”ti uppannasaṃvego teneva liṅgena āgantvā āgantukavattaṃ na sādiyati, bhikkhūhi puṭṭho vā apuṭṭho vā yathābhūtamattānaṃ āvikatvāva pabbajjaṃ yācati, liṅgaṃ apanetvā pabbājetabbo. Sace pana vattaṃ sādiyati, pabbajitālayaṃ dasseti, sabbaṃ pubbe vuttaṃ vassagaṇanādibhedaṃ paṭipajjati, ayaṃ pana na pabbājetabbo.

If a king becomes angry with someone, that person, thinking, 'Thus I will be safe,' takes on the outward sign himself and flees. Seeing him, they inform the king. The king, thinking, 'If he has gone forth, nothing can be done to him,' abandons his anger toward him. That person, thinking, 'The danger from the king has passed,' without having approached the midst of the Sangha, comes back having taken the lay sign; he should be given the going-forth. But if, with a sense of spiritual urgency having arisen, thinking, 'I have gained my life by relying on the Dispensation; now I will go forth,' he comes back with that same outward sign but does not perform the duties of a newcomer, and when questioned by the monks or even unasked, he reveals himself as he truly is and requests the going-forth, the outward sign should be removed, and he should be given the going-forth. If, however, he performs the duties, shows an inclination for the ordained life, and follows all the previously mentioned procedures, such as the counting of years, this one, however, should not be given the going-forth.

Idha panekacco dubbhikkhe jīvituṃ asakkonto sayameva liṅgaṃ gahetvā sabbapāsaṇḍiyabhattāni [V 0.0161] bhuñjanto dubbhikkhe vītivatte saṅghamajjhaṃ anosaritvāva gihiliṅgaṃ gahetvā āgatoti sabbaṃ purimasadisameva.

Here, a certain person, unable to live during a famine, takes on the outward sign himself and eats the food of all sectarians. When the famine has passed, without having approached the midst of the Sangha, he comes back having taken the lay sign. Everything is just like the previous case.

Aparo mahākantāraṃ nittharitukāmo hoti, satthavāho ca pabbajite gahetvā gacchati. So “evaṃ maṃ satthavāho gahetvā gamissatī”ti sayameva liṅgaṃ gahetvā satthavāhena saddhiṃ kantāraṃ nittharitvā khemantaṃ patvā saṅghamajjhaṃ anosaritvāva gihiliṅgaṃ gahetvā āgatoti sabbaṃ purimasadisameva.

Another wishes to cross a great wilderness, and a caravan leader takes ordained ones along. Thinking, 'Thus the caravan leader will take me along,' he takes the outward sign himself and crosses the wilderness with the caravan leader. Having reached a safe place, without having approached the midst of the Sangha, he comes back having taken the lay sign. Everything is just like the previous case.

Aparo rogabhaye (mahāva. aṭṭha. 110; vi. saṅga. aṭṭha. 138) uppanne jīvituṃ asakkonto sayameva liṅgaṃ gahetvā sabbapāsaṇḍiyabhattāni bhuñjanto rogabhaye vūpasante saṅghamajjhaṃ anosaritvāva gihiliṅgaṃ gahetvā āgatoti sabbaṃ purimasadisameva.

Another, when the danger of disease has arisen and he is unable to live, takes on the outward sign himself and eats the food of all sectarians. When the danger of disease has ceased, without having approached the midst of the Sangha, he comes back having taken the lay sign. Everything is just like the previous case.

Aparassa eko veriko kuddho hoti, ghātetukāmo naṃ vicarati. So “evaṃ me sotthi bhavissatī”ti sayameva liṅgaṃ gahetvā palāyati. Veriko “kuhiṃ so”ti pariyesanto “pabbajitvā palāto”ti sutvā “sace pabbajito, na taṃ labbhā kiñci kātu”nti tasmiṃ kodhaṃ paṭivineti. So “vūpasantaṃ me veribhaya”nti saṅghamajjhaṃ anosaritvāva gihiliṅgaṃ gahetvā āgatoti sabbaṃ purimasadisameva.

Another has an angry enemy who goes about seeking to kill him. Thinking, 'Thus I will be safe,' he takes on the outward sign himself and flees. The enemy, searching for him and hearing, 'He has gone forth and fled,' thinks, 'If he has gone forth, nothing can be done to him,' and abandons his anger toward him. That person, thinking, 'The danger from the enemy has ceased,' without having approached the midst of the Sangha, comes back having taken the lay sign. Everything is just like the previous case.

Aparo ñātikulaṃ gantvā sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya gihī hutvā “imāni cīvarāni idha vinassissanti, sacepi imāni gahetvā vihāraṃ gamissāmi, antarāmagge maṃ ‘coro’ti gahessanti, yaṃnūnāhaṃ kāyaparihāriyāni katvā gaccheyya”nti cīvarāharaṇatthaṃ nivāsetvā ca pārupitvā ca vihāraṃ gacchati. Taṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ disvā sāmaṇerā ca daharā ca abbhuggacchanti, vattaṃ [M 0.0171] dassenti. So na sādiyati, yathābhūtamattānaṃ āvikaroti. Sace bhikkhū “na dāni mayaṃ taṃ muñcissāmā”ti balakkārena pabbājetukāmā honti, kāsāyāni apanetvā puna pabbājetabbo. Sace pana “na ime mama hīnāyāvattabhāvaṃ jānantī”ti taṃyeva bhikkhubhāvaṃ paṭijānitvā sabbaṃ pubbe vuttavassagaṇanādibhedaṃ vidhiṃ paṭipajjati, ayaṃ na pabbājetabbo. Tenāha “rājadubbhikkhakantāra-rogaverībhayena vā”tiādi. Bhayasaddo cettha paccekaṃ yojetabbo “rājabhayena, dubbhikkhabhayenā”tiādinā. Liṅgaṃ ādiyatīti vesaṃ gaṇhāti. Idhāti imasmiṃ sāsane. Saṃvāsaṃ nādhivāseti, yāva so suddhamānasoti bhikkhūnaṃ vañcetukāmatāya abhāvato yo suddhamānaso yāva saṃvāsaṃ nādhivāseti, tāva esa “gihī maṃ [V 0.0162] ‘samaṇo’ti jānantū”ti vañcanacitte satipi bhikkhūnaṃ vañcetukāmatāya abhāvato doso natthīti theyyasaṃvāsako nāmāti na vuccatīti attho.

Another, having gone to his relatives' family, renounced the training and became a layperson. Thinking, 'These robes will be ruined here. If I take them and go to the monastery, they might seize me as a thief on the way. What if I were to go wearing them as a body-covering?' for the purpose of carrying the robes, he puts on the lower and upper robes and goes to the monastery. Seeing him coming from afar, the novices and young monks go out to meet him and show their respect. He does not consent, and reveals himself as he truly is. If the monks, thinking, 'We will not release him now,' wish to give him the going-forth by force, the saffron robes should be removed, and he should be given the going-forth again. But if, thinking, 'These monks do not know of my return to the lower state,' he claims that very state of a bhikkhu and follows the entire procedure previously mentioned, such as the counting of years, this one should not be given the going-forth. Therefore, it is said: 'due to fear of a king, famine, wilderness, disease, or an enemy,' etc. Here, the word 'fear' should be connected with each: 'fear of a king, fear of famine,' and so on. 'He takes the outward sign' means he assumes the appearance. 'Here' means in this Dispensation. 'He does not consent to communion, as long as he is pure-minded' means: because of the absence of the desire to deceive the monks, one who is pure-minded, as long as he does not consent to communion, for that long, even though there is a deceptive thought, 'Let laypeople know me as a recluse,' because of the absence of the desire to deceive the monks, there is no fault. Thus, he is not called 'one who lives in communion by theft.' This is the meaning.

Titthiyesu pakkantako paviṭṭhoti titthiyapakkantako. So ca na kevalaṃ tattha paviṭṭhamatteneva titthiyapakkantako hoti, atha kho tesaṃ laddhiggahaṇena. Tenāha “yo panā”tiādi. “Upasampanno”ti iminā anupasampanno titthiyapakkantako na hotīti dasseti. Vuttañhetaṃ kurundiaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “ayañca titthiyapakkantako nāma upasampannabhikkhunā kathito, tasmā sāmaṇero saliṅgena titthāyatanaṃ gatopi puna pabbajjañca upasampadañca labhatī”ti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 110). Kusacīrādikanti etthādisaddena phalakakkhaṇḍajaṭādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Sacepi “ayaṃ pabbajjā seṭṭhā”ti seṭṭhabhāvaṃ vā upagacchati, na muccati, titthiyapakkantakova hoti. Vatānīti ukkuṭikappadhānādīni vatāni. Sace pana “sobhati nu kho me titthiyapabbajjā, nanu kho sobhatī”ti vīmaṃsanatthaṃ kusacīrādīni nivāseti, jaṭaṃ vā bandhati, khārikājaṃ vā ādiyati, yāva na sampaṭicchati taṃ laddhiṃ, tāva rakkhati, sampaṭicchitamatte titthiyapakkantako hoti. Acchinnacīvaro pana kusacīrādīni nivāsento, rājabhayādīhi vā titthiyaliṅgaṃ gaṇhanto laddhiyā abhāvena neva titthiyapakkantako hoti.

One who has gone over to and entered among the sectarians is a 'sectarian-gone-over.' And he is not a sectarian-gone-over merely by having entered there, but rather by grasping their doctrine. Therefore, it is said, 'But whoever,' etc. By 'fully ordained,' it is shown that one who is not fully ordained is not a sectarian-gone-over. For it is stated in the Kurundī commentary: 'This so-called sectarian-gone-over is spoken of in relation to a fully ordained monk. Therefore, a novice, even if he goes to a sectarian abode with his own outward sign, can again receive the going-forth and full ordination.' 'Grass robes, etc.': here, by the word 'etc.,' the inclusion of bark-cloth garments, matted hair, and the like is meant. Even if one accepts its superiority, thinking, 'This going-forth is the best,' he is not released; he is still a sectarian-gone-over. 'Observances' means observances such as the squatting posture and strenuous exertion. If, however, for the sake of investigation, thinking, 'Does this sectarian going-forth suit me, or does it not suit me?' one wears grass robes, etc., or ties up matted hair, or takes up a carrying-pole, as long as he does not accept that doctrine, he is protected. The moment he accepts it, he becomes a sectarian-gone-over. However, one who has not given up his robe, who wears grass robes, etc., or who takes on the outward sign of sectarians due to fear of a king or other such reasons, is not a sectarian-gone-over because of the absence of the doctrine.

Avaseso sabbopīti nāgasupaṇṇayakkhagandhabbādiko. Yañhettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva.

'The rest, all of them' means nāgas, supaṇṇas, yakkhas, gandhabbas, and so on. Whatever is to be said on this has already been stated below.

Yathā [M 0.0172] samānajātikassa (sārattha. ṭī. mahāvagga 3.112) vikopane kammaṃ garutaraṃ, na tathā vijātikassāti āha “manussajātikā”ti. Puttasambandhena mātāpitusamaññā, dattakittimādivasenapi puttavohāro loke dissati, so ca kho pariyāyatoti nippariyāyasiddhataṃ dassetuṃ “janettī”ti vuttaṃ. Janettīti janikā, mātāti attho. Yathā manussattabhāve ṭhitasseva kusaladhammānaṃ tikkhavisadasūrabhāvāpatti, yathā taṃ tiṇṇampi bodhisattānaṃ bodhittayanipphattiyaṃ, evaṃ manussattabhāve ṭhitasseva akusaladhammānampi tikkhavisadasūrabhāvāpattīti āha “manussabhūtenevā”ti. Sañciccāti “pāṇo”ti saññāya saddhiṃ vadhakacetanāya cetetvā. Ayaṃ mātughātako nāmāti ayaṃ ānantariyena mātughātakakammena mātughātako nāma. Yena pana manussitthibhūtāpi ajanikā posāvanikamātā vā mahāmātā vā cūḷamātā vā janikāpi vā amanussitthibhūtā mātā ghātitā, tassa pabbajjā na vāritā, na ca ānantariko hoti. Yena sayaṃ tiracchānabhūtena manussitthibhūtā [V 0.0163] mātā ghātitā, sopi ānantariko na hoti. Tiracchānagatattā panassa pabbajjā paṭikkhittā, kammaṃ panassa bhāriyaṃ hoti, ānantariyaṃ āhacceva tiṭṭhati.

Just as the act of harming one of the same kind is more serious than harming one of a different kind, so it is said, 'of human birth.' The terms 'mother' and 'father' are used due to the connection with a child, and in the world, the designation of 'son' is also seen through adoption and the like—but that is only in a figurative sense. To show the non-figurative, established meaning, the term 'janettī' is used. 'Janettī' means the birth-giver, that is, the mother. Just as, while existing in the state of being human, the attainment of sharp, clear, and intense wholesome qualities is possible—as seen in the three Bodhisattas in the accomplishment of the three types of enlightenment—so too, while existing in the state of being human, the attainment of sharp, clear, and intense unwholesome qualities is possible. Hence, it is said, 'only while being human.' 'Sañcicca' means having intentionally thought with the intention to kill, together with the perception that it is a living being. This one is called a matricide—this person, by the action of matricide with immediate retribution, is named a matricide. However, if someone kills a woman who is human but not their birth-giver—such as a foster-mother, a stepmother, or an aunt—or if someone kills a non-human female who is their birth-giver, their ordination is not prohibited, nor do they commit an act with immediate retribution. If someone, while being an animal themselves, kills a human woman who is their mother, they too do not commit an act with immediate retribution. However, because of being in the animal realm, their ordination is rejected, but their kamma remains weighty, and it borders on being an act with immediate retribution.

Yena manussabhūto janako pitā sayampi manussajātikeneva satā sañcicca jīvitā voropito, ayaṃ ānantariyena pitughātakakammena pitughātako nāmāti imamatthaṃ atidisanto “pitughātakepi eseva nayo”ti āha. Sacepi hi vesiyā putto hoti, “ayaṃ me pitā”ti na jānāti, yassa sambhavena nibbatto, so ca tena ghātito, “pitughātako”tveva saṅkhaṃ gacchati, ānantariyañca phusati (mahāva. aṭṭha. 114).

When a progenitor father who is human is intentionally deprived of life by one who is also of human birth, this one is called a patricide by the action of patricide with immediate retribution. Extending this meaning, it is said: 'In the case of a patricide, too, this is the same principle.' For even if one is the son of a prostitute and does not know, 'This is my father,' if he kills the one from whom he was born, he is reckoned a patricide and commits an act with immediate retribution.

Eḷakacatukkaṃ (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 3.128; a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.275; vibha. aṭṭha. 809; sārattha. ṭī. mahāvagga 3.112), saṅgāmacatukkaṃ, coracatukkañcettha kathetabbaṃ. “Eḷakaṃ māremī”ti abhisandhināpi hi eḷakaṭṭhāne ṭhitaṃ manussabhūtaṃ mātaraṃ vā pitaraṃ vā mārento ānantariyaṃ phusati māraṇādhippāyeneva ānantariyavatthuno vikopitattā. Eḷakābhisandhinā, pana mātāpitiabhisandhinā vā eḷakaṃ mārento ānantariyaṃ na phusati ānantariyavatthuabhāvato. Mātāpitiabhisandhinā mātāpitaro mārento phusateva[M 0.0173]. Eseva nayo itarasmimpi catukkadvaye. Sabbattha hi purimaṃ abhisandhicittaṃ appamāṇaṃ, vadhakacittaṃ, pana tadārammaṇajīvitindriyañca ānantariyānānantariyabhāve pamāṇaṃ.

The Goat Quartet, the Battle Quartet, and the Thief Quartet should be discussed here. For even with the intention, 'I will kill a goat,' one who kills their mother or father, being human and standing in the place of a goat, commits an act with immediate retribution, because the object of an act with immediate retribution was destroyed with murderous intent. However, one who kills a goat with the intention of killing a goat, or with the intention of killing a mother or father, does not commit an act with immediate retribution, due to the absence of the object of an act with immediate retribution. One who kills a mother or father with the intention of killing a mother or father certainly commits such an act. This same principle applies to the other two quartets. For in all cases, the prior thought of intention is not the determining factor; rather, the thought at the moment of killing, and the life faculty that is its object, are the determining factors for whether or not the act has immediate retribution.

Arahantaghātakopi manussaarahantavaseneva veditabboti āha “yena antamaso gihiliṅge ṭhitopī”tiādi. Amanussajātikaṃ pana arahantaṃ, manussajātikaṃ vā avasesaṃ ariyapuggalaṃ ghātetvā ānantariko na hoti, pabbajjāpissa na vāritā, kammaṃ pana balavaṃ hoti. Tiracchāno manussaarahantampi ghātetvā ānantariko na hoti, kammaṃ pana bhāriyanti ayamettha vinicchayo. Yathā mātāpitūsu, evaṃ arahantepi eḷakacatukkādīni veditabbāni.

A killer of an Arahant should also be understood by way of a human Arahant; thus it is said: 'by whom, even if one is standing in the guise of a householder,' and so on. However, having killed a non-human Arahant, or a human who is one of the other noble persons, one does not commit an act with immediate retribution, nor is their ordination prohibited, but the kamma is strong. An animal, even having killed a human Arahant, does not commit an act with immediate retribution, but the kamma is weighty—this is the judgment here. Just as in the case of mother and father, so too in the case of an Arahant, the quartets beginning with the goat should be understood.

Pakatattaṃ bhikkhuninti parisuddhasīlaṃ ubhatosaṅghe upasampannaṃ bhikkhuniṃ. Yo (mahāva. aṭṭha. 115) pana kāyasaṃsaggena sīlavināsaṃ pāpeti, tassa pabbajjā ca upasampadā ca na vāritā. Balakkārena odātavatthavasanaṃ katvā anicchamānaṃyeva dūsentopi bhikkhunidūsakoyeva, balakkārena pana odātavatthavasanaṃ katvā icchamānaṃ dūsento bhikkhunidūsako na hoti. Kasmā? Yasmā gihibhāve sampaṭicchitamatteyeva sā abhikkhunī hoti[V 0.0164]. Sakiṃ sīlavipannaṃ pana pacchā dūsento sikkhamānasāmaṇerīsu ca vippaṭipajjanto neva bhikkhunidūsako hoti, pabbajjaṃ, upasampadañca labhatīti.

'A bhikkhunī in her natural state' means a bhikkhunī of pure virtue, ordained in both Saṅghas. For one who causes the destruction of her virtue through physical contact, their going forth and full ordination are not prohibited. One who, having forcibly made her wear white clothes, corrupts an unwilling bhikkhunī is indeed a corrupter of a bhikkhunī. But one who, having forcibly made her wear white clothes, corrupts her with her consent is not a corrupter of a bhikkhunī. Why? Because as soon as she has accepted the lay state, she is no longer a bhikkhunī. However, one who corrupts her after her virtue has already been ruined once, or who misbehaves with female trainees or female novices, is not a corrupter of a bhikkhunī, and can obtain the going forth and full ordination.

Dhammato uggataṃ apagataṃ uddhammaṃ. Ubbinayanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Catunnaṃ kammānanti apalokanañattiñattidutiyañatticatutthasaṅkhātānaṃ catunnaṃ kammānaṃ. Imesañhi aññataraṃ saṅghakammaṃ ekasīmāyaṃ visuṃ visuṃ karontena saṅgho bhinno nāma hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “catunnaṃ kammānaṃ aññataravasena saṅghaṃ bhindatī”ti.

That which has arisen from and departed from the Dhamma is non-Dhamma. In 'they cause agitation,' this same principle applies. 'Of the four acts' means the four acts designated as an act of announcement, an act of motion, an act of motion with a second proclamation, and an act of motion with a fourth proclamation. For the Saṅgha is said to be divided by one who performs any of these Saṅgha acts separately within a single boundary. Therefore it was said: 'divides the Saṅgha by means of one of the four acts.'

“Duṭṭhacittenā”ti vuttamevatthaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “vadhakacittenā”ti vuttaṃ. Vadhakacetanāya hi dūsitaṃ cittaṃ idha duṭṭhacittaṃ nāma. Lohitaṃ uppādetīti antosarīreyeva lohitaṃ uppādeti, sañcitaṃ karotīti adhippāyo. Na hi tathāgatassa abhejjakāyatāya parūpakkamena dhammaṃ bhinditvā lohitaṃ paggharati, sarīrassa pana antoyeva ekasmiṃ ṭhāne lohitaṃ samosarati, āghātena pakuppamānaṃ sañcitaṃ hoti, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ [M 0.0174] vuttaṃ. Yo pana rogavūpasamanatthaṃ jīvako viya satthena phāletvā pūtimaṃsañca lohitañca nīharitvā phāsukaṃ karoti, ayaṃ lohituppādako na hoti, bahuṃ pana so puññaṃ pasavati (mahāva. aṭṭha. 115).

To explain the meaning of the phrase 'with a malicious mind,' the phrase 'with a murderous mind' was stated. For here, a mind corrupted by murderous intent is called a malicious mind. 'Produces blood' means produces blood internally within the body; the intention is that one causes it to accumulate. For due to the Tathāgata's impenetrable body, blood does not flow out from another's attack by breaking the skin. Rather, within the body, blood collects in one place; being agitated by the impact, it accumulates. This was said in reference to that. But one who, for the purpose of curing an illness, like Jīvaka, makes an incision with a knife, removes putrid flesh and blood, and brings comfort, is not a producer of blood; on the contrary, they generate much merit.

Duvidhampi byañjananti yathāvuttakammadvayato samuṭṭhitaṃ itthinimittaṃ, purisanimittañcāti duvidhampi byañjanaṃ. Iminā ca viggahena “ubhatobyañjanako”ti asamānādhikaraṇavisayo bāhiratthasamāsoyaṃ, purimapade ca vibhattialopoti dasseti. So duvidho hoti itthiubhatobyañjanako, purisaubhatobyañjanako cāti. Tattha itthiubhatobyañjanakassa itthinimittaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, purisanimittaṃ paṭicchannaṃ. Purisaubhatobyañjanakassa purisanimittaṃ pākaṭaṃ, itthinimittaṃ paṭicchannaṃ. Itthiubhatobyañjanakassa itthīsu purisattaṃ karontassa itthinimittaṃ paṭicchannaṃ hoti, purisanimittaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti. Purisaubhatobyañjanakassa purisānaṃ itthibhāvaṃ upagacchantassa purisanimittaṃ paṭicchannaṃ hoti, itthinimittaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti. Itthiubhatobyañjanako sayañca gabbhaṃ gaṇhāti, parañca gaṇhāpeti. Purisaubhatobyañjanako pana sayaṃ na gaṇhāti, paraṃ gaṇhāpetīti idametesaṃ nānākaraṇaṃ.

'The characteristic is also of two kinds' means: the female characteristic and the male characteristic, which arise from the two kinds of kamma as stated before; thus the characteristic is of two kinds. And by this analysis, it is shown that the term ‘ubhatobyañjanaka’ is an external compound whose members have different referents, and that there is no elision of the case ending in the first member. This is of two kinds: a female ubhatobyañjanaka and a male ubhatobyañjanaka. In this case, for a female ubhatobyañjanaka, the female characteristic is manifest, while the male characteristic is concealed. For a male ubhatobyañjanaka, the male characteristic is manifest, while the female characteristic is concealed. When a female ubhatobyañjanaka acts as a male towards women, the female characteristic becomes concealed and the male characteristic becomes manifest. When a male ubhatobyañjanaka assumes the state of a female for men, the male characteristic becomes concealed and the female characteristic becomes manifest. A female ubhatobyañjanaka both conceives herself and causes another to conceive. A male ubhatobyañjanaka, however, does not conceive himself but causes another to conceive. This is the distinction between them.

Aparāmasanānīti aggahaṇāni avacanāni. “Ayaṃ itthannāmo”ti upasampadāpekkhassa akittananti yassa upasampadā karīyati, tassa akittanaṃ, “suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho, ayaṃ dhammarakkhito āyasmato buddharakkhitassa upasampadāpekkho”ti vattabbe “ayaṃ dhammarakkhito”ti (pari. aṭṭha. 484) [V 0.0165] avacananti vuttaṃ hoti. “Itthannāmassa upasampadāpekkho”ti upajjhāyassa akittananti “suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho, ayaṃ dhammarakkhito āyasmato buddharakkhitassa upasampadāpekkho”ti vattabbe “suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho, ayaṃ dhammarakkhito upasampadāpekkho”ti vatvā “āyasmato buddharakkhitassā”ti avacanaṃ. Sabbena sabbaṃ ñattiyā anuccāraṇanti ñattiṃ aṭṭhapetvā catukkhattuṃ kammavācāya eva anussāvanakammassa karaṇaṃ. Sampannanti upetaṃ.

Non-mentioning means not taking up, not stating. Not stating the name of the ordination candidate means not announcing the one for whom the ordination is being performed. For example, when it should be said, ‘Venerable sirs, let the Sangha hear me. This Dhammarakkhita is the ordination candidate of the Venerable Buddharakkhita,’ it is not stated, but only ‘This Dhammarakkhita’ is said. Not stating the name of the preceptor means that when it should be said, ‘Venerable sirs, let the Sangha hear me. This Dhammarakkhita is the ordination candidate of the Venerable Buddharakkhita,’ one says, ‘Venerable sirs, let the Sangha hear me. This Dhammarakkhita is an ordination candidate,’ thus not stating ‘of the Venerable Buddharakkhita.’ Not reciting the motion at all means that, having omitted the motion, the act is performed by reciting only the proclamation four times. Complete means endowed.

Hāpanaṃ pariccajanaṃ. Yopi ekaṃ ñattiṃ ṭhapetvā sakiṃyeva vā dvikkhattuṃ vā anussāvanaṃ karoti, ayampi sāvanaṃ hāpetiyeva. Duruccāraṇaṃ nāma aññasmiṃ [M 0.0175] akkhare vattabbe aññassa vacanaṃ. Tasmā kammavācaṃ karontena bhikkhunā yvāyaṃ –

Omission is abandoning. Even one who, after stating the one motion, makes the proclamation only once or twice, also omits the proclamation. Mispronunciation is the uttering of a different syllable when another syllable should be uttered. Therefore, a bhikkhu performing a formal act of the Sangha should—

“Sithilaṃ dhanitañca dīgharassaṃ;

Garukaṃ lahukañceva niggahītaṃ;

Sambandhavavatthitaṃ vimuttaṃ;

Dasadhā byañjanabuddhiyā pabhedo”ti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.190; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.291; a. ni. aṭṭha. 2.3.64, pari. aṭṭha. 485; vi. saṅga. aṭṭha. 252) –

“Unaspirated and aspirated, long and short; heavy and light, and the suppressed sound; connected, separated, and released—this is the tenfold division in the understanding of articulation.”

Vutto, ayaṃ suṭṭhu upalakkhetabbo. Ettha hi sithilaṃ nāma pañcasu vaggesu paṭhamatatiyaṃ. Dhanitaṃ nāma tesveva dutiyacatutthaṃ. Dīghanti dīghena kālena vattabbaṃ ā-kārādi. Rassanti tato upaḍḍhakālena vattabbaṃ a-kārādi. Garukanti dīghameva, yaṃ vā “āyasmato buddharakkhitattherassa yassa nakkhamatī”ti evaṃ saṃyogaparaṃ katvā vuccati. Lahukanti rassameva, yaṃ vā “āyasmato buddharakkhitattherassa yassa na khamatī”ti evaṃ asaṃyogaparaṃ katvā vuccati. Niggahītanti yaṃ karaṇāni niggahetvā avissajjetvā avivaṭena mukhena sānunāsikaṃ katvā vattabbaṃ. Sambandhanti yaṃ parapadena sambandhitvā “tuṇhissā”ti vā “tuṇhassā”ti vā vuccati. Vavatthitanti yaṃ parapadena sambandhaṃ akatvā vicchinditvā “tuṇhī assā”ti vā “tuṇha assā”ti vā vuccati. Vimuttanti yaṃ karaṇāni aniggahetvā vissajjetvā vivaṭena mukhena anunāsikaṃ akatvā vuccati.

This which has been stated should be carefully noted. Here, ‘sithila’ (unaspirated) refers to the first and third consonants of the five classes. ‘Dhanita’ (aspirated) refers to the second and fourth of those same classes. ‘Dīgha’ (long) means to be pronounced with a long duration, like the vowel ā. ‘Rassa’ (short) means to be pronounced with half that duration, like the vowel a. ‘Garu’ (heavy) refers to a long vowel, or a short vowel that is followed by a conjunct consonant, as in ‘yassa nakkhamatī.’ ‘Lahu’ (light) refers to a short vowel that is not followed by a conjunct consonant, as in ‘yassa na khamatī.’ ‘Niggahīta’ (suppressed) refers to what is pronounced by restraining the organs of articulation, not releasing them, with the mouth not open, and with nasalization. ‘Sambandha’ (connected) refers to what is connected with the following word, as when saying ‘tuṇhissā’ or ‘tuṇhassā.’ ‘Vavatthita’ (separated) refers to what is not connected with the following word but is separated, as when saying ‘tuṇhī assā’ or ‘tuṇha assā.’ ‘Vimutta’ (released) refers to what is pronounced without restraining the organs of articulation, releasing them, with an open mouth and without nasalization.

Tattha “suṇātu me”ti vattabbe ta-kārassa tha-kāraṃ katvā “suṇāthu me”ti vacanaṃ sithilassa [V 0.0166] dhanitakaraṇaṃ nāma, tathā “pattakallaṃ esā ñattī”ti vattabbe “patthakallaṃ esā ñattī”tiādivacanañca. “Bhante, saṅgho”ti vattabbe bha-kāra gha-kārānaṃ ba-kāra ga-kāre katvā “bante saṃgo”ti vacanaṃ dhanitassa sithilakaraṇaṃ nāma. “Suṇātu me”ti vivaṭena mukhena vattabbe “suṇaṃtu me”ti vā “esā ñattī”ti vattabbe “esaṃ ñattī”ti vā avivaṭena mukhena anunāsikaṃ katvā vacanaṃ vimuttassa niggahitavacanaṃ nāma. “Pattakalla”nti avivaṭena mukhena anunāsikaṃ katvā vattabbe “pattakallā”ti vivaṭena mukhena anunāsikaṃ akatvā vacanaṃ niggahitassa vimuttavacanaṃ nāma. Iti sithile kattabbe dhanitaṃ, dhanite kattabbe sithilaṃ, vimutte kattabbe niggahitaṃ, niggahite kattabbe vimuttanti imāni cattāri byañjanāni [M 0.0176] antokammavācāya kammaṃ dūsenti. Evaṃ vadanto hi aññasmiṃ akkhare vattabbe aññaṃ vadati, duruttaṃ karotīti vuccati.

Here, when one should say ‘suṇātu me,’ but instead says ‘suṇāthu me’ by making the letter t into th, this is called making an aspirated consonant out of an unaspirated one. Similarly, when one should say ‘pattakallaṃ esā ñattī,’ but says ‘patthakallaṃ esā ñattī,’ and so on. When one should say ‘bhante, saṅgho,’ but instead says ‘bante saṃgo’ by changing the bh and gh into b and g, this is called making an unaspirated consonant out of an aspirated one. When one should say ‘suṇātu me’ with an open mouth, but instead says ‘suṇaṃtu me’ with the mouth not open and with nasalization, or when one should say ‘esā ñattī,’ but says ‘esaṃ ñattī,’ this is called uttering a suppressed sound for a released one. When one should say ‘pattakallaṃ’ with the mouth not open and with nasalization, but instead says ‘pattakallā’ with an open mouth and without nasalization, this is called uttering a released sound for a suppressed one. Thus, making an aspirated consonant when an unaspirated one should be made, an unaspirated one when an aspirated one should be made, a suppressed sound when a released one should be made, and a released sound when a suppressed one should be made—these four mispronunciations of articulation spoil the formal act when they occur within the proclamation. For one who speaks thus utters a different syllable when another should be uttered; this is called a faulty utterance.

Itaresu pana dīgharassādīsu chasu byañjanesu dīghaṭṭhāne dīghameva. Rassaṭṭhāne ca rassamevāti evaṃ yathāṭhāne taṃ tadeva akkharaṃ bhāsantena anukkamāgataṃ paveṇiṃ avināsentena kammavācā kātabbā. Sace pana evaṃ akatvā dīghe vattabbe rassaṃ, rasse vā vattabbe dīghaṃ vadati, tathā garuke vattabbe lahukaṃ, lahuke vā vattabbe garukaṃ vadati, sambandhe vā pana vattabbe vavatthitaṃ, vavatthite vā vattabbe sambandhaṃ vadati, evaṃ vuttepi kammavācā na kuppati. Imāni hi cha byañjanāni kammaṃ na kopenti.

But in the case of the other six phonetic features, a long vowel should be pronounced where it is long, and a short vowel where it is short. Thus, the formal act of the Sangha should be performed by speaking each letter in its proper place, without destroying the tradition that has come down in sequence. However, if one does not do this and pronounces a short vowel where a long one should be pronounced, or a long vowel where a short one should be pronounced; or a light syllable where a heavy one should be pronounced, or a heavy syllable where a light one should be pronounced; or a separated word where a connected one should be pronounced, or a connected word where a separated one should be pronounced—even when spoken thus, the formal act of the Sangha is not spoiled. For these six phonetic features do not spoil the formal act.

Yaṃ pana suttantikattherā “da-kāro ta-kāramāpajjati, ta-kāro da-kāramāpajjati, ca-kāro ja-kāramāpajjati, ja-kāro ca-kāramāpajjati, ya-kāro ka-kāramāpajjati, ka-kāro ya-kāramāpajjati, tasmā da-kārādīsu vattabbesu ta-kārādīnaṃ vacanaṃ na virujjhatī”ti vadanti, taṃ kammavācaṃ patvā na vaṭṭati. Tasmā vinayadharena neva da-kāro ta-kāro kātabbo…pe… na ka-kāro ya-kāro. Yathāpāḷiyā niruttiṃ sodhetvā dasavidhāya byañjananiruttiyā vuttadose pariharantena kammavācā kātabbā. Itarathā hi sāvanaṃ hāpeti nāma. Ñattiṃ aṭṭhapetvā paṭhamaṃ anussāvanakaraṇanti sambandho.

As for what the Suttantika elders say, ‘The letter d becomes t, t becomes d, c becomes j, j becomes c, y becomes k, and k becomes y; therefore, when words with d, etc., should be spoken, the utterance of t, etc., is not incorrect’—this is not allowable with respect to the formal act of the Sangha. Therefore, a master of the Vinaya should not make d into t... nor k into y. The formal act of the Sangha should be performed after purifying the phrasing according to the Pāḷi text and avoiding the faults mentioned in the tenfold analysis of articulation. Otherwise, it is called omitting the proclamation. The connection is: ‘having established the motion, the first proclamation is to be made.’

Yāvatikā bhikkhū kammappattāti yattakā bhikkhū tassa upasampadākammassa pattā yuttā anurūpā. Te ca kho sabbantimena pariyāyena hatthapāsaṃ avijahitvā ekasīmaṭṭhā pañca pakatattā bhikkhū. Na hi tehi vinā taṃ kammaṃ karīyati, na tesaṃ chando eti. Avasesā pana sacepi sahassamattā honti, sace ekasīmaṭṭhā ekasmiṃ ṭhāne samānasaṃvāsakā, sabbe chandārahāva [V 0.0167] honti, chandaṃ datvā āgacchantu vā, mā vā, kammaṃ na kuppati. Paṭikkosananti nivāraṇaṃ. Tiṭṭhati ettha phalaṃ tadāyattavuttitāyāti ṭhānaṃ, kāraṇaṃ. Idha pana upasampadākammakaraṇassa kāraṇattā upasampadākammavācāsaṅkhātaṃ bhagavato vacanaṃ vuccati. Tenāha “kāraṇārahattā pana satthu sāsanārahattā”ti. Yathā ca “taṃ kattabba”nti bhagavatā anusiṭṭhaṃ, tathākaraṇaṃ upasampadākammassa kāraṇaṃ hotīti [M 0.0177] ṭhānārahaṃ nāma. Keci (sārattha. ṭī. 2.45) pana “ṭhānārahenāti ettha ‘na, bhikkhave, hatthacchinno pabbājetabbo’tiādi (mahāva. 119) satthusāsanaṃ ṭhāna”nti vadanti. Idhāti imasmiṃ pārājike. Yathā ca idha, evaṃ sabbatthāpi lokavajjasikkhāpadesu ayameva adhippetoti veditabbaṃ. Tenāha “paṇṇattivajjesu panā”tiādi. Aññepīti ehibhikkhūpasampannādayopi. Kathametaṃ viññāyati paṇṇattivajjesu sikkhāpadesu aññepi saṅgahaṃ gacchantīti? Atthato āpannattā. Tathā hi “dve puggalā abhabbā āpattiṃ āpajjituṃ buddhā ca paccekabuddhā ca, dve puggalā bhabbā āpattiṃ āpajjituṃ bhikkhū ca bhikkhuniyo cā”ti (pari. 322) sāmaññato vuttattā. Ehibhikkhūpasampannādayopi asañcicca assatiyā acittakaṃ sahaseyyāpattiādibhedaṃ paṇṇattivajjaṃ āpajjantīti (sārattha. ṭī. 2.45) atthato āpannaṃ.

‘As many monks as are qualified for the act’ means as many monks as are suitable, fit, and appropriate for that act of higher ordination. At the very least, there must be five monks of normal status present within a single boundary, not having left hand’s-reach. For without them that act cannot be performed, nor can their consent be brought. As for the remaining monks, even if they number a thousand, if they are within the same boundary and share the same residence, they are all eligible to give their consent. Whether they come and give their consent or not, the act is not invalidated. ‘Objection’ means prevention. A ‘foundation’ (ṭhāna) is so called because the fruit stands on it, its existence being dependent on that; it means a cause. But here, because it is the cause for performing the act of higher ordination, the Blessed One’s word, designated as the formal declaration of the act of higher ordination, is meant. Therefore it is said: ‘because it is worthy of being a cause, and worthy of the Teacher’s instruction.’ And just as the Blessed One instructed, ‘That should be done,’ so the performance in that way is the cause for the act of higher ordination; thus it is called ‘worthy of being a foundation.’ Some, however, say (Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā 2.45): ‘Here, by “worthy of being a foundation,” the Teacher’s instruction, such as, “Bhikkhus, one whose hand has been cut off should not be given the going-forth” (Mahāvagga 119), is meant as the “foundation.”’ ‘Here’ means in this Pārājika rule. And it should be understood that just as here, so too everywhere in the training rules concerning offenses blameworthy in the world, this is the intended meaning. Therefore it is said: ‘But in the case of prescribed offenses…,’ and so on. ‘Others’ means those given the higher ordination with the ‘Come, bhikkhu’ formula, and so on. How is it to be understood that in the training rules concerning prescribed offenses, others are also included? Because of having committed it in substance. For it is stated in general: ‘Two persons are incapable of committing an offense: Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas. Two persons are capable of committing an offense: bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs’ (Parivāra 322). Even those given the higher ordination with the ‘Come, bhikkhu’ formula, etc., may unintentionally, through lack of mindfulness or inattentiveness, commit a prescribed offense, of which the offense of sharing a bed is one kind. Thus they are considered to have committed it in substance (Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā 2.45).

Idāni “bhikkhūna”nti imaṃ padaṃ visesatthābhāvato visuṃ avaṇṇetvāva yaṃ sikkhañca sājīvañca samāpannattā bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno hoti, taṃ dassento “bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno”tiādimāha. Sikkhitabbāti sikkhā, pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ, saha jīvanti etthāti sājīvaṃ, mātikādibhedā paṇṇatti, sikkhā ca sājīvañca sikkhāsājīvaṃ, tadubhayaṃ samāpanno upagatoti sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno. Tenāha “yā bhikkhūna”ntiādi. Ettha ca “sikkhā”ti sājīvasahacariyato adhisīlasikkhāva adhippetāti āha “adhisīlasaṅkhātā”ti. Adhikaṃ uttamaṃ sīlanti adhisīlaṃ, “adhisīla”nti saṅkhātā adhisīlasaṅkhātā.

Now, without explaining the word ‘of the bhikkhus’ separately since it has no special meaning, to show that because one has undertaken the training and the common livelihood, one is ‘one who has undertaken the training and common livelihood of the bhikkhus,’ he says, ‘one who has undertaken the training and common livelihood of the bhikkhus,’ etc. Training (sikkhā) is what should be trained in; it is the virtue of the Pātimokkha restraint. A common livelihood (sājīvaṃ) is that wherein they live together; it is the prescription with its divisions such as the mātikā. Training and common livelihood are ‘the training and common livelihood’ (sikkhāsājīvaṃ). One who has undertaken (samāpanno), entered upon (upagato), that pair is ‘one who has undertaken the training and common livelihood’ (sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno). Therefore he says: ‘which for the bhikkhus…,’ and so on. And here, because of its association with the common livelihood, by ‘training’ only the training in the higher virtue is intended; thus he says, ‘designated as the higher virtue.’ The higher virtue (adhisīlaṃ) is superior and supreme virtue. What is designated as ‘the higher virtue’ is ‘designated as the higher virtue’ (adhisīlasaṅkhātā).

Katamaṃ panettha sīlaṃ, katamaṃ adhisīlanti? Vuccate – pañcaṅgadasaṅgasīlaṃ tāva sīlameva, na taṃ adhisīlaṃ. Pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ pana adhisīla”nti vuccati. Tañhi sūriyo viya pajjotānaṃ, sineru viya ca pabbatānaṃ sabbalokiyasīlānaṃ adhikañceva uttamañca, buddhuppādeyeva ca pavattati, na vinā buddhuppādā. Na hi taṃ paññattiṃ uddharitvā añño satto paññāpetuṃ sakkoti, buddhāyeva panassa sabbaso kāyavacīdvārajjhācārasotaṃ chinditvā tassa tassa vītikkamassa anucchavikaṃ taṃ taṃ sīlasaṃvaraṃ paññāpenti. Pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlatopi [V 0.0168] ca maggaphalasampayuttameva sīlaṃ adhisīlaṃ, taṃ pana idha na adhippetaṃ. Na hi taṃ samāpanno methunadhammaṃ paṭisevati.

Herein, what is virtue and what is the higher virtue? It is said: To begin with, the virtue of five and ten factors is just virtue; it is not the higher virtue. But the virtue of the Pātimokkha restraint is called ‘the higher virtue.’ For that virtue, like the sun among luminaries and Mount Sineru among mountains, is superior and supreme to all worldly virtues. It exists only when a Buddha arises, not when a Buddha does not arise. For no other being can formulate and prescribe that rule. Only Buddhas, having completely cut off the stream of misconduct through the doors of body and speech, prescribe the appropriate virtuous restraint for each particular transgression. Moreover, the virtue associated with the path and fruition is a higher virtue even than the virtue of the Pātimokkha restraint, but that is not intended here. For one who has attained that does not engage in the sexual act.

Eteti [M 0.0178] nānādesajātigottādibhedabhinnā bhikkhū. Saha jīvantīti ekuddesādivasena saha pavattanti. Tenāha “ekajīvikā sabhāgavuttino”ti. Sikkhāpadasaṅkhātanti paṇṇattisaṅkhātaṃ. Sāpi hi viratiādīnaṃ dīpanato “sikkhāpada”nti vuccati. Vuttampi cetaṃ “sikkhāpadanti yo tattha nāmakāyo padakāyo niruttikāyo byañjanakāyo”ti. Tatthāti tesu. Sikkhaṃ paripūrentoti akattabbaparivajjanakattabbakaraṇavasena vārittacārittasaṅkhātaṃ duvidhaṃ sīlaṃ paripūrentoti attho, vārittasīlavasena viratisampayuttacetanaṃ, cārittasīlavasena virativippayuttacetanañca attani pavattentoti vuttaṃ hoti. Sājīvañca avītikkamantoti sikkhāpadañca amaddanto, sīlasaṃvaraṇaṃ, sājīvānatikkamanañcāti idameva dvayaṃ idha samāpajjanaṃ nāmāti adhippāyo. Tattha sājīvānatikkamo sikkhāpāripūriyā paccayo. Tassānatikkamanato hi yāva maggā sikkhā paripūrati. Apicettha “sikkhaṃ paripūrento”ti iminā viraticetanāsaṅkhātassa sīlasaṃvarassa visesato santāne pavattanakālova gahito, “avītikkamanto”ti iminā pana appavattanakālopi. Sikkhañhi paripūraṇavasena attani pavattentopi niddādivasena appavattentopi vītikkamābhāvā sikkhanavasena samāpannoti vuccati.

‘These’ means these bhikkhus who are distinguished by differences of country, birth, clan, etc. ‘They live together’ means they carry on together by way of a common recitation, etc. Therefore it is said: ‘those with a common livelihood, those with a similar way of life.’ ‘Designated as a training rule’ means designated as a prescription. For it is called a ‘training rule’ because it illuminates abstinence, etc. And this is said: ‘A training rule is the body of nouns, the body of phrases, the body of expressions, the body of letters therein.’ ‘Therein’ means in them. ‘Fulfilling the training’ means one fulfills the twofold virtue designated as the virtue of avoidance and the virtue of observance, by way of avoiding what should not be done and doing what should be done. This is to say that one causes to arise in oneself volition associated with abstinence by way of the virtue of avoidance, and volition dissociated from abstinence by way of the virtue of observance. ‘And not transgressing the common livelihood’ means not violating the training rule. The intention is that these two things here—virtuous restraint and the non-transgression of the common livelihood—are what is called ‘undertaking.’ Therein, non-transgression of the common livelihood is a condition for the fulfillment of the training. For by not transgressing it, the training is fulfilled up to the path. Moreover, here by ‘fulfilling the training,’ the time is taken when the virtuous restraint, designated as the volition of abstinence, is specifically arising in one’s mental continuity; but by ‘not transgressing,’ the time when it is not arising is also taken. For whether one is causing the training to arise in oneself by way of fulfillment, or not causing it to arise, as when one is asleep, one is said to have undertaken the training because of the absence of transgression.

Yasmā sikkhāpaccakkhānassa ekaccaṃ dubbalyāvikammaṃ attho hoti, tasmā taṃ sandhāya “sikkhaṃ apaccakkhāyā”ti padassa atthaṃ vivaranto “dubbalyaṃ anāvikatvā”ti āhāti dassetuṃ “sikkhaṃ apaccakkhāya dubbalyaṃ anāvikatvā”tiādimāha. Tattha siyā (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.45 sikkhāpaccakkhānavibhaṅgavaṇṇanā), yasmā na sabbaṃ dubbalyāvikammaṃ sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ, tasmā “dubbalyaṃ anāvikatvā”ti paṭhamaṃ vatvā tassa atthaniyamanatthaṃ “sikkhaṃ apaccakkhāyā”ti vattabbanti? Taṃ na, kasmā? Atthānukkamābhāvato. “Sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno”ti hi vuttattā yaṃ sikkhaṃ samāpanno, taṃ apaccakkhāya, yañca sājīvaṃ samāpanno, tattha dubbalyaṃ anāvikatvāti vuccamāne anukkameneva attho vutto hoti, na aññathā. Tasmā idameva paṭhamaṃ vuttanti.

Since a certain revealing of weakness is the meaning of ‘renouncing the training,’ therefore, with reference to that, to show that in explaining the meaning of the phrase ‘without renouncing the training’ he says ‘without revealing weakness,’ the author says ‘without renouncing the training, without revealing weakness,’ etc. Here one might ask (see Pārājika-aṭṭhakathā 1.45, Exposition of the Analysis of Renouncing the Training): since not every revealing of weakness is a renunciation of the training, should one first say ‘without revealing weakness,’ and then, in order to define its meaning, say ‘without renouncing the training’? That is not so. Why? Because there would be no proper sequence of meaning. For since it was said ‘one who has undertaken the training and common livelihood,’ when it is said, ‘without renouncing the training that one has undertaken, and without revealing weakness in the common livelihood that one has undertaken,’ the meaning is stated in the proper sequence, not otherwise. Therefore, this was stated first.

Idāni tadubhayameva pākaṭaṃ katvā dassetuṃ “tatthā”tiādimāha. Tadabhāvenāti tesaṃ cittādīnaṃ abhāvena. Cavitukāmatācittenāti apagantukāmatācittena[M 0.0179]. Davāti sahasā. Yo hi [V 0.0169] aññaṃ bhaṇitukāmo sahasā “buddhaṃ paccakkhāmī”ti bhaṇati, ayaṃ davā vadati nāma. Ravāti virajjhitvā. Yo hi aññaṃ bhaṇitukāmo virujjhitvā “buddhaṃ paccakkhāmī”ti bhaṇati, ayaṃ ravā bhaṇati nāma. Purimena ko visesoti ce? Purimaṃ paṇḍitassāpi sahasāvasena aññabhaṇanaṃ, idaṃ pana mandattā momūhattā pakkhalantassa “aññaṃ bhaṇissāmī”ti aññabhaṇanaṃ. “Akkharasamayānabhiññātatāya vā karaṇasampattiyā abhāvato vā kathetabbaṃ kathetumasakkonto hutvā aññaṃ kathento ravā bhaṇati nāmā”ti (sārattha. ṭī. 2.54) eke.

Now, to show this pair clearly, he says, ‘Therein…,’ etc. ‘By their absence’ means by the absence of those minds, etc. ‘With a mind desiring to fall away’ means with a mind desiring to depart. ‘In play’ (davā) means suddenly (sahasā). For one who, intending to say something else, suddenly says, ‘I renounce the Buddha,’ is one who speaks in play. ‘In anger’ (ravā) means having become disaffected (virajjhitvā). For one who, intending to say something else, says out of vexation, ‘I renounce the Buddha,’ is one who speaks in anger. If it is asked, ‘What is the difference from the former?’ The former is the saying of something else by way of suddenness even on the part of a wise person; but this latter is the saying of something else by one who is slow and bewildered and stumbles, thinking, ‘I will say something else.’ Some say (Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā 2.54): ‘One who, being unable to say what should be said either because of unfamiliarity with the combination of syllables or because of a lack of accomplishment in the organ of speech, says something else, is one who speaks in anger.’

Vajjāvajjaṃ upanijjhāyatīti upajjhāyo, taṃ upajjhāyaṃ. “Evaṃ sajjhāyitabbaṃ, evaṃ abhikkamitabba”ntiādinā ācārasikkhāpanako ācariyo. Ante samīpe vasati sīlenāti antevāsī, vibhattialopena yathā “vanekaserukā”ti. Samāno upajjhāyo assāti samānupajjhāyako. Evaṃ samānācariyako. Sabrahmacārinti bhikkhuṃ. So hi “ekakammaṃ, ekuddeso, samasikkhatā”ti imaṃ brahmaṃ samānaṃ carati, tasmā “sabrahmacārī”ti vuccati. Evaṃ vuttānanti evaṃ padabhājanīye vuttānaṃ. Yathā hi loke sassānaṃ viruhanaṭṭhānaṃ “khetta”nti vuccati, evamimānipi buddhādīni padāni sikkhāpaccakkhānassa viruhanaṭṭhānatthā “khetta”nti vuccantīti āha “imesaṃ dvāvīsatiyā khettapadāna”nti. Yasmā panetesaṃ vevacanehipi sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hoti, tasmā “savevacanassā”ti vuttaṃ. Vividhaṃ ekasmiṃyeva atthe vacanaṃ vivacanaṃ, vivacanameva vevacanaṃ, pariyāyanāmaṃ, saha vevacanehīti savevacanaṃ, tassa savevacanassa. Ettha ca vaṇṇapaṭṭhāne (sārattha. ṭī. 2.52; vi. vi. ṭī. 1.53; vajira. ṭī. 53) āgataṃ nāmasahassaṃ, upāligāthāsu (ma. ni. 2.76) nāmasataṃ, aññāni ca guṇato labbhamānāni nāmāni “buddhavevacanānī”ti veditabbāni. Sabbānipi dhammassa nāmāni “dhammavevacanānī”ti veditabbāni. Esa nayo sabbattha.

He who reflects on what is blameworthy and blameless is an upajjhāya (preceptor); that is, 'the upajjhāya.' The ācariya (teacher) is one who instructs in conduct, saying, 'Thus should it be recited, thus should one proceed,' and so on. An antevāsī (pupil) is one who lives near, possessing virtue; the elision of the case ending is as in 'vanekaserukā.' A samānupajjhāyaka is one who has the same preceptor. Similarly, a samānācariyaka is one who has the same teacher. 'Sabrahmacārī' (fellow in the holy life) refers to a bhikkhu. For he lives a shared holy life—being 'of one act, one recitation, and equal training'—and therefore he is called a 'sabrahmacārī.' 'Of those thus stated' means of those thus stated in the word analysis. Just as in the world a place where crops grow is called a 'field,' so too these words—beginning with 'Buddha'—are called 'fields' because they are the place for the arising of the rejection of the training. Hence it is said, 'of these twenty-two field-words.' And since the rejection of the training also comes about through their synonyms, it is said, 'including its synonyms.' A diverse expression for one and the same meaning is a 'vivacana'; 'vivacana' is just 'vevacana,' a synonymous name. 'With synonyms' is 'savevacana'; 'of that which has synonyms' is 'savevacanassa.' Here, in the Vaṇṇapaṭṭhāna, a thousand names are mentioned; in the Upāligāthā, a hundred names; and other names obtainable from qualities should be understood as 'synonyms of the Buddha.' All the names of the Dhamma should be understood as 'synonyms of the Dhamma.' This is the method in all cases.

Tesu yaṃ kiñci vattukāmassa yaṃ kiñci vadato sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hotīti tesu dvāvīsatiyā khettapadesu yaṃ kiñci ekaṃ padaṃ vattukāmassa tato aññaṃ yaṃ kiñci padampi vacībhedaṃ katvā vadato khettapadantogadhattā sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ [M 0.0180] hotīti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – sace panāyaṃ “buddhaṃ paccakkhāmī”ti vattukāmo padapaccābhaṭṭhaṃ katvā “paccakkhāmi buddha”nti vā vadeyya, milakkhabhāsādīsu vā aññatarabhāsāya tamatthaṃ vadeyya, “buddhaṃ paccakkhāmī”ti vattukāmo uppaṭipāṭiyā “dhammaṃ paccakkhāmī”ti vā “sabrahmacāriṃ paccakkhāmī”ti vā vadeyya, seyyathāpi uttarimanussadhammavibhaṅge “paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajjāmī”ti [V 0.0170] vattukāmo “dutiyaṃ jhāna”nti vadati. Sace “yassa vadati, so ayaṃ bhikkhubhāvaṃ cajitukāmo etamatthaṃ vadatī”ti ettakamattampi jānāti, viraddhaṃ nāma natthi, khettameva otiṇṇaṃ, paccakkhātāva hoti sikkhā. Sakkattā vā brahmattā vā cutasatto viya cutova hoti sāsanāti.

The statement 'For one who wishes to say anything among them, and who says anything, there is a rejection of the training' means this: among these twenty-two field-words, for one who wishes to say any one word, but who, having made a verbal slip, says any other word, because it falls within the field-words, there is a rejection of the training. This is what is said: If, for instance, one wishing to say, 'I reject the Buddha,' having transposed the words, should say, 'Reject I Buddha,' or should express that meaning in some other language such as a barbarian tongue, or if one wishing to say, 'I reject the Buddha,' should say in the wrong order, 'I reject the Dhamma,' or 'I reject a fellow in the holy life'—just as in the analysis of superhuman states, one who wishes to say, 'I am attaining the first jhāna,' says, 'the second jhāna.' If the one to whom he speaks knows just this much: 'This person wishes to abandon the state of a bhikkhu and is saying this for that purpose,' then there is no mistake; it has entered the field, and the training is indeed rejected. Like a being fallen from the state of Sakka or Brahmā, he has indeed fallen from the Dispensation.

Alanti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.52) hotu, pariyattanti attho. Kiṃ nu meti kiṃ mayhaṃ kiccaṃ, kiṃ karaṇīyaṃ, kiṃ sādhetabbanti attho. Na mamatthoti natthi mama attho. Sumuttāhanti suṭṭhu mutto ahaṃ. Purimehi cuddasahi padehīti buddhādīhi sabrahmacāripariyantehi purimehi cuddasahi padehi. Yannūnāhaṃ paccakkheyyanti ettha “yannūnā”ti parivitakkadassane nipāto. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “sacāhaṃ buddhaṃ paccakkheyyaṃ, sādhu vata me siyā”ti. Ādisaddena “paccakkhi”nti vā “paccakkhissāmī”ti vā “bhavissāmī”ti vā “homī”ti vā “jātomhī”ti vā “amhī”ti vā evaṃbhūtānaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Sace pana “ajja paṭṭhāya ‘gihī’ti maṃ dhārehī”ti vā “jānāhī”ti vā “sañjānāhī”ti vā “manasi karohī”ti vā vadati, ariyakena vā vadati, milakkhakena vā. Evametasmiṃ atthe vutte yassa vadati, sace so jānāti, paccakkhātā hoti sikkhā. Esa nayo sesesupi “upāsako”tiādīsu sattasu padesu. Ettha ca ariyakaṃ nāma māgadhavohāro. Milakkhakaṃ nāma anariyako andhadamiḷādi.

'Enough!' means let it be; the meaning is 'it is sufficient.' 'What is it to me?' means: What is my business? What is to be done by me? What is to be accomplished by me? 'It is of no use to me' means 'there is no use for me.' 'I am well freed' means 'I am thoroughly freed.' 'By the first fourteen terms' means by the first fourteen terms beginning with the Buddha and ending with the fellow in the holy life. 'What if I were to reject?'—here 'what if' is a particle showing deliberation. This is what is said: 'If I were to reject the Buddha, it would indeed be good for me!' By the word 'etc.' is included such expressions as 'I have rejected,' 'I will reject,' 'I will be,' 'I am,' 'I have become,' 'I am.' But if one says, 'From today onward, consider me a householder,' or 'know me as such,' or 'recognize me as such,' or 'bear me in mind as such,' whether one speaks in the Aryan tongue or in a barbarian tongue. When this meaning is expressed, if the one to whom he speaks understands, the training is rejected. This is the method also in the remaining seven terms, such as 'lay follower.' Here, the Aryan tongue is the Magadhan dialect. The barbarian tongue is a non-Aryan one, such as Andha and Damiḷa.

Akkharalikhananti “buddhaṃ paccakkhāmī”tiādinā aññesaṃ dassanatthaṃ akkharalikhanaṃ. Adhippāyaviññāpako aṅgulisaṅkocanādiko hatthavikāro hatthamuddā, hatthasaddo cettha tadekadesesu aṅgulīsu daṭṭhabbo “na bhuñjamāno sabbaṃ hatthaṃ mukhe pakkhipissāmī”tiādīsu (pāci. 618) viya. Tasmā adhippāyaviññāpakassa aṅgulisaṅkocanādino hatthavikārassa dassanaṃ hatthamuddādidassananti [M 0.0181] (sārattha. ṭī. 2.51) evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Ādisaddena sīsakampanadassanādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

'Writing letters' means writing letters with phrases like 'I reject the Buddha,' etc., for the purpose of showing others. A hand gesture (hatthamuddā) is a motion of the hand, such as contracting the fingers, that conveys one's intention. Here, the word 'hand' should be understood as referring to a part of it, the fingers, as in such cases as 'While eating, I will not put the whole hand into my mouth.' Therefore, 'seeing a hand gesture, etc.' means seeing a motion of the hand, such as contracting the fingers, that conveys one's intention. This is how the meaning should be understood here. By the word 'etc.' is included seeing things like the shaking of the head.

Ummattakakhittacittavedanāṭṭānanti ettha ummattakoti pittummattako. Khittacittoti yakkhehi katacittavikkhepo, yakkhummattakoti vuttaṃ hoti. Ubhinnaṃ pana viseso anāpattivāre āvibhavissati. Vedanāṭṭoti balavatiyā dukkhavedanāya phuṭṭho mucchāpareto, tena vippalapantena paccakkhātāpi apaccakkhātāva hoti. Manussajātiko hotīti sabhāgo vā visabhāgo vā gahaṭṭho vā pabbajito vā viññū yokoci manusso hoti. Ummattakādīnanti etthādisaddena khittacittavedanāṭṭadevatātiracchānagatānaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Tatra ummattakakhittacittavedanāṭṭatiracchānagatānaṃ santike paccakkhātāpi ajānanabhāvena apaccakkhātāva hoti. Devatāya pana santike atikhippaṃ jānanabhāvena. Devatā nāma mahāpaññā tihetukappaṭisandhikā atikhippaṃ jānanti, cittañca nāmetaṃ lahuparivattaṃ, tasmā “cittalahukassa puggalassa cittavaseneva mā atikhippaṃ vināso ahosī”ti devatāya santike [V 0.0171] sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ paṭikkhipi. Tena vuttaṃ “na ca ummattakādīnaṃ aññataro”ti. Dūtena vāti “mama sikkhāpaccakkhānabhāvaṃ kathehī”ti mukhasāsanavasena dūtena vā. Paṇṇena vāti paṇṇe likhitvā pahiṇavasena paṇṇena vā.

Regarding 'an insane person, one of deranged mind, or one afflicted by pain': here, 'insane person' (ummattaka) is one insane due to bile. 'One of deranged mind' (khittacitta) is one whose mind is deranged by yakkhas; that is to say, one insane due to yakkhas. The distinction between the two will become clear in the chapter on non-offenses. 'One afflicted by pain' (vedanāṭṭa) is one overcome by fainting, afflicted by intense painful feeling; even if such a person, while delirious, renounces the training, it is not renounced. 'He is of human birth' means he is any discerning human being, whether of the same kind or a different kind, a householder or one gone forth. 'Of an insane person, etc.': here, by the word 'etc.' is included one of deranged mind, one afflicted by pain, a deva, and an animal. In that case, if one renounces the training in the presence of an insane person, one of deranged mind, one afflicted by pain, or an animal, because they do not understand, it is not renounced. But in the presence of a deva, it is because they understand too quickly. Devas, it is said, are of great wisdom, having a three-rooted rebirth-linking consciousness, and they understand very quickly. And this mind is fickle. Therefore, in order that a person with a fickle mind should not be too quickly ruined by the influence of his own mind, the renunciation of the training in the presence of a deva is disallowed. Hence it is said, 'and not any of an insane person, etc.' 'Or by a messenger' means by a messenger with a verbal message, saying, 'Announce my renunciation of the training.' 'Or by a letter' means by writing it on a leaf and sending it.

Sace te sikkhāpaccakkhānabhāvaṃ jānantīti sambandho. Āvajjanasamayeti atthābhogasamaye. Iminā taṃ khaṇaṃyeva pana apubbaṃ acarimaṃ dujjānanti dasseti. Vacanānantaramevāti vacanassa anantarameva, āvajjanasamayevāti attho. Eva-saddena pana cirena jānanaṃ paṭikkhipati. Ukkaṇṭhitoti anabhiratiyā imasmiṃ sāsane kicchajīvikaṃ patto. Atha vā “ajja yāmi, sve yāmi, ito yāmi, ettha yāmī”ti uddhaṃ kaṇṭhaṃ katvā viharamāno vikkhitto, anekaggoti vuttaṃ hoti. Idañca “anabhirato sāmaññā cavitukāmo”tiādīnaṃ (pārā. 45) upalakkhaṇaṃ. Yena kenaci…pe… jānantīti sace te“ukkaṇṭhito”ti vā “gihibhāvaṃ patthetī”ti vā “anabhirato”ti vā “sāmaññā cavitukāmo”ti vā yena kenaci ākārena sikkhāpaccakkhānabhāvaṃ jānanti. Idañhi sikkhāpaccakkhānañca upari [M 0.0182] abhūtārocanaduṭṭhullavācāattakāmaduṭṭhadosabhūtārocanasikkhāpadāni ca ekaparicchedāni, āvajjanasamaye ñāte eva sīsaṃ enti. “Kiṃ ayaṃ bhaṇatī”ti kaṅkhatā cirena ñāte sīsaṃ na enti. Tenāha “atha aparabhāge”tiādi. Atha dvinnaṃ ṭhitaṭṭhāne dvinnampi niyametvā “etesaṃ ārocemī”ti vadati, tesu ekasmiṃ jānantepi dvīsu jānantesupi paccakkhātāva hoti sikkhā. Evaṃ sambahulesupi veditabbaṃ. Vuttanayenāti “tassa vacanānantara”ntiādinā vuttena nayena. Yo koci manussajātikoti antamaso navakammikaṃ upādāya yo koci manusso. Vuttañhetaṃ samantapāsādikāyaṃ –

The connection is: 'If they know the fact of his renunciation of the training.' 'At the time of adverting' means at the time of attending to the meaning. By this he shows that that very moment, not before and not after, is difficult to know. 'Immediately after the statement' means right after the statement, that is, at the time of adverting. By the word 'eva' (immediately), he rejects knowing it after a long time. 'Discontented' means one who, through dissatisfaction, has come to a difficult livelihood in this Dispensation. Or else, one who lives with his neck craned, thinking, 'I'll go today, I'll go tomorrow, I'll go from here, I'll go there,' is distracted; that is to say, his mind is not unified. And this is an illustration of such phrases as 'displeased, wishing to fall away from the ascetic's life,' etc. 'By whatever means... they know' means: if they know by whatever means the fact of his renunciation of the training—whether that he is 'discontented,' or 'longs for the household life,' or is 'displeased,' or 'wishes to fall away from the ascetic's life.' For this renunciation of the training and the subsequent training rules—on making a groundless charge, on abusive speech, on acting from one's own desire, on making a charge out of malice, and on making a groundless charge—are all in one section. They are fulfilled only when known at the time of adverting. They are not fulfilled when known after a long time by one who is wondering, 'What is he saying?' Therefore he said, 'Then, at a later time,' etc. Then, in a place where two are standing, having specified both, he says, 'I am informing these two.' The training is renounced when one of them knows, or when both know. The same should be understood in the case of many. 'By the stated method' means by the method stated as 'immediately after his statement,' etc. 'Any human being' means any human, up to and including a new workman. For this is stated in the Samantapāsādikā:

“Sace pana anabhiratiyā pīḷito sabhāge bhikkhū parisaṅkamāno ‘yo koci jānātū’ti uccāsaddaṃ karonto ‘buddhaṃ paccakkhāmī’ti vadati, tañca avidūre ṭhito navakammiko vā añño vā samayaññū puriso sutvā ‘ukkaṇṭhito ayaṃ samaṇo gihibhāvaṃ pattheti, sāsanato cuto’ti jānāti, paccakkhātāva hoti sikkhā”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.51).

'If, being afflicted by discontent, a monk, approaching his fellow monks, making a loud noise so that anyone may know, declares, 'I renounce the Buddha,' and a new workman or another person who understands the situation, standing not far away, hears it and understands, 'This ascetic is discontented, he desires the householder's life, he has fallen away from the teaching,' then the training is renounced.' (Pārā. aṭṭha. 1.51).

Sace [V 0.0172] vacanatthaṃ ñatvāpi “ayaṃ ukkaṇṭhito”ti vā “gihibhāvaṃ patthetī”ti vā na jānāti, apaccakkhātāva hoti sikkhā. Sace pana vacanatthaṃ ajānitvāpi “ukkaṇṭhito”ti vā “gihibhāvaṃ patthetī”ti vā jānāti, paccakkhātāva hoti sikkhā. Davāyapīti kīḷādhippāyenapi. Cittādīnaṃ vā vasenāti cittādīnaṃ vā chaḷaṅgānaṃ vasena. Hoti cettha –

If, even knowing the meaning of the statement, one does not understand that 'this person is discontented' or 'desires the householder life,' the training is not renounced. But if, without knowing the meaning of the statement, one understands that he is 'discontented' or 'desires the householder life,' then the training is renounced. 'Even in play' means even with the intention of sport. 'Or by the power of the mind, etc.' means by the power of the mind and the other five factors. Here, there is this:

“Cittaṃ khettañca kālo ca, payogo puggalo tathā;

Vijānananti sikkhāya, paccakkhānaṃ chaḷaṅgika”nti.

'Mind, field, and time, effort and the person as well; discernment: the renunciation of the training is six-factored.'

Sabbaso vā pana apaccakkhānenāti “buddhaṃ paccakkhāmī”tiādīsu yena yena pariyāyena sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hoti, tato ekassapi paccakkhānassa abhāvena. Iminā pana “idaṃ padaṃ sāvessāmi, sikkhaṃ paccakkhāmī”ti evaṃ pavattacittuppādassa abhāvaṃ dasseti. Yassa hi evarūpo cittuppādo natthi, so sabbaso na paccakkhāti nāmāti. Sikkhāpaccakkhānassāti “buddhaṃ paccakkhāmī”tiādisikkhāpaccakkhānassa. Atthabhūtaṃ ekaccaṃ dubbalyanti “buddhaṃ paccakkhāmī”ti vadati viññāpeti, evampi, bhikkhave, dubbalyāvikammañceva hoti, sikkhā [M 0.0183] ca paccakkhātā”tiādinā (pārā. 53) vuttehi yehi vacanehi sikkhāpaccakkhānañceva hoti dubbalyāvikammañca, taṃ “buddhaṃ paccakkhāmī”tiādikaṃ atthabhūtaṃ dubbalyaṃ anāvikatvā. “Buddhaṃ paccakkhāmī”tiādimhi pana vutte sikkhāparipūraṇe dubbalabhāvassāpi gamyamānattā sikkhāpaccakkhānassa idaṃ dubbalyāvikammaṃ atthoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ettha ca “atthabhūta”nti iminā “yannūnāhaṃ buddhaṃ paccakkheyya”ntiādikaṃ dubbalyāvikammaṃ paṭikkhipati. Yena hi sikkhāpaccakkhānañceva hoti dubbalyāvikammañca, tadeva sikkhāpaccakkhānassa atthabhūtaṃ. Yena pana dubbalyāvikammameva hoti, na sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ, na taṃ tassa atthabhūtanti.

'Or, by not renouncing at all' means by the absence of even a single renunciation among those various ways in which the renunciation of the training occurs, such as 'I renounce the Buddha.' This, however, indicates the absence of a thought-process arising like, 'I will utter this phrase, I renounce the training.' For one who lacks such a thought-process is said not to renounce at all. 'Of the renunciation of the training' means of the renunciation of the training such as 'I renounce the Buddha.' 'A certain actual weakness' means without revealing that actual weakness, such as 'I renounce the Buddha,' etc.—by which words, as stated (in Pārā. 53), 'when one says or declares, "I renounce the Buddha," even so, monks, it is both an act of revealing weakness and the training is renounced,' both the renunciation of training and an act of revealing weakness occur. But when 'I renounce the Buddha,' etc., is said, since a state of weakness is also implied in the fulfillment of the renunciation, this act of revealing weakness should be understood as belonging to the renunciation of training. Here, by 'actual,' he rejects acts of revealing weakness such as, 'Suppose I were to renounce the Buddha,' etc. For only that by which both the renunciation of training and an act of revealing weakness occur is actual for the renunciation of training. But that by which only an act of revealing weakness occurs, and not a renunciation of training, is not actual for it.

Rāgapariyuṭṭhānena sadisabhāvāpattiyā mithunānaṃ ayanti “methuno”ti dhammova vuccatīti āha “rāgapariyuṭṭhānenā”tiādi. Tattha rāgapariyuṭṭhānenāti rāgassa pariyuṭṭhānena, methunarāgassa pavattiyā pariyonaddhacittatāyāti attho. Dhammoti ajjhācāro. “Palambate vilambate”tiādīsu viya upasaggassa koci atthaviseso natthīti āha “seveyyā”ti. Ajjhāpajjeyyāti abhibhuyya pajjeyya. Sabbantimenāti paranimmitavasavatti…pe… cātumahārājikamanussitthināgagaruḷamāṇavikādīnaṃ sabbāsaṃ antimena. Tiracchānagatāyāti tiracchānesu [V 0.0173] uppannāya. Tenāha “paṭisandhivasenā”ti. Pārājikāya vatthubhūtā eva cettha tiracchānagatitthī “tiracchānagatā”ti gahetabbā, na sabbā. Tatrāyaṃ paricchedo –

Because this is a practice of couples that is attained through a similar state due to the obsession of lust, it is called 'sexual intercourse' (methuno dhammo); thus he says, 'by the obsession of lust,' etc. Herein, 'by the obsession of lust' means by the obsession of lust, by the arising of sexual desire, by having one's mind bound by it. 'Practice' (dhamma) means transgression. As in 'delays' (palambate) and 'lingers' (vilambate), there is no special meaning of the prefix; thus he says, 'one should engage' (seveyya). 'One should commit' (ajjhāpajjeyya) means one should commit it, being overcome. 'By the very last' refers to the very last of all of them, such as human females, female nāgas, female garuḷas, and young women, from the Paranimmitavasavatti realm down to the Cātumahārājika realm. 'With one of animal birth' means with one born among animals. Therefore, he says, 'by way of rebirth-linking.' Here, only the female animal who constitutes the object of a Pārājika offense should be taken as 'one of animal birth,' not all. Herein, this is the delimitation:

“Apadānaṃ ahimacchā, dvipadānañca kukkuṭī;

Catuppadānaṃ majjārī, vatthu pārājikassimā”ti. (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.55)

For the footless, a snake and a fish; for the two-footed, a hen; for the four-footed, a cat—these are the objects for a pārājika offense.

Tattha ahiggahaṇena sabbāpi ajagaragonasādibhedā dīghajāti saṅgahitā. Tasmā dīghajātīsu yattha tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ aññatarasmiṃ sakkā tilaphalamattampi pavesetuṃ, sā pārājikavatthu, avasesā dukkaṭavatthūti veditabbā. Macchaggahaṇena sabbāpi macchakacchapamaṇḍūkādibhedā odakajāti saṅgahitā. Tatrāpi dīghajātiyaṃ vuttanayeneva pārājikavatthu ca dukkaṭavatthu ca veditabbaṃ. Ayaṃ pana viseso – pataṅgamukhamaṇḍūkā nāma honti, tesaṃ mukhasaṇṭhānaṃ mahantaṃ, chiddaṃ appakaṃ, tattha pavesanaṃ nappahoti, mukhasaṇṭhānaṃ pana vaṇasaṅkhepaṃ gacchati, tasmā taṃ thullaccayavatthūti veditabbaṃ[M 0.0184]. Kukkuṭiggahaṇena sabbāpi kākakapotādibhedā pakkhijāti saṅgahitā. Tatrāpi vuttanayeneva pārājikavatthu ca dukkaṭavatthu ca veditabbaṃ. Majjāriggahaṇena sabbāpi rukkhasunakhamaṅgusagodhādibhedā catuppadajāti saṅgahitā. Tatrāpi vuttanayeneva pārājikavatthu ca dukkaṭavatthu ca veditabbaṃ.

Herein, by the term 'serpent,' all long-bodied species of such varieties as pythons, gonasa snakes, and the like, are included. Therefore, among long-bodied creatures, wherever it is possible to insert even to the measure of a sesame seed into any of the three orifices, that constitutes an object for a pārājika offense; the rest should be understood as objects for a dukkaṭa offense. By the term 'fish,' all water-dwelling species of such varieties as fish, turtles, frogs, and the like, are included. Here too, the object for a pārājika offense and the object for a dukkaṭa offense should be understood in the same way as stated for the long-bodied species. However, there is this distinction: there are those called 'moth-mouthed frogs'; their mouth-shape is large, but the aperture is small. Insertion there is not possible, but the mouth-shape is reckoned as a wound. Therefore, that should be understood as an object for a thullaccaya offense. By the term 'hen,' all winged species of such varieties as crows, pigeons, and the like, are included. Here too, the object for a pārājika offense and the object for a dukkaṭa offense should be understood in the same way as previously stated. By the term 'cat,' all four-legged species of such varieties as tree-dwelling animals, dogs, mongooses, monitor lizards, and the like, are included. Here too, the object for a pārājika offense and the object for a dukkaṭa offense should be understood in the same way as previously stated.

Pārājiko hotīti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.55) parājito hoti parājayaṃ apanno. Ayañhi pārājikasaddo sikkhāpadāpattipuggalesu vattati. Tattha “aṭṭhānametaṃ, ānanda, anavakāso, yaṃ tathāgato vajjīnaṃ vā vajjiputtakānaṃ vā kāraṇā sāvakānaṃ pārājikaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ samūhaneyyā”ti (pārā. 43) evaṃ sikkhāpade vattamāno veditabbo. “Āpattiṃ tvaṃ bhikkhu āpanno pārājika”nti (pārā. 67) evaṃ āpattiyaṃ. “Na mayaṃ pārājikā, yo avahaṭo, so pārājiko”ti (pārā. 155) evaṃ puggale vattamāno veditabbo. “Pārājikena dhammena anuddhaṃseyyā”tiādīsu (pārā. 384) pana dhamme vattatīti vadanti. Yasmā pana tattha “dhammo”ti katthaci āpatti, katthaci sikkhāpadameva adhippetaṃ, tasmā so visuṃ na vattabbo. Tattha sikkhāpadaṃ yo taṃ atikkamati, taṃ parājeti, tasmā “pārājika”nti vuccati. Āpatti pana yo naṃ ajjhāpajjati, taṃ parājeti, tasmā “pārājikā”ti vuccati. Puggalo yasmā parājito parājayamāpanno, tasmā “pārājiko”ti vuccati. Idha pana puggalo veditabboti āha “pārājiko hotī”tiādi. Imināpi [V 0.0174] idaṃ dasseti – “parājitasadde upasaggassa vuddhiṃ katvā, ta-kārassa ca ka-kāraṃ katvā pārājiko hotīti niddiṭṭho”ti.

He is defeated (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 1.55): he is vanquished, having fallen into defeat. Indeed, this term 'pārājika' applies to training rules, offenses, and individuals. In this regard, it should be understood as referring to the training rule in the following passage: 'It is impossible, Ānanda, there is no possibility that the Tathāgata would revoke a pārājika training rule prescribed for the disciples because of the Vajjians or the Vajjian princes' (Pārā. 43). Regarding the offense, it is stated: 'You, monk, have committed a pārājika offense' (Pārā. 67). Regarding the individual, it should be understood as stated: 'We are not pārājikas; whoever is expelled is the pārājika' (Pārā. 155). However, in passages such as 'he should not charge him with a pārājika matter' (Pārā. 384), they say it applies to the 'dhamma'. But since in that context, 'dhamma' sometimes means the offense and sometimes the training rule itself, it should not be stated separately. Therein, the training rule is called 'pārājika' because it defeats whoever transgresses it. The offense is called 'pārājikā' because it defeats whoever commits it. The individual is called 'pārājiko' because he is vanquished, having fallen into defeat. Here, however, the individual is to be understood, as stated: 'he is defeated,' etc. This also indicates: 'By strengthening the prefix of the word 'parājita' and changing the letter 'ta' to 'ka,' it is designated as 'pārājiko'.'

Apalokanādi catubbidhampi saṅghakammaṃ sīmāparicchinnehi pakatattehi bhikkhūhi ekato kattabbattā ekakammaṃ nāma. Ādisaddena ekuddesasamasikkhatānaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Tattha pañcavidhopi pātimokkhuddeso ekato uddisitabbattā ekuddeso nāma. Nahāpitapubbakādīnaṃ viya odissa anuññātaṃ ṭhapetvā avasesaṃ sabbampi sikkhāpadaṃ sabbehipi lajjipuggalehi samaṃ sikkhitabbabhāvato samasikkhatā nāma. Yasmā sabbepi lajjino etesu [M 0.0185] ekakammādīsu saha vasanti, na ekopi tato bahiddhā sandissati, tasmā tāni sabbānipi gahetvā ekakammādiko tividhopi saṃvāso nāmāti āha “so ca vuttappakāro saṃvāso tena puggalena saddhiṃ natthi, tena kāraṇena so pārājiko puggalo ‘asaṃvāso’ti vuccatī”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.55).

The fourfold Sangha act, beginning with announcement, must be performed together by the monks who are within a boundary and in good standing; hence it is called a 'single act' (ekakamma). By the word 'beginning' (ādi), 'single recitation' (ekuddesa) and 'equal training' (samasikkhatā) are included. Therein, the fivefold recitation of the Pātimokkha must be recited together; hence it is called a 'single recitation'. Setting aside what is permitted for a specific case, such as that of the former barber, all remaining training rules must be trained in equally by all conscientious individuals; hence it is called 'equal training'. Because all conscientious individuals dwell together in these—the single act, and so on—and not even one is found apart from them, therefore, taking all these together, the threefold communion, consisting of the single act and so on, is so called. Thus it is said: 'That kind of communion, as described, does not exist with that individual. For that reason, that person guilty of a pārājika offense is called ‘one with whom there is no communion’ (asaṃvāso)' (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 1.55).

Idāni yasmā na kevalaṃ manussitthiyā eva nimittaṃ pārājikavatthu, atha kho amanussitthitiracchānagatitthīnampi. Na ca itthiyā eva. Atha kho ubhatobyañjanakapaṇḍakapurisānampi, tasmā te satte, tesañca yaṃ yaṃ nimittaṃ vatthu hoti, taṃ taṃ nimittaṃ, tattha ca yathā paṭisevanto pārājiko hoti, tañca sabbaṃ vitthāretvā dassetuṃ “ayaṃ panettha vinicchayo”tiādimāha. Etthāti imasmiṃ sikkhāpade. Tesūti ye tiṃsamaggā vuttā, tesu. Attano vāti lambimudupiṭṭhike sandhāya vuttaṃ. Santhatassa vāti yena kenaci vatthena vā paṇṇena vā vākapaṭṭena vā cammena vā tipusīsādīnaṃ paṭṭena vā paliveṭhetvā, anto vā pavesetvā paṭicchannassa. Akkhāyitassa vāti soṇasiṅgālādīhi akkhāditassa. Yebhuyyena akkhāyitassāti yāva upaḍḍhakkhāyito nāma na hoti, evaṃ akkhāyitassa. Allokāseti tintokāse. Santhatanti tesaṃyeva vatthādīnaṃ yena kenaci paṭicchannaṃ. Ayañhettha saṅkhepattho – na hettha anupādinnakaṃ anupādinnakena chupati, mutti atthi, atha kho upādinnakena vā anupādinnakaṃ ghaṭṭiyatu, anupādinnakena vā upādinnakaṃ, anupādinnakena vā anupādinnakaṃ, upādinnakena vā upādinnakaṃ. Sace yattake paviṭṭhe pārājikaṃ hotīti vuttaṃ, tattakaṃ sevanacittena paveseti, sabbatthāyaṃ pārājikāpattiṃ āpanno nāma hotīti.

Now, since the object for a pārājika offense is not only the sexual organ of a human woman, but also that of a non-human woman and a female animal—and not only of a female, but also of a hermaphrodite, a eunuch, and a male—therefore, to explain in detail those beings, and of them whichever organ is the object, and how one who engages in intercourse there becomes guilty of a pārājika offense, and all that, he said, 'Herein is the decision,' and so on. 'Herein' means in this training rule. 'Among them' means among those thirty orifices that were mentioned. 'Or one’s own' is said with reference to the fleshy parts and the soft back. 'Of an uneaten one' means not devoured by dogs, jackals, and so on. 'Mostly uneaten' means uneaten to the extent that it is not what is called 'half-eaten'. 'In a wet place' means in a moist place. 'Covered' means concealed by any of those things, such as cloth, a leaf, bark, hide, or a sheet of tin, either by being wrapped around or inserted inside. Here is the summary meaning: It is not the case that there is release from the offense if what is not clung to touches what is not clung to; rather, whether what is clung to is in contact with what is not clung to, or what is not clung to with what is clung to, or what is not clung to with what is not clung to, or what is clung to with what is clung to—if one inserts to the extent that has been stated to constitute a pārājika offense, with the intention of sexual congress, then in every case one is said to have incurred a pārājika offense.

Evaṃ sevanacitteneva pavesentassa āpattiṃ dassetvā idāni yasmā taṃ pavesanaṃ nāma na kevalaṃ attūpakkameneva, parūpakkamenāpi hoti. Tatrāpi sādiyantasseva āpatti paṭisevanacittasamaṅgissa[V 0.0175], na itarassāti dassetuṃ “parena vā”tiādimāha. Tattha parenāti bhikkhupaccatthikādinā yena kenaci aññena. Pavesanapaviṭṭhaṭṭhitauddharaṇesūti ettha aggato (sārattha. ṭī. 2.58) yāva mūlā pavesanaṃ pavesanaṃ nāma. Aṅgajātassa yattakaṃ ṭhānaṃ pavesanārahaṃ, tattakaṃ anavasesato paviṭṭhaṃ paviṭṭhaṃ nāma. Evaṃ [M 0.0186] paviṭṭhassa uddharaṇārambhato antarā ṭhitakālo ṭhitaṃ nāma. Samantapāsādikāyaṃ pana mātugāmassa sukkavisaṭṭhiṃ patvā sabbathā vāyāmato oramitvā ṭhitakālaṃ sandhāya “sukkavisaṭṭhisamaye”ti vuttaṃ. Uddharaṇaṃ nāma yāva aggā nīharaṇakālo. Sādiyatīti sevanacittaṃ upaṭṭhapeti. Asādhāraṇavinicchayoti adinnādānādīhi sabbehi sikkhāpadehi asādhāraṇo vinicchayo.

Having thus shown the offense for one who inserts with a mind of indulgence, now, since that insertion occurs not only by one’s own initiative but also by another’s, to show that in that case too, the offense is only for one who consents, being endowed with a mind of indulgence, and not for the other, it is said, 'or by another,' and so forth. Herein, 'by another' means by any other, such as a monk's adversary. Regarding 'entering, having entered, remaining, and withdrawing': herein, from the tip down to the root, the insertion is called 'entering'. As much of the sexual organ as is the part suitable for insertion, that much having entered without remainder is called 'having entered'. For one thus entered, the period of remaining still before the start of withdrawal is called 'remaining'. However, in the Samantapāsādikā, referring to the time of remaining still after having reached the woman’s emission and having ceased from all effort, it is said, 'at the time of emission.' 'Withdrawal' is the time of drawing out up to the tip. 'Consents' means one establishes a mind of indulgence. 'Uncommon decision' means a decision not shared with all the other training rules, such as that on stealing.

Sādhāraṇavinicchayatthanti parivāravasena sādhāraṇavinicchayatthaṃ. Mātikāti mātā, janettīti attho. Nidadāti desanaṃ desavasena aviditaṃ viditaṃ katvā nidassetīti nidānaṃ. Paññāpīyatīti paññatti, tassā pakāro paññattividhi aṅgeti gameti ñāpetīti aṅgaṃ, kāraṇaṃ. Samuṭṭhahanti āpattiyo etenāti samuṭṭhānaṃ, uppattikāraṇaṃ, tassa vidhi samuṭṭhānavidhi. Vajjakammappabhedañcāti ettha pabhedasaddo paccekaṃ yojetabbo “vajjappabhedaṃ, kammappabhedañcā”ti. Tattha tatthāti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ sikkhāpade.

'For the purpose of a shared judgment' means for the purpose of a shared judgment by way of the Parivāra. 'Mātikā' means mother; the meaning is 'progenitrix.' It lays down the teaching; by way of teaching, it makes known what was unknown and displays it; thus it is the 'source' (nidāna). It is prescribed, thus 'prescription' (paññatti); its manner is the 'method of prescription' (paññattividhi). It indicates, conveys, and makes known, thus it is a 'factor' (aṅga), a cause. Offenses arise from this, thus it is the 'origin' (samuṭṭhāna), the cause of arising; its method is the 'method of origin' (samuṭṭhānavidhi). And the classification of offenses and legal procedures: here the word 'classification' (pabheda) should be connected separately as 'the classification of offenses and the classification of legal procedures.' 'Here and there' means in each and every training rule.

Paññattiṭṭhānanti paññattiṭṭhapanassa ṭhānaṃ, sikkhāpadānaṃ paññattidesoti attho. Puggaloti ettha ādikammikoyeva adhippetoti āha “puggalo nāma yaṃ yaṃ ārabbha taṃ taṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññatta”nti, so so puggaloti adhippāyo. Honti cettha –

'The basis for the prescription' means the ground for establishing the prescription; the meaning is the place where the training rules are prescribed. 'Person' here means that only the original offender is intended, as it is said, "'Person' is whoever, in reference to whom, that particular training rule was prescribed." The meaning is: that particular person. And here there are—

“Sudinno dhaniyo sambahulā vaggumudantikā;

Seyyasako udāyi cā-ḷavakā channamettiyā.
