"Sudinna, Dhanika, and many from the Vaggumudā; Seyyasaka, Udāyi, the Āḷavakas, Channa and Mettiya.

“Devadattassajipunabbasu-chabbaggiyopanandaññataropi ca;

Hatthako cānuruddho ca, sattarasa cūḷapanthako.

"Devadatta, Assaji and Punabbasu, the Group of Six, Upananda, and another; Hatthaka and Anuruddha, the group of seventeen, and Cūḷapanthaka.

“Belaṭṭhasīso cānando, sāgatoriṭṭhanāmako;

Nandattherena tevīsa, bhikkhūnaṃ ādikammikā.

"Belaṭṭhasīsa, Ānanda, and the one named Ariṭṭha; with the elder Nanda, the original offenders among the monks are twenty-three.

“Sundarīnandā [V 0.0176] thullanandā, chabbaggiyaññatarāpi ca;

Caṇḍakāḷī sambahulā, dve ca bhikkhuniyo parā;

Bhikkhunīnaṃ tu satteva, honti tā ādikammikā”ti.

"Sundarī Nandā, Thullanandā, one of the Group of Six nuns, Caṇḍakālī, many others, and two other nuns—indeed, these seven are the original offenders among the nuns."

Tassa tassa puggalassāti yaṃ yaṃ sudinnādikaṃ puggalaṃ ārabbha sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ, tassa tassa puggalassa. Paññattīti paṭhamapaññatti. Paṭhamapaññattiyā pacchā [M 0.0187] ṭhapitā paññatti anupaññatti. Anuppanne dose ṭhapitā paññatti anuppannapaññatti. Sabbattha majjhimadese ceva paccantimesu janapadesu cāti sabbesu padesesu ṭhapitā paññatti sabbatthapaññatti. Majjhimadeseyeva ṭhapitā paññatti padesapaññatti. Bhikkhūnañceva bhikkhunīnañca sādhāraṇabhūtā paññatti sādhāraṇapaññatti. Suddhabhikkhūnameva, suddhabhikkhunīnaṃ vā paññattaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ asādhāraṇapaññatti. Ubhinnampi paññatti ubhatopaññatti. Vinayadharapañcamenāti anussāvanakācariyapañcamena. Guṇaṅguṇūpāhanāti catuppaṭalato paṭṭhāya katā upāhanā, na ekadvitipaṭalā. Cammattharaṇanti attharitabbaṃ cammaṃ. Etesaṃ vasena catubbidhā padesapaññatti nāmāti etesaṃ vasena catubbidhā paññatti majjhimadeseyeva paññattāti padesapaññatti nāma. Tenevāha “majjhimadeseyeva hī”tiādi. Yasmā majjhimadeseyeva yathāvuttavatthuvītikkame āpatti hoti, na paccantimajanapade, tasmā padesapaññattīti attho. Dhuvanhānaṃ paṭikkhepamattanti niccanahānappaṭisedhanameva. Ettha ca mattasaddena aññāni tīṇi sikkhāpadāni paṭikkhipati. Tāni hi “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sabbapaccantimesu janapadesu vinayadharapañcamena gaṇena upasampada”ntiādinā (mahāva. 259) cammakkhandhake āgatāni. Tenevāha “tato aññā padesapaññatti nāma natthī”ti. Sabbānīti tato avasesāni sabbāni sikkhāpadāni. Tasmāti yasmā anuppannapaññatti aṭṭhagarudhammavasena bhikkhunīnaṃyeva āgatā, yasmā ca dhuvanhānaṃ paṭikkhepamattaṃ ṭhapetvā pātimokkhe sabbāni sikkhāpadāni sabbatthapaññattiyeva honti, yasmā ca sādhāraṇapaññattidukañca ekatopaññattidukañca byañjanamattaṃ nānaṃ, atthato ekaṃ, tasmā. Sabbatthāti sabbesu sikkhāpadesu. Āpattibhedo hettha uttarapadalopena “āpattī”ti vuttoti āha “āpattīti pubbappayogādivasena āpattibhedo”ti. Sīlaācāradiṭṭhiājīvavipattīnanti ettha paṭhamā dve āpattikkhandhā sīlavipatti nāma, avasesā pañca ācāravipatti nāma, micchādiṭṭhi ca antaggāhikādiṭṭhi ca diṭṭhivipatti nāma, ājīvahetu paññattāni cha sikkhāpadāni ājīvavipatti nāma, iti imāsaṃ sīlaācāradiṭṭhiājīvavipattīnaṃ aññatarāti attho.

'For each individual' means for each individual, such as Sudinna, in reference to whom a training rule was prescribed. 'Prescription' (paññatti) refers to the first prescription. A prescription established after the first prescription is a 'subsequent prescription' (anupaññatti). A prescription established for faults that have not yet arisen is an 'unarisen prescription' (anuppannapaññatti). A prescription established everywhere—both in the Middle Country and in the border regions, that is, in all regions—is a 'universal prescription' (sabbatthapaññatti). A prescription established only in the Middle Country is a 'regional prescription' (padesapaññatti). A prescription common to both monks and nuns is a 'shared prescription' (sādhāraṇapaññatti). A training rule prescribed exclusively for monks, or exclusively for nuns, is an 'unshared prescription' (asādhāraṇapaññatti). A prescription for both is a 'dual prescription' (ubhatopaññatti). 'By the fifth Vinaya expert' means with the proclaiming teacher as the fifth. 'Sandals with multiple layers' (guṇaṅguṇūpāhanā) are sandals made from four layers upwards, not one, two, or three layers. 'A leather covering' (cammattharaṇa) is leather that should be spread. Through these, the fourfold regional prescription is named—meaning that through these, the fourfold prescription is prescribed only in the Middle Country, hence it is called a regional prescription. Therefore it is said, 'Indeed, only in the Middle Country,' and so forth. Because an offense occurs for transgressing the stated grounds only in the Middle Country, not in the border regions, therefore it has the meaning of 'regional prescription.' 'Only the prohibition against constant bathing' means merely the prohibition of habitual bathing. And here, by the word 'only,' three other training rules are excluded. For these are found in the chapter on leather in the Mahāvagga, beginning with 'Monks, I allow ordination by a group with the fifth being a Vinaya expert in all border regions' (Mahāva. 259). Therefore it is said, 'Beyond that, there is no other regional prescription.' 'All' means all the remaining training rules from that. 'Therefore' (tasmā) means because the unarisen prescription applies exclusively to nuns by way of the eight weighty rules; and because, apart from merely the prohibition against constant bathing, all training rules in the Pātimokkha are universal prescriptions; and because the pair of shared prescriptions and the pair of dual prescriptions differ only in expression, but are one in meaning—therefore. 'Everywhere' means in all training rules. Here, 'offense' (āpatti) is stated by the omission of the subsequent word, meaning 'types of offenses.' Hence, it is said, "'Offense' refers to the divisions of offenses based on prior application, etc." 'Failures in moral conduct, behavior, views, and livelihood': here, the first two categories of offenses are called 'failure in moral conduct'; the remaining five are called 'failure in behavior'; wrong view and extreme views are called 'failure in views'; and the six training rules prescribed due to livelihood are called 'failure in livelihood.' Thus, the meaning is 'any one of these failures in moral conduct, behavior, views, or livelihood'.

Na [V 0.0177] kevalaṃ yathāvuttanayeneva vuccantīti āha “yāni sikkhāpadasamuṭṭhānānītipi vuccantī”ti. Etāni hi kiñcāpi āpattiyā samuṭṭhānāni, na [M 0.0188] sikkhāpadassa, vohārasukhatthaṃ panevaṃ vuccantīti. Tatthāti tesu chasu samuṭṭhānesu. Tesūti sacittakācittakesu. Ekaṃ samuṭṭhānaṃ uppattikāraṇaṃ etissāti ekasamuṭṭhānā, ekena vā samuṭṭhānaṃ etissāti ekasamuṭṭhānā. “Dvisamuṭṭhānā”tiādīsupi eseva nayo.

It is said that they are not only spoken of in the manner just stated, but also as 'the origins of the training rules.' For although these are indeed the origins of offenses, not of the training rule itself, they are spoken of thus merely for the sake of convenience in expression. 'Herein' means among those six origins. 'Among them' means among the volitional and non-volitional. One origin is the cause of its arising, thus 'single-origin' (ekasamuṭṭhānā); or, by one origin it arises, thus 'single-origin.' In the case of 'dual-origin' and so forth, the method is the same.

Samuṭṭhānavasenāti samuṭṭhānasīsavasena. Paṭhamapārājikaṃ samuṭṭhānaṃ etissāti paṭhamapārājikasamuṭṭhānā. Tathā adinnādānasamuṭṭhānā”tiādīsupi.

'By way of origin' means by way of the principal origin. The first pārājika has this as its origin; hence, 'origin of the first pārājika.' Similarly, in 'origin of stealing,' and so forth.

Sayaṃ pathavikhaṇane kāyena, pare āṇāpetvā khaṇāpane vācāya ca āpattisambhavato “pathavikhaṇanādīsu viyā”ti vuttaṃ. Ādisaddena adinnādānādīnaṃ pariggaho. Paṭhamakathināpatti kāyavācato kattabbaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ vā vikappanaṃ vā akarontassa hoti, no karontassāti āha “paṭhamakathināpatti viyā”ti. Aññātikāya bhikkhuniyā hatthato cīvarappaṭiggahaṇāpatti tassā hatthato cīvaraṃ paṭiggaṇhantassa, parivattakaṃ adentassa ca hotīti kiriyākiriyato samuṭṭhāti. “Siyā karontassā”tiādīsu siyāti “siyā kho pana te brāhmaṇa evamassā”tiādīsu viya “kadācī”ti iminā samānattho nipāto. Rūpiyappaṭiggahaṇāpatti siyā kiriyā gahaṇena āpajjanato, siyā akiriyā paṭikkhepassa akaraṇatoti āha “rūpiyappaṭiggahaṇāpatti viyā”ti. Kuṭikārāpatti vatthuṃ desāpetvā pamāṇātikkantakaraṇe karontassa siyā, adesāpetvā pana pamāṇātikkantakaraṇe pamāṇayuttaṃ vā karontassa ca akarontassa ca siyāti āha “kuṭikārāpatti viyā”ti.

Since an offense occurs through the body when digging the earth oneself, and through speech when ordering others to dig, it is said, 'as in digging the earth, etc.' By the word 'etc.' is included taking what is not given and so on. The first Kathina offense occurs for one who does not make the determination or the assignment by body or speech, not for one who does so; thus it is said, 'as in the first Kathina offense.' The offense of accepting a robe from the hand of an unrelated bhikkhunī occurs for one who accepts the robe from her hand and does not give an exchange item; thus it arises from an action and an inaction. In such phrases as 'it might be for one who does,' the word 'siyā' is a particle with the same meaning as 'sometimes,' as in such phrases as 'it might be, brahmin, that it is so for you.' The offense of accepting gold and silver might arise from the action of accepting it, or it might arise from the inaction of not refusing it; thus it is said, 'as in the offense of accepting gold and silver.' The offense concerning building a kuṭi might arise for one who, having had a site indicated, builds it exceeding the proper measure; but if one has not had a site indicated, it might arise for one who acts—by building it exceeding the measure or according to the measure—and for one who does not act; thus it is said, 'as in the offense concerning building a kuṭi.'

Saññāya abhāvena vimokkho assāti saññāvimokkhoti majjhepadalopasamāso daṭṭhabboti āha “yato vītikkamasaññāyā”tiādi. Itarā nāma yato vītikkamasaññāya abhāvena na muccati, sā itarasaddassa vuttappaṭiyogivisayattā. Yā acittakena vā sacittakamissakena vā samuṭṭhātīti yā āpatti kadāci acittakena vā kadāci sacittakamissakena vā samuṭṭhānena samuṭṭhāti. Ettha ca saññādukaṃ anāpattimukhena vuttaṃ, sacittakadukaṃ āpattimukhenāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

'Liberation-by-perception' (saññāvimokkha) means 'there is liberation due to the absence of perception'; it should be seen as a compound with an elided middle term. Thus it is said, 'because of the perception of transgression,' etc. The other kind is so called because one is not freed by the absence of the perception of transgression, for the word 'other' refers to the opposite case of what was stated. 'That which arises either from the unintentional or from a mixture with the intentional' means an offense that arises sometimes from an unintentional origin, sometimes from an origin mixed with the intentional. And here it should be understood that the dyad concerning perception is stated from the perspective of non-offense, while the dyad concerning intention is stated from the perspective of offense.

Yassā [M 0.0189] sacittakapakkhe cittaṃ akusalameva hotīti yassā sacittakāya āpattiyā cittaṃ akusalameva hoti, yassā ca sacittakācittakasaṅkhātāya surāpānādiacittakāya āpattiyā vatthuvijānanacittena [V 0.0178] sacittakapakkhe cittaṃ akusalameva hoti, ayaṃ lokavajjā. “Sacittakapakkhe”ti hi idaṃ vacanaṃ sacittakācittakaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Na hi ekaṃsato sacittakassa “sacittakapakkhe”ti visesane payojanaṃ atthīti. Yaṃ panettha gaṇṭhipade “surāpānasmiñhi ‘surā’ti vā ‘na vaṭṭatī’ti vā jānitvā pivane akusalamevā”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha “na vaṭṭatīti vā jānitvā”ti vuttavacanaṃ na yujjati paṇṇattivajjassāpi lokavajjabhāvappasaṅgato. Yassā pana “sacittakapakkhe cittaṃ akusalamevā”ti niyamo natthi, sā paṇṇattivajjāti imamatthaṃ dassento āha “sesā paṇṇattivajjā”ti. Tathā hi tassā vatthuvijānanacittena sacittakapakkhe cittaṃ siyā kusalaṃ, siyā akusalaṃ, siyā abyākatanti “akusalamevā”ti niyamo natthi. Ubhayattha āpajjitabbāti kāyadvāre, vacīdvāre cāti ubhayattha āpajjitabbā āpatti, tā pana adinnādānādayo. “Manodvāre āpatti nāma natthī”ti idaṃ yebhuyyavasena vuttaṃ upanikkhittasādiyanādīsu āpattisambhavatoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

'That for which, in the intentional case, the mind is only unwholesome': this refers to an intentional offense where the mind is only unwholesome, and to an offense classified as both intentional and unintentional, such as the unintentional offense of drinking liquor, where in the intentional case—when the mind knows the object—the mind is only unwholesome. This is what is blameworthy in the world. For the phrase 'in the intentional case' is stated with reference to what is both intentional and unintentional, since there is no purpose in qualifying what is exclusively intentional with the phrase 'in the intentional case.' What is said here in the difficult passage: 'In drinking liquor, when one drinks knowing it is 'liquor' or 'it is not allowable,' it is only unwholesome.' There, the statement 'knowing it is not allowable' is not tenable, as it would lead to the consequence that what is blameworthy by regulation would also be blameworthy in the world. But that for which there is no rule that 'in the intentional case, the mind is only unwholesome,' that is what is blameworthy by regulation. To show this meaning, it is said: 'The rest are blameworthy by regulation.' For in that case, when the mind knows the object, in the intentional case the mind might be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate; thus there is no rule that it is 'only unwholesome.' 'To be incurred in both places' means an offense to be incurred through both the body-door and the speech-door; these are taking what is not given and so on. The statement 'There is no offense, as such, through the mind-door' is said as a general rule, for it should be understood that an offense can occur in cases such as consenting to what has been deposited.

Akusalacitto vā āpajjatīti pārājikasukkavisaṭṭhikāyasaṃsaggaduṭṭhullaattakāmapāricariyaduṭṭhadosasaṅghabhedappahāradānatalasattikādibhedaṃ āpattiṃ akusalacitto āpajjati. Anupasampannaṃ padasodhammaṃ vācento, mātugāmassa dhammaṃ desentoti evarūpaṃ āpattiṃ kusalacitto āpajjati. Asañciccasahaseyyādiṃ abyākatacitto āpajjati. Yaṃ arahā āpajjati, sabbaṃ abyākatacittova āpajjati. Tenāha “kusalābyākatacitto vā”ti.

'Or one with an unwholesome mind commits an offense': one with an unwholesome mind commits an offense of the kind involving defeat, emission of semen, bodily contact, lewd speech, attending to one's own lusts, malice, schism in the Sangha, giving a blow, raising a weapon, and so on. One with a wholesome mind commits an offense of the kind such as teaching the Dhamma word by word to an unordained person, or teaching the Dhamma to a woman. One with an indeterminate mind commits an offense such as unintentionally lying down together. Whatever offense an arahant commits, he commits it all with an indeterminate mind. Therefore it is said: 'or with a wholesome or indeterminate mind.'

Dukkhavedanāsamaṅgī vāti duṭṭhadosādibhedaṃ āpattiṃ āpajjanto dukkhavedanāsamaṅgī āpajjati. Methunadhammādibhedaṃ pana sukhavedanāsamaṅgī āpajjati. Yaṃ sukhavedanāsamaṅgī āpajjati, taṃyeva majjhatto hutvā āpajjanto adukkhamasukhavedanāsamaṅgī āpajjati. Tenāha “itaravedanādvayasamaṅgī vā”ti. Idampi ca tikadvayaṃ yebhuyyavaseneva vuttaṃ. Nipajjitvā [M 0.0190] nirodhasamāpanno hi acittako avedano sahaseyyāpattiṃ āpajjatīti. Kiñcāpi evaṃ aniyamena vuttaṃ, viseso panettha atthīti dassetuṃ “evaṃ santepī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Evaṃ santepīti hi visesābhidhānanimittābhyūpagameva yujjati. Sabbesaṃ vasena tīṇi cittānīti kusalākusalābyākatānaṃ vasena padasodhammādīsu tīṇi cittāni.

'Or one endowed with painful feeling': one committing an offense of the kind involving malice, etc., commits it endowed with painful feeling. But one commits an offense of the kind involving sexual intercourse, etc., endowed with pleasant feeling. When one commits with equanimity the very same offense that one commits endowed with pleasant feeling, one commits it endowed with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Therefore it is said: 'or endowed with the other two feelings.' This dyad of triplets, too, is stated as a general rule. For one who has lain down and attained the cessation attainment is without mind and without feeling, yet he commits the offense of lying down together. Although it is thus stated without a fixed rule, to show that there is a distinction here, it is said, 'even so,' etc. For the phrase 'even so' is fitting only for acknowledging the sign of a special statement. 'By way of all, there are three minds': by way of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate, there are three minds in cases such as teaching the Dhamma word by word.

Idāni taṃ yathāvuttanidānādivedanāttikapariyosānaṃ sattarasappakāraṃ imasmiṃ sikkhāpade yojetuṃ “idha panā”tiādimāha. Idhāti imasmiṃ paṭhamapārājikasikkhāpade. Vesāliyanti evaṃnāmake [V 0.0179] itthiliṅgavasena pavattavohāre nagare. Tañhi nagaraṃ tikkhattuṃ pākāraparikkhepavaḍḍhanena visālībhūtattā “vesālī”ti vuccati. Idampi ca nagaraṃ sabbaññutaṃ sampatteyeva sammāsambuddhe sabbākāravepullattaṃ pattanti veditabbaṃ. “Sikkhaṃ apaccakkhāyā”ti ca “antamaso tiracchānagatāyapī”ti ca dve anupaññattiyoti makkaṭivajjiputtakavatthūnaṃ vasena vuttā. “Antamaso tiracchānagatāyā”ti ca “sikkhaṃ apaccakkhāyā”ti ca imā dve anupaññattiyo. Āpattikarā ca hotīti paṭhamapaññattito visuṃyevāpattikarā ca hoti. Aññavādakasikkhāpadādīsu viyāti aññavādakasikkhāpadādīsu “vihesake”tiādikā (pāci. 98) viyāti attho. Ādisaddena ujjhāpanakassa pariggaho. Ettha hi aññavādakādito visuṃyeva vihesakādīsupi pācittiyaṃ hoti. Yathāha “ropite vihesake saṅghamajjhe vatthusmiṃ vā āpattiyā vā anayuñjiyamāno taṃ nakathetukāmo taṃ naugghāṭetukāmo tuṇhībhūto saṅghaṃ viheseti, āpatti pācittiyassā”tiādi (pārā. 100). Supinante vijjamānāpi mocanassādacetanā abbohārikattā anāpattikarāti āha “aññatra supinantātiādikā viyā”ti. Tathā hi thinamiddhena abhibhūtattā supine cittaṃ abbohārikaṃ, cittassa abbohārikattā opakkamanakiriyāpavattanikāpi cetanā abbohārikā. Vuttañhetaṃ “atthesā, bhikkhave, cetanā, sā ca kho abbohārikā”ti (pārā. 235), tasmā “aññatra supinantā”ti ayaṃ anupaññatti anāpattikarā jātā. Ādisaddena “aññatra adhimānā”tiādikaṃ (pārā. 197) saṅgaṇhāti. Adinnādānādīsu viyāti adinnādānādīsu [M 0.0191] “araññā vā”tiādikā (pārā. 91) viyāti attho. Ettha pana ādisaddena paṭhamapārājikādīnaṃ saṅgaho. Ettha hi “tañca kho gāme, no araññe”tiādinā (pārā. 90) nayena lesaṃ oḍḍentānaṃ lesapidahanatthaṃ “araññā vā”tiādikā anupaññatti vuttāti upatthambhakarāva hoti. Teneva hi “nanu, āvuso, tathevetaṃ hotī”ti (pārā. 90) bhikkhūhi vuttaṃ.

Now, to apply to this training rule those seventeen types of analysis, beginning with the origin and ending with the triplet on feeling, as they have been described, he says, 'But here,' etc. 'Here' means in this first pārājika training rule. 'In Vesālī' means in the city of that name, a term used in the feminine gender by convention. For that city, having become extensive by the enlargement of its surrounding wall three times, is called 'Vesālī.' And it should be understood that this city attained its full prosperity in every way only when the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One had attained omniscience. 'Without having renounced the training' and 'even with a female animal' are two supplementary clauses stated on the basis of the stories of the monkey and the Vajjian son. 'Even with a female animal' and 'without having renounced the training'—these are the two supplementary clauses. 'And it entails an offense' means it entails an offense quite apart from the original ruling. 'As in the training rule on evasive speech, etc.': the meaning is, as in the training rule on evasive speech, etc., with the clause 'by being vexatious,' etc. By 'etc.' is included contemptuous speech. For here, a pācittiya offense is incurred for being vexatious, etc., quite apart from the offense for evasive speech. As it is said: 'If, when a matter or an offense is raised in the midst of the Sangha, one, not wanting to speak about it, not wanting to disclose it, remains silent and thus vexes the Sangha, it is an offense of pācittiya,' etc. Since the intention to enjoy the release, though present in a dream, is non-transactional, it does not entail an offense; thus he says, 'as in "except in a dream," etc.' For in a dream, since the mind is overcome by sloth and torpor, it is non-transactional, and because the mind is non-transactional, the intention that initiates the action is also non-transactional. This has been said: 'There is, bhikkhus, that intention, but it is non-transactional.' Therefore this supplementary clause 'except in a dream' has become one that makes for no offense. By 'etc.' is included 'except in the case of overestimation,' etc. 'As in taking what is not given, etc.': the meaning is, as in taking what is not given, etc., with the clause 'or from the wilderness,' etc. By 'etc.' here is included the first pārājika, etc. For here, the supplementary clause 'or from the wilderness,' etc., was stated to close a loophole for those who were setting up a pretext in the way shown by 'and that, too, in a village, not in the wilderness,' etc. Thus it is merely supportive. For that very reason the bhikkhus said: 'But, friend, is it not just so?'

Vuttappakāre maggeti “manussāmanussatiracchānagatavasenā”tiādinā (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. paṭhamapārājikavaṇṇanā) vuttappakāre tiṃsamagge. Imassa pana “chinne”ti iminā sambandho. Tacādīni anavasesetvāti nimittappadese bahi ṭhitāni chavicammāni anavasesetvā. Nimittasaṇṭhānamattaṃ paññāyatīti nimittamaṃsassa pana abbhantare chavicammassa ca vijjamānattā vuttaṃ. Cammakhilanti cammakkhaṇḍaṃ. “Uṇṇigaṇḍo”tipi (sārattha. ṭī. 2.55; vi. vi. ṭī. 1.55) vadanti. Tañhi nimitte jātattā nimittameva. Tenāha “sevanacitte sati pārājika”nti. Sevanacitteti methunasevanacitte. Kāyasaṃsaggasevanacitte pana sati saṅghādisesova[V 0.0180]. Naṭṭho kāyappasādo etthāti naṭṭhakāyappasādaṃ, sukkhapīḷakaṃ vā matacammaṃ vāti attho. Mate akkhāyite, yebhuyyena akkhāyite ca pārājikāpattivacanato (pārā. 61) pana naṭṭhakāyappasādepi itthinimitte pavesentassa pārājikāpattiyeva. Nimittasaṇṭhānamattampi anavasesetvāti nimittākārena ṭhitaṃ yathāvuttanimittamaṃsādimpi anavasesetvā. Vaṇasaṅkhepavasenāti vaṇasaṅgahavasena. Vaṇe thullaccayañca “amaggena amaggaṃ paveseti, āpatti thullaccayassā”ti (pārā. 66) imassa suttassa vasena veditabbaṃ. Tasmiñhi sutte dvīsu sambhinnavaṇesu ekena vaṇena pavesetvā dutiyena nīharantassa thullaccayaṃ vuttaṃ. Vuttañhi samantapāsādikāyaṃ “imassa sattassa anulomavasena sabbattha vaṇasaṅkhepe thullaccayaṃ veditabba”nti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.66). Manussānaṃ pana akkhiādayopi vaṇasaṅgahaṃ gacchantīti vaṇena ekaparicchedaṃ katvā dassento “tathā”tiādimāha. Tesaṃ vaṇasaṅgaho “navadvāro mahāvaṇo”ti (mi. pa. 2.6.1) evamādisuttānusārena veditabbo. Tattha manussānanti itthipurisapaṇḍakaubhatobyañjanakavasena catubbidhānaṃ manussānaṃ. Vatthikosesūti [M 0.0192] vatthipuṭesu purisānaṃ aṅgajātakosesu. Hatthiassādīnañca tiracchānānanti hatthiassagoṇagadrabhaoṭṭhamahiṃsādīnaṃ tiracchānagatānaṃ. Tiracchānānaṃ panāti sabbesampi tiracchānagatānaṃ. Sabbesanti yathāvuttamanussādīnaṃ sabbesaṃ.

The path is sought in the manner stated, 'by way of humans, non-humans, and animals,' etc. (Kaṅkhā. Aṭṭha. First Pārājikā Commentary), in the thirty paths described in this manner. Its connection, however, is with 'cut off.' 'Without leaving out the skin, etc.' means without leaving out the skin and hide that remain outside in the area of the mark. 'Only the shape of the mark is discernible' is said because the flesh of the mark and the inner skin are still present within it. 'Cammakhila' means a piece of skin. Some also call it 'uṇṇigaṇḍa' (Sārattha. Ṭī. 2.55; Vi. Vi. Ṭī. 1.55). Since it arises from the mark, it is the mark itself. Hence, it is said: 'When there is an intention for intercourse, it is a pārājikā offense.' 'Intention for intercourse' means the intention for sexual union. If, however, there is an intention for bodily contact, it is only a saṅghādisesa offense. 'Naṭṭhakāyappasādaṃ' means 'where the bodily sensitivity is destroyed,' that is, a dry sore or dead skin. However, since it is stated that a pārājikā offense is incurred when it is dead and not apparent, or mostly not apparent (Pārā. 61), even if the bodily sensitivity is lost, one who inserts into a female mark still incurs a pārājikā offense. 'Without leaving out even the mere shape of the mark' means without leaving out even the aforementioned flesh of the mark, etc., that remains in the form of a mark. 'By way of classifying as a wound' means by way of including as a wound. And a grave offense in the case of a wound should be understood according to the rule: 'If one inserts into a non-passage through a non-passage, there is an offense of grave offense' (Pārā. 66). For in that rule, it is stated that for one who inserts through one of two connected wounds and withdraws through the second, a grave offense is incurred. It is also stated in the Samantapāsādikā: 'For this being, a grave offense is to be understood everywhere by way of classifying as a wound, in due order' (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 1.66). However, since even the eyes, etc., of humans are included in the category of wounds, to show this by making a single classification with the wound, it says 'so too,' etc. Their inclusion in the category of wounds should be understood according to such suttas as 'the great wound with nine doors' (Mi. Pa. 2.6.1). There, 'humans' means the four types of humans: women, men, neuters, and hermaphrodites. 'Vatthikosesu' means in the scrotal sacs, the pouches of the male genitalia. And 'of elephants, horses, etc., and of animals' means of animals such as elephants, horses, oxen, donkeys, camels, buffaloes, etc. And 'of animals' means of all animals. 'All' means all the aforementioned humans, etc.

Evaṃ jīvamānakasarīre labbhamānaṃ āpattivisesaṃ dassetvā idāni matasarīre labbhamānaṃ āpattivisesaṃ dassetuṃ “matasarīre”tiādimāha. Vaccamaggapassāvamaggamukhamaggānaṃ catūsu koṭṭhāsesu dve koṭṭhāse ṭhapetvā yadā apare dve koṭṭhāsā khāditā, tadā upaḍḍhakkhāyitaṃ nāma hoti. Na kuthitaṃ hotīti uddhumātakādibhāvena kuthitaṃ na hoti, allanti attho. Yadā pana sarīraṃ uddhumātakaṃ hoti kuthitaṃ nīlamakkhikasamākiṇṇaṃ kimikulasamākulaṃ navahi vaṇamukhehi paggaḷitapubbakuṇapabhāvena upagantumpi asakkuṇeyyaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.59-60), tadā pārājikavatthuñca thullaccayavatthuñca vijahati, dukkaṭavatthumeva hotīti āha “kuthite dukkaṭa”nti. Kuthiteti uddhumātakabhāvappatte. Īdise hi sarīre yattha katthaci upakkamato dukkaṭaṃ. Tathā vaṭṭakate mukhe acchupantaṃ aṅgajātaṃ pavesentassāti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.73) vivaṭṭe mukhe cattāri passāni, tālukañca apphusantaṃ aṅgajātaṃ pavesentassa dukkaṭanti attho. Sace pana heṭṭhā vā upari vā ubhayapassehi vā chupantaṃ paveseti, pārājikaṃ. Catūhi passehi acchupantaṃ pavesetvā abbhantare tālukaṃ chupati, pārājikameva. Bahi nikkhantajivhāya vā dantesu vā aṅgajātaṃ pavesentassa thullaccayanti sambandho. Jīvamānakasarīrepi bahi nikkhantajivhāya thullaccayameva. Yadi pana bahi jivhāya paliveṭhetvā antomukhaṃ paveseti, pārājikameva. Yadi pana dantā suphusitā, antomukhe okāso [V 0.0181] natthi, dantā ca bahi oṭṭhamaṃsena paṭicchannā, tattha vātena asamphuṭṭhaṃ allokāsaṃ tilaphalamattampi pavesentassa pārājikameva. Uppāṭite pana oṭṭhamaṃse dantesuyeva upakkamantassa thullaccayaṃ. Yopi danto bahi nikkhamanto tiṭṭhati, na sakkā oṭṭhehi pidahituṃ, tatthāpi eseva nayo.

Having thus shown the specific offense incurred in a living body, now, to show the specific offense incurred in a dead body, it begins with 'in a dead body.' When, of the four parts of the anal, urinary, and mouth passages, two parts are set aside and the other two are eaten, then it is called 'half-eaten.' 'It is not decayed' means it is not decayed in the state of being bloated, etc.; it is fresh. However, when the body is bloated, decayed, infested with blue flies, swarming with worms, and oozing from its nine orifices with the nature of a putrid corpse, such that it is impossible even to approach (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 1.59-60), at that time, it abandons the grounds for both a pārājikā and a thullaccaya offense, becoming only a dukkaṭa offense—hence it is said, 'in a decayed state, a dukkaṭa.' 'In a decayed state' means having reached the condition of being bloated. For in such a body, a dukkaṭa is incurred by any attempt whatsoever. Similarly, 'in the case of one inserting the genital organ into an open mouth without touching' (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 1.73) means that for one who inserts the genital organ into an open mouth without it touching the four sides and the palate, a dukkaṭa is incurred. However, if one inserts it while it is touching below, above, or both sides, it is a pārājikā. If one inserts it without it touching the four sides but it touches the palate inside, it is still a pārājikā. The connection is that for one who inserts the genital organ into a tongue protruding outside or between the teeth, it is a thullaccaya. Even in a living body, for a tongue protruding outside, it is only a thullaccaya. However, if one wraps the organ with the tongue outside and then inserts it into the mouth, it is a pārājikā. If, however, the teeth are closely set, leaving no space inside the mouth, and the teeth are covered by the flesh of the lip, and one inserts even a sesame-seed-sized wet space there that is untouched by wind, it is still a pārājikā. But if the flesh of the lip is torn and one attempts between the teeth themselves, it is a thullaccaya. And even if a tooth protrudes outside and cannot be covered by the lips, this same principle applies.

Vedanāya aṭṭo pīḷito vedanāṭṭo. Ummattakoti cettha pittummattako adhippetoti āha “yo pittavasenā”tiādi. Pittavasenāti [M 0.0193] baddhapittavasena. Tasmiñhi baddhapitte pittakosato calitvā bahi nikkhamante sattā ummattakā honti, vipallatthasaññā hirottappaṃ chaḍḍetvā asāruppacariyaṃ caranti, lahukagarukāni sikkhāpadāni maddantāpi na jānanti, bhesajjakiriyāyapi atekicchā honti, evarūpassa ummattakassa anāpatti. Abaddhapittaṃ pana lohitaṃ viya sabbaṅgagataṃ, tamhi kupite sattānaṃ kaṇḍukacchusarīrakampādīni honti, tāni bhesajjakiriyāya vūpasamanti. Tena vuttaṃ “baddhapittavasenā”ti. Khittacitto nāma vissaṭṭhacitto yakkhummattako vuccatīti āha “yakkhehi katacittavikkhepo khittacitto”ti. Yakkhā kira bheravāni ārammaṇāni dassetvā mukhena hatthaṃ pavesetvā, hadayarūpaṃ vā maddantā satte vikkhittacitte vipallatthasaññe karonti, evarūpassa khittacittassa anāpatti. Tesaṃ pana ubhinnaṃ ayaṃ viseso – pittummattako niccameva ummattako hoti, pakatisaññaṃ na labhati. Yakkhummattako antarantarā pakatisaññaṃ paṭilabhati. Idha pana pittummattako vā hotu, yakkhummattako vā, yo sabbaso muṭṭhassati kiñci na jānāti, aggimpi suvaṇṇampi gūthampi candanampi ekasadisaṃ maddantova vicarati, evarūpassa anāpatti. Antarantarā pakatisaññaṃ paṭilabhitvā ñatvā karontassa pana āpattiyeva. Tenāha “dvinnampi ca etesa”ntiādi.

One afflicted and tormented by feeling is 'afflicted by feeling.' Here, 'madman' is intended to mean one mad due to bile; hence it is said, 'one who, due to bile,' etc. 'Due to bile' means due to constricted bile. For when that constricted bile moves from the gall bladder and exits, beings become mad; with their perceptions distorted, they abandon shame and fear and engage in unsuitable behavior. Even when they violate minor and major training rules, they do not know it, and they are incurable by medical treatment. For such a madman, there is no offense. Unconstricted bile, however, like blood, spreads throughout the entire body. When it is aggravated, beings experience itching, scabies, bodily tremors, etc. These are calmed by medical treatment. Therefore, it is said, 'due to constricted bile.' 'One with a deranged mind' means one whose mind is scattered, who is called 'one made mad by a spirit'; hence it is said, 'one whose mind is disturbed by spirits is 'deranged-minded'.' Spirits, it is said, show terrifying objects, insert their hands into the mouth, or crush the physical heart, making beings' minds scattered and their perceptions distorted. For such a deranged-minded one, there is no offense. However, there is this distinction between the two: one mad due to bile is always mad and does not regain normal perception. One made mad by a spirit regains normal perception intermittently. Here, however, whether one is mad due to bile or made mad by a spirit, if one is entirely forgetful and knows nothing—treating fire, gold, excrement, and sandalwood as the same, and wandering about crushing them—for such a one, there is no offense. But for one who regains normal perception intermittently and acts knowingly, there is an offense. Therefore, it is said: 'For both of these,' etc.

Adhimattavedanāyāti adhikappamāṇāya dukkhavedanāya. Ādikamme niyutto ādikammiko, yo ca ādikamme niyutto, so tasmiṃ kamme ādibhūto hotīti āha “yo”tiādi. Idha pana sudinnatthero ādikammiko, tassa anāpatti. Avasesānaṃ makkaṭisamaṇavajjiputtakādīnaṃ āpattiyeva. Paṭipādanaṃ sampādanaṃ. Karontoyeva hi taṃ āpajjatīti kiriyaṃ. Idaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. 2.66) pana yebhuyyavasena vuttaṃ methunadhamme parūpakkame sati sādiyantassa akiriyasamuṭṭhānabhāvato. Methunappaṭisaṃyuttāya hi kāmasaññāya abhāvena muccanato saññāvimokkhaṃ. “Anāpatti ajānantassa, asādiyantassā”ti (pārā. 66) hi vuttaṃ. Methunacitteneva naṃ āpajjati, na vinā cittenāti sacittakaṃ. Rāgavaseneva āpajjitabbato lokavajjaṃ. Kāyadvāreneva samuṭṭhānato kāyakammaṃ. Cittaṃ panettha aṅgamattaṃ hoti[V 0.0182], na tassa vasena kammabhāvo labbhati. Lobhacitteneva [M 0.0194] āpajjitabbato akusalacittaṃ. Sukhasamaṅgī vā upekkhāsamaṅgī vā āpajjatīti dvivedanaṃ. Nanu samuṭṭhānādīni āpattiyā honti, na sikkhāpadassa, atha kasmā sikkhāpadassa samuṭṭhānādīni vuttānīti āha “imāni ca samuṭṭhānādīni nāmā”tiādi. Āpattiyā hontīti ajjhācārassa honti.

'Adhimattavedanāyāti' means by a painful feeling of excessive measure. 'Ādikamme niyutto ādikammiko' means 'one engaged in the first action is the first doer'; and 'one who is engaged in the first action is the first in that action', hence it is said, 'one who,' and so on. Here, however, the Elder Sudinna was the first doer; for him, there is no offense. For the rest—such as the monkey ascetic and the Vajjiputtakas—there is indeed an offense. 'Paṭipādanaṃ' means 'sampādanaṃ' (accomplishment). For it is only by doing it that one incurs it; hence it is an action (kiriya). This, however, is stated for the most part, because for one who consents when there is an attempt at sexual intercourse by another, the offense arises from non-action. For it is liberation by perception (saññāvimokkha) because one is freed by the absence of a perception of sensuality connected with sexual intercourse. For it is stated: 'There is no offense for one who is unaware, or unconsenting' (Pārā. 66). One incurs it only with a mind intent on sexual intercourse, not without a mind—hence it is 'with mind' (sacittaka). Since it is to be incurred through the power of lust, it is a worldly fault (lokavajja). Because it arises only through the body-door, it is a bodily action (kāyakamma). Here, the mind is merely a factor; the nature of the action is not obtained through it. Since it is to be incurred only through a greedy mind, it is an unwholesome mind (akusalacitta). One incurs it either accompanied by pleasure or accompanied by equanimity—hence it is twofold in feeling (dvivedana). Now, are not the origins and so on of the offense, not of the training rule? Then why are the origins and so on stated for the training rule?' To this, he says: 'These origins and so on are indeed called...' 'They are of the offense' means they are of the transgression (ajjhācāra).

Munanato anumunanato muti, ñāṇaṃ, taṃ etassa atthīti mutimā, ñāṇavāti attho.

From 'munana' (knowing) and 'anumunana' (repeatedly knowing) comes 'muti', which is knowledge (ñāṇa). One who possesses this is 'mutimā', meaning 'ñāṇavā' (endowed with knowledge).

Paṭhamapārājikavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the First Pārājika is concluded.

2. Dutiyapārājikavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Second Pārājika

Etthāti etesu dvīsu. Ekakuṭikādibhedo sabbopi gāmoti veditabboti sambandho. Tattha ekakuṭikādibhedoti yasmiṃ gāme ekā eva kuṭi ekaṃ gehaṃ seyyathāpi malayajanapade, ayaṃ ekakuṭiko gāmo nāma. Ādisaddena “dvikuṭikopi gāmo, tikuṭikopi gāmo, catukkuṭikopi gāmo”ti (pārā. 92) vuttappabhedaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Abhinavaniviṭṭho ekakuṭikādigāmo pana yāva manussā pavisitvā vāsaṃ na kappenti, tāva gāmasaṅkhaṃ na gacchati. Kiṃbhūtoti āha “parikkhitto vā”tiādi. Tattha parikkhitto nāma iṭṭhakapākāraṃ ādiṃ katvā antamaso kaṇṭakasākhāhipi parikkhitto. Tabbiparīto aparikkhitto. Amanusso nāma yo sabbaso vā manussānaṃ abhāvena yakkhapariggahabhūto, yato vā manussā kenaci karaṇīyena punapi āgantukāmā eva apakkantā, yato pana nirapekkhā hutvā pakkamanti, so gāmasaṅkhaṃ na gacchati. Na kevalaṃ ekakuṭikādibhedovāti āha “antamaso”tiādi. Yo koci satthopīti jaṅghasatthasakaṭasatthādīsu yo koci satthopi. Imasmiṃ sikkhāpade nigamanagarāni viya gāmaggahaṇeneva gāmūpacāropi saṅgahitoti āha “ṭhapetvā gāmañca gāmūpacārañcā”ti. Aññathā pana mātikāya anavasesato avahāraṭṭhānapariggaho kato nāma na hoti, na ca buddhā sāvasesaṃ pārājikaṃ paññāpenti.

'Ettha' means in these two. The connection is that every type, such as a single-hut village, should be understood as a 'village'. Therein, 'the various types such as a single-hut village' means a village in which there is only one hut, one house—for instance, in the Malaya country—this is called a single-hut village. By the word 'ādi' (and so on), it includes the distinctions mentioned: 'a two-hut village, a three-hut village, a four-hut village' (Pārā. 92). However, a newly established village of one hut and so on does not count as a village as long as people have not entered and taken up residence. 'Of what kind?' To this, he says: 'whether enclosed,' and so on. Therein, 'enclosed' means enclosed by anything from a brick wall down to thorny branches. The opposite is 'unenclosed'. 'Non-human' means a place that is either completely without humans and has become possessed by yakkhas, or from which humans have departed with the intention of returning for some business; but when they depart without attachment, it does not count as a village. To show that it is not only the types such as a single-hut village, he says 'even,' and so on. 'Any caravan' means any caravan among foot-caravans, cart-caravans, and so on. To show that in this training rule the village vicinity is also included by the very term 'village', just as market towns and cities are, he says: 'excluding the village and the village vicinity.' Otherwise, the determination of the location of theft in the matrix would not be exhaustive, and the Buddhas do not lay down a pārājika offense that is incomplete.

Tatthāti tesu gāmagāmūpacāresu. Dvāreti nibbakosassa udakapatanaṭṭhānato abbhantare. Antogeheti pamukhassa abbhantare. Kataparikkhepoti [M 0.0195] pākāravatiādīhi kataparikkhepo. Suppapatanādiparicchedo panettha aparikkhittagharaṃ sandhāya vutto. Na kevalaṃ gharassa purato, atha kho samantato tattakova paricchedo gharūpacāro nāmāti gahetabbaṃ. “Purato”tiādikaṃ pana lokiyehi [V 0.0183] tathākaraṇato vuttaṃ. Thāmamajjhimassāti majjhimathāmassa, neva appathāmassa, na mahāthāmassāti vuttaṃ hoti. “Yathā taruṇamanussā”tiādinā yathā mātugāmo kāke uḍḍāpento ujukameva hatthaṃ ukkhipitvā leḍḍuṃ khipati, yathā ca udakukkhepe udakaṃ khipanti, evaṃ khittassa leḍḍussa patitaṭṭhānaṃ paṭikkhipati. Pavattitvāti luṭhitvā, parivattitvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tassa sace dve indakhīlā hontīti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.92) tassa parikkhittassa gāmassa sace anurādhapurasseva dve ummārā honti. Yassa pana eko, tassa gāmadvārabāhānaṃ vemajjhe ṭhitassa leḍḍupātabbhantaraṃ gāmūpacāro nāma. Yatra pana indakhīlo natthi, tatra gāmadvārabāhānaṃ vemajjhaṃ. Yatra dvārabāhāpi natthi, tattha ubhosu passesu vatiyā vā pākārassa vā koṭivemajjhaṃva indakhīlaṭṭhāniyattā indakhīloti gahetabbaṃ. Yo pana gāmo pubbe mahā hutvā pacchā kulesu naṭṭhesu appako hoti, so gharūpacārato leḍḍupāteneva paricchinditabbo. Purimaparicchedo panassa parikkhittassāpi aparikkhittassāpi appamāṇamevāti. Nanu cetaṃ aparikkhittassa upacāradassanaṃ padabhājanena viruddhamiva dissati. Tattha hi “gāmūpacāro nāma parikkhittassa gāmassa indakhīle ṭhitassa majjhimassa purisassa leḍḍupāto”ti (pārā. 92) vatvā “aparikkhittassa gāmassa gharūpacāre ṭhitassa majjhimassa purisassa leḍḍupāto”ti (pārā. 92) ettakameva vuttaṃ, na pana taṃ leḍḍupātaṃ gāmasaṅkhepaṃ katvā tato paraṃ gāmūpacāroti vuttoti āha “padabhājanepi hi imināva nayena attho veditabbo”ti.

'Tattha' means in those, that is, in the village and the village vicinity. 'At the door' means inside from the place where water falls from a house without a projection. 'Inside the house' means inside the entrance hall. 'Having a boundary made' means having a boundary made by a wall, fence, and so on. The determination here by the fall of a well-thrown clod, and so on, is stated with reference to an unenclosed house. It should be understood that the house vicinity is not only in front of the house, but is that same extent all around. 'In front,' and so on, is said because that is how worldly people do it. 'Of medium strength' means of moderate strength; it is said to be neither of little strength nor of great strength. By 'as a young person,' and so on, it rejects the landing spot of a clod thrown in the way a woman scaring away crows raises her hand straight up and throws, or as one throws water when splashing. 'Having rolled' means having tumbled, having turned over. 'If it has two boundary posts' (Pārā. aṭṭha. 1.92) means if that enclosed village has two gate-towers, like Anurādhapura. But for one that has only one, the village vicinity is the area within the range of a clod thrown by one standing midway between the village gateposts. Where there is no boundary post, it is midway between the gateposts. Where there are not even gateposts, the midpoint between the corners of the fence or wall on both sides should be taken as the boundary post, as it is in the position of a boundary post. But a village that was formerly large and later becomes small when families have been lost should be defined by a clod's throw from the house vicinity. Its former boundary, however, whether it was enclosed or unenclosed, is indeed immeasurable. Now, does not this explanation of the vicinity of an unenclosed village seem to conflict with the Word-Analysis? For there, after stating, 'The village vicinity of an enclosed village is the range of a clod thrown by a man of average strength standing at the boundary post' (Pārā. 92), it is said only this much: 'For an unenclosed village, it is the range of a clod thrown by a man of average strength standing in the house vicinity' (Pārā. 92). It is not stated that this clod's throw defines the village boundary and what is beyond that is the village vicinity. To this, he says: 'Even in the Word-Analysis, the meaning should be understood in this same way'.

Ayamettha adhippāyo – idha gāmo nāma duvidho hoti parikkhitto ca aparikkhitto ca (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.92). Tatra parikkhittassa parikkhepoyeva paricchedo. Tasmā tassa visuṃ paricchedaṃ avatvā “gāmūpacāro nāma parikkhittassa gāmassa indakhīle ṭhitassa majjhimassa purisassa leḍḍupāto”ti pāḷiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Aparikkhittassa pana gāmassa gāmaparicchedo vattabbo. Tasmā tassa [M 0.0196] gāmassa gāmaparicchedadassanatthaṃ “aparikkhittassa gāmassa gharūpacāre ṭhitassa majjhimassa purisassa leḍḍupāto”ti (pārā. 92) vuttaṃ. Gāmaparicchede ca dassite gāmūpacāralakkhaṇaṃ pubbe vuttanayeneva sakkā ñātunti puna “tattha ṭhitassa majjhimassa purisassa leḍḍupāto”ti na vuttaṃ, attho pana tatthāpi ayameva yathāvuttoti. Yo pana gharūpacāre ṭhitassa leḍḍupātaṃyeva “gāmūpacāro”ti vadati, tassa gharūpacāro “gāmo”ti āpajjati. Tato gharaṃ gharūpacāro, gāmo gāmūpacāroti esa vibhāgo saṅkarīyati. Asaṃkarato cettha vinicchayo veditabbo. Tasmā pāḷiñca aṭṭhakathañca saṃsanditvā vuttanayenevettha gāmo, gāmūpacāro ca veditabboti.

Here, the meaning is this: In this context, a village is of two kinds—enclosed and unenclosed (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 1.92). For an enclosed village, the enclosure itself is the limit. Therefore, without separately stating its limit, it is said in the Pāli: "The vicinity of a village, in the case of an enclosed village, is the distance a clod can be thrown by an average man standing at the boundary post." However, for an unenclosed village, the village boundary must be defined. Thus, to show the boundary of such a village, it is said (Pārā. 92): "For an unenclosed village, it is the distance a clod can be thrown by an average man standing in the house vicinity." Once the village boundary is shown, the characteristic of the village vicinity can be understood in the way previously explained. Therefore, it is not repeated, "the distance a clod can be thrown by an average man standing there," but the meaning there is also the same as stated. However, for one who says that the clod-throw from the house-vicinity is itself the 'village vicinity', for him it follows that the house-vicinity is the 'village.' Then this distinction between a house and its vicinity, and a village and its vicinity, becomes confused. The decision here should be understood without confusion. Therefore, by reconciling the Pāli and the commentary, the village and the village vicinity should be understood in the way stated herein.

Tatthāti [V 0.0184] tesu dvīsu upacāresu. Yvāyaṃ upacāro dassitoti sambandho. Vikāle gāmappavesanādīsūti ettha ādisaddena asaṃkaccikāgāmappavesanaṃ (pāci. 1225) saṅgaṇhāti. Yo pana parikkhittassa gāmassa upacāro vutto, so na katthaci vinayapiṭake upayogaṃ gato. Kevalaṃ aparikkhittassa parikkhepokāsato aparo eko leḍḍupāto gāmūpacāro nāmāti ñāpanatthaṃ vutto. Evaṃ vutte hi ñāyati “parikkhittassāpi ce gāmassa eko leḍḍupāto kappiyabhūmi samāno upacāroti vutto, pageva aparikkhittassa parikkhepokāsato eko”ti. Imesaṃ paricchedadassanatthanti imesaṃ gāmāraññānaṃ paricchedadassanatthaṃ vuttā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ. Pārājikavatthunti pādagghanakaṃ. Avaharantassāti gaṇhantassa.

'Herein' means in those two vicinities. The connection is: 'This vicinity which is shown.' In the phrase 'At an improper time, entering the village, etc.,' the word 'etc.' includes entering the village without the saṅkaccikā (Pāc. 1225). However, the vicinity mentioned for an enclosed village has not been applied anywhere in the Vinaya Piṭaka. It was stated merely to make known that for an unenclosed village, another single clod's throw from the place of its boundary is called the village vicinity. For when it is stated thus, it is understood: 'If even for an enclosed village, a single clod's throw, being a permissible area, is called a vicinity, how much more so for an unenclosed village is one from the place of its boundary.' 'To show the boundaries of these' means it is said in the commentary to show the boundaries of these villages and forests. The ground for a pārājika offense means worth a pāda. 'For one who takes' means for one who seizes.

Adinnanti (pārā. aṭṭha. 92) dantaponasikkhāpade attano santakampi appaṭiggahitakaṃ kappiyaṃ ajjhoharaṇīyaṃ vuccati, idha pana yaṃ kiñci parapariggahitaṃ sasāmikaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ, tadetaṃ tehi sāmikehi kāyena vā vācāya vā na dinnanti adinnaṃ. Avahārappahonakameva pana dassetuṃ “aññassa manussajātikassa santaka”nti vuttaṃ. Saṅkhāsaddasseva ta-kārena vaḍḍhetvā vuttattā “saṅkhā saṅkhātanti atthato eka”nti vuttaṃ. Tattha atthato ekanti padatthato ekaṃ, anatthantaranti vuttaṃ hoti. Koṭṭhāsassetaṃ nāmaṃ bhāgato [M 0.0197] saṅkhāyati upaṭṭhātīti katvā. Papañcasaṅkhāti sattānaṃ saṃsāre papañcenti cirāyantīti papañcā, taṇhāmānadiṭṭhiyo, yassa vā uppannā, taṃ “ratto”ti vā “matto”ti vā “micchādiṭṭhiniviṭṭho”ti vā papañcenti byañjentīti papañcā, saṅkhā vuccati koṭṭhāso, papañcāva saṅkhā papañcasaṅkhā, papañcakoṭṭhāsāti attho, taṇhāmānadiṭṭhiyoti vuttaṃ hoti. Theyyacittasaṅkhātoti “theyyacitto”ti kathito. Eko cittakoṭṭhāsoti vissāsatāvakālikādiggāhavasappavattaatheyyacittakoṭṭhāsato añño cittakoṭṭhāso. Theyyasaṅkhātenāti theyyabhūtacittakoṭṭhāsena. Yadi evaṃ atha kasmā etassa vibhaṅge “theyyacitto avaharaṇacitto”ti (pārā. 92) vuttanti āha “yo cā”tiādi. Byañjanaṃ anādiyitvāti byañjane ādaraṃ akatvāti attho, saddatthamanapekkhitvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Atthamevāti bhāvatthameva.

"Not given" (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 92): In the training rule concerning tooth-sticks, even one's own suitable item for consumption, if unreceived, is called 'not given'. Here, however, any item whatever that is possessed by another, belonging to an owner, is 'not given' if it has not been given by those owners through body or speech. But to show that it is sufficient for an act of theft, it is stated: 'belonging to another human being.' Because the word 'saṅkhā' is stated expanded with a 'ta', it is said: 'saṅkhā' and 'saṅkhāta' are one in meaning. There, 'one in meaning' means one in terms of word-meaning, that is to say, there is no difference in meaning. This is the name for a portion (koṭṭhāsa) because it is reckoned or appears as a part. 'Papañcasaṅkhā': that which proliferates (papañcenti) for beings in saṃsāra, that which makes them delay long (cirāyanti), are proliferations (papañcā), namely craving, conceit, and wrong views. Or, when they have arisen in someone, they manifest (papañcenti) him as 'impassioned,' 'infatuated,' or 'entrenched in wrong view'; therefore they are proliferations. 'Saṅkhā' is called a portion; 'papañcasaṅkhā' is the proliferation-portion, meaning the portion of proliferation; that is to say, craving, conceit, and wrong views. 'Theyyacittasaṅkhāto' means 'called a thieving mind.' 'One portion of mind' means a portion of mind different from the non-thieving portion of mind that proceeds by way of taking with trust, for a temporary period, and so on. 'Theyyasaṅkhātena' means 'by the portion of mind that has become thieving.' If so, why is it stated in its analysis (vibhaṅga) as 'a thieving mind, a mind of taking away' (Pārā. 92)? To this, he says 'yo cā,' etc. 'Byañjanaṃ anādiyitvā' means 'not having regard for the letter,' that is to say, not considering the literal meaning of the word. 'Atthameva' means 'the essential meaning alone.'

Te pana avahārāti te pañcavīsati avahārā. Saviññāṇakāviññāṇakavasena nānāvidho bhaṇḍo etassa pañcakassāti nānābhaṇḍaṃ, pañcannaṃ avahārānaṃ samūho pañcakaṃ, pañcaparimāṇamassāti vā pañcakaṃ, nānābhaṇḍameva pañcakaṃ nānābhaṇḍapañcakaṃ. Saviññāṇakavasena eko bhaṇḍo etassāti ekabhaṇḍaṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Sāhatthikova pañcakaṃ [V 0.0185] sāhatthikapañcakaṃ. Ādipadavasena cetaṃ nāmaṃ kusalādittikassa kusalattikavohāro viya. Tasmā sāhatthikādipañcakanti atthato daṭṭhabbaṃ. Esa nayo sesesu pañcakadvayesu. Etassevāti “ādiyeyyā”ti etasseva mātikāpadassa. Imesaṃ padānaṃ vasenāti imesaṃ pañcannaṃ padānaṃ vasena. Ettha ca paṭhamapadaṃ abhiyogavasena vuttaṃ, dutiyapadaṃ aññesaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ harantassa gacchato vasena, tatiyapadaṃ upanikkhittabhaṇḍavasena, catutthaṃ saviññāṇakavasena, pañcamaṃ thale nikkhittādivasena vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

But those 'modes of theft' (avahārā) are the twenty-five modes of theft. 'Diverse goods' (nānābhaṇḍa) means that various goods, animate or inanimate, belong to this pentad. A 'pentad' (pañcaka) is a collection of five modes of theft, or it is a pentad because it has the measure of five. The 'diverse-goods pentad' (nānābhaṇḍapañcaka) is simply the pentad of diverse goods. 'Single item' (ekabhaṇḍa) means that one item, in the sense of being animate, belongs to it. The rest is in the same way as stated. The pentad of personal action (sāhatthika) is the sāhatthikapañcaka. This name is given by way of the initial term, just as the 'wholesome triad' (kusalattika) is the designation for the triad beginning with 'wholesome' (kusalādittika). Therefore, it should be understood in meaning as the 'pentad beginning with personal action' (sāhatthikādipañcaka). This same method applies to the remaining two pentads. 'Of this very' refers to this very matrix term 'should take' (ādiyeyya). 'By means of these terms' means by means of these five terms. And here it should be understood that the first term is stated in the sense of a claim; the second term, in the sense of one going while carrying another's goods; the third term, in the sense of deposited goods; the fourth, in the sense of animate goods; and the fifth, in the sense of goods placed on the ground, and so forth.

Idāni nesaṃ atthayojanaṃ dassetuṃ “tatthā”tiādimāha. Tattha tatthāti tesu dvīsu pañcakesu. Itaranti ekabhaṇḍapañcakaṃ. Ārāmanti pupphārāmaphalārāmaṃ. Abhiyuñjatīti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.102) parasantakaṃ “mama santakova aya”nti musā bhaṇitvā abhiyuñjati codeti, aṭṭaṃ karotīti attho. Sampajānamusāvādepi adinnādānassa pubbapayogattā dukkaṭanti āha “āpatti [M 0.0198] dukkaṭassā”ti, dukkaṭasaṅkhātā āpatti bhaveyyāti attho. Atha vā dukkaṭasaññitassa vītikkamassa āpajjananti attho. Esa nayo “āpatti thullaccayassā”tiādīsu. Sāmikassa vimatiṃ uppādetīti vinicchayakusalatāya, balavanissitādibhāvena vā ārāmasāmikassa saṃsayaṃ janeti. Kathaṃ? Tañhi tathā vinicchayappasutaṃ disvā sāmiko cinteti “sakkhissāmi nu kho ahaṃ imaṃ ārāmaṃ attano kātuṃ, na sakkhissāmi nu kho”ti. Evaṃ tassa vimati uppajjamānā tena uppāditā hoti. Dhuraṃ nikkhipatīti yadā pana sāmiko “ayaṃ thaddho kakkhaḷo jīvitabrahmacariyantarāyampi me kareyya, alaṃ dāni mayhaṃ iminā ārāmenā”ti dhuraṃ nikkhipati, ussāhaṃ ṭhapeti, attano santakakaraṇe nirussāho hotīti attho. Āpatti pārājikassa sace sayampi katadhuranikkhepo cāti adhippāyo. Atha pana sāmikena dhure nikkhittepi abhiyuñjako dhuraṃ anikkhipitvāva “imaṃ suṭṭhu pīḷetvā mama āṇāpavattiṃ dassetvā kiṅkārappaṭissāvibhāve ṭhapetvā dassāmī”ti dātabbabhāve saussāho, rakkhati tāva. Athāpi abhiyuñjako acchinditvā “na dāni imaṃ imassa dassāmī”ti dhuraṃ nikkhipati, sāmiko pana dhuraṃ na nikkhipati, pakkhaṃ pariyesati, kālaṃ āgameti, “lajjiparisaṃ tāva labhāmi, pacchā jānissāmī”ti gahaṇeyeva saussāho hoti, rakkhatiyeva. Yadā pana “sopi na dassāmī”ti, “sāmikopi na lacchāmī”ti evaṃ ubho dhuraṃ nikkhipanti, tadā abhiyuñjakassa pārājikaṃ.

Now, to show their meaning, it begins with 'there' (tatthā) and so forth. 'There' (tatthā) refers to those two pentads. 'The other' (itara) is the single-item pentad. 'Ārāma' refers to a flower garden or a fruit garden. 'He makes a claim' (abhiyuñjati) (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 1.102) means that he falsely claims another's property as his own, saying 'This belongs to me,' and presses the claim, making a case; this is the meaning. Even in the case of knowingly false speech, because it is a preliminary act to taking what is not given, it is said, 'The offense is a dukkaṭa.' The meaning is that there would be an offense classified as a dukkaṭa. Alternatively, it means incurring a transgression designated as a dukkaṭa. This same method applies to phrases like 'The offense is a grave offense' (thullaccaya), and so forth. 'He causes doubt in the owner' means that either through skill in adjudication or by being supported by a powerful person, etc., he creates uncertainty in the garden owner. How? Seeing him so intent on adjudication, the owner thinks, 'Will I be able to make this garden mine, or will I not?' Thus, the doubt arising in him is caused by that person. 'He abandons the burden' means that when the owner thinks, 'This person is stubborn and harsh; he might even endanger my life and my holy life. Enough of this garden for me now,' he abandons the burden, puts aside effort, and becomes disinterested in making it his own property—this is the meaning. The offense is a pārājika if he himself has also abandoned the burden—this is the meaning. However, even if the owner has abandoned the burden, if the claimant, without abandoning the burden, is enthusiastic about giving it back, thinking, 'After thoroughly harassing him and demonstrating my authority, establishing him in a state of subservience, I will give it back,' he continues to guard it for a time. Or again, if the claimant, without having seized it, thinks, 'I will not give this to him now,' and abandons the burden, while the owner does not abandon the burden but seeks support and bides his time, thinking, 'Let me first find an assembly of scrupulous monks; afterwards I will know what to do,' he remains enthusiastic about taking it and continues to guard it. But when the one thinks, 'I will not give it,' and the owner thinks, 'I will not get it,' and thus both abandon the burden, then the claimant incurs a pārājika.

Aññassa bhaṇḍaṃ harantoti vetanena vā mittabhāvena vā aññassa bhaṇḍaṃ haranto. Sīse bhāranti [V 0.0186] sīse ṭhitabhāraṃ. Sīsassa tāva purimagale galavāṭako, piṭṭhigale kesañci kesante āvaṭṭo hoti, galasseva ubhosu passesu kesañci kesā oruyha jāyanti, ye “kaṇṇacūḷikā”ti vuccanti, tesaṃ adhobhāgo cāti ayaṃ heṭṭhimako paricchedo, tato upari sīsaṃ, etthantare ṭhitabhāranti vuttaṃ hoti. Khandhaṃ oropetīti ubhosu passesu kaṇṇacūḷikāhi paṭṭhāya heṭṭhā, kapparehi paṭṭhāya upari, piṭṭhigalāvaṭṭato ca galavāṭakato ca paṭṭhāya heṭṭhā, piṭṭhivemajjhāvaṭṭato ca uraparicchedamajjhe, hadayāvāṭakato ca paṭṭhāya upari khandho, taṃ oropeti.

'One carrying another's goods' (Aññassa bhaṇḍaṃ haranto) means one who is carrying another's goods, whether for wages or out of friendship. 'A burden on the head' (sīse bhāra) refers to a burden placed on the head. As for the head: at the front of the neck is the throat-hollow; at the back of the neck, for some, there is a curl at the end of the hair; and on both sides of the neck, for some, hair grows hanging down, which are called 'ear-locks' (kaṇṇacūḷikā); the lower part of these is the lower boundary. Above this is the head, and it is said to be 'a burden placed on the head' when it is placed within this area. 'He lowers it onto the shoulder' (khandhaṃ oropeti). The shoulder is the area on both sides: downwards from the ear-locks; upwards from the collarbones; downwards from the curl at the back of the neck and from the throat-hollow; and upwards from the curl in the middle of the back, from the middle of the chest boundary, and from the heart-hollow. He lowers it onto that.

Ayaṃ [M 0.0199] panettha vinicchayo – yo bhikkhu “idaṃ gahetvā ettha yāhī”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.101) sāmikehi anāṇatto sayameva “mayhaṃ idaṃ nāma detha, ahaṃ vo bhaṇḍaṃ vahāmī”ti tesaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ sīsena ādāya gacchanto theyyacittena taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ āmasati, dukkaṭaṃ. Yathāvuttasīsaparicchedaṃ anatikkamantova ito cito ca ghaṃsanto sāretipi paccāsāretipi, thullaccayaṃ. Khandhaṃ oropitamatte kiñcāpi sāmikānaṃ “vahatū”ti cittaṃ atthi, tehi pana anāṇattattā pārājikaṃ. Khandhaṃ pana anoropetvāpi sīsato kesaggamattampi cāventassa pārājikaṃ. Yamakabhārassa pana eko bhāgo sīse patiṭṭhāti, eko piṭṭhiyaṃ, tattha dvinnaṃ ṭhānānaṃ vasena vinicchayo veditabbo. Ayaṃ pana suddhasīsabhārasseva vasena vutto. Yo cāyaṃ sīsabhāre vutto, khandhabhārādīsupi ayameva vinicchayo veditabbo.

Here is the judgment in this matter: If a monk, not being authorized by the owners by being told, 'Take this and go there,' (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 1.101) on his own accord says, 'Give me such-and-such, I will carry your goods,' and, taking their goods on his head, proceeds with the intention to steal, upon touching those goods, it is a dukkaṭa offense. If, without exceeding the aforementioned boundary of the head, he jostles it here and there, moving it forward and backward, it is a thullaccaya offense. At the very moment of lowering it onto his shoulder, even though the owners may have the thought, 'Let him carry it,' because he has not been authorized by them, it is a pārājika offense. Furthermore, even without lowering it onto his shoulder, for one who moves it from the head by as much as a hair's breadth, it is a pārājika offense. In the case of a double load, however, one part rests on the head and one on the back; in that case, the judgment should be understood according to the two positions. This, however, has been stated with reference to a load purely on the head. And this judgment which has been stated for a head-load should be understood as the very same for shoulder-loads and so forth.

Upanikkhittaṃ bhaṇḍanti saṅgopanatthāya attano hatthe parehi ṭhapitabhaṇḍaṃ. Ahaṃ na gaṇhāmīti sambandho. Atītatthe cetaṃ vattamānavacanaṃ, nāhaṃ gahesinti attho. Dukkaṭaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.111) sampajānamusāvādepi adinnādānassa pubbapayogattā. “Kiṃ tumhe bhaṇatha, nevidaṃ mayhaṃ anurūpaṃ, na tumhāka”ntiādīni vadantassāpi dukkaṭameva. Sāmikassa vimatiṃ uppādetīti “raho mayā etassa hatthe ṭhapitaṃ, na añño koci jānāti, dassati nu kho me, no”ti sāmikassa vimatiṃ uppādeti. Dhuraṃ nikkhipatīti tassa pharusādibhāvaṃ disvā ussāhaṃ ṭhapeti. Tatra sacāyaṃ bhikkhu “kilametvā naṃ dassāmī”ti dāne saussāho, rakkhati tāva. Sace so dāne nirussāho, bhaṇḍasāmiko pana gahaṇe saussāho, rakkhateva. Yadi pana so tasmiṃ dāne nirussāho, bhaṇḍasāmikopi “na mayhaṃ dassatī”ti dhuraṃ nikkhipati, evaṃ ubhinnaṃ dhuranikkhepena bhikkhuno pārājikaṃ. Yadipi mukhena “dassāmī”ti vadati, cittena pana adātukāmo, evampi sāmikassa dhuranikkhepena bhikkhuno pārājikaṃ.

'Deposited goods' (upanikkhittaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ) means goods placed in one's hand by others for the purpose of safekeeping. The connection is, 'I do not take it.' This present-tense expression is used in the sense of the past; the meaning is, 'I did not take it.' It is a dukkaṭa offense (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 1.111), as even knowingly false speech is a preliminary act to taking what is not given. For one who says such things as, 'What are you saying? This is not suitable for me, nor for you,' it is also a dukkaṭa offense. 'He causes doubt in the owner' means that he creates doubt in the owner, who thinks, 'This was secretly placed in his hand by me; no one else knows. Will he give it to me, or not?' 'He abandons the burden' means that seeing the monk's harshness or other such qualities, the owner gives up the effort. In this case, if this monk is enthusiastic about giving, thinking, 'After wearying him, I will give it,' he guards it for the time being. If he is unenthusiastic about giving, but the owner of the goods is enthusiastic about taking, it is still guarded. If, however, he is unenthusiastic about giving, and the owner of the goods also abandons the burden, thinking, 'He will not give it to me,' then by the abandonment of the burden by both, it is a pārājika offense for the monk. Even if he says with his mouth, 'I will give it,' but in his mind is unwilling to give, in that case also, by the owner's abandonment of the burden, it is a pārājika offense for the monk.

Sahabhaṇḍahārakaṃ [V 0.0187] nessāmīti “sahabhaṇḍahārakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ nessāmī”ti cintetvā. Paṭhamaṃ pādaṃ atikkāmetīti bhaṇḍahārakaṃ tajjetvā tassa gamanapathaṃ vāretvā attanā rucitamaggaṃ ekapādaṃ atikkāmeti. Thalaṭṭhanti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.95) thale nikkhittaṃ, bhūmitale vā pāsāṇapabbatatalādīsu vā yattha katthaci paṭicchanne vā appaṭicchanne vā ṭhapitanti attho. Phandāpeti, thullaccayanti yo phandāpeti[M 0.0200], tassa payoge payoge thullaccayaṃ, āmasane dukkaṭaṃ, phandāpane thullaccayañca visuṃ visuṃ theyyacittena āmasanaphandāpanapayoge karontasseva hoti. “Ekapayogena gaṇhantassa pana uddhāre pārājikameva, na dukkaṭathullaccayānī”ti vadanti. Ṭhānāti ṭhitaṭṭhānato. Sace taṃ thalaṭṭhaṃ rāsikataṃ hoti, antokumbhiyaṃ bhājanagatakaraṇamuṭṭhicchedanavinicchayena vinicchinitabbaṃ. Sace ekābaddhaṃ silesaniyyāsādi, pakkamadhuphāṇitavinicchayena vinicchinitabbaṃ. Sace garukaṃ hoti bhārabaddhaṃ lohapiṇḍitelamadhughaṭādi vā, kumbhiyaṃ ṭhānācāvanavinicchayena vinicchinitabbaṃ. Saṅkhalikābaddhassa ca ṭhānabhedo sallakkhetabbo. Pattharitvā ṭhapitaṃ pana pāvārattharaṇakaṭasārakādiṃ ujukaṃ gahetvā ākaḍḍhati, pārimante orimantena phuṭṭhokāsaṃ atikkante pārājikaṃ. Tatheva gahetvā parato pellati, pārimante phuṭṭhokāsaṃ orimante atikkante pārājikaṃ. Vāmato vā dakkhiṇato vā apanāmentassa vāmantena vā dakkhiṇantena vā phuṭṭhokāsaṃ dakkhiṇante vā vāmante vā atikkante pārājikaṃ. Veṭhetvā uddharati, kesaggamattaṃ ākāsagataṃ karontassa pārājikaṃ.

He thinks, 'I will take the goods along with the carrier,' intending, 'I will take the goods along with the carrier.' 'First, he makes it cross the first step' means: having threatened the carrier and blocked his path, he himself makes it cross one step along a preferred route. 'Placed on the ground' (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 1.95) means placed on the ground, whether on the surface of the earth, on stone, on the surface of a mountain, or anywhere else, whether concealed or unconcealed. 'He causes it to move, it is a grave offense' means: for one who causes it to move, for each attempt there is a grave offense; for touching, a wrongdoing; and for causing it to move, a grave offense. These occur separately for one who acts with the intention of theft in the attempts of touching and causing movement. Some say, 'For one who takes it in a single attempt, only the offense entailing expulsion is incurred, not wrongdoings or grave offenses.' 'From its place' means from the place where it was standing. If the item placed on the ground is in a pile, it should be determined by the legal precedent concerning making it contained within a pot, contained within a vessel, or by cutting with a measuring scoop. If it is bound as one item, such as with glue or resin, it should be determined by the legal precedent concerning cooked honey or molasses. If it is heavy, being bound as a load, such as a lump of iron, a pot of oil, or a pot of honey, it should be determined by the legal precedent concerning moving a pot from its place. The breaking from its place of a chain-bound item should also be noted. If something is spread out and placed, such as a cloak, a rug, or a coarse mat, and one pulls it straight, when the far end has crossed the space touched by the near end, it is an offense entailing expulsion. Similarly, if one takes it and pushes it forward, when the near end has crossed the space touched by the far end, it is an offense entailing expulsion. If one moves it to the left or right, when the right end or the left end crosses the space touched by the left end or the right end, it is an offense entailing expulsion. If one rolls it up and lifts it, it is an offense entailing expulsion for one who makes it go into the air even by a hair's breadth.

Sako hattho sahattho, tena nibbatto, tassa vā sambandhīti sāhatthiko, avahāro. Āṇāpanaṃ āṇatti, tāya āṇattiyā nibbatto avahāro āṇattiko. Nissajjanaṃ nissaggo, suṅkaghātaṭṭhāne, parikappitokāse ca ṭhatvā bhaṇḍassa bahi nipātanaṃ, nissaggova nissaggiyo. Kiriyāsiddhito puretarameva pārājikāpattisaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ sādhetīti atthasādhako. Dhurassa ālayasaṅkhātassa bhārassa nikkhipanaṃ pariccajanaṃ nirussāhabhāvāpajjanaṃ dhuranikkhepo. Idāni byañjane ādaraṃ akatvā tesaṃ atthamattameva dassento “tattha sāhatthiko nāmā”tiādimāha. Sahatthāti sahatthena. Karaṇatthe hi idaṃ nissakkavacanaṃ. “Asukassa bhaṇḍaṃ avaharā”ti aññaṃ āṇāpetīti etthāpi āṇattikkhaṇe eva āpatti daṭṭhabbā. Yadi evaṃ imassa, atthasādhakassa ca ko visesoti? Taṃ khaṇaṃ eva gahaṇe niyuñjanaṃ āṇattikapayogo, kālantarena gahaṇatthaṃ niyogo atthasādhakoti (sārattha. ṭī. 2.92; vi. vi. ṭī. 1.92) ayametesaṃ visesoti. Tenevāha “asukassa bhaṇḍaṃ yadā sakkosi, tadā taṃ avaharāti āṇāpetī”ti.

One's own hand is 'sahattha'; a taking away produced by it, or connected to it, is 'sāhatthika.' 'Āṇāpana' is a command; a taking away produced by that command is 'āṇattika.' 'Nissajjana' is abandonment. Standing at a customs evasion place or a pre-arranged place and throwing goods outside is abandonment; that which is related to abandonment is 'nissaggika.' That which accomplishes the purpose, designated as an offense entailing expulsion, even before the completion of the act is 'atthasādhaka,' purpose-accomplishing. The laying down of the burden, designated as a charge, which is the abandoning or giving up due to becoming unenthusiastic, is 'dhuranikkhepa,' the laying down of the burden. Now, without paying attention to the phrasing, showing only their meaning, he says, 'Here, "sāhatthika" means...' 'Sahatthā' means by one's own hand. Indeed, this is a word indicating separation used in the sense of the instrumental. When he orders another, 'Take away so-and-so's goods,' here too the offense should be understood as occurring at the very moment of the order. If so, what is the distinction between this and 'atthasādhaka'? The employment for taking at that very moment is the application of 'āṇattika,' whereas the assignment for taking after some time is 'atthasādhaka' (Sārattha. Ṭī. 2.92; Vi. Vi. Ṭī. 1.92)—this is their distinction. Therefore, he said, 'He orders thus: "When you are able, take away so-and-so's goods."

Suṅkaghātaparikappitokāsānanti [M 0.0201] suṅkaghātañca parikappitokāso ca suṅkaghātaparikappitokāsā, [V 0.0188] tesaṃ. Tattha suṅkaghātanti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.113) rukkhapabbatādisaññāṇena niyamitassa suṅkaṭṭhānassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tañhi yasmā tato rājadeyyabhāgaṃ suṅkaṃ adatvā nīharantā rañño suṅkaṃ hananti vināsenti, tasmā “suṅkaghāta”nti vuttaṃ.

The phrase ‘of customs evasion places and pre-arranged places’ is a compound of ‘customs evasion place’ and ‘pre-arranged place’. Herein, ‘customs evasion place’ (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 1.113) is a designation for a customs post fixed by a sign, such as a tree or a mountain. Indeed, because those who take goods out from there without paying the king's due share of customs duty destroy or evade the king's customs, it is called a ‘customs evasion place’.

Koci parapariveṇādīni paviṭṭho kiñci lobhaneyyabhaṇḍaṃ disvā dvārappamukhādivasena yaṃ ṭhānaṃ “sace maṃ etthantare passissanti, daṭṭhukāmatāya gahetvā vicaranto viya dassāmi, no ce passissanti, harissāmī”ti parikappeti, ayaṃ parikappitokāso. Āṇattikkhaṇeyeva pārājikanti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.121) atthasādhakacetanākkhaṇeyeva pārājikaṃ. Sacepi avahārako saṭṭhivassātikkamenapi taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ avaharati, āṇāpako ca antarāyeva kālaṃ karoti, hīnāya vā āvattati, assamaṇova hutvā kālaṃ vā karissati, hīnāya vā āvattissati, avahārakassa pana avahārakkhaṇeyeva pārājikaṃ. Pādagghanakatelanti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.94) ettha pādo nāma kahāpaṇassa catuttho bhāgo, taṃ agghatīti pādagghanakaṃ, pādagghanakañca taṃ telañcāti pādagghanakatelaṃ. Upāhanā ādi yesaṃ vatthūnaṃ tāni upāhanādīni. Ādisaddena dukūlasāṭakacammakkhaṇḍādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Pakkhipatīti theyyacittena pakkhipati. Tenāha “hatthato muttamatteyeva pārājika”nti sace pana attanopi kumbhiyaṃ añño sappiṃ vā telaṃ vā ākirati, tatra cāyaṃ theyyacittena telapivanakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ pakkhipati, vuttanayeneva pārājikaṃ.

Someone who enters another's monastic residence or the like and sees some desirable object, then pre-arranges a place such as a doorway, thinking: 'If they see me in here, I will show myself as if wandering around having picked it up out of a desire to look at it; but if they do not see me, I will take it'—this is a pre-arranged place. 'At the very moment of the command, it is an offense entailing expulsion' (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 1.121) means it is an offense entailing expulsion at the very moment of the intention that accomplishes the purpose. Even if the one who carries out the theft steals the object after sixty years have passed, and the one who gave the order in the meantime dies, or reverts to the lower life, or will die as a non-monk, or will revert to the lower life—for the one who carries out the theft, however, the offense entailing expulsion occurs at the very moment of the theft. 'Oil worth a pāda' (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 1.94): Here, a pāda is the fourth part of a kahāpaṇa. That which is worth it is 'pādagghanaka'; and that oil is 'pādagghanakatela.' 'Footwear and the like' refers to those items of which footwear is the first. By the word 'like,' the inclusion of fine cloth garments, pieces of leather, and so forth is to be understood. 'He puts it in' means he puts it in with a thieving mind. Therefore, it was said: 'The moment it is released from the hand, it is an offense entailing expulsion.' But if another person is pouring ghee or oil into one's own pot, and this person, with a thieving mind, puts in an oil-absorbing object, it is an offense entailing expulsion in the manner already stated.

Kāyena vā vācāya vā payuñjanaṃ āṇāpanaṃ payogo, āṇattassa bhaṇḍaggahaṇato pubbattā pubbo, iti pubbo ca so payogo cāti pubbapayogo. Payogena saha vattamāno avahāro sahapayogo. Samaṃ ekī hutvā vidahitvā mantetvā avaharaṇaṃ saṃvidhāvahāro, aññamaññaṃ saññuppattiyā katāvahāroti vuttaṃ hoti. Pubbaṇhādikālaparicchedena sañjānanaṃ saṅketo, tassa kammaṃ saṅketakammaṃ. Nimittassa kammaṃ nimittakammaṃ, saññuppādanatthaṃ kassaci nimittassa karaṇanti attho. Tatthāti yathāvuttesu pubbapayogādīsu pañcasu. Khilādīni saṅkāmetvā khettādiggahaṇavasenāti khilaṃ, rajjuṃ, vatiṃ, mariyādaṃ vā pākāraṃ [M 0.0202] vā saṅkāmetvā khettaggahaṇavasena, khilaṃ, rajjuṃ, vatiṃ, mariyādaṃ vā pākāraṃ vā saṅkāmetvā vatthuggahaṇavasena. Sace pana dvīhi khilehi gahetabbaṃ hoti, paṭhame khile thullaccayaṃ, dutiye pārājikaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.104). Sace tīhi gahetabbaṃ hoti, paṭhame dukkaṭaṃ, dutiye thullaccayaṃ, tatiye pārājikaṃ. Evaṃ bahukesupi avasāne dve ṭhapetvā purimehi dukkaṭaṃ, avasāne dvinnaṃ ekena thullaccayaṃ[V 0.0189], itarena pārājikaṃ. Rajjupasāraṇādīsupi eseva nayo. Yaṃ pana samantapāsādikāyaṃ “tañca kho sāmikānaṃ dhuranikkhepenā”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.104) vuttaṃ, taṃ “khettaṃ abhiyuñjati, āpatti dukkaṭassā”tiādi (pārā. 104) -adhikāre vuttattā abhiyogavasena gahaṇaṃ sandhāyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Saṃvidahitvāti etasseva vevacanaṃ. Saṃmantayitvāti ekacchandatāya ekajjhāsayatāya bhaṇitvāti attho. Imasmiṃ avahāre asammohatthaṃ “evaṃ saṃvidahitvā gatesu hī”tiādimāha. Sañjānanakammanti pubbaṇhādikālaparicchedavasena saññāṇakaraṇaṃ. Tenāha “sace hī”tiādi.

The application by body or speech, or the command, is the effort. Because it is prior to the taking of the goods by the one commanded, it is prior; thus, it is both prior and an effort, hence 'prior effort' (pubbapayoga). A taking away occurring together with the effort is 'concurrent effort' (sahapayoga). The taking away after having become equal, united, arranged, and consulted is 'agreed taking' (saṃvidhāvahāra); it is said to be a taking away done by mutual agreement. The designation by means of a division of time, such as morning, is 'a signal' (saṅketa); the act of that is 'signal-making' (saṅketakamma). The act of making a sign is 'sign-making' (nimittakamma); the meaning is the making of some sign for the purpose of arousing recognition. 'Herein' refers to the five, such as prior effort, etc., as stated. 'By means of taking a field, etc., by moving stakes, etc.' means by moving a stake, a rope, a fence, a boundary, or a wall, by means of taking a field; and by moving a stake, a rope, a fence, a boundary, or a wall, by means of taking a plot of land. But if it is to be taken by two stakes, for the first stake, it is a grave offense; for the second, an offense entailing expulsion. If it is to be taken by three, for the first, it is a wrong-doing; for the second, a grave offense; for the third, an offense entailing expulsion. Similarly, even with many, setting aside the last two, for the preceding ones it is a wrong-doing; of the final two, for one it is a grave offense, and for the other, an offense entailing expulsion. The same method applies to extending a rope, etc. As for what is stated in the Samantapāsādikā: 'But that is by the owners relinquishing their responsibility,' this should be understood as referring to taking by means of accusation, as it is said in the section on 'He challenges the field, an offense of wrong-doing,' etc. 'Saṃvidahitvā' is a synonym for this very thing. 'Saṃmantayitvā' means having spoken with one consent, with one intention. To avoid confusion in this taking away, he says, 'Having arranged thus, when they have gone,' etc. 'Sañjānanakamma' means making a signal by means of a division of time, such as morning. Therefore, he says, 'If,' etc.

Ettha ca “purebhattaṃ avaharā”ti vutte (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.119) ajja vā purebhattaṃ avaharatu, sve vā, anāgate vā saṃvacchare, natthi visaṅketo, ubhinnampi pārājikaṃ. Sace pana “ajja purebhattaṃ avaharā”ti vutte sve avaharati. “Ajjā”ti niyamitaṃ saṅketaṃ atikkamma pacchā avahaṭaṃ hoti. Sace “sve purebhattaṃ avaharā”ti vutte ajja purebhattaṃ avaharati, “sve”ti niyamitaṃ taṃ saṅketaṃ apatvā pure avahaṭaṃ hoti, evaṃ avaharantassa avahārakasseva pārājikaṃ, mūlaṭṭhassa anāpatti. “Sveva purebhatta”nti vutte tadaheva vā, sve pacchābhattaṃ vā avaharantopi taṃsaṅketato pure ca pacchā ca avaharati. Yo pana evaṃakatvā yathāparicchinnakālameva avaharati, ayaṃ saṅketato apure apacchā taṃ avaharatīti veditabbo. Esa nayo pacchābhattarattindivesupi, purimayāmamajjhimayāmapacchimayāmakāḷajuṇhamāsautusaṃvaccharādivasenāpi ettha saṅketavisaṅketatā veditabbā. Parabhaṇḍāvahārasaññuppādassa hetuttā akkhinikhaṇādīneva nimittanti akkhinikhaṇādinimittaṃ, tassa karaṇaṃ akkhinikhaṇādinimittakaraṇaṃ. Ādisaddena bhamukukkhepasīsakampanahatthalaṅghanapāṇippahāraaṅguliphoṭanagīvunnāmanaukkāsanādianekappakāraṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Sesamettha saṅketakamme vuttanayameva.

Here, when it is said, 'Steal before the meal,' whether one steals today before the meal, or tomorrow, or in a future year, there is no breach of the stipulation; both incur an offense entailing expulsion. However, if it is said, 'Steal today before the meal,' and one steals tomorrow, the stipulated 'today' is transgressed, and the theft occurs later. If it is said, 'Steal tomorrow before the meal,' and one steals today before the meal, that stipulated 'tomorrow' is not reached, and the theft occurs earlier. In such a case, only the one who steals incurs an offense entailing expulsion, while the instigator is not liable to an offense. If it is said, 'Steal tomorrow itself before the meal,' and one steals on that very day or tomorrow after the meal, one steals both before and after that stipulation. But if one, not doing so, steals only within the specified time, they should be understood as stealing it neither before nor after that stipulation. The same principle applies to after the meal, at night, and during the day, and also by way of the first, middle, or last watch of the night, the dark fortnight, the bright fortnight, the season, or the year. Here, the distinction between stipulated and non-stipulated times should be understood in these ways. Because it is the cause for the arising of the perception of taking another's property, the blinking of an eye, etc., are the signs; the making of such a sign is called 'making the sign of blinking an eye, etc.' The word 'etc.' includes many other actions, such as raising the eyebrows, shaking the head, a wave of the hand, a clap of the hands, snapping the fingers, raising the neck, clearing the throat, and so on. The rest here follows the same method as explained in the case of signal-making.

Theno [M 0.0203] vuccati coro, tassa bhāvo theyyaṃ, tena avaharaṇaṃ theyyāvahāro. Pasayha abhibhavitvā avaharaṇaṃ pasayhāvahāro. Vatthasuttādikaṃ paricchijja kappanaṃ parikappo, tena avaharaṇaṃ parikappāvahāro. Tiṇapaṇṇādīhi paṭicchannassa avahāro paṭicchannāvahāro. Kusena avahāro kusāvahāro. Kūṭamānakūṭakahāpaṇādīhīti ettha kūṭamānaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.10; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.293; pu. pa. aṭṭha. 179) nāma hadayabhedasikhābhedarajjubhedavasena tividhaṃ mānakūṭaṃ. Tattha hadayanti nāḷiādimānabhājanānaṃ abbhantaraṃ, tassa bhedo chiddakaraṇaṃ hadayabhedo, so sappitelādiminanakāle labbhati. Tāni hi gaṇhanto heṭṭhāchiddena mānena “saṇikaṃ [V 0.0190] āsiñcā”ti vatvā antobhājane bahuṃ paggharāpetvā gaṇhāti, dadanto ca chiddaṃ pidhāya sīghaṃ pūretvā deti.

A thief is called a 'theno' or 'cora'. His state is theft (theyya), and taking by means of that is called 'theft-taking' (theyyāvahāra). Taking by overpowering force is 'forceful-taking' (pasayhāvahāra).
