Contriving by demarcating and arranging cloth, thread, etc., is 'contrivance' (parikappa); taking by means of that is 'contrived-taking' (parikappāvahāra). Taking what is concealed by grass, leaves, etc., is 'concealed-taking' (paṭicchannāvahāra). Taking by fraud is 'fraudulent-taking' (kusāvahāra). 'By false measures, false coins, etc.': here, 'false measure' (kūṭamāna) refers to three kinds of fraudulent measurement: by 'heart-breaking,' 'peak-breaking,' or 'cord-breaking.' Therein, 'heart' refers to the interior of measuring vessels like tubes; breaking it means making a hole—this is 'heart-breaking,' which is employed when measuring ghee, oil, etc. For when taking, one says, 'Pour slowly,' while causing much to flow out from below through the hole in the measure into an inner vessel. And when giving, one covers the hole, fills it quickly, and gives it.

Sikhābhedo pana tilataṇḍulādiminanakāle labbhati. Tāni hi gaṇhanto saṇikaṃ sikhaṃ ussāpetvā gaṇhāti, dadanto vegena pūretvā sikhaṃ chindanto deti.

'Peak-breaking,' however, is employed when measuring sesame seeds, rice grains, etc. For when taking them, one slowly raises the peak and takes the measure; and when giving, one quickly fills it and gives it, cutting off the peak.

Rajjubhedo khettavatthuminanakāle labbhati. Khettādiṃ minantā hi amahantampi mahantaṃ katvā minanti, mahantampi amahantaṃ.

'Cord-breaking' is employed when measuring fields or plots of land. For those who measure fields, etc., they measure even a small area as if it were large, and a large area as if it were small.

Tambakaṃsādimayo kūṭo kahāpaṇo kūṭakahāpaṇo. Ādisaddena tulākūṭakaṃsakūṭavañcanādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Tattha tulākūṭaṃ rūpakūṭaṃ, aṅgakūṭaṃ, gahaṇakūṭaṃ, paṭicchannakūṭanti catubbidhaṃ hoti. Tattha rūpakūṭaṃ nāma dve tulā samarūpā katvā gaṇhanto mahatiyā gaṇhāti, dadanto khuddikāya deti. Aṅgakūṭaṃ nāma gaṇhanto pacchābhāge hatthena tulaṃ akkamati, dadanto pubbabhāge akkamati. Gahaṇakūṭaṃ nāma gaṇhanto mūle rajjuṃ gaṇhāti, dadanto agge. Paṭicchannakūṭaṃ nāma tulaṃ susiraṃ katvā anto ayacuṇṇaṃ pakkhipitvā gaṇhanto taṃ pacchābhāge karoti, dadanto aggabhāge.

A counterfeit kahāpaṇa made of copper, bronze, etc., is a 'false coin' (kūṭakahāpaṇa). The word 'etc.' includes false scales, false bowls, deception, and so on. Therein, false scales (tulākūṭa) are of four kinds: false in form, false in manipulation, false in holding, and false in concealment. Therein, 'false in form' (rūpakūṭa) means making two scales of similar appearance, but when taking, one uses the larger scale, and when giving, one uses the smaller one. 'False in manipulation' (aṅgakūṭa) means when taking, one presses the scale down with the hand on the back part, and when giving, one presses the front part. 'False in holding' (gahaṇakūṭa) means when taking, one holds the rope at the base, and when giving, at the tip. 'False in concealment' (paṭicchannakūṭa) means making the scale hollow, filling it inside with iron filings, and when taking, causing them to be in the back part, and when giving, in the front part.

Kaṃso vuccati suvaṇṇapāti, tāya vañcanaṃ kaṃsakūṭaṃ. Kathaṃ? Ekaṃ suvaṇṇapātiṃ katvā aññā dve tisso lohapātiyo suvaṇṇavaṇṇā karonti. Tato janapadaṃ gantvā kiñcideva aḍḍhaṃ kulaṃ pavisitvā “suvaṇṇabhājanāni kiṇāthā”ti vatvā agghe pucchite samagghataraṃ dātukāmā honti[M 0.0204]. Tato tehi “kathaṃ imesaṃ suvaṇṇabhāvo jānitabbo”ti vutte “vīmaṃsitvā gaṇhathā”ti suvaṇṇapātiṃ pāsāṇe ghaṃsitvā sabbā pātiyo datvā gacchati.

A 'kaṃsa' is called a golden bowl; deception with it is 'bowl-fraud' (kaṃsakūṭa). How? They make one golden bowl and two or three other metal bowls colored like gold. Then, going to the countryside, they enter some wealthy household and say, 'Will you buy golden vessels?' When asked the price, they are willing to sell at a very reasonable price. Then, when asked by the buyers, 'How can we know these are truly golden?' they say, 'Examine them and take them,' rub the golden bowl on a touchstone, give all the bowls, and leave.

Vañcanaṃ nāma tehi tehi upāyehi paresaṃ vañcanaṃ. Tatridamekaṃ vatthu – eko kira luddako migañca migapotakañca gahetvā āgacchati, tameko dhutto “kiṃ bho migo agghati, kiṃ migapotako”ti āha. “Migo dve kahāpaṇe, migapotako eka”nti vutte ekaṃ kahāpaṇaṃ datvā migapotakaṃ gahetvā thokaṃ gantvā nivattento “na me bho migapotakena attho, migaṃ me dehī”ti āha. “Tena hi dve kahāpaṇe dehī”ti āha. So āha “nanu bho mayā paṭhamaṃ eko kahāpaṇo dinno”ti. Āma dinno, imaṃ migapotakaṃ gaṇha, evaṃ so ca kahāpaṇo[V 0.0191], ayañca kahāpaṇagghanako migapotakoti dve kahāpaṇā bhavissantīti. So “kāraṇaṃ vadatī”ti sallakkhetvā migapotakaṃ gahetvā migaṃ adāsīti.

'Deception' means deceiving others by various means. Here is an instance: A hunter, it seems, caught a deer and a fawn and was coming. A rogue asked him, "What is the deer worth, and what is the fawn worth?" When he said, "The deer is two kahāpaṇas, the fawn one," the rogue gave one kahāpaṇa, took the fawn, went a little way, and turning back said, "I have no need of the fawn; give me the deer." The hunter said, "Then give two kahāpaṇas." The rogue said, "But surely I gave one kahāpaṇa earlier? Yes, it was given. Take this fawn. Thus, that kahāpaṇa and this fawn, worth one kahāpaṇa, will be two kahāpaṇas." The hunter, thinking, "He is stating a reason," took the fawn and gave the deer.

Pasayhāti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.138) pare abhibhuyya. Gāmaṃ ghātentīti gāmaghātakā, gāmaṃ paharantā corā, te ādi yesaṃ te gāmaghātakādayo. Ādisaddena cettha panthaghātakādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Uddhāreyeva pārājikanti “sace sāṭako bhavissati, gaṇhissāmī”ti parikappassa pavattattā, sāṭakassa ca tattha sabbhāvato. Padavārena kāretabboti bhūmiyaṃ anikkhipitvāva vīmaṃsitattā vuttaṃ. Bhaṇḍadeyyanti yaṃ parassa naṭṭhaṃ, tassa mūlaṃ vā tadeva vā bhaṇḍaṃ dātabbanti attho.

'By force' (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 1.138) means overpowering others. Those who destroy villages are 'village-destroyers,' thieves who strike villages; 'village-destroyers and so forth' are those of whom such are the first. By the term 'and so forth' here is meant the inclusion of highway robbers and others. It is a pārājika offense at the very moment of lifting because the thought arises, 'If there is a cloak, I will take it,' and the cloak is actually present there. 'It is to be effected by the foot-turn' is said because it was examined without being placed on the ground. 'Goods to be repaid' means that whatever is lost by another, either its value or the item itself, must be given back; this is the meaning.

Tassāti yo evaṃ parikappeti, tassa. Imassa “avahāro hotī”ti iminā sambandho.

'Of that one' means of the one who contrives thus. This is connected with 'there is misappropriation.'

Paresanti kīḷantānaṃ, pavisantānaṃ vā paresaṃ manussānaṃ. “Pacchā gaṇhissāmī”ti paṃsunā vā paṇṇena vā paṭicchādetīti “sace idāneva onamitvā gaṇhissāmi, ‘kiṃ samaṇo gaṇhātī’ti maṃ jānitvā viheṭheyyuṃ pacchā gaṇhissāmī”ti paṃsunā vā paṇṇena vā paṭicchādeti. Uddhāro natthīti ṭhānācāvanaṃ natthīti attho. Sāmikāti antāgāmaṃ pavisitukāmā bhaṇḍasāmikā manussā. Uddhāreti uddharaṇe, ṭhānācāvaneti attho[M 0.0205]. Ṭhānācāvanañcettha heṭṭhā vuttanayānusārena veditabbaṃ. Pavesetīti ṭhānācāvanavasena paveseti, heṭṭhimantena phuṭṭhokāsaṃ kesaggamattampi uparimantena atikkāmento pavesetīti attho.

'Among others' means among other people who are playing or entering. He thinks, 'I will take it later,' and covers it with dust or leaves; this means: 'If I bend down to take it now, they might see me and, knowing "the ascetic is taking something," harass me. Therefore, I will take it later,' and he covers it with dust or leaves. 'There is no removal' means there is no displacement; this is the meaning. 'Owners' means people who are owners of goods, wishing to enter the inner village. 'He removes' means in the sense of removal, that is, displacement. Displacement here should be understood according to the method explained below. 'He inserts' means he inserts by way of displacement; that is, he inserts by causing the upper edge to pass over the place touched by the lower edge, even by a hair's breadth.

Samagghataranti appagghataraṃ. Uddhaṭamatte avahāroti sakabhāvappayogassa niṭṭhāpitattā, na atthasādhakavasena. Uddhāre rakkhati attano koṭṭhāse pātetukāmatāya uddhaṭattā. Eseva nayo pātanepi rakkhatīti etthāpi. “Uddhāreyeva rakkhatī”ti imināva pātane na rakkhatīti atthe siddhepi atthasādhakavasena atthaṃ dassetuṃ “taṃ uddharitvā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sace pana dvīsupi koṭṭhāsesu patitadaṇḍake adassanaṃ gameti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.138), tato avasesabhikkhūsu gatesu itaro “mayhaṃ, bhante, daṇḍako na paññāyatī”ti, “mayhampi, āvuso, na paññāyatī”ti, “katamo pana, bhante, mayhaṃ bhāgo”ti. “Ayaṃ tuyhaṃ bhāgo”ti attano bhāgaṃ dasseti. Tasmiṃ vivaditvā vā avivaditvā vā taṃ gaṇhitvā gate itaro tassa bhāgaṃ uddharati, uddhāre [V 0.0192] pārājikaṃ. Sacepi tena “ahaṃ mama bhāgaṃ tuyhaṃ na demi, tvaṃ pana attano bhāgaṃ ñatvā gaṇhā”ti vuttepi “nāyaṃ mamā”ti jānantopi tasseva bhāgaṃ gaṇhāti, uddhāre pārājikaṃ. Sace pana itaro “ayaṃ tuyhaṃ bhāgo, ayaṃ mayhaṃ bhāgoti kiṃ iminā vivādenā”ti cintetvā “mayhaṃ vā patto hotu, tumhākaṃ vā, yo varabhāgo, taṃ tumhe gaṇhathā”ti vadati, dinnakaṃ nāma gahitaṃ hoti, natthettha avahāro. Sace so vivādabhīruko bhikkhu “yaṃ tuyhaṃ ruccati, taṃ gaṇhā”ti vutto attano pattaṃ varabhāgaṃ ṭhapetvā lāmakaṃyeva gahetvā gacchati, tato itarassa vicinitāvasesaṃ gaṇhantassāpi avahāro nattheva. Evamimāni pañca pañcakāni samodhānetvā ime pañcavīsati avahārā veditabbā. Niṭṭhito “ādiyeyyā”ti imassa padassa vinicchayo. Tenāha “iti yaṃ vuttaṃ…pe… yassattho pakāsito hotī”ti.

'More valuable' means less valuable. Theft occurs at the very moment of removal because the application of one's own state has been established, not because of the accomplishment of the purpose. In removing, he guards it because it has been removed with the desire to make it fall into his own share. This is the same method here too in the case of 'in making it fall, he guards it.' Although the meaning 'he does not guard it in making it fall' is established by this very phrase 'he guards it only in removing,' the words 'having removed that,' etc., are stated to show the meaning in terms of accomplishing the purpose. But if, in both shares, the marked stick goes unseen (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 1.138), then after the remaining bhikkhus have left, the other says: 'Venerable sir, my stick is not to be seen.' 'Friend, mine is not to be seen either.' 'But, venerable sir, which is my portion?' 'This is your portion,' he says, showing his own portion. After that one has taken it and left, whether they disputed it or not, the other removes that one's portion; in the removal, it is an offense entailing expulsion. Even if that one had said, 'I will not give you my portion, but you, knowing your own portion, should take it,' if he, knowing 'this is not mine,' takes that very portion, in the removal, it is an offense entailing expulsion. But if the other, fearing a dispute, thinks, 'What is the use of this dispute over "this is your portion, this is my portion"?' and says, 'Let the bowl be mine or yours; you take the better share,' what is taken is considered a gift; there is no theft here. If that bhikkhu who fears a dispute, having been told, 'Take what you prefer,' sets aside his own better portion, takes only the inferior one, and leaves, then there is no theft even for the other who takes what remains after searching. Thus, by combining these five pentads, these twenty-five kinds of theft should be understood. The analysis of the word 'one might take' is finished. Therefore it was said: 'Thus what was said...pe... whose meaning has been clarified.'

Rājānoti kiñcāpi avisesena vuttaṃ, aparādhānurūpaṃ pana chejjabhejjānusāsako pamāṇabhūtova idhādhippetoti āha “rājānoti idaṃ bimbisāraṃyeva sandhāya vutta”nti. So hi dhammikarājattā yathāpaveṇiyāva karoti. Aññe pana kākaṇikamattassapi sīsaṃ chindeyyuṃ[M 0.0206], bahukassāpi na vā kiñci kareyyuṃ. Tenāha “aññe panā”tiādi. Hananaṃ nāma pothanañceva chedanañcāti āha “hatthādīhi vā”tiādi. Ādisaddena pādakasāvettaaḍḍhadaṇḍakānaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Rajjubandhanādīhīti ādisaddena andubandhanasaṅkhalikābandhanagharabandhananagarabandhanapurisaguttīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Nīhareyyunti raṭṭhato nikkhāmeyyuṃ. Corosi…pe… thenosīti ettha “paribhāseyyu”nti padaṃ ajjhāharitabbaṃ ūnattā padappayogassa. Tenāha “imehi vacanehi paribhāseyyu”nti. Yathārūpaṃ pana yasmā pādato paṭṭhāya hoti, tasmā “pādassa vā pādārahassa vā”ti āha. Porāṇakassa kahāpaṇassa catuttho bhāgo pādo, pādaṃ arahatīti pādāraho, tassa pādassa vā pādārahassa vā. Ettha ca pādena kahāpaṇassa catutthabhāgaṃ akappiyabhaṇḍameva dasseti, pādārahena pādagghanakaṃ kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ. Ettāvatā heṭṭhimantadassanena sabbākārena dutiyapārājikappahonakavatthu dassitaṃ hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Porāṇakassāti (sārattha. ṭī. 2.88; vi. vi. ṭī. 1.88) porāṇasatthānurūpaṃ uppāditassa lakkhaṇasampannassa nīlakahāpaṇasadisassa kahāpaṇassa. Etena rudradāmakādīni paṭikkhipati.

Although 'king' is stated without specification, here one who imposes punishments involving cutting and breaking in accordance with the crime, being the standard, is intended. Thus he said: 'The word "king" is stated with reference to Bimbisāra alone.' For he, being a righteous king, acts only in accordance with tradition. But others might cut off a head for a mere kākaṇika, or do nothing at all even for a large amount. Therefore it is said: 'but others,' etc. 'Killing' means both striking and cutting, as stated: 'with hands, etc.' By the word 'etc.' is included seizing by the feet, ropes, and half-staffs. In 'by binding with ropes, etc.,' by the word 'etc.' is included binding with fetters, binding with chains, house-confinement, city-confinement, and guarding by men. 'They might banish' means they might expel from the country. Here in 'You are a robber...pe... you are a thief,' the word 'they might revile' should be supplied because the use of the word is deficient. Therefore it is said: 'with these words they might revile.' But since 'in accordance with the value' starts from a pāda, he said 'of a pāda or what is worth a pāda.' A pāda is the fourth part of an ancient kahāpaṇa. What is worth a pāda is pādāraha. Thus, 'of a pāda or what is worth a pāda.' And here, by 'pāda' he indicates only unallowable goods worth a quarter of a kahāpaṇa; by 'pādāraha,' allowable goods worth a pāda. It should be seen that by this much, through the lower limit shown, the object sufficient for a second pārājika offense has been indicated in all its aspects. 'Of an ancient one' (Sārattha. Ṭī. 2.88; Vi. Vi. Ṭī. 1.88) means of a kahāpaṇa produced in accordance with ancient treatises, endowed with marks, similar to a blue kahāpaṇa. By this he rejects the rudradāmakas and so on.

Evaṃ asādhāraṇavinicchayaṃ dassetvā idāni sādhāraṇavinicchayaṃ dassetuṃ “rājagahe”tiādimāha. Raññoti bimbisārarañño. Māsako nāma porāṇakassa kahāpaṇassa vīsatimo bhāgo. Yo loke “mañjeṭṭhī”tipi vuccati. Idāni imasmiṃ adinnādāne vinicchayaṃ dassetuṃ “sabbatthā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sabbatthāti ūnamāsakātirekamāsakapañcamāsakesu. Parihīnāparihīnavasenāti agghassa parihīnāparihīnavasena. Ayamettha saṅkhepo[V 0.0193], vitthāro pana evaṃ veditabbo – idañhi adinnādānaṃ vinicchinantena otiṇṇe vatthusmiṃ sahasā avinicchinitvā pañca ṭhānāni oloketabbāni. Yāni sandhāya porāṇā āhu –

Having thus shown the specific ruling, now to show the general ruling, he stated, 'In Rājagaha,' etc. 'Of the king' means of King Bimbisāra. A māsaka is the twentieth part of an ancient kahāpaṇa, which is also called a 'mañjeṭṭhī' in the world. Now, to show the ruling on this taking of what is not given, 'in all cases,' etc., was said. 'In all cases' means in cases of less than a māsaka, more than a māsaka, and five māsakas. 'According to decrease and non-decrease' means according to the decrease and non-decrease of the value. This is the summary here; the detail, however, should be understood thus: When judging this taking of what is not given, one should not decide hastily about the matter that has come up for judgment but should examine five points. With reference to which the ancients have said:

“Vatthuṃ kālañca desañca, agghaṃ paribhogapañcamaṃ;

Tulayitvā pañcaṭhānāni, dhāreyyatthaṃ vicakkhaṇo”ti. (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.92);

'The object, the time, and the place, the value, and its use as the fifth—having weighed these five grounds, the discerning one should decide the case.'

Tattha ca vatthūti bhaṇḍaṃ. Avahārakena hi “mayā idaṃ nāma avahaṭa”nti vuttepi āpattiṃ anāropetvāva taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ sasāmikaṃ vā asāmikaṃ vāti [M 0.0207] upaparikkhitabbaṃ. Sasāmikepi sāmikānaṃ sālayabhāvo vā nirālayabhāvo vā upaparikkhitabbo. Sace tesaṃ sālayakāle avahaṭaṃ, bhaṇḍaṃ agghāpetvā āpatti kāretabbā. Sace nirālayakāle, na pārājikena kāretabbo. Bhaṇḍasāmikesu pana bhaṇḍaṃ āharāpentesu bhaṇḍaṃ dātabbaṃ. Ayamettha sāmīci. Evaṃ vatthu oloketabbaṃ.

Therein, 'object' means goods. For even if the thief says, 'I have stolen such-and-such an item,' without imposing an offense, it should first be investigated whether those goods have an owner or are ownerless. Even when they have an owner, it should be investigated whether the owners have attachment or non-attachment to them. If the goods were stolen at a time when they had attachment, an offense should be charged after having the goods valued. If it was at a time of non-attachment, he should not be charged with a pārājika offense. But when the owners of the goods have them brought back, the goods should be returned. This is the proper course here. Thus the object should be examined.

Kāloti avahārakālo. Tadeva hi bhaṇḍaṃ kadāci samagghaṃ hoti, kadāci mahagghaṃ. Tasmā taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ yasmiṃ kāle avahaṭaṃ, tasmiṃyeva kāle yo tassa aggho, tena agghena āpatti kāretabbā. Evaṃ kālo oloketabbo.

'Time' means the time of the theft. For the very same item is sometimes of low value and sometimes of high value. Therefore, an offense should be charged according to whatever the value of that item is at the very time it was stolen. Thus the time should be examined.

Desoti avahāradeso. Tañhi bhaṇḍaṃ yasmiṃ dese avahaṭaṃ, tasmiṃyeva dese yo tassa aggho, tena agghena āpatti kāretabbā. Bhaṇḍuṭṭhānadese hi bhaṇḍaṃ samagghaṃ hoti, aññattha mahagghaṃ. Evaṃ deso oloketabbo.

'Place' means the place of the theft. For an offense should be charged according to whatever the value of that item is in the very place where it was stolen. For in the place where the goods are produced, they are of low value; elsewhere they are of high value. Thus the place should be examined.

Agghoti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.92) bhaṇḍaggho. Navabhaṇḍassa hi yo aggho, so pacchā parihāyati. Yathā navadhoto patto aṭṭha vā dasa vā agghati, so pacchā bhinno vā chiddo vā āṇigaṇṭhikāhato vā appaggho hoti, tasmā na sabbadā bhaṇḍaṃ pakatiaggheneva kātabbanti. Evaṃ aggho oloketabbo.

'Value' means the value of the goods. For whatever the value of new goods is, it diminishes later. Just as a newly washed bowl is worth eight or ten, but later, being broken, or having a hole, or being struck by a nail-knot, it becomes of little value. Therefore, the goods should not always be valued at their normal price. Thus the value should be examined.

Paribhogoti bhaṇḍassa paribhogo. Paribhogenāpi hi vāsiādibhaṇḍassa aggho parihāyati, tasmā evaṃ upaparikkhitabbaṃ – sace koci kassaci pādagghanakaṃ vāsiṃ harati, tatra [V 0.0194] vāsisāmiko pucchitabbo “tayā ayaṃ vāsi kittakena kītā”ti. “Pādena, bhante”ti. “Kiṃ pana te kiṇitvāva ṭhapitā, udāhu taṃ valañjesī”ti? Sace vadati “ekadivasaṃ me dantakaṭṭhaṃ vā rajanachalli vā pattapacanadāru vā chinnaṃ, ghaṃsitvā vā nisitā”ti. Athassa porāṇo aggho bhaṭṭhoti veditabbo. Yathā ca vāsiyā, evaṃ añjaniyā vā añjanisalākāya vā kuñcikāya vā palālena vā thusehi vā iṭṭhakacuṇṇena vā ekavāraṃ ghaṃsitvā dhovanamattenāpi aggho bhassati. Tipumaṇḍalassa makaradantacchedanenāpi parimaddanamattenāpi, udakasāṭikāya sakiṃ nivāsanapārupanenāpi, paribhogasīsena [M 0.0208] aṃse vā sīse vā ṭhapanamattenāpi, taṇḍulādīnaṃ papphoṭanenāpi tato ekaṃ vā dve vā apanayanenapi, antamaso ekaṃ pāsāṇasakkharaṃ uddharitvā chaḍḍitamattenāpi, sappitelādīnaṃ bhājanantaraparivattanenapi, antamaso tato makkhikaṃ vā kipillikaṃ vā uddharitvā chaḍḍitamattenapi, guḷapiṇḍakassa madhurabhāvajānanatthaṃ nakhena vijjhitvā aṇumattaṃ gahitamattenapi aggho bhassati. Tasmā yaṃ kiñci pādagghanakaṃ vuttanayeneva sāmikena paribhogena ūnaṃ kataṃ hoti, na taṃ avahārako bhikkhu pārājikena kāretabboti. Evaṃ paribhogo oloketabbo.

'Use' means the use of an item. For by use, too, the value of items such as an adze diminishes. Therefore, it should be investigated thus: If someone steals an adze worth a pāda, the owner of the adze should be asked: 'For how much did you buy this adze?' 'For a pāda, venerable sir.' 'But was it just bought and set aside, or did you make use of it?' If he says, 'For one day I cut a tooth-stick with it, or bark for dyeing, or firewood for cooking with the bowl, or I rubbed or sharpened it,' then its former value should be understood as lost. And just as with the adze, so too with an ointment pot, an ointment applicator, a key, straw, husks, or brick powder, the value is lost even by the mere act of rubbing and washing once. The value is also lost for a tin circle even by the mere act of rubbing it after cutting a makara-tooth pattern; for a water-strainer, even by wearing it once as a lower or upper garment; for a shoulder-cloth, even by the mere act of placing it on the shoulder or head; for rice and so on, even by winnowing it and removing one or two grains; even by the mere act of picking up and discarding a single stone or pebble; for ghee, oil, and so on, even by transferring it to another vessel; even by the mere act of picking out and discarding a fly or an ant from it; for a lump of molasses, even by the mere act of piercing it with a fingernail to find out its sweetness and taking a tiny amount. Therefore, if any item worth a pāda has been made deficient by the owner's use in the way described, the bhikkhu who steals it should not be charged with a pārājika offense. Thus use should be examined.

Evaṃ imāni tulayitvā pañca ṭhānāni dhāreyya atthaṃ vicakkhaṇo āpattiṃ vā anāpattiṃ vā garukaṃ vā lahukaṃ vā āpattiṃ yathāṭhāne ṭhapeyyāti.

Having thus weighed these five factors, a discerning person should determine the matter and place the offense or non-offense, a serious offense or a light one, in its proper place.

Evaṃ tattha vinicchayaṃ dassetvā idāni anāpattiṃ dassento “sakasaññissā”tiādimāha. Tattha sakasaññissāti “mayhaṃ santakaṃ idaṃ bhaṇḍa”nti evaṃ sakasaññissa parabhaṇḍampi gaṇhato gahaṇe anāpatti, gahitaṃ pana puna dātabbaṃ. Sace sāmikehi “dehī”ti vutto na deti, tesaṃ dhuranikkhepe pārājikaṃ. Vissāsaggāheti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.131) vissāsaggahaṇepi anāpatti. Vissāsaggāhalakkhaṇaṃ pana iminā suttena jānitabbaṃ –

Having thus explained the decision in that case, now showing the non-offense, he says, 'with the perception of one's own,' etc. Here, 'with the perception of one's own' means that for one who has the perception, 'This is my own property,' there is no offense in taking another's goods, but the item taken must be returned. If, when told by the owners, 'Give it back,' one does not give it back, then it is a pārājika for abandoning the obligation. 'Taking through trust': even in taking through trust, there is no offense. However, the characteristic of taking through trust should be understood through this Sutta:

“Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pañcahaṅgehi samannāgatassa vissāsaṃ gahetuṃ, sandiṭṭho ca hoti, sambhatto ca ālapito ca jīvati ca jānāti ca ‘gahite me attamano’”ti (mahāva. 356).

'Monks, I allow one to take on trust from a person endowed with five qualities: he is seen, he is familiar, he has been conversed with, he is alive, and one knows, 'He will be pleased when it is taken by me.''

Tattha sandiṭṭhoti diṭṭhamattakamitto. Sambhattoti daḷhamitto. Ālapitoti “mama santakaṃ yaṃ icchasi, taṃ gaṇheyyāsi, āpucchitvā gahaṇe kāraṇaṃ natthī”ti vutto. Jīvatīti anuṭṭhānaseyyāya [V 0.0195] sayitopi yāva jīvitindriyupacchedaṃ na pāpuṇāti. Gahite ca attamanoti gahite tuṭṭhacitto. Evarūpassa santakaṃ “gahite me attamano bhavissatī”ti jānantena gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Anavasesapariyādānavasena cetāni pañcaṅgāni vuttāni. Vissāsaggāho pana tīhi aṅgehi ruhati. Kathaṃ? Sandiṭṭho, jīvati, gahite attamano, sambhatto, jīvati, gahite attamano, ālapito, jīvati, gahite attamanoti evaṃ.

Here, `sandiṭṭho` means an acquaintance. `Sambhatto` means a close friend. `Ālapito` means one who has been told: “Take whatever you wish of my belongings; there is no need to ask before taking.” `Jīvati` means that even if he is lying down unable to rise, he has not reached the termination of the life faculty. `Gahite ca attamano` means he is pleased when something is taken. It is permissible for one who knows, “He will be pleased if I take his belongings,” to take from such a person. These five factors are stated in the sense of taking completely without leaving a remainder. Taking based on trust, however, is allowable with three factors. How? An acquaintance, alive, and pleased when it is taken; a close friend, alive, and pleased when it is taken; one who has given permission, alive, and pleased when it is taken. Thus.

Yo [M 0.0209] pana jīvati, na ca gahite attamano hoti, tassa santakaṃ vissāsabhāvena gahitampi puna dātabbaṃ. Dadantena ca matakadhanaṃ tāva ye tassa dhane issarā gahaṭṭhā vā pabbajitā vā, tesaṃ dātabbaṃ. Anattamanassa santakaṃ tasseva dātabbaṃ. Yo pana paṭhamaṃyeva “suṭṭhu kataṃ tayā mama santakaṃ gaṇhantenā”ti vacībhedena vā cittuppādamattena vā anumoditvā pacchā kenaci kāraṇena kupito, so paccāharāpetuṃ na labhati. Yo ca adātukāmo, cittena pana adhivāseti, na kiñci vadati, sopi puna paccāharāpetuṃ na labhati. Yo pana “mayā tumhākaṃ santakaṃ gahita”nti vā “paribhutta”nti vā vutto gahitaṃ vā hotu, paribhuttaṃ vā, “mayā pana taṃ kenacideva karaṇīyena ṭhapitaṃ, pākatikaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadati, ayaṃ paccāharāpetuṃ labhati.

But in the case of one who is alive but is not pleased when something is taken, what was taken from his belongings based on trust must be given back. And when giving, the wealth of a deceased person should first be given to those who are masters of that wealth, whether they are householders or renunciates. What belongs to one who is displeased should be given back to that same person. But if one at first approves, either by verbal expression or by a mere thought, saying, “You did well to take my belongings,” and later becomes angry for some reason, he does not get to have it returned. And one who is unwilling to give but mentally consents and says nothing, he too does not get to have it returned. But if, when told, “I have taken your belongings,” or “I have used them,” whether it was taken or used, one says, “But I had set that aside for some purpose; it should be restored,” this one gets to have it returned.

Tāvakāliketi “paṭidassāmi paṭikarissāmī”ti evaṃ gaṇhantassa tāvakālikepi gahaṇe anāpatti. Gahitaṃ pana sace bhaṇḍasāmiko puggalo vā gaṇo vā “tuyhevetaṃ hotū”ti anujānāti, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. No ce anujānāti, āharāpente dātabbaṃ. Saṅghasantakaṃ pana paṭidātumeva vaṭṭati.

Temporarily: For one who takes something thinking, “I will give it back, I will make it right,” there is no offense even in taking it temporarily. But if the owner of the goods, whether an individual or a group, consents, saying, “Let this be yours,” this is good. If they do not consent, it must be given back when they ask for its return. But what belongs to the Saṅgha must certainly be returned.

Petapariggaheti ettha pana pettivisaye upapannāpi, kālaṃ katvā tasmiṃyeva attabhāve nibbattāpi, cātumahārājikādayo devāpi sabbe “petā”tveva saṅkhyaṃ gatā, tesaṃ pariggahe anāpatti. Devatāya pana uddissa balikammaṃ karontehi rukkhādīsu laggitasāṭake vattabbameva natthi. Tañca kho ārakkhakehi apariggahite, pariggahitaṃ pana gahetuṃ na vaṭṭati (sārattha. ṭī. 2.131).

Taking what belongs to petas: Here, even those reborn in the peta-realm, those reborn in the very same body after death, and all the devas such as those of the Four Great Kings—all are reckoned as ‘petas.’ There is no offense in taking what belongs to them. Further, when people perform offering-rites dedicated to a deity, there is nothing to be said about cloths hung on trees and so on. But this is when they are not claimed by guardians; it is not permissible to take what has been claimed. (Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā 2.131).

Tiracchānagatapariggaheti nāgasupaṇṇādīnaṃ tiracchānagatānaṃ pariggahe. Sacepi hi devo vā nāgasupaṇṇo vā manussarūpena āpaṇaṃ pasāreti, tato cassa santakaṃ koci dibbacakkhuko bhikkhu taṃ ñatvā gahetvā gacchati, vaṭṭati.

Taking what belongs to animals: This is the taking of what belongs to animals such as nāgas and supaṇṇas. For even if a deva or a nāga or a supaṇṇa should set up a shop in human form, and some bhikkhu with the divine eye, knowing this, should take his property and go, it is permissible.

Paṃsukūlasaññissāti [V 0.0196] “asāmikaṃ idaṃ paṃsukūla”nti evasaññissāpi gahaṇe anāpatti. Sace pana taṃ sasāmikaṃ hoti, āharāpente dātabbaṃ. Ummattakādīni pubbe vuttappakārāneva. Ādikammiko panettha dhaniyo[M 0.0210]. Avasesānaṃ pana rajakabhaṇḍikādicorānaṃ chabbaggiyādīnaṃ āpattiyeva.

For one with the perception of it being a dust-heap rag: There is no offense in taking it even for one with the perception: “This is an ownerless dust-heap rag.” But if it has an owner, it must be given back when they ask for its return. The cases of the insane and so on are just as stated before. Here, the original offender is Dhaniya. But for the rest, such as the thieves of the washerman’s bundle and the group-of-six bhikkhus, there is an offense.

Sacittakehi tīhi samuṭṭhānehi idaṃ samuṭṭhātīti āha “adinnādānasamuṭṭhāna”nti. Tathā hi sāhatthikaṃ kāyacittato samuṭṭhāti. Āṇattikaṃ vācācittato samuṭṭhāti. Sāhattikāṇattikaṃ kāyavācācittato samuṭṭhāti, tañca kho “bhāriyamidaṃ, tvaṃ ekapassaṃ gaṇha, ahaṃ ekapassa”nti saṃvidhāya ubhayesaṃ payogena ekassa vatthuno ṭhānācāvane labbhati. “Kāyavacīkamma”nti avacanaṃ pana kāyavācānaṃ īdise ṭhāne aṅgamattattā. Yāya pana cetanāya samuṭṭhāpito payogo sāhatthiko vā āṇattiko vā padhānabhāvena ṭhānācāvanaṃ sādheti, tassā vasena āpatti kāretabbā. Aññathā sāhatthikaṃ vā āṇattikassa aṅgaṃ na hoti, āṇattikaṃ vā sāhatthikassāti idaṃ virujjhati. “Adinnaṃ ādiyāmī”ti saññāya abhāvena muccanato saññāvimokkhaṃ. Kāyena kataṃ kammaṃ kāyakammaṃ, kāyadvārena katanti attho. Vacīkammanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Tuṭṭho vā bhīto vā majjhatto vā naṃ āpajjatīti tivedanaṃ. Sesaṃ paṭhamasikkhāpade vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

It is said, 'The origin of taking what is not given,' because this offense arises from three origins involving consciousness. For an act by one’s own hand arises from body and mind. An act by command arises from speech and mind. An act by one’s own hand and by command arises from body, speech, and mind; this occurs when, having arranged, “This is heavy, you take one side, I’ll take the other,” an object is moved from its place by the effort of both. The term 'bodily and verbal action' is not used because in such a case body and speech are mere components. The offense should be incurred in accordance with the volition by which the effort—whether by one’s own hand or by command—is instigated, which as the principal factor accomplishes the moving from the place. Otherwise, this would be contradicted: that an act by one’s own hand is not a component of one by command, or that an act by command is not a component of one by one’s own hand. It is a release through perception because one is absolved due to the absence of the perception, 'I am taking what is not given.' An action done by the body is a bodily action; the meaning is that it is done through the body-door. The same method applies to verbal action. It has three feelings because one commits it while pleased, afraid, or neutral. The rest should be understood in the way stated in the first training rule.

Dutiyapārājikavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Second Pārājika is finished.

3. Tatiyapārājikavaṇṇanā

3. The Explanation of the Third Pārājika

Santi sahatthe upasaggo. Tena saddhiṃ ussukkavacanametaṃ “sañciccā”ti āha “sañcetetvā”tiādi. Ussukkavacananti ettha ussukkavacanaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. 2.172) nāma pubbakālakiriyāvacanaṃ. Ayañhi samānakattukesu pubbāparakālakiriyāvacanesu pubbakālakiriyāvacanassa niruttivohāro. Idāni “saddhiṃ cetetvā”ti iminā saṅkhepena vuttamevatthaṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā dassetuṃ “pāṇo”tiādimāha. Tattha “pāṇo”ti saññāya saddhiṃyevāti “pāṇo”ti saññaṃ avijahitvā eva, “pāṇo”ti saññuppattiyā anantaranti vuttaṃ hoti. Evañca katvā kathaṃ ekakkhaṇe ekassa cittassa ubhayārammaṇabhāvoti edisī codanā anavakāsāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Keci pana “ñātapariññāya [M 0.0211] diṭṭhasabhāvesu dhammesu tīraṇapariññāya tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā (sārattha. ṭī. 2.172) ‘rūpaṃ anicca’ntiādinā sabhāvena [V 0.0197] saddhiṃ ekakkhaṇe aniccādilakkhaṇajānanaṃ viya ‘pāṇo’ti saññāya saddhiṃyeva ‘vadhāmi na’nti jānātī”ti vadanti. Apare pana ācariyā tatthāpi evaṃ na kathenti. Ettha ca manussaviggaho”ti avatvā “pāṇo”ti vacanaṃ “manusso aya”nti ajānitvā kevalaṃ sattasaññāya ghātentassāpi pārājikabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Cetetvāti cintetvā. Pakappetvāti abhivicāretvā, sanniṭṭhānaṃ karitvāti attho.

The prefix saṃ has the sense of 'together with.' Along with that, this word for endeavor, sañcicca, is stated, as in sañcetetvā ('having intended'), and so on. Here, 'word for endeavor' (ussukkavacana) is a term for a prior action. For this is the linguistic convention for a term for a prior action among terms for prior and subsequent actions that have the same agent. Now, to make plain and show the meaning that was stated concisely by 'having intended together,' he says 'a living being,' etc. Therein, 'a living being' means 'together with the perception'; that is, 'without having abandoned the perception "it is a living being,"' which means 'immediately after the arising of the perception "it is a living being."' This being so, the objection, 'How can a single consciousness have two objects at a single moment?' should be seen as baseless. Some, however, say that just as one, by means of discernment by comprehension (tīraṇapariññā), applies the three characteristics to phenomena whose nature has been seen by means of discernment by full knowledge (ñātapariññā) and knows, for instance, 'form is impermanent,' knowing the characteristic of impermanence, etc., at the same moment as the nature, so too, one knows 'I will kill' or 'I will not' at the very same moment as the perception 'it is a living being.' But other teachers do not explain it thus. And here, instead of saying 'a human form,' the word 'a living being' is used to show that a pārājika is incurred even by one who kills merely with the perception of a being, without knowing 'this is a human.' Cetetvā means having thought. Pakappetvā means having deliberated, that is, having made a determination.

Idāni manussaattabhāvaṃ ādito paṭṭhāya dassetuṃ “manussaviggaha”ntiādimāha. Tattha kalalato paṭṭhāyāti paṭisandhiviññāṇena saddhiṃ uppannakalalarūpato paṭṭhāya. Kalalarūpaṃ nāma itthipurisānaṃ kāyavatthubhāvadasakavasena samatiṃsa rūpāni, napuṃsakānaṃ kāyavatthudasakavasena vīsati. Tattha itthipurisānaṃ kalalarūpaṃ jātiuṇṇāya ekena aṃsunā uddhaṭatelabindumattaṃ hoti acchaṃ vippasannaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ –

Now, to explain the human individual existence from the beginning, he says 'a human form,' etc. Here, 'starting from the kalala' means starting from the material form of the kalala that arises together with the rebirth-linking consciousness. The material form of the kalala consists of thirty material phenomena for males and females (the body-decad, the heart-basis-decad, and the sex-decad) and twenty for neuters (the body-decad and the heart-basis-decad). Therein, the material form of the kalala for males and females is the size of a drop of oil lifted up by a single thread of fine wool; it is clear and very bright. For it is said in the commentary:

“Tilatelassa yathā bindu, sappimaṇḍo anāvilo;

Evaṃvaṇṇappaṭibhāgaṃ, ‘kalala’nti pavuccatī”ti. (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.235; vibha. aṭṭha. 26; pārā. aṭṭha. 2.172);

“Just as a drop of sesame oil, or the clear surface of ghee, unstirred; of such a color and appearance, it is called the ‘kalala.’”

Evaṃ parittakaṃ vatthuṃ ādiṃ katvā yāva maraṇakālā etthantare anupubbena vuḍḍhippatto attabhāvo manussaviggaho nāmāti vuttaṃ hoti. Idañca yebhuyyavaseneva vuttaṃ. Opapātikasaṃsedajāpi hi manussā pārājikavatthuyeva. Kalalakālepīti paṭhamasattāhepi. Tattha hi santativasena pavattamānaṃ kalalasaṅkhātaṃ attabhāvaṃ jīvitā voropetuṃ sakkā, na pana sabbapaṭhamaṃ kalalarūpaṃ. Paṭisandhicittena hi saddhiṃ tiṃsa kammajarūpāni nibbattanti. Tesu pana ṭhitesuyeva soḷasa bhavaṅgacittāni uppajjitvā nirujjhanti. Etasmiṃ antare gahitapaṭisandhikassa dārakassa vā mātuyā vā panassa antarāyo natthi. Ayañhi maraṇassa anokāso nāma. Bhesajjasampadānenāti gabbhapātanabhesajjadānena. Tato vā uddhampīti abbudapesikālādīsupi. Jīvitā viyojeyyāti santativikopanavasena jīvitindriyato apaneyya.

This means that the individual existence which, having started from such a tiny basis, has gradually developed in the interval up to the time of death, is called 'a human form.' And this is stated as a general rule, for even humans who are spontaneously born or moisture-born are objects of a pārājika offense. Even in the kalala stage—that is, in the first week—it is possible to deprive of life the individual existence called the kalala, which proceeds by way of continuity, but not the very first material form of the kalala. For along with the rebirth-linking consciousness, thirty kamma-born material phenomena are generated. While these still exist, sixteen moments of life-continuum consciousness arise and cease. During this interval, there is no danger either for the child who has taken rebirth-linking or for its mother. This is indeed called a time when death is impossible. 'By giving medicine' means by giving medicine that causes an abortion. 'Or even beyond that' means in the abbuda and pesi stages, etc. 'One might deprive of life' means one might remove from the life-faculty by way of disrupting the continuity.

Imassa [M 0.0212] panatthassāti “sañcicca manussaviggahaṃ jīvitā voropeyyā”ti (pārā. 171) imassa atthassa. Āvibhāvatthanti pakāsanatthaṃ. Pāṇassa atipāto pāṇātipāto, pāṇavadho pāṇaghātoti vuttaṃ hoti. Sattoti khandhasantāno. Tattha hi sattapaññatti. Jīvitindriyanti [V 0.0198] rūpārūpajīvitindriyaṃ. Rūpajīvitindriye hi vikopite itarampi taṃsambandhatāya vinassatīti. Yāya cetanāyāti tasmiṃ pāṇe pāṇasaññino kāyavacīdvārānaṃ aññataradvārappavattāya yāya cetanāya. Manodvāre pana pavattāya vadhakacetanāya pāṇātipātabhāvo natthi. Sā cetanāti sā jīvitindriyupacchedakaupakkamasamuṭṭhāpikā kāyavacīdvārānaṃ aññataradvārappavattā vadhakacetanā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yāya cetanāya pavattamānassa jīvitindriyassa nissayabhūtesu mahābhūtesu upakkamakaraṇahetu taṃmahābhūtapaccayā uppajjanakamahābhūtā nuppajjissanti (sārattha. ṭī. 2.172), sā tādisapayogasamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā pāṇātipāto. Laddhūpakkamāni hi mahābhūtāni itarabhūtāni viya na visadānīti samānajātikānaṃ kāraṇaṃ na hontīti.

'Of this meaning' means: of the meaning of this statement, 'one might intentionally deprive a human form of life.' 'For the purpose of manifestation' means for the purpose of clarification. The destruction of a living being (pāṇassa atipāto) is pāṇātipāto; this means the slaying of a living being (pāṇavadho), the killing of a living being (pāṇaghāto). 'A being' means the continuum of the aggregates, for the designation 'being' applies to that. 'The life faculty' means the material and immaterial life faculty. For when the material life faculty is damaged, the other also perishes because of its connection with it. 'By which volition' means: by that volition, in one who perceives a living being as such, that proceeds through one of the two doors, the body-door or the speech-door. But there is no state of killing a living being by a murderous volition that proceeds through the mind-door. 'That volition' means: that murderous volition, proceeding through one of the two doors, the body-door or the speech-door, which initiates the effort to cut off the life faculty. This is what is meant: that volition which, by causing an attack on the great elements that are the support for the proceeding life faculty, is the reason why the great elements that would have arisen conditioned by those great elements do not arise—that volition, which originates such an application, is the destruction of life. For the great elements that have been attacked, unlike other elements, are not clear and thus do not become a cause for others of the same kind.

Pāṇātipāto assa atthīti pāṇātipātī. Saṃsagge ayamīkāro. Tenāha “vuttacetanāya samaṅgipuggalo”ti. Sako hattho sahattho, tena nibbatto payogo sāhatthiko. Nissajjanaṃ nissaggo, sova nissaggiyo. Evaṃ āṇattiko. Vijjāmayo mantaparijappanayogo. Iddhimayo kammavipākajiddhimayo.

A destroyer of life (pāṇātipātī) is one for whom there is destruction of life (pāṇātipāto). This ī-suffix denotes connection. Therefore he says, 'a person endowed with the aforesaid volition.' One's own hand is sahattho; the application produced by that is sāhatthiko (by one's own hand). Letting go is nissaggo; the application related to that is nissaggiyo (by throwing). Similarly, āṇattiko (by command). Vijjāmayo (by means of spells) is the application of muttering mantras. Iddhimayo (by means of psychic power) is that consisting of psychic power that is the result of kamma.

Idāni yathāvutteyeva cha payoge vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “tatthā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tesu chasu payogesu. Sāhatthikoti ettha hattho upalakkhaṇabhāvena gahitoti āha “kāyena vā”tiādi. Tattha kāyenāti hatthena vā pādena vā muṭṭhinā vā jāṇunā vā yena kenaci aṅgapaccaṅgena. Kāyekadeso hettha hatthādikāyo avayave samudāyopacāro yathā “gāmo daḍḍho”ti. Kāyappaṭibaddhenāti kāyato amocitena asiādinā paharaṇena. Paharaṇanti kāyaviññattisahitāya vadhakacetanāya adhippetatthasādhanaṃ. Kāyena vā sattiādīnaṃ, kāyappaṭibaddhena vā usuyantapāsāṇādīnaṃ nissajjananti yathāsambhavaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Tatthāti tesu sāhatthikanissaggiyesu[M 0.0213]. Uddissānuddissabhedatoti uddisitvā ca anuddisitvā ca pavattibhedena. Uddisanaṃ uddiso, so etassa atthīti uddisako, payogo, tasmiṃ. Bajjhati etenāti baddho, kammameva baddho kammabaddho, pāṇātipātoti attho. Atha vā bandhanaṃ baddho, kammunā baddho kammabaddho, so assa hoti, pāṇātipātakammamassa siddhanti vuttaṃ hoti. Ubhayatthāpīti uddisake, anuddisake cāti dvīsupi. Pacchā vā teneva rogena maratūti yojanā. Paharitakkhaṇeyevāti maraṇāya pahonakappahārassa laddhakkhaṇeyeva kammabaddho. Yadi avassaṃ tena maratīti adhippāyo. Sace pana maraṇādhippāyena pahāraṃ datvā tena amatassa puna aññena cittena pahāre dinne pacchāpi paṭhamappahāreneva marati, tadāva kammabaddho. Atha dutiyapahārena marati[V 0.0199], natthi pāṇātipāto. Ubhayehi matepi paṭhamappahāreneva kammabaddho, ubhayehipi amate nevatti pāṇātipāto. Esa nayo bahūhipi ekassa pahāre dinne. Tatrāpi hi yassa pahārena marati, tasseva kammabaddhoti. Āṇāpanaṃ nāma vacīviññattisahitāya vadhakacetanāya adhippetatthasādhanaṃ.

Now, to show the six applications just mentioned by analyzing them, 'therein,' etc., is said. 'Therein' means in those six applications. In sāhatthiko (by one's own hand), the hand is taken as a synecdoche, thus he says 'with the body,' etc. Here, 'with the body' means with the hand, foot, fist, knee, or any other limb. A part of the body, the hand, stands for the whole body; this is a metaphorical usage of the part for the whole, as in 'the village was burned.' 'With something connected to the body' means with a weapon such as a sword that is not released from the body. A 'weapon' (paharaṇa) is a means of accomplishing the intended purpose by a murderous volition accompanied by bodily intimation. The releasing of a spear, etc., is with the body, while the releasing of an arrow from a bow, a stone from a sling, etc., is with something connected to the body; this should be connected as is appropriate. 'Therein' means in those cases of sāhatthika (by one's own hand) and nissaggiya (by throwing). 'By the distinction of specified and unspecified' means by the difference in occurrence, whether having specified or not having specified. Specifying is uddiso; one for whom this exists is an uddisako (specifier); in that application. 'He is bound by it' (baddho); the kamma itself is what binds, so kammabaddho means the destruction of life. Or, binding is baddho; he is bound by kamma, kammabaddho; this means the kamma of destroying life is accomplished for him. 'In both cases' means in both the specified and unspecified cases. The connection is: 'or he dies later from that same affliction.' 'At the very moment of striking' means he is bound by the kamma at the very moment when the blow, sufficient to cause death, has found its opportunity, that is, if he will inevitably die from it. But if, having delivered a blow with the intention to kill, the victim does not die from it, and one delivers another blow with a different state of mind, and he then dies from the first blow, one is bound by the kamma at that time. If he dies from the second blow, there is no destruction of life. Even if he dies from both, one is bound by the kamma of the first blow. If he does not die from either, there is no destruction of life. This is the method also when many people deliver a blow to one person; for there too, the one by whose blow he dies is the one who is bound by the kamma. 'Commanding' (āṇāpanaṃ) is a means of accomplishing the intended purpose by a murderous volition accompanied by verbal intimation.

Idāni imasmiṃ āṇattikapayoge saṅketavisaṅketabhāvajānanatthaṃ chabbidhaṃ niyamaṃ dassento “tatthā”tiādimāha. Tattha tatthāti tasmiṃ āṇattikapayoge. Āṇattiniyāmakāti āṇattikapayogasādhikā. Etesu hi avirajjhitesuyeva āṇattikapayogo hoti, na aññathāti.

Now, showing the sixfold principle for the purpose of knowing the state of agreement and disagreement in this application by command, he says 'therein,' etc. 'Therein' means in that application by command. 'Regulators of the command' (āṇattiniyāmakā) are what accomplish the application by command. For it is only when these are not contravened that the application by command occurs, not otherwise.

Puggaloti māretabbo puggalo. Tenāha “yaṃ hī”tiādi. Āṇāpakassa āpattīti āṇāpakassa āṇattikkhaṇe āpatti, āṇattassa māraṇakkhaṇe. Āṇāpako muccatīti āṇattasseva kammabaddho, vatthuvisesena panettha kammaviseso ca āpattiviseso ca hotīti. “Purebhattaṃ mārehī”ti āṇatto purebhattameva māretīti “ajja sve”ti aniyametvā “purebhattaṃ mārehī”ti āṇatto yadā kadāci purebhattaṃ māreti. Yo pana “ajja pubbaṇhe”ti vutto majjhanhe vā sāyanhe vā sve vā pubbaṇhe māreti, visaṅketo hoti, āṇāpakassa natthi kammabaddho. Pubbaṇhe māretuṃ vāyamantassa majjhanhe [M 0.0214] jātepi eseva nayo. Etena nayena sabbakālappabhedesu saṅketavisaṅketatā veditabbā.

A person means a person to be killed. Hence it is said, 'Because,' etc. The offense for the one who commands is at the moment of the command, and for the one commanded, at the moment of the killing. The statement 'The one who commands is freed' means that only the one commanded is bound by the kamma; but here, due to the particularity of the object, there is also a particularity of kamma and a particularity of offense. When commanded, 'Kill him before the meal,' he kills him only before the meal. When, without specifying 'today or tomorrow,' one is commanded, 'Kill him before the meal,' he kills him at some time or other before the meal. But if one who is told, 'Kill him this forenoon,' kills him at midday, or in the evening, or on the next day's forenoon, it is a deviation from the instruction; the one who commanded is not bound by the kamma. This same principle applies even if, while attempting to kill in the forenoon, it happens at midday. By this method, agreement and deviation should be understood in all divisions of time.

Evaṃ vatthukālesu saṅketavisaṅketataṃ dassetvā idāni okāsādīsu saṅketavisaṅketataṃ atidisanto “iminā nayenā”tiādimāha. Tattha okāsoti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.174) gāmo vā vanaṃ vā gehadvāraṃ vāti evamādiko. Āvudhanti asi vā usu vā satti vāti evamādi. Iriyāpathoti māretabbassa gamanaṃ vā nisajjā vāti evamādi. Kiriyāvisesoti vijjhanaṃ vā chedanaṃ vā bhedanaṃ vā saṅkhamuṇḍakaṃ vāti evamādi. Imesu yathā yathā vadhako āṇatto, tathā tathā kate āṇāpakassa āpatti, aññathā kate visaṅketo hoti. Tenāha “iminā nayenā”tiādi. Tattha sabbatthāti okāsādīsu catūsu. Hoti cettha –

Having thus shown agreement and deviation in regard to the object and time, now, applying by extension the agreement and deviation to location and so forth, he says, 'By this method,' etc. Herein, 'location' refers to a village, a forest, a house door, and so on. 'Weapon' refers to a sword, an arrow, a spear, and the like. 'Posture' refers to the walking or sitting of the one to be killed, and so on. 'Specific action' refers to piercing, cutting, breaking, or making a 'conch-shell tonsure' (saṅkhamuṇḍaka), and so on. In these cases, just as the killer is instructed, if he acts in just that way, the one who commands incurs an offense; if he acts otherwise, it is a deviation from the instruction. Therefore he said, 'By this method,' etc. Herein, 'in all cases' means in the four beginning with location. And here there is this:

“Yathāṇattivaseneva, āṇattena kate sati;

Āṇāpakassa āpatti, visaṅketoññathā kate”ti.

"When it is done by the one commanded

exactly as the command was given,

the one who commands incurs an offense;

if it is done otherwise, it is a deviation."

Āṇattiyaṃ [V 0.0200] pana ayaṃ viseso – adhiṭṭhāyāti adhiṭṭhahitvā āṇāpeti “evaṃ vijjha, evaṃ pahara, evaṃ ghātehī”ti (pārā. 174) vuttāya pāḷiyā labbhatīti ñātabbo.

But in the case of a command, this is the specific point: it should be understood that `adhiṭṭhāya` means having determined and then commanding, 'Pierce thus, strike thus, kill thus,' which is obtained from the Pāḷi text that has been cited (Pārā. 174).

Opatanti etthāti opāto, āvāṭo, tassa khaṇanaṃ opātakkhaṇanaṃ. Apassenasaṃvidhānanti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.177) apassenassa saṃvidhānaṃ. Niccaparibhogo mañco vā pīṭhaṃ vā apassenaphalakaṃ vā divāṭṭhāne nisīdantassa apassenakatthambho vā tatthajātakarukkho vā caṅkame apassāya tiṭṭhantassa ālambanarukkho vā ālambanaphalakaṃ vā, sabbampetaṃ apassanīyaṭṭhena apassenaṃ nāma, tasmiṃ apassene yathā apassayantaṃ vijjhati vā chindati vā, tathā katvā vāsipharasusattiārakaṇṭakādīsu aññatarassa satthassa ṭhapananti attho.

`Opāta` means that into which they fall; a pit. The digging of it is `opātakkhaṇana` (pit-digging). `Apassenasaṃvidhāna` is the arranging of a support (`apassena`). A constantly used couch or chair; a leaning-board; for one sitting in a day-time resting place, a leaning-post or a tree that grew there; for one standing on a walking path to lean on, a supporting tree or a supporting board—all this is called a 'support' (`apassena`) in the sense of something to be leaned on. The meaning is the placing of some weapon—such as an adze, axe, knife, spike, thorn, etc.—on such a support in such a way that it would pierce or cut one who leans on it.

Upanikkhipanaṃ nāma samīpe nikkhipanaṃ. Manāpassa vā amanāpassa vā rūpassa upaharaṇaṃ samīpe ṭhapanaṃ rūpūpahāro, attanā vā yakkhapetādivesaṃ gahetvā tiṭṭhanaṃ. Ādisaddena saddūpahārādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Etthāpīti thāvarapayogepi[M 0.0215]. Uddissānuddissabhedo veditabbo, yato tatthapi pubbe vuttanayeneva kammabaddho hoti. Ayaṃ pana viseso – mūlaṭṭhena opātādīsu paresaṃ mūlena vā mudhā vā dinnesupi yadi tappaccayā koci marati, mūlaṭṭhasseva kammabaddho. Yadipi tena, aññena vā tatra opāte vināsetvā bhūmisame katepi paṃsuhārakā vā paṃsuṃ gaṇhantā, mūlakhaṇakā vā mūlāni khaṇantā āvāṭaṃ karonti, deve vā vassante kaddamo jāyati, tattha ca koci otaritvā vā laggitvā vā marati, mūlaṭṭhasseva kammabaddho. Yadi pana yena laddhaṃ, so vā añño vā vitthatataraṃ vā gambhīrataraṃ vā karoti, tappaccayā ca koci marati, ubhayesampi kammabaddho. Yathā tu mūlāni mūlehi saṃsandanti, tathā tattha thale kate muccati. Evaṃ apassenasaṃvidhānādīsupi yāva tesaṃ pavatti, tāva yathāsambhavaṃ kammabaddho veditabbo.

`Upanikkhipana` means placing nearby. `Rūpūpahāra` is the presenting of a pleasing or unpleasing form, placing it nearby, or taking on the guise of a yakkha, a peta, etc., and standing there. By the word 'etc.' (`ādi`), the offering of sound and so on is included. 'Here too' means even in the case of a stationary device. The distinction between specified and unspecified should be understood, for there too one is bound by kamma in the way previously stated. This, however, is the specific point: in the case of pits and so on, even if they are given to others by the original owner for a price or for free, if someone dies on account of that, the original owner is bound by the kamma. Even if he or another destroys that pit and makes the ground level, if then dust-collectors taking dust or root-diggers digging for roots make a hole, or if mud forms when it rains, and someone, having entered or gotten stuck there, dies, the original owner is bound by the kamma. If, however, the one who received it, or another, makes it wider or deeper, and someone dies on account of that, both are bound by the kamma. But when the place has been made into level ground, he is freed, just as roots are connected with roots. Similarly, in the cases of arranging a support and so on, as long as they are operative, one should be understood to be bound by kamma as is possible.

Vijjāparijappananti āthabbaṇikehi, vijjādharehi ca mantaparijappanaṃ. Kammavipākajāya iddhiyāti sātisayakammanibbattāya kammavipākena sahajātāya iddhiyā, kammassa vā vipākabhāvena jātāya iddhiyā. Payojananti pavattanaṃ, karaṇanti attho, dāṭhāvudhādīnaṃ dāṭhākoṭanādīnamiva māraṇatthaṃ kammavipākajiddhivikārakaraṇanti vuttaṃ hoti.

`Vijjāparijappana` (muttering of lore) is the muttering of spells by sorcerers and bearers of lore. `By psychic power born of kamma-result` means by the psychic power that is produced by exceptional kamma and is co-nascent with the kamma-result, or by the psychic power born by way of being the result of kamma. `Application` means setting in motion; the meaning is instrumentality. This is said to be the causing of a transformation in the psychic power born of kamma-result for the purpose of killing, just like the striking with fangs and so on by those whose fangs are their weapons.

Kammasādhano vāyaṃ hārakasaddo bahulaṃvidhānena tatthāpi ṇvupaccayassa sijjhanatoti āha “atha vā”tiādi. Jīvitaharaṇakaṃ, upanikkhipitabbaṃ vā satthameva hārakanti (sārattha. ṭī. 2.172) vikappadvayena [V 0.0201] vuttanti āha “satthañca taṃ hārakañcāti satthahāraka”nti. “Hārakasattha”nti vattabbe visesanassa paranipātaṃ katvā evaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Pariyeseyyāti gaveseyya. “Yathā labhati, tathā kareyyā”ti iminā pana adhippāyatthamāha, “upanikkhipeyyā”ti iminā sikhāpattamatthaṃ. Itarathā hi “pariyeseyyā”ti imassa “upanikkhipeyyā”ti ayamattho adhippeto na siyā. Pariyiṭṭhamatteyevāti pariyesitamatteyeva. Yadi evaṃ atha kasmā pāḷiyaṃ “satthahārakaṃ vāssa pariyeseyyāti asiṃ vā sattiṃ vā bheṇḍiṃ vā laguḷaṃ vā pāsāṇaṃ vā satthaṃ vā visaṃ vā rajjuṃ vā”ti (pārā. 172) vuttanti āha “padabhājane panā”tiādi. Assāti “satthahārakaṃ vāssa pariyeseyyā”ti imassa padassa. Byañjanānurūpato paripuṇṇaṃ katvā atthassa avuttattā [M 0.0216] “byañjanaṃ anādiyitvā”ti vuttaṃ. Sasati hiṃsatīti satthaṃ, sasanti hiṃsanti etenāti vā satthaṃ. Ādisaddena “sattiṃ vā”tiādipāḷisesaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Tattha laguḷanti muggaro. Satthanti vuttāvasesaṃ yaṃ kiñci samukhaṃ veditabbaṃ.

He says, 'Or alternatively,' etc., because this word `hāraka` is an agent noun, and the suffix `ṇvu` is also accomplished there by the rule of frequent application. He says, 'A weapon that is also a taker is a `satthahāraka`,' because it is stated with a twofold alternative: 'A `hāraka` is that which takes life, or a weapon to be placed nearby.' It should be seen that this is stated by placing the adjective after the noun, when `hārakasattha` should have been said. `Pariyeseyya` means he should search. But by 'He should act as he obtains it,' he states the intended meaning; by 'he should place it nearby,' he states the meaning at the peak of the training. Otherwise, 'he should place it nearby' would not be the intended meaning of 'he should search for it.' `Pariyiṭṭhamatteyeva` means merely upon having searched. If so, why is it stated in the Pāḷi: 'Or he might search for a weapon-bringer for him, that is, a sword, a spear, a dart, a club, a stone, a knife, poison, or a rope'? He says, 'But in the word-analysis,' etc. Regarding this phrase, 'Or he might search for a weapon-bringer for him': because the meaning is not stated completely in accordance with the letter, it is said, 'without regarding the letter.' `Sattha` is so called because 'it injures' (`sasati hiṃsati`), or because 'they injure with it.' By the word 'etc.' (`ādi`), he includes the rest of the Pāḷi passage, 'a spear, or…' etc. Therein, `laguḷa` is a club. `Sattha` should be understood as any remaining item that has a point or edge.

Yo evaṃ maratīti yo satthaṃ vā āharitvā, visaṃ vā khāditvā, rajjuyā vā ubbandhitvā, sobbhādīsu vā patitvā, aññehi vā aggipavesanaudakapavesanādīhi upāyehi marati. “So dhanaṃ vā labhatī”tiādinā nayenāti so dhanaṃ vā labhati, yasaṃ vā labhati, saggaṃ vā gacchati, dhammo vāssa hotīti iminā nayena. Kimanena veditabbanti āha “etenā”tiādi. Tattha etenāti “maraṇavaṇṇaṃ vā saṃvaṇṇeyyā”ti etena vacanena. Nayidha evanti idha manussaviggahapārājike na evaṃ, na pariyāyakathāya muccatīti attho. Tenāha “saṃvaṇṇeyyā”tiādi.

`One who dies thus` means one who dies by taking a weapon, or by eating poison, or by hanging himself with a rope, or by falling into a pit or the like, or by other means such as entering a fire or entering water. `By the method of 'He obtains wealth,' etc.` means by this method: 'He obtains wealth, or he obtains fame, or he goes to heaven, or it is righteous for him.' When it is asked, 'What is to be understood by this?' he says, 'By this,' etc. Therein, 'by this' means by this statement: 'or he might praise the beauty of death.' `Not so here` means: here, in the case of the Pārājika offense concerning a human being, it is not so; the meaning is that one is not absolved by indirect speech. Therefore he said, 'he might praise,' etc.

“Satthaṃ vā āharā”tiādināti ettha ādisaddena “visaṃ vā khāda, rajjuyā vā ubbandhitvā kālaṃ karohi, sobbhe vā narake vā papāte vā papatā”tiādiṃ (pārā. 172) sabbaṃ maraṇūpāyaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Ettha ca narako (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.172) nāma tattha tattha phalantiyā bhūmiyā sayameva nibbattā mahādarī, yattha hatthīpi patanti, corāpi nilīyitvā tiṭṭhanti. Papātoti pabbatantare vā thalantare vā ekato chinno. Pāpakenāti lāmakena. Dujjīvitenāti dukkhabahulattā dukkhena jīvitena. Mataṃ te jīvitā seyyāti tava maraṇaṃ jīvitā sundarataraṃ. Cittamassa atthīti citto. Tathā mano. Iti-saddo “sabbamatthīti kho, kaccāna, ayameko anto, sabbaṃ natthīti kho, kaccāna, ayaṃ dutiyo anto”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 2.15; 3.90) viya [V 0.0202] nidassane daṭṭhabbo yathāvuttassa buddhiyaṃ viparivattamānassa maraṇassa nidassanato. Tenevāha “mataṃ te jīvitā seyyo”tiādi.

In 'Bring a weapon,' etc., here by the word 'etc.' (`ādi`) he includes every means of death, such as 'Eat poison,' 'Die by hanging with a rope,' or 'Fall into a pit, a chasm, or an abyss.' And here `naraka` (chasm) is a great fissure that forms by itself in ground that splits open here and there, into which even elephants fall and where thieves hide. `Papāta` (abyss) is a sheer drop on one side within a mountain range or on level ground. `By what is bad` means by what is inferior. `Than a bad life` means than a life that is difficult because it is full of suffering. `Better for you is death than life` means your death is more excellent than your life. He has a mind (citta), thus he is 'citto'. Likewise for 'mano'. The word `iti` should be seen here as an illustration, as in such passages as 'That all exists, Kaccāna, is one extreme. That all does not exist, Kaccāna, is the second extreme,' because it illustrates the death that is revolving in the mind as described. For that reason he said, 'Better for you is death than life,' etc.

Nanu cettha “mano”ti idampi atthato cittameva, atha kasmā vuttanti āha “ettha cā”tiādi. Cittassa atthadīpanatthaṃ vuttanti nāyaṃ cittasaddo “cittasaṅkappo”tiādīsu (pārā. 171) viya vicittādiattho, atha kho viññāṇavacanoti tassa atthadīpanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Iminā punaruttidosābhāvaṃ dasseti. Kathametaṃ viññāyatīti āha “tenevassā”tiādi. Citto [M 0.0217] nānāppakārako saṅkappo assāti cittasaṅkappo. Vicittattho hettha cittasaddo “nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, aññaṃ ekanikāyampi samanupassāmi evaṃ cittaṃ, yathayidaṃ, bhikkhave, tiracchānagatā”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 3.100) viya. Tenāha “vicittasaṅkappo”ti. Etthāpi itisaddo āharitabboti “cittasaṅkappo”ti imasmiṃ padepi adhikāravasena itisaddo āharitabbo. Idañhi “iti cittasaṅkappo”ti evaṃ avuttampi adhikārato vuttameva hotīti. Saṅkappoti cettha “takko vitakko saṅkappo”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 7) viya na vitakkasseva nāmaṃ, atha kho tassa ca aññesañcāti dassetuṃ “saṅkappoti cā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Saṃvidahanamattassāti saññācetanāvitakkasaṅkhātassa sabbassa saṃvidahanassa. Sāmaññattho hettha mattasaddo “brāhmaṇamattaṃ bhojetī”tiādīsu viya. Tenāha “tañca saṃvidahana”ntiādi. Iminā saṃvidahanaṃ nāmettha na vidhānanti dasseti. Adhippāyo nāma vitakko.

But here, is not 'mind' also in meaning the same as consciousness? Then why was it stated? He says: 'Here too…' and so on. It was stated to clarify the meaning of consciousness. The word 'citta' here does not have the meaning of 'variegated,' as in 'cittasaṅkappa,' but is a term for cognition; this was stated to clarify its meaning. By this, he shows there is no redundancy. How is this to be understood? He says: 'By that very…' and so on. Cittasaṅkappa means 'a thought that is variegated, of various kinds.' Here the word 'citta' does mean 'variegated,' as in: 'Bhikkhus, I do not see any other single class of beings so variegated as animals.' Therefore he says, 'variegated thought.' Here too the particle 'iti' should be supplied; in the phrase 'cittasaṅkappa,' the particle 'iti' should be supplied by reason of the context. For this, even though not stated as 'iti cittasaṅkappa,' is nevertheless stated by reason of the context. And here 'thought' is not just a name for 'initial thought,' as in 'reasoning, initial thought, thought,' but to show that it includes that and others, he begins, 'And thought…' and so on. 'Of the mere arranging' refers to all that arranging designated as perception, volition, and initial thought. Here the word 'merely' has a general sense, as in 'he feeds a mere brahmin.' Therefore he says, 'and that arranging…' and so on. By this he shows that 'arranging' here does not mean 'prescribing.' 'Intention' is initial thought.

Uccāvacena kāraṇenāti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.172) mahantāmahantena upāyena. Tattha maraṇavaṇṇasaṃvaṇṇane tāva jīvite ādīnavadassanavasena avacākāratā, maraṇe vaṇṇabhaṇanavasena uccākāratā veditabbā. Samādapane pana muṭṭhijāṇunippothanādīhi maraṇasamādapanavasena uccākāratā, ekato bhuñjantassa nakhe visaṃ pakkhipitvā maraṇādisamādapanavasena avacākāratā veditabbā.

'By high and low means' means by great and small methods. Here, in praising death, the low aspect should be understood as seeing the danger in life, and the high aspect as speaking in praise of death. But in inciting, the high aspect should be understood as inciting death by striking the knee with the fist, etc., and the low aspect as inciting death by putting poison on the nail of one eating together with him.

Evaṃ asādhāraṇavinicchayaṃ vatvā idāni sādhāraṇavinicchayaṃ dassetuṃ “vesāliya”ntiādimāha. Opātakkhaṇanādīsu dukkaṭanti ettha sacepi jātapathaviṃ khaṇati, pāṇātipātassa pubbapayogattā payoge payoge dukkaṭaṃ. Manussaviggaho nāgasupaṇṇādisadiso tiracchānagato tiracchānagatamanussaviggaho, yakkho ca peto ca tiracchānagatamanussaviggaho ca yakkhapetatiracchānagatamanussaviggahā, tesaṃ. “Tathā”ti iminā thullaccayaṃ atidisati. Idāni “iminā [V 0.0203] nayenā”tiādinā apassenasaṃvidhānādīsupi yathāvuttaāpattibhedaṃ atidisati. Sabbatthāti apassenasaṃvidhānādīsu sabbesu payogesu.

Having thus stated the specific ruling, now to show the general ruling, he says, 'at Vesālī…' and so on. In digging a pitfall, etc., there is a dukkaṭa offense. Here, even if one digs living earth, because it is a preliminary act to destroying life, for each act there is a dukkaṭa offense. A human form similar to that of a nāga, supaṇṇa, or other animal is an animal-like human form. A yakkha, a peta, and an animal-like human form make up the yakkha-peta-animal-like-human-forms. Of these... By 'similarly,' he extends this to a thullaccaya offense. Now, by 'by this method,' etc., he extends the aforesaid classification of offenses also to arranging a screen, etc. 'In all cases' means in all acts such as arranging a screen, etc.

Idāni anāpattiṃ dassetuṃ “asañciccā”tiādimāha. Ettha ca “asañciccā”ti (sārattha. ṭī. 2.179) idaṃ maraṇasaṃvattanikaupakkamassa asallakkhaṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ[M 0.0218], “ajānantassā”ti idaṃ pana maraṇasaṃvattanikaupakaraṇassa ajānanaṃ sandhāya, “namaraṇādhippāyassā”ti idaṃ upakkamaṃ jānantassāpi maraṇādhippāyassa abhāvaṃ. Tenāha “asañciccā”tiādi. Acetetvāti asallakkhetvā, virajjhitvāti vuttaṃ hoti.

Now, to show what is not an offense, he says 'unintentionally…' and so on. Here, 'unintentionally' is said with reference to not noticing an undertaking leading to death; 'of one not knowing' is said with reference to not knowing an instrument leading to death; and 'of one without the intention to kill' refers to the absence of the intention to kill even while knowing the undertaking. Therefore he says, 'unintentionally…' and so on. 'Without intending' means not noticing; it is said to be 'having failed'.

Musalussāpanavatthusmiṃ viyāti “tena kho pana samayena aññataro bhikkhu bhattagge antaraghare āsanaṃ paññapento musale ussite ekaṃ musalaṃ aggahesi. Dutiyo musalo paripatitvā aññatarassa dārakassa matthake avatthāsi. So kālamakāsi. Tassa kukkuccaṃ ahosi…pe… kiṃcitto tvaṃ bhikkhūti. Asañcicca ahaṃ bhagavāti. Anāpatti bhikkhu asañciccā”ti (pārā. 180) imasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ viya.

As in the Story of Lifting the Pestle: 'Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu, while preparing a seat in a refectory in a house, took one pestle from a pile of pestles. A second pestle fell and landed on the head of a certain boy. He died. The bhikkhu felt remorse… “Bhikkhu, what was your intention?” “Blessed One, I had no intention.” “Bhikkhu, there is no offense when there is no intention.”' As in this story.

Visagatapiṇḍapātavatthusmiṃ viyāti “tena kho pana samayena aññataro piṇḍacāriko bhikkhu visagataṃ piṇḍapātaṃ labhitvā paṭikkamanaṃ haritvā bhikkhūnaṃ aggakārikaṃ adāsi. Te bhikkhū kālamakaṃsu. Tassa kukkuccaṃ ahosi…pe… kiṃcitto tvaṃ bhikkhūti. Nāhaṃ bhagavā jānāmīti. Anāpatti bhikkhu ajānantassā”ti (pārā. 181) imasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ viya.

As in the Story of the Poisoned Almsfood: 'Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu on his alms round received poisoned almsfood. Taking it on his return, he gave the first portion to the bhikkhus. Those bhikkhus died. He felt remorse… “Bhikkhu, what was your intention?” “Blessed One, I did not know.” “Bhikkhu, there is no offense for one who does not know.”' As in this story.

Bhesajjavatthusmiṃ viyāti “tena kho pana samayena aññatarā vañjhā itthī kulūpakaṃ bhikkhuṃ etadavoca “iṅghāyya bhesajjaṃ jānāhi, yenāhaṃ vijāyeyya’nti. ‘Suṭṭhu bhaginī’ti tassā bhesajjaṃ adāsi. Sā kālamakāsi. Tassa kukkuccaṃ ahosi…pe… anāpatti bhikkhu pārājikassa, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (pārā. 187) imasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ viya. Idha ādikammikā aññamaññaṃ jīvitā voropitabhikkhū, tesaṃ anāpatti. Avasesānaṃ maraṇavaṇṇasaṃvaṇṇanakādīnaṃ āpattiyeva.

As in the Story about the Medicine: 'Now at that time, a certain barren woman said to a bhikkhu who was a frequenter of her family: “Come now, venerable sir, find out a medicine by which I might give birth.” “Very well, sister,” he said, and gave her a medicine. She died. He felt remorse… “Bhikkhu, there is no pārājika offense, but there is an offense of wrong-doing.”' As in this story. Here, for the bhikkhus who were the original offenders, who deprived one another of life, there is no offense. For the rest, for praising death and so on, there is indeed an offense.

Atha kathaṃ dukkhavedananti, nanu rājāno coraṃ disvā hasamānāpi “gacchatha, naṃ ghātethā”ti vadantīti? Saccaṃ hasamānā vadanti, so pana hāso tesaṃ aññavisayo, sanniṭṭhāpakacetanā [V 0.0204] dukkhasampayuttāva. Vuttañhetaṃ samantapāsādikāyaṃ “sacepi hi sirisayanaṃ āruḷho rajjasampattisukhamanubhavanto rājā ‘coro deva ānīto’ti vutte ‘gacchatha naṃ mārethā’ti hasamāno bhaṇati, domanassacitteneva bhaṇatīti [M 0.0219] veditabbo. Sukhavokiṇṇattā, pana anuppabandhābhāvā ca dujjānametaṃ puthujjanehī”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.179).

Then how is the feeling painful? Do not kings, on seeing a thief, say, even while laughing, 'Go, kill him'? It is true they speak while laughing, but that laughter of theirs has a different object; the conclusive volition is associated with pain. For this is said in the Samantapāsādikā: 'Even if a king, enjoying the happiness of royal prosperity while seated on his royal couch, says laughing when told, “Your majesty, a thief has been brought,” “Go and kill him,” it should be understood that he speaks with a mind of displeasure. But because it is interspersed with happiness and because its continuity is not apparent, this is hard for ordinary people to understand.' (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.179).

Tatiyapārājikavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the third Pārājika is concluded.

4. Catutthapārājikavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Fourth Pārājika

Anabhijānanti na abhijānaṃ. Yena hi yo dhammo adhigato, so tassa pākaṭo hotīti āha “sakasantāne”tiādi. Uttarimanussānanti pakatimanussehi uttaritarānaṃ manussānaṃ, ukkaṭṭhamanussānanti attho. Dhammanti mahaggatalokuttarabhūtaṃ adhigatadhammaṃ. Atha vā uttarimanussadhammāti uttarimanussadhammo. Manussadhammo nāma vinā bhāvanāmanasikārena pakatiyā manussehi nibbattetabbo dasakusalakammapathadhammo. So hi manussānaṃ cittādhiṭṭhānamattena ijjhanato tesaṃ so bhāvitadhammo viya ṭhitoti tathā vutto, manussaggahaṇañcettha tesu bahulaṃ pavattanato. Jhānādikaṃ pana tabbidhuranti tatuttari, iti uttari manussadhammāti uttarimanussadhammo, taṃ uttarimanussadhammanti evampettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Samudācarantoti ārocento.

`Anabhijānanti`: not knowing directly. For whatever Dhamma has been attained by a person, that becomes manifest to him; thus it is said, “in his own continuity,” and so on. `Uttarimanussānaṃ`: of humans who are superior to ordinary humans; that is, of excellent humans. `Dhammaṃ`: the attained Dhamma, which is exalted or supramundane. Or, `uttarimanussadhamma` is a superhuman state. “Human Dhamma” is the Dhamma of the ten wholesome courses of action, which is to be produced by humans naturally, without cultivation or special attention. Since it is accomplished by humans merely through mental determination, it stands as if it were a cultivated Dhamma for them; and the word ‘human’ is used here because it occurs frequently among them. But jhāna and the like are devoid of that, hence they are superior to it. Thus `uttari manussadhamma` is `uttarimanussadhammo`. The meaning of `uttarimanussadhammaṃ` should be understood here in this way. `Samudācaranto` means announcing.

Kiñcāpi lokiyalokuttarā sabbāva paññā “ñāṇa”nti vuccati, idha pana mahaggatalokuttarāva veditabbāti āha “mahaggatalokuttarapaññā jānanaṭṭhena ñāṇa”nti. Kilesehi ārakattā parisuddhaṭṭhena ariyanti āha “ariyaṃ visuddhaṃ uttama”nti. Ariyasaddo cettha visuddhapariyāyo, na lokuttarapariyāyo. Jhānādibhedeti ādisaddena “vimokkho, samādhi, samāpatti, ñāṇadassanaṃ, maggabhāvanā, phalasacchikiriyā, kilesappahānaṃ, vinīvaraṇatā cittassa, suññāgāre abhiratī”ti (pārā. 198) ime saṅgaṇhāti. Viññussa manussajātikassāti ārocetabbapuggalanidassanaṃ. Etassa hi ārocite ārocitaṃ hoti, na devabrahmānaṃ, nāpi petayakkhatiracchānagatānanti. Āroceyyāti vadeyya, viññāpeyyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Vinā aññāpadesenāti “yo te vihāre vasati, so bhikkhu paṭhamassa jhānassa lābhī”tiādinā (pārā. 220) nayena aññāpadesaṃ vināti [M 0.0220] attho. Idhevāti “iti jānāmi, iti passāmī”ti imasmiṃyeva pade. “Tena vutta”ntiādi nigamanaṃ.

Although all wisdom, both mundane and supramundane, is called 'knowledge,' here it should be understood as only exalted and supramundane wisdom. Thus it is said: 'Exalted and supramundane wisdom is knowledge in the sense of knowing.' Because it is far from the defilements and pure, it is called noble. Thus it is said: 'Noble, pure, supreme.' Here the word 'noble' is a synonym for 'pure,' not for 'supramundane.' In the phrase 'jhāna and its divisions,' the word 'etc.' includes the following: liberation, concentration, attainment, knowledge and vision, development of the path, realization of the fruit, abandonment of defilements, the mind’s freedom from hindrances, and delight in a secluded dwelling (Pārā. 198). `Viññussa manussajātikassa` (to a wise human being): this indicates the person to whom the announcement should be made. For when it is announced to such a one, it is truly announced; not so when announced to devas, brahmās, or to those in the ghost, yakkha, or animal realms. `Āroceyya` (one should announce) means one should speak, one should make it known. `Vinā aññāpadesena` (without indirect reference) means without an indirect reference in the way of, for example, 'The bhikkhu who lives in your monastery is an attainer of the first jhāna' (Pārā. 220). `Idheva` (right here) means in this very phrase: 'Thus I know, thus I see.' The words 'Therefore it was said,' etc., are the conclusion.

Samanuggāhīyamānoti [V 0.0205] codiyamāno, yaṃ vatthu ārocitaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ “kiṃ te adhigataṃ, kinti te adhigataṃ, kadā te adhigataṃ, kattha te adhigataṃ, katame te kilesā pahīnā, katamesaṃ tvaṃ dhammānaṃ lābhī’ti kenaci vuccamāno”ti vuttaṃ hoti. Asamanuggāhīyamānoti na kenaci vuccamāno.

`Samanuggāhīyamāno` (being pressed) means being interrogated. When a matter has been announced, concerning that matter one is asked by someone: 'What have you attained? How have you attained it? When did you attain it? Where did you attain it? Which defilements have you abandoned? Of which states are you an attainer?' `Asamanuggāhīyamāno` (not being pressed) means not being asked by anyone.

“Bhikkhubhāve ṭhatvā abhabbo jhānādīni adhigantu”nti sikkhāpadātikkamassa antarāyakarattā vuttaṃ. Bhikkhubhāvo hissa saggantarāyo ceva hoti maggantarāyo ca (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.198). Vuttañhetaṃ “sāmaññaṃ dupparāmaṭṭhaṃ, nirayāyupakaḍḍhatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.89; dha. pa. 311). Aparampi vuttaṃ “sithilo hi paribbājo, bhiyyo ākirate raja”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.89; dha. pa. 313). Bhikkhubhāvoti pārājikaṃ āpajjitvā “samaṇo aha”nti paṭijānanato vohāramattasiddho bhikkhubhāvo. Dānādīhīti dānasaraṇasīlasaṃvarādīhi.

“While remaining in the state of a bhikkhu, he is incapable of attaining jhāna and other such states”—this is said because transgression of the training rule creates an obstacle. For him, the state of a bhikkhu is an obstacle to heaven and an obstacle to the path (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.198). For it is said: “The ascetic life, if wrongly handled, drags one down to hell” (SN 1.89; Dhp 311). And further it is said: “A lax wanderer stirs up still more dust” (SN 1.89; Dhp 313). “The state of a bhikkhu”: this refers to the state of a bhikkhu that is established merely in designation, from one’s professing, “I am an ascetic,” after having committed a pārājika offense. “By giving, etc.”: by giving, taking refuge, virtue, restraint, and so on.

Ajānamevāti ettha evāti avadhāraṇatthe nipāto. “Ajānameva”ntipi paṭhanti. Tattha pana “evaṃ jānāmi, evaṃ passāmī”ti avacanti yojetabbaṃ. Vacanatthavirahatoti “paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajji”nti ādivacanassa (pārā. 209) atthabhūtena jhānādinā vajjitattā tucchaṃ udakādisuññaṃ bhājanaṃ viya. Musāti visaṃvādanapurekkhārassa paravisaṃvādako vacīpayogo, kāyapayogo vā. Tenāha “vañcanādhippāyato musā”ti. Musā ca vañcanādhippāyo ca pubbabhāgakkhaṇe, taṅkhaṇe ca. Vuttañhi “pubbe vāssa hoti ‘musā bhaṇissa’nti, bhaṇantassa hoti ‘musā bhaṇāmī’”ti (pārā. 200). Etañhi dvayaṃ aṅgabhūtaṃ, itaraṃ pana hotu vā, mā vā, akāraṇametaṃ. Abhaṇinti viññāpanaṃ akāsiṃ.

In `ajānameva`, the word `eva` is a particle with the sense of emphasis. Some also read it as `ajānamevaṃ`. In that case, however, it should be connected with not saying, 'Thus I know, thus I see.' `Vacanatthavirahato` (because of being devoid of the statement’s meaning): because it is devoid of jhāna and so on, which are the meaning of the statement 'he attained the first jhāna' (Pārā. 209), it is empty like a vessel devoid of water and other such things. `Musā` (falsehood): this is a verbal or bodily application that deceives another, preceded by the intention to deceive. Hence it is said: 'A falsehood is from the intention to deceive.' Both the falsehood and the intention to deceive are present in the preceding moment and in that very moment. For it is said: 'Beforehand he has the thought, “I will speak falsely,” and while speaking he has the thought, “I am speaking falsely”' (Pārā. 200). These two are the essential factors; as for the other, whether it is present or not, it is not a cause. `Abhaṇiṃ` (I did not speak): I did not make a declaration.

Aññatra adhimānāti adhigato māno, adhiko vā māno adhimāno, thaddhamānoti attho, taṃ vināti attho. Kassa panāyaṃ adhimāno uppajjati, kassa nuppajjati? Ariyasāvakassa tāva nuppajjati (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.196). So hi maggaphalanibbānapahīnakilesāvasiṭṭhakilesapaccavekkhaṇena sañjātasomanasso [M 0.0221] ariyaguṇappaṭivedhe nikkaṅkho, tasmā sotāpannādīnaṃ “ahaṃ sakadāgāmī”tiādivasena māno nuppajjati. Dussīlassa nuppajjati. So hi ariyaguṇādhigame nirāsova. Sīlavatopi pariccattakammaṭṭhānassa niddārāmatādimanuyuttassa nuppajjati, suparisuddhasīlassa pana kammaṭṭhāne appamattassa nāmarūpaṃ vavatthapetvā paccayapariggahena vitiṇṇakaṅkhassa tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā saṅkhāre [V 0.0206] sammasantassa āraddhavipassakassa uppajjati. Tenāha “yvāya”ntiādi. Tattha tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvāti (sārattha. ṭī. 2.196) kalāpasammasanavasena aniccādilakkhaṇattayaṃ āropetvā. Sammasantassāti vipassantassa. Āraddhavipassakassāti udayabbayānupassanāya āraddhavipassakassa. Apatteti attano santāne uppattivasena apatte, anadhigateti vuttaṃ hoti. Pattasaññitāsaṅkhātoti “patto mayā uttarimanussadhammo”ti evaṃsaññitāsaṅkhāto adhimāno uppajjati. Uppanno ca suddhasamathalābhiṃ vā suddhavipassanālābhiṃ vā antarā ṭhapeti. So hi dasapi vīsampi tiṃsampi vassāni kilesasamudācāraṃ apassanto “ahaṃ sotāpanno”ti vā “sakadāgāmī”ti vā “anāgāmī”ti vā maññati. Samathavipassanālābhiṃ pana arahatteyeva ṭhapeti. Tassa hi samādhibalena kilesā vikkhambhitā, vipassanābalena saṅkhārā supariggahitā, tasmā saṭṭhimpi vassāni, asītimpi vassāni, vassasatampi kilesā na samudācaranti, khīṇāsavasseva cittācāro hoti. So evaṃ dīgharattaṃ kilesasamudācāraṃ apassanto antarā aṭṭhatvāva “arahā aha”nti maññatīti. “Taṃ adhimānaṃ ṭhapetvā”ti iminā “aññatrā”ti padaṃ apekkhitvā “adhimānā”ti upayogatthe nissakkavacananti dasseti.

`Aññatra adhimānā` (except for conceit): `adhimāno` is an attained conceit or an excessive conceit; the meaning is stiff pride. The meaning is ‘apart from that.’ But for whom does this conceit arise, and for whom does it not? For a noble disciple, it does not arise (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.196). For he is joyful from reviewing the defilements that remain after those abandoned by the path, fruit, and Nibbāna, and he is free from doubt about the penetration of the noble qualities.
