Therefore, in a stream-enterer and others, conceit such as “I am a once-returner” does not arise. It does not arise in an immoral person, for he is without hope of attaining the noble qualities. It also does not arise in a virtuous person who has given up his meditation subject and is devoted to sleep and laziness. But it does arise in one of very pure virtue who is diligent in his meditation subject, who has defined name-and-form, has crossed beyond doubt by grasping the conditions, has applied the three characteristics to formations, and is contemplating them, having thus begun insight meditation. Hence it is said, “whatsoever,” and so on. Here, “applies the three characteristics” means applying the three characteristics of impermanence, etc., by way of comprehension by groups. `Sammasantassa` means of one who is practicing insight. `Āraddhavipassakassa` means of one who has begun insight with the contemplation of arising and passing away. `Apatte` (in what is not attained): in what has not arisen in one's own continuity; that is to say, not achieved. `Pattasaññitāsaṅkhāto` (designated by the perception of attainment): conceit so designated arises with the thought, “The superhuman state has been attained by me.” Once arisen, it stops one who has gained either pure serenity or pure insight midway. For such a person, not seeing the manifestation of defilements for ten, twenty, or thirty years, thinks, “I am a stream-enterer,” or “a once-returner,” or “a non-returner.” But in one who has gained both serenity and insight, it makes him stuck only with regard to arahantship. For in him, the defilements are suppressed by the power of concentration, and formations are well-grasped by the power of insight. Thus, for sixty, eighty, or even a hundred years, the defilements do not manifest, and his mental conduct is like that of one whose taints are destroyed. Not seeing the manifestation of defilements for such a long time, he gets stuck in between and thinks, “I am an arahant.” By the phrase “setting aside that conceit,” it shows that, in connection with the word `aññatra`, the word `adhimānā` is an ablative of exception.

Pāpicchatāyāti pāpā icchā etassāti pāpiccho, tassa bhāvo pāpicchatā, tāya, pāpikāya icchāyāti attho. Yā sā “idhekacco dussīlova samāno ‘sīlavā’ti maṃ jano jānātū”tiādinā (vibha. 851) nayena vuttā, tāya asantaguṇasambhāvanicchāyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Iminā pana mandattā momūhattā samudācarantassa anāpattīti dasseti. Ayampīti pi-saddena na kevalaṃ purimā tayovāti dasseti.

`Pāpicchatāya` (because of evil wishes): one who has an evil wish is a `pāpiccho`; his state is `pāpicchatā`. The meaning is: because of a wicked wish. This is the wish to make it seem one possesses good qualities that are non-existent, as spoken of in the way beginning: 'Here, someone, being immoral, wishes: “Let people know me as virtuous”' (Vibh 851). This shows, however, that there is no offense for one who makes the claim out of dullness or delusion. `Ayampi` (this too): the particle `pi` shows that it is not only the previous three.

Asantanti [M 0.0222] abhūtaṃ. Jhānādidhammanti jhānaṃ, vimokkho, samādhi, samāpatti, ñāṇadassanaṃ, maggabhāvanā, phalasacchikiriyā, kilesappahānaṃ, vinīvaraṇatā cittassa, suññāgāre abhiratī”ti (pārā. 198) evaṃ vuttaṃ uttarimanussadhammaṃ. Yassa ārocetīti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.215) vācāya vā hatthavikārādīhi vā aṅgapaccaṅgacopanehi viññattipathe ṭhitassa yassa puggalassa āroceti. Viññattipathaṃ pana atikkamitvā ṭhito koci ce dibbena cakkhunā (sārattha. ṭī. 2.215), dibbāya ca sotadhātuyā disvā ca sutvā ca jānāti, na pārājikaṃ. Yopi “kiṃ ayaṃ bhaṇatī”ti saṃsayaṃ vā āpajjati, ciraṃ vīmaṃsitvā vā pacchā jānāti, “avijānanto”icceva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Yo pana jhānādīni attano adhigamavasena vā uggahaparipucchādivasena vā na jānāti, kevalaṃ “jhāna”nti vā “vimokkho”ti [V 0.0207] vā vacanamattameva sutaṃ hoti, sopi tena vutte “jhānaṃ kira samāpajjī”ti esa vadatīti yadi ettakamattampi jānāti, “jānāti”cceva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati, tassa vutte pārājikameva. Seso pana ekassa vā dvinnaṃ vā bahūnaṃ vā niyamitāniyamitavasena viseso sabbo sikkhāpaccakkhānakathāyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Pariyāyabhāsane pana “aha”nti avuttattā paṭivijānantassa vuttepi thullaccayaṃ. Visaṃvādanādhippāyena musāvādapayogassa katattā appaṭivijānantassāpi dukkaṭanti āha “yo te vihāre vasati…pe… dukkaṭa”nti. Anullapanādhippāyassāti ullapanādhippāyavirahitassa, abhūtārocanādhippāyavirahitassāti attho. Ummattakādayo pubbe vuttanayā eva. Idha pana ādikammikā vaggumudātīriyabhikkhū, tesaṃ anāpatti.

`Unreal` means non-existent. `A state such as jhāna` means a superior human state spoken of thus: “Jhāna, liberation, concentration, attainment, knowledge and vision, development of the path, realization of the fruit, abandonment of defilements, the mind’s freedom from hindrances, delight in an empty dwelling.” `To whom he declares it`: to whichever person standing in the path of communication he declares it, whether by speech, by hand gestures, or by movements of the major and minor limbs. But if someone, standing beyond the path of communication, knows by seeing with the divine eye and hearing with the divine ear-element, it is not a pārājika. Even one who falls into doubt, thinking, “What is he saying?” or who understands only after long investigation, is reckoned as “not knowing.” But as to one who does not know about jhāna and so on either by way of attainment or by way of study and inquiry, but has only heard the mere words “jhāna” or “liberation,” if, when the other speaks, he knows just this much—“He is saying, ‘It seems I have attained jhāna’”—he is reckoned as “knowing,” and when one speaks to him, it is a pārājika. The rest—the distinction concerning one, two, or many, specified or unspecified—should all be understood in the way stated in the discussion on giving up the training. In the case of indirect speech, however, because “I” is not said, even if it is said to one who understands, it is a thullaccaya. Because an utterance of falsehood has been made with the intention to deceive, even for one who does not understand it is a dukkaṭa. Thus it is said: “Whoever lives in your monastery… a dukkaṭa.” `Without the intention to boast` means: without the intention to praise, that is, without the intention to declare what is unreal. The cases of the insane and so on are as stated before. Here, however, the original offenders are the bhikkhus from the bank of the Vaggumudā river; for them there is no offense.

Catutthapārājikavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Fourth Pārājika is finished.

Pārājikanigamanavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Conclusion of the Pārājikas

Idhāti imasmiṃ bhikkhupātimokkhe. Uddiṭṭhapārājikaparidīpanamevāti uddiṭṭhānaṃ catunnaṃ pārājikānaṃ paridīpanavacanameva. Avadhāraṇaṃ pana na aññesampīti dassanatthaṃ. Tenāha “samodhānetvā panā”tiādi. Tattha samodhānetvāti tattha tattha āgatāni ettheva samodahitvā, pakkhipitvā rāsiṃ katvāti attho. Pāḷiyaṃ āgatānīti uddesapāḷiyaṃ āgatāni[M 0.0223]. Bhikkhunīnaṃ asādhāraṇāni cattārīti ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalikā, vajjappaṭicchādikā, ukkhittānuvattikā, aṭṭhavatthukāti imāni bhikkhunīnaṃ bhikkhūhi asādhāraṇāni cattāri. Paṇḍakādīnañhi ekādasannaṃ abhabbabhāvo pārājikāpattisadisattā pārājikoti āha “ekādasanna”ntiādi. Abhabbabhāvasaṅkhātehīti vatthuvipannatādinā pabbajjūpasampadāya naarahabhāvasaṅkhātehi. Paṇḍakatiracchānagataubhatobyañjanakā (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.233) hi tayo vatthuvipannā ahetukappaṭisandhikā, tesaṃ saggo avārito, maggo pana vārito. Abhabbā hi te maggappaṭilābhāya vatthuvipannattā. Pabbajjāpi nesaṃ paṭikkhittā, tasmā tepi pārājikāva. Theyyasaṃvāsako, titthiyapakkantako, mātughātako, pitughātako, arahantaghātako, bhikkhunidūsako, lohituppādako, saṅghabhedakoti ime aṭṭha attano kiriyāya vipannattā abhabbaṭṭhānaṃ pattāti pārājikāva. Tesu theyyasaṃvāsako, titthiyapakkantako, bhikkhunidūsakoti imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ saggo avārito, maggo pana vāritova. Itaresaṃ pañcannaṃ ubhayampi vāritaṃ. Te hi anantarāva narake nibbattanakasattā. Yadā bhikkhunī vibbhamitukāmā hutvā kāsāvameva [V 0.0208] vā gihivatthaṃ vā gihinivāsanākārena nivāseti, tadā pārājikamāpannā nāma hotīti āha “gihibhāvaṃ patthayamānāyā”tiādi. Sā hi ajjhācāravītikkamaṃ akatvāpi ettāvatā assamaṇī nāma hoti.

Here, 'idha' refers to this Bhikkhu Pātimokkha. 'Uddiṭṭhapārājikaparidīpanamevāti' means only the explanation regarding the four Pārājika offenses that have been recited. The emphasis, 'pana na aññesampīti,' is stated to show that it does not apply to others. Therefore, it is said, 'samodhānetvā panā,' and so on. In this context, 'samodhānetvā' means gathering what has been mentioned in various places here, compiling them into a collection. 'Pāḷiyaṃ āgatānīti' refers to what has been included in the recitation text. The four offenses not shared with bhikkhus, specific to bhikkhunīs, are: ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalikā, vajjappaṭicchādikā, ukkhittānuvattikā, and aṭṭhavatthukā. Regarding the eleven types, such as paṇḍakas, their state of being incapable (abhabbabhāva) is similar to a Pārājika offense; hence it is said, 'ekādasanna,' and so on. 'Abhabbabhāvasaṅkhātehi' refers to those who are counted as unworthy of the going forth or higher ordination due to a defect of their person (vatthuvipannatā). The paṇḍaka, tiracchānagata, and ubhatobyañjanaka—these three are defective in their person and have a rootless relinking-consciousness; for them, heaven is not barred, but the path is barred. They are incapable of attaining the path due to their defective person. Even their going forth is prohibited, so they too are like Pārājikas. The theyyasaṃvāsaka, titthiyapakkantaka, mātughātaka, pitughātaka, arahantaghātaka, bhikkhunidūsaka, lohituppādako, and saṅghabhedaka—these eight, having reached a state of incapacity due to their own corrupted actions, are also Pārājikas. Among them, for the theyyasaṃvāsaka, titthiyapakkantaka, and bhikkhunidūsaka, heaven is not barred, but the path is barred. For the remaining five, both are barred, as they are beings destined to be reborn in hell immediately after. When a bhikkhunī, desiring to disrobe, wears either the monastic robe or lay clothing in the manner of a laywoman, she is considered to have incurred a Pārājika offense. This is stated as 'gihibhāvaṃ patthayamānāyā,' and so on. Even without committing a transgression of misconduct, she is by that much no longer considered a recluse.

Dīghatāya lambamānaṃ aṅgajātametassāti lambī (sārattha. ṭī. 2.233). Na so ettāvatā pārājiko, atha kho yadā anabhiratiyā pīḷito attano aṅgajātaṃ mukhe vā vaccamagge vā paveseti, tadā pārājiko hoti. Mudukatā piṭṭhi etassāti mudupiṭṭhiko, kataparikammāya mudukāya piṭṭhiyā samannāgato. Sopi yadā anabhiratiyā pīḷito attano aṅgajātaṃ attano mukhamaggavaccamaggesu aññataraṃ paveseti, tadā pārājiko hoti. Parassa aṅgajātaṃ mukhena gaṇhātīti yo anabhiratiyā pīḷito parassa suttassa vā pamattassa vā aṅgajātaṃ mukhena gaṇhāti. Parassa aṅgajāte abhinisīdatīti yo anabhiratiyā pīḷito parassa aṅgajātaṃ kammaniyaṃ disvā attano vaccamaggena tassūpari nisīdati, taṃ attano vaccamaggaṃ pavesetīti attho. Etāni hi cattāri yasmā [M 0.0224] ubhinnaṃ rāgavasena sadisabhāvūpagatānaṃ dhammo “methunadhammo”ti vuccati, tasmā ekena pariyāyena methunadhammaṃ appaṭisevitvāyeva kevalaṃ maggena maggappavesanavasena āpajjitabbattā methunadhammapārājikassa anulomentīti “anulomapārājikānī”ti vuccanti.

His sexual organ hangs down due to its length, hence 'lambī' (Sāratthadīpanī, ṭīkā 2.233). He does not become a Pārājika by that alone, but when, oppressed by discontent, he inserts his own sexual organ into his mouth or excretory passage, then he becomes a Pārājika. His back is soft, hence 'mudupiṭṭhiko,' one endowed with a back made soft by preparation. He too, when oppressed by discontent, inserts his own sexual organ into either his own mouth or excretory passage, then he becomes a Pārājika. 'He takes another's sexual organ with his mouth' means one who, oppressed by discontent, takes into his mouth the sexual organ of another who is asleep or heedless. 'He sits down upon another's sexual organ' means one who, oppressed by discontent, seeing another's sexual organ to be suitable for the act, sits down upon it with his own excretory passage; the meaning is that he causes it to enter his own excretory passage. Indeed, these four are called 'conforming pārājikas' (anuloma-pārājikāni). This is because, while the practice of two people who have reached a similar state through lust is called 'sexual intercourse' (methunadhamma), these offenses—though in one way not involving the act of sexual intercourse—are incurred merely by the entry of a passage into a passage, and thus they conform to the Pārājika offense of sexual intercourse.

Etthāha – mātughātakapitughātakaarahantaghātakā tatiyapārājikaṃ āpannā, bhikkhunidūsako, lambiādayo cattāro ca paṭhamapārājikaṃ āpannā evāti katvā kuto catuvīsatīti (sārattha. ṭī. 2.233)? Vuccate – mātughātakādayo hi cattāro idha anupasampannā eva adhippetā, lambiādayo cattāro kiñcāpi paṭhamapārājikena saṅgahitā, yasmā pana ekena pariyāyena methunadhammaṃ appaṭisevino honti, tasmā visuṃ vuttāti. Dutiyavikappe kaccitthāti ettha kacci atthāti padacchedo kātabbo.

Here it is asked: 'Since the matricide, the patricide, and the murderer of an Arahant have incurred the third Pārājika, and the violator of a bhikkhunī and the four beginning with lambī have incurred the first Pārājika, how then are there twenty-four?' (Sāratthadīpanī, ṭīkā 2.233). It is replied: The four beginning with the matricide are here intended as those who are not ordained. And although the four beginning with lambī are included under the first Pārājika, they are mentioned separately because in one respect they do not engage in sexual intercourse. In the second alternative, 'kaccitthāti' should be parsed as 'kacci atthāti'.

Iti kaṅkhāvitaraṇiyā pātimokkhavaṇṇanāya

Thus in the Pātimokkha-explanation of the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī,

Vinayatthamañjūsāyaṃ līnatthappakāsaniyaṃ

In the Vinayatthamañjūsā, the Elucidation of Subtle Meanings,

Pārājikavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Pārājikas is concluded.

Saṅghādisesakaṇḍaṃ

The Section on Saṅghādisesa Offenses

Piyavacanena [M 0.0225][V 0.0209] ālapananti piyāyitabbavacanenālapanaṃ, sādhūnaṃ samālapananti vuttaṃ hoti. Sādhavo hi pare “bhonto”ti vā “devānaṃpiyā”ti vā “bhadrabhava”nti vā “āyasmanto”ti vā samālapanti.

‘Addressing with pleasing speech’ means addressing with endearing words; this is said to be the way the virtuous address others. For the virtuous address others as 'bhonto,' or 'devānaṃpiya,' or 'bhadra bhava,' or 'āyasmanto.'

1. Sukkavissaṭṭhisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Training Rule on Intentional Emission of Semen

Saṃ-saddo vijjamānatthoti āha “saṃvijjatī”ti. Cetanāti vītikkamavasappavattā pubbabhāgacetanā, mocanassādacetanāti attho. Assāti sukkavissaṭṭhiyā. Aññapadatthasamāseneva sukkavissaṭṭhiyā vuttattā ika-saddassa visuṃ attho natthīti āha “sañcetanāva sañcetanikā”ti. Idāni ika-saddova atthiatthaṃ pakāsetīti dassento “sañcetanā vā”tiādimāha. Saṃvijjamānā cetanā sañcetanā. Sukkassāti sambhavassa. Visaṭṭhīti vissaggo.

He said: 'The prefix 'saṃ-' has the meaning of 'existing,' as in 'saṃvijjati' (it exists).' 'Cetanā' is the preliminary volition that proceeds by way of the transgression; the meaning is the volition of delighting in the release. 'Assā' refers to the emission of semen. Because the emission of semen is spoken of by way of a relative compound, the suffix '-ika' has no separate meaning; thus he says, 'sañcetanāva sañcetanikā' (volition itself is what is volitional). Now, showing that the suffix '-ika' itself indicates the meaning of 'possessing,' he says, 'sañcetanā vā,' and so on. 'Saṃvijjamānā cetanā' is 'sañcetanā.' 'Sukkassa' means of what is produced. 'Visaṭṭhi' means emission.

Idāni taṃ yasmiṃ kāle moceti, yenādhippāyena moceti, yena copāyena moceti, yañca tassa adhippāyassa vatthu, taṃ sabbaṃ saṅkhepato vibhāvetvā sarūpato taṃ visaṭṭhiṃ dassetuṃ “rāgūpatthambhādīsū”tiādimāha. Tattha rāgassa balavabhāvo, rāgena vā aṅgajātassūpatthambho thaddhabhāvo rāgūpatthambho, so ādi yesaṃ te rāgūpatthambhādayo, tesu rāgūpatthambhādīsu. Ādisaddena (pārā. 238) vaccūpatthambhapassāvūpatthambhavātūpatthambhauccāliṅgapāṇakadaṭṭhūpatthambhānaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Kammaññataṃ patteti mocanakammakkhamatāya kammaniyataṃ patte, ajjhattarūpādīsu upakkamārahabhāvaṃ patteti attho. Arogassa bhāvo ārogyaṃ, taṃ ādi yesaṃ te ārogyādayo, tesu ārogyādīsu. Ādisaddena sukhabhesajjadānapuññayaññasaggabījavīmaṃsadavānaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Ajjhattarūpaṃ ajjhattaṃ upādinnarūpaṃ, taṃ ādi yesaṃ te ajjhattarūpādayo, tesu. Ādisaddena bahiddhārūpaajjhattabahiddhārūpaākāsekaṭikampanānaṃ [V 0.0210] gahaṇaṃ. Mocane assādo sukhavedanā mocanassādo, mocanatthaṃ pubbabhāge pavattarāgo, sampayuttaassādasīsena cettha rāgo vutto, tena sampayuttā cetanā mocanassādacetanā, tāya[M 0.0226]. Iminā muccanassādo (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.240) muttassādo methunassādo phassassādo kaṇḍuvanassādo dassanassādo nisajjassādo vācassādo gehasitapemaṃ vanabhaṅgiyanti imehi sampayuttā cetanāyo paṭikkhipati, tāhi nimitte upakkamantassa muttepi anāpatti. “Nimitte upakkamantassā”ti iminā pana ūrumaddāpanādīni paṭikkhipati. Tena hi satipi mocanassāde nimitte upakkamābhāvato muttepi anāpatti. Vuttañhetaṃ samantapāsādikāyaṃ “sā ca kho nimitte upakkamantasseva, hatthaparikammapādaparikammagattaparikammakaraṇena sacepi asuci muccati, anāpattī”ti.

Now, having briefly analyzed all this—at what time one emits it, with what intention one emits it, by what means one emits it, and what is the object of that intention—in order to show that emission in its own nature, he states, ‘due to the support of lust, etc.’ Herein, the powerful state of lust, or the stiffening—the rigidity—of the generative organ by lust, is ‘the support of lust.’ That is the first of those things, hence they are ‘the support of lust, etc.’; thus, ‘due to the support of lust, etc.’ By the word ‘etc.’ is included the stiffening due to feces, urine, or wind, and the stiffening due to an insect bite. ‘Having become workable’ means having become fit for the act of emission, having become suitable for the action; the meaning is that it has reached a state suitable for making an effort with regard to internal forms, etc. The state of being not ill is ‘health.’ That is the first of those things, hence ‘for the sake of health, etc.’ By the word ‘etc.’ is included for the sake of happiness, as a medicine, as a gift, for merit, for a sacrifice, for heaven, for testing the seed, and for sport. ‘Internal form’ is clung-to form within oneself. That is the first of those things, hence ‘in internal form, etc.’ By the word ‘etc.’ is included external form, both internal and external form, and shaking the hips in space. The pleasure in emission is the pleasant feeling, the delight of emission. The lust that arises in the preliminary stage for the purpose of emission—lust is spoken of here under the heading of its associated delight. The volition associated with that is the ‘volition for the delight of emission.’ By this, he excludes volitions associated with these: delight in being released, delight in being freed, delight in sexual intercourse, delight in touch, delight in scratching, delight in seeing, delight in sitting, delight in speech, household affection, and breaking the monotony of the forest. For one making an effort at the sign with these other volitions, there is no offense even if there is an emission. But by the phrase ‘for one making an effort at the sign,’ he excludes such things as having one’s thighs rubbed. For in that case, even if there is delight in emission, since there is no effort made at the sign, there is no offense even if there is an emission. And this was stated in the Samantapāsādikā: ‘And this is only for one who makes an effort at the sign. If an impurity is emitted through having one’s hands massaged, feet massaged, or body massaged, there is no offense.’

Āsayadhātunānāttatoti pittasemhapubbalohitāsayānañceva pathavīdhātuādīnañca catunnaṃ dhātūnaṃ, rasasoṇitādīnaṃ vā sattannaṃ dhātūnaṃ nānāttato. Ṭhānā cāvanāti sukkassa yaṃ ṭhānaṃ, tato cuti. Sukkassa hi vatthisīsaṃ kaṭi kāyoti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.237) tidhā ṭhānaṃ pakappenti. Eko kirācariyo “vatthisīsaṃ sukkassa ṭhāna”nti āha, eko “kaṭī”ti, eko “sakalo kāyo”ti. Tesu tatiyassa bhāsitaṃ subhāsitaṃ. Kesalomanakhadantānañhi maṃsavinimuttaṭṭhānaṃ, uccārapassāvakheḷasiṅghāṇikā, thaddhasukkhacammāni ca vajjetvā avaseso chavimaṃsalohitānugato sabbopi kāyo kāyappasādabhāvajīvitindriyābaddhapittānaṃ, sambhavassa ca ṭhānameva. Tathā hi rāgapariyuṭṭhānenābhibhūtānaṃ hatthīnaṃ ubhohi kaṇṇacūḷikāhi sambhavo nikkhamati.

‘Due to the diversity of the repository elements’ means due to the diversity of the repositories of bile, phlegm, pus, and blood, and of the four great elements beginning with the earth element, or of the seven elements beginning with nutritive essence and blood. ‘Falling from its place’ means falling from whatever is the place of the semen. For they posit three places for semen: the head of the bladder, the waist, and the entire body. One teacher, it seems, said, ‘The place of semen is the head of the bladder’; another, ‘the waist’; another, ‘the entire body.’ Among these, the statement of the third is well-spoken. For, excluding the places free from flesh—hair of the head, body hair, nails, and teeth—and excluding feces, urine, saliva, snot, and hardened, dry skin, the entire rest of the body, pervaded by skin, flesh, and blood, and bound up with the body sensitivity, the state of being, the life faculty, and bile, is the very place of semen. For when elephants are overcome by an outbreak of lust, semen comes out from both tips of their ears.

Ettha ca “rāgūpatthambhādīsū”tiādinā (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.237) kālo dassito. Rāgūpatthambhādikālesu hi aṅgajātaṃ kammaniyaṃ hoti. Yassa kammaniyatte sati moceti, ito paraṃ añño kālo natthi. Na hi vinā rāgūpatthambhādīhi pubbaṇhādayo kālabhedā mocane nimittaṃ honti. “Ārogyādīsū”tiādinā pana adhippāyo dassito. Evarūpena hi adhippāyabhedena moceti, na aññathā. “Ajjhattarūpādīsū”tiādinā upāyo dassito. Ajjhattarūpe vā hi moceyya, bahiddhārūpe vā, ubhayattha vā, ākāse vā kaṭiṃ kampento, ito paraṃ añño upāyo natthi. Nīlādivasenā”tiādīhi pana dasahi navamassa adhippāyassa vatthu dassitaṃ. Vīmaṃsanto hi nīlādīsu aññataravasena vīmaṃsati, na tehi vinimuttanti. “Ṭhānā cāvanā”ti iminā pana atthato vissaṭṭhi dassitā[M 0.0227]. Yathāha “vissaṭṭhīti ṭhānato cāvanā vuccatī”ti (pārā. 237). Sā cāyaṃ tassa sukkassa ṭhānā cāvanā rāgavasena. Vuttañhetaṃ [V 0.0211] kathāvatthuaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “sukkavissaṭṭhi nāma rāgasamuṭṭhānā hotī”ti (kathā. aṭṭha. 307). Aññatra supinantāti supino eva supinanto, taṃ ṭhapetvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tenāha “yā supine”tiādi. Saṅghādisesoti imassa āpattinikāyassa nāmaṃ. Tenāha “yā aññatra supinantā”tiādi. Āpattinikāyoti āpattisamūho. Kiñcāpi ayaṃ ekāva āpatti, ruḷhisaddena, pana avayave samūhavohārena vā “nikāyo”ti vutto “eko vedanākkhandho, eko viññāṇakkhandho”tiādīsu viya.

And here, by the phrase ‘due to the support of lust, etc.,’ the time is shown. For it is at such times as when there is stiffening due to lust that the generative organ becomes workable. When it has become workable, one emits; apart from this there is no other time. For without stiffening due to lust and so on, divisions of time such as morning are not the cause for emission. By the phrase ‘for the sake of health, etc.,’ the intention is shown. For one emits with such a distinction of intention, not otherwise. By the phrase ‘in internal form, etc.,’ the means is shown. For one might emit in relation to an internal form, or an external form, or both, or by shaking the hips in space; apart from these there is no other means. By the ten phrases beginning with ‘by way of blue, etc.,’ the object of the ninth intention, that of testing the seed, is shown. For one who is testing does so by way of one or another of these, such as blue; he is not separate from them. By the phrase ‘falling from its place,’ emission is shown in its meaning. As it is said: ‘Emission is called falling from its place.’ And this falling of that semen from its place is due to lust. For it is stated in the Kathāvatthu Commentary: ‘The emission of semen, it is said, is rooted in lust.’ ‘Except in a dream’: a dream itself is a ‘supinanta’; ‘excluding that’ is what is meant. Thus he says, ‘that which is in a dream,’ etc. ‘Saṅghādisesa’ is the name of this class of offenses. Thus he says, ‘that which is other than in a dream,’ etc. ‘Class of offenses’ means a collection of offenses. Although this is a single offense, it is called a ‘class’ by a conventional term or by using a collective term for a part, as in such cases as ‘the one feeling aggregate’ and ‘the one consciousness aggregate.’

Assāti (sārattha. ṭī. 2.16 saṃghādisesakaṇḍa) āpattinikāyassa. Nanu ca ayuttoyaṃ niddeso “saṅgho ādimhi ceva sese ca icchitabbo assā”ti. Na hi āpattinikāyassa ādimhi ceva sese ca saṅgho icchito, kiñcarahi vuṭṭhānassāti imaṃ codanaṃ manasi nidhāya yathā na virujjhati, tathā adhippāyaṃ vivarituṃ “kiṃ vuttaṃ hotī”tiādimāha. Āpattito vuṭṭhānassa ādimhi ceva sese ca icchito saṅgho āpattiyāva icchito nāma hotīti ayamettha adhippāyo. Āpattivuṭṭhānanti āpattito vuṭṭhānaṃ, anāpattikabhāvūpagamananti attho.

‘Assā’ refers to this class of offenses. But is not this explanation unsuitable: ‘For it, the Saṅgha is required at the beginning and at the remainder’? For the Saṅgha is not required for the class of offenses at the beginning and at the remainder, but rather for the rehabilitation. Keeping this objection in mind, in order that there be no contradiction, to clarify the intention he says, ‘What is meant?’ and so on. The intention here is this: the Saṅgha that is required at the beginning and at the remainder for rehabilitation from the offense is, in fact, required on account of the offense itself. ‘Rehabilitation from the offense’ means rising up from the offense; the meaning is the attainment of a state of being without an offense.

Dakasotanti passāvamaggaṃ, aṅgajātappadesanti vuttaṃ hoti. Yadi evaṃ atha kasmā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “dakasotaṃ otiṇṇamatte”ti vuttanti āha “ṭhānato pana cuta”ntiādi. Avassameva dakasotaṃ otarati adhivāsetvā antarā nivāretuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā. Dakasotorohanato (sārattha. ṭī. 2.236-237) paṭṭhāya pana upādinnato vinimuttattā sambhavarūpaṃ utusamuṭṭhānameva avasissati, sesaṃ tisamuṭṭhānaṃ natthīti veditabbaṃ. Tasmāti yasmā ṭhānato cutaṃ dakasotaṃ otarati, tasmā.

‘The water-channel’ means the urinary passage; it is said to be the region of the generative organ. If so, why then is it said in the Commentary, ‘as soon as it has descended into the water-channel’? He says, ‘but having fallen from its place,’ etc. It inevitably descends into the water-channel because one is unable to endure and prevent it midway. But from its descent into the water-channel onwards, because it is freed from what is clung-to, only the material form of the semen originated by temperature remains; it should be understood that what is originated from the other three sources is no longer present. ‘Therefore’ means: because what has fallen from its place descends into the water-channel, for that reason.

Amocanādhippāyassāti bhesajjena nimittaṃ ālimpantassa uccārādīni vā karontassa. Supinaṃ passantassāti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.237) dhātukkhobhato vā anubhūtapubbato vā devatopasaṃhārato vā pubbanimittato vāti imehi catūhi kāraṇehi supinaṃ passantassa. Kiṃ panetaṃ passanto sutto passati, paṭibuddho, udāhu neva sutto, na paṭibuddhoti? Kiñcettha – yadi [M 0.0228] tāva sutto passati, abhidhammavirodho āpajjati. Bhavaṅgacittena hi supati, taṃ rūpanimittādiārammaṇaṃ vā rāgādisampayuttaṃ vā na hoti. Supinaṃ passantassa ca īdisāni cittāni uppajjanti. Atha paṭibuddho passati, vinayavirodho āpajjati. Yañhi paṭibuddho passati, taṃ sabbohārikacittena passati. Sabbohārikacittena ca kate vītikkame anāpatti nāma [V 0.0212] natthi. Supinaṃ passantena pana katepi vītikkame ekantaṃ anāpatti eva. Atha neva sutto na paṭibuddho passati, ko nāma passati, evañca sati supinassa abhāvova āpajjatīti? Na abhāvo, kasmā? Yasmā kapimiddhapareto passati. Vuttañhetaṃ “kapimiddhapareto kho mahārāja supinaṃ passatī”ti (mi. pa. 5.3.5). Kapimiddhaparetoti makkaṭaniddāya yutto. Yathā hi makkaṭassa niddā lahuparivattā hoti, evaṃ yā niddā punappunaṃ kusalādicittavokiṇṇattā lahuparivattā, yassā pavattiyaṃ punappunaṃ bhavaṅgato uttaraṇaṃ hoti, tāya yutto supinaṃ passati. Yassa ca evaṃ passantassa supine methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevantassa viya, kāyasaṃsaggādīni āpajjantassa viya ca supinanteneva kāraṇena asuci muccati, tassapi anāpatti. Supine (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.262) pana uppannāya assādacetanāya sacassa visayo hoti, niccalena bhavitabbaṃ, na hatthena nimittaṃ kīḷāpetabbaṃ. Kāsāvapaccattharaṇarakkhaṇatthaṃ pana hatthapuṭena gahetvā jagganatthāya udakaṭṭhānaṃ gantuṃ vaṭṭati.

With the intention of not releasing: this refers to one applying medicine to the organ or while urinating, etc. For one seeing a dream: this means for one seeing a dream due to one of these four causes: a disturbance of the elements, a previous experience, an intervention by a deity, or a premonitory sign. Now, does one see this while asleep, while awake, or while neither asleep nor awake? Herein, if one sees it while asleep, a contradiction with the Abhidhamma arises. For one sleeps with the life-continuum consciousness, which does not take a form-sign, etc., as its object, nor is it associated with lust, etc. But for one seeing a dream, such states of mind arise. If one sees it while awake, a contradiction with the Vinaya arises. For what one sees while awake, one sees with the fully active consciousness, and when a transgression is committed with the fully active consciousness, there is no such thing as no offense. But when a transgression is committed by one seeing a dream, there is definitely no offense. If one sees it while neither asleep nor awake, then who sees it? And if so, would it not follow that the dream is nonexistent? It is not nonexistent. Why? Because one sees it when overcome by 'monkey-sleep.' For it is said: 'Great king, one sees a dream when overcome by monkey-sleep.' 'Overcome by monkey-sleep' means endowed with a monkey's sleep. For just as a monkey's sleep is light and easily broken, so too one sees a dream when endowed with that sleep which, because it is repeatedly interspersed with wholesome and other kinds of consciousness, is light and easily broken, during the course of which there is repeated emergence from the life-continuum. For one who, while seeing a dream in this way, acts as if engaging in sexual intercourse or as if committing bodily contact, etc., and emits semen for the sole reason of the dream, for him, too, there is no offense. However, if in a dream a consciousness of enjoyment arises, one should be still regarding the object itself; one should not manipulate the organ with the hand. But for the sake of protecting the ochre robe and the ground-covering, it is permissible to catch it in the cup of one's hands and go to a place with water in order to wake up.

Sukkavissaṭṭhisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on the emission of semen is finished.

2. Kāyasaṃsaggasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Training Rule on Bodily Contact

“Otiṇṇo”ti (sārattha. ṭī. 2.270) idaṃ kammasādhanaṃ, kattusādhanaṃ vā hotīti tadubhayavasena atthaṃ dassento “yakkhādīhi viya sattā”tiādimāha. Asamapekkhitvāti yathāsabhāvaṃ anupaparikkhitvā, yathā te ratijanakā rūpādayo visayā aniccadukkhāsubhānattākārena avaṭṭhitā, tathā apassitvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Pariṇatenāti parivattena. Tenāha “yathā parivattamāna”ntiādi. Vuttarāgavasenāti kāyasaṃsaggarāgavasena. Tadahujātāyapīti tasmiṃ ahani jātaṃ jananaṃ etissāti [M 0.0229] tadahujātā, tasmiṃ ahani jātāti vā tadahujātā, tāya, taṃ divasaṃ jātāyapīti attho, jātamattāya allamaṃsapesivaṇṇāyapīti vuttaṃ hoti.

Otiṇṇo (overcome): this word can be derived in the sense of the action or in the sense of the agent. Showing the meaning in both ways, he says: 'like beings such as yakkhas,' etc. Without having regard for means without investigating their intrinsic nature; that is, it means not seeing how those sense objects that arouse delight, such as forms, are established in the modes of impermanence, suffering, foulness, and not-self. By one that is transformed means by one that is altered. Hence he says: 'as when transforming,' etc. Through the power of the aforesaid lust means through the power of lust for bodily contact. Even for one born on that very day: this means for one for whom birth occurred on that day, or one born on that day; the meaning is, even for one born on that very day, that is, for one just born, having the color of a lump of moist flesh.

Assāti “kāyasaṃsaggaṃ samāpajjeyyā”ti padassa. Idāni hatthādīnaṃ vibhāgadassanatthaṃ “tattha hattho nāma kapparato paṭṭhāyā”tiādimāha. Kapparato paṭṭhāyāti dutiyamahāsandhiṃ upādāya. Aññattha pana maṇibandhato paṭṭhāya yāva agganakhā hattho. Vinandhitvā vā avinandhitvā vā katakesakalāpassetaṃ adhivacananti sambandho. Tattha vinandhitvāti tīhi kesavaṭṭīhi [V 0.0213] ganthitvā. Suvaṇṇacīrakanti suvaṇṇapāḷiṃ. Hatthañca veṇiñca ṭhapetvā avasesasarīraṃ aṅganti āha “avasesassa sarīrassā”tiādi.

Of this: this refers to the phrase 'should engage in bodily contact.' Now, to show the division of the hand, etc., he says: 'Therein, the hand is from the elbow onwards,' etc. From the elbow onwards means from the second major joint. Elsewhere, however, the hand is from the wrist up to the tips of the fingernails. The connection is: this is a designation for an arranged mass of hair, whether plaited or not plaited. Therein, plaited means tied with three strands of hair. A golden strip means a golden fillet. Excluding the hand and the braid, the rest of the body is a 'limb'; thus he says: 'of the remaining body,' etc.

Yo hi sevanādhippāyopi niccalena kāyena kevalaṃ phassaṃ paṭivijānāti sādiyati anubhoti, tassa cittuppādamatte āpattiyā abhāvato anāpattīti āha “kāyena avāyamitvā”tiādi. Mokkhādhippāyenāti itthito muccitukāmatādhippāyena. Asañciccāti “iminā upāyena imaṃ phusissāmī”ti acetetvā. Evañhi acetetvā pattappaṭiggahaṇādīsu mātugāmassa aṅge phuṭṭhepi anāpatti. Asatiyāti aññavihito hoti, “mātugāmaṃ phusissāmī”ti sati natthi, evaṃ asatiyā hatthapādapasāraṇādikāle phusantassa anāpatti. Ajānantassāti dārakavesena ṭhitaṃ dārikaṃ “itthī”ti ajānanto kenacideva karaṇīyena phusati, evaṃ “itthī”ti ajānantassa phusato anāpatti. Asādiyantassāti kāyasaṃsaggaṃ asādiyantassa bāhāparamparāya nītabhikkhussa viya anāpatti. Idha pana udāyitthero ādikammiko. Tassa anāpatti ādikammikassāti.

For one who, though having the intention to indulge, merely feels, consents to, and experiences the contact with an unmoving body, there is no offense because there is no offense in a mere arising of consciousness. Thus he says: 'without making an effort with the body,' etc. With the intention of release means with the intention of wishing to be freed from a woman. Unintentionally means without having intended, 'By this means I will touch her.' For if one touches a woman's limb without such an intention while receiving a bowl and so on, there is no offense. Through lack of mindfulness means one is distracted, there is no mindfulness, 'I will touch a woman.' Thus for one who touches through lack of mindfulness while stretching out his hands and feet, there is no offense. For one who does not know means one touches a girl standing in the guise of a boy for some reason, not knowing she is a woman. Thus for one who touches without knowing she is a woman, there is no offense. For one not consenting means there is no offense for one who does not consent to the bodily contact, like a bhikkhu being led away arm-in-arm. Here, however, the Elder Udāyī was the originator of the case. For him, there is no offense means for the originator of the case.

Kāyasaṃsaggasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on bodily contact is finished.

3. Duṭṭhullavācāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Training Rule on Offensive Speech

Duṭṭhullavācassādarāgavasenāti duṭṭhullā vācā duṭṭhullavācā, tāya assādacetanā duṭṭhullavācassādo, tena sampayuttarāgavasena. Etthādhippetaṃ [M 0.0230] mātugāmaṃ dassetuṃ “mātugāma”ntiādimāha. Duṭṭhullāduṭṭhullasaṃlakkhaṇasamatthanti asaddhammasaddhammappaṭisaṃyuttaṃ kathaṃ jānituṃ samatthaṃ. Yā pana mahallikāpi bālā eḷamūgā, ayaṃ idhānadhippetā. Vaṇṇo nāma dve magge uddissa “itthilakkhaṇena subhalakkhaṇena samannāgatāsī”tiādinā (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.285) thomanā. Avaṇṇo nāma dve magge uddissa vuttavipariyāyena garahanā, “itthilakkhaṇena subhalakkhaṇena asamannāgatāsī”tiādīhi khuṃsanāti vuttaṃ hoti. Yācanā nāma “dehi me, arahasi me dātu”nti (pārā. 285) vacanaṃ. Āyācanā nāma “kadā te mātā pasīdissati, kadā te pitā pasīdissati, kadā te devatāyo pasīdissanti, kadā te sukhaṇo sulayo sumuhutto bhavissati, kadā te methunaṃ dhammaṃ labhissāmī”ti (pārā. 285) vacanaṃ[V 0.0214]. Pucchanaṃ nāma “kathaṃ tvaṃ sāmikassa desi, kathaṃ jārassa desī”ti (pārā. 285) vacanaṃ. Paṭipucchanaṃ nāma “evaṃ kira tvaṃ sāmikassa deti, evaṃ jārassa desī”ti (pārā. 285) vacanaṃ. Ācikkhanaṃ nāma puṭṭhassa “evaṃ dehi, evaṃ dentā sāmikassa piyā bhavissasi, manāpā cā”ti (pārā. 285) bhaṇanaṃ. Anusāsanaṃ nāma apuṭṭhassa “evaṃ dehi, evaṃ dentā sāmikassa piyā bhavissasi, manāpā cā”ti (pārā. 285) bhavanaṃ. Akkosanaṃ (pārā. 285) nāma “animittāsi, nimittamattāsi, alohitāsi, dhuvalohitāsi, dhuvacoḷāsi, paggharantīsi, sikharaṇīsi, itthipaṇḍakāsi, vepurisikāsi, sambhinnāsi, ubhatobyañjanakāsī”ti (pārā. 285) vacanaṃ. Yasmā methunupasaṃhitāya vācāya adhikaṃ duṭṭhullaṃ nāma natthi, tasmā “methunupasaṃhitāhī”ti idaṃ duṭṭhullavācāya sikhāpattalakkhaṇadassananti vuttaṃ, na pana methunupasaṃhitāyeva duṭṭhullavācattā. Sikharaṇīsīti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.285) bahinikkhantaāṇimaṃsā. Sambhinnāsīti sambhinnavaccamaggapassāvamaggā. Ubhatobyañjanakāsīti purisanimittena, itthinimittena cāti ubhatobyañjanehi samannāgatā.

‘By the power of lust for the delight in indecent speech’ means: indecent speech is duṭṭhullavācā; the volition of delight in it is duṭṭhullavācassādo; by the power of lust associated with that. Here, to indicate a woman, it is said, “woman,” and so on. “Capable of recognizing what is indecent and what is not” means able to distinguish between speech connected with the false Dhamma and the true Dhamma. Even an elderly woman who is foolish, deaf, and mute is not intended here. Praise (vaṇṇo) refers to extolling concerning the two paths, saying, “You are endowed with feminine characteristics and auspicious marks,” and so on. Disparagement (avaṇṇo) refers to the opposite, condemning with statements like, “You are devoid of feminine characteristics and auspicious marks,” and so forth; that is to say, denigrating. Requesting (yācanā) means saying, “Give to me; you should give to me.” Pleading (āyācanā) means saying, “When will your mother be pleased? When will your father be pleased? When will the deities be pleased? When will there be a favorable time, a lucky moment, a good instant for you? When will I obtain sexual intercourse?” Questioning (pucchanaṃ) means saying, “How do you give to your husband? How do you give to your lover?” Counter-questioning (paṭipucchanaṃ) means saying, “Is it true that you give to your husband like this, that you give to your lover like this?” Informing (ācikkhanaṃ) means telling one who has been asked, “Give like this; by giving like this, you will become dear and pleasing to your husband.” Instructing (anusāsanaṃ) means telling one who has not been asked, “Give like this; by giving like this, you will become dear and pleasing to your husband.” Reviling (akkosanaṃ) means saying, “You are without a mark, you are only a mark, you are bloodless, you are ever bloody, you are ever ragged, you are oozing, you are a sikharaṇī, you are a female eunuch, you are a mannish woman, you are a sambhinnā, you are an ubhatobyañjanakā.” Because there is nothing more indecent than speech connected with sexual intercourse, therefore, the statement “connected with sexual intercourse” is made to show the characteristic of indecent speech that has reached its peak, but it is not the case that only speech connected with sexual intercourse is indecent. Sikharaṇī means one whose inner flesh protrudes. Sambhinnā means one whose anal and urinary passages are joined. Ubhatobyañjanakā means one endowed with both male and female characteristics.

Ettha ca vaṇṇabhaṇane tāva “itthilakkhaṇena subhalakkhaṇena samannāgatāsī”ti vadati, na tāva sīsaṃ eti. “Tava vaccamaggo ca passāvamaggo ca subho subhasaṇṭhāno dassanīyo, īdisena nāma itthilakkhaṇena subhalakkhaṇena samannāgatāsī”ti vadati, sīsaṃ eti, saṅghādiseso hotīti attho.

Here, in speaking of praise, when one says, “You are endowed with the characteristics of a woman, with auspicious marks,” it does not yet reach the peak. But when one says, “Your anal passage and urinary passage are beautiful, well-formed, and pleasing to behold—you are endowed with such characteristics of a woman, with such auspicious marks,” then it reaches the peak; the meaning is that it becomes a Saṅghādisesa offense.

Avaṇṇabhaṇane [M 0.0231] pana “animittāsī”tiādīhi ekādasahi padehi avaṇṇe aghaṭite sīsaṃ na eti, ghaṭitepi tesu “sikharaṇīsi sambhinnāsi ubhatobyañjanakāsī”ti imehi tīhi ghaṭiteyeva saṅghādiseso.

In speaking of disparagement, however, with the eleven phrases beginning with ‘You are without a mark,’ if the disparagement is unconnected, it does not reach the peak. Even when connected, among them, it is a Saṅghādisesa only with these three: ‘You are a sikharaṇī, you are a sambhinnā, you are an ubhatobyañjanakā.’

Yācanāyapi “dehi me”ti ettakeneva sīsaṃ na eti, “methunaṃ dhammaṃ dehī”ti evaṃ methunadhammena ghaṭite eva saṅghādiseso.

In requesting, too, merely saying, “Give me,” does not reach the peak. Only when it is connected with sexual intercourse, as in, “Give me sexual intercourse,” is it a Saṅghādisesa.

“Kadā te mātā pasīdissatī”tiādīsu āyācanavacanesupi ettakeneva sīsaṃ na eti, “kadā te mātā pasīdissati, kadā te methunaṃ dhammaṃ labhissāmī”ti vā “tava mātari pasannāya vā methunaṃ dhammaṃ labhissāmī”tiādinā pana nayena methunadhammena ghaṭiteyeva saṅghādiseso.

In words of pleading, too, such as, “When will your mother be pleased?” it does not reach the peak with just that much. But only when it is connected with sexual intercourse, by way of saying, “When will your mother be pleased? When will I obtain sexual intercourse?” or, “When your mother is pleased, I will obtain sexual intercourse,” and so on, is it a Saṅghādisesa.

“Kathaṃ tvaṃ sāmikassa desī”tiādīsu (pārā. 285) pucchāvacanesupi “methunaṃ dhamma”nti [V 0.0215] vutteyeva saṅghādiseso. “Evaṃ kira tvaṃ sāmikassa desī”ti (pārā. 285) paṭipucchāvacanesupi eseva nayo.

In words of questioning, too, such as, “How do you give to your husband?” it is a Saṅghādisesa only when “sexual intercourse” is said. This same principle applies to words of counter-questioning, such as, “Is it true that you give to your husband in this way?”

Ācikkhanāya ca “evaṃ dehī”ti, “evaṃ dadamānā”ti vuttepi sīsaṃ na eti, “methunaṃ dhammaṃ evaṃ dehi, evaṃ upanehi, evaṃ methunaṃ dhammaṃ dadamānā upanayamānā sāmikassa piyā hotī”tiādinā pana nayena methunadhammena ghaṭiteyeva saṅghādiseso. Anusāsanivacanesupi eseva nayo.

And in informing, even when one says, “Give in this way,” or, “Giving in this way,” it does not reach the peak. But it is a Saṅghādisesa only when connected with sexual intercourse, by way of saying, “Give sexual intercourse in this way, offer it in this way; by giving and offering sexual intercourse in this way, you become dear to your husband,” and so on. This same principle applies to words of instruction.

Akkosavacanesu pana ekādasasu “sikharaṇīsi sambhinnāsi ubhatobyañjanakāsī”ti imāni tīṇiyeva padāni suddhāni sīsaṃ enti, iti imāni ca tīṇi, purimāni ca vaccamaggapassāvamaggamethunadhammapadāni tīṇīti cha padāni suddhāni āpattikarāni, sesāni “animittāsī”tiādīni animitte “methunaṃ dhammaṃ me dehī”ti vā “animittāsi, methunaṃ dhammaṃ me dehī”ti vā ādinā nayena methunadhammena ghaṭitāneva āpattikarāni hontīti veditabbāni.

In words of reviling, however, among the eleven phrases, only these three—‘You are a sikharaṇī, you are a sambhinnā, you are an ubhatobyañjanakā’—reach the peak by themselves. Thus, these three, along with the previous three phrases related to the anal passage, urinary passage, and sexual intercourse, make six phrases that are offense-making in themselves. The remaining phrases, such as ‘You are without a mark,’ should be understood to be offense-making only when connected with sexual intercourse, by way of saying, for instance, ‘Give me sexual intercourse,’ or ‘You are without a mark; give me sexual intercourse,’ and so on.

Adhakkhakanti akkhakato paṭṭhāya adho. Ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalanti jāṇumaṇḍalato paṭṭhāya uddhaṃ. Ubbhakkhakanti akkhakato paṭṭhāya uddhaṃ. Adhojāṇumaṇḍalanti jāṇumaṇḍalato paṭṭhāya adho. Akkhakaṃ, pana jāṇumaṇḍalañca ettheva dukkaṭakhette saṅgahaṃ gacchati bhikkhuniyā kāyasaṃsagge viya[M 0.0232]. Na hi buddhā garukāpattiṃ sāvasesaṃ paññāpentīti. Kāyappaṭibaddhanti vatthaṃ vā pupphaṃ vā ābharaṇaṃ vā.

‘Below the collarbone’ means downward, starting from the collarbone. ‘Above the knee-circle’ means upward, starting from the knee-circle. ‘Above the collarbone’ means upward, starting from the collarbone. ‘Below the knee-circle’ means downward, starting from the knee-circle. The collarbone and the knee-circle, however, are included here in the area of a Dukkaṭa offense, as in the case of bodily contact with a bhikkhunī. For the Buddhas do not prescribe a grave offense that leaves a remainder. ‘Bound to the body’ means a cloth, a flower, or an ornament.

Atthadhammaanusāsanipurekkhārānanti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.287) ettha “animittā”tiādīnaṃ padānaṃ atthaṃ kathento, aṭṭhakathaṃ vā sajjhāyaṃ karonto atthapurekkhāro nāma, pāḷiṃ vācento, sajjhāyaṃ vā karonto dhammapurekkhāro nāma, “idānipi animittāsi, ubhatobyañjanakāsi, appamādaṃ dāni kareyyāsi, yathā āyatimpi evarūpā mā hohisī”ti bhaṇanto anusāsanipurekkhāro nāma. Iti atthañca dhammañca anusāsaniñca purakkhitvā bhaṇantānaṃ anāpatti. Yo pana bhikkhunīnaṃ pāḷiṃ vācento pakativācanāmaggaṃ pahāya hasanto hasanto “sikharaṇīsi, sambhinnāsi, ubhatobyañjanakāsī”ti punappunaṃ bhaṇati, tassa āpattiyeva. Idha ādikammiko udāyitthero, tassa anāpatti ādikammikassa. Nanu “sikharaṇī”tiādīhi akkosantassa paṭighacittaṃ uppajjatīti dukkhavedanāyapi bhavitabbaṃ, atha [V 0.0216] kasmā dvivedananti? Nāyaṃ doso. Rāgavasena hi ayaṃ āpatti, na paṭighavasena, tasmā rāgavaseneva pavatto akkoso idhādhippeto, na paṭighavasenāpīti.

Regarding ‘those who prioritize meaning, Dhamma, and instruction’: Here, one who explains the meaning of words such as ‘animittā,’ or who recites the commentary, is called one who prioritizes meaning. One who teaches the Pāli text, or who recites it, is called one who prioritizes the Dhamma. One who says, ‘Now you are without a mark, you are an ubhatobyañjanakā; you should now be heedful, so that in the future you will not be of such a kind,’ is called one who prioritizes instruction. Thus, for those who speak prioritizing meaning, Dhamma, and instruction, there is no offense. But if a monk, while teaching the Pāli text to bhikkhunīs, abandons the normal way of recitation and, laughing repeatedly, says, ‘You are a sikharaṇī, you are a sambhinnā, you are an ubhatobyañjanakā,’ for him there is an offense. Here, the first offender was the Elder Udāyi; for him, as the first offender, there was no offense. But is it not the case that for one who reviles with words like ‘sikharaṇī,’ a mind of aversion arises, and so there should also be painful feeling? Why then is it said to be with two feelings? This is not a fault. For this offense is due to lust, not aversion. Therefore, the reviling intended here is that which proceeds from lust, not also that which proceeds from aversion.

Duṭṭhullavācāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on indecent speech is concluded.

4. Attakāmasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. Explanation of the Training Rule on Self-serving Desire

Attakāmapāricariyāvasenāti attakāmapāricariyāya rāgavasena. Idhāpi duṭṭhullāduṭṭhullajānanasamatthāva itthī adhippetāti āha “duṭṭhullobhāsena vuttappakārāya itthiyā”ti. Samīpeti savanūpacāre. “Ṭhatvā”ti pāṭhaseso. Attakāmapāricariyāti kāmīyatīti kāmo, methunadhammo, paricaraṇaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ paricariyā, sāva pāricariyā, kāmena pāricariyā kāmapāricariyā, attano kāmapāricariyā attakāmapāricariyā, attano atthāya methunadhammena upaṭṭhānanti attho. Atha vā kāmitāti kāmā, pāricariyā, attano kāmā attakāmā, attakāmā ca sā pāricariyā cāti attakāmapāricariyā, sayaṃ methunarāgavasena [M 0.0233] patthitaupaṭṭhānanti attho. Tenāha “methunadhammasaṅkhātenā”tiādi. Ettha ca paṭhamena atthavikappena kāmahetupāricariyāsaṅkhātaṃ atthattayaṃ dasseti, dutiyena adhippāyapāricariyāsaṅkhātaṃ atthadvayaṃ. Byañjane (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.291) pana ādaraṃ akatvā atthamattameva dassetuṃ “attano kāmaṃ attano hetuṃ attano adhippāyaṃ attano pāricariya”nti (pārā. 292) padabhājanaṃ vuttaṃ. “Attano kāmaṃ attano hetuṃ attano pāricariya”nti hi vutte jānissanti paṇḍitā “ettāvatā attano atthāya kāmapāricariyā vuttā”ti, “attano adhippāyaṃ attano pāricariya”nti (pārā. 292) vuttepi jānissanti “ettāvatā attanā icchitakāmitaṭṭhena attakāmapāricariyā vuttā”ti.

'By way of service for one's own desire' means by way of lust for service for one's own desire. Here too, a woman capable of understanding what is lewd and not lewd is intended, hence it is said: 'by lewd speech, to a woman of the kind described.' 'In the vicinity' means within earshot. 'Having stood' is the rest of the text. 'Service for one's own desire' means: what is desired is desire (kāma), the sexual act; attending is serving, that itself is service; serving with desire is desire-service; serving one's own desires is service for one's own desire—the meaning is attending for one's own benefit through the act of sexual intercourse. Alternatively, what is desired is desire, service is serving; one's own desires are one's own desires, and that service is service for one's own desire—the meaning is attendance, sought out by one's own lust for intercourse. Hence it is said: 'designated as the act of sexual intercourse,' etc. Here, with the first interpretation, it shows three meanings, designated as 'service caused by desire'; with the second, two meanings, designated as 'service according to intention.' In the commentary (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.291), however, without paying attention to the wording, only the meaning is shown: 'one's own desire, one's own reason, one's own intention, one's own service' (Pārā. 292), the division of words is stated. For if it is said: 'one's own desire, one's own reason, one's own service,' the wise will understand: 'to this extent, service with desire for one's own benefit is stated.' And if it is said: 'one's own intention, one's own service' (Pārā. 292), they will understand: 'to this extent, service for one's own desire, in the sense of desired by oneself, is stated.'

Kalyāṇena bhaddakena guṇena samannāgatattā kalyāṇadhammaṃ. Tenāha “tadubhayenāpī”tiādi. Abhirameyyāti toseyya. Etadagganti esā aggā. Pāricariyānanti pāricariyānaṃ majjhe, niddhāraṇe cetaṃ sāmivacanaṃ. Nanu duṭṭhallavācāsikkhāpade (pārā. 285) methunayācanaṃ āgataṃ, atha kasmā idaṃ vuttaṃ? Nāyaṃ doso. Tattha (sārattha. ṭī. 2.291) hi duṭṭhullavācassādarāgavasena vuttaṃ, idha pana attano methunassādarāgavasenāti.

Because it is endowed with a good, excellent quality, it is a 'good practice.' Hence he said, 'by both of them,' etc. 'One should take delight' means 'one should please.' 'This is the highest' means 'this is the best.' 'Of services' means 'among services'; this is a genitive of specification. Now, in the training rule on lewd speech (Pārā. 285), a request for sexual intercourse is mentioned—so why is this stated here? This is not a fault. For there (Sārattha. Ṭī. 2.291), it is said due to lustful fondness for lewd speech, but here it is due to lustful fondness for one's own sexual intercourse.

Tasmiṃyeva khaṇeti bhaṇitakkhaṇe. Ubhatobyañjanako pana paṇḍakagatikattā visuṃ na vutto[V 0.0217]. “Imasmiṃ sikkhāpadadvaye kāyasaṃsagge viya yakkhipetīsupi duṭṭhullattakāmavacane thullaccaya”nti (vajira. ṭī. pārājika 295) vadanti. Tasmiṃyevāti paṇḍakeyeva itthisaññino attakāmapāricariyāya vaṇṇabhaṇanepi dukkaṭaṃ. “Yo te vihāre vasati, tassa aggadānaṃ methunaṃ dhammaṃ dehī”ti pariyāyavacanepi dukkaṭaṃ. “Attakāmapāricariyāya vaṇṇaṃ bhāseyya yā mādisaṃ ‘sīlavanta’nti vuttattā”ti (vajira. ṭī. pārājika 295) eke. “Pañcasu aṅgesu sabbhāvā saṅghādisesovā”ti apare. “Methunupasaṃhitenā”ti vuttattā “cīvarādīhi…pe… bhāsantassa anāpattī”ti vuttaṃ.

'At that very moment' means at the moment of speaking. However, one with both sexual characteristics is not mentioned separately because they are included in the category of paṇḍaka. They say: 'In these two training rules, as in the case of physical contact, in the case of lewd speech and speech for one's own desire towards yakkhas and petas, there is a thullaccaya offense' (Vajira. Ṭī. Pārājika 295). Regarding 'at that very moment': for a paṇḍaka who perceives himself as a woman, there is a dukkaṭa offense even for praising service for one's own desire. Even in indirect speech such as, 'Give the highest gift, the sexual act, to the one who dwells in your monastery,' there is a dukkaṭa offense. Some say: '[It is an offense] because it is said, "One might speak in praise of service for one's own desire to a woman who regards one like me as virtuous"' (Vajira. Ṭī. Pārājika 295). Others say: 'If the five factors are present, it is a Saṅghādisesa offense.' Because it is stated 'connected with sexual intercourse,' it is said: 'for one speaking about robes, etc. ... there is no offense.'

Attakāmasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning one's own desire is concluded.

5. Sañcarittasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

5. Explanation of the Training Rule on Acting as a Go-between

Sañcaraṇaṃ [M 0.0234] sañcaro, so etassa atthīti sañcarī, sañcaraṇasīloti vā sañcarī, tassa bhāvo sañcarittaṃ, sañcaraṇanti attho. Tañca parato “itthiyā vā purisamati”ntiādivacanato itthipurisānaṃ vemajjheti āha “itthipurisānaṃ antare sañcaraṇabhāva”nti. Paṭiggaṇhanavīmaṃsanapaccāharaṇānīti ettha paṭiggaṇhanaṃ nāma purisena vā itthiyā vā ubhinnaṃ mātādīhi vā “bhante, itthannāmaṃ itthiṃ vā purisaṃ vā evaṃ bhaṇāhī”ti vutte tesaṃ vacanaṃ “sādhū”ti vā “hotū”ti vā “bhaṇāmī”ti vā yena kenaci ākārena vacībhedaṃ katvā, sīsakampanādīhi vā sampaṭicchanaṃ. Vīmaṃsanaṃ nāma vuttappakārena sāsanaṃ gahetvā tassā itthiyā vā purisassa vā tesaṃ avassaṃ ārocanakānaṃ mātāpitubhātābhaginiādīnaṃ vā santikaṃ gantvā tassa sāsanassa ārocanaṃ. Paccāharaṇaṃ nāma tena gantvā ārocite sā itthī vā puriso vā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchatu vā, mā vā, lajjāya vā tuṇhī hotu, puna āgantvā tassā itthiyā vā purisassa vā tassā pavattiyā ārocanaṃ. Āpajjeyyāti paṭipajjeyya.

Going between (sañcaraṇa) is sañcara; one who does this is a sañcarī (go-between); or one whose nature is to go between is a sañcarī; the state of that is sañcarittaṃ, meaning the act of going between. And that, from the subsequent statement 'a woman's intention towards a man,' etc., is being in the middle of women and men, thus he says 'the state of going between women and men.' 'Accepting, conveying, and reporting back': here, 'accepting' is when a man or a woman, or the parents, etc., of both, say: 'Venerable sir, speak thus to such-and-such a woman or man,' and one assents to their words by saying 'Good,' or 'So be it,' or 'I will speak,' or by making some verbal utterance, or by nodding the head, etc. 'Conveying' is, having accepted the message in the way described, going to that woman or man, or to their parents, brother, sister, etc., who must be informed, and announcing that message. 'Reporting back' is, after one has gone and announced it, whether that woman or man accepts it saying 'Good' or not, or remains silent out of shame, one returns and reports that event to the first woman or man. 'He would incur' means he would engage in.

Itthiyā vā purisamatiṃ purisassa vā itthimatinti ettha “āroceyyā”ti pāṭhaseso daṭṭhabbo. Tenevāha “tatthā”tiādi. Jāyābhāveti bhariyābhāve. Jārabhāveti patibhāve, nimittatthe cetaṃ bhummavacanaṃ. Tasmā bhariyābhāvanimittaṃ patibhāvanimittaṃ, bhariyābhāvahetu patibhāvahetu, bhariyābhāvapaccayā patibhāvapaccayā ārocetīti attho. Esa nayo “jāyattane ārocetī”tiādīsupi. “Jāyattane vā jārattane vā”ti hi idaṃ yadatthaṃ taṃ tesaṃ matiṃ āroceti[V 0.0218], taṃ dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Idāni pana padabhājaniyaṃ (pārā. 302) vuttanayenāpi atthaṃ dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādimāha. Kiñcāpi itthiliṅgavasena padabhājaniyaṃ vuttaṃ, “jāyattane vā jārattane vā”ti pana niddesassa ubhayaliṅgasādhāraṇattā purisaliṅgavasenāpi yojetvā vattabbanti āha “eteneva upāyenā”tiādi. Muhuttikāti gaṇikā. “Antamaso taṅkhaṇikāyapī”ti idaṃ nidassanamattanti āha “eteneva upāyenā”tiādi.

In the phrase 'a woman's intention towards a man or a man's intention towards a woman,' the rest of the text, 'he should report,' should be understood. Hence he said, 'in that case,' etc. 'As a wife' means in the state of being a wife. 'As a paramour' means in the state of being a lover; this is a locative of purpose. Therefore, the meaning is: he reports for the purpose of her being a wife, for the purpose of his being a paramour; for the reason of her being a wife, for the reason of his being a paramour; on account of her being a wife, on account of his being a paramour. This same method applies to phrases like 'reports as a wife,' etc. For 'as a wife or as a paramour' is stated to show the purpose for which he reports their intention. Now, to show the meaning also according to the method of the word analysis (Pārā. 302), he said, 'moreover,' etc. Although the word analysis is given in the feminine gender, because the expression 'as a wife or as a paramour' is common to both genders, it should be construed and stated in the masculine gender as well; hence he said, 'by this very method,' etc. 'A temporary wife' means a courtesan. 'Even for a momentary one' is just an example; hence he said, 'by this very method,' etc.

Aññatra [M 0.0235] nālaṃvacanīyāyāti (sārattha. ṭī. 2.339-340) desacārittavasena paṇṇadānādinā apariccattaṃ ṭhapetvā. Sañcarittavasena bhikkhunā vacanīyā na hotīti nālaṃvacanīyā, taṃ ṭhapetvāti keci. Appena vā bahunā vā dhanena kītā dhanakkītā. Yasmā pana sā na kītamattāyeva bhariyā, saṃvāsatthāya pana kītattā bhariyā, tasmāssa niddese “dhanena kiṇitvā vāsetī”ti (pārā. 304) vuttaṃ. Chandavāsinīti chandena attano ruciyā vasatīti chandavāsinī. Yasmā pana sā na attano chandamatteneva bhariyā hoti, purisena pana sampaṭicchitattā, tasmāssa niddese “piyo piyaṃ vāsetī”ti (pārā. 304) vuttaṃ. Ādisaddena “bhogavāsinī, paṭavāsinī, odapattakinī, obhaṭacumbaṭā, dāsī ca bhariyā ca, kammakārī ca bhariyā ca, dhajāhaṭā, muhuttikā”ti (pārā. 304) imesaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ ākārānaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Yathā ca “chandavāsinī”tiādīsu aññataravasena vadato visaṅketo natthi, evaṃ pāḷiyaṃ avuttesupi “hohi kira itthannāmassa bhariyā, jāyā, pajāpati, puttamātā, gharaṇī, gharasāminī, bhattarandhikā, sussūsikā, paricārikā”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.305) evamādīsu saṃvāsaparidīpakesu vacanesu aññataravasena vadantassāpi visaṅketo natthi, tivaṅgasampattiyā āpattiyeva.

'Except for one who is unfit to be addressed' (Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā 2.339-340) means setting aside one not given up by way of local custom through the giving of a leaf, etc. Some say: she is 'unfit to be addressed' because she should not be addressed by a bhikkhu by way of acting as a go-between; setting that aside. 'Bought with wealth' means bought with little or much wealth. But since she is not a wife merely by being bought, but is a wife because she was bought for the purpose of cohabitation, it is therefore said in the explanation: 'having bought her with wealth, he cohabits with her' (Pārājika 304). 'One who cohabits by consent' means one who cohabits by her own wish and liking. But since she does not become a wife merely by her own consent, but because she is accepted by the man, it is therefore said in the explanation: 'a dear one cohabits with a dear one' (Pārājika 304). By the word 'etc.' the inclusion of these eight types is to be understood: 'a wife through wealth, a wife through clothing, a water-bowl wife, one with head-pad removed, a slave who is also a wife, a worker who is also a wife, one brought under the flag, and a temporary wife' (Pārājika 304). And just as there is no misunderstanding when one speaks in terms of any of these, such as 'one who cohabits by consent,' so too, even in cases not mentioned in the Pāli, there is no misunderstanding when one speaks in terms of any of these expressions that indicate cohabitation, such as: 'Be the wife of so-and-so, his spouse, his mate, the mother of his children, his housewife, the lady of his house, his cook, his attendant, his servant' (Pārājika-aṭṭhakathā 2.305); with the fulfillment of the three factors, there is an offense.

Māturakkhitaṃ brūhīti ettha māturakkhitā nāma mātarā rakkhitā, yathā purisena saha saṃvāsaṃ na kappeti, evaṃ mātarā rakkhitāti attho. Tenevassa padabhājanepi “mātā rakkhati gopeti, issariyaṃ kāreti, vasaṃ vattetī”ti (pārā. 304) vuttaṃ. Piturakkhitādīsūti “piturakkhitā, mātāpiturakkhitā, bhāturakkhitā, bhaginirakkhitā, ñātirakkhitā, gottarakkhitā, dhammarakkhitā, sārakkhā, saparidaṇḍā”ti (pārā. 303) evaṃ vuttesu piturakkhitādīsu. Yathā ca ettha, evaṃ “piturakkhitaṃ brūhī”tiādīsupi nayo veditabbo.

In the phrase 'Speak to one protected by her mother,' 'one protected by her mother' means one guarded by her mother; the meaning is that she is guarded by her mother so that she does not engage in cohabitation with a man. Hence in its word analysis it is said: 'The mother protects her, guards her, exercises authority over her, and keeps her under her control' (Pārājika 304). 'In the case of one protected by her father, etc.' refers to those mentioned as: 'one protected by her father, one protected by her mother and father, one protected by her brother, one protected by her sister, one protected by relatives, one protected by her clan, one protected by the Dhamma, one with a guardian, and one subject to punishment' (Pārājika 303). And as here, so too the method should be understood in cases such as 'Speak to one protected by her father,' etc.

Saṅghassa vā cetiyassa vā gilānassa vā kiccena gacchantassāti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.340) ettha bhikkhusaṅghassa uposathāgāraṃ vā kiñci vā vippakataṃ hoti. Tattha kārukānaṃ bhattavetanatthāya [V 0.0219] upāsako vā upāsikāya santikaṃ bhikkhuṃ pahiṇeyya, upāsikā vā upāsakassa, evarūpena saṅghakiccena gacchantassa anāpatti. Cetiyakamme kariyamānepi eseva nayo. Gilānassa [M 0.0236] bhesajjatthāyapi upāsakena vā upāsikāya santikaṃ, upāsikāya vā upāsakassa santikaṃ pahitassa gacchato anāpatti.

Regarding ‘going on business for the Saṅgha, or for a shrine, or for a sick person’ (Pārājika-aṭṭhakathā 2.340): Here, something belonging to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, such as an Uposatha hall, or anything else, is unfinished or damaged. There, for the purpose of food and wages for the workers, a layman may send a bhikkhu to a laywoman, or a laywoman to a layman. For one going on such business of the Saṅgha, there is no offense. The same principle applies when work is being done for a shrine. Also, for obtaining medicine for a sick person, if someone is sent by a layman to a laywoman, or by a laywoman to a layman, there is no offense for the one who goes.

Kiñcāpi ettha “itthī nāma manussitthī, na yakkhī na petī na tiracchānagatā. Puriso nāma manussapuriso, na yakkho”tiādi (sārattha. ṭī. 2.341) natthi, tathāpi manussajātikāva itthipurisā idha adhippetāti āha “tesaṃ manussajātikatā”ti. Nanālaṃvacanīyatāti yathāvuttanayena pariccattā alaṃvacanīyā. Nivāraṇattho hi ettha alaṃ-saddo. Na alaṃvacanīyā nālaṃvacanīyā, na nālaṃvacanīyā, tassā bhāvo nanālaṃvacanīyatā, “alaṃvacanīyatā”icceva vuttaṃ hoti.

Although here there is no statement such as ‘a woman means a human woman, not a female spirit, ghost, or animal; a man means a human man, not a male spirit,’ etc. (Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā 2.341), it is nevertheless human women and men that are intended here. Hence, it is said, ‘their being of human birth.’ Regarding the state of not being unfit to be addressed (`nanālaṃvacanīyatā`): this means that, according to the method described, one who is abandoned is fit to be addressed. For here the word `alaṃ` has the meaning of prevention. `Na alaṃvacanīyā` becomes `nālaṃvacanīyā` (unfit to be addressed). The negation of this, `na nālaṃvacanīyā`, means ‘not unfit to be addressed.’ The state of this is `nanālaṃvacanīyatā`, which is the same as saying `alaṃvacanīyatā`, ‘the state of being fit to be addressed.’

Paṇṇattinti, imaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ. Kāyavikārenāti sīsukkhipanādikāyavikārena. Tatheva vīmaṃsitvā tatheva paccāharantassāti hatthamuddādinā kāyavikārena vīmaṃsitvā puna āgantvā tatheva ārocentassa. Āgamissatīti tava santike dhammassavanādiatthaṃ āgamissati. Kenaci vutteti āsanasālādīsu nisinnassa kenaci purisena vutte. Sace hi khīṇāsavassa mātāpitaro kujjhitvā alaṃvacanīyā honti, tañca bhikkhuṃ gharaṃ upagataṃ pitā vadati “mātā te, tāta, maṃ mahallakaṃ chaḍḍetvā ñātikulaṃ gatā, gaccha naṃ maṃ upaṭṭhātuṃ pesehī”ti. So ce gantvā taṃ vatvā puna pituno tassā āgamanaṃ vā anāgamanaṃ vā āroceti, evaṃ ārocentassa tassapi kāyavācato samuṭṭhāti. Tenāha “paṇṇattiṃ ajānantassa panā”tiādi. Khīṇāsavassapīti ettha pi-saddena sekkhaputhujjanānaṃ vattabbameva natthīti dīpeti. Pituvacanenāti attano pituvacanena. Gantvāti tassā samīpaṃ gantvā. Paṇṇattiṃ, alaṃvacanīyabhāvañcāti ubhayaṃ ajānantassapi kāyavācato samuṭṭhāti. Tadubhayanti paṇṇattiṃ, alaṃvacanīyabhāvañca. Yaṃ pana paṇṇattiṃ jānitvā eteheva tīhi nayehi sañcarittaṃ samāpajjato kāyacittato, vācācittato, kāyavācācittato ca samuṭṭhāti. Imāni tīṇi paṇṇattijānanacittena “sacittakasamuṭṭhānānī”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ ayuttaṃ. Na hi paṇṇattiṃ jānitvāpi “nālaṃvacanīyā”ti maññamānassa sacittakehi samuṭṭhānehi āpatti samuṭṭhātīti vattuṃ yujjati vītikkamacetanāya asambhavato.

`Paṇṇatti` means this training rule. By bodily gesture: by a bodily gesture such as raising the head. Having investigated in the same way and reporting back in the same way: having investigated by a bodily gesture such as a hand signal, and then returning to report in the same way. He will come: he will come to your presence for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma, etc. Spoken by someone: when it is spoken by some man seated in a meeting hall, etc. For instance, if the parents of an arahant become angry and become a case to which the rule applies, and the father says to the bhikkhu who has come to the house, 'Dear son, your mother has abandoned me, an old man, and gone to her relatives’ house. Go and send her to attend to me,' and if he goes and says this and then reports back to his father whether she is coming or not, for one reporting in this way, the offense arises from his body and speech. Therefore, it is said, 'For one who does not know the rule,' etc. Even for an arahant: here the word 'even' indicates that there is nothing to be said for trainees and ordinary people. By the father’s words: by his own father’s words. Having gone: having gone near her. For one who does not know both the rule and the state of being fit to be addressed, the offense arises from body and speech. Both means the rule and the state of being fit to be addressed. But for one who knows the rule and engages as a go-between in these three ways, it arises from body and mind, speech and mind, and body, speech, and mind. It is said that these three are 'intentional arisings' because of the mind that knows the rule, but that is incorrect. For it is not right to say that for one who knows the rule but thinks, 'She is unfit to be addressed,' an offense arises from intentional arisings, because of the absence of an intention to transgress.

Sañcarittasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on acting as a go-between is finished.

6. Kuṭikārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. Explanation of the Training Rule on Building Huts

Saññācikāya [M 0.0237][V 0.0220] panāti ettha santi attavācako tatiyatthe nipāto, yācikāti bhāvasādhano, tesañca majjhepadalopasamāso. Panāti nipātamattameva. Tenāha “sayaṃ pavattitayācanā vuccatī”ti. Yā hi attanā pavattitā, sā attano nāma hotīti āha “tasmā”tiādi. Nanu na sakkā yācanāyeva kuṭiṃ kātunti anuyogaṃ sandhāya tassādhippāyatthaṃ dassetuṃ “sayaṃ yācitakehī”tiādimāha. Tattha sayaṃ yācitakehīti “vāsiṃ detha, pharasuṃ dethā”tiādinā (pārā. 342) sayaṃ yācitakehi. Upakaraṇehīti vāsiyādīhi. Parena bhaṇḍasāmikena “mama ida”nti apariccāgārakkhaṇagopanavasena pariggahitaṃ parapariggahitakaṃ, parasantakanti vuttaṃ hoti. Mūlacchedavasenāti mūlassa chindanavasena, parasantakabhāvato mocetvā attano santakaṃ katvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Evañhi aññātakaappavāritaṭṭhānato yācantassa aññātakaviññattiyā dukkaṭaṃ. Tāvakālikaṃ pana vaṭṭatīti tāvakālikaṃ katvā yācituṃ vaṭṭati. Sakakammaṃ na yācitabbāti pāṇātipātasikkhāpadarakkhaṇatthaṃ vuttaṃ. “Hatthakammaṃ dethā”ti aniyametvāpi na yācitabbā. Evaṃ yācitā hi te “sādhu, bhante”ti bhikkhuṃ uyyojetvā migepi māretvā āhareyyuṃ. Niyametvā pana “vihāre kiñci kattabbaṃ atthi, tattha hatthakammaṃ dethā”ti yācitabbā. “Kuṭi nāma ullittā vā hoti, avalittā vā ullittāvalittā vā”ti (pārā. 345) padabhājane vuttattā “kuṭinti ullittādīsu aññatara”nti vuttaṃ. Tattha uddhaṃ mukhaṃ littā ullittā. Anto limpantā hi evaṃ limpanti. Adho mukhaṃ littā avalittā. Bahi limpantā hi evaṃ limpanti. Tenāha “tattha ullittā nāmā”tiādi. Piṭṭhasaṅghāṭoti dvārabāhā. “Sudhāya vā mattikāya vā”ti etena ṭhapetvā ime dve lepe avaseso bhasmāgomayādibhedo alepoti dasseti.

As for 'saññācikāya pana': here, 'sa' is a particle denoting 'self' in the sense of the instrumental, and 'yācikā' is a derivative expressing the state. Between them is a compound with elision of the middle term. 'Pana' is merely a particle. Therefore, it is said, 'It is called a request initiated by oneself.' For what is initiated by oneself is indeed called one's own; thus it is stated, 'therefore,' etc. Now, 'Is it not possible to build a hut simply by asking?'—addressing this objection, to show the intended meaning, he stated, 'by things requested by oneself,' etc. Here, 'by things requested by oneself' means with things requested by oneself, such as, 'Give an adze, give an axe,' etc. 'With tools' means with adzes and the like. That which is possessed by another, the owner of the goods, by way of not giving it up, guarding, and protecting it, saying, 'This is mine,' is called 'possessed by another'; it means belonging to another. 'By way of cutting the root' means by way of cutting the root, that is, having freed it from being another's possession and made it one's own. Thus, for one asking from an unrelated, uninvited place, there is a dukkaṭa offense for intimating to an unrelated person. However, what is for temporary use is allowable; it is allowable to ask for something making it for temporary use. 'One should not ask for one's own work': this is stated for the sake of protecting the training rule against taking life. Even without specifying, one should not ask, 'Give manual labor.' For if asked thus, they might say, 'Very well, venerable sir,' send the bhikkhu away, and then kill deer and bring them. But by specifying, one may ask, 'There is some work to be done in the monastery; give your manual labor there.' 'A hut is either plastered above, or plastered below, or plastered both above and below.' Since this is stated in the word analysis (padabhājana), it is said, 'a hut means any one of these—plastered above, etc.' Therein, 'plastered above' (ullittā) means plastered on the upper surface. For those who plaster the interior plaster thus. 'Plastered below' (avalittā) means plastered on the lower surface. For those who plaster the exterior plaster thus. Hence it is said, 'therein, "plastered above" means,' etc. 'Piṭṭhasaṅghāṭa' means the doorjambs. 'With lime or clay': by this, having excluded these two plasters, he indicates that the remainder—the various kinds such as ashes and cow dung—is 'not plaster'.

Yasmā pana saññācikāya kuṭiṃ karontenāpi idha vuttanayeneva paṭipajjitabbaṃ, tasmā “sayaṃ vā karontena āṇattiyā vā kārāpentenā”ti vuttaṃ. Ettha ca “sayaṃ vā karontenā”ti iminā sāmatthiyato labbhamānamatthamāha, na tu padatthato. “Āṇattiyā vā kārāpentenā”ti [M 0.0238] (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.348-349) pana padatthato. Evañca katvā yadi pana “karontena vā kārāpentena vā”ti vadeyya, byañjanaṃ vilomitaṃ bhaveyya. Na hi kārāpento karonto nāma hotīti edisī codanā anavakāsāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Natthi sāmī pati etissāti asāmikā, taṃ [V 0.0221] asāmikaṃ, anissaranti attho. Anissaratā cettha kārāpanenāti āha “kāretā dāyakena virahita”nti. Uddesoti uddisitabbo.

Since even when building a hut by solicitation, one must proceed in the manner described here, it is therefore said, 'either by doing it oneself or by having it done through a command.' And here, by 'either by doing it oneself,' he states the meaning obtainable from the implication, not from the literal meaning of the word. But 'or by having it done through a command' is from the literal meaning of the word. This being so, if one were to say, 'either by doing or by having it done,' the expression would be contrary. For 'one who causes something to be done is not called the doer'—such an objection should be seen as groundless. 'There is no owner or master for it,' thus asāmikā. That is asāmikaṃ, meaning 'without a master' (anissara). And here, the state of being without a master is through causing it to be done; thus he says, 'the agent is without a donor.' Uddeso means 'to be designated'.

Tatrāti sāmismiṃ bhummavacananti āha “tassā kuṭiyā”ti. Dīghasoti nissakkavacananti āha “dīghato”ti. Bahikuṭṭeti kuṭṭassa bahi, thusena missako piṇḍo thusapiṇḍo, tassa pariyanto thusapiṇḍapariyanto, tena, thusamissakamattikāpiṇḍapariyantenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Thusapiṇḍassūpari setakammaṃ pana abbohārikaṃ. Abbhantare bhavo abbhantarimo, tena. Yatthāti yassaṃ kuṭiyaṃ. Pamāṇayuttoti pakatividatthiyā navavidatthipamāṇo. “Tiriyaṃ sattantarā”ti (pārā. 348) ukkaṃsato pamāṇassa vuttattā “heṭṭhimakoṭiyā catuhatthavitthārā na hotī”ti vuttaṃ.

'Tatra' is a locative expression in the sense of relation; hence he says, 'of that hut.' 'Dīghaso' is a word indicating extension; hence he says, 'in length.' 'Bahikuṭṭe' means outside the wall. A lump mixed with chaff is a chaff-lump; its boundary is the boundary of the chaff-lump; by that, it means 'by the boundary of a lump of clay mixed with chaff.' However, whitewashing over the chaff-lump is not conventional. 'That which is inside' is abbhantarima; by that. 'Yattha' means 'in which hut.' 'Of appropriate size' means a measure of nine spans by the standard span. Since 'seven spans across' is stated as the maximum measure, it is said, 'at the lower limit, it is not four cubits in width.'

Sodhetvāti samatalasīmamaṇḍalasadisaṃ katvā. Padabhājane vuttanayena saṅghaṃ tikkhattuṃ yācitvāti “saṅghaṃ upasaṅkamitvā ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā vuḍḍhānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ pāde vanditvā ukkuṭikaṃ nisīditvā añjaliṃ paggahetvā evamassa vacanīyo ‘ahaṃ, bhante, saññācikāya kuṭiṃ kattukāmo asāmikaṃ attuddesaṃ, sohaṃ, bhante, saṅghaṃ kuṭivatthuolokanaṃ yācāmī’”ti (pārā. 349) padabhājane vuttanayena tikkhattuṃ yācitvā. Saṅghena vā sammatāti padabhājaniyaṃ (pārā. 350) vuttena ñattidutiyakammena, apalokanakammavasena vā saṅghena sammatā. Vatthūti kuṭivatthu. Anārambhanti anupaddavaṃ. Parito kamati gacchati etthāti parikkamanaṃ, tena saha vattatīti saparikkamanaṃ, saupacāranti attho. Tenāha “tehi bhikkhūhī”tiādi.

'Having cleared it' means having made it like a level, bounded circle. 'Having requested the Saṅgha three times in the manner stated in the word analysis' means having requested three times in the manner stated in the word analysis: 'Having approached the Saṅgha, having arranged the upper robe over one shoulder, having paid homage at the feet of the senior bhikkhus, having sat down in a squatting position, having raised the joined palms, he should speak thus: "Venerable sirs, I desire to build a hut by solicitation, without an owner, for my own use. I, venerable sirs, request the Saṅgha for an inspection of the hut site."' 'Or approved by the Saṅgha' means approved by the Saṅgha by means of the act with a motion as the second part, as stated in the word analysis, or by way of an act of seeking consent. 'The site' means the hut site. 'Without obstruction' means without trouble. 'One walks or goes around it,' thus parikkamana. 'That which has that' is saparikkamanaṃ; the meaning is 'with an approach-way.' Therefore, he says, 'by those bhikkhus,' etc.

Kipillikādīnanti ettha kipillikā (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.353) nāma rattakāḷapiṅgalādibhedā yā kāci, tā ādi yesaṃ tāni kipillikādīni, tesaṃ. Ādisaddena upacikādīnaṃ saṅgahaṇaṃ. Āsayoti nibaddhavasanaṭṭhānaṃ, so ādi [M 0.0239] yesaṃ te āsayādayo, tehi. Ādisaddena cettha nissitassa gahaṇaṃ. Soḷasahi upaddavehīti “kipillikānaṃ vā āsayo hoti, upacikānaṃ vā undūrānaṃ vā ahīnaṃ vā vicchikānaṃ vā satapadīnaṃ vā hatthīnaṃ vā assānaṃ vā sīhānaṃ vā byagghānaṃ vā dīpīnaṃ vā acchānaṃ vā taracchānaṃ vā yesaṃ kesañci tiracchānagatānaṃ pāṇānaṃ vā āsayo hoti, pubbaṇṇanissitaṃ vā hoti, aparaṇṇaabbhāghātaāghātanasusānauyyānarājavatthuhatthisālāassasālābandhanāgārapānāgārasūnaracchācaccarasabhāsaṃsaraṇanissitaṃ vā hotī”ti (pārā. 353) evaṃ vuttehi soḷasahi upaddavehi. Tattha [V 0.0222] ca abbhāghātaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.353) nāma kāraṇāgharaṃ. Āghātanaṃ nāma dhammagandhikā. Susānanti mahāsusānaṃ. Saṃsaraṇaṃ nāma anibbijjhagamanīyo gatapaccāgatamaggo.

Here, in 'of ants and so on' (kipillikādīnaṃ), 'ants' (kipillikā) means any of the various kinds, such as red, black, or tawny. Those which have these as their beginning are 'ants and so on'; this refers to them. By the word 'and so on' (ādi), termites and others are included. 'A dwelling' (āsayo) means a permanent place of residence. Those which have this as their beginning are 'dwellings and so on' (āsayādayo); this refers to them. And here, by the word 'and so on' (ādi), that which is dependent is included. 'By the sixteen troubles' refers to the sixteen troubles stated thus: 'There may be a dwelling of ants, or termites, rats, snakes, scorpions, centipedes, elephants, horses, lions, tigers, leopards, bears, hyenas, or any other kind of animal. Or it may be dependent on early grain, or late grain, a place of torture, an execution ground, a charnel ground, a park, a royal property, an elephant stable, a horse stable, a prison, a tavern, a butcher's shop, a street, a crossroads, an assembly hall, or a thoroughfare.' And there, abbhāghāta is a house of torture. Āghātana is an execution ground. Susāna means a great charnel ground. Saṃsaraṇa means a path of coming and going that is difficult to penetrate.

Āvijjhituṃ sakkuṇeyyatāyāti chinnataṭādīnamabhāvato anupariyāyituṃ sakkuṇeyyatāya. Tena bhikkhunāti kuṭikārakena bhikkhunā. Yācitehīti “ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā vuḍḍhānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ pāde vanditvā ukkuṭikaṃ nisīditvā añjaliṃ paggahetvā evamassa vacanīyo ‘ahaṃ, bhante, saññācikāya kuṭiṃ kattukāmo asāmikaṃ attuddesaṃ, sohaṃ, bhante, saṅghaṃ kuṭivatthudesanaṃ yācāmī’”ti (pārā. 351) tikkhattuṃ yācitehi. Ñattidutiyena kammenāti –

'Because of the ability to encompass it' means because of the ability to go all around it, due to the absence of broken banks and so on. 'By that bhikkhu' means by the bhikkhu who is the hut-maker.
