But since marine pearls are mostly seen in the world, and among them those from oysters, with the others being rare, therefore in the Sammohavinodanī it is said: 'Pearls means marine pearls.' Gem should be understood as every variety of blue, yellow, etc., color, apart from beryl, down to and including natural crystal. However, only a glass gem, which is made by firing, is allowable to be accepted for the value of goods such as a bowl. Beryl is a gem the color of bamboo. Conch means a blowing conch, washed and polished, mixed with gems; but a drinking conch is not mixed with gems, and it is allowable to accept it for the purpose of medicine such as collyrium and for the value of goods. Stone means a stone of mung-bean color, washed and polished, conjoined with gems. But one not mixed with gems is allowable to be accepted for purposes such as a knife-sharpener. And here some say: 'Conjoined with gems means fused with gold and made by firing.' Coral means all coral, whether washed or unwashed. Lohitaṅka is a red gem. Masāragalla is a variegated gem, which is also called 'emerald.'

Satta dhaññānīti sānulomāni sāliādīni satta dhaññāni. Nīvārādiupadhaññassa pana sāliādimūladhaññantogadhattā “satta dhaññānī”ti vuttaṃ. Dāsidāsakhettavatthupupphārāmaphalārāmādayoti [V 0.0286] ettha dāsī nāma antojātadhanakkītakaramarānītappabhedā. Tathā dāso. Khettaṃ nāma yasmiṃ pubbaṇṇaṃ ruhati. Vatthu nāma yasmiṃ aparaṇṇaṃ ruhati. Yattha vā ubhayampi ruhati, taṃ khettaṃ. Tadatthāya akatabhūmibhāgo vatthu. Khettavatthusīsena cettha vāpitaḷākādīnipi saṅgahitāneva. Vassikādīnaṃ pupphanako pupphārāmo. Ambaphalādīnaṃ phalanako phalārāmo. Na kevalañca attanoyevatthāya sampaṭicchituṃ na vaṭṭati, sacepi koci jātarūparajataṃ ānetvā “idaṃ saṅghassa dammi, ārāmaṃ vā karotha, cetiyaṃ vā bhojanasālādīnaṃ vā aññatara”nti vadati, idampi sampaṭicchituṃ na vaṭṭati. “Yassa kassaci hi aññassa atthāya sampaṭicchantassa dukkaṭaṃ hotī”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.538-539) mahāpaccariyaṃ vuttaṃ. Tenāha “cetiyasaṅghagaṇapuggalānaṃ vā atthāya sampaṭicchituṃ na vaṭṭantī”ti.

The seven kinds of grain means the seven kinds of grain such as rice, etc., along with their derivatives. But since secondary grains such as wild rice are included within the primary grains such as rice, it is said, 'the seven kinds of grain.' Female slaves, male slaves, fields, land, flower parks, fruit parks, etc.: here, a female slave is of different kinds, such as one born in the house, bought with money, or brought as a captive of war. Likewise a male slave. A field is where early grain grows. Land is where late grain grows. Or, where both grow is a field; a piece of ground not prepared for that purpose is land. And here, under the heading of fields and land, reservoirs and ponds, etc., are also included. A flower park is a place of flowers such as jasmine. A fruit park is a place of fruits such as mangoes. And it is not only unallowable to accept these for oneself, but even if someone brings gold and silver and says, 'I give this to the Sangha; build a park, or a cetiya, or one of the buildings such as a dining hall,' it is unallowable to accept this. In the Mahāpaccarī it is said: 'For one who accepts for the sake of anyone else at all, there is an offense of wrong-doing.' For that reason it is said: 'It is not allowable to accept for the sake of a cetiya, the Sangha, a group, or an individual.'

Sace pana saṅghaṃ vā gaṇaṃ vā puggalaṃ vā anāmasitvā “idaṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ cetiyassa dema, vihārassa dema, navakammassa demā”ti vadanti, paṭikkhipituṃ na vaṭṭati. “Ime idaṃ bhaṇantī”ti kappiyakārakānaṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ. “Cetiyādīnaṃ atthāya tumhe gahetvā ṭhapethā”ti vutte pana “amhākaṃ gahetuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti paṭikkhipitabbaṃ.

But if, without addressing the Sangha, a group, or an individual, they say, 'We give this gold and silver to the cetiya, to the monastery, for new construction,' it is not allowable to refuse. The lay attendants should be told: 'These people are saying this.' But if it is said, 'You take and keep it for the sake of the cetiya, etc.,' it should be refused with: 'It is not allowable for us to take it.'

Veyyāvaccakaroti kiccakaro. Idha pana sabbo kiccakarova “veyyāvaccakaro”ti adhippetoti āha “kappiyakārako”ti. Eso khoti “asukavīthiyaṃ asukaghare asukanāmo”ti parammukhaṃ vadati. Itarampīti parammukhāniddiṭṭhampi. “Attho me, āvuso, cīvarenā”ti etaṃ codanālakkhaṇanidassananti sambandho. Tattha codanālakkhaṇanidassananti vācāya [M 0.0312] codanālakkhaṇanidassanaṃ. Tenāha “sace hī”tiādi. Idaṃ vā vacanaṃ vattabbanti sambandho. Etassa vā attho yāya kāyaci bhāsāya vattabboti sambandho. “Dehi me cīvaraṃ, āhara me cīvaraṃ, parivattehi me cīvaraṃ, cetāpehi me cīvara”nti etāni pana vacanāni etesaṃ vā attho yāya kāyaci bhāsāya na vattabbo. Tenāha “dehi me”tiādi. Sādheyyāti nipphādeyya. Iccetaṃ kusalanti evaṃ yāvatatiyaṃ codanena tassa cīvarassa yadetaṃ abhinipphādanaṃ, etaṃ kusalaṃ sādhu suṭṭhūti attho. Tenāha “etaṃ sundara”nti.

One who performs a service means a worker. Here, however, by the term 'veyyāvaccakaro' every worker is intended; thus it is said, 'one who makes things allowable.' This one, indeed, speaks indirectly, saying: 'In such-and-such a street, in such-and-such a house, is one named so-and-so.' And the other also means one who is indicated indirectly. The connection is: 'Friend, I have need of a robe' is an example showing the characteristic of a reminder. Therein, 'an example showing the characteristic of a reminder' is an example showing the characteristic of a verbal reminder. For that reason it is said: 'For if,' etc. The connection is: 'Or this statement should be spoken.' The connection is: 'Or the meaning of this should be spoken in any language whatsoever.' But these statements—'Give me a robe,' 'Bring me a robe,' 'Exchange a robe for me,' 'Have a robe acquired for me'—or their meaning should not be spoken in any language whatsoever. For that reason it is said: 'Give me,' etc. 'He should accomplish it' means he should bring it to completion. Thus this is skillful: this accomplishment of that robe by reminding up to the third time is skillful, good, excellent. For that reason it is said: 'This is fine.'

Chakkhattuṃ paramo paricchedo assāti chakkhattuparamaṃ. Idañhi “ṭhātabba”nti imissā kiriyāya visesanaṃ, chakkhattuparamaṃ ṭhānaṃ kātabbanti attho. Tenāha “bhāvanapuṃsakavacanameta”nti, etaṃ bhāve ṭhātabbanti vuttadhātvatthamatte sādhetabbe napuṃsakaliṅgavacananti attho. Na nisīditabbanti “idha, bhante, nisīdathā”ti vuttepi na nisīditabbaṃ[V 0.0287]. Na āmisaṃ paṭiggahetabbanti yāgukhajjakādibhedaṃ kiñci āmisaṃ “gaṇhatha, bhante”ti yāciyamānenāpi na gaṇhitabbaṃ. Na dhammo bhāsitabboti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.538-539) “maṅgalaṃ vā anumodanaṃ vā bhāsathā”ti yāciyamānenāpi na kiñci bhāsitabbaṃ. Ṭhānaṃ bhañjatīti ṭhitiṃ vināseti. Ṭhatvā cīvaraṃ gahetuṃ āgatena hi taṃ uddissa tuṇhībhūtena ṭhātabbameva, na nisajjādikaṃ kātabbaṃ. Iminā pana taṃ katanti ṭhānaṃ vināsitaṃ hoti. Tenāha “āgatakāraṇaṃ vināsetī”ti. “Āgatakāraṇaṃ nāma ṭhānameva, tasmā ‘na kātabba’nti vāritassa katattā nisajjādīsu katesu chasu ṭhānesu ekaṃ ṭhānaṃ bhañjatī”ti (sārattha. ṭī. 2.537-539) ayamettha adhippāyo. Chakkhattuparamaṃ tuṇhībhūtena uddissa ṭhātabbaṃ. “Na aññaṃ kiñci kātabba”nti hi idaṃ ṭhānalakkhaṇaṃ. Tenevāha “ida”ntiādi. Tattha idanti “catukkhattuṃ pañcakkhattuṃ, chakkhattuparamaṃ tuṇhībhūtena uddissa ṭhātabba”nti vacanaṃ. Ettha ca “nisīdanādimhi kate puna cīvaraṃ gahetuṃ na labhatī”ti keci. “Dve ṭhānāni parihāyantī”ti aññe. “Ekaṃ ṭhānaṃ parihāyatī”ti apare. Ubhayaṃ karotīti codetipi tiṭṭhatipi.

The limit is six times at most, hence 'chakkhattuparamaṃ.' This is a qualifier for the action 'one should stand,' meaning one should stand up to six times at most. Therefore it is said: 'This is a neuter word in the sense of an action,' meaning it is a neuter gender word used when the mere meaning of the verbal root 'to stand' is to be accomplished. 'One should not sit down': even if told, 'Venerable sir, sit here,' one should not sit down. 'One should not accept a material offering': even if requested, 'Venerable sir, take this,' one should not accept any material offering such as gruel or solid food. 'The Dhamma should not be spoken': even if requested, 'Please speak on a blessing or give words of appreciation,' one should not say anything. 'Breaks the standing' means one destroys the standing. For one who has come to receive a robe should just stand in silence with that intention; one should not sit down or do anything similar. But when this is done, the standing is destroyed. Therefore it is said: 'one destroys the reason for coming.' The meaning here is: 'The reason for coming is the standing itself. Therefore, because one has done what was forbidden by 'should not be done,' when one does things like sitting down, one breaks one of the six standings.' One should stand in silence with that intention up to six times at most. For 'Nothing else should be done' is the characteristic of this standing. Therefore it is said, 'this,' etc. Here, 'this' refers to the statement: 'Four times, five times, up to six times at most, one should stand in silence with that intention.' In this regard, some say: 'If one sits down or does something similar, one does not get to receive the robe again.' Others say: 'Two standings are lost.' Still others say: 'One standing is lost.' 'He does both' means he both reminds and stands.

“Tatra tatra ṭhāne tiṭṭhatī”ti idaṃ codakassa ṭhitaṭṭhitaṭṭhānato apakkamma tatra tatra cīvaraṃ uddissa ṭhānaṃyeva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Etthāti etesu dvīsu codanāṭṭhānesu.

'He stands in this or that place': this is said with reference to the very act of standing with the intention for the robe in this or that place, after having moved from the place where the one who reminds was standing. 'Here' means in these two instances of reminding.

Kiṃ [M 0.0313] pana sabbakappiyakārakesu (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.538-539; vi. saṅga. aṭṭha. 65) evaṃ paṭipajjitabbanti? Na paṭipajjitabbaṃ. Ayañhi kappiyakārako nāma saṅkhepato duvidho niddiṭṭho ca aniddiṭṭho ca. Tattha ca niddiṭṭho duvidho bhikkhunā niddiṭṭho, dūtena niddiṭṭhoti. Aniddiṭṭhopi duvidho mukhavevaṭikakappiyakārako, parammukhakappiyakārakoti. Tesu bhikkhunā niddiṭṭho sammukhāsammukhavasena catubbidho hoti, tathā dūtena niddiṭṭhopi.

But should one act in this way with all lay attendants? One should not. For this lay attendant is, in brief, of two kinds: designated and undesignated. Among these, the designated one is of two kinds: designated by a bhikkhu and designated by a messenger. The undesignated one is also of two kinds: a lay attendant by word of mouth and a lay attendant in one's absence. Among these, the one designated by a bhikkhu is fourfold, based on whether it is in his presence or absence; similarly for the one designated by a messenger.

Kathaṃ? Idhekacco bhikkhussa cīvaratthāya dūtena akappiyavatthuṃ pahiṇati, dūto ca taṃ bhikkhuṃ upasaṅkamitvā “idaṃ, bhante, itthannāmena tumhākaṃ cīvaratthāya pahitaṃ, gaṇhatha na”nti vadati. Bhikkhu “idaṃ na kappatī”ti paṭikkhipati. Dūto “atthi pana te, bhante, veyyāvaccakaro”ti pucchati, puññatthikehi ca upāsakehi “bhikkhūnaṃ veyyāvaccaṃ karothā”ti āṇattā vā bhikkhūnaṃ vā sandiṭṭhā sambhattā keci veyyāvaccakarā honti, tesaṃ aññataro tasmiṃ khaṇe bhikkhussa santike nisinno hoti, bhikkhu taṃ niddisati “ayaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ veyyāvaccakaro”ti[V 0.0288]. Dūto tassa hatthe akappiyavatthuṃ datvā “therassa cīvaraṃ kiṇitvā dehī”ti gacchati, ayaṃ bhikkhunā sammukhāniddiṭṭho.

How so? Here, a certain person sends an unallowable item through a messenger to a bhikkhu for the purpose of a robe. The messenger approaches the bhikkhu and says: 'Venerable sir, this has been sent by so-and-so for your robe. Will you accept it?' The bhikkhu refuses, saying: 'This is not allowable.' The messenger then asks: 'Venerable sir, do you have an attendant?' Now, there are some attendants who have been instructed by merit-seeking lay followers, 'Perform services for the bhikkhus,' or who are known to and intimate with the bhikkhus. One of them happens to be sitting near the bhikkhu at that moment. The bhikkhu points him out, saying: 'This is an attendant of the bhikkhus.' The messenger places the unallowable item in his hand, says, 'Buy a robe for the Elder and give it to him,' and departs. This is one designated by a bhikkhu in his presence.

No ce bhikkhussa (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.537; vi. saṅga. aṭṭha. 65) santike nisinno hoti, apica kho bhikkhu niddisati “asukasmiṃ nāma gāme itthannāmo bhikkhūnaṃ veyyāvaccakaro”ti. So gantvā tassa hatthe akappiyavatthuṃ datvā “therassa cīvaraṃ kiṇitvā dadeyyāsī”ti āgantvā bhikkhussa ārocetvā gacchati, ayameko bhikkhunā asammukhāniddiṭṭho.

But if no one is sitting near the bhikkhu, the bhikkhu might instead point out: 'In such-and-such village, so-and-so is an attendant of the bhikkhus.' The messenger goes, places the unallowable item in his hand, and says: 'You should buy a robe for the Elder and give it to him.' Then he returns, informs the bhikkhu, and departs. This is one designated by a bhikkhu in his absence.

Na heva kho so dūto attanā āgantvā āroceti, apica kho aññaṃ pahiṇati “dinnaṃ mayā, bhante, tassa hatthe cīvaracetāpannaṃ, cīvaraṃ gaṇheyyāthā”ti, ayaṃ dutiyo bhikkhunā asammukhāniddiṭṭho.

Or that messenger does not come himself to inform him, but instead sends another to say: 'Venerable sir, I have given the price for the robe into his hand; you should receive the robe.' This is the second case of one designated by a bhikkhu in his absence.

Na heva kho aññaṃ pahiṇati, apica kho gacchantova bhikkhuṃ vadati “ahaṃ tassa hatthe cīvaracetāpannaṃ dassāmi, tumhe cīvaraṃ gaṇheyyāthā”ti, ayaṃ tatiyo bhikkhunā asammukhāniddiṭṭhoti evaṃ eko sammukhāniddiṭṭho tayo asammukhāniddiṭṭhāti ime cattāro bhikkhunā niddiṭṭhaveyyāvaccakarā nāma. Etesu imasmiṃ rājasikkhāpade vuttanayeneva paṭipajjitabbaṃ.

Or he does not send another, but as he is leaving he tells the bhikkhu: 'I will give the price for the robe into his hand; you should receive the robe.' This is the third case of one designated by a bhikkhu in his absence. Thus, one is designated in his presence and three are designated in his absence—these are the four kinds of attendants designated by a bhikkhu. In regard to these, one should proceed in the very manner stated in this Royal Sikkhāpada.

Aparo [M 0.0314] bhikkhu purimanayeneva dūtena pucchito natthitāya vā avicāretukāmatāya vā “natthamhākaṃ kappiyakārako”ti vadati, tasmiñca khaṇe koci manusso āgacchati, dūto tassa hatthe akappiyavatthuṃ datvā “imassa hatthato cīvaraṃ gaṇheyyāthā”ti vatvā gacchati, ayaṃ dūtena sammukhāniddiṭṭho.

Another bhikkhu, when asked by the messenger in the same way as before, says, 'We have no attendant who makes things allowable,' either because there is none or because he does not wish to investigate. At that moment some person arrives. The messenger places the unallowable item in that person's hand, says, 'You should receive the robe from this person's hand,' and departs. This is one designated by the messenger in his presence.

Aparo dūto gāmaṃ pavisitvā attanā abhirucitassa kassaci hatthe akappiyavatthuṃ datvā purimanayeneva āgantvā vā āroceti, aññaṃ vā pahiṇati, “ahaṃ asukassa nāma hatthe cīvaracetāpannaṃ dassāmi, tumhe cīvaraṃ gaṇheyyāthā”ti vatvā vā gacchati, ayaṃ tatiyo dūtena asammukhāniddiṭṭhoti evaṃ eko sammukhāniddiṭṭho, tayo asammukhāniddiṭṭhāti ime cattāro dūtena niddiṭṭhaveyyāvaccakarā nāma. Etesu meṇḍakasikkhāpade vuttanayeneva paṭipajjitabbaṃ.

Another messenger enters a village and gives the unallowable item into the hand of someone he himself chooses. Then, in the same way as before, he either returns and informs the bhikkhu, or sends another, or says as he is leaving, 'I will give the price for the robe into the hand of so-and-so; you should receive the robe.' This is the third case of one designated by the messenger in his absence. Thus, one is designated in his presence and three are designated in his absence—these are the four kinds of attendants designated by a messenger. In regard to these, one should proceed in the very manner stated in the Meṇḍaka Sikkhāpada.

Vuttañhetaṃ [V 0.0289] –

For this has been said:

“Santi, bhikkhave, manussā saddhā pasannā, te kappiyakārakānaṃ hatthe hiraññaṃ upanikkhipanti ‘iminā ayyassa yaṃ kappiyaṃ, taṃ dethā’ti. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, yaṃ tato kappiyaṃ, taṃ sādituṃ, na tvevāhaṃ, bhikkhave, kenaci pariyāyena jātarūparajataṃ sāditabbaṃ pariyesitabbanti vadāmī”ti (mahāva. 299).

'Bhikkhus, there are faithful, believing people who deposit gold in the hands of attendants who make things allowable, saying: "With this, give the noble one whatever is allowable." Bhikkhus, I allow you to consent to what is allowable from that. But, bhikkhus, I do not say that in any way at all gold and silver should be sought for or consented to.'

Ettha ca codanāya parimāṇaṃ natthi. Mūlaṃ asādiyantena sahassakkhattumpi codanāya vā ṭhānena vā kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ sādituṃ vaṭṭati. No ce deti, aññaṃ kappiyakārakaṃ ṭhapetvāpi āharāpetabbaṃ. Sace icchati, mūlasāmikānampi kathetabbaṃ. No ce icchati, na kathetabbaṃ.

Here there is no limit to the reminding. Without consenting to the principal item, it is proper to consent to the allowable goods by reminding or by standing even a thousand times. If he does not give it, it should be procured by appointing another attendant who makes things allowable. If one wishes, one may also speak to the original owners. If one does not wish, one should not speak to them.

Aparo bhikkhu purimanayeneva dūtena pucchito “natthamhākaṃ kappiyakārako”ti vadati, tadañño samīpe ṭhito sutvā “āhara, bho, ahaṃ ayyassa cīvaraṃ cetāpetvā dassāmī”ti vadati. Dūto “handa, bho, dadeyyāsī”ti tassa hatthe datvā bhikkhussa anārocetvāva gacchati, ayaṃ mukhavevaṭikakappiyakārako.

Another bhikkhu, when asked by the messenger in the same way as before, says: 'We have no attendant who makes things allowable.' Another person standing nearby hears this and says: 'Bring it, good sir, I will have a robe purchased for the noble one and give it.' The messenger says, 'Very well, good sir, you should give it,' places it in his hand, and departs without informing the bhikkhu. This is an attendant who makes things allowable by word of mouth.

Aparo (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.538-539; vi. saṅga. aṭṭha. 65) bhikkhuno upaṭṭhākassa vā aññassa vā hatthe akappiyavatthuṃ datvā “therassa cīvaraṃ dadeyyāsī”ti ettova pakkamati, ayaṃ parammukhakappiyakārakoti [M 0.0315] ime dve aniddiṭṭhakappiyakārakā nāma. Etesu aññātakaappavāritesu viya paṭipajjitabbaṃ.

Another person gives an unallowable item into the hand of the bhikkhu's attendant or someone else and departs, saying only: 'You should give the robe to the Elder.' This is an attendant who makes things allowable in one's absence. These two are called undesignated attendants who make things allowable. In regard to these, one should act as one would towards those who are not relatives and have not extended an invitation.

Sace sayameva cīvaraṃ ānetvā denti, gahetabbaṃ. No ce, na kiñci vattabbā. Tenāha “sace”tiādi. Kappiyakāraketi sammukhāsammukhavasena cattāro kappiyakāraketi attho. “Dāyako sayamevā”ti iminā bhikkhuṃ paṭikkhipati, na dūtaṃ. Tasmā dūtena niddiṭṭhopi yathāruci codetuṃ vaṭṭati. Mukhaṃ vivaritvā sayameva kappiyakārakattaṃ upagatoti mukhavevaṭikakappiyakārako. Evanti “eso kho”tiādinā yathāvuttena ākārena. Dassitā honti saṅkhepatoti adhippāyo.

If they bring the robe themselves and give it, it should be accepted. If not, nothing should be said. Therefore it is said, 'If,' etc. 'Attendants who make things allowable': the meaning is the four kinds of attendants who make things allowable, based on whether it is in one's presence or absence. 'The donor himself': by this, one refuses the bhikkhu, not the messenger. Therefore, even if designated by a messenger, it is proper to remind as one wishes. 'An attendant who makes things allowable by word of mouth' is so called because, having opened his mouth, he himself has undertaken the task of making things allowable. 'Thus' refers to the manner stated beginning with 'this indeed.' The intention is that they are shown concisely.

Vuttacodanāṭṭhānaparimāṇatoti vuttacodanāparimāṇato ca vuttaṭṭhānaparimāṇato ca. Santikanti samīpaṃ. Tatthāti ettha kathamayamattho labbhatīti āha “samīpatthe hi idaṃ bhummavacana”nti[V 0.0290]. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “gaṅgāyaṃ goyūthāni caranti, kūpe gaggakūla”ntiādīsu viya yasmā samīpādhāre idaṃ sattamīvibhattivacanaṃ, tasmā ayamattho labbhatīti. Evaṃ akarontoti sāmaṃ vā agacchanto, dūtaṃ vā apāhento.

“Regarding the extent of the stated reminding and standing” means both from the extent of the stated reminding and from the extent of the stated standing. “Santika” means proximity. How is this meaning obtained here from the word “tattha” (there)? It is said: “For this locative expression is in the sense of proximity.” This is what is said: just as in such phrases as “herds of cattle roam along the Ganges” and “the Gaggā’s bank is in the well,” this meaning is obtained because this locative case expression indicates proximity as the location. “Thus, not doing so” means either not going oneself or not sending a messenger.

Ajjaṇho, bhante, āgamehīti, bhante, ajja ekadivasaṃ amhākaṃ tiṭṭha, adhivāsehīti attho. Tikapācittiyanti atirekesu codanāṭṭhānesu atirekasaññivematikaūnakasaññīnaṃ vasena tīṇi pācittiyāni. Tikkhattuṃ codanāya chakkhattuṃ ṭhānena, ūnakatikkhattuṃ codanāya ūnakacchakkhattuṃ ṭhānena laddhepi anāpatti. Appitatāti patiṭṭhāpitatā, “saññatto so mayā”tiādinā (pārā. 538) kathitatāti vuttaṃ hoti.

The phrase “Venerable sir, please come today” means: “Venerable sir, please stay with us for one day; please consent.” “A pācittiya in three cases” refers to three pācittiya offenses in the case of exceeding the limits for reminding and standing, arising for one who perceives excess, is in doubt, or perceives a deficit. There is no offense for what is obtained by reminding three times and standing six times, or by reminding fewer than three times and standing fewer than six times. “Appitatā” means being established, that is, being stated in the way beginning, “He has been instructed by me” (Pārā. 538).

Rājasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning kings is finished.

Cīvaravaggo paṭhamo.

The Chapter on Robes: The First.

2. Eḷakalomavaggo

2. The Chapter on Sheep’s Wool

1. Kosiyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Training Rule on Silk

Kosiyamissakanti [M 0.0316] “kosakārakā”ti laddhavohārānaṃ pāṇakānaṃ kosato nibbattaṃ aṃsu kosiyaṃ, tena missaṃ kosiyamissakaṃ. Tena pana kosiyena appakenāpi missitaṃ kosiyamissakameva, na idaṃ abbohārikanti vattuṃ labbhā. Tenāha “ekenāpī”tiādi. Kosiyaṃsunāti kimikosasambhavena aṃsunā. “Antamaso”tiādikaṃ pana imassa sikkhāpadassa acittakattā vuttaṃ. Santhataṃ nāma santharitvā kataṃ avāyimaṃ. Tenāha “same bhūmibhāge”tiādi. Imasseva vacanassa anusārenāti imasseva paṭhamasanthatassa nissajjanavidhānavacanānusārena. Sabbasanthatanti sabbasanthatanissajjanavidhānaṃ.

“Mixed with silk” means mixed with kosiya, which is fiber produced from the cocoons of creatures designated as “cocoon-makers.” But even if mixed with only a little silk, it is still “mixed with silk”; it cannot be said that this is unconventional. Therefore he said: “Even with one,” and so on. “With silk thread” means with thread originating from an insect’s cocoon. The phrase beginning “Even at the very least” is said because this training rule is unintentional. “Felt mat” means something made by spreading out, not woven. Therefore it is said: “On a level patch of ground,” and so on. “In accordance with this very statement” means in accordance with the statement on the procedure for forfeiting this very first felt mat. “All felt mats” means the procedure for forfeiting all felt mats.

Aññassatthāya kārāpane dukkaṭattā attano atthāya kārāpanavasena “sāṇattika”nti vuttaṃ. Attanā vippakatapariyosāpananayenāti “attanā vippakataṃ attanā pariyosāpeti, nissaggiyaṃ [V 0.0291] pācittiyaṃ. Attanā vippakataṃ parehi pariyosāpeti, nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. Parehi vippakataṃ attanā pariyosāpeti, nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. Parehi vippakataṃ parehi pariyosāpeti, nissaggiyaṃ pācittiya”nti (pārā. 545) iminā nayena. Vitānādikaraṇeti vitānabhūmattharaṇasāṇipākārabhisibibbohanakaraṇe. Yathā ca vitānādikaraṇe, evaṃ tenākārena paribhogepi anāpatti. “Avāyima”nti (pārā. 544) vuttattā vāyitvā karontassāpi anāpatti.

Since it is a dukkaṭa offense to have it made for another's sake, it is called “sāṇattika” when one has it made for one's own sake. “By the method of finishing what was started by oneself” means by this method: “If one completes what was begun by oneself, it is an offense of expiation with forfeiture. If others complete what was begun by oneself, it is an offense of expiation with forfeiture. If one completes what was begun by others, it is an offense of expiation with forfeiture. If others complete what was begun by others, it is an offense of expiation with forfeiture” (Pārā 545). “In making a canopy, etc.” means in making a canopy, a ground-covering, a curtain-wall, a cushion, or a bolster. And just as in making a canopy, etc., so too there is no offense in using it in that way. Because it is said “unwoven” (Pārā 544), there is no offense for one who makes it by weaving.

Kosiyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on silk is finished.

2. Suddhakāḷakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Training Rule on Pure Black

Kāḷakānanti sabhāvena vā rajanena vā kāḷakānaṃ. Yathāha “kāḷakaṃ nāma dve kāḷakāni jātiyā kāḷakaṃ vā rajanakāḷakaṃ vā”ti. Aññehi amissitānanti aññehi amissitakāḷakānanti attho. “Yathā paṭhame ‘ekenāpi kosiyaṃsunā’ti (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. kosiyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) vuttaṃ, tathā idhāpi [M 0.0317] ‘ekenāpi aññena amissetvā’ti avuttattā aññena pana missakabhogepi apaññāyamānarūpakaṃ ce ‘suddhakāḷaka’micceva vuccatī”ti (vajira. ṭī. pārājika 547) vadanti.

“Of black” means of what is black either by nature or by dye. As it is said: “‘Black’ means two kinds of black: naturally black or dyed black.” “Unmixed with others” means black unmixed with others. They say: “Just as in the first case it is said, ‘even with a single silk thread,’ so here too, since it is not said ‘unmixed with even one other,’ if it is used mixed with another but its form is not discernible, it is still called ‘pure black’” (Vajira. Ṭī. Pārājika 547).

Ettha ca “idaṃ me, bhante, suddhakāḷakānaṃ eḷakalomānaṃ santhata”ntiādinā (pārā. 549) nissajjanavidhānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sesanti pubbapayogadukkaṭacatukkapācittiyādikaṃ. Aṅgesu pana “suddhakāḷakabhāvo”ti ayaṃ viseso.

And here the procedure for forfeiture should be known from the passage beginning: “Venerable sir, this felt mat of mine is made of pure black sheep's wool…” (Pārā 549). “The rest” means the preliminary effort, the fourfold dukkaṭa, the pācittiya offense, and so on. But among the factors, “the state of being pure black” is the distinction.

Suddhakāḷakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on pure black is finished.

3. Dvebhāgasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Training Rule on Two Parts

Gahetabbāti yathā kāḷakā adhikā na honti, tathā gahetabbā. Ṭhapetvā cettha kāḷakaodāte avasesā gocariyesuyeva saṅgahaṃ gacchantīti (sārattha. ṭī. 2.552) daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ettha ca dve bhāgāti ukkaṭṭhaparicchedo kāḷakānaṃ adhikaggahaṇassa paṭikkhepavasena sikkhāpadassa paññattattā. Tasmā kāḷakānaṃ bhāgadvayato adhikaṃ na vaṭṭati, ūnakaṃ vaṭṭati. Tenāha [V 0.0292] “ekassāpī”tiādi. Ekassāpi kāḷakalomassa atirekabhāveti tulāya dhārayitvā ṭhapitesu antamaso vātavegenapi pahitassa ekassāpi kāḷakalomassa adhikabhāve satīti attho. “Tatiyaṃ odātānaṃ, catutthaṃ gocariyāna”nti idaṃ pana heṭṭhimaparicchedo tesaṃ adhikaggahaṇe paṭikkhepābhāvato. Tasmā tesaṃ vuttappamāṇato adhikampi vaṭṭati.

“Should be taken” means they should be taken in such a way that the black ones are not in excess. It should be seen that here, apart from the black and white ones, the remaining ones are included under “tawny-colored” (Sārattha. Ṭī. 2.552). And here, “two parts” is the upper limit, since the training rule was laid down to reject the taking of an excess of black wool. Therefore, more than two parts of black is not allowed; less is allowed. Hence he said, “even of one,” and so on. This means that there is an excess if there is an excess of even a single black hair from what has been weighed and set aside—even one blown away by the force of the wind. But this, “a third of white, a fourth of tawny-colored,” is the lower limit, since there is no prohibition against taking them in excess. Therefore, even more than the stated amount of them is allowed.

Ettha ca “idaṃ me, bhante, santhataṃ anādiyitvā dve tule suddhakāḷakānaṃ eḷakalomānaṃ, tulaṃ odātānaṃ, tulaṃ gocariyānaṃ santhataṃ kārāpitaṃ nissaggiya”nti (pārā. 554) iminā nayena nissajjanavidhānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ādāya ca vuttaparicchedena anādāya ca karaṇato kiriyākiriyaṃ. Sesanti pubbapayogadukkaṭacatukkapācittiyādikaṃ. Ayaṃ pana viseso – tulaṃ odātānaṃ tulaṃ gocariyānaṃ ādiyitvā karaṇe, bahutaraṃ odātānaṃ bahutaraṃ gocariyānaṃ ādiyitvā karaṇe[M 0.0318], suddhaṃ odātānaṃ suddhaṃ gocariyānaṃ ādiyitvā karaṇe ca anāpattīti.

And here the procedure for forfeiture should be known by this method: “Venerable sir, this felt mat of mine, made with two measures of pure black sheep’s wool, one measure of white, and one measure of tawny-colored, is to be forfeited for not taking [the wool] correctly” (Pārā 554). The offense is one of both action and non-action, since it is committed both by taking and by not taking in accordance with the stated limit. “The rest” means the preliminary effort, the fourfold dukkaṭa, the pācittiya offense, and so on. But this is the distinction: there is no offense in making it after taking one measure of white wool and one measure of tawny-colored wool; in making it after taking more white wool and more tawny-colored wool; or in making it after taking only white wool or only tawny-colored wool.

Aṅgesu pana paṭhamaṅgaṃ kāḷakānaṃ dvebhāgato atirekabhāvoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Imāni tīṇi na kevalaṃ anissaṭṭhāneva paribhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭantīti āha “imāni panā”tiādi. “Paribhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭantī”ti iminā yadi paribhuñjati, dukkaṭanti dasseti.

But among the factors, the first factor should be understood as the black wool exceeding two parts. He says, “But these…” and so on, to show that it is not allowable to use these three things, and not only when they are unforfeited. By the words “it is not allowable to use,” he shows that if one does use them, there is a dukkaṭa offense.

Dvebhāgasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on two parts is finished.

4. Chabbassasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. Explanation of the Training Rule on Six Years

Yaṃ santhatasammutiṃ detīti sambandho. Gilānassa bhikkhunoti yassa vinā santhatā na phāsu hoti, na sakkoti ca santhataṃ ādāya pakkamituṃ, evaṃbhūtassa gilānassa bhikkhuno. Santhatasammutiṃ detīti “suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho, ayaṃ itthannāmo bhikkhu gilāno na sakkoti santhataṃ ādāya pakkamitu”ntiādinā (pārā. 560) padabhājane vuttāya ñattidutiyakammavācāya santhatasammutiṃ deti.

That which gives the felt mat allowance is the connection. "A sick bhikkhu" refers to a sick bhikkhu for whom it is not comfortable without a felt mat, and who is unable to depart carrying a felt mat. "Gives the felt mat allowance" means giving the felt mat allowance through a motion with a single proclamation, as stated in the word analysis (Pārā. 560), beginning with, "Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha listen to me. This bhikkhu, named so-and-so, is sick and unable to depart carrying a felt mat."

Sāti santhatasammuti. Vūpasanto vā puna kuppatīti vūpasanto vā so ābādho puna kuppati, anuvassampi kātuṃ vaṭṭati, puna sammutidānakiccaṃ natthīti adhippāyo. Na kevalaṃ tasmiṃyeva roge kuppite, atha kho aññasmiṃ roge kuppitepi gatagataṭṭhāne anuvassaṃ kātuṃ labhati. Teneva hi samantapāsādikāyaṃ “sace arogo hutvā puna mūlabyādhināva gilāno hoti[V 0.0293], soyeva parihāro, natthaññaṃ ‘sammutikicca’nti phussadevatthero āha. Upatissatthero pana so vā byādhi paṭikuppatu, añño vā, sakiṃ ‘gilāno’ti nāmaṃ laddhaṃ laddhameva, puna ‘sammutikiccaṃ natthī’ti āhā”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.557) upatissattheravādo pacchā vutto.

That is the felt mat allowance. The phrase 'vūpasanto vā puna kuppati' means that the ailment, having subsided, flares up again. It is permissible to make one even annually, and the meaning is that there is no need for a further act of granting consent. Not only when that very disease flares up, but even when another disease flares up, wherever one goes, it is permissible to make one annually. Therefore, in the Samantapāsādikā it is said: "If, having become healthy, he again becomes sick with the very same original disease, that same dispensation applies; there is no other 'act of consent'," so said the Elder Phussadeva. But the Elder Upatissa said: "Whether that disease recurs or another one does, once the designation 'sick' has been obtained, it is obtained for good; there is no further 'act of consent' needed." The Elder Upatissa's saying was stated later.

Ettha ca “idaṃ me, bhante, santhataṃ ūnakachabbassāni kārāpitaṃ aññatra bhikkhusammutiyā nissaggiya”nti (pārā. 562) iminā nayena nissajjanavidhānaṃ veditabbaṃ. “Sesaṃ paṭhamasadisamevā”ti iminā “attanā kataṃ parehi pariyosāpetī”tiādikaṃ atidiṭṭhaṃ. Ayaṃ pana viseso – paripuṇṇe chabbasse vā atirekachabbasse [M 0.0319] vā anāpatti. Aṅgesu ca chabbassānaṃ antobhāvo nānāttaṃ.

Here, the procedure for forfeiture should be understood in this way: "Venerable sir, this felt mat, made by me in less than six years without the Saṅgha's agreement, is to be forfeited." The rest is just like the first case, as in "what one has made oneself, others finish," etc., which has been referred to. This, however, is the difference: There is no offense when six years are complete or six years are exceeded. And, among the factors, the diversity lies in the inclusion of the six years.

Chabbassasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on six years is finished.

5. Nisīdanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

5. Explanation of the Training Rule on the Sitting Cloth

Nisīdanasanthatanti “nisīdanaṃ nāma sadasaṃ vuccatī”ti ettha padabhājaniyaṃ (pārā. 568) vuttattā sadasaṃ santhataṃ, ettha ca nisīdanaggahaṇaṃ santhate cīvarasaññānivāraṇatthaṃ, yato te bhikkhū kambalacīvarasaññāya santhataṃ chaḍḍetvā dhutaṅgāni samādiyiṃsu. Sayanāsanappayojanattā santhatassa “purāṇasanthataṃ nāmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yatthāti yasmiṃ santhate. Vidatthimattanti sugatavidatthimattaṃ. Ukkaṭṭhaparicchedo cāyaṃ “anāpatti alabhanto thokataraṃ ādiyitvā karotī”ti (pārā. 570) padabhājane vuttattā. Ekadeseti idāni kattabbanavasanthatassa ekappadese. Vijaṭetvāti viddhaṃsetvā. Anādāti ya-kāralopenāyaṃ niddesoti āha “sati purāṇasanthate aggahetvā”ti.

Nisīdanasanthataṃ (sitting felt mat) means 'a felt mat with a border', as it is stated in the word analysis (Pārā. 568) that 'nisīdana is called sadasa'. Here, the inclusion of 'sitting' in 'felt mat' is to prevent the perception of it as a robe, since those bhikkhus discarded the felt mat under the perception of it being a woolen robe and undertook ascetic practices. Because the felt mat is used for bedding and sitting, it is called 'old felt mat,' etc. 'Where' means on which felt mat. 'Of a hand-span' means of the size of the Sugata's hand-span. This is a highest measure, as stated in the word analysis: 'There is no offense if one cannot obtain it and takes a slightly smaller portion to make it.' The word 'ekadesa' (a portion) refers to one part of the new felt mat that is now to be made. 'Vijaṭetvā' means disassembling. The expression 'anādā' (without taking) is by the omission of the letter 'ya', as he says, 'if, there being an old felt mat, without taking it.'

Ettha ca “idaṃ me, bhante, nisīdanasanthataṃ anādiyitvā purāṇasanthatassa sāmantā sugatavidatthiṃ kārāpitaṃ nissaggiya”nti (pārā. 568) iminā nayena nissajjanavidhānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Santhatavissajjanavatthusmiṃ paññattanti bhagavatā santhatāni vippakiṇṇāni disvā “saddhādeyyavinipātane kāraṇaṃ natthi, paribhogupāyaṃ nesaṃ dassessāmī”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.566) santhatavissajjanavatthusmiṃ paññattaṃ. Kiriyākiriyattā imassa sikkhāpadassa “sesaṃ tatiyasadisamevā”ti vuttaṃ, dvebhāgasikkhāpadasadisamevāti attho. Ayaṃ pana viseso – purāṇasanthatassa [V 0.0294] sāmantā sugatavidatthiyā ādāya karaṇe, alabhantassa thokataraṃ ādāya karaṇe, sabbathā alabhantassa anādāya karaṇe ca anāpattīti. Aṅgesu panettha paṭhamaṅgapurāṇasanthatassa sāmantā sugatavidatthianādiyanāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Here, the method of relinquishment should be understood according to this formula: "Venerable sir, this sitting-rug of mine, which was made without taking a Sugata's span from the border of the old rug, is to be forfeited." (Pārā. 568) It was laid down in the case of relinquishing a rug because the Blessed One, seeing rugs scattered about, thought: "There is no reason for the waste of gifts given in faith. I will show them a way to make use of them." (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.566) Because this training rule involves both action and non-action, it is said, "The rest is just like the third," meaning it is just like the training rule concerning two parts. This, however, is the distinction: there is no offense in making it by taking a Sugata's span from the border of the old rug; or, if that is not available, by taking a smaller portion; or, if it is not available at all, by making it without taking anything. Among the factors here, the first factor should be understood as not taking a Sugata's span from the border of the old rug.

Nisīdanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule concerning the Sitting-Rug is concluded.

6. Eḷakalomasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Sheep's Wool

Addhānamaggappaṭipannassāti [M 0.0320] addhānameva maggo addhānamaggo, taṃ paṭipannassāti attho. Tenāha “addhānasaṅkhāta”ntiādi. Addhānasaddena visesitattā pana “dīghamagga”nti vuttaṃ. Addhānagamanasamayassa vibhaṅge “addhayojanaṃ gacchissāmīti bhuñjitabba”ntiādivacanato (pāci. 218) addhayojanampi addhānamaggo hoti. Eḷakalomāni cetāni addhānamaggato aññattha uppannāni paṭiggahetuṃ na vaṭṭanti, yato “addhānamaggappaṭipannassā”tiādikaṃ vuttanti anuyogaṃ sandhāyāha “sabbañceta”ntiādi. Tattha sabbañcetanti “bhikkhuno paneva addhānamaggappaṭipannassa eḷakalomāni uppajjeyyu”ntiādikaṃ etaṃ sabbaṃ. Vatthumattadīpanamevāti “tena kho pana samayena aññatarassa bhikkhuno kosalesu janapade sāvatthiṃ gacchantassa antarāmagge eḷakalomāni uppajjiṃsū”tiādikassa (pārā. 571) vatthumattassa dīpanameva. Yattha katthacīti addhānato aññatthāpi yattha katthaci ṭhānesu. Sahatthāti karaṇatthe nissakkavacananti āha “sahatthenā”ti. Lakkhaṇavacanañcetaṃ, tasmā yena kenaci sarīrāvayavenāti attho daṭṭhabbo. Tenāha “attanā haritabbānīti attho”ti. Asante hāraketi ettha padānaṃ antogadhāvadhāraṇato avadhāraṇattho labbhatīti āha “asanteyevā”tiādi.

The term 'addhānamaggappaṭipannassa' means 'for one who has set out on a journey-path'; a journey is the path, hence 'journey-path', and 'for one who has set out on it' is the meaning. Therefore, it is said, 'designated as a journey,' and so on. Because it is qualified by the word 'journey,' it is called 'a long road.' In the analysis of the time for traveling a journey, from the statement, 'One should eat thinking, "I will travel half a yojana,"' and so on (Pāc. 218), even half a yojana is a journey-path. These sheep's wool, if they arise elsewhere than on the journey-path, are not permissible to receive, since it is said, 'for a bhikkhu traveling on a journey,' and so on. With reference to this question, it is said, 'all this,' and so on. Here, 'all this' refers to the entire passage beginning, 'If sheep's wool should arise for a bhikkhu traveling on a journey…' It is merely an explanation of the incident, that is, it is only an explanation of the incident beginning, 'At that time, for a certain bhikkhu traveling through the Kosala country to Sāvatthī, sheep's wool arose along the way…' (Pārā. 571). 'Wherever' means in any place other than on the journey. 'With his own hand'—this is a term of agency in the instrumental sense, hence it is said, 'with his own hand.' And this is a descriptive term; therefore, the meaning should be understood as 'with any part of the body.' Hence, it is said, 'meaning they must be carried by oneself.' In 'if there is no carrier,' the emphatic sense is obtained from the implied emphasis within the words; therefore, it is said, 'only if there is no one,' and so on.

Ettha ca “imāni me, bhante, eḷakalomāni tiyojanaṃ atikkāmitāni nissaggiyānī”tiādinā (pārā. 573) nissajjanavidhānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tikapācittiyanti atirekatiyojane atirekatiyojanasaññivematikaūnakasaññīnaṃ vasena tīṇi pācittiyāni. Vāsādhippāyena gantvā tato paraṃ haraṇeti yattha gato, tattha uddesaparipucchādīnaṃ vā paccayādīnaṃ vā alābhena tato paraṃ aññattha haraṇe, tatopi aññatthāti evaṃ yojanasatampi haraṇe anāpatti. Acchinnaṃ vā nissaṭṭhaṃ vāti corehi acchinnaṃ vā vinayakammakataṃ vā. Katabhaṇḍanti kataṃ bhaṇḍaṃ kambalakojavasanthatādi yaṃ kiñci antamaso suttakena baddhamattampi. Tenāha “antamaso”tiādi. Yo pana tanukapattatthavikantare (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.575) vā āyogaaṃsabaddhakakāyabandhanādīnaṃ [V 0.0295] antaresu vā pipphalikādīnaṃ malarakkhaṇatthaṃ sipāṭikāyaṃ vā antamaso vātābādhiko kaṇṇacchiddepi lomāni pakkhipitvā gacchati[M 0.0321], āpattiyeva. Suttakena pana bandhitvā pakkhittaṃ katabhaṇḍaṭṭhāne tiṭṭhati, veṇiṃ katvā harati, idaṃ nidhānamukhaṃ nāma, āpattiyeva.

Here, the method of relinquishment should be understood according to the formula beginning, "Venerable sir, this sheep's wool of mine, having been carried beyond three yojanas, is to be relinquished…" (Pārā. 573). A 'threefold pācittiya' means that when one has exceeded three yojanas, there are three pācittiya offenses, based on whether one perceives it as exceeding, is doubtful, or perceives it as less. If one goes with the intention of residing, but then carries it further—if, at the place one has gone, one does not obtain instruction, questioning, or requisites, and so carries it further to another place, and from there to yet another, there is no offense even if one carries it a hundred yojanas. 'Snatched away or relinquished' means either snatched away by thieves or relinquished through a formal Vinaya act. 'A manufactured item' means any made article, such as a woolen blanket, a rug with long pile, or a spread, or even something merely bound with a thread. Hence, it is said, 'even as little as…' and so on. However, if one goes having placed wool in the fold of a bag made of thin leaves (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.575), or in the gaps of a yoke, shoulder-strap, or body-binding, or in a small bag for protecting things like peppercorns from dirt, or even if a person with a wind-illness stuffs it into their ear-hole, there is an offense. But if, having bound it with a thread, it is put down, it stands in the place of a manufactured item. If one carries it having made it into a braid, this is called a 'means of concealment,' and there is an offense.

Paṭhamappaṭilābhoti attano atthāya eḷakalomānaṃ paṭhamuppatti. Etena acchinnanissaṭṭhappaṭiladdhānaṃ paṭikkhepo. Aññassa ajānantassa yāne pakkhipitvāti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.572) gacchante rathādike vā hatthipiṭṭhiādīsu vā sāmikassa ajānantasseva “harissatī”ti pakkhipitvā. Agacchantepi eseva nayo. Sace pana agacchante rathādimhi vā hatthipiṭṭhiādīsu vā ṭhapetvā ārohitvā sāreti, heṭṭhā vā gacchanto codeti, pakkosanto vā anubandhāpeti, “aññaṃ harāpetī”ti (pārā. 575) vacanato anāpatti. Ettha ca “ajānantassa yāne”ti iminā jānantassa ce yāne pakkhipati, aññaṃ harāpeti nāmāti dasseti. Aharaṇapaccāharaṇanti haraṇapaccāharaṇānamabhāvo.

'First acquisition' means the first arising of sheep's wool for one's own purpose. By this is excluded that which is re-obtained after having been snatched away or relinquished. 'Placing it in another's vehicle without his knowing' (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.572) means placing it in a moving cart or the like, or on an elephant's back or the like, without the owner's knowledge, thinking, 'He will carry it.' This same principle applies even if it is not moving. But if one places it in a non-moving cart or the like, or on an elephant's back or the like, and then, having mounted, makes it go, or, while walking below, urges it on, or, while calling out, has it followed, there is no offense, according to the phrase 'causes another to carry it' (Pārā. 575). And here, the phrase 'in the vehicle without his knowing' shows that if one places it in the vehicle with his knowledge, it is called 'causing another to carry it.' 'Non-carrying and non-bringing back' means the absence of carrying and bringing back.

Eḷakalomasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Sheep's Wool is concluded.

7. Eḷakalomadhovāpanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Having Sheep's Wool Washed

Sakkesūti “sakyā vata, bho kumārā”ti (dī. ni. 1.267) udānaṃ paṭicca “sakyā”ti laddhanāmānaṃ nivāso ekopi janapado ruḷhisaddena “sakkā”ti vuccati, tasmiṃ sakkesu janapade. Chabbaggiyā nāma paṇḍukalohitakādayo chamūlakā, tesaṃ sissā ca.

'Among the Sakyans' means: in the country of the Sakyans. Their dwelling place, even a single country, is conventionally called 'Sakkā', for they obtained the name 'Sakyans' on account of the inspired utterance, "Indeed, sirs, the princes are capable (sakyā)!" (Dī. Ni. 1.267). The Group of Six by name are the six principal ones—Paṇḍuka, Lohitaka, and the others—and their disciples.

Eḷakalomadhovāpanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Having Sheep's Wool Washed is concluded.

8. Jātarūpasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Gold and Silver

Rajatanti na kevalaṃ rūpiyameva idhādhippetaṃ, atha kho yaṃ kiñci vohāragamanīyaṃ kahāpaṇādi ca etaṃ adhippetanti āha “apicā”tiādi. Tattha kahāpaṇoti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.583-584) suvaṇṇamayo vā rūpiyamayo vā pākatiko vā. Lohamāsako nāma tambalohādīhi katamāsako. Dārumāsako nāma sāradārunā vā veḷupesikāya vā [M 0.0322] antamaso tālapaṇṇenapi [V 0.0296] rūpaṃ chinditvā katamāsako. Jatumāsako nāma lākhāya vā niyyāsena vā rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā katamāsako. “Ye vohāraṃ gacchantī”ti iminā pana padena yo yo yattha yattha janapade yadā yadā vohāraṃ gacchati, antamaso aṭṭhimayopi cammamayopi rukkhaphalabījamayopi samuṭṭhāpitarūpopi asamuṭṭhāpitarūpopi sabbo saṅgahito. Tadevāti jātarūparajatameva. Hiraññaṃ nāma kahāpaṇo.

'Silver': not only silver coin is intended here, but rather whatever is used in transactions, such as a kahāpaṇa and so on; this is what is meant, as stated by 'moreover,' etc. Here, a 'kahāpaṇa' (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.583-584) is one made of gold, or of silver, or a common one. A 'lohamāsaka' is a māsaka made of copper, bronze, or other metals. A 'dārumāsaka' is a māsaka made by cutting a shape from hardwood, a strip of bamboo, or even from a palm leaf. A 'jatumāsaka' is a māsaka made by forming a shape from lac or resin. By the phrase 'those that are used in transactions,' whatever is used as currency in any country at any time is included, even if made of bone, leather, or the seeds of fruit trees, whether it has a raised image or not. 'That very thing' means gold and silver itself. 'Hirañña' means a kahāpaṇa.

“Sādiyatī”ti vuttamevatthaṃ vibhāveti “gaṇhitukāmo hotī”ti. Na kevalaṃ kāyavācāhi paṭikkhittameva paṭikkhittaṃ hoti, atha kho manasāpi paṭikkhittaṃ paṭikkhittameva hotīti āha “kāyavācāhī”tiādi. Sace pana kāyavācāhi appaṭikkhipitvā cittena adhivāseti, kāyavācāhi kattabbassa paṭikkhepassa akaraṇato akiriyasamuṭṭhānaṃ kāyavacīdvāre āpattiṃ āpajjati. Manodvāre pana āpatti nāma natthi.

He explains the meaning of 'sādiyati' (he consents) as 'he desires to take.' Not only is what is rejected by body and speech considered rejected, but also what is rejected by mind is considered rejected, as indicated by the phrase 'by body and speech,' and so on. But if, without rejecting by body and speech, he acquiesces in mind, then, because of the non-performance of the rejection that should be done by body and speech, he incurs an offense at the doors of body and speech, which arises from non-action. But there is no offense at the mind-door.

Eko sataṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.583-584) vā sahassaṃ vā pādamūle ṭhapeti “tuyhidaṃ hotū”ti, bhikkhu “nayidaṃ kappatī”ti paṭikkhipati. Upāsako “pariccattaṃ mayā tumhāka”nti gato, añño tattha āgantvā pucchati “kiṃ, bhante, ida”nti. Yaṃ tena ca attanā ca vuttaṃ, taṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ. So ce vadati “gopessāmi, bhante, guttaṭṭhānaṃ dassethā”ti, sattabhūmikampi pāsādaṃ abhiruhitvā “idaṃ guttaṭṭhāna”nti ācikkhitabbaṃ, “idha nikkhipāhī”ti na vattabbaṃ. Ettāvatā kappiyañca akappiyañca nissāya ṭhitaṃ hoti, dvāraṃ pidahitvā rakkhantena vasitabbaṃ. Sace kiñci vikkāyikabhaṇḍaṃ pattaṃ vā cīvaraṃ vā āgacchati, “idaṃ gahessatha, bhante”ti vutte “upāsaka, atthi amhākaṃ iminā attho, vatthu ca evarūpaṃ nāma saṃvijjati, kappiyakārako natthī”ti vattabbaṃ. Sace so vadati “ahaṃ kappiyakārako bhavissāmi, dvāraṃ vivaritvā dethā”ti, dvāraṃ vivaritvā “imasmiṃ okāse ṭhapita”nti vattabbaṃ, “imaṃ gaṇhā”ti na vattabbaṃ. Evañca kappiyañca akappiyañca nissāya ṭhitameva hoti. So cetaṃ gahetvā tassa kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ deti, vaṭṭati. Sace adhikaṃ gaṇhāti, “na mayaṃ tava bhaṇḍaṃ gaṇhāma, nikkhamāhī”ti vattabbo.

Someone places a hundred or a thousand (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.583-584) at his feet with the words, 'This is for you.' The monk refuses, saying, 'This is not allowable.' The lay follower goes away saying, 'I have relinquished it to you.' Another person arrives there and asks, 'What is this, venerable sir?' Whatever was said by that person and oneself should be explained. If he says, 'I will guard it, venerable sir; show me a safe place,' even a seven-storied mansion may be ascended, and it should be pointed out, saying, 'This is a safe place.' But one should not say, 'Place it here.' By this much, it stands in a state involving both the allowable and the unallowable. The door should be closed, and one should dwell guarding it. If any merchandise for sale, such as a bowl or robe, arrives, and someone says, 'Take this, venerable sir,' one should say, 'Lay follower, we have a need for this, and such an item is available, but there is no one to make it allowable.' If he says, 'I will be the one to make it allowable; open the door and give it,' the door should be opened, and it should be said, 'It is placed in this spot.' But one should not say, 'Take this.' And thus, it remains in a state involving both the allowable and the unallowable. If he takes this and gives him allowable goods, it is permissible. If he takes more, he should be told, 'We are not taking your goods; leave.'

Saṅghamajjheyeva [M 0.0323] nissajjitabbanti ettha yasmā rūpiyaṃ nāma akappiyaṃ, tasmā “nissajjitabbaṃ saṅghassa vā gaṇassa vā puggalassa vā”ti na vuttaṃ. Yasmā pana taṃ paṭiggahitamattameva, na tena kiñci kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ cetāpitaṃ, tasmā upāyena paribhogadassanatthaṃ “saṅghamajjheyeva nissajjitabba”nti vuttaṃ. Ādi-saddena telādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Soti yo gahaṭṭho “sappi [V 0.0297] vā telaṃ vā vaṭṭati upāsakā”tiādinā nayena vutto, so. Aññena labhitvāti bhikkhunā vā ārāmikena vā attano vassaggena labhitvā. Tato nibbattarukkhacchāyāpīti nissaggiyavatthunā āhaṭabījato nibbattarukkhaparicchedena ṭhitacchāyāpi, paricchedātikkantā pana āgantukattā vaṭṭati. No ce chaḍḍetīti atha neva gahetvā gacchati, na chaḍḍeti, “kiṃ mayhaṃ iminā byāpārenā”ti yenakāmaṃ pakkamati. Pañcaṅgasamannāgato “yo na chandāgatiṃ gaccheyya, na dosāgatiṃ gaccheyya, na mohāgatiṃ gaccheyya, na bhayāgatiṃ gaccheyya, chaḍḍitāchaḍḍitañca jāneyyā”ti (pārā. 584) evaṃ vuttapañcaṅgehi samannāgato. Sammannitabboti “suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho, yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, saṅgho itthannāmaṃ bhikkhuṃ rūpiyachaḍḍakaṃ sammanneyyā”tiādinā padabhājane vuttāya ñattidutiyakammavācāya sammannitabbo.

In the midst of the Sangha alone it should be relinquished—here, because money is unallowable, it is not said, 'It should be relinquished to the Sangha, a group, or an individual.' However, since it was merely received and no allowable goods were procured with it, therefore, to show a method for its use, it is said, 'It should be relinquished in the midst of the Sangha alone.' By the word 'ādi' (etc.), oil and so on are included. 'He' refers to the householder mentioned in the phrase, 'Ghee or oil is allowable, lay followers,' and so on. 'Obtained by another' means obtained by a monk, a monastery worker, or by one of equal seniority. 'Even the shade produced from it' refers to even the shade cast by a tree grown from seeds brought with the relinquished item, standing within its boundary; if it extends beyond the boundary, it is permissible because it is adventitious. 'If he does not discard it' means he neither takes it nor discards it, but thinking, 'What use is this trouble to me?' he departs as he pleases. 'Endowed with five qualities' refers to one who does not act out of favoritism, ill will, delusion, or fear, and knows what has and has not been discarded, as stated (Pārā. 584). 'Should be appointed' means appointed by a formal act with a motion and one announcement, as described in the procedure: 'Venerable sirs, may the Sangha hear me. If it is timely for the Sangha, the Sangha should appoint the monk so-and-so as the discarder of money.'

Animittaṃ katvā gūthaṃ viya chaḍḍetabbanti patitaṭṭhānaṃ sallakkhaṇavasena nimittaṃ akatvā gūthaṃ viya chaḍḍetabbaṃ, akkhīni nimīletvāva nadiyā vā papāte vā vanagahane vā gūthaṃ viya anapekkhena patitokāsaṃ asamannāharantena pātetabbanti vuttaṃ hoti. Tenāha “gūthaṃ viya chaḍḍetabba”nti. Tikapācittiyanti rūpiyasaññivematikaarūpiyasaññīnaṃ vasena tīṇi pācittiyāni. Arūpiye rūpiyasaññinoti kharapattādīsu suvaṇṇādisaññino. Ratanasikkhāpadanayenāti “ajjhārāme vā ajjhāvasathe vā”ti (pāci. 505) ettha vuttavidhinā.

'Having made no sign, it should be discarded like excrement' means it should be discarded like excrement without making a sign by observing the place where it falls. It is said that one should drop it, as if closing one's eyes, into a river, a precipice, or a dense forest, like excrement, without attachment and without paying attention to the place where it falls. Hence it is said, 'It should be discarded like excrement.' 'Three Pācittiyas' refers to the three Pācittiya offenses based on perception: perceiving it as money, being in doubt, and perceiving what is not money as money. 'Perceiving what is not money as money' means having the perception of gold, etc., in things like rough leaves. 'According to the method of the Ratanasikkhāpada' means according to the procedure explained there, as stated in the rule, 'in a monastery or a dwelling place' (Pāci. 505).

Jātarūpasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Gold and Silver is concluded.

9. Rūpiyasaṃvohārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Monetary Transactions

Katādivasenāti [M 0.0324] kataakatakatākatavasena. Suvaṇṇādicatubbidhampi nissaggiyavatthu idha rūpiyaggahaṇena gahitanti āha “jātarūparajataparivattana”nti. Idañca ukkaṭṭhaparicchedena vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tenāha “purimasikkhāpadena hī”tiādi. Parivattananti sāditarūpiyassa parivattanaṃ. Purimanayānusārenāti “ahaṃ, bhante, nānappakārakaṃ rūpiyasaṃvohāraṃ samāpajjiṃ, idaṃ me nissaggiya”ntiādinā (pārā. 589).

Regarding 'katādivasena,' it means by way of what is done, not done, and partially done. Even the four kinds of items subject to relinquishment, such as gold, are included here under the term 'money,' as stated in the phrase 'jātarūparajataparivattana' (exchange of gold and silver). This should be understood as being stated according to the highest standard. Hence it is said, 'as in the previous training rule,' and so forth. 'Parivattana' refers to the exchange of money that has been accepted. Following the previous method means saying, 'Venerable sir, I have engaged in various kinds of monetary transactions; this is to be relinquished,' and so forth (Pārā. 589).

Rūpiyasaṃvohāravatthusminti paṭiggahaṇasseva paṭikkhittattā paṭiggahitaparivattane dosaṃ adisvā rūpiyaparivattane. Tassa vāti parivattitassa vā. Dhanassa vāti attano mūladhanassa vā[V 0.0298]. Attano vā hi arūpiyena parassa rūpiyaṃ cetāpeyya, attano vā rūpiyena parassa arūpiyaṃ, ubhayathāpi rūpiyasaṃvohāro katova hotīti.

Regarding the matter of monetary transaction: since the acceptance itself is prohibited, one might not see a fault in exchanging what has already been accepted; the fault is in the exchange of money itself. 'Of that' means of what has been exchanged. 'Of wealth' means of one's own principal wealth. For if one were to obtain another's money with one's own non-money, or another's non-money with one's own money, in both cases, a monetary transaction is indeed performed.

Rūpiyasaṃvohārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Monetary Transactions is concluded.

10. Kayavikkayasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Buying and Selling

Rūpiyasaṃvohārassa pana heṭṭhāsikkhāpadena gahitattā kappiyabhaṇḍānamevettha gahaṇanti āha “cīvarādīna”ntiādi. Tattha cīvarādīnaṃ kappiyabhaṇḍānanti antamaso dasikasuttaṃ upādāya cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayānaṃ yesaṃ kesañci kappiyabhaṇḍānaṃ. Kayaṃ nāma parabhaṇḍassa gahaṇaṃ. Vikkayaṃ nāma attano bhaṇḍassa dānaṃ. Tenāha “iminā imaṃ dehī”tiādi. Parassāti ṭhapetvā pañca sahadhammike aññassa. Ettha ca “ahaṃ, bhante, nānappakārakaṃ kayavikkayaṃ samāpajjiṃ, idaṃ me nissaggiyaṃ, imāhaṃ saṅghassa nissajjāmī”tiādinā (pārā. 595) nayena nissajjitabbaṃ. Tenāha “vuttalakkhaṇavasenā”tiādi. Nanu cettha cīvaradhovane vā kesacchedane vā bhūmisodhanādinavakamme vā parabhaṇḍaṃ attano hatthagataṃ nissajjitabbaṃ nāma natthi, tattha kiṃ kātabbanti āha “asante pācittiyaṃ desetabbamevā”ti. Yathā nissaggiyavatthumhi paribhutte vā naṭṭhe vā pācittiyaṃ deseti, evaṃ idhāpi desetabbamevāti adhippāyo.

However, since monetary transactions are covered by the preceding training rule, only allowable goods are to be taken here, as stated, 'such as robes,' and so forth. In this context, 'allowable goods such as robes' refers to any allowable goods whatsoever, such as robes, almsfood, lodging, or medicinal requisites, down to a single thread. 'Buying' means acquiring another's goods. 'Selling' means giving away one's own goods. Hence it is said, 'Give me this for that,' and so forth. 'Another' means anyone other than the five fellow monastics. Here, one should relinquish by the method of saying, 'Venerable sir, I have engaged in various kinds of buying and selling; this is to be relinquished; this I relinquish to the Sangha,' and so forth (Pārā. 595). Therefore it is said, 'according to the stated characteristics,' and so forth. Now, one might ask: 'In cases like washing robes, cutting hair, or performing new construction work such as cleaning the ground, if another's goods come into one's possession, is there nothing to relinquish? What should be done then?' The reply is: 'If there is no item to be relinquished, only a pācittiya should be declared.' Just as when an item subject to relinquishment has been used or lost, one declares a pācittiya, so too here—only a pācittiya should be declared. This is the meaning.

Idaṃ [M 0.0325] amhākaṃ atthīti idaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ telaṃ vā sappi vā amhākaṃ saṃvijjati. Amhākañca iminā ca iminā ca atthoti amhākañca tadaññena iminā ca iminā ca appaṭiggahitakena attho. “Rūpiyasaṃvohāre vuttanayamevā”ti iminā “tikapācittiyaṃ akayavikkaye kayavikkayasaññino ca vematikassa ca dukkaṭa”nti imaṃ nayamatidisati.

'This is ours' means this accepted oil or ghee exists for us. 'And we have need of this and that' means we have need of this and that which is unaccepted, along with something else. 'The same method applies as stated for monetary transactions.' By this, it refers to the method whereby 'a threefold pācittiya offense arises for not engaging in buying and selling, and a dukkaṭa for one who perceives buying and selling when there is none, or for one who is uncertain.'

Kayavikkayasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Buying and Selling is concluded.

Eḷakalomavaggo dutiyo.

The Second Chapter on Wool.

3. Pattavaggo

3. The Chapter on Bowls.

1. Pattasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Bowl.

Avikappitoti [V 0.0299] “imaṃ pattaṃ tuyhaṃ vikappemī”tiādinā nayena avikappito. Aḍḍhāḷhakodanaṃ gaṇhātīti magadhanāḷiyā dvinnaṃ taṇḍulanāḷīnaṃ odanaṃ gaṇhāti. “Magadhanāḷi nāma aḍḍhaterasapalā hotī”ti andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. “Sīhaḷadīpe pakatināḷi mahantā, damiḷanāḷi khuddakā, magadhanāḷi pamāṇayuttā, tāya magadhanāḷiyā diyaḍḍhanāḷi ekā sīhaḷanāḷi hotī”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.602) mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Anuttaṇḍulanti pākato ukkantaṃ taṇḍulaṃ uttaṇḍulaṃ, na uttaṇḍulaṃ anuttaṇḍulaṃ. Sabbasambhārasaṅkhatoti jīrakādisabbasambhārehi saṅkhato. Ālopassa catutthabhāgappamāṇaṃ byañjanaṃ ālopassa anurūpabyañjanaṃ.

'Avikappita' means not designated by the method of saying, 'I designate this bowl to you,' and so forth. 'Takes half an āḷhaka of cooked rice' means takes cooked rice from two nāḷis of uncooked rice by Magadhan measure. 'The Magadhan nāḷi is said to be twelve and a half palas,' as stated in the Andhakaṭṭhakathā. 'In the island of the Sinhalese, the standard nāḷi is large, the Tamil nāḷi is small, and the Magadhan nāḷi is of proper measure; one and a half of that Magadhan nāḷi make one Sinhalese nāḷi,' as mentioned in the Mahāaṭṭhakathā. 'Anuttaṇḍula' means 'uttaṇḍula' is rice that is overcooked; 'anuttaṇḍula' is not 'uttaṇḍula.' 'Prepared with all condiments' means prepared with all condiments such as cumin and so forth. 'Condiment proportionate to the morsel' means condiment to the measure of a fourth part of the morsel.

Evaṃ ukkaṭṭhapattaṃ dassetvā idāni majjhimomakāni dassetuṃ “ukkaṭṭhato”tiādimāha. Tatrāyaṃ nayo – sace nāḷikodanādi sabbampi pakkhittaṃ vuttanayeneva heṭṭhimarājisamaṃ tiṭṭhati, ayaṃ majjhimo nāma patto. Sace taṃ rājiṃ atikkamma thūpīkataṃ tiṭṭhati, ayaṃ majjhimomako nāma patto. Sace taṃ rājiṃ na sampāpuṇāti, antogadhameva hoti, ayaṃ majjhimukkaṭṭho nāma patto. Sace pattodanādi sabbampi pakkhittaṃ heṭṭhimarājisamaṃ tiṭṭhati, ayaṃ omako nāma patto. Sace taṃ rājiṃ atikkamma thūpīkataṃ tiṭṭhati, ayaṃ omakomako nāma patto. Sace taṃ rājiṃ [M 0.0326] na sampāpuṇāti, antogadhameva hoti, ayaṃ omakukkaṭṭho nāma pattoti. Tenāha “tesampi vuttanayeneva bhedo veditabbo”ti.

Having thus shown the excellent bowl, now to show the medium and inferior ones, it is said, 'from the excellent,' and so forth. Here, the method is as follows: If all the nāḷi of cooked rice and so forth, having been placed as described, stands level with the lower line, this is called a medium bowl. If it stands heaped up, exceeding that line, this is called a medium-inferior bowl. If it does not reach that line but remains contained within, this is called a medium-excellent bowl. If all the bowl’s contents, such as cooked rice, having been placed as described, stand level with the lower line, this is called an inferior bowl. If it stands heaped up, exceeding that line, this is called an inferior-inferior bowl. If it does not reach that line but remains contained within, this is called an inferior-excellent bowl. Therefore, it is said, 'for these too, the distinctions should be understood in the same way.'

Idāni tesu adhiṭṭhānavikappanānadhiṭṭhānāvikappanupage dassetuṃ “iccetesū”tiādimāha. Tattha ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭhoti ukkaṭṭhato ukkaṭṭho. Tato hi so “apatto”ti vutto. Omakomakoti omakato omako. Tato hi so “apatto”ti vutto. Ete pana bhājanaparibhogena paribhuñjitabbā, na adhiṭṭhānupagā na vikappanupagā, itare pana satta adhiṭṭhahitvā vā vikappetvā vā paribhuñjitabbā. Tenāha “sesā satta pattā pamāṇayuttā nāmā”ti.

Now, to show among these bowls those that are suitable for determination and designation and those that are not, it is said, 'Herein, these,' and so forth. In this context, 'ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭha' means the most excellent of the excellent. For that reason, it is said to be 'not a bowl.' 'Omakomaka' means the most inferior of the inferior. For that reason, it is said to be 'not a bowl.' These, however, should be used as ordinary vessels, not being suitable for determination or designation; but the other seven should be used after determining or designating them. Therefore it is said, 'The remaining seven bowls are called 'of proper measure.''

Tasmāti [V 0.0300] yasmā satta pattā pamāṇayuttā, tasmā. Samaṇasāruppena pakkanti ettha ayopatto pañcahi pākehi (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.608) pakko samaṇasāruppena pakko hoti, mattikāpatto dvīhi pākehi. Sace eko pāko ūno hoti, na adhiṭṭhānupago. Yathā ca samaṇasāruppena pakkoyeva adhiṭṭhānupago, tathā ubhopi yaṃ mūlaṃ dātabbaṃ, tasmiṃ dinneyeva adhiṭṭhānupagā. Yadi pana appakampi adinnaṃ hoti, na adhiṭṭhānupagā. Tenāha “sace panā”tiādi. “Kākaṇikamattaṃ nāma diyaḍḍhavīhī”ti vadanti. Sacepi pattasāmiko vadati “yadā tumhākaṃ mūlaṃ bhavissati, tadā dassatha, adhiṭṭhahitvā paribhuñjathā”ti, neva adhiṭṭhānupago hoti. Pākassa hi ūnattā pattasaṅkhaṃ na gacchati. Mūlassa sakalassa vā ekadesassa vā adinnattā sakabhāvaṃ na upeti, aññasseva santako hoti. Tasmā pāke ca mūle ca niṭṭhiteyeva adhiṭṭhānupago hoti. Yo adhiṭṭhānupago, sveva vikappanupago ca. Tenāha “apaccuddharantenā”tiādi. Apaccuddharantena vikappetabboti purāṇapattaṃ apaccuddharantena navo patto vikappetabboti attho, ṭhapetabboti adhippāyo. Kaṅgusitthanti sattannaṃ dhaññānaṃ lāmakadhaññasitthanti āha “kaṅgusitthanikkhamanamattena chiddenā”ti.

'Therefore' means because the seven bowls are of proper measure, therefore. 'Properly fired for an ascetic' means here an iron bowl, fired five times, is properly fired for an ascetic; an earthen bowl is properly fired by two firings. If even one firing is lacking, it is not suitable for determination. Just as only a bowl properly fired for an ascetic is suitable for determination, so too both types of bowls are suitable for determination only when the full price that is to be given has been given. But if even a little is not given, they are not suitable for determination. Therefore it is said, 'But if,' and so forth. They say, 'A kākaṇika's worth is one and a half rice grains.' Even if the owner of the bowl says, 'When you have the price, then give it; determine it and use it,' it is still not suitable for determination. For due to the lack of a firing, it does not count as a bowl. And due to the price, whether whole or partial, not being given, it does not become one's own property but belongs to someone else. Therefore, only when both the firing and the price are complete is it suitable for determination. What is suitable for determination is also suitable for designation. Therefore it is said, 'Without setting aside,' and so forth. 'It should be designated without setting aside' means the new bowl should be designated without setting aside the old bowl; the intention is that it should be put aside. 'Kaṅgusittha' means a grain of millet, an inferior grain among the seven kinds of grains; it is said, 'with a hole just large enough for a millet grain to pass through.'

Pattasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Bowl is concluded.

2. Ūnapañcabandhanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Fewer Than Five Bonds.

Assāti [M 0.0327] imassa pattassa. Tena ūnapañcabandhanenāti tena ūnapañcabandhanena pattena upalakkhito hutvāti attho. Ūnapañcabandhano hi patto ettha lakkhaṇabhāvena gahito. Tenevāha “itthambhūtassa lakkhaṇe karaṇavacana”nti. Tattha itthambhūtassāti kañci pakāraṃ pattassa. Lakkhīyate anenāti lakkhaṇaṃ, tasmiṃ karaṇavacanaṃ, tatiyāvibhattīti attho. “Pakāro”ti ca sāmaññassa bhedako viseso vuccati. Tathā hi ūnapañcabandhanena pattenāti ettha bhikkhubhāvasāmaññassa ūnapañcabandhanapattabhāvo pakāro, taṃ bhikkhu āpanno, tassa patto lakkhaṇaṃ. Yadi aparipuṇṇapañcabandhano patto ūnapañcabandhano nāma hoti, atha kasmā imassa padabhājaniyaṃ abandhanopi vuttoti āha “tatthā”tiādi. Tattha tatthāti vākyopaññāse. Bandhanokāse sati vā asati vā bandhanavirahito patto abandhano, pañcabandhanānaṃ okāso assāti pañcabandhanokāso. Apattoti patto nāma na hotīti attho, pākatikaṃ kātuṃ asamatthoti vuttaṃ hoti. Idañca aññassa viññāpane kāraṇavacanaṃ. Tenāha “tasmā aññaṃ viññāpetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti.

“Assa” means ‘of this bowl.’ “Tena ūnapañcabandhanena” (by that with fewer than five bonds) means “being characterized by a bowl with fewer than five bonds.” Indeed, a bowl with fewer than five bonds is here taken as the characteristic. Therefore, it is said, “the instrumental case in the sense of ‘characteristic of such a state’.” In this context, “of such a state” refers to some condition one has attained. “Characteristic” means that by which something is characterized; in that sense, it is the instrumental case, meaning the third case ending. And “kind” refers to a specific distinction that differentiates the general. Thus, in “by a bowl with fewer than five bonds,” the state of having a bowl with fewer than five bonds is the kind that distinguishes the general state of being a monk; the monk has attained that state, and his bowl is the characteristic. If a bowl that is not fully bound with five bonds is called “one with fewer than five bonds,” then why is “without binding” also mentioned in the analysis of terms? He says, “herein,” and so on. “Herein, herein” is for introducing the statement. Whether there is an occasion for binding or not, a bowl devoid of binding is “without binding.” “Occasion for five bonds” means there is an occasion for five bonds. “Not a bowl” means it is not considered a bowl; it is said to be incapable of being made serviceable. This is also an instrumental expression of cause for informing another. Therefore, it is said, “Hence, it is proper to inform another.”

Bandhanañca [V 0.0301] nāmetaṃ yasmā bandhanokāse sati hoti, asati na hoti, tasmā tassa lakkhaṇaṃ, bandhanavidhiñca dassetuṃ “yasmiṃ panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Mukhavaṭṭisamīpe pana pattavedhakena vijjhiyamāne kapālassa bahalattā bhijjati, tasmā heṭṭhā vijjhitabbo. Tenāha “heṭṭhimapariyante”tiādi. Sukhumaṃ vā chiddaṃ katvā bandhitabboti sukhume chidde tipupaṭṭādīhi payojanaṃ natthi, suttaṃ pakkhipitvāva adhiṭṭhātabboti adhippāyo. Na kevalaṃ tipusuttakādināva bandhitabboti āha “phāṇita”ntiādi. Phāṇitaṃ jhāpetvā pāsāṇacuṇṇenāti pāsāṇacuṇṇena saddhiṃ phāṇitaṃ pacitvā tathāpakkena pāsāṇacuṇṇenāti attho. Nissajjitabboti “ayaṃ me, bhante, patto ūnapañcabandhanena pattena cetāpito nissaggiyo, imāhaṃ saṅghassa nissajjāmī”ti (pārā. 613) nissajjitabbo. Tenāha “nissajjantenā”tiādi. Sammatenāti –

And this is called a binding because it exists when there is an occasion for binding, and does not exist when there is not. Therefore, to show its characteristic and the method of binding, “in which case…” and so on, is stated. Moreover, when the bowl is pierced near the rim, the bowl breaks due to its thickness. Therefore, it should be pierced below. Hence it is said, “at the lower edge” and so on. Or, a fine hole should be made and then it should be bound. If the hole is fine, there is no need for tin-plates and so on; the meaning is that the thread should be inserted and then fixed. It should not be bound only with tin-thread and so on; therefore, it is said, “with molasses” and so on. “Molasses should be heated with stone powder” means molasses should be cooked together with stone powder; the meaning is with stone powder cooked in that way. It should be relinquished: saying, “Venerable sir, this bowl of mine, purchased with a bowl with fewer than five bonds, is subject to relinquishment; I relinquish it to the Sangha” (Pārā. 613), it should be relinquished. Therefore, it is said, “by the one who relinquishes” and so on. “By one who is appointed” means…

“Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho, yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, saṅgho itthannāmaṃ bhikkhuṃ pattaggāhāpakaṃ sammanneyya, esā ñatti[M 0.0328]. Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho, saṅgho itthannāmaṃ bhikkhuṃ pattaggāhāpakaṃ sammannati, yassāyasmato khamati itthannāmassa bhikkhuno pattaggāhāpakassa sammuti, so tuṇhassa. Yassa nakkhamati, so bhāseyya. Sammato saṅghena itthannāmo bhikkhu pattaggāhāpako, khamati saṅghassa, tasmā tuṇhī, evametaṃ dhārayāmī”ti (pārā. 614) –

“Venerable sirs, may the Sangha listen to me. If it is the proper time for the Sangha, the Sangha should appoint the monk named so-and-so as the bowl-receiver. This is the motion. Venerable sirs, may the Sangha listen to me. The Sangha appoints the monk named so-and-so as the bowl-receiver. If the appointment of the monk named so-and-so as the bowl-receiver is agreeable to the venerable ones, let them remain silent. If anyone disagrees, they should speak. The monk named so-and-so has been appointed by the Sangha as the bowl-receiver. It is agreeable to the Sangha, therefore it is silent. Thus do I hold it.” (Pārā. 614)

Evaṃ padabhājane vuttāya ñattidutiyakammavācāya sammatena. Pattassa vijjamānaguṇaṃ vatvāti “ayaṃ, bhante, patto pamāṇayutto sundaro therānurūpo”tiādinā (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.615) vijjamānānisaṃsaṃ vatvā. Pattapariyantoti pariyante ṭhitapatto. Adeseti mañcapīṭhacchattanāgadantakādike adese. Pattassa hi nikkhipanadeso “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ādhāraka”ntiādinā nayena khandhake vuttoyeva. Aparibhogenāti yāgurandhanarajanapacanādinā ayuttaparibhogena. Antarāmagge pana byādhimhi uppanne aññasmiṃ bhājane asati mattikāya limpitvā yāguṃ pacituṃ, udakaṃ vā tāpetuṃ vaṭṭati. Vissajjetīti aññassa deti. Sace pana saddhivihāriko vā antevāsiko vā aññaṃ varapattaṃ ṭhapetvā “ayaṃ mayhaṃ sāruppo, ayaṃ therassā”ti gaṇhāti, vaṭṭati. Añño vā taṃ gahetvā attano pattaṃ deti, vaṭṭati. “Mayhameva pattaṃ āharā”ti vattabbakiccaṃ natthi.

Thus, by the one appointed by the formal act consisting of a motion and one announcement, as stated in the analysis of the words. ‘Having stated the existing qualities of the bowl’ means having stated the existing benefits, such as: “Venerable sir, this bowl is of proper measure, beautiful, and suitable for the elder,” and so on (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.615). ‘At the edge of the bowl’ means a bowl placed at the edge. ‘In an unsuitable place’ means on such things as beds, chairs, sunshades, and wall-pegs. Indeed, the place for setting down the bowl has already been stated in the Khandhaka in the manner of saying, “I allow, monks, a stand,” and so on. ‘By improper use’ means by unsuitable use, such as cooking gruel or cooking dye. However, if illness arises while on the road and no other vessel is available, it is permissible to smear the bowl with clay and cook gruel, or to heat water. ‘He relinquishes it’ means he gives it to another. But if a co-resident or a pupil sets aside another superior bowl, thinking, “This one suits me, this one suits the elder,” and takes it, it is permissible. Or if another takes it and gives his own bowl in return, it is permissible. There is no need to say, “Bring my bowl only.”

Ñātakappavāriteti ettha saṅghavasena pavāritaṭṭhāne pañcabandhaneneva vaṭṭati, puggalavasena pana pavāritaṭṭhāne [V 0.0302] ūnapañcabandhanenāpi. Akataviññatti nāma “vada, bhante, paccayenā”ti evaṃ akataṭṭhāne viññatti.

Regarding ‘when invited by relatives’: here, in the case of an invitation to the Sangha, it is allowable only with five bonds; but in the case of an invitation to an individual, it is allowable even with fewer than five bonds. ‘An uninvited request’ means a request made in a situation where one has not been prompted with words such as, ‘Speak, venerable sir, what requisite do you need?’

Ūnapañcabandhanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning fewer than five bonds is concluded.

3. Bhesajjasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Medicine

Uggahetvāti uggahitakaṃ katvā, appaṭiggahitaṃ sayameva gahetvāti attho. Sattāhātikkamepi anāpattikatā cettha anajjhoharaṇīyataṃ āpannattāti veditabbaṃ. Kasmā etena idaṃ dassitaṃ hotīti āha “tāni hī”tiādi. Bhisakkassa imāni tena anuññātattāti bhesajjāni, yesaṃ [M 0.0329] kesañci sappāyānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tenāha “bhesajjakiccaṃ karontu vā, mā vā, evaṃ laddhavohārānī”ti. Idāni sattāhakālikaṃ nissaggiyavatthubhūtaṃ sappinavanītaṃ dassetuṃ “sappi nāma gavādīna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Ādisaddena ajikādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ. “Yesaṃ maṃsaṃ kappatī”ti iminā pākaṭehi goajikādīhi aññānipi migarohitādīni saṅgaṇhāti. Yesañhi khīraṃ atthi, sappipi tesaṃ atthiyeva. Taṃ pana sulabhaṃ vā hotu, dullabhaṃ vā, asaṃmohatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Makkhikāmadhumevāti khuddakabhamaramadhukarīhi tīhi makkhikāhi kataṃ madhumeva. Ucchurasanti suddhodakasambhinnānaṃ vasena duvidhampi ucchurasaṃ. “Agilānassa guḷodaka”nti (mahāva. 284) pana uddissa anuññātattā udakasambhinno agilānassa vaṭṭati. “Avatthukapakkā vā”ti iminā savatthukapakkā na vaṭṭatīti dasseti. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana “etaṃ savatthukapakkaṃ vaṭṭati, no vaṭṭatīti pucchaṃ katvā ucchuphāṇitaṃ pacchābhattaṃ novaṭṭanakaṃ nāma natthī”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ yuttanti samantapāsādikāyaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.623) vuttaṃ. Ucchuvikatīti ucchumhā nibbattā rasalasikādikā. Pakatattānaṃ paṭiniddesattā taṃ-saddassa tena pakatānaṃ bhesajjānaṃ eva gahaṇaṃ, na tesaṃ vatthūnanti āha “tāni bhesajjānī”tiādi. Na tesaṃ vatthūnīti tesaṃ sappiādīnaṃ kāraṇāni khīrādīni appaṭiggahetvāti attho.

‘Having taken up’ means having made it taken up; the meaning is taking it oneself without having received it. Here, it should be understood that even after seven days there is no offense because it has become something not to be consumed. Why is this shown by this? He said, “For these,” and so on. These are medicines because they are permitted by the physician; this is a designation for whatever is suitable for anyone. Therefore, he said, “Whether they are performing a medicinal function or not, they are thus designated.” Now, to show ghee and butter, which are allowable for seven days and are grounds for relinquishment, it was said, “Ghee is from cows,” and so on. The word “and so on” includes goats, and so on. By “whose flesh is allowable,” it includes other animals like deer and antelope, in addition to the obvious cows and goats. For those that have milk, ghee also exists for them. But it was stated to avoid confusion, whether it is easily available or hard to obtain. ‘Bee-honey’ refers only to honey made by three types of bees: small bees, large black bees, and honeybees. ‘Sugarcane juice’ means sugarcane juice of two kinds, depending on whether it is mixed with pure water or not. But since ‘sugar-water for the non-ill’ (Mahāva. 284) was permitted specifically, that which is mixed with water is allowable for the non-ill. By ‘or juice cooked without ingredients,’ it indicates that juice cooked with ingredients is not allowable. However, in the Mahāpaccariya it is said, “This juice cooked with ingredients is allowable, and when asked whether it is allowable or not, there is nothing called ‘non-allowable’ regarding sugarcane molasses after the meal.” This is said to be correct in the Samantapāsādikā (Pārā. aṭṭha. 2.623). ‘Sugarcane products’ means juice, syrup, and so on, derived from sugarcane. Since it is a reference to what has been previously mentioned, the word ‘those’ refers only to those medicines that have been mentioned, not their ingredients. Therefore, he said, “Those are medicines,” and so on. ‘Not their ingredients’ means not receiving the milk, and so on, which are the causes of ghee, and so on—this is the meaning.

Vasātelanti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.623) “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, vasāni bhesajjāni acchavasaṃ macchavasaṃ susukāvasaṃ sūkaravasaṃ gadrabhavasa”nti (mahāva. 262) evaṃ anuññātavasānaṃ telaṃ.
