Yānīti yāni bhesajjāni. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, vasāni bhesajjāni acchavasaṃ macchavasaṃ susukāvasaṃ sūkaravasaṃ gadrabhavasaṃ kāle paṭiggahitaṃ kāle nippakkaṃ [V 0.0303] kāle saṃsaṭṭhaṃ telaparibhogena paribhuñjitu”nti evaṃ telatthaṃ vasāpaṭiggahaṇassa anuññātattā “vasātelaṃ panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Kāleti purebhattaṃ. Saṃsaṭṭhanti parissāvitaṃ. Tasmāti yasmā anuññātaṃ, tasmā. “Acchavasa”nti vacanena ṭhapetvā manussavasaṃ sabbesaṃ akappiyamaṃsānaṃ vasāya anuññātattā “ṭhapetvā manussavasa”nti vuttaṃ.

‘Fat-oil’ (Pārā. aṭṭha. 2.623) refers to the oil from fats thus permitted: “Monks, I allow fats as medicines: bear fat, fish fat, porpoise fat, pig fat, and donkey fat” (Mahāva. 262). ‘Which’ refers to which medicines. Because the acceptance of fat for the purpose of oil is permitted in this way—“Monks, I allow fats as medicines: bear fat, fish fat, porpoise fat, pig fat, and donkey fat—when received at the proper time, prepared at the proper time, and mixed at the proper time, to be consumed for the use of oil”—therefore, it was said, “But fat-oil,” and so on. ‘At the proper time’ means before the midday meal. ‘Mixed’ means strained. ‘Therefore’ means because it is permitted, therefore. By the word ‘bear fat,’ since the fat of an animal with impermissible meat is allowed, the fat of all animals with impermissible meat—except for human fat—is also allowed. Hence, it was said, “except for human fat.”

Sāmaṃ pacitvāti kāleyeva sāmaṃ pacitvā. Nibbattitatelampīti kāleyeva attanā vivecitatelampi. Tividhampi cetaṃ kāleyeva vaṭṭati. Vuttampi cetaṃ “kāle ce, bhikkhave, paṭiggahitaṃ kāle nippakkaṃ kāle [M 0.0330] saṃsaṭṭhaṃ, taṃ ce paribhuñjeyya, anāpattī”ti. Pacchābhattaṃ pana paṭiggahetuṃ vā kātuṃ vā na vaṭṭatiyeva. Vuttampi cetaṃ “vikāle ce, bhikkhave, paṭiggahitaṃ vikāle nippakkaṃ vikāle saṃsaṭṭhaṃ, taṃ ce paribhuñjeyya, āpatti tiṇṇaṃ dukkaṭānaṃ. Kāle ce, bhikkhave, paṭiggahitaṃ vikāle nippakkaṃ vikāle saṃsaṭṭhaṃ, taṃ ce paribhuñjeyya, āpatti dvinnaṃ dukkaṭānaṃ. Kāle ce, bhikkhave, paṭiggahitaṃ kāle nippakkaṃ vikāle saṃsaṭṭhaṃ, taṃ ce paribhuñjeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 262). “Sattāhaṃ nirāmisaparibhogena vaṭṭatī”ti iminā pana “kāle paṭiggahitaṃ kāle nippakkaṃ kāle saṃsaṭṭhaṃ telaparibhogena paribhuñjitu”nti idaṃ nirāmisaparibhogaṃ sandhāya vuttanti dasseti.

“Having cooked it himself” means having cooked it himself at the proper time. “Even oil extracted by himself” means even oil separated by himself at the proper time. And all three of these are allowable only at the proper time. For it was also said: “Monks, if it is received at the proper time, cooked at the proper time, and mixed at the proper time, and one consumes it, there is no offense.” But to receive or prepare it after the meal-time is never allowable. For it was also said: “Monks, if it is received at the wrong time, cooked at the wrong time, and mixed at the wrong time, and one consumes it, there is an offense of three dukkaṭas. If, monks, it is received at the proper time, but cooked at the wrong time and mixed at the wrong time, and one consumes it, there is an offense of two dukkaṭas. If, monks, it is received at the proper time, cooked at the proper time, but mixed at the wrong time, and one consumes it, there is an offense of one dukkaṭa” (Mahāvagga 262). But by “it is allowable to use it for seven days as non-flesh nourishment,” it shows that this refers to “to be consumed for the use of oil, when received at the proper time, properly prepared, and properly mixed,” with reference to non-flesh nourishment.

Yaṃ panettha (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.623) sukhumarajasadisaṃ maṃsaṃ vā nhāru vā aṭṭhi vā lohitaṃ vā hoti, taṃ abbohārikaṃ. Sace pana anupasampanno tāya paṭiggahitavasāya telaṃ katvā deti, taṃ kathanti āha “anupasampannenā”tiādi. Tadahūti yasmiṃ ahani paṭiggahitaṃ, tadahu. Pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya pana sattāhaṃ nirāmisameva vaṭṭati. Tatrāpi abbohārikaṃ abbohārikameva. Yāvakālikavatthūnaṃ aññesaṃ vatthuṃ pacituṃ na vaṭṭatīti sambandho. Tattha yāvakālikavatthūnanti yāvakālikaṃ vatthu etesanti yāvakālikavatthūni, tesaṃ, yāvakālikavatthumantānanti attho. Aññesanti vasātelato aññesaṃ sappiādīnaṃ. Vatthunti khīrādikaṃ yāvakālikabhūtaṃ vatthuṃ, pacituṃ na vaṭṭatiyeva, sāmaṃpākattāti adhippāyo.

Whatever here (Pārā. aṭṭha. 2.623) is flesh like fine dust, or sinew, or bone, or blood, that is unusable. But if an unordained person, having received that fat, makes oil and gives it, how is that? He said, “by an unordained person,” and so on. “On that very day” means the day it was received. But from after the meal onward, it is allowable only as non-flesh for seven days. Even in that case, what is unusable is still unusable. The connection is that it is not allowable to cook other things for temporary requisites. Herein, “temporary requisites” means “things that are temporary for them,” that is, “for those who possess temporary requisites.” “Other things” refers to ghee, and so on, other than fat-oil. “Thing” means milk, and so on, which are temporary requisites. It is indeed not permissible to cook them, because they are to be cooked by oneself—this is the intention.

Nibbattitasappiṃ vāti yāvakālikavatthuto vivecitasappiṃ vā. Yathā tattha dadhigataṃ vā takkagataṃ vā khayaṃ gamissati, evaṃ jhāpitaṃ vāti attho. Navanītaṃ vāti takkabindūnipi dadhiguḷikāyopi apanetvā sudhotanavanītaṃ pacituṃ vaṭṭati sāmaṃpakkābhāvatoti adhippāyo. Yadi sayaṃpacitasattāhakālikena saddhiṃ āmisaṃ bhuñjati, taṃ āmisaṃ sayaṃpacitasattāhakālikena missitaṃ attano yāvakālikabhāvaṃ sattāhakālikena gaṇhāpeti. Tathā [V 0.0304] ca yāvakālikaṃ apakkampi sayaṃpakkabhāvaṃ upagacchatīti “taṃ pana tadahupurebhattampi sāmisaṃ paribhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Yathā sayaṃpakkasattāhakālikaṃ vasātelaṃ, sayaṃbhajjitasāsapādiyāvajīvikavatthūnaṃ telañca sāmisaṃ tadahupurebhattampi na vaṭṭati, tathā navanītasappīti veditabbaṃ. Vuttañca –

“Ghee that has been produced” means ghee that has been separated from a temporary requisite. The meaning is that just as yogurt or buttermilk will eventually spoil there, so too will ghee that has been rendered. “Fresh butter” refers to butter that has been thoroughly cleaned by removing even buttermilk droplets and curd particles, and is suitable for cooking because it is not self-prepared—this is the intention. If one eats flesh with a self-prepared seven-day allowance, that flesh, being mixed with the self-prepared seven-day allowance, is caused by it to take on the nature of a seven-day allowance. And thus, even an uncooked temporary allowance becomes self-prepared. Therefore, it was said, “But even on that day before the meal, it is not permissible to consume such an allowance with flesh.” Just as self-prepared fat-oil that is a seven-day allowance, and oil from mustard and so on, which are lifelong requisites prepared by oneself, cannot be consumed with flesh even on that day before the meal, so too should fresh butter and ghee be understood. And it was said—

“Yāvakālikaādīni[M 0.0331], saṃsaṭṭhāni sahattanā;

Gāhāpayanti sabbhāva”nti ca;

“Teheva bhikkhunā pattaṃ, kappate yāvajīvikaṃ;

Nirāmisaṃva sattāhaṃ, sāmise sāmapākatā”ti ca.

“Temporary requisites and so on, when mixed with their own kind, cause the mixture to take on that nature,” and also; “With these, a bowl obtained by a monk is allowable for life; like non-flesh for seven days, and with flesh, it is self-cooked.”

Khīrāditoti ettha ādisaddena tilādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Sāmisānipīti na kevalaṃ nirāmisānevāti attho. Pacchābhattato pana paṭṭhāya na vaṭṭantiyeva. Sattāhātikkamepi anāpatti savatthukānaṃ paṭiggahitattā. “Tāni paṭiggahetvā”ti (pārā. 622) hi vuttaṃ. Tenāha “pacchābhattato paṭṭhāyā”tiādi. Pacchābhattaṃ paṭiggahitakehi kataṃ pana abbhañjanādīsu upanetabbaṃ, purebhattampi ca uggahitakehi kataṃ. Ubhayesampi sattāhātikkamepi anāpatti. Antosattāheti sattāhabbhantare. Abbhañjanādīnanti ettha ādisaddena muddhanitelaarumakkhanagharadhūpanādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Adhiṭṭhahitvāti “idāni na mayhaṃ ajjhoharaṇatthāya bhavissati, idaṃ sappi ca telañca vasā ca muddhanitelatthaṃ vā abbhañjanatthaṃ vā bhavissati, madhu arumakkhanatthaṃ vā phāṇitaṃ gharadhūpanatthaṃ vā bhavissatī”ti evaṃ cittaṃ uppādetvā.

“From milk, and so on”—here, the word “and so on” includes sesame, and so on. “Even with flesh” means not only non-flesh foods. However, from after the meal onward, they are never allowable. Even if seven days pass, there is no offense, because they were received with a valid reason. For it was said, “Having accepted them” (Pārā. 622). Therefore, he said, “starting from after the meal,” and so on. But what is prepared after the meal by those who have received it should be applied to ointments, and so on; and what is prepared before the meal by those who have taken it for themselves should also be applied. In both cases, even if seven days pass, there is no offense. “Within seven days” means within the period of seven days. “Ointments, and so on”—here, the word “and so on” includes head oil, body oil, ointment for sores, house fumigation, and so on. “Having determined” means generating the thought thus: “Now this will not be for my consumption; this ghee, oil, or fat will be for head oil or for anointing; this honey will be for ointment for sores or this molasses for house fumigation.”

Ko panettha yāvakālikayāvajīvikavatthūsu visesoti āha “yāvajīvikānī”tiādi. Yāva aruṇassa uggamanā tiṭṭhatīti sattamadivase katatelaṃ sace yāva aruṇuggamanā tiṭṭhatīti attho. Pāḷiyaṃ anāgatasappiādīnanti ettha tāva migarohitādīnaṃ sappi pāḷiyaṃ anāgatasappi, tathā navanītaṃ, nāḷikeranimbakosambakaramandasāsapaādīnaṃ telaṃ pana pāḷiyaṃ anāgatatelaṃ, tathā madhukapupphaphāṇitaṃ pāḷiyaṃ anāgataphāṇitanti veditabbaṃ. Na sabbaṃ madhukapupphaphāṇitaṃ phāṇitagatikanti āha “sītudakenā”tiādi. Sītudakena katanti madhukapupphāni sītudake pakkhipitvā amadditvā puppharase udakagate sati taṃ udakaṃ gahetvā pacitvā kataṃ. “Phāṇitagatikamevā”ti iminā sattāhakālikanti dasseti, na pana nissaggiyavatthunti. Tasmā sattāhaṃ atikkāmayato dukkaṭanti veditabbaṃ. Vuttampi cetaṃ samantapāsādikāyaṃ sītudakena kataṃ madhukapupphaphāṇitaṃ purebhattaṃ sāmisaṃ vaṭṭati[M 0.0332], pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya [V 0.0305] sattāhaṃ nirāmisameva, sattāhātikkame vatthugaṇanāya dukkaṭa”nti. Sace pana khīraṃ pakkhipitvā kataṃ, yāvakālikaṃ. Khaṇḍasakkharaṃ pana khīrajallikaṃ apanetvā sodhenti, tasmā vaṭṭati, ambajambupanasakadalikhajjuriciñcādīnaṃ sabbesaṃ yāvakālikaphalānaṃ phāṇitaṃ yāvakālikamevāti āha “ambaphāṇitādīni yāvakālikānī”ti.

Here, regarding the distinction among items permissible for only the day and those permissible for life, he said, "Things permissible for life," and so on. "Until the rising of the sun" means if oil prepared on the seventh day lasts until sunrise, that is the meaning. In the Pāli, "unspecified ghee, etc."—here, first, the ghee from deer etc. is "unspecified ghee" in the Pāli; likewise, fresh butter is also considered so. However, oil from coconut, neem, kosamba, karamanda, mustard, etc., is "unspecified oil" in the Pāli. Likewise, treacle from madhuka flowers is known as "unspecified treacle" in the Pāli. He said, "With cold water," etc., because not all treacle from madhuka flowers is treated as treacle. "Made with cold water" means having put madhuka flowers into cold water, without crushing them, when the essence of the flowers has gone into the water, having taken that water and cooked and made it. "It is indeed of the nature of treacle"—by this he shows that it is permissible for seven days, but it is not an item requiring forfeiture. Therefore, it should be understood that there is an offense of wrong-doing for one who keeps it beyond seven days. This was also said in the Samantapāsādikā: "Treacle made from madhuka flowers with cold water is permissible with meat before the meal, but from after the meal onwards, for seven days, only without meat; beyond seven days, an offense of wrong-doing by counting the articles." But if it is made having put milk in, it is permissible for only the day. However, they purify lump sugar, having removed the milk scum; therefore it is permissible. He said, "Mango treacle, etc., are permissible for only the day," because the treacle from all fruits permissible for only the day, such as mango, rose apple, jackfruit, banana, date, tamarind, etc., is itself permissible for only the day.

Kāyikaparibhogaṃ vaṭṭatīti kāyassa vā kāye aruno vā makkhanaṃ vaṭṭati, ajjhoharituṃ pana na vaṭṭati. Yanti sattāhātikkantaṃ bhesajjaṃ. Nirapekkho pariccajitvāti anapekkho sāmaṇerassa datvā. Tanti evaṃ pariccajitvā puna laddhabhesajjaṃ. Evañhi dinnaṃ bhesajjaṃ sace so sāmaṇero abhisaṅkharitvā vā anabhisaṅkharitvā vā tassa bhikkhuno dadeyya, gahetvā natthukammaṃ vā kātabbaṃ, aññaṃ vā kañci paribhogaṃ. Tenāha “ajjhoharitumpi vaṭṭatī”ti. Sace so bālo hoti, dātuṃ na jānāti, aññena bhikkhunā vattabbo “atthi te, sāmaṇera, bhesajja”nti, “āma, bhante, atthī”ti. “Āhara, therassa bhesajjaṃ karissāmā”ti, evampi vaṭṭati. Vatthugaṇanāyāti sappiādivatthugaṇanāya ceva sappipiṇḍādivatthugaṇanāya ca. Missitesu pana ekaṃ nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. Ettha ca “idaṃ me, bhante, bhesajjaṃ sattāhātikkantaṃ nissaggiyaṃ, imāhaṃ saṅghassa nissajjāmī”ti (pārā. 623) nissajjanavidhānaṃ veditabbaṃ.

“It is permissible for bodily use” means it is permissible to anoint the body or a wound on the body, but it is not permissible to consume it. “That” refers to medicine that has exceeded seven days. “Having relinquished it without concern” means having given it to a novice without concern. “That” means medicine obtained again after having relinquished it in this way. For if medicine is given in this way, should that novice give it to that bhikkhu, whether having prepared it or not having prepared it, it should be taken and used for a nasal treatment or any other use. Therefore he said, “It is permissible even to consume it.” If that novice is foolish and does not know how to give, another bhikkhu should say to him, “Novice, do you have medicine?” “Yes, venerable sir, I do.” “Bring it, we will make medicine for the elder.” This too is permissible. “By counting the articles” means by counting the articles such as ghee, and by counting the articles such as lumps of ghee. But in mixed cases, there is one Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense. And here, the procedure for forfeiture should be understood thus: “Venerable sir, this medicine of mine has exceeded seven days and is to be forfeited. I forfeit this to the Saṅgha.” (Pārā. 623)

Sādhāraṇapaññatti. Sattāhaṃ anatikkantepi atikkantasaññino ceva vematikassa ca dukkaṭaṃ. Atikkante anatikkantasaññinopi vematikassapi nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyameva, tathā anadhiṭṭhitāvissajjitānaṭṭhāvinaṭṭhādaḍḍhāviluttesu adhiṭṭhitādisaññino. Antosattāhaṃ adhiṭṭhite, vissajjite, naṭṭhe, vinaṭṭhe, daḍḍhe, acchinne, vissāsena gahite ummattakādīnañca anāpatti. Ācāravipatti. Sappiādīnaṃ attano santakatā, gaṇanupagatā, sattāhātikkamoti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni. Kathinasamuṭṭhānaṃ, akiriyaṃ, nosaññāvimokkhaṃ, acittakaṃ, paṇṇattivajjaṃ, kāyakammaṃ, vacīkammaṃ, ticittaṃ, tivedanaṃ. Tenāha “sesaṃ cīvaravaggassa paṭhamasikkhāpade vuttanayeneva veditabba”nti (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. kathinasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā).

A general promulgation. Even if it has not exceeded seven days, for one who perceives it as exceeded and for one who is uncertain, there is an offense of wrong-doing. When it has exceeded, for one who perceives it as not exceeded and for one who is uncertain, there is indeed a Nissaggiya Pācittiya. Similarly, for one who perceives as determined, etc., an item that is undetermined, relinquished, lost, destroyed, burnt, or seized, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Within seven days, if it is determined, relinquished, lost, destroyed, burnt, not seized, taken with confidence, and for the insane and so on, there is no offense. This is a failure in conduct. Ghee and so on being one's own possession, being subject to counting, and exceeding seven days: these are the three factors here. It is suspended by the Kathina, it is non-action, it is not absolved by perception, it can be unintentional, it is an offense by regulation, it is a bodily action and a verbal action, with three kinds of consciousness and three kinds of feeling. Therefore, it is said: “The rest should be understood in the same way as explained in the first training rule of the Robe Chapter” (Kaṅkhāvitaranī-aṭṭhakathā, Kathinasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā).

Bhesajjasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on medicine is concluded.

4. Vassikasāṭikasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. The Explanation of the Training Rule on the Rains-Cloth

Pacchimamāsassa [M 0.0333][V 0.0306] paṭhamadivasato paṭṭhāyāti jeṭṭhamūlapuṇṇamāsiyā pacchimapāṭipadadivasato paṭṭhāya. Tāvāti tāva parimāṇe kāle. Jeṭṭhamūlapuṇṇamāsiyā pacchimapāṭipadadivasato paṭṭhāya yāva kattikapuṇṇamā, imasmiṃ pañcamāseti attho. Kālo vassikasāṭikāyātiādināti ettha ādisaddena “samayo vassikasāṭikāya, aññepi manussā vassikasāṭikacīvaraṃ dentī”ti (pārā. 628) imesaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Detha me vassikasāṭikacīvarantiādikāyāti ettha ādisaddena pana “āharatha me vassikasāṭikacīvaraṃ, parivattetha me vassikasāṭikacīvaraṃ, cetāpetha me vassikasāṭikacīvara”nti imesaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Attano aññātakaappavāritesu tadubhayaṃ karontassa kiṃ hotīti āha “aññātakaappavāritaṭṭhāne”tiādi. “Vattabhede dukkaṭa”nti idaṃ vassikasāṭikaṃ pubbe adente sandhāya vuttaṃ. Ye pana pubbepi denti, tesu vattabhedo natthi. Vuttañhi samantapāsādikāyaṃ “ye manussā pubbepi vassikasāṭikacīvaraṃ denti, ime pana sacepi attano aññātakaappavāritā honti, vattabhedo natthi tesu satuppādakaraṇassa anuññātattā”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.628). Aññātakaviññattisikkhāpadena nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyanti “yo pana bhikkhu aññātakaṃ gahapatiṃ vā gahapatāniṃ vā cīvaraṃ viññāpeyya aññatra samayā, nissaggiyaṃ pācittiya”nti (pārā. 518) iminā sikkhāpadena nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. Idaṃ pana pakatiyā vassikasāṭikadāyakesupi hotiyeva.

“Starting from the first day of the last month” means starting from the day after the full-moon day of Jeṭṭhamūla. “So long” means for that measured time. The meaning is: from the day after the full-moon day of Jeṭṭhamūla until the full-moon day of Kattika, during these five months. In the phrase “The time for the rains-cloth, etc.,” the word “etc.” includes: “the season for the rains-cloth, and other people also give rains-cloth robes” (Pārā. 628). In the phrase “Give me a rains-cloth robe, etc.,” the word “etc.” includes: “Bring me a rains-cloth robe, exchange a rains-cloth robe for me, acquire a rains-cloth robe for me.” As to what happens to one who does both of these in regard to those who are unrelated and uninvited, he says, “In the case of unrelated and uninvited persons,” etc. “For a breach of the custom, there is an offense of wrong-doing”—this is said with reference to those who previously did not give a rains-cloth robe. But for those who did give it previously, there is no breach of the custom. For it is stated in the Samantapāsādikā: “Even if these people who previously gave the rains-cloth robe are unrelated and uninvited, there is no breach of the custom for them, because reminding them of the opportunity is permitted” (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.628). By the training rule on requesting from an unrelated person, there is a Nissaggiya Pācittiya—by this training rule, “Whatever bhikkhu should request a robe from a householder or householder's wife who is unrelated to him, except at the proper time, it is a Nissaggiya Pācittiya” (Pārā. 518), there is a Nissaggiya Pācittiya. However, this offense is incurred even with those who are regular donors of the rains-cloth.

Gimhānaṃ pacchimaddhamāsassa paṭhamadivasato paṭṭhāyāti ettha jeṭṭhamūlakāḷapakkhūposathassa pacchimapāṭipadadivasato paṭṭhāya yāva āsāḷhipuṇṇamā, ayamaddhamāso gimhānaṃ pacchimaddhamāso nāma, tassa paṭhamadivasato paṭṭhāyāti attho, addhamāsassa paṭhamapāṭipadadivasato paṭṭhāyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Kattikamāsassa pacchimadivaso nāma pacchimakattikamāsassa puṇṇamā. Ettāvatāti “māso seso gimhānanti bhikkhunā vassikasāṭikacīvaraṃ pariyesitabbaṃ, addhamāso seso gimhānanti katvā nivāsetabba”nti ettakena gaṇanena. Pariyesanakkhettanti pariyesanassa khettaṃ. Etasmiñhi māse vassikasāṭikaṃ aladdhaṃ pariyesituṃ vaṭṭati. Karaṇanivāsanakkhettampīti karaṇakkhettañceva nivāsanakkhettañca. Pi-saddena pariyesanakkhettaṃ [M 0.0334] sampiṇḍeti. Etasmiñhi addhamāse pariyesituṃ, kātuṃ, nivāsetuñca vaṭṭati, adhiṭṭhātuṃyeva na vaṭṭati. Yaṃ pana samantapāsādikāyaṃ katthaci potthake “jeṭṭhamūlapuṇṇamāsiyā pacchimapāṭipadadivasato paṭṭhāya yāva kālapakkhuposatho, ayameko addhamāso pariyesanakkhettañceva karaṇakkhettañca. Etasmiñhi antare vassikasāṭikaṃ aladdhaṃ pariyesituṃ[V 0.0307], laddhaṃ kātuñca vaṭṭati, nivāsetuṃ, adhiṭṭhātuñca na vaṭṭatī”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.628) vacanaṃ dissati, taṃ pamādalikhitaṃ mātikāya virodhatoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Addhamāso seso gimhānanti katvā nivāsetabba”nti (pārā. 627) hi pāḷi. Sabbampīti pariyesanaṃ, karaṇaṃ, nivāsanaṃ, adhiṭṭhānañcāti sabbampi. Iminā ime cattāro māsā pariyesanakaraṇanivāsanādhiṭṭhānānaṃ catunnampi khettanti dasseti. Etesu hi catūsu māsesu aladdhaṃ pariyesituṃ, laddhaṃ kātuṃ, nivāsetuṃ, adhiṭṭhātuñca vaṭṭati.

“Starting from the first day of the last half-month of the hot season”: here, this means starting from the day after the Uposatha of the dark fortnight of Jeṭṭhamūla until the full moon of Āsāḷhī. This half-month is called the last half-month of the hot season, and the meaning is starting from its first day; that is to say, starting from the first day of the half-month. The last day of the month of Kattika is the full moon of the last Kattika month. “Up to this point” refers to this calculation: “When one month of the hot season remains, a bhikkhu should search for a rains-cloth robe; when half a month of the hot season remains, having made it, it should be worn.” The field for searching means the domain for searching. For during this month, it is permissible to search for a rains-cloth that has not been obtained. The field for making and wearing as well means both the field for making and the field for wearing. The particle 'pi' also includes the field for searching. For during this half-month, it is permissible to search, to make, and to wear; it is just not permissible to determine it. As for the statement found in some manuscripts of the Samantapāsādikā, “From the day after the full moon of Jeṭṭhamūla until the Uposatha of the dark fortnight, this one half-month is both the field for searching and the field for making. During this interval, it is permissible to search for a rains-cloth that has not been obtained and, having obtained it, to make it; but it is not permissible to wear or to determine it” (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.628), that should be seen as a scribal error, as it contradicts the matrix. For the Pāli states: “When half a month of the hot season remains, having made it, it should be worn” (Pārā. 627). “All” means all of these: searching, making, wearing, and determining. By this, it is shown that these four months are the field for all four: searching, making, wearing, and determining. For during these four months, it is permissible to search for what has not been obtained, to make what has been obtained, to wear it, and to determine it.

Vassaṃ ukkaḍḍhīyatīti saṃvaccharaṃ uddhaṃ kaḍḍhīyati vaḍḍhīyati, āruyhatīti attho, vassānassa paṭhamamāsaṃ ukkaḍḍhitvā gimhānaṃ pacchimamāsameva karontīti vuttaṃ hoti. Vassūpanāyikadivase adhiṭṭhātabbāti vassānato pubbeyeva dasāhassa atikkantattā vassūpanāyikadivaseyeva adhiṭṭhātabbā. Tañhi divasaṃ atikkāmetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Antovasse pana laddhā ceva niṭṭhitā ca tasmiṃyeva antovasse laddhadivasato paṭṭhāya dasāhaṃ nātikkāmetabbā, dasāhātikkame niṭṭhitā pana tadaheva adhiṭṭhātabbā. Dasāhe appahonte cīvarakālaṃ nātikkāmetabbā. Ayaṃ tāva katāya parihāro. Akatāya pana ko parihāroti āha “sace”tiādi. Ekāhampi na labhati ito aññassa parihārassābhāvatoti adhippāyo.

“The year is drawn out” means that the year is pulled upwards, increased, it ascends—this is the meaning. It is said that by drawing out the first month of the rainy season, they make it the very last month of the hot season. It should be determined on the day of entering the rains-residence—because the ten-day period before the rains-residence has already passed, it must be determined on the very day of entering the rains-residence. It is not proper to let that day pass. However, if one obtains and completes it within the rains, then starting from the day it was obtained within the rains, ten days should not be exceeded. But if it is completed after the ten days have passed, it must be determined on that very day. If the ten days are not sufficient, the robe-season should not be exceeded. This, then, is the allowance for one who has done it. But what is the allowance for one who has not done it? He says, “If,” etc. The meaning is that not even a single day is obtained, as there is no other allowance beyond this.

So kuto hotīti āha “yāva hemantassa paṭhamadivaso”ti, jeṭṭhamūlapuṇṇamāsito paṭṭhāya yāva kattikapuṇṇamāsiyā pacchimapāṭipadadivaso, tāvāti attho. Etesu sattasu piṭṭhisamayamāsesūti paṭilomakkamena vuttesu kattikapuṇṇamāsiyā pacchimapāṭipadādīsu jeṭṭhamūlapuṇṇamāsāvasānesu etesu sattasu piṭṭhisamayanāmakesu māsesu. Satuppādakaraṇenāti “kālo vassikasāṭikāyā”tiādinā nayena satuppādakaraṇena. Viññāpentassāti “detha [M 0.0335] me vassikasāṭikacīvara”ntiādinā (pārā. 628) nayena viññattiṃ karontassa. Tena sikkhāpadena anāpattīti aññātakaviññattisikkhāpadena anāpatti, iminā pana sikkhāpadena āpattiyeva asamayattā. Vuttañhetaṃ bhadantabuddhadattācariyena –

“From where does that come?” he asks. It is said, “Up to the first day of winter.” This means starting from the full moon of Jeṭṭhamūla up to the day after the Kattika full moon—that is the meaning of “up to that point.” In these seven months called “back-season months,” spoken of in reverse order—beginning from the day after the Kattika full moon and ending with the Jeṭṭhamūla full moon—in these seven months. “By creating an occasion” means by creating an occasion in the manner of “It is time for the rainy-season robe,” and so forth. “For one who makes a request” means for one making a request in the manner of “Give me the rainy-season robe-cloth,” and so forth (Pārā. 628). “There is no offense by that training rule” means there is no offense by the training rule concerning requesting from non-relatives, but by this training rule, there is indeed an offense because it is not the proper time. For this was said by the venerable teacher Buddhadatta:

“Katvā pana satuppādaṃ, vassasāṭikacīvaraṃ;

Nipphādentassa bhikkhussa, samaye piṭṭhisammate.

“But having created an occasion for a rainy-season robe-cloth, for a monk who accomplishes it at the agreed-upon back-season time.”

“Hoti [V 0.0308] nissaggiyāpatti, ñātakāññātakādino;

Tesuyeva ca viññattiṃ, katvā nipphādane tathā”ti.

“There is an offense entailing forfeiture, whether from relatives or non-relatives; and likewise, by making a request to them and having it accomplished.”

Ettha ca “idaṃ me, bhante, vassikasāṭikacīvaraṃ atirekamāse sese gimhāne pariyiṭṭhaṃ atirekaddhamāse sese gimhāne katvā paridahitaṃ nissaggiya”nti iminā (pārā. 628) nayena nissajjanavidhānaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Here, the procedure for forfeiture should be understood in this way: “Venerable sir, this rainy-season robe-cloth was sought when more than a month of the hot season remained, and made and worn when more than half a month of the hot season remained. It is to be forfeited”—in this manner (Pārā. 628).

Vassikasāṭikapariyesanavatthusminti paṭikacceva vassikasāṭikapariyesanavatthusmiṃ. Tikapācittiyanti atirekamāsaddhamāsesu atirekasaññivematikaūnakasaññīnaṃ pariyesananivāsanavasena tīṇi pācittiyāni, ekasesaniddeso cāyaṃ, sāmaññaniddeso vā. Ūnakamāsaddhamāsesūti ūnakamāse ceva ūnakaddhamāse ca. Atirekasaññino, vematikassa vā dukkaṭanti ettha “pariyesananivāsanaṃ karontassā”ti pāṭhaseso. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “ūnakamāse sese gimhāne atirekasaññino, vematikassa vā pariyesantassa dukkaṭaṃ, ūnakaddhamāse sese gimhāne ca atirekasaññino, vematikassa vā nivāsentassa dukkaṭa”nti. “Tathā”ti iminā dukkaṭaṃ atidisati, tañca dukkaṭaṃ udakaphusitagaṇanāya akatvā nhānapariyosānavasena payoge payoge kāretabbaṃ, tañca kho vivaṭaṅgaṇe ākāsato patitaudakeneva nhāyantassa, na nhānakoṭṭhakavāpiādīsu ghaṭehi āsittūdakena nhāyantassa. Tenevāha “satiyā vassikasāṭikāyā”tiādi. Pokkharaṇiyādīsu pana naggassa nhāyantassa anāpattīti sambandho, pokkharaṇiyādīsu pana satiyāpi vassikasāṭikāya naggassa nhāyantassa natthi dukkaṭāpattīti attho.

In the matter of seeking a rains-cloth: first of all, in the matter of seeking a rains-cloth. Three pācittiya offenses: in the cases of exceeding a month and half a month, for those who perceive it as exceeding, are in doubt, or perceive it as deficient, there are three pācittiya offenses by way of seeking and wearing. This is an explanation by way of ellipsis, or a general explanation. “Less than a month and half a month” means less than a month and less than half a month. “For one who perceives it as exceeding or is in doubt, there is a dukkaṭa offense”—here, the remaining part of the text is “for one who is seeking or wearing.” This means: “For one who perceives it as exceeding or is in doubt while seeking when less than a month of the hot season remains, there is a dukkaṭa offense; and for one who perceives it as exceeding or is in doubt while wearing when less than half a month of the hot season remains, there is a dukkaṭa offense.” The word “tathā” (thus) here extends to the dukkaṭa offense, and that dukkaṭa offense should be incurred for each act at the conclusion of bathing, not by counting splashes of water. And that applies only to one bathing in an open courtyard with water fallen from the sky, not to one bathing in a bathing enclosure, pond, etc., with water poured from pots. Hence it is said, “when a rains-cloth is available,” and so forth. But there is no offense for one bathing naked in a pond or similar place—this is the connection. Moreover, even when a rains-cloth is available, there is no dukkaṭa offense for one bathing naked in a pond or similar place—this is the meaning.

Evaṃ [M 0.0336] antarāpattiyā anāpattiṃ dassetvā idāni nissaggiyena anāpattiṃ dassetuṃ “acchinnacīvarassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha acchinnacīvarassāti acchinnasesacīvarassa. Tassāpi asamaye nivāsato anāpatti. Esa nayo naṭṭhacīvarassa vāti etthāpi. Yathā cettha nivāsentānaṃ tesaṃ anāpatti, evaṃ tattha pariyesantānampīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ettha pana mahagghavassikasāṭikaṃ ṭhapetvā nhāyantassa corūpaddavo āpadā nāmāti āha “anivattha”ntiādi. Āpadāsu vā nivāsayatoti āpadāsu vijjamānāsu asamaye nivāsentassa. Yaṃ pana samantapāsādikāyaṃ “acchinnacīvarassāti etaṃ vassikasāṭikaṃyeva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tesañhi naggānaṃ kāyovassāpane anāpatti. Ettha ca mahagghavassikasāṭikaṃ nivāsetvā nhāyantassa corūpaddavo āpadā nāmā”ti acchinnacīvarādino nissaggiyena anāpattiṃ [V 0.0309] adassetvā naggassa nhāyato dukkaṭeneva anāpattidassanaṃ, taṃ yuttaṃ viya na dissati. Sabbasikkhāpadesu hi mūlāpattiyā eva āpattippasaṅge anāpattidassanatthaṃ anāpattivāro ārabhīyati, na antarāpattiyāti, tasmā upaparikkhitabbaṃ. Sacīvaratāti antaravāsakauttarāsaṅgehi sacīvaratā.

Having thus shown the non-offense regarding an intermediate offense, now, to show the non-offense regarding the offense entailing forfeiture, it is stated, “for one whose robe is not taken away,” and so forth. Herein, “for one whose robe is not taken away” means for one whose remaining robe is not taken away. For him, there is no offense in wearing it at an improper time. This principle also applies to one whose robe is lost. Just as in this case, there is no offense for those wearing it, so too for those seeking it—this should be understood. Here, however, danger from thieves is called an emergency for one bathing having put aside an expensive rains-cloak; he says, “not wearing,” and so forth. Or, “for one who wears during emergencies” means for one wearing at an improper time when emergencies are present. But in the Samantapāsādikā, it is said: “‘For one whose robe is not taken away’—this is said with reference only to the rains-cloak. For them, there is no offense in exposing the body to the rain while naked. And here, for one bathing having worn an expensive rains-cloak, danger from thieves is called an emergency.” To show non-offense for one bathing naked only by way of a dukkaṭa offense, without showing non-offense regarding the forfeiture for one whose robe is not taken away, etc., does not seem appropriate. For in all training rules, the section on non-offense is introduced to show non-offense in cases where a root offense is possible, not for intermediate offenses. Therefore, it should be examined. “Being properly robed” means being properly robed with the lower robe and upper robe.

Vassikasāṭikasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning the rainy-season bathing-cloth is finished.

5. Cīvaraacchindanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

5. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Forcibly Taking a Robe

“Datvā”ti yaṃ kiñci paccāsīsamānasseva dānamiha adhippetaṃ, na nissaṭṭhadānanti āha “veyyāvaccādīnī”tiādi. Sakasaññāyāti “saka”nti saññāya. Iminā pārājikābhāvaṃ dasseti. Cajitvā dinnampi hi sakasaññāya gaṇhato natthi pārājikaṃ. Acchindantassāti ekato abaddhāni, visuṃ ṭhapitāni ca bahūni acchindato, “saṅghāṭiṃ āhara, uttarāsaṅgaṃ āharā”ti evaṃ āharāpayato ca. Tenāha “vatthugaṇanāya āpattiyo”ti. “Mayā dinnāni sabbāni āharā”ti vadatopi ekavacaneneva sambahulā āpattiyo. Ekaṃ cīvaraṃ pana ekābaddhāni ca bahūni acchindato ekā āpatti. “Acchindā”ti āṇattiyā dukkaṭanti “mayā dinnāni sabbāni gaṇhā”ti āṇattiyā ekaṃ dukkaṭaṃ, acchinnesu pana [M 0.0337] ekavacaneneva sambahulā pācittiyo. Tenāha “acchinnesu vatthugaṇanāya āpattiyo”ti. Acchinnesūti tenāṇattena acchinnesu cīvaresu. Yattha pana potthakesu “acchinnesu yattakāni āṇattāni, tesaṃ gaṇanāya āpattiyo”ti pāṭho, tattha yattakāni āṇattānīti yattakāni cīvarāni gaṇhituṃ āṇattānīti attho. Yaṃ pana samantapāsādikāyaṃ “cīvaraṃ ‘gaṇhā’ti āṇāpeti, ekaṃ dukkaṭaṃ. Āṇatto bahūni gaṇhāti, ekaṃ pācittiya”nti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.633) vuttaṃ, taṃ ekābaddhaṃ sandhāya. Evañca katvā samantapāsādikāya saddhiṃ imāya aṭṭhakathāya na koci virodho. Sace pana “saṅghāṭiṃ gaṇha, uttarāsaṅgaṃ gaṇhā”ti āṇāpeti, vācāya vācāya dukkaṭaṃ. Acchinnesu vatthugaṇanāya āpattiyo. Ettha ca “idaṃ me, bhante, cīvaraṃ bhikkhussa sāmaṃ datvā acchinnaṃ nissaggiya”nti (pārā. 633) iminā nayena nissajjanavidhānaṃ veditabbaṃ.

“Having given” here refers to a gift given with some expectation of return, not a relinquished gift—hence the mention of “services and so on.” “With the perception of ownership” means with the perception of it being “one’s own.” This indicates the absence of a pārājika offense. Even if one takes back what has been given away, there is no pārājika offense if done with the perception of it being one’s own. “By forcibly taking” refers to one who forcibly takes many items that are not bound together, or that are placed separately, or one who causes them to be brought by saying, “Bring the saṅghāṭi, bring the uttarāsaṅga.” Therefore it is said, “the offenses are counted by the number of garments.” Even if one says, “Bring all the things that I have given,” multiple offenses arise from a single utterance. However, for a single robe or many items bound together forcibly taken, there is one offense. By the command “forcibly take,” there is a dukkaṭa. By the command “Take all the things that I have given,” there is one dukkaṭa, but when they are forcibly taken, multiple pācittiya offenses arise, even if by a single utterance. Therefore it is said, “When forcibly taken, the offenses are counted by the number of garments.” “When forcibly taken” refers to robes forcibly taken by the one commanded. However, where in the texts the reading is “when forcibly taken, the offenses are counted by the number of items commanded,” there “yattakāni āṇattāni” means “the number of robes commanded to be taken.” However, what is said in the Samantapāsādikā: “If one commands, ‘Take a robe,’ there is one dukkaṭa. If the commanded person takes many, there is one pācittiya” (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.633), refers to a single item bound together. Thus, there is no contradiction between the Samantapāsādikā and this commentary. But if one commands, “Take the saṅghāṭi, take the uttarāsaṅga,” each utterance incurs a dukkaṭa. When forcibly taken, the offenses are counted by the number of garments. Here, the procedure for relinquishment should be understood according to this method: “Venerable sir, this robe, having been given by me personally to the monk and then forcibly taken back, is to be relinquished with forfeiture.”

Tikapācittiyanti upasampanne upasampannasaññivematikaanupasampannasaññīnaṃ vasena tīṇi pācittiyāni. Aññaṃ parikkhāranti pattādiṃ aññaṃ parikkhāraṃ, antamaso sūcimpīti attho. Na [V 0.0310] kevalaṃ anupasampannassa cīvaraṃyeva acchindato dukkaṭanti āha “anupasampannassa cā”tiādi. Tattha yaṃ kiñcīti cīvaraṃ vā hotu, pattādi, yaṃ kiñci parikkhāraṃ vā. Tassa vissāsaṃ gaṇhantassāti yassa dinnaṃ, tassa vissāsena gaṇhantassa, tatiyatthe cetaṃ upayogavacanaṃ. Upasampannatāti acchindanasamaye upasampannabhāvo. Kiñcāpi upasampannabhāvo pāḷiyaṃ, mātikaṭṭhakathāyañca dānaggahaṇesu dissati, tathāpi anupasampannakāle cīvaraṃ datvā upasampannakāle acchindantassa āpattito acchindanakāleyeva upasampannatā aṅganti veditabbaṃ.

“Tika-pācittiya” means three pācittiya offenses in the case of an ordained person, depending on whether one perceives them as ordained, is uncertain, or perceives them as unordained. “Aññaṃ parikkhāraṃ” refers to any other requisite, such as a bowl, or even a needle; that is the meaning. A dukkaṭa offense is not only for forcibly taking the robe of an unordained person, hence it is said, “and of an unordained person,” and so on. Here, “yaṃ kiñci” means anything, whether a robe, a bowl, or any other requisite. “Tassa vissāsaṃ gaṇhantassāti” refers to one who takes with the trust of the one to whom it was given; this is a usage in the sense of the instrumental case. “Upasampannatā” means the state of being ordained at the time of forcibly taking. Although the state of being ordained is seen in the Pāli text and the Mātika commentary in relation to acts of giving and receiving, it should be understood that the state of being ordained at the time of forcibly taking is the relevant factor for the offense, even if the robe was given when one was not yet ordained and then forcibly taken when one was ordained.

Cīvaraacchindanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Forcibly Taking Robes is concluded.

6. Suttaviññattisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Requesting Thread.

Chabbidhaṃ khomasuttādinti “suttaṃ nāma cha suttāni khomaṃ kappāsikaṃ koseyyaṃ kambalaṃ sāṇaṃ bhaṅga”nti (pārā. 638) evaṃ vuttaṃ chabbidhaṃ khomasuttādiṃ. Tattha [M 0.0338] khomanti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.636-38) khomavākehi katasuttaṃ. Kappāsikanti kappāsato nibbattaṃ. Koseyyanti kosiyaṃsūhi kantitvā katasuttaṃ. Kambalanti eḷakalomasuttaṃ. Sāṇanti sāṇavākena katasuttaṃ. Bhaṅganti pāṭekkaṃ vākasuttamevāti eke. Pañcahipi missetvā katasuttaṃ pana “bhaṅga”nti veditabbaṃ. Tesaṃ anulomanti tesaṃ khomādīnaṃ anulomaṃ dukūlaṃ pattuṇṇaṃ somārapaṭṭaṃ cīnapaṭṭaṃ iddhijaṃ devadinnanti chabbidhaṃ suttaṃ.

The six kinds of thread, beginning with linen thread: “Thread means six kinds of thread: linen, cotton, silk, wool, hemp, and bhaṅga” (Pārā. 638) – thus is said the six kinds of thread beginning with linen. Herein, “linen” means thread made from linen fibers (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.636-38). “Cotton” means that produced from cotton. “Silk” means thread made by spinning silk threads. “Wool” means thread from sheep’s wool. “Hemp” means thread made from hemp fibers. Some say that “bhaṅga” means thread from individual fibers. However, thread made by mixing these five should be understood as “bhaṅga.” Their counterparts: corresponding to these—linen, etc.—are six kinds of thread: fine linen, fine wool, Somāra cloth, Chinese cloth, cloth born of psychic power, and cloth given by the gods.

Turīti vāyanūpakaraṇo eko daṇḍo, vītavītaṭṭhānaṃ yattha saṃharitvā ṭhapenti. Vemanti vāyanūpakaraṇo eko daṇḍo, suttaṃ pavesetvā yena ākoṭento ghanabhāvaṃ sampādenti. Tassa sabbappayogesu dukkaṭanti tantavāyassa ye te turivemasajjanādikā payogā, tesu sabbesu payogesu bhikkhussa dukkaṭaṃ, tassa tantavāyassa payoge payoge bhikkhussa dukkaṭanti vuttaṃ hoti. Turiādīnaṃ abhāve tesaṃ karaṇatthaṃ vāsipharasuādīnaṃ maggananisānarukkhacchedanādisabbappayogepi eseva nayo. Tantūnaṃ attano santakattā vītavītaṭṭhānaṃ paṭiladdhameva hotīti āha “paṭilābhena nissaggiyaṃ hotī”ti, vikappanupagapacchimacīvarappamāṇe vīte nissaggiyaṃ hotīti vuttaṃ hoti. Teneva vakkhati “dīghato vidatthimatte, tiriyañca hatthamatte vīte nissaggiyaṃ pācittiya”nti. Ettha ca “idaṃ me, bhante, cīvaraṃ sāmaṃ suttaṃ viññāpetvā tantavāyehi vāyāpitaṃ nissaggiya”nti iminā nayena nissajjanavidhānaṃ veditabbaṃ.

A turī is a stick, a weaving tool, where they gather and place the threads that have been stretched taut. A vema is a stick, a weaving tool, by which, inserting the thread, they beat it to achieve firmness. For all these applications, there is a dukkaṭa. This means that for all those applications of the weaver, such as preparing the turī and vema, etc., for all those applications, a dukkaṭa is incurred by the bhikkhu. It is said that for each application by the weaver, a dukkaṭa is incurred by the bhikkhu. In the absence of tools like the turī, etc., the same principle applies to all applications for making them, such as searching for, sharpening, cutting trees, etc., with axes, adzes, and so on. Because the threads belong to oneself, the area stretched taut is considered acquired. Hence, it is said: “It becomes forfeitable upon acquisition.” It is said that when it is woven to the measure of a final robe not subject to designation, it becomes forfeitable. Therefore it will be said: “If it is woven to the measure of a span in length and a cubit in width, it is forfeitable and entails a pācittiya offense.” Here, the procedure for relinquishment should be understood according to this method: “Venerable sir, this robe, having had the thread requested by me personally and woven by weavers, is to be relinquished with forfeiture.”

Tenevāti [V 0.0311] viññāpitatantavāyeneva. Evaṃ idha dukkaṭanti idhāpi tantavāyeneva dīghato vidatthimatte, tiriyaṃ hatthamatte vīte dukkaṭanti attho. Akappiyasuttamayeti viññāpitasuttamaye. Itarasminti aviññattisuttamaye paricchede. Tato ce ūnatarāti vuttappamāṇato ce ūnatarā, antamaso (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.636-638) acchimaṇḍalappamāṇāpīti adhippāyo. Kappiyatantavāyenapi akappiyasuttaṃ vāyāpentassa yathā pubbe nissaggiyaṃ, evamidha dukkaṭaṃ. Teneva kappiyañca akappiyañca suttaṃ vāyāpentassa sace pacchimacīvarappamāṇā vā ūnakā vā akappiyasuttaparicchedā honti, tesu paricchedagaṇanāya dukkaṭaṃ. Kappiyasuttaparicchedesu anāpatti. Atha ekantarikena vā suttena, dīghato vā kappiyaṃ tiriyaṃ akappiyaṃ katvā vītaṃ hoti, pamāṇayutte paricchede paricchede dukkaṭaṃ.

‘Teneva’ means by that very weaver who was requested. Thus, here, “dukkaṭa” means that even here, when woven by the weaver to the measure of a span in length and a cubit in width, there is a dukkaṭa. “Made of unallowable thread” means made of requested thread. “In the other case” refers to the section made of unrequested thread. “If it is less than that” means if it is less than the stated measure, even if it is as small as the socket of the eye, that is the intention. Even if one causes unallowable thread to be woven by an allowable weaver, just as before there is a nissaggiya, so here there is a dukkaṭa. Similarly, if one causes both allowable and unallowable thread to be woven, and if the sections of unallowable thread are equal to or less than the size of the final robe, then a dukkaṭa offense results from counting those sections. For sections of allowable thread, there is no offense. But if it is woven with a single intervening thread, or if the length is allowable but the width is unallowable, for each section that meets the required measurement, it is a dukkaṭa offense.

Yadi [M 0.0339] pana (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.636-638) dve tantavāyā honti eko kappiyo eko akappiyo, suttañca akappiyaṃ, te ce vārena vinanti, akappiyatantavāyena vīte pamāṇayutte paricchede paricchede pācittiyaṃ, ūnatare dukkaṭaṃ. Itarena vīte ubhayattha dukkaṭaṃ. Sace dvepi vemaṃ gahetvā ekato vinanti, pamāṇayutte paricchede paricchede pācittiyaṃ. Atha suttaṃ kappiyaṃ, cīvarañca kedārabaddhādīhi saparicchedaṃ, akappiyatantavāyena vīte paricchede paricchede dukkaṭaṃ, itarena vīte anāpatti. Sace dvepi ekato vinanti, pamāṇayutte paricchede paricchede dukkaṭaṃ. Atha suttampi kappiyañca akappiyañca, te ce vārena vinanti, akappiyatantavāyena akappiyasuttamayesu pacchimacīvarappamāṇesu paricchedesu vītesu paricchedagaṇanāya pācittiyaṃ, ūnataresu kappiyasuttamayesu ca dukkaṭaṃ. Kappiyatantavāyena akappiyasuttamayesu pamāṇayuttesu vā ūnakesu vā dukkaṭameva, kappiyasuttamayesu anāpatti.

If there are two weavers (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.636-638), one allowable and one unallowable, and the thread is unallowable, and they weave by turns, for each section woven by the unallowable weaver that meets the measure, it is a pācittiya offense; if less, it is a dukkaṭa offense. If woven by the other, there is a dukkaṭa offense in both cases. If both weave together, holding the shuttle, for each section that meets the measure, it is a pācittiya offense. Now, if the thread is allowable, and the robe has sections like a paddy field, for each section woven by the unallowable weaver, it is a dukkaṭa offense; if woven by the other, there is no offense. If both weave together, for each section that meets the measure, it is a dukkaṭa offense. Now, if the thread is both allowable and unallowable, and they weave by turns, for the sections made of unallowable thread woven by the unallowable weaver, which are of the measure for the final robe, there is a pācittiya offense for each section counted; for those that are less, and for those made of allowable thread, it is a dukkaṭa offense. If woven by the allowable weaver using unallowable thread, whether of the standard measure or less, it is only a dukkaṭa offense; for sections made of allowable thread, there is no offense.

Atha ekantarikena vā suttena, dīghato vā akappiyaṃ tiriyaṃ akappiyaṃ katvā vinanti, ubhopi vā te vemaṃ gahetvā ekato vinanti, aparicchede cīvare pamāṇayutte paricchede paricchede dukkaṭaṃ, saparicchede paricchedavasena dukkaṭāni. Tenāha “eteneva upāyenā”tiādi.

Then, if they weave it with an alternating thread, or by making the length unallowable or the width unallowable, or if both of them take the shuttle and weave together, in the case of an unsectioned robe, for each section that meets the measure, there is a dukkaṭa offense; in the case of a sectioned robe, dukkaṭa offenses arise according to the sections. Therefore it is said, “By this very method,” and so on.

Ettha ca tantavāyo tāva aññātakaappavāritato viññattiyā laddho akappiyo, seso kappiyo. Suttampi sāmaṃ viññāpitaṃ akappiyaṃ, sesaṃ, ñātakādivasena uppannañca kappiyanti veditabbaṃ. Tikapācittiyanti vāyāpite vāyāpitasaññivematikaavāyāpitasaññīnaṃ vasena tīṇi pācittiyāni. Cīvaratthāya viññāpitasuttanti sāmaṃ vā aññena vā cīvaratthāya viññāpitasuttaṃ[V 0.0312]. Kiñcāpi pāḷiyaṃ “sāmaṃ suttaṃ viññāpetvā”ti vuttaṃ, tathāpi idha “cīvaratthāya sāmaṃ viññāpitasutta”nti avatvā kevalaṃ “cīvaratthāya viññāpitasutta”nti aṅgesu vuttattā aññena cīvaratthāya viññāpitasuttampi saṅgahaṃ gacchatīti veditabbaṃ. Akappiyaviññattiyāti “cīvaraṃ me, āvuso, vāyathā”ti evaṃbhūtāya akappiyaviññattiyā.

Here, first, a weaver obtained through a request from an unrelated and uninvited person is unallowable; the rest are allowable. Thread requested by oneself is also unallowable; the rest, and that which arises through relatives and so on, should be understood as allowable. Tikapācittiya means there are three pācittiya offenses based on these perceptions regarding the weaving: perceiving it as woven, being uncertain, and perceiving it as not woven. ‘Thread requested for the purpose of a robe’ means thread requested for the purpose of a robe, whether by oneself or by another. Although in the Pāli text it is stated, ‘having oneself requested thread,’ nevertheless, here, because in the factors of the offense it is stated simply as ‘thread requested for the purpose of a robe,’ without explicitly saying ‘thread requested by oneself for the purpose of a robe,’ it should be understood that thread requested by another for the purpose of a robe is also included. ‘Unallowable request’ means an unallowable request of this sort: ‘Friend, weave a robe for me.’

Suttaviññattisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning the request for thread is concluded.

7. Mahāpesakārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

7. The Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning a Master Weaver

Cīvarasāmikehi [M 0.0340] pubbe appavārito hutvāti “kīdisena te, bhante, cīvarena attho, kīdisaṃ te cīvaraṃ vāyāpemi, vada, bhante, yadicchasī”ti cīvarasāmikehi pubbe avutto hutvā. Ettha ca āyatādīhi tīhi suttavaḍḍhanākārena saha vāyanākāraṃ dasseti, suvītādīhi catūhi vāyanākārameva. “Kiñcimattaṃ anupadajjeyyāmā”tiādi tassa kattabbākāramattadassanaṃ, na pana aṅgadassanaṃ suttavaḍḍhanavaseneva āpajjitabbattāti āha “na bhikkhuno piṇḍapātadānamattenā”tiādi. Ettha ca “idaṃ me, bhante, cīvaraṃ pubbe appavāritena aññātakassa gahapatikassa tantavāye upasaṅkamitvā cīvare vikappaṃ āpannaṃ nissaggiya”nti (pārā. 643) iminā nayena nissajjanavidhānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tikapācittiyanti aññātake aññātakasaññivematikañātakasaññīnaṃ vasena tīṇi pācittiyāni.

‘Having not been previously invited by the robe-owners’ means having not been addressed beforehand by the robe-owners with words such as, ‘What kind of robe do you need, venerable sir? What kind of robe should I have woven for you? Speak, venerable sir, whatever you desire.’ Here, with the three qualities beginning with ‘long,’ he shows the manner of weaving along with the manner of increasing the thread; with the four qualities beginning with ‘well-woven,’ he shows only the manner of weaving. The phrase, ‘We would give just a little,’ and so forth, shows only the manner of what is to be done, but it does not show a factor of the offense, because the offense is incurred only on account of increasing the thread. Therefore, it is said, ‘Not by the mere giving of almsfood to a monk,’ and so forth. Here, the procedure for relinquishment should be understood by this method: ‘Venerable sir, this robe of mine, having approached an unrelated householder weaver when not previously invited and made a stipulation regarding the robe, is to be relinquished’ (Pārā. 643). Tikapācittiya means there are three pācittiya offenses based on these perceptions: perceiving an unrelated person as unrelated, being uncertain, and perceiving a related person as unrelated.

Mahāpesakārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning a master weaver is concluded.

8. Accekacīvarasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

8. Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning an Emergency Robe

Paṭhamapadassāti “dasāhānāgata”nti padassa. Purimanayenevāti accantasaṃyogavaseneva. Tāni divasānīti tesu divasesu. Accantamevāti nirantarameva, tesu dasāhesu yattha katthaci divaseti vuttaṃ hoti. Pavāraṇāmāsassāti pubbakattikamāsassa. So hi idha paṭhamapavāraṇāyogato “pavāraṇāmāso”ti vutto. Juṇhapakkhapañcamito paṭṭhāyāti sukkapakkhapañcamiṃ ādiṃ katvā. Pavāraṇāmāsassa juṇhapakkhapañcamitoti vā pavāraṇāmāsassa pakāsanato purimassa juṇhapakkhassa pañcamito paṭṭhāyāti attho. Yo panettha “kāmañcesa (sārattha. ṭī. 2.650) ‘dasāhaparamaṃ atirekacīvaraṃ dhāretabba’nti (pārā. 463) imināva [V 0.0313] siddho, aṭṭhuppattivasena pana apubbaṃ viya atthaṃ dassetvā sikkhāpadaṃ ṭhapita”nti pāṭho dissati, so pamādapāṭho “dasāhānāgata”nti iminā virodhatoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kiñca “juṇhapakkhapañcamito paṭṭhāyā”ti vuttattā aṭṭhakathāyeva pubbāparavirodhopi siyā.

‘Of the first phrase’ means of the phrase ‘when less than ten days remain.’ ‘By the previous method’ means by way of absolute connection. ‘Those days’ refers to during those days. ‘Absolutely’ means continuously; it is said that it refers to any day whatsoever within those ten days. ‘Of the month of Pavāraṇā’ means of the first month of Kattika. For here, due to its connection with the first Pavāraṇā, it is called ‘the month of Pavāraṇā.’ ‘Starting from the fifth day of the bright fortnight’ means beginning with the fifth day of the bright fortnight. ‘From the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pavāraṇā’ or, it means starting from the fifth day of the bright fortnight that precedes the declaration of the Pavāraṇā month. However, if a reading is found here stating, ‘If one wishes, “An extra robe may be kept for a maximum of ten days” (Pārā. 463), this is already established by that; but a training rule was laid down displaying a meaning as if it were new, by way of the arising of the matter’ (Sārattha. Ṭī. 2.650), then that reading should be seen as a careless reading because it contradicts ‘when less than ten days remain.’ Furthermore, since it is said, ‘starting from the fifth day of the bright fortnight,’ there might even be a contradiction between the beginning and the end of the commentary itself.

Accekacīvaranti [M 0.0341] accāyikacīvaraṃ vuccati, so ca accāyikabhāvo dāyakassa gamikādibhāvenāti dassetuṃ “gamikagilānagabbhiniabhinavuppannasaddhānaṃ puggalāna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha gamiko nāma “senāya vā gantukāmo hoti, pavāsaṃ vā gantukāmo hotī”ti (pārā. 649) vutto. Aññatarena “vassāvāsikaṃ dassāmī”ti evaṃ ārocetvā dinnanti gamikādīnaṃ aññatarena gamanādīhi kāraṇehi dātukāmena dūtaṃ vā pesetvā, sayaṃ vā āgantvā “vassāvāsikaṃ dassāmī”ti evaṃ ārocetvā dinnaṃ cīvaraṃ. Ettha ca “idaṃ me, bhante, accekacīvaraṃ cīvarakālasamayaṃ atikkāmitaṃ nissaggiya”nti (pārā. 649) iminā nayena nissajjanavidhānaṃ veditabbaṃ.

An emergency robe is called an urgent robe, and to show that this state of urgency arises from the donor’s condition, such as being a traveler, it is said, ‘for individuals who are travelers, sick, pregnant, or in whom faith has newly arisen,’ and so forth. Here, a traveler is defined as ‘one who intends to go with an army or intends to go on a journey’ (Pārā. 649). ‘A robe given by someone who, having announced, “I will give a rains-residence robe”’ means a robe given by one of the travelers and so forth, who, due to reasons such as travel, sends a messenger or comes in person and gives the robe after announcing, ‘I will give a rains-residence robe.’ Here, the procedure for relinquishment should be understood by this method: ‘Venerable sir, this emergency robe of mine has exceeded the robe season and is to be relinquished’ (Pārā. 649).

Sesanti “sādhāraṇapaññattī”tiādikaṃ. Ayaṃ pana viseso – tattha atirekacīvare atirekacīvarasaññiādino dasāhātikkamo, idha accekacīvare accekacīvarasaññiādino cīvarakālātikkamo. Tathā anaccekacīvare accekacīvarasaññino, vematikassa ca dukkaṭaṃ. Jātippamāṇasampannassa accekacīvarassa attano santakatā, dasāhānāgatāya kattikatemāsikapuṇṇamāya uppannabhāvo, anadhiṭṭhitaavikappitatā, cīvarakālātikkamoti caturaṅgabhāvova ettha viseso.

The rest refers to ‘the general regulation’ and so forth. However, there is this distinction: there, in the case of an extra robe, the offense is the exceeding of ten days by one who perceives it as an extra robe and so forth; whereas here, in the case of an emergency robe, the offense is the exceeding of the robe season by one who perceives it as an emergency robe and so forth. Similarly, for one who perceives a non-emergency robe as an emergency robe, and for one who is uncertain, there is a dukkaṭa offense. The specific condition here is its fourfold nature: (1) its being one's own emergency robe of the proper kind and size; (2) its having arisen when the Kattika full moon is less than ten days away; (3) its not having been determined or shared; and (4) its exceeding the robe season.

Accekacīvarasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning the emergency robe is concluded.

9. Sāsaṅkasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

9. Explanation of the Training Rule Regarding a Suspicious Place

Upasampajjantiādīsu viyāti “paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharatī”ti (vibha. 508) imassa vibhaṅge “upasampajjā”ti uddharitabbe “upasampajja”nti uddhaṭaṃ. Tadiha nidassanaṃ kataṃ. Ādisaddena pana “anāpucchaṃ vā gaccheyyā”tiādīnaṃ (pāci. 111, 115) saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Upagantvāti upasaddassatthamāha. Vasitvāti akkhaṇḍaṃ vasitvā. “Yena yassa hi sambandho, dūraṭṭhampi ca tassa ta”nti vacanato “imassa…pe… iminā sambandho”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha imassāti “upavassa”nti padassa. Vinayapariyāyena araññalakkhaṇaṃ adinnādānapārājike [V 0.0314] āgataṃ. Tattha hi “gāmā vā araññā vā”ti anavasesato avahāraṭṭhānapariggahena [M 0.0342] tadubhayaṃ asaṅkarato dassetuṃ “ṭhapetvā gāmañcā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Gāmūpacāro hi loke gāmasaṅkhameva gacchatīti. Idha pana suttantapariyāyena “pañcadhanusatikaṃ pacchima”nti (pārā. 654) āgataṃ āraññakaṃ bhikkhuṃ sandhāya. Na hi so vinayapariyāyike araññe vasanto “āraññako panthasenāsano”ti (ma. ni. 1.61) sutte vutto, tasmā tattha āgatameva lakkhaṇaṃ gahetabbanti dassento “sabbapacchimāni āropitena ācariyadhanunā”tiādimāha. Tattha “ācariyadhanu nāma pakatihatthena navavidatthipamāṇaṃ. Jiyāya pana āropitāya catuhatthapamāṇa”nti vadanti. Gāmassāti parikkhittassa gāmassa. Indakhīlatoti ummārato. Parikkhepārahaṭṭhānatoti pariyante ṭhitagharassa upacāre ṭhitassa majjhimassa purisassa paṭhamaleḍḍupātato. Kittakena maggena minitabbanti āha “sace”tiādi. Majjhimaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “vihārassāpi gāmasseva upacāraṃ nīharitvā ubhinnaṃ leḍḍupātānaṃ antarā minitabba”nti vuttaṃ. Corānaṃ niviṭṭhokāsādidassanenāti ārāme, ārāmūpacāre ca corānaṃ niviṭṭhokāsādidassanena kāraṇena. Ādisaddena bhuttokāsaṭṭhitokāsanisinnokāsanipannokāsānaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Corehi manussānaṃ hataviluttākoṭitabhāvadassanatoti ārāme, ārāmūpacāre ca hataviluttākoṭitabhāvadassanato.

As in 'upasampajjanti', etc.: in the analysis of 'he dwells having attained the first jhāna' (Vibha. 508), where 'upasampajjā' should be extracted, 'upasampajja' is extracted. This is given here as an example. By the word 'ādi', the inclusion of such phrases as 'he may go without asking permission' (Pācittiya 111, 115) should be understood. Upagantvā: he states the meaning of the prefix 'upa'. Vasitvā means having dwelt continuously. According to the saying, 'Whatever connection one has, even if distant, that belongs to him,' it is stated: 'This... connection with this.' Here, 'this' refers to the word 'upavassa'. According to the Vinaya method, the characteristic of a forest is found in the Pārājika on theft. There, in order to show both without confusion by encompassing all places of theft without remainder with 'from a village or from a forest', it is said 'excluding the village', etc. For the vicinity of a village is counted as the village itself in the world. Here, however, according to the Suttanta method, it is said: 'five hundred bow-lengths as the final limit' (Pārā. 654), with reference to a forest-dwelling monk. For he, dwelling in a forest as defined by the Vinaya, is not called 'a forest-dweller, one whose lodging is by the path' in the sutta (MN 1.61). Therefore, to show that the characteristic mentioned there should be taken, he says, 'all the final boundaries are measured by the teacher’s strung bow', etc. There, they say, 'A teacher's bow is nine spans in length by the natural hand, but when strung, it is four cubits.' 'Of the village' means of an enclosed village. 'From the Indakhīla' means from the threshold post. 'From the place suitable for enclosure' means from the first clod-throw of a man of medium height standing in the vicinity of a house situated at the boundary. He says 'if', etc., asking 'by how much of the path should it be measured?' But in the Majjhima Commentary it is said: 'Having determined the vicinity of the monastery just as for the village, the distance between the two clod-throws should be measured.' 'By seeing the settled places of thieves, etc.' means because of seeing the settled places, etc., of thieves in the monastery and its vicinity. By the word 'ādi', the inclusion of places where they have eaten, stood, sat, and lain down is to be understood. 'From seeing the state of people being killed, plundered, and assaulted by thieves' means from seeing the state of being killed, plundered, and assaulted in the monastery and its vicinity.

Antaraghare nikkhipeyyāti antare antare gharāni ettha, etassāti vā antaragharaṃ, gāmo, tasmiṃ ṭhapeyyāti attho. Tenāha “āraññakassā”tiādi. Tañcāti nikkhipanañca. “Mahāpavāraṇāya pavārito hotī”ti idaṃ vassacchedaṃ akatvā vuṭṭhabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ, na pana pavāraṇāya aṅgabhāvaṃ. Teneva hi byatirekaṃ dassentena samantapāsādikāyaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.653-654) vuttaṃ “sace pacchimikāya vā upagato hoti chinnavasso vā, nikkhipituṃ na labhatī”ti. Kattikamāso nāma pubbakattikamāsassa kāḷapakkhapāṭipadato paṭṭhāya yāva aparakattikapuṇṇamā, tāva ekūnattiṃsa rattindivā. Eva-saddena kattikamāsato paraṃ na labhatīti dasseti. Ūnappamāṇe tāva araññalakkhaṇāyogato na labhatu, kasmā gāvutato atirekappamāṇe na labhatīti āha “yatra [M 0.0343] hī”tiādi. Nimantito pana addhayojanampi yojanampi gantvā vasituṃ pacceti, idamappamāṇaṃ. Sāsaṅkasappaṭibhayameva hotīti sāsaṅkañceva sappaṭibhayañca hoti. Eva-saddena anāsaṅkaappaṭibhayehi aṅgayuttepi senāsane vasanto nikkhipituṃ na labhatīti dasseti. Ettāvatā purimikāya upagantvā akkhaṇḍaṃ katvā vuṭṭhavasso yaṃ gāmaṃ gocaragāmaṃ katvā pañcadhanusatikapacchime āraññakasenāsane viharati, tasmiṃ gāme cīvaraṃ ṭhapetvā sakalakattikamāsaṃ tasmiṃyeva senāsane tena cīvarena vinā vatthuṃ anujānitvā [V 0.0315] idāni vihārato aññattha vasantassa chārattaṃ vippavāsaṃ anujānanto “siyā ca tassa bhikkhuno”tiādimāha. Asamādānacārañhi atthatakathinā eva labhanti, netareti ettha idampi kāraṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tattha chārattaparamaṃ tena bhikkhunā tena cīvarena vippavasitabbanti yo bhikkhu vihāre vasanto tato aññattha gamanakicce sati antaraghare cīvaraṃ nikkhipati, tena bhikkhunā tena cīvarena chārattaparamaṃ vippavasitabbaṃ, cha rattiyo tamhā vihārā aññattha vasitabbāti vuttaṃ hoti. Vuttañhi bhadantena buddhadattācariyena –

'He should deposit it in an inhabited area' means: an inhabited area is where there are houses here and there, or it is his village; the meaning is he should place it there. Therefore, he says, 'for the forest-dwelling one,' etc. And that refers to the depositing. The phrase 'he has been invited for the great Pavāraṇā' is said to show the state of having completed the rains-residence without a break, but not that it is a factor of the Pavāraṇā. For this very reason, to indicate the exception, it is said in the Samantapāsādikā (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.653-654): 'If he has entered upon the later rains-residence or has a broken rains-residence, he is not allowed to deposit it.' The month of Kattika means twenty-nine days and nights, starting from the first day of the dark fortnight of the earlier Kattika month until the full moon of the later Kattika month. By the word 'eva,' it is shown that this is not allowed after the month of Kattika. Let him not be allowed in a lesser measure because the characteristic of a forest does not apply; why is he not allowed in a measure exceeding a gāvuta? He says, 'where indeed,' etc. But if invited, he returns to stay having gone even half a yojana or a full yojana; this is without limit. 'It is indeed with suspicion and with danger' means it is both with suspicion and with danger. By the word 'eva,' it is shown that even while dwelling in a lodging endowed with the factors of being without suspicion and without danger, he is not allowed to deposit it. Up to this point, for a monk who, having entered upon the earlier rains-residence and completed it unbroken, and having made a certain village his alms-resort, dwells in a forest lodging at the final limit of five hundred bow-lengths, it has been allowed that he may deposit his robe in that village and dwell for the entire month of Kattika in that very lodging without that robe. Now, allowing a six-night absence for one dwelling elsewhere than the monastery, he says, 'And there might be for that monk,' etc. For only those who have received the kathina privilege are allowed the practice without formal undertaking, not others. Here this reason should also be seen. Therein, 'that monk should be absent from that robe for at most six nights' means: whichever monk, while dwelling in the monastery, deposits his robe in an inhabited area when there is some business to go elsewhere, that monk should be absent from that robe for at most six nights; it is said that he should dwell elsewhere than that monastery for six nights. For it has been said by the venerable teacher Buddhadatta—

“Yaṃ gāmaṃ gocaraṃ katvā, bhikkhu āraññake vase;

Tasmiṃ gāme ṭhapetuṃ taṃ, māsamekaṃ tu vaṭṭati.

For a monk dwelling in the forest who has made a certain village his alms-resort, it is allowable to deposit it in that village for one month.

“Aññattheva vasantassa, chārattaparamaṃ mataṃ;

Ayamassa adhippāyo, paṭicchanno pakāsito”ti.

For one dwelling elsewhere, at most six nights is considered allowable; this is his intention, concealed and now revealed.

Tenevāha “tato ce uttari vippavaseyyāti chārattato uttari tasmiṃ senāsane sattamaṃ aruṇaṃ uṭṭhāpeyyā”tiādi. Tathā asakkontenāti gataṭṭhānassa dūratāya senāsanaṃ āgantvā sattamaṃ aruṇaṃ uṭṭhāpetuṃ asakkontena. Evampi asakkontena tatreva ṭhitena paccuddharitabbaṃ “atirekacīvaraṭṭhāne ṭhassatī”ti. Vasitvāti aruṇaṃ uṭṭhāpetvā. Bhikkhusammuti udositasikkhāpade vuttāva.

Therefore, he says, 'If he should be absent beyond that,' that is, 'beyond six nights, he should cause the seventh dawn to arise in that lodging,' etc. 'Thus, if unable' means being unable to return to the lodging and cause the seventh dawn to arise because of the distance of the place one has gone to. Even being unable in this way, while remaining right there, it should be relinquished with the thought, 'It will stand in the place of an extra robe.' 'Having dwelt' means after causing the dawn to arise. The consent of the monks is as stated in the Udosita Training Rule.

Sesanti “aññatra bhikkhusammutiyāti ayamettha anupaññattī”tiādikaṃ. Tattha hi aṅgesu yaṃ rattivippavāso catutthamaṅgaṃ, taṃ idha chārattato uttari vippavāso hotīti ayameva viseso.

'The rest' means 'except by the consent of the monks,' this is the supplementary regulation here,' and so on. For there, among the factors, that which is absence for a night is the fourth factor; here, that it is an absence beyond six nights is the only difference.

Sāsaṅkasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Sāsaṅka Training Rule is concluded.

10. Pariṇatasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

10. The explanation of the Training Rule on What is Designated

Nanu [M 0.0344] cāyaṃ saṅghassa pariṇato, na pariccatto, atha kathaṃ saṅghasantako hotīti āha “so hī”tiādi. Tattha soti lābho. Ekena pariyāyenāti pariṇatabhāvasaṅkhātena ekena pariyāyena. “Labhitabba”nti iminā lābhasaddassa kammasādhanamāha. Cīvarādivatthunti cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhāraṃ [V 0.0316] antamaso cuṇṇapiṇḍampi dantakaṭṭhampi dasikasuttampi. Pariṇatanti saṅghassa ninnaṃ saṅghassa poṇaṃ saṅghassa pabbhāraṃ hutvā ṭhitanti attho. Yena pana kāraṇena so pariṇato hoti, taṃ dassetvā tassa atthaṃ dassetuṃ “dassāma karissāmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Attano pariṇāmentassāti “idaṃ mayhaṃ dehī”ti saṅghassa pariṇatabhāvaṃ ñatvā attano pariṇāmetvā gaṇhantassa. Payogeti pariṇāmanappayoge. Ettha ca “idaṃ me, bhante, jānaṃ saṅghikaṃ lābhaṃ pariṇataṃ attano pariṇāmikaṃ nissaggiya”nti iminā nayena nissajjanavidhānaṃ veditabbaṃ.

“But was this not designated for the Sangha, not relinquished? How then does it belong to the Sangha?” To this it is said: “For that...” and so on. Here, “that” refers to the gain. “By one method” means by one method, namely, the state of being designated. “Should be obtained”—by this, the objective sense of the word “gain” is stated. “Robes and other requisites” means robes, almsfood, dwellings, medicines for the sick, and accessories, even down to a ball of powder, a tooth-stick, or a needle-thread. “Designated” means having become inclined towards the Sangha, sloping towards the Sangha, tending towards the Sangha. To show the reason why it is designated, and to explain its meaning, “We will give, we will do...” and so on is stated. “Of one who designates for oneself” means of one who, knowing that it is designated for the Sangha, takes it after designating it for oneself, thinking, “Give this to me.” “In the application” means in the application of designating. Here, the procedure of relinquishment should be understood according to this method: “Venerable sir, this gain, known by me as designated for the Sangha, having been designated for myself, is to be forfeited.”

Saṅghacetiyapuggalesūti ettha ca antamaso sunakhaṃ upādāya yo koci satto “puggalo”ti veditabbo. Aññasaṅghādīnanti aññasaṅghacetiyapuggalānaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “saṅghassa pariṇataṃ aññassa saṅghassa vā cetiyassa vā puggalassa vā, cetiyassa pariṇataṃ aññassa cetiyassa vā saṅghassa vā puggalassa vā, puggalassa pariṇataṃ aññassa puggalassa vā saṅghassa vā cetiyassa vā pariṇāmentassa dukkaṭa”nti.

“To the Sangha, a shrine, or an individual”—here, even down to a dog, any living being should be understood as an “individual.” “Of another Sangha, etc.” means of another Sangha, shrine, or individual. This is what is meant: “For one who designates what is designated for the Sangha to another Sangha, or a shrine, or an individual; or what is designated for a shrine to another shrine, or the Sangha, or an individual; or what is designated for an individual to another individual, or the Sangha, or a shrine—there is an offense of wrong-doing.”

Idāni anāpattiṃ dassetuṃ “apariṇatasaññino”tiādimāha. Pariṇate, apariṇate ca apariṇatasaññino cāti sambandho, pariṇate, apariṇate cāti ubhayatthāpi anāpattīti attho. Vuttañhetaṃ “pariṇate apariṇatasaññī attano pariṇāmeti, anāpatti. Apariṇate apariṇatasaññī anāpattī”ti (pārā. 660). Deyyadhammoti cattāro paccayā. Ādisaddena “paṭisaṅkhāraṃ vā labheyya, ciraṭṭhitiko vā assa, yattha vā pana tumhākaṃ cittaṃ pasīdati, tattha dethā”ti (pārā. 661) vacanānaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Sace pana dāyakā “mayaṃ [M 0.0345] saṅghabhattaṃ kattukāmā, cetiyapūjaṃ kattukāmā, ekassa bhikkhuno parikkhāraṃ dātukāmā, tumhākaṃ ruciyā dassāma. Bhaṇatha, kattha demā”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.660) vadanti, evaṃ vutte tena bhikkhunā “yattha icchatha, tattha dethā”ti vattabbā.

Now, to show the non-offense, he states “for one who perceives it as undesignated,” and so on. The connection is that ‘for one who perceives it as undesignated’ applies to both ‘when it is designated’ and ‘when it is undesignated’; the meaning is that there is no offense in either case. For it is said: “If one perceives it as undesignated when it is designated and designates it for oneself, there is no offense. If one perceives it as undesignated when it is undesignated, there is no offense” (Pārā. 660). “Things to be given” refers to the four requisites. The word “etc.” includes such statements as: “Or he may receive it for repairs, or if it will last long, or give it where your mind is pleased” (Pārā. 661). But if the donors say, “We wish to offer a meal to the Sangha, we wish to make an offering to a shrine, we wish to give requisites to a single monk—we will give according to your preference. Tell us, where should we give?” (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.660), then when this is said, that monk should say, “Give it where you wish.”

Pariṇatasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on What is Designated is concluded.

Pattavaggo tatiyo.

The Third Chapter, on the Bowl.

Iti kaṅkhāvitaraṇiyā pātimokkhavaṇṇanāya

Thus, in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī, the Explanation of the Pātimokkha,

Vinayatthamañjūsāyaṃ līnatthappakāsaniyaṃ

in the Vinayatthamañjūsā, the Elucidation of Hidden Meanings,

Nissaggiyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

the Explanation of the Nissaggiyas is concluded.

Pācittiyakaṇḍaṃ

The Section on Pācittiya Offenses

1. Musāvādavaggo

1. The Chapter on False Speech

1. Musāvādasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Training Rule on False Speech

Sampajānamusāvādeti [M 0.0346][V 0.0317] ettha musāti abhūtaṃ atacchaṃ vatthu, vādoti tassa bhūtato tacchato viññāpanaṃ, sampajānassa musāvādo sampajānamusāvādo, tasmiṃ sampajānamusāvādeti attho. Tenāha “pubbe”tiādi. So ca pana musāvādo pubbabhāgakkhaṇe, taṅkhaṇe ca vijānantassa hoti “pubbevassa hoti ‘musā bhaṇissa’nti, bhaṇantassa hoti ‘musā bhaṇāmī’”ti (pāci. 4) vuttattāti āha “pubbepi jānitvā vacanakkhaṇepi jānantassā”ti. Etañhi dvayaṃ aṅgabhūtaṃ, itaraṃ pana hotu vā, mā vā, akāraṇametaṃ. Nanu cetaṃ bhaṇanameva ñāyatīti āha “bhaṇanañca nāmā”tiādi. Abhūtassāti atacchassa.

In “knowingly false speech”: here, “false” (musā) means what is untrue, unreal; “speech” (vāda) means making that known as true and real. The false speech of one who is aware is “knowingly false speech”; in this, “knowingly false speech” is the meaning. Therefore, he said: “previously,” and so on. Moreover, that false speech occurs for one who knows both at the prior moment and at the moment of speaking, as it is said: “Before, he has the thought, ‘I will speak falsely,’ and while speaking, he thinks, ‘I am speaking falsely’” (Pāc. 4). Thus, it is said: “of one who knows beforehand and also knows at the moment of speaking.” For these two are essential factors; as for the other, whether it occurs or not, it is not a cause. “But surely this is just known as speaking?” To this, he said: “And speaking is called,” and so on. “Of what is untrue” means of what is unreal.

Hatthakaṃ sakyaputtanti ettha hatthakoti tassa therassa nāmaṃ. Sakyānaṃ puttoti sakyaputto. Buddhakāle kira sakyakulato asīti purisasahassāni pabbajiṃsu, tesaṃ so aññataro. Avajānitvā paṭijānanādivatthusminti ettha avajānitvā paṭijānanaṃ nāma titthiyehi saddhiṃ kathento attano vāde kañci dosaṃ sallakkhento “nāyaṃ mama vādo”ti avajānitvā puna kathento kathento niddosataṃ sallakkhetvā “mameva ayaṃ vādo”ti paṭijānāti. Ādisaddena paṭijānitvā avajānanaṃ, aññenaññaṃ paṭicaraṇaṃ, sampajānamusābhāsanaṃ, saṅketaṃ katvā visaṃvādakaraṇañca saṅgaṇhāti. Idāni āpattibhedadassanatthaṃ “uttarimanussadhammārocanattha”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

In “Hatthaka, the Sakyan's son”: here, “Hatthaka” is the name of that elder. “Son of the Sakyans” means Sakyan-born. During the Buddha's time, it is said that eighty thousand men from the Sakyan clan went forth, and he was one of them. In the case of “rejecting and then asserting,” and so on: here, “rejecting and then asserting” is when someone, while conversing with sectarians, detects some fault in his own argument and, rejecting it, says, “This is not my view.” But then later, while speaking on, he perceives it to be faultless and asserts, “This is indeed my view.” The word “etc.” includes: asserting and then rejecting, prevarication, knowingly speaking falsehood, and making an agreement and then breaking it. Now, to show the distinctions of offenses, “for the purpose of declaring superhuman states,” and so on, is stated.

Anupadhāretvā sahasā bhaṇantassāti avīmaṃsitvā vegena diṭṭhampi “adiṭṭhaṃ me”tiādinā bhaṇantassa[V 0.0318]. “Aññaṃ bhaṇissāmī”ti aññaṃ bhaṇantassāti yo mandattā momūhattā pakkhalanto “cīvara”nti vattabbe “cīra”ntiādīni bhaṇati, ayaṃ “aññaṃ bhaṇissāmī”ti aññaṃ bhaṇati nāma. Yo pana sāmaṇerena “api, bhante, mayhaṃ upajjhāyaṃ passitthā”ti [M 0.0347] vutto keḷiṃ kurumāno “tava upajjhāyo dārusakaṭaṃ yojetvā gato bhavissatī”ti vā siṅgālasaddaṃ sutvā “kassāyaṃ saddo”ti vutto “mātuyā te yānena gacchantiyā kaddame laggacakkaṃ uddharantānaṃ ayaṃ saddo”ti vā evaṃ neva davā, na ravā aññaṃ bhaṇati, so āpattiṃ āpajjatiyeva. Aññā pūraṇakathā nāma hoti – eko gāme thokaṃ telaṃ labhitvā vihāraṃ āgato sāmaṇeraṃ bhaṇati “tvaṃ ajja kuhiṃ gato, gāmo ekatelo ahosī”ti vā, pacchikāya ṭhapitaṃ pūvakhaṇḍaṃ labhitvā “ajja gāme pacchikāhi pūve cāresu”nti vā, ayaṃ musāvādova hoti. Visaṃvādanapurekkhāratāti visaṃ vādenti etenāti visaṃvādanaṃ, vañcanādhippāyavasappavattaṃ cittaṃ, tassa purekkhāratā visaṃvādanapurekkhāratā, visaṃvādanacittassa purato karaṇanti attho.

“Of one speaking hastily without considering” means of one speaking quickly without reflection, for instance, saying, “I have not seen it” even when something has been seen. “Of one speaking something else while intending to say something else” refers to one who, due to dullness and confusion, stumbles and says “cīra” when he should say “cīvara,” and so on—this is called “speaking something else while intending to say something else.” But if, when a novice asks, “Venerable sir, have you seen my preceptor?” he jokingly replies, “Your preceptor must have gone off in a wooden cart,” or, having heard the cry of a jackal and being asked, “Whose sound is this?” he says, “That is the sound of people pulling out the stuck wheel of your mother’s carriage as she was traveling through the mud”—if he thus speaks something else, not as a slip of the tongue, he certainly commits an offense. Another case is called “exaggeration”: for instance, a monk receives a little oil in the village, returns to the monastery, and says to a novice, “Where did you go today? The village was flowing with oil,” or, having received a piece of cake placed in a basket, he says, “Today in the village they were distributing cakes by the basketful”—this is simply false speech. “With the intention to deceive”: ‘deception’ is that by which one deceives, that is, a mind proceeding from an intention to cheat. ‘Having that as a forerunner’ means placing a deceptive mind at the forefront.

Musāvādasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on False Speech is concluded.

2. Omasavādasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Training Rule on Contemptuous Speech

Omasavādeti khuṃsanagarahaṇavacane. Yasmā pana taṃ neva kaṇṇasukhaṃ, na hadayasukhaṃ, tasmā tena kaṇṇañceva hadayañca vijjhatīti āha “ovijjhanavacane”ti, jātiādīhi ghaṭetvā vacaneti vuttaṃ hoti. Tenāha “jātināmā”tiādi. Tattha jāti nāma brāhmaṇādi ukkaṭṭhā ceva caṇḍālādi hīnā ca jāti. Nāmaṃ nāma avakaṇṇakādi hīnañceva buddharakkhitādi ukkaṭṭhañca nāmaṃ. Gottaṃ nāma kosiyādi hīnañceva gotamādi ukkaṭṭhañca gottaṃ. Kammaṃ nāma pupphachaḍḍakādi hīnañceva kasivaṇijjādi ukkaṭṭhañca kammaṃ. Sippaṃ nāma naḷakārādi hīnañceva muddāgaṇanādi ukkaṭṭhañca sippaṃ. Ābādho nāma sabbopi rogo hīnoyeva. Atha vā madhumeho ukkaṭṭho, seso hīnoti veditabbo. Liṅgaṃ nāma atidīghādi hīnañceva nātidīghādi ukkaṭṭhañca liṅgaṃ. Kileso nāma rāgādiko sabbopi kileso. Āpatti nāma sotāpattādikā ukkaṭṭhā ceva pārājikādi anukkaṭṭhā ca āpatti. Akkoso nāma “oṭṭhosī”tiādiko hīno ceva “paṇḍitosī”tiādiko (pāci. 15) ukkaṭṭho ca akkoso.

`Omasavāda` means words of contempt and blame. Since such speech is neither pleasant to the ear nor pleasing to the heart, it is said to pierce both the ear and the heart; hence it is called 'piercing speech,' which means speech connected with birth and so forth. Thus it is said, 'birth, name,' and so on. Herein, 'birth' refers to high births such as that of a brahmin, and low births such as that of an outcaste. 'Name' refers to low names such as 'Crooked-ear,' and high names such as 'Buddha-protected.' 'Clan' refers to low clans such as the Kosiya, and high clans such as the Gotama. 'Work' refers to low occupations such as a flower-sweeper, and high occupations such as farming and trade. 'Craft' refers to low crafts such as basket-weaving, and high crafts such as accounting and reckoning. 'Affliction' refers to any disease, which is considered low. Alternatively, diabetes may be considered high, while the rest are to be understood as low.
