'Characteristic' refers to low characteristics such as being excessively tall, and high characteristics such as not being excessively tall. 'Defilement' refers to any defilement, such as lust. 'Offense' refers to high offenses such as those related to stream-entry, and inferior offenses such as a pārājika. 'Abuse' refers to low abuse such as 'You are a camel!' and high abuse such as 'You are wise!'

Yathā [M 0.0348][V 0.0319] tathāti pāḷiāgatānāgatapadānaṃ yena kenaci ākārena. Imasmiṃ sikkhāpade ṭhapetvā bhikkhuṃ bhikkhuniādayo sabbe sattā anupasampannaṭṭhāne ṭhitāti āha “idha cā”tiādi. Davakamyatā nāma keḷihasādhippāyatā. Sabbatthāti upasampannānupasampannesu ceva pāḷiāgatānāgatapadesu cāti sabbattha. Atthadhammaanusāsanipurekkhārānanti ettha “caṇḍālosī”tiādikāya pāḷiyā atthaṃ vaṇṇento atthapurekkhāro nāma. Pāḷiṃ vācento dhammapurekkhāro nāma. Anusiṭṭhiyaṃ ṭhatvā “idānipi caṇḍālosi, pāpaṃ mā akāsi. Mā tamotamaparāyaṇo ahosī”tiādinā (pāci. aṭṭha. 35) nayena kathento anusāsanipurekkhāro nāmāti veditabbo.

'However it may be' means in any manner whatsoever regarding words that are in the Pāli text and those that are not. In this training rule, excepting a monk, all beings—nuns and so on—stand in the position of one not fully ordained; thus it is said, 'and here,' and so on. 'Wantonness' means the intention of play and laughter. 'In all cases' means in all cases, regarding both the fully ordained and the not fully ordained, and regarding words that are in the Pāli text and those that are not. Regarding 'with the aim of meaning, Dhamma, or instruction': here, one who explains the meaning of a Pāli passage such as 'You are an outcaste' is called 'one who has meaning as his aim.' One who recites the Pāli is called 'one who has the Dhamma as his aim.' One who speaks by way of instruction, saying 'Even now you are an outcaste; do not do evil. Do not be one for whom darkness is the final destination,' is to be understood as 'one who has instruction as his aim.'

Omasavādasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on contemptuous speech is concluded.

3. Pesuññasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Divisive Speech.

Bhikkhupesuññeti pisatīti pisuṇā, yāya vācāya samagge satte avayavabhūte vagge bhinne karoti, sā vācā pisuṇā, pisuṇā eva pesuññaṃ, tāya vācāya samannāgato pisuṇo, tassa kammaṃ pesuññaṃ, bhikkhussa pesuññaṃ bhikkhupesuññaṃ, tasmiṃ bhikkhupesuññe, bhikkhuto sutvā bhikkhunā, bhikkhussa vā upasaṃhaṭapesuññeti attho. Tenāha “jātiādīhī”tiādi. Tañca kho dvīhi kāraṇehi upasaṃharatīti āha “bhikkhuno piyakamyatāya vā”tiādi. Tattha bhikkhuno piyakamyatāyāti yassa taṃ bhāsati, tassa bhikkhuno “evamahaṃ etassa piyo bhavissāmī”ti attano piyabhāvaṃ patthayamānatāya. Bhedādhippāyenāti “evamayaṃ tena saddhiṃ bhijjissatī”ti parassa parena bhedaṃ icchantena. Atha vā piyasuññakaraṇato pesuññaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. pācittiya 3.36) niruttinayena, yāya vācāya yassa taṃ bhāsati, tassa hadaye attano piyabhāvaṃ, parassa ca suññabhāvaṃ karoti, sā vācā, “bhikkhussa pesuññaṃ bhikkhupesuñña”ntiādinā evampettha attho daṭṭhabbo. “Vuttanayenevāti “jātiādīhi akkosavatthūhī”tiādinā vuttanayena.

Regarding divisive speech concerning a monk (`bhikkhupesuññe`): because it crushes (`pisati`), it is called `pisuṇā`. That speech by which one makes united beings divided, or those already in factions more divided—that speech is `pisuṇā`. `Pisuṇā` itself is divisive speech (`pesuñña`). One endowed with such speech is a slanderer (`pisuṇo`). His action is divisive speech (`pesuñña`). Divisive speech concerning a monk is `bhikkhupesuñña`. Regarding that `bhikkhupesuñña`, the meaning is divisive speech reported to a monk by another monk after having heard it from a monk. Hence it is said, 'by birth,' and so on. And one reports it for two reasons, as it is said: 'from a desire to be dear to a monk,' and so on. Here, 'from a desire to be dear to a monk' means desiring to make oneself dear, thinking, 'In this way, I will become dear to this monk to whom I speak.' 'With the intention of causing division' means wishing for a division between one person and another, thinking, 'In this way, he will be divided from him.' Alternatively, according to etymology, `pesuñña` comes from 'making dear' (`piya`) and 'making empty' (`suñña`). That speech by which one makes oneself dear in the heart of the one to whom one speaks, and makes the other person empty—that is the meaning to be understood here by such phrases as 'divisive speech concerning a monk is `bhikkhupesuñña`.' 'In the manner already stated' means in the manner stated by 'through the grounds for abuse, such as birth, etc.'

Pāḷimuttakaakkosūpasaṃhāreti [M 0.0349] “corosī”tiādinā akkosassa upasaṃhāre. “Anakkosavatthubhūtaṃ pana pesuññakaraṃ tassa kiriyaṃ, vacanaṃ vā piyakamyatāya upasaṃharantassa kiñcāpi iminā sikkhāpadena āpatti na dissati, tathāpi dukkaṭena bhavitabba”nti (sārattha. ṭī. pācittiya 3.36) vadanti. Pāpagarahitāya vadantassāti ekaṃ akkosantaṃ, ekañca [V 0.0320] khamantaṃ disvā “aho nillajjo, īdisampi nāma bhavantaṃ puna vattabbaṃ maññissatī”ti evaṃ kevalaṃ pāpagarahitāya bhaṇantassa.

'Bringing in abuse not found in the Pāli text' means bringing in abuse such as 'You are a thief!' They say: 'However, for one who, out of a desire to be liked, reports an action or a word that causes division but is not a ground for abuse, although an offense under this training rule is not seen, there should still be an offense of wrong-doing.' 'For one who speaks out of condemnation for what is evil' means: for one who, having seen one person abusing and another enduring it, speaks merely out of condemnation for what is evil, saying, 'Oh, the shameless one! That he should think to speak to a venerable one like you again in this way!'

Pesuññasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on divisive speech is concluded.

4. Padasodhammasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Reciting the Dhamma Word by Word.

Padaso dhammaṃ vāceyyāti ekato padaṃ padaṃ dhammaṃ vāceyya, koṭṭhāsaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ vāceyyāti attho. Yasmā na kevalaṃ tisso saṅgītiyo āruḷhadhammaṃyeva padaso vācentassa āpatti, tasmā “saṅgītittayaṃ anāruḷhampī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ādi-saddena (pāci. aṭṭha. 45) sīlūpadesa dhutaṅgapañhaārammaṇakathā buddhikadaṇḍakaññāṇavatthuasubhakathādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Meṇḍakamilindapañhesu therassa sakappaṭibhāne anāpatti. Yaṃ rañño saññāpanatthaṃ āharitvā vuttaṃ, tattha āpatti. Vaṇṇapiṭakaaṅgulimālapiṭakaraṭṭhapālagajjitaāḷavakagajjitagūḷhamaggagūḷhavessantaragūḷhavinayavedallapiṭakādīni pana abuddhavacanāniyeva.

'One should teach the Dhamma word by word' means to teach the Dhamma together word by word, or to teach it section by section; this is the meaning. An offense is incurred not only when teaching word by word the Dhamma that was included in the three Councils, but also, as it is said, that which was 'not included in the three Councils,' and so on. By the word 'and so on,' the following are included: instruction on virtue, questions on ascetic practices, discussions on meditation objects, the Buddhika Daṇḍaka, the Ñāṇa Vatthu, the discourse on the unattractive, and so on. In the Meṇḍaka and Milinda questions, there is no offense in the elder’s own spontaneous inspiration. But where it was brought forth and spoken for the purpose of convincing the king, there is an offense. However, the Vaṇṇa Piṭaka, Aṅgulimāla Piṭaka, Raṭṭhapāla’s Roar, Āḷavaka’s Roar, the Hidden Path, the Hidden Vessantara, the Hidden Vinaya Vedalla Piṭaka, and so on are indeed not the words of the Buddha.

Yasmā pana taṃ padaṃ catubbidhaṃ hoti, tasmā taṃ dassetuṃ “padānupadaanvakkharānubyañjanesū”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha padanti eko gāthāpādo adhippeto. Anupadanti dutiyapādo. Anvakkharanti ekekaṃ akkharaṃ. Anubyañjananti purimabyañjanena sadisaṃ pacchābyañjanaṃ. Yaṃ kiñci vā ekaṃ akkharaṃ anvakkharaṃ. Akkharasamūho anubyañjanaṃ. Akkharānubyañjanasamūho padaṃ. Paṭhamaṃ padaṃ padameva, dutiyaṃ anupadanti evamettha nānākaraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Etesu padādīsu yaṃ kañci koṭṭhāsaṃ bhikkhuñca bhikkhuniñca ṭhapetvā avasesapuggalehi saddhiṃ ekato bhaṇantassa padādigaṇanāya pācittiyanti sambandho.

And since that unit of recitation (`pada`) is fourfold, to show this it is said: 'in `pada`s, `anupada`s, `anvakkhara`s, and `anubyañjana`s.' Herein, by '`pada`' is meant one line of a verse. By '`anupada`' is meant the second line. By '`anvakkhara`' is meant each individual letter. By '`anubyañjana`' is meant a subsequent consonant similar to a preceding consonant. Alternatively, any single letter is an '`anvakkhara`.' A group of letters is an '`anubyañjana`.' A group of letters and consonants is a '`pada`.' The first `pada` is just a `pada`, the second is an `anupada`—thus the distinction here should be understood. The connection is this: for one who recites any portion of these—`pada`s and so on—together with other individuals, excluding monks and nuns, there is a `pācittiya` offense for each `pada`, and so on, that is counted.

Ettha [M 0.0350] gāthābandhesu (pāci. aṭṭha. 45) tāva “manopubbaṅgamā dhammā”ti (dha. pa. 1, 2) ekamekaṃ padaṃ sāmaṇerena saddhiṃ ekato ārabhitvā ekatoyeva niṭṭhāpentassa padagaṇanāya pācittiyaṃ. Therena “manopubbaṅgamā dhammā”ti vutte taṃ padaṃ apāpuṇitvā “manoseṭṭhā manomayā”ti vacanakāle pattena sāmaṇerena ekato bhaṇantassa anupadagaṇanāya. “Rūpaṃ anicca”ntiādi (ma. ni. 1.353, 356) vacanakāle tena saddhiṃ “rū” kāramattameva vācentassa anvakkharagaṇanāya. Esa nayo gāthābandhepi. “Rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ, vedanā aniccā”ti (ma. ni. 1.353, 356) imaṃ suttaṃ vācayamāno therena “rūpaṃ [V 0.0321] anicca”nti vuccamāne sāmaṇero sīghapaññatāya “vedanā aniccā”ti imaṃ aniccapadaṃ therassa “rūpaṃ anicca”nti etena aniccapadena saddhiṃ ekato bhaṇanto vācaṃ nicchāreti, evaṃ vācentassa anubyañjanagaṇanāya pācittiyanti veditabbaṃ.

Here, in the case of verses (Pācittiya Aṭṭhakathā 45), firstly, regarding 'Mind precedes phenomena' (Dhp. 1, 2), for one who begins each word together with a novice and finishes it together, it is a pācittiya by counting the words. When the elder has said 'Mind precedes phenomena,' and the novice, not having reached that phrase, recites 'Mind is chief, mind-made' together with him as he reaches it, it is by counting the subsequent phrases. When reciting 'Form is impermanent,' etc. (MN 1.353, 356), for one who has him recite only the syllable 'rū' along with him, it is by counting the syllables. This same method applies also in the case of verses. When teaching the sutta 'Form, monks, is impermanent; feeling is impermanent' (MN 1.353, 356), while the elder is saying 'Form is impermanent,' if the novice, due to quick wisdom, utters 'Feeling is impermanent,' pronouncing this word 'impermanent' together with the elder's word 'impermanent' from 'Form is impermanent,' thus emitting speech, it should be understood that for one teaching in this way, it is a pācittiya by counting the consonants.

Tikapācittiyanti anupasampanne anupasampannasaññivematikaupasampannasaññīnaṃ vasena tīṇi pācittiyāni. Anupasampannena saddhiṃ ekato uddesaggahaṇe ekato bhaṇantassa anāpattīti sambandho. Esa nayo “sajjhāyakaraṇe, tassa santike uddesaggahaṇe”ti etthāpi. Tatrāyaṃ vinicchayo – upasampanno ca anupasampanno ca nisīditvā uddisāpenti. Ācariyo “nisinnānaṃ bhaṇāmī”ti tehi saddhiṃ ekato vadati, ācariyasseva āpatti. Anupasampannena saddhiṃ gaṇhantassa anāpatti. Dvepi ṭhitā gaṇhanti, eseva nayo. Daharabhikkhu nisinno, sāmaṇero ṭhito, “nisinnassa bhaṇāmī”ti bhaṇato anāpatti. Sace daharo tiṭṭhati, itaro nisīdati, “ṭhitassa bhaṇāmī”ti bhaṇatopi anāpatti. Sace bahūnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ antare eko sāmaṇero nisinno hoti, tasmiṃ nisinne padaso dhammaṃ vācentassa acittakā āpatti. Sace sāmaṇero upacāraṃ muñcitvā ṭhito vā nisinno vā hoti, yesaṃ vāceti, tesu apariyāpannattā ekena disābhāgena palāyanakaganthaṃ nāma gaṇhātīti saṅkhaṃ gacchati, tasmā anāpatti.

'A threefold pācittiya' means there are three pācittiyas in the case of one who is not fully ordained: with the perception that he is not fully ordained, with doubt, and with the perception that he is fully ordained. The connection is: 'There is no offense for one who receives instruction together or recites together with one who is not fully ordained.' This same method applies also to: 'in joint recitation, in receiving instruction in his presence.' Herein, this is the decision: A fully ordained one and one not fully ordained sit down and have the text recited to them. If the teacher says, 'I am reciting for those who are seated,' and recites together with them, the offense is for the teacher alone. There is no offense for one who is learning together with one who is not fully ordained. If both are standing and learning, this is the same method. If a junior bhikkhu is seated and a novice is standing, there is no offense for one who recites saying, 'I am reciting for the one who is seated.' If the junior stands and the other sits, there is also no offense for one who recites saying, 'I am reciting for the one who is standing.' If one novice is seated among many bhikkhus, for one who teaches the Dhamma word by word while he is seated there, there is an unintentional offense. If the novice, having left the vicinity, is standing or sitting, because he is not included among those for whom one is reciting, it is reckoned that he is learning a 'getaway text' from one side; therefore, there is no offense.

Sajjhāyakaraṇeti anupasampannena saddhiṃ ekato sajjhāyakaraṇe. Tassa santike uddesaggahaṇeti anupasampannassa santike uddesaggahaṇe. Yebhuyyena paguṇaganthaṃ bhaṇantassāti sace ekagāthāya eko [M 0.0351] pādo nāgacchati, avasesā āgacchanti, ayaṃ yebhuyyena paguṇagantho nāma. Etena nayena suttepi veditabbo, taṃ bhaṇantassa. Osārentassa cāti parisāmajjhe suttaṃ uccārentassa ca.

'In joint recitation' means in joint recitation with one who is not fully ordained. 'In receiving instruction in his presence' means in receiving instruction in the presence of one who is not fully ordained. 'For one who recites a text that is mostly familiar' means: if one line of a verse does not come to mind, but the remaining ones do, this is called a 'text that is mostly familiar.' This should be understood in the same way in the case of a sutta, for one who recites it. 'And for one who leads a recitation' means for one who recites a sutta aloud in the midst of an assembly.

Padasodhammasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Training Rule on Teaching the Dhamma Word by Word is finished.

5. Paṭhamasahaseyyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

5. The Explanation of the First Training Rule on Lying Down Together

Idha “bhikkhuṃ ṭhapetvā avaseso anupasampanno nāmā”ti (pāci. 52) vacanato tiracchānagatopi anupasampannoyeva, so ca kho na sabbo, methunadhammāpattiyā vatthubhūtovāti āha “antamaso”tiādi. Tassa ca paricchedo methunadhammāpattiyā vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Dirattatirattanti [V 0.0322] ettha dirattavacanena na koci visesattho labbhati, kevalaṃ lokavohāravasena byañjanasiliṭṭhatāya, mukhāruḷhatāya evaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Dvinnaṃ vā tiṇṇaṃ vā rattīnanti pana vacanatthamattadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, nirantaratirattadassanatthaṃ vā dirattaggahaṇaṃ katanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sahaseyyanti ekato seyyaṃ. Seyyāti ca kāyappasāraṇasaṅkhātaṃ sayanampi vuccati “sayanaṃ seyyā”ti katvā, yasmiṃ senāsane sayanti, tampi “sayanti etthāti seyyā”ti katvā. Tadubhayampi idha sāmaññena, ekasesanayena vā gahitanti āha “sabbacchannaparicchanne”tiādi.

Here, in accordance with the passage, 'Setting aside a bhikkhu, the remainder are called “not fully ordained”' (Pāc. 52), even an animal is one who is not fully ordained. But not every one, only one that has become the basis for an offense of sexual intercourse; thus he said, 'at least,' etc. And the delimitation of this should be understood in the same way as was stated for the offense of sexual intercourse. Regarding 'for two or three nights,' here the term 'two nights' conveys no special meaning; it should be understood that it is said thus merely as a worldly expression, for smoothness of phrasing and ease of speech. However, 'of two or three nights' is said just to show the meaning of the words, or it should be seen that the inclusion of 'two nights' is done to show three uninterrupted nights. 'Lying down together' means a sleeping place together. And 'sleeping place' refers to both the lying down, defined as the stretching out of the body, because 'lying down is a sleeping place,' and also the lodging in which they lie down, because 'they lie down in it, thus it is a sleeping place.' That both are taken here, either in a general sense or by the principle of ellipsis, he states by 'in a fully covered and enclosed' etc.

Tattha yaṃ senāsanaṃ upari pañcahi chadanehi (pāci. aṭṭha. 51), aññena vā kenaci antamaso vatthenāpi sabbameva paricchannaṃ, bhūmito paṭṭhāya yāva chadanaṃ āhacca, anāhaccāpi vā sabbantimena pariyāyena diyaḍḍhahatthubbedhena pākārena vā aññena vā kenaci antamaso vatthenāpi parikkhittaṃ, idaṃ sabbacchannasabbaparicchannaṃ nāma. Yassa pana upari bahutaraṃ ṭhānaṃ channaṃ, appaṃ acchannaṃ, samantato ca bahutaraṃ parikkhittaṃ, appaṃ aparikkhittaṃ, idaṃ yebhuyyena channaṃ yebhuyyena paricchannaṃ nāma. Tasmiṃ sabbacchannaparicchanne, yebhuyyena channaparicchanne vā.

Therein, whatever lodging is completely covered above by five kinds of roofing (Pāc. Aṭṭha. 51), or by anything else, even by a cloth; and is enclosed from the ground up to the roof, whether touching it or not, or in the very last alternative, is surrounded by a wall one and a half cubits high, or by anything else, even by a cloth—this is called 'fully covered and fully enclosed.' But that of which the greater part above is covered and a small part is uncovered, and all around the greater part is enclosed and a small part is unenclosed—this is called 'mostly covered and mostly enclosed.' In such a fully covered and enclosed, or mostly covered and enclosed place.

Vidaheyyāti kareyya, tañca kho atthato sampādananti āha “sampādeyyā”ti. Ayañhettha saṅkhepattho “senāsanasaṅkhātaṃ seyyaṃ pavisitvā kāyappasāraṇasaṅkhātaṃ [M 0.0352] seyyaṃ kappeyya vidaheyya sampādeyyā”ti. Diyaḍḍhahatthubbedho vaḍḍhakihatthena gahetabbo. Ekūpacāroti valañjanadvārassa ekattaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Satagabbhaṃ vā catusālaṃ ekūpacāraṃ hotīti sambandho. Tattha vāti purimapurimadivase yattha vuṭṭhaṃ, tasmiṃyeva senāsane vā. Aññattha vā tādiseti yathāvuttalakkhaṇena samannāgate aññasmiṃ pubbe avuṭṭhasenāsane vā. Tena vāti yena saha purimapurimadivase vuṭṭhaṃ, tena vā. Aññena vāti yena saha purimapurimasmiṃ divase vuṭṭhaṃ, tato aññena vā. Saṅkhepoti saṅkhepavaṇṇanā. Yadi evaṃ vitthāro kathaṃ veditabboti āha “vitthāro panā”tiādi.

'One should prepare' means 'one should do'; and that, in terms of meaning, is 'to accomplish,' thus it is said, 'one should accomplish.' Herein, this is the concise meaning: 'Having entered the sleeping place known as a lodging, one should arrange, prepare, and accomplish the sleeping place known as the stretching out of the body.' A height of one and a half cubits should be taken by the carpenter's cubit. 'Of single access' is said with reference to the singleness of the door for use. The connection is: 'A hundred-chambered or four-winged hall is of single access.' 'Therein, or' means: in that same lodging where one stayed on the previous days. 'Or in another such' means: in another lodging, not previously stayed in, that is endowed with the aforesaid characteristics. 'Or with that one' means: with that same one with whom one stayed on the previous days. 'Or with another' means: with another than the one with whom one stayed on the previous days. 'Concisely' means the concise explanation. If so, how is the detailed explanation to be understood? He said, 'But the detailed explanation...' and so on.

Upaḍḍhacchannaparicchannādīsūti ādisaddena “sabbacchanne cūḷakaparicchanne dukkaṭaṃ, yebhuyyena channe cūḷakaparicchanne dukkaṭaṃ, sabbaparicchanne cūḷakacchanne dukkaṭaṃ, yebhuyyena paricchanne cūḷakacchanne dukkaṭa”nti (pāci. aṭṭha. 53) aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttānaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Tatiyāya rattiyā purāruṇā nikkhamitvā puna vasantassāti tatiyāya rattiyā aruṇato puretarameva nikkhamitvā aruṇaṃ bahi uṭṭhāpetvā catutthadivase atthaṅgate sūriye puna vasantassa. Sabbacchannasabbāparicchannādīsūti [V 0.0323] ettha pana ādisaddena “sabbaparicchanne sabbaacchanne, yebhuyyena acchanne yebhuyyena aparicchanne”ti (pāci. 54) pāḷiyaṃ āgatānaṃ, “upaḍḍhacchanne cūḷakaparicchanne anāpatti, upaḍḍhaparicchanne cūḷakacchanne anāpatti, cūḷakacchanne cūḷakaparicchanne anāpattī”ti (pāci. aṭṭha. 53) aṭṭhakathāyaṃ āgatānañca gahaṇaṃ.

“In the case of being half-covered and half-enclosed, etc.” Here, the word “etc.” includes what is stated in the commentary (Pācittiya Aṭṭhakathā 53): “In a fully covered but slightly enclosed space, it is a dukkaṭa offense; in a mostly covered but slightly enclosed space, it is a dukkaṭa offense; in a fully enclosed but slightly covered space, it is a dukkaṭa offense; in a mostly enclosed but slightly covered space, it is a dukkaṭa offense.” “Having left before dawn on the third night and dwelling again.” This means leaving before dawn on the third night, letting the dawn rise outside, and dwelling again after the sun has set on the fourth day. “In the case of being fully covered and fully unenclosed, etc.” Here, the word “etc.” includes what is stated in the Pāli (Pācittiya 54): “In a fully enclosed but fully uncovered space, or in a mostly uncovered but mostly unenclosed space,” and what is stated in the commentary (Pācittiya Aṭṭhakathā 53): “In a half-covered but slightly enclosed space, there is no offense; in a half-enclosed but slightly covered space, there is no offense; in a slightly covered and slightly enclosed space, there is no offense.”

Paṭhamasahaseyyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the first training rule on sharing a sleeping place is concluded.

6. Dutiyasahaseyyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. The Explanation of the Second Training Rule Concerning Shared Bedding

Manussitthiyāti jīvamānakamanussitthiyā. “Matitthī pana kiñcāpi pārājikavatthubhūtā, anupādinnapakkhe pana ṭhitattā sahaseyyāpattiṃ na karotī”ti (vajira. ṭī. pācittiya 55) vadanti. Adissamānarūpāhi pana yakkhipetīhi, methunassa avatthubhūtāya [M 0.0353] ca tiracchānagatitthiyā anāpatti. Paṭhamadivasepīti paṭhamasmiṃ viya sikkhāpade na catuttheyeva divase, atha kho idha paṭhamadivasepīti attho. Iminā idha divasaparicchedo natthīti dasseti. Aṅgesu pana pācittiyavatthukasenāsanaṃ, tattha mātugāmena saha nipajjanaṃ, sūriyatthaṅgamananti tīṇi aṅgānīti ayampi viseso daṭṭhabbo.

“A human woman” means a living human woman. They say that “even if a dead woman is a basis for a pārājika offense, since she remains in the unappropriated category, she does not incur an offense of shared bedding” (Vajira. Ṭī. Pācittiya 55). However, there is no offense regarding invisible female yakkhas and petīs, or a female animal who is not a basis for sexual intercourse. “Even on the first day” means that, unlike in the first training rule where it is only on the fourth day, here it means even on the first day. By this, it is shown that there is no restriction of days here. However, regarding the factors, the lodging that is the basis for a pācittiya offense, lying down together with a woman there, and the setting of the sun—these are the three factors. This distinction should also be noted.

Dutiyasahaseyyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Second Training Rule Concerning Shared Bedding is concluded.

7. Dhammadesanāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

7. Explanation of the Training Rule on Teaching the Dhamma

Chappañcavācāhīti chahi pañcahi vācāhi. Vācāparicchedo panettha kathaṃ veditabboti āha “uttari chappañcavācāhī”tiādi. Sabbatthāti sutte, aṭṭhakathāyañca. Sace aṭṭhakathaṃ, dhammapadaṃ, jātakādivatthuṃ vā kathetukāmo hoti, chappadamattameva kathetuṃ vaṭṭati. Pāḷiyā saddhiṃ kathentena ekaṃ padaṃ pāḷito, pañca aṭṭhakathātoti evaṃ cha padāni anatikkamitvāva kathetabbo. Purisenāti manussapurisena. Tenāha “manussaviggahaṃ gahetvā panā”tiādi.

“Chappañcavācāhi” means with six or five words. How should the division of words be understood here? It is said, “beyond six or five words,” and so on. “Everywhere” means in the Sutta and in the Commentary. If one wishes to relate a commentary, a Dhammapada verse, a Jātaka story, or the like, it is proper to speak only six words. When speaking along with the Pāḷi text, one should not exceed six words: one word from the Pāḷi and five from the Commentary. “By a man” means by a human male. Therefore, it is said, “having taken on a human form, however…” and so on.

Tikapācittiyanti mātugāme mātugāmasaññivematikaamātugāmasaññīnaṃ vasena tīṇi pācittiyāni. Aññassa vā mātugāmassāti ekassa mātugāmassa desetvā nisinne puna āgatassa aññassa mātugāmassa, evaṃ pana ekāsane nisinnena mātugāmasatassāpi desetuṃ vaṭṭati[V 0.0324]. “Viññumanussitthiyā”ti vacanato aviññitthiyāpi desayato anāpatti. Iriyāpathaparivattābhāvoti attano vā mātugāmassa vā iriyāpathaparivattābhāvo. Kappiyakārakassābhāvoti viññussa kappiyakārakassābhāvo, dutiyāniyate vuttalakkhaṇassa manussassa abhāvoti vuttaṃ hoti. Kiriyākiriyanti ettha uttari chappañcavācāhi dhammadesanā kiriyā, kappiyakārakassa aggahaṇaṃ akiriyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

“Tika-pācittiya” means three pācittiya offenses, namely in the case of a woman, when one perceives her as a woman, is uncertain, or perceives her as not a woman. “For another woman” means that having taught one woman who is seated, if another woman arrives, it is permissible to teach even a hundred women seated in the same place. From the statement “a woman who understands,” there is no offense if one teaches a woman who does not understand. The absence of changing postures means the absence of changing one’s own posture or the woman’s posture. The absence of a suitable attendant refers to the absence of a suitable attendant who understands. It is said that this means the absence of a person with the characteristics mentioned in the second undetermined rule (dutiya-aniyata). Regarding “doing and not doing”—here, teaching the Dhamma with more than five or six phrases is considered doing, while not taking a suitable attendant is considered not doing.

Dhammadesanāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Teaching the Dhamma is concluded.

8. Bhūtārocanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

8. Explanation of the Training Rule on Reporting a True Attainment

Nippariyāyenāti [M 0.0354] “paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajji”ntiādinā (pāci. 71) ujukameva. Pariyāyena ārocitanti “yo te vihāre vasi, so bhikkhu paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajji, samāpajjati, samāpanno”tiādinā (pāci. 75) aññāpadesena bhaṇitaṃ. Parinibbānakāle (pāci. aṭṭha. 77), pana antarā vā atikaḍḍhiyamānena upasampannassa bhūtaṃ ārocetuṃ vaṭṭati. Anatikaḍḍhiyamānenāpi (sārattha. ṭī. pācittiya 3.77) tathārūpe kāraṇe sati ārocetuṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Teneva aññatarena daharabhikkhunā upavadito aññataro thero “āvuso, uparimaggatthāya vāyāmaṃ mā akāsi, khīṇāsavo tayā upavadito”ti āha. Therena ca “atthi te, āvuso, imasmiṃ sāsane patiṭṭhā”ti puṭṭho daharabhikkhu “āma, bhante, sotāpanno āha”nti avoca. “Kārako aya”nti ñatvāpi paṭipattiyā amoghabhāvadassanena samuttejanāya, sampahaṃsanāya ca ariyā attānaṃ pakāsentiyeva. Tenāha “tathārūpe kāraṇe sati upasampannassa ārocayato”ti. Sutapariyattisīlaguṇaṃ pana anupasampannassapi ārocetuṃ vaṭṭati. Kasmā na idha ummattakādayo gahitāti āha “yasmā panā”tiādi. Ādisaddena khittacittavedanāṭṭānaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Tasmiṃ satīti ummattakādibhāve sati. Idha na gahitāti imasmiṃ sikkhāpade padabhājaniyaṃ na gahitā. Acittakanti paṇṇattijānanacittābhāvena acittakaṃ. Kusalābyākatacittehi dvicitta”nti idaṃ ukkaṭṭhaparicchedena ariyapuggaleyeva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Na hi paṇṇattiṃ ajānantā jhānalābhino puthujjanā vatthumhi lobhavasena akusalacittenāpi na ārocentīti. Dukkhavedanāya vā abhāvato “dvivedana”nti imassa anurūpaṃ katvā evaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

“Without circumlocution” means straightforwardly, as in “he attained the first jhāna” (Pāc. 71), and so on. “Reported by circumlocution” refers to speaking indirectly, as in “the bhikkhu who stayed in your dwelling attained the first jhāna, is attaining it, or has attained it” (Pāc. 75), and so on, which is stated by way of indirection. However, at the time of final Nibbāna (Pāc. Aṭṭha. 77), or if one is being excessively pressed, it is permissible to report the truth about one who is ordained. Even without being excessively pressed (Sārattha. Ṭī. Pācittiya 3.77), it is still permissible to report in such a case if there is sufficient cause. For this reason, when a certain elder reproached a certain young bhikkhu, the young bhikkhu said, “Friend, do not strive for the higher path; an arahant has been reproached by you.” And when the elder asked, “Friend, do you have a footing in this Dispensation?” the young bhikkhu replied, “Yes, venerable sir, I am a stream-enterer.” Even knowing that “this one is a doer,” the noble ones reveal themselves for the sake of inspiration and praise, by showing the effectiveness of their practice. Thus it is said, “In such a case, it is permissible for an ordained one to report.” However, it is also permissible for a non-ordained person to report qualities such as learning, virtue, and conduct. Why are the insane and others not included here? It is said, “Because, however…” and so on. The word “etc.” includes those whose minds are deranged or afflicted by pain. “When such conditions are present” means when there is insanity and so on. “Not included here” means they are not included in the word analysis of this training rule. “Mindless” means mindless due to the absence of a mind that knows concepts. “With two types of mind” (wholesome and indeterminate minds)—this is said with reference to noble individuals in the highest sense. For ordinary people who attain jhāna but do not know concepts, it is not that they do not report the object even with an unwholesome mind due to greed. Or, due to the absence of painful feeling, “two feelings” should be understood as being made suitable accordingly. Thus it is to be seen.

Bhūtārocanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Reporting a True Attainment is concluded.

9. Duṭṭhullārocanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

9. Explanation of the Training Rule on Reporting a Gross Offense

Dvinnaṃ [V 0.0325] ‘āpattikkhandhānanti pārājikasaṅghādisesasaṅkhātānaṃ dvinnaṃ āpattikkhandhānaṃ. Āyatiṃ saṃvaratthāyāti “evamesa paresu hirottappenāpi āyatiṃ [M 0.0355] saṃvaraṃ āpajjissatī”ti āyatiṃ saṃvaratthāya. Āpattīnañca kulānañca pariyantaṃ katvā vā akatvā vāti “ettakā āpattiyo ārocetabbā, ettakesu kulesu ārocetabbā”ti evaṃ āpattīnañca kulānañca pariyantaṃ katvā vā akatvā vā.

Of the two categories of offenses: namely, the two categories of offenses called pārājika and saṅghādisesa. For the sake of future restraint: thinking, 'In this way, through shame and fear of wrongdoing towards others, he will achieve future restraint.' Having set a limit or not set a limit for the offenses and the families: meaning, 'This many offenses should be reported, and to this many families,' thus having set a limit or not set a limit for the offenses and the families.

Aduṭṭhullāyāti pārājikasaṅghādisesaṃ ṭhapetvā avasesapañcāpattikkhandhasaṅkhātāya aduṭṭhullāya āpattiyā. Avasese cha āpattikkhandheti saṅghādisesavajjite sese cha āpattikkhandhe. Purimapañcasikkhāpadavītikkamasaṅkhātaṃ duṭṭhullanti pāṇātipātaveramaṇiādikassa ādito pañcasikkhāpadassa vītikkamasaṅkhātaṃ duṭṭhullaṃ. Itaraṃ aduṭṭhullaṃ vā ajjhācāranti tato aññaṃ vikālabhojanādikapañcakaṃ, sukkavisaṭṭhikāyasaṃsaggaduṭṭhullaattakāmañceti aduṭṭhullaṃ vā ajjhācāraṃ. Vatthumattanti “ayaṃ sukkavissaṭṭhiṃ āpanno, duṭṭhullaṃ, attakāmaṃ, kāyasaṃsaggaṃ āpanno”ti evaṃ vatthumattaṃ vā ārocentassa. Āpattimattanti “ayaṃ pārājikaṃ āpanno, saṅghādisesaṃ, thullaccayaṃ, pācittiyaṃ, pāṭidesanīyaṃ, dukkaṭaṃ, dubbhāsitaṃ āpanno”ti evaṃ āpattimattaṃ vā ārocentassa. Vuttalakkhaṇassāti “pārājikaṃ anajjhāpannassā”ti kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. duṭṭhullārocanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) evaṃ vuttalakkhaṇassa. Savatthukoti vatthunā saha ghaṭito.

Aduṭṭhullā (not gross) refers to an offense counted as one of the remaining five categories of offenses, excluding Pārājika and Saṅghādisesa. The remaining six categories of offenses means the remaining six categories of offenses excluding Saṅghādisesa. Duṭṭhulla (gross) refers to what is counted as a transgression of the first five precepts, beginning with abstaining from the destruction of life. The other, 'not gross' or 'misconduct,' refers to the other five precepts, such as eating at the wrong time, and also the offenses of emission of semen, physical contact, lewd speech, and self-indulgence, which are considered 'not gross' or 'misconduct.' Merely stating the matter means reporting in this way: 'This person has committed emission of semen, lewd speech, self-indulgence, or physical contact.' Merely stating the offense means reporting in this way: 'This person has committed a Pārājika offense, a Saṅghādisesa offense, a Thullaccaya offense, a Pācittiya offense, a Pāṭidesanīya offense, a Dukkaṭa offense, or a Dubbhāsita offense.' Of the stated characteristics: this refers to the doubt regarding one who has not committed a Pārājika offense (Commentary on the Training Rule on Reporting a Gross Offense); thus, of the stated characteristics. Savatthuka (with its basis) means connected with a specific matter.

Duṭṭhullārocanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning reporting a gross offense is completed.

10. Pathavīkhaṇanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Training Rule on Digging the Ground

Pāsāṇasakkharakathalamarumbavālukādīsūti ettha muṭṭhippamāṇato upari pāsāṇāti veditabbā. Muṭṭhippamāṇā sakkharā. Kathalāti kapālakhaṇḍāni. Marumbāti kaṭasakkharā. Vālukā vālikāyeva. Aññatarassa tatiyabhāgo hotīti tatiyo bhāgo hoti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yato paṃsuṃ vā mattikaṃ vā āharāpetvā visuṃ visuṃ kate dve koṭṭhāsā paṃsu vā mattikā vā eko pāsāṇādīsu aññataro hoti, ayaṃ missakapathavī nāmāti. Ovaṭṭho nāma devena ovaṭṭho (pāci. 86). Vuttanti padabhājaniyaṃ, sīhaḷaṭṭhakathāyameva vā vuttaṃ[M 0.0356]. Adhikatarapāsāṇādimissāti [V 0.0326] adhikatarapāsāṇādīhi missā, adaḍḍhāpi vuttappamāṇato adhikatarapāsāṇādimissāti adhippāyo. Vā-saddo avuttavikappattho, tena ūnakacatumāsovaṭṭhapathaviṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Suddhapāsāṇādibhedāyāti suddhā pāsāṇā etthāti suddhapāsāṇā, sā ādi yassa bhedassa so suddhapāsāṇādi. Ādi-saddena suddhasakkharādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Suddhapāsāṇādibhedo yassā sā suddhapāsāṇādibhedā, tāya suddhapāsāṇādibhedāya, suddhapāsāṇādippakārāyāti attho.

Here, regarding 'stones, pebbles, potsherds, gravel, sand, etc.': 'stones' (pāsāṇa) should be understood as those larger than a fist. 'Pebbles' (sakkharā) are fist-sized. 'Potsherds' (kathala) mean fragments of pots. 'Gravel' (marumba) refers to coarse pebbles. 'Sand' (vālukā) is simply sand. 'It is a third part of any of these' means it is a third part. This is what is said: when soil or clay is brought and divided separately, so that two parts are soil or clay and one part is any of the stones, etc., this is called 'mixed earth.' Ovaṭṭha means 'rained upon by the sky' (Pāc. 86). Vutta (stated) refers to the word analysis, or it is said in the Sinhalese commentary itself. 'Mixed with a greater amount of stones, etc.' means mixed with a predominance of stones, etc.; the intention is that even if not burnt, it is mixed with more stones, etc., than the stated measure. The particle 'vā' indicates an unstated alternative; thus, it includes earth rained upon for less than four months. Regarding Suddhapāsāṇādibhedāya (of the type of pure stone, etc.): 'pure-stoned' (suddhapāsāṇā) is so called because 'pure stones are in it'. That is the beginning of this type. The term 'etc.' includes pure pebbles and the like. That which is of the type beginning with pure stones is suddhapāsāṇādibhedā. By suddhapāsāṇādibhedāya is meant 'of the kind consisting of pure stones, etc.'

Sayaṃ khaṇatīti ettha yo antamaso pādaṅguṭṭhakenapi khaṇati, udakampi chaḍḍento bhindati, pādaṅguṭṭhakenapi vilikhati, pattampi pacanto dahati, so sabbo khaṇatiyevāti veditabbo. Tenāha “khaṇanabhedanavilekhanapacanādīhi vikopetīti. Pattaṃ pacantena (pāci. aṭṭha. 87) hi pubbe pakkaṭṭhāneyeva pacitabbo. Adaḍḍhāya pathaviyā aggiṃ ṭhapetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Pattapacanakapālassa pana upari aggiṃ ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati. Dārūnaṃ upari ṭhapeti, so aggi tāni dahanto gantvā pathaviṃ dahati, na vaṭṭati. Iṭṭhakapāsāṇādīsupi eseva nayo. Tatrāpi hi iṭṭhakādīnaṃyeva upari ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati. Kasmā? Tesaṃ anupādānattā. Na hi tāni aggissa upādānasaṅkhaṃ gacchanti. Sukkhakhāṇurukkhādīsupi aggiṃ dātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Sace pana “pathaviṃ apattameva nibbāpetvā gamissāmī”ti deti, vaṭṭati. Pacchā nibbāpetuṃ na sakkoti, avisayattā anāpatti. Vuttanayenevāti “khaṇanabhedanavilikhanapacanādīhī”ti vutteneva nayena. Niyametvāti sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā. Itaroti āṇāpako.

Here, 'he digs by himself' means that even if one digs with just the tip of a toe, or discards water and breaks the ground, scratches with the tip of a toe, or burns the ground while cooking a leaf, all such actions are to be understood as digging. Hence it is said: 'It is disturbed by digging, breaking, scratching, burning, etc.' For when cooking a leaf (Pāc. Aṭṭha. 87), one should cook it only in a place already burnt. It is not permissible to place fire on unburnt ground. However, it is permissible to place fire above a potsherd for cooking leaves. If one places fire on wood, and the fire, burning the wood, then goes and burns the ground—this is not permissible. The same principle applies to bricks, stones, etc. There too, fire may only be placed on top of the bricks and such. Why? Because they do not serve as fuel. They do not become fuel for the fire. It is also not permissible to light a fire on dry stumps or trees. But if one thinks, 'I will extinguish the fire before it reaches the ground,' then it is permissible. If one later cannot extinguish it due to it being beyond one's control, there is no offense. Vuttanayeneva (by the method stated) means by the method stated as 'by digging, breaking, scratching, burning, etc.' Niyametvā (having determined) means having made a resolution. Itara (the other) refers to the one who gives the order.

“Pokkharaṇiṃ khaṇā”ti (pāci. aṭṭha. 86) vadati, vaṭṭati. Khatāyeva pokkharaṇī nāma hoti, tasmā ayaṃ kappiyavohāro. Esa nayo “vāpiṃ, taḷākaṃ, āvāṭaṃ khaṇā”tiādīsupi. “Imaṃ okāsaṃ khaṇa, imasmiṃ okāse pokkharaṇiṃ khaṇā”ti pana vattuṃ na vaṭṭati. “Kandaṃ khaṇa mūlaṃ khaṇā”ti aniyametvā vattuṃ vaṭṭati. “Imaṃ valliṃ khaṇa, imasmiṃ okāse kandaṃ vā mūlaṃ vā khaṇā”ti vattuṃ na vaṭṭati. Tenāha “okāsaṃ aniyametvā…pe… bhaṇantassā”ti. Ātapena sukkhakaddamo ca phalati, tatra yo heṭṭhā pathaviyā asambaddho, tameva apanetuṃ vaṭṭati. Esa nayo gokaṇṭakepi[M 0.0357]. Tenāha “ātapena…pe… asambaddha”nti. Tattha gokaṇṭako (pāci. aṭṭha. 86) nāma gāvīnaṃ khuracchinnakaddamo vuccati. Sace pana heṭṭhimatalena bhūmisambandho, vikopetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Bhijjitvā patitanaditaṭanti bhijjitvā nadisāmantā patitaṃ omakacātumāsaṃ ovaṭṭhaṃ naditaṭaṃ. Sace pana bhijjitvā udakeyeva pakati, deve atirekacātumāsaṃ ovaṭṭhepi udakeyeva udakassa patitattā [V 0.0327] vaṭṭati. Mahantampi naṅgalacchinnamattikāpiṇḍanti mahantampi kasitaṭṭhāne heṭṭhā pathaviyā asambaddhaṃ naṅgalacchinnamattikāpiṇḍaṃ. Evamādisaddena kūṭāsiñcanayoggatanukakaddamādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Asañcicca rukkhādipavaṭṭanena bhindantassāti pāsāṇarukkhādīni vā pavaṭṭentassa, kattaradaṇḍena vā āhacca āhacca gacchantassa pathavī bhijjati, sā “tena bhindissāmī”ti evaṃ sañcicca abhinnattā asañcicca bhinnā nāma hoti, iti asañcicca rukkhādippavaṭṭanena bhindantassa anāpatti. Asatiyā pādaṅguṭṭhakādīhi vilikhantassāti yo aññavihito kenaci saddhiṃ kiñci kathento pādaṅguṭṭhakena vā kattarayaṭṭhiyā vā pathaviṃ vilikhanto tiṭṭhati, tassa evaṃ asatiyā pādaṅguṭṭhakādīhi vilikhantassa anāpatti.

'Dig a pond,' (Pāc. Aṭṭha. 86) it is said, is permissible. For a pond is called a pond only when it has been dug; therefore, this is an allowable expression. The same principle applies to phrases like 'dig a reservoir, a lake, a pit,' and so on. However, it is not permissible to say, 'Dig this spot; dig a pond in this spot.' It is permissible to say without specifying, 'Dig a tuber; dig a root.' But it is not permissible to say, 'Dig this vine; dig a tuber or root in this spot.' Therefore, it is said, 'Without specifying a spot... when speaking.' Dried mud cracked by the sun also crumbles, and whatever is not connected to the ground below may be removed. The same principle applies to cow-thorn. Hence, it is said, 'By the sun... not connected.' Here, 'cow-thorn' (Pāc. Aṭṭha. 86) refers to mud cut by a cow's hoof. But if it is connected to the lower layer of earth, it is not permissible to disrupt it. A riverbank that has collapsed and fallen refers to a section of the river's edge that has broken off and fallen near the river, if it has been rained upon for less than four months. But if after breaking, it naturally remains in the water, even if it has been rained upon by the sky for more than four months, since it has fallen into the water, it is permissible. A large clod of earth cut by a plow refers to a large clod of earth in a plowed field that is not connected to the ground below. By the term 'etc.', things like thin dried mud suitable for plastering are included. For one who breaks unintentionally by rolling a tree, etc.: if one rolls stones or trees, or walks while repeatedly striking the ground with a staff, and the ground breaks, that is called 'broken unintentionally' because it was not broken with the intention 'I will break it with this.' Thus, there is no offense for one who breaks the ground unintentionally by rolling a tree, etc. For one who scratches absentmindedly with a toe, etc.: if someone, while engaged in conversation with another, absentmindedly scratches the ground with a toe or a staff, there is no offense for one who scratches absentmindedly with a toe, etc.

Pathavīkhaṇanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning digging the ground is completed.

Musāvādavaggo paṭhamo.

The First Chapter on False Speech.

2. Bhūtagāmavaggo

2. The Plant Life Chapter

1. Bhūtagāmasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Training Rule on Seed and Plant Life

“Bhavantī”ti (sārattha. ṭī. pācittiya 3.90) iminā viruḷhamūle nīlabhāvaṃ āpajjitvā vaḍḍhamānake taruṇagacche dasseti. “Ahesu”nti iminā pana vaḍḍhitvā ṭhite mahante rukkhagacchādike dasseti. Tenāha “jāyantī”tiādi. Ettha ca “bhavantī”ti imassa vivaraṇaṃ “jāyanti vaḍḍhantī”ti, “ahesu”nti imassa “jātā vaḍḍhitā”ti. Gāmoti samūho. Patiṭṭhitaharitatiṇarukkhādīnanti bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhitassa haritatiṇassa ceva haritarukkhādīnañca. Ādisaddena osadhigacchalatādayo veditabbā. Nimittatthe ca bhummaṃ. Yo attho sampajjati, tamāha “bhūtagāmapātabyatāyā”tiādinā.

“Bhavantī” (Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā, Pācittiya 3.90): by this, it indicates young, growing plants that are taking on a green color at their sprouting roots. By “Ahesu,” however, it indicates large, fully grown trees and similar plants that are established. Therefore it is said, “jāyanti,” and so on. Here, the explanation of “bhavantī” is “jāyanti vaḍḍhanti” (they are born and grow), and of “ahesu” is “jātā vaḍḍhitā” (they were born and grew). “Gāma” means a group. “Patiṭṭhitaharitatiṇarukkhādīnaṃ” refers to green grass and green trees, etc., established on the ground. By the term “ādi,” medicinal plants, shrubs, creepers, and the like should be understood. And “bhummaṃ” is in the sense of a condition. The meaning that results is stated by “bhūtagāmapātabyatāyā” and so on.

Nanu [M 0.0358] ca rukkhādayo cittarahitatāya na jīvā, cittarahitatā ca pariphandābhāvato, chinnepi viruhanato, visadisajātikabhāvato, catuyoniyaṃ apariyāpannato ca veditabbā, vuḍḍhi pana pavāḷasilālavaṇānampi vijjatīti na tesaṃ jīvabhāve kāraṇaṃ, visayaggahaṇañca nesaṃ parikappanāmattaṃ [V 0.0328] supanaṃ viya ciñcādīnaṃ, tathā dohaḷādayo, atha kasmā bhūtagāmassa pātabyatāya pācittiyaṃ icchitanti? Samaṇaasāruppato, tannissitasattānurakkhaṇato ca. Tenevāha “jīvasaññino hi moghapurisā manussā rukkhasmi”ntiādi (pāci. 89). Sāsapabījakasevālampīti sāsapabījakasaṅkhātaṃ sevālampi, sāsapasevālaṃ, bījakasevālampīti attho. Tattha sāsapasevālo nāma sāsapamatto khuddakasevālo. Bījakasevālo nāma upari khuddakapatto heṭṭhā khuddakamūlo sevālo.

Are not trees and the like non-living because they lack consciousness? And their lack of consciousness is to be understood from their absence of movement, their sprouting even when cut, their being of a dissimilar nature, and their non-inclusion in the four modes of birth. But growth is also found in coral, rock-salt, and the like; therefore, that is not a reason for them to be considered living. And their perception of objects is merely conceptual, like a dream of tamarind trees, etc., and similarly with cravings and the like. Then why is a Pācittiya offense prescribed for the destruction of plant life? It is because it is unsuitable for an ascetic, and for the protection of beings dependent on them. Therefore it was said, “For, foolish man, humans have the perception of life in a tree,” etc. (Pācittiya 89). “Sāsapabījakasevālampīti” means even the moss known as mustard-seed moss; the meaning is mustard-moss and seed-moss. Here, “sāsapasevālo” means small moss the size of a mustard seed. “Bījakasevālo” means moss with small leaves on top and small roots below.

Mūlabījakhandhabījaphaḷubījaaggabījabījabījānanti ettha mūlameva bījaṃ mūlabījaṃ. Evaṃ sesesupi. Tattha mūlabījaṃ haliddiādikaṃ. Khandhabījaṃ assatthādikaṃ. Phaḷubījaṃ ucchuādikaṃ. Aggabījaṃ hiriverādikaṃ. Bījaṃbījaṃ pubbaṇṇādikaṃ. Bhājanagatanti sarāvādibhājanagataṃ. Nikkhantaṃ mūlamattaṃ etasmāti nikkhantamūlamattaṃ. Matta saddena cettha paṇṇassa nikkhamanaṃ paṭikkhipati. Esa nayo nikkhantaaṅkuramattanti etthāpi. Sace pana mūlañca paṇṇañca niggataṃ, bhūtagāmasaṅkhaṃ gacchati. Vidatthimattā pattavaṭṭi niggacchatīti vidatthimattā anīlavaṇṇā pattavaṭṭi nikkhamati. Tenāha “nikkhante”tiādi. Harito na hotīti nīlavaṇṇo na hoti. Muggādīnaṃ pana paṇṇesu uṭṭhitesu, vīhiādīnaṃ vā aṅkure harite bhūtagāmasaṅgahaṃ gacchanti. Esa nayo ambaṭṭhiādīsu.

Regarding root-seeds, stem-seeds, joint-seeds, shoot-seeds, and seed-seeds: here, the root itself is the seed, a root-seed. Similarly for the rest. Among these, a root-seed is like turmeric and so on. A stem-seed is like the sacred fig tree and so on. A joint-seed is like sugarcane and so on. A shoot-seed is like hirivera and so on. A seed-seed is like early grains and so on. 'Bhājanagata' means placed in a dish or similar container. 'Nikkhantamūlamattaṃ' means that only the root has emerged from it. Here, the word 'matta' (only) excludes the emergence of a leaf. The same principle applies to 'just emerged to the extent of a sprout.' However, if both the root and a leaf have emerged, it is classified as a plant (bhūtagāma). 'The leaf-rim emerges to the width of a span' means the leaf-rim, not yet of a green color, emerges to the width of a span. Hence it is said, 'when emerged,' etc. 'It is not green' means it is not of a green color. For mung beans and the like, once the leaves have appeared, or for rice and the like, once the sprouts are green, they are classified as plants (bhūtagāma). The same principle applies to mango stones and the like.

Bhūtagāmabījagāmeti ettha bhūtagāmato viyojitaṃ viruhanasamatthameva mūlabījādikaṃ bījagāmo nāmāti veditabbaṃ. Ubhayatthāti bhūtagāmabījagāmesu. Atathāsaññissāti abhūtagāmābījagāmasaññissa. Ko pana vādo abhūtagāmābījagāmesu abhūtagāmābījagāmasaññissa. Asañciccāti pāsāṇarukkhādīni vā pavaṭṭentassa, sākhaṃ vā kaḍḍhantassa, kattaradaṇḍena vā bhūmiṃ paharitvā gacchantassa tiṇāni kuppanti. Tāni tena “vikopessāmī”ti evaṃ sañcicca avikopitattā asañcicca vikopitāni nāma honti. Iti asañcicca vikopentassa anāpatti.

In the phrase 'bhūtagāma and bījagāma,' here, that which is separated from a plant but is capable of sprouting, such as root-seeds and so on, is to be understood as bījagāma. 'In both cases' refers to bhūtagāma and bījagāma. 'For one who perceives it as otherwise' refers to one who perceives it as not being a plant or a seed. What then needs to be said of one who perceives something that is not a plant or a seed as not being a plant or a seed? 'Unintentionally' means, for example, when someone is rolling down stones or trees, or pulling a branch, or walking while striking the ground with a cutting-staff, grass is disturbed. Because these were not intentionally disturbed by him with the thought, 'I will disturb them,' they are called unintentionally disturbed. Thus, for one who disturbs unintentionally, there is no offense.

Asatiyāti [M 0.0359] aññavihito kenaci saddhiṃ kiñci kathento pādaṅguṭṭhakena vā hatthena vā tiṇaṃ vā lataṃ vā vikopento tiṭṭhati, evaṃ asatiyā vikopentassa anāpatti.

'Unmindfully' means that one stands with one's mind directed elsewhere, talking with someone about something, and disturbs grass or a creeper with one's big toe or hand. In such a case, for one who disturbs it unmindfully, there is no offense.

Ajānitvāti ettha abbhantare “bījagāmo”ti vā “bhūtagāmo”ti vā na jānāti, “vikopemī”ti pana jānāti. Evaṃ tiṇe vā palālapuñje vā khaṇittiṃ vā kudālaṃ vā saṅgopanatthāya [V 0.0329] ṭhapeti, ḍayhamānahattho vā aggiṃ pāteti. Tatra ce tiṇāni chijjanti vā ḍayhanti vā, evaṃ ajānitvā vikopentassa anāpatti.

'Not knowing' here means that one does not know internally whether it is 'seed-growth' or 'plant-growth,' but one does know, 'I am disturbing.' Similarly, if one places a digging tool or a hoe on grass or a pile of straw for safekeeping, or if one with a burning hand drops fire, and if the grass there is cut or burns, for one who disturbs it without knowing, there is no offense.

Yena kenaci aggināti kaṭṭhaggigomayaggiādīsu yena kenaci agginā, antamaso lohakhaṇḍenapi ādittena. “Kappiya”nti vatvāvāti yāya kāyaci bhāsāya “kappiya”nti vatvāva. Eva-saddena paṭhamaṃ agginā phusitvā pacchā “kappiya”nti vattuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti dasseti. “Paṭhamaṃ aggiṃ nikkhipitvā taṃ anuddharitvāva ‘kappiya’nti vutte pana vaṭṭatī”ti (sārattha. ṭī. pācittiya 3.93) vadanti. Esa nayo sesesupi. Tathevāti ‘kappiya’nti vatvāva. Assamahiṃsasūkaramigagorūpānaṃ pana khurā atikhiṇā, tasmā tehi na kātabbaṃ, katampi akataṃ hotīti āha “ṭhapetvā gomahiṃsādīnaṃ khure”ti. Hatthinakhā pana khurā na honti, tasmā tehi vaṭṭati. Tiracchānānanti sīhabyagghadīpimakkaṭānaṃ, sakuntānañca. Tesañhi nakhā tikhiṇā honti, tasmā tehi kātabbaṃ. “Antamaso chinditvā āhaṭenapī”ti iminā yehi kātuṃ vaṭṭati, tehi tatthajātakehi kātabbanti ettha vattabbameva natthīti dasseti. “Satthe vuttanayenevā”ti iminā chedaṃ vā vedhaṃ vā dassentena “kappiyanti vatvāvā”ti vuttamatidisati. Ettha ca kiñcāpi “kappiyanti vatvāva kātabba”ntiādinā kappiyaṃ karontena kattabbākārameva dassitaṃ, tathāpi bhikkhunā “kappiyaṃ karohī”ti vutteyeva anupasampannena “kappiya”nti vatvā aggiparijitādi kātabbanti gahetabbaṃ. Avacanaṃ pana “punapi kappiyaṃ karohīti kāretvāva paribhuñjitabba”nti paṭhamameva vuttattā.

'By any kind of fire' means by any fire, such as a wood fire or a dung fire, even with a heated piece of metal. 'Having said "permissible"' means having said "permissible" in whatever language. The word 'eva' (only) indicates that it is not permissible to first touch it with the fire and then say 'permissible.' However, they say: 'If one first places the fire down, and says "permissible" without having picked it up, then it is permissible' (Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā, Pācittiya 3.93). This same principle applies in the other cases. 'Likewise' means having said 'permissible' first. The hooves of asses, buffaloes, pigs, deer, and cows, however, are too blunt; therefore, it should not be done with them. Even if it is done, it is as if not done. Hence, it is said, 'except for the hooves of cattle, buffaloes, etc.' Elephant nails, however, are not hooves, so it is permissible with them. 'Of animals' refers to lions, tigers, leopards, monkeys, and birds. For their claws are sharp; therefore, it should be done with them. 'Even with one that is cut off and brought'—this indicates that if it is permissible to do it with these, there is no need to state that it should be done with those that are naturally in place. By the phrase 'in the same way as stated for a knife,' it extends the statement 'having said "permissible"' to the act of showing a cut or a piercing. Here, although the method for one making something permissible has been shown by the words 'it must be done only after saying "permissible,"' etc., it should nevertheless be understood that only when a monk says, 'Make it permissible,' should an unordained person say 'permissible' and then perform the act of touching with fire, etc. No instruction on this is given here, however, because it was already stated at the beginning that 'it must be used only after having it made permissible by instructing again, "Make it permissible."

Ekasmiṃ…pe… kappiye kate sabbaṃ kataṃ hotīti ekaṃyeva “kappiyaṃ karomī”ti adhippāyenapi kappiye kate ekābaddhattā sabbaṃ kataṃ [M 0.0360] hoti. Dārukaṃ vijjhatīti jānitvā vā ajānitvā vā vijjhati vā vijjhāpeti vā, vaṭṭatiyeva. Bhattasitthe vijjhatīti etthāpi eseva nayo. Taṃ vijjhati, na vaṭṭatīti valliādīnaṃ bhājanagatikattāti adhippāyo. Bhindāpetvā kappiyaṃ kāretabbanti bījato muttassa kaṭāhassa bhājanagatikattā vuttaṃ. Abījanti aṅkurajananasamatthabījarahitataruṇambaphalādi. Tenāha “yaṃ pana phalaṃ taruṇaṃ hoti, abīja”nti. Nibbattabījaṃ nāma bījaṃ nibbattetvā visuṃ katvā paribhuñjituṃ sakkuṇeyyaṃ ambapanasādiphalaṃ. Tenāha “bījaṃ apanetvā paribhuñjitabba”nti. Tattha kappiyakaraṇakiccaṃ natthi, sayameva kappiyānīti adhippāyo.

When one thing... is made permissible, all is done. Thus, even with the intention, 'I make it permissible,' when one thing is made permissible, because of its interconnectedness, all is done. Regarding piercing a wooden object: whether one pierces it or has it pierced, knowingly or unknowingly, it is indeed permissible. Regarding piercing a lump of cooked rice, here too the same principle applies. 'That is pierced, it is not permissible'—the meaning is that this refers to vines and the like because they are considered containers. 'Having had it broken, one should have it made permissible'—this is said because a husk detached from a seed is considered a container. 'Non-seed' refers to young mango fruits and the like that lack seeds capable of producing sprouts. Therefore, it is said, 'But any fruit that is young is non-seed.' 'A developed seed' refers to a mango, jackfruit, or other fruit where the seed has developed and can be separated and consumed. Therefore, it is said, 'The seed should be removed before it is eaten.' In that case, there is no need to make it permissible, as they are permissible by themselves—this is the meaning.

Bhūtagāmasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on plant life is concluded.

2. Aññavādakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Training Rule on Speaking Otherwise

Yamatthanti [V 0.0330] “tvaṃ kira dukkaṭāpattiṃ āpanno”tiādikaṃ yaṃ kiñci atthaṃ. Tato aññanti pucchitatthato aññamatthaṃ. Aññenaññaṃ paṭicaraṇassāti vinayadharena yaṃ vacanaṃ dosapucchanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, tato aññena vacanena paṭicchādanassa. Paṭicchādanatthopi hi carasaddo hoti anekatthattā dhātūnaṃ. Vuttanti pāḷiyaṃ vuttaṃ.

‘Whatever matter’ means any matter, such as, ‘It is said you have incurred a dukkaṭa offense.’ ‘Other than that’ means a matter other than the one asked about. ‘Of dealing with one by another’ means the concealment by another statement of what was spoken by a Vinaya expert for the purpose of asking about a fault. For the root ‘car’ can also have the meaning of concealment, since roots have multiple meanings. ‘It is said’ means it is said in the Pāḷi.

Sāvasesaṃ āpattiṃ āpannoti ettha ṭhapetvā pārājikaṃ sesā sāvasesāpatti nāma, taṃ āpanno. Anuyuñjiyamānoti “kiṃ, āvuso, itthannāmaṃ āpattiṃ āpannosī”ti pucchiyamāno. Aññena vacanenāti “ko āpanno? Kiṃ āpanno? Kismiṃ āpanno? Kathaṃ āpanno? Kaṃ bhaṇatha? Kiṃ bhaṇathā”ti aññena vacanena. Aññanti “kiṃ tvaṃ itthannāmaṃ āpattiṃ āpannosī”tiādikaṃ anuyuñjakavacanaṃ. Tathā tathā vikkhipatīti tena tena pakārena vikkhipati. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? So (pāci. aṭṭha. 94) kiñci vītikkamaṃ disvā “āvuso, āpattiṃ āpannosī”ti saṅghamajjhe āpattiyā anuyuñjiyamāno “ko āpanno”ti vadati. Tato “tva”nti vutte “ahaṃ kiṃ āpanno”ti vadati. Atha “pācittiyaṃ vā dukkaṭaṃ vā”ti vutte “ahaṃ kismiṃ āpanno”ti [M 0.0361] vadati. Tato “amukasmiṃ nāma vatthusmi”nti vutte “ahaṃ kathaṃ āpanno, kiṃ karonto āpannomhī”ti pucchati. Atha “idaṃ nāma karonto āpanno”ti vutte “kaṃ bhaṇathā”ti vadati. Tato “taṃ bhaṇāmā”ti vutte “kiṃ bhaṇathā”ti evamanekehi pakārehi vikkhipatīti vuttaṃ hoti.

‘One who has incurred a residual offense’ means, here, that apart from a pārājika, the remaining offenses are called ‘residual offenses,’ and one has incurred such an offense. ‘Being questioned’ means being asked, ‘Friend, have you incurred such-and-such an offense?’ ‘By other speech’ means by other speech such as, ‘Who has incurred it? What has been incurred? In what has it been incurred? How was it incurred? Whom are you speaking about? What are you saying?’ ‘Other’ refers to the questioning speech, such as, ‘Have you incurred such-and-such an offense?’ ‘He diverts in various ways’ means he diverts in this and that manner. What is being said? Seeing some transgression, when questioned in the midst of the Saṅgha about the offense, ‘Friend, you have incurred an offense,’ he says, ‘Who has incurred it?’ Then, when told, ‘You,’ he says, ‘What have I incurred?’ Next, when told, ‘A pācittiya or a dukkaṭa,’ he says, ‘In what have I incurred it?’ Then, when told, ‘In such-and-such a matter,’ he asks, ‘How have I incurred it? What was I doing when I incurred it?’ When told, ‘You incurred it while doing this,’ he says, ‘Whom are you speaking about?’ Then, when told, ‘We are speaking about you,’ he says, ‘What are you saying?’ Thus, it is said that he diverts in many ways.

Yo pana bhikkhu sāvasesaṃ āpattiṃ āpanno, taṃ na kathetukāmo tuṇhībhāvena vihesetīti sambandho. Vihesetīti ciranisajjācirabhāsanehi piṭṭhiāgilāyanatālusosādivasena saṅghaṃ viheseti, parissamaṃ tesaṃ karotīti attho. Parissamo hi vihesā nāma. Aññavādakakammanti aññavādakassa bhikkhuno aññavādakāropanatthaṃ kātabbaṃ ñattidutiyakammaṃ. Vihesakakammanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Tasmiṃ saṅghena kateti tasmiṃ aññavādakakamme ca vihesakakamme ca saṅghena ñattidutiyakammavācāya kate. Tathā karontānanti taṃ pakāraṃ karontānaṃ, aññavādakañca vihesakañca karontānanti attho.

The connection is that a bhikkhu who has incurred a residual offense, being unwilling to confess it, harasses the Saṅgha by remaining silent. ‘He harasses’ means he harasses the Saṅgha by means of prolonged sitting and prolonged speaking, causing backaches, dryness of the palate, and so on; the meaning is that he causes them fatigue. For fatigue is indeed called harassment. ‘Action for one who speaks otherwise’ means the motion-and-second procedure to be performed for a bhikkhu who speaks otherwise, for the purpose of charging him with speaking otherwise. ‘Action for a harasser’—here too, the same principle applies. ‘When the Saṅgha has performed that’ means when the Saṅgha has performed, by means of the motion-and-second procedure, both the action for one who speaks otherwise and the action for a harasser. ‘Of those acting thus’ means of those acting in that manner, that is, of those performing the action for one who speaks otherwise and the action for a harasser.

“Vihesaketi ayamettha anupaññattī”ti avacanañcettha “āpattikarā ca hoti aññavādakasikkhāpadādīsu viyā”ti (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. paṭhamapārājikavaṇṇanā) vuttattāyeva paññāyatīti [V 0.0331] katvā. Esa nayo upari sikkhāpadesu. Dhammakamme tikapācittiyanti dhammakamme dhammakammasaññivematikaadhammakammasaññīnaṃ vasena tīṇi pācittiyāni. Adhammakamme tikadukkaṭanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Anāropiteti kammavācāya anāropite, appatiṭṭhāpiteti attho. Gelaññenāti yena kathetuṃ na sakkoti, mukhe tādisena byādhinā. Saṅghassa bhaṇḍanādīni bhavissantīti saṅghamajjhe kathite tappaccayā saṅghassa bhaṇḍanaṃ vā kalaho vā viggaho vā vivādo vā saṅghabhedo vā saṅgharāji vā bhavissantīti iminā vā adhippāyena na kathentassa. Ettha ca adhammenāti abhūtena vatthunā.

And the non-statement here that ‘this is a supplementary rule for harassment’ is understood because it is said (in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī commentary on the first pārājika) that ‘it also causes an offense, as in the training rule on speaking otherwise, etc.’ This principle applies to the subsequent training rules. ‘A triad of pācittiya offenses in a legal act’ means three pācittiya offenses in a legal act, depending on whether one perceives the act as legal, is doubtful about it, or perceives it as illegal. ‘A triad of dukkaṭa offenses in an illegal act’—here too, the same principle applies. ‘Not initiated’ means not initiated by a formal motion; the meaning is not established. ‘Due to illness’ means by such a disease in the mouth that one cannot speak. ‘There will be disputes in the Saṅgha’ means that if it is spoken of in the midst of the Saṅgha, disputes, quarrels, contentions, disagreements, schisms, or factions may arise in the Saṅgha because of that—or it is of one who refrains from speaking with this intention. Here, ‘unjustly’ means with an untrue matter.

“Samuṭṭhānādīni adinnādānasadisānī”ti avisesaṃ atidisitvā visesaṃ dassetuṃ “idaṃ panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Siyā kiriyaṃ aññenaññaṃ paṭicarantassa. Siyā akiriyaṃ tuṇhībhāvena vihesentassa.

‘The origins, etc., are similar to those of taking what is not given’—having thus indicated the general similarity, ‘but this,’ etc., is stated to show the specific difference. There may be an action for one who deals with one thing by another. There may be an inaction for one who harasses by remaining silent.

Aññavādakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Training Rule on Speaking Otherwise is concluded.

3. Ujjhāpanakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Training Rule on Causing Discontent

Yena [M 0.0362] vacanenāti “chandāya itthannāmo idaṃ nāma karotī”tiādikena yena vacanena. Tenāha “chandāyā”tiādi. Tattha chandāyāti chandena pakkhapātena. “Akkharāya vācetī”tiādīsu (pāci. 46) viya liṅgavipallāso esa. Idaṃ nāma karotīti attano sandiṭṭhasambhattānaṃ paṇītaṃ senāsanaṃ vā paññapeti, bhattādikaṃ vāti adhippāyo. Senāsanapaññāpakādibhedanti ettha ādisaddena bhattuddesakayāgubhājakaphalabhājakādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Anekatthattā dhātūnaṃ jhe-saddo olokanatthopi hotīti āha “avaññāya olokāpentī”ti. Cintanatthoyeva vā gahetabboti āha “lāmakato vā cintāpentī”ti. Tatheva vadantāti “chandāya itthannāmo idaṃ nāma karotī”tiādīni vadantā. Vuttanti pāḷiyaṃ vuttaṃ. “Khiyyanake”ti (pāci. aṭṭha. 105) ayamettha anupaññatti.

‘By which speech’ means by such speech as, ‘So-and-so does this and that out of desire.’ Therefore it is said, ‘out of desire,’ etc. Herein, ‘out of desire’ means by inclination, by partiality. This is a case of gender inversion, as in ‘he teaches letters,’ etc. ‘He does this and that’ means he assigns superior lodgings or meals, etc., to those he has personally seen and associated with—this is the intended meaning. ‘The varieties of assigners of lodgings, etc.’—here, the word ‘etc.’ includes the distributors of food, allocators of rice-gruel, and allocators of fruit. Because roots have multiple meanings, the root ‘jhe’ can also have the meaning of looking at—hence it is said, ‘making them look with contempt.’ Or it should be taken simply as having the meaning of pondering—hence it is said, ‘or making them think poorly.’ ‘Those who speak thus’ means those who say, ‘So-and-so does this and that out of desire,’ etc. ‘It is stated’ means it is stated in the Pāḷi. ‘To the one who is angry’—this here is a supplementary rule.

Asammatassāti saṅghena kammavācāya asammatassa. Kevalaṃ “taveso bhāro”ti saṅghena āropitabhārassa, bhikkhūnaṃ vā phāsuvihāratthāya sayameva bhāraṃ vahantassa, yatra vā dve tayo bhikkhū viharanti, tatra tādisaṃ kammaṃ karontassāti adhippāyo. Yassa kassacīti upasampannassa vā anupasampannassa vā yassa kassaci. Anupasampannassa pana sammatassa vā asammatassa [V 0.0332] vāti ettha pana (pāci. aṭṭha. 106) kiñcāpi anupasampannassa terasa sammatiyo dātuṃ na vaṭṭanti, tathāpi yo upasampannakāle laddhasammutiko pacchā anupasampannabhāve ṭhito, taṃ sandhāya “sammatassa vā”ti vuttaṃ. Yassa pana byattassa sāmaṇerassa kevalaṃ saṅghena vā sammatena vā bhikkhunā “tvaṃ idaṃ kammaṃ karohī”ti bhāro kato, taṃ sandhāya “asammatassa vā”ti vuttaṃ. Yasmā ujjhāpanañca khiyyanañca musāvādavasena pavattaṃ, tasmā ādikammikassa imināva anāpatti, musāvādena pana āpattiyevāti gahetabbaṃ.

‘Not appointed’ means one who has not been appointed by the Saṅgha through a formal act of declaration. It refers to someone whose burden is merely imposed by the Saṅgha with the words, ‘This is your burden,’ or to one who voluntarily carries the burden for the comfortable living of the bhikkhus, or to one performing such an act where two or three bhikkhus reside—this is the intended meaning. ‘Of anyone’ refers to anyone, whether fully ordained or not fully ordained. However, regarding the not fully ordained, whether appointed or not—here, although thirteen appointments cannot be given to the not fully ordained, still, one who obtained appointment at the time of full ordination but later came to be in the state of one not fully ordained is intended by the phrase ‘or appointed.’ But concerning a competent novice who is merely assigned the task by the Saṅgha or by an appointed bhikkhu with the words, ‘You perform this act,’ the phrase ‘or not appointed’ is intended. Because complaining and scorn arise based on false speech, therefore, for the first offender, there is no offense by this alone, but an offense is incurred only through false speech—this should be understood.

Ujjhāpanakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Training Rule on Complaining is concluded.

4. Paṭhamasenāsanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. Explanation of the First Training Rule on Lodgings

Mañcaṃ [M 0.0363] vāti masārako, bundikābaddho, kuḷīrapādako, āhaccapādakoti imesu catūsu yaṃ kañci mañcaṃ vā. Pīṭhaṃ vāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Bhisiṃ vāti uṇṇabhisi, coḷabhisi, vākabhisi, tiṇabhisi, paṇṇabhisīti imāsu pañcasu bhisīsu yaṃ kañci bhisiṃ vā. Tenāha “mañcādīsū”tiādi. Tattha “mañcasaṅkhepenā”ti iminā pīṭhasaṅkhepaṃ paṭikkhipati. Kappiyacammenāti migājeḷakacammena. Ettha pana migacamme eṇimigo, vātamigo, pasadamigo, kuruṅgamigo, migamātuko, rohitamigoti etesaṃyeva cammāni vaṭṭanti, aññesaṃ pana –

A bed (mañca) means one made of woven cane (masārako), bound with cords (bundikābaddho), with crab-like legs (kuḷīrapādako), or with detachable legs (āhaccapādako); among these four, any such bed. A chair (pīṭha) means here too the same applies. A mattress (bhisi) means a woolen mattress, a cotton mattress, a bark mattress, a grass mattress, or a leaf mattress; among these five kinds of mattresses, any such mattress. Hence it is said, 'among beds and so on.' Here, by the summary term 'bed' (mañcasaṅkhepena), the summary inclusion of 'chair' (pīṭhasaṅkhepaṃ) is rejected. 'With allowable hide' (kappiyacammena) means with the hide of a deer or goat. In this case, among deer hides, only the hides of the eṇi deer, vāta deer, pasada deer, kuruṅga deer, female deer (migamātuka), and rohita deer are allowable. But for others—

Makkaṭo kāḷasīho ca, sarabho kadalīmigo;

Ye ca vāḷamigā keci, tesaṃ cammaṃ na vaṭṭatīti. (mahāva. aṭṭha. 259);

The monkey and the black lion, the sarabha and the plantain deer, and whatever other wild animals there are, their skins are not allowable.

Tattha vāḷamigāti sīhabyagghaacchataracchā. Na kevalañca eteyeva, yesaṃ pana cammaṃ vaṭṭatīti vuttaṃ, te ṭhapetvā avasesā antamaso gomahiṃsasasabiḷārādayopi sabbe imasmiṃ atthe “vāḷamigā”tveva veditabbā. Etesañhi sabbesaṃ cammaṃ na vaṭṭati. Tālīsapattanti suddhaṃ tamālapattaṃ, aññena missaṃ pana vaṭṭati. Tiṇavākacoḷesu akappiyaṃ nāma natthi. Kiṃ panettha bibbohane viya nisīdituñca nipajjituñca na vaṭṭatīti āha “tatthā”tiādi. Na kevalañcedamevāti āha “pamāṇaparicchedopi cettha natthī”ti, “ettakameva kātabba”nti bhisiyā [V 0.0333] pamāṇaniyamopi natthīti attho. Mañcabhisipīṭhabhisibhūmattharaṇabhisicaṅkamanabhisipādapuñchanabhisīti etāsaṃ pana anurūpato sallakkhetvā attano rucivasena pamāṇaṃ kātabbaṃ. Anto saṃvellitvā baddhanti yathā vemajjhaṃ saṃkhittaṃ hoti, evaṃ majjhe suṭṭhu veṭhetvā baddhaṃ.

Here, 'wild animals' (vāḷamigā) refers to lions, tigers, bears, and hyenas. Not only these, but excluding those whose skins are said to be allowable, all the rest—even down to cows, buffaloes, rabbits, cats, and the like—are to be understood as 'wild animals' in this context. For the skins of all these are not allowable. 'Tālisa leaves' (tālīsapattanti) means pure tamāla leaves, but if mixed with others, it is permissible. Regarding grass, bark, and cloth, there is nothing unallowable. What then, is it not allowable to sit or lie down on it as if on a cushion (bibbohane)? He says, 'in that case' (tatthā), etc. Not only this, but he also says, 'there is no fixed measure here' (pamāṇaparicchedopi cettha natthī), meaning there is no prescribed limit for the size of a mattress (bhisi). For bed-mattresses, seat-mattresses, ground-covering mattresses, walking-path mattresses, foot-wiping mattresses, and the like—one should determine the appropriate size according to one's preference. 'Bound by rolling inward' (anto saṃvellitvā baddhaṃ) means, just as something is contracted in the middle, it should be tightly wound and secured in the center.

Ye aṭṭha māsāti sambandho. “Avassikasaṅketā”ti etasseva vivaraṇaṃ “vassānamāsāti evaṃ apaññātā”ti, appatitā appasiddhāti attho. “Asaññitā”tipi pāṭho, tattha aviññātāti attho. Aṭṭha māsāti cattāro hemantikā, cattāro gimhikā māsāti aṭṭha māsā. Ovassakamaṇḍapeti sākhāmaṇḍapapadaramaṇḍapānaṃ yattha katthaci ovassake maṇḍape. Yatthāti yesu janapadesu. Sabbatthāti sabbesu janapadesu[M 0.0364]. Kākādīnaṃ nibaddhavāsarukkhamūleti yattha dhuvanivāsena kākā vā kulālā vā aññe vā sakuntā kulāvake katvā vasanti, tādisassa kākādīnaṃ nibaddhavāsassa yassa kassaci rukkhassa heṭṭhā. Yattha pana gocarappasutā sakuntā vissamitvā gacchanti, tassa rukkhassa mūle nikkhipituṃ vaṭṭati. “Kadācipī”ti iminā na kevalaṃ vassikasaṅketeyevāti dasseti. Yatthāti yasmiṃ padese. Yadāti yasmiṃ kāle.

The connection is to 'the eight months.' 'Not designated for the rains' (Avassikasaṅketā) is explained by 'not known as the months of the rains' (vassānamāsāti evaṃ apaññātā), meaning not established or not ascertained. 'Unmarked' (Asaññitā) is another reading, meaning not recognized. 'Eight months' refers to four winter months and four summer months, totaling eight months. 'In a shelter exposed to rain' (Ovassakamaṇḍape) means in any kind of shelter exposed to rain, such as a branch-shelter or a leaf-shelter. 'Wherever' (Yatthā) means in whichever regions. 'Everywhere' (Sabbatthā) means in all regions. 'At the base of a tree where crows and others have a fixed dwelling' (Kākādīnaṃ nibaddhavāsarukkhamūle) means at the base of any tree where crows, potter wasps, or other birds habitually dwell, having built nests and settled there. But wherever birds, intent on foraging, rest before moving on, it is permissible to place it at the base of such a tree. 'At any time' (Kadācipī) indicates that this is not only for the period designated for the rains. 'Wherever' (Yatthā) means in whatever place. 'Whenever' (Yadā) means at whatever time.

Soti yassatthāya santhato, so. Pakatisanthateti pakatiyāva santhate, yaṃ nevattanā santhataṃ, na parena santharāpitaṃ, tasminti vuttaṃ hoti. Lajjī hotīti lajjanasīlo hoti, parikkhāravināsane bhītoti attho. Tenāha “attano palibodhaṃ viya maññatī”ti, iminā alajjiṃ āpucchitvā gantuṃ na vaṭṭatīti dasseti. Nirapekkhoti “āgantvā uddharissāmī”ti apekkhārahito, iminā sāpekkho ce gacchati, anāpattīti dasseti. Teneva hi anāpattivāre “otāpento gacchatī”ti (pāci. 113) vuttaṃ. Aññattha gacchantoti taṃ maggaṃ atikkamitvā aññattha gacchanto. Leḍḍupātūpacārato bahi ṭhitattā “pāduddhārena kāretabbo”ti vuttaṃ, aññattha gacchantassa paṭhamapāduddhāre dukkaṭaṃ, dutiyapāduddhāre pācittiyanti attho.

‘He’ (so) means he for whose sake it was spread. 'Naturally spread' (pakatisanthate) means spread by nature itself; that which is neither spread by oneself nor caused to be spread by another. Thus it is said. 'He is conscientious' (lajjī hoti) means he is of a scrupulous character; the meaning is he is afraid of the destruction of the requisites. Hence it is said, 'he regards it as his own impediment,' showing that it is not proper to leave after asking leave of a shameless person. 'Without concern' (nirapekkho) means devoid of the expectation of thinking, 'I will retrieve it when I return,' showing that if one leaves with expectation, there is no offense. For this reason, in the section on non-offenses, it is said, 'one leaves while putting it out to sun' (otāpento gacchati). 'Going elsewhere' (aññattha gacchanto) means going beyond that path to another place. Because of standing outside the range of a clod's throw, it is said, 'the action is to be done by the lifting of the foot' (pāduddhārena kāretabbo). For one going elsewhere, there is a dukkaṭa at the first lifting of the foot, and a pācittiya at the second lifting of the foot—this is the meaning.

Tikapācittiyaṃ saṅghike saṅghikasaññivematikapuggalikasaññīnaṃ vasena. Imināva nayena tikadukkaṭampi veditabbaṃ. Cimilikādīnaṃ attho dutiyasikkhāpade dassitova. Pādapuñchanī (pāci. aṭṭha. 112) nāma rajjukehi vā pilotikāhi vā pādapuñchanatthaṃ katā. Phalakapīṭhaṃ nāma phalakamayaṃ pīṭhaṃ. Na kevalaṃ cimilikādīniyeva ajjhokāse ṭhapetvā gacchantassa dukkaṭanti āha “yaṃ vā panā”tiādi. Yaṃ kiñci dārubhaṇḍaṃ, yaṃ kiñci mattikābhaṇḍanti [V 0.0334] sambandho. “Antamaso pattādhārakampī”ti iminā tālavaṇṭabījanipattapānīyauḷauṅkapānīyasaṅkhādīsu vattabbameva natthīti dasseti.

The threefold Pācittiya applies to what belongs to the Saṅgha, for one who perceives it as belonging to the Saṅgha, or who is in doubt, or who perceives it as personal. In this same way, the threefold dukkaṭa should also be understood. The meaning of 'ground-covering' (cimilikā) and so on has already been shown in the second training rule. 'Foot-wiping mat' (pādapuñchanī) means one made with strings or rags for the purpose of wiping feet. 'Wooden bench' (phalakapīṭhaṃ) means a bench made of planks. Not only for a ground-covering and so on, but he also says, 'whatever else' (yaṃ vā pana), etc., that a dukkaṭa is incurred for leaving it in the open air when going. The connection is with 'any wooden item, any earthenware item.' 'Even a bowl stand' (antamaso pattādhārakampi)—by this, it is shown that there is no need to mention palm-leaf fans, seed-leaves, water ladles, water conches, and so on.

Araññe (pāci. aṭṭha. 110) paṇṇakuṭīsu vasantānaṃ sīlasampadāya pasannacittā manussā mañcapīṭhādīni denti “saṅghikaparibhogena paribhuñjathā”ti, tattha kiṃ kātabbanti āha “āraññakena panā”tiādi. Tattha asati anovassaketi pabbhārādianovassakaṭṭhāne asati. Idañca lakkhaṇavacanaṃ “sabhāgānaṃ [M 0.0365] abhāve”ti ca icchitabbattā. Āraññakena hi bhikkhunā tattha vasitvā aññattha gacchantena sāmantavihāre bhikkhūnaṃ pesetvā gantabbaṃ. Sabhāgānaṃ abhāve anovassake nikkhipitvā gantabbaṃ. Anovassake asati rukkhe laggetvā gantabbaṃ.

In the wilderness, people, with minds pleased by the virtuous conduct of those dwelling in leaf huts, give beds, benches, and so on, saying, 'Use these as communal property.' There, what should be done? He says, 'But by a wilderness-dweller,' etc. There, 'when there is no rain shelter' (asati anovassake) means when there is no place serving as a rain shelter, such as a cave. And this is a descriptive statement, as it should also be understood to mean 'in the absence of those sharing the same possessions.' For a wilderness-dwelling bhikkhu, having stayed there and then going elsewhere, should send word to the bhikkhus in a nearby monastery before leaving. In the absence of those sharing the same possessions, he should leave it in a rain shelter before going. If there is no rain shelter, he should hang it on a tree and leave.

Na kevalaṃ idaṃyeva katvā gantuṃ vaṭṭatīti āha “yathā vā”tiādi. Yathā vā upacikāhi na khajjatīti yathā ṭhapite upacikāhi senāsanaṃ na khajjati, evaṃ tathā pāsāṇānaṃ upari ṭhapanaṃ katvāti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – catūsu (pāci. aṭṭha. 116) pāsāṇesu mañcaṃ ṭhapetvā mañce avasesamañcapīṭhāni āropetvā upari bhisiādikaṃ rāsiṃ katvā dārubhaṇḍaṃ mattikābhaṇḍaṃ paṭisāmetvā gamikavattaṃ pūretvā gantabbanti.

Not only is it allowable to go having done this, but he also says, 'or just as' (yathā vā), and so on. 'Or just as it is not eaten by termites' (yathā vā upacikāhi na khajjati) means: just as a lodging (senāsanaṃ), when placed thus, is not eaten by termites, so too, having placed it upon stones—this is the meaning. This is what is meant: Having placed the bed (mañca) on four stones (Pāci. Aṭṭha. 116), and having placed the remaining beds and chairs (mañcapīṭhāni) on the bed, then piling up bedding (bhisi) and the like on top, and putting away wooden and earthenware utensils, one should fulfill the duties of a traveler (gamikavattaṃ) and then depart.

Abbhokāsikenāpi “ahaṃ ukkaṭṭhaabbhokāsiko”ti cīvarakuṭimpi akatvā asamaye ajjhokāse paññapetvā nisīdituṃ vā nipajjituṃ vā na vaṭṭatīti dassento āha “abbhokāsikenā”tiādi. Sace pana catugguṇenapi cīvarena katakuṭi atementaṃ rakkhituṃ neva sakkoti, sattāhavaddalikādīni bhavanti, bhikkhuno kāyānugatikattā vaṭṭati. Rukkhamūlikassāpi eseva nayo.

Even for one who dwells in the open air (abbhokāsika), thinking 'I am an eminent dweller in the open air' (ukkaṭṭhaabbhokāsiko), it is not allowable to prepare a place to sit or lie down in an open space at an unsuitable time without even making a robe-hut (cīvarakuṭi). This is shown by 'by one who dwells in the open air' (abbhokāsikena), and so on. But if even a hut made with a fourfold robe (catugguṇena cīvarena katakuṭi) cannot adequately protect from the elements, and there are seven-day rains (sattāhavaddalikādīni bhavanti), then it is permissible for a monk, since it is for the body's needs (kāyānugatikattā). The same principle applies to one who dwells at the foot of a tree (rukkhamūlika).

Yasmiṃ vissāsaggāho ruhati, tassa santakaṃ attano puggalikamiva hotīti āha “vissāsikapuggalike”ti. Yasmiṃ pana vissāso na ruhati, tassa santake dukkaṭameva. Amanussoti yakkho vā peto vā. Palibuddhaṃ hotīti upaddutaṃ hoti.

In whom trust takes root, his belongings become as if one's own personal property—thus it is said, 'trustworthy, personal' (vissāsikapuggalike). But concerning the belongings of one in whom trust does not take root, there is only a dukkaṭa offense. 'Non-human' (amanusso) means a yakkha or a departed spirit (peta). 'Palibuddhaṃ hoti' means it is afflicted (upaddutaṃ hoti).

Paṭhamasenāsanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the first training rule concerning lodgings is concluded.

5. Dutiyasenāsanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

5. The Explanation of the Second Training Rule on Lodgings

Yaṃ [V 0.0335] kiñci cammanti kappiyākappiyaṃ yaṃ kiñci cammaṃ. Nanu “na, bhikkhave, mahācammāni dhāretabbāni sīhacammaṃ byagghacammaṃ dīpicammaṃ, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 255) khandhake sīhacammādīnaṃ paṭikkhepo katoti āha “sīhacammādīnañhī”tiādi. Pariharaṇeyeva paṭikkhepoti attano santakaṃ [M 0.0366] katvā taṃ taṃ vihāraṃ haritvā mañcapīṭhādīsu attharitvā paribhogeyeva paṭikkhepo, senāsanasantakaṃ katvā bhūmattharaṇavasena pana paribhoge nevatthi doso. Tenāha “senāsanaparibhoge pana akappiyacammaṃ nāma natthī”ti. Pāvārenti sañchādenti sarīraṃ etenāti pāvāro. Kojavoti uddalomiekantalomiādikojavattharaṇaṃ.
