Sesanti bhisi nisīdanaṃ tiṇasanthāro paṇṇasanthāroti avasiṭṭhaṃ senāsanaṃ. Tattha bhisīti mañcakabhisi vā pīṭhakabhisi vā. Nisīdananti sadasaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tiṇasanthāroti yesaṃ kesañci tiṇānaṃ santhāro. Esa nayo paṇṇasanthāre. Ettha ca bhisi heṭṭhā vuttattā pākaṭā. Nisīdanaṃ nisīdanasikkhāpadeneva (pāci. 531 ādayo) pākaṭaṃ. Tiṇasanthārapaṇṇasanthārāni pana lokapasiddhāniyeva. Tenevāha “pākaṭamevā”ti.

Whatever hide (yaṃ kiñci cammaṃ) means any hide, whether permissible or not. Indeed, in the Khandhaka, it is stated: “Monks, large hides—lion hide, tiger hide, leopard hide—should not be worn. Whoever wears them commits an offense of wrong-doing” (Mahāvagga 255). Thus, the prohibition of lion hides and the like is made. Therefore, it is said, “For lion hides and the like,” and so on. The prohibition applies only to personal use: having made it one’s own property, bringing it to this or that monastery, spreading it on beds, benches, and so on, and using it. However, there is no fault in using it as the lodging's property, for instance, as a ground-covering. Therefore, it is said: “But in the use of lodging, there is no such thing as an impermissible hide.” Pāvāro is so called because one covers the body with it. Kojavo means a fleecy covering, such as one with long fleece or fleece on one side. The rest (sesaṃ) refers to the remaining lodging items: a mattress or cushion (bhisi), a sitting mat (nisīdana), a grass spread (tiṇasanthāro), and a leaf spread (paṇṇasanthāro). Among these, a bhisi is a mattress or cushion for a bed or a bench. A nisīdana should be understood as a sitting cloth with a border. A tiṇasanthāro is a spread made of any kind of grass. The same applies to a leaf spread. Here, the bhisi is evident because it was mentioned below. The nisīdana is evident from the training rule on sitting mats (Pācittiya 531 onwards). Grass spreads and leaf spreads, however, are well-known in the world. Therefore, it is said: “They are evident.”

Neva uddhareyya, na uddharāpeyyāti attanā vā uddharitvā patirūpe ṭhāne na ṭhapeyya, parena vā tathā na kāreyya. Tenāha “yathā ṭhapita”ntiādi. Taṃ ṭhapentena ca “catūsu pāsāṇesū”tiādinā (pāci. aṭṭha. 116) pubbe vuttanayeneva antogehe anovassake nikkhipitabbaṃ. Sace pana senāsanaṃ ovassati, chadanatthañca tiṇaṃ vā iṭṭhakā vā ānītā honti. Sace ussahati, chādetabbaṃ. No ce sakkoti, yo okāso anovassako, tattha nikkhipitabbaṃ. Sace sabbampi ovassati, ussahantena antogāme upāsakānaṃ ghare ṭhapetabbaṃ. Sace tepi “saṅghikaṃ nāma, bhante, bhāriyaṃ, aggidāhādīnaṃ bhāyāmā”ti na sampaṭicchanti, ajjhokāse pāsāṇānaṃ upari mañcaṃ ṭhapetvā sesaṃ pubbe vuttanayeneva nikkhipitvā tiṇehi ca paṇṇehi ca paṭicchādetabbaṃ. Yañhi tattha aṅgamattampi avasissati, taṃ aññesaṃ tattha āgatānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ upakāraṃ bhavissatīti. Upacāranti sabbapacchimasenāsanato dve leḍḍupātā.

“He should not remove it, nor should he have it removed” means that he himself does not remove it and place it in a suitable place, nor does he have another do so. Therefore, it is said, “as it was placed,” and so on. When placing it, it should be deposited inside a building that does not leak, in the manner previously stated, beginning with “on four stones” (Pāc. Aṭṭha. 116). However, if the lodging leaks, and grass or tiles have been brought for roofing, if one is able, it should be roofed. If one is not able, it should be deposited in a place that does not leak. If the entire lodging leaks, one who is able should place it in the house of a lay follower within the village. If they do not accept, saying, “Venerable sir, that which belongs to the Sangha is a heavy responsibility; we fear fire and such dangers,” then one should place a bed outside on top of stones and deposit the rest in the manner previously instructed, covering it with grass and leaves. For whatever remains there, even a small portion, will be of use to other bhikkhus who arrive there. Upacāra means two clod-throws away from the farthest lodging.

Ayamettha āpucchitabbānāpucchitabbavinicchayo – (pāci. aṭṭha. 118) yā tāva bhūmiyaṃ dīghasālā vā paṇṇasālā vā hoti, yaṃ vā rukkhatthambhesu katagehaṃ upacikānaṃ uṭṭhānaṭṭhānaṃ hoti, tato pakkamantena āpucchitvāva pakkamitabbaṃ. Tasmiñhi katipayāni divasāni ajaggiyamāne vammikāva santiṭṭhanti. Yaṃ pana pāsāṇapiṭṭhiyaṃ vā pāsāṇatthambhesu vā [V 0.0336] katasenāsanaṃ siluccayaleṇaṃ vā sudhālittasenāsanaṃ vā, yattha upacikāsaṅkā natthi, tato [M 0.0367] pakkamantassa āpucchitvāpi anāpucchitvāpi gantuṃ vaṭṭati. Tenāha “yattha panā”tiādi. Sace tādisepi senāsane ekena passena upacikā ārohanti, āpucchitvāva gantabbaṃ. Āpucchanaṃ pana vattanti āpucchanaṃ gamikavattaṃ. Idañca itikattabbatādassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, na pana vattabhedadukkaṭanti (sārattha. ṭī. pācittiya 3.118) dassanatthaṃ. Keci pana “dukkaṭanti dassanattha”nti vadanti, taṃ na yujjati vattakkhandhakaṭṭhakathāya “yaṃ pāsāṇapiṭṭhiyaṃ vā pāsāṇatthambhesu vā katasenāsanaṃ, yattha upacikānārohanti, taṃ anāpucchantassāpi anāpattī”ti (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 360) vuttattā. Āpucchantena pana bhikkhumhi (pāci. aṭṭha. 116) sati bhikkhu āpucchitabbo, tasmiṃ asati sāmaṇero, tasmiṃ asati ārāmiko, tasmimpi asati yena vihāro kārāpito, so vihārasāmiko, tassa vā kule yo koci āpucchitabbo.

Herein is the determination of what should and should not be announced (Pāc. Aṭṭha. 118): First, if there is a long hall or a leaf-hut on the ground, or a dwelling built on tree stumps that is a place for termites to arise, one must announce one’s departure before leaving. For if it is not looked after for a few days, termite mounds will indeed form. However, if the dwelling is built on a stone slab or stone pillars, or is a rock cave or a plastered dwelling where there is no suspicion of termites, one may depart either with or without announcing. Therefore, it is said, “But where,” and so on. If even in such a dwelling termites climb up on one side, one must announce before leaving. Announcing, however, is a duty, the proper conduct for one who is departing. And this is stated to show what ought to be done, not to show that it is an offense of wrong-doing for breaking the duty (Sārattha. Ṭī. Pācittiya 3.118). Some, however, say it is stated to show it is a wrong-doing, but this is incorrect because the commentary on the section of duties (Vattakkhandha) states: “Regarding a dwelling built on a stone slab or stone pillars where termites do not climb—there is no offense for one who departs without announcing” (Cūḷava. Aṭṭha. 360). When announcing, if a bhikkhu is present, the bhikkhu should be informed. If he is not present, a sāmaṇera. If he is not present, a monastery attendant. If even he is not present, the person who had the monastery built—the owner of the monastery—or anyone in his household should be informed.

“Upacāre”ti etasseva vivaraṇaṃ “bahi āsanne”ti, vihārassa bahi āsannaṭṭhāneti attho. Upaṭṭhānasālāya vāti bhojanasālāyaṃ vā. Dukkaṭamevāti vuttappakārañhi dasavidhaṃ seyyaṃ antogabbhādimhi guttaṭṭhāne paññapetvā gacchantassa yasmā seyyāpi senāsanampi upacikāhi palujjati, vammikarāsiyeva hoti, tasmā pācittiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Bahi pana upaṭṭhānasālādīsu paññapetvā gacchantassa seyyāmattameva nasseyya ṭhānassa aguttatāya, na senāsanaṃ, tasmā ettha dukkaṭaṃ vuttaṃ. Mañcapīṭhaṃ pana yasmā na sakkā sahasā upacikāhi khāyituṃ, tasmā taṃ vihārepi santharitvā gacchantassa dukkaṭaṃ vuttaṃ. Vihārūpacāre pana taṃ vihāracārikaṃ āhiṇḍantā disvāva paṭisāmenti.

The explanation of “in the vicinity” (upacāre) is “near the outside” (bahi āsanne), meaning in a place near the outside of the monastery. “Or in the service hall” (upaṭṭhānasālāya vā) means in the dining hall. Regarding “only a dukkaṭa offense”: For one who departs having spread out the ten kinds of bedding described inside a guarded place, such as an inner room, since both the bedding and the lodging may be destroyed by termites and become a mere termite mound, a pācittiya offense is stated. However, for one who departs having spread out bedding outside, such as in the service hall, only the bedding itself might be lost because the place is unguarded, not the lodging. Therefore, a dukkaṭa offense is stated here. As for a bed or bench, since termites cannot quickly consume them, a dukkaṭa offense is stated for one who departs even if it is left spread out inside the monastery. But in the vicinity of the monastery, those wandering around the monastery will see it and put it away.

Uddharaṇāni katvāti ettha uddharitvā gacchantena mañcapīṭhakavānaṃ sabbaṃ apanetvā (pāci. aṭṭha. 118) saṃharitvā cīvaravaṃse laggetvā gantabbaṃ. Pacchā āgantvā vasanakabhikkhunāpi puna mañcapīṭhaṃ vā paññapetvā sayitvā gacchantena tatheva kātabbaṃ. Antokuṭṭato seyyaṃ bahikuṭṭe paññapetvā vasantena gamanakāle puna gahitaṭṭhāneyeva paṭisāmetabbaṃ. Uparipāsādato oropetvā heṭṭhāpāsāde vasantassāpi eseva nayo. Rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānesu mañcapīṭhaṃ paññapetvāpi gamanakāle puna gahitaṭṭhāneyeva ṭhapetabbaṃ. Uddharāpetvā gamanepi eseva nayo. Āpucchitvā gacchantena pana [M 0.0368] “bhikkhumhi sati bhikkhu āpucchitabbo”tiādinā (pāci. aṭṭha. 116) heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva āpucchitvā gantabbaṃ.

“Having taken up” (uddharaṇāni katvā): Here, when leaving after taking up, all bedding from the bed and bench should be removed (Pāc. Aṭṭha. 118), gathered, and hung on the robe-rail, and then one should depart. Later, when a resident bhikkhu returns, that bhikkhu should again set up the bed or bench, lie down, and upon departing, do likewise. If one stays after setting up a sleeping place from inside a room to outside the room, when leaving, it should be restored to the place from which it was taken. The same principle applies to one who stays in a lower-storied building after bringing furnishings down from an upper-storied building. Even if a bed or bench is set up in a place for the night or a place for the day, when leaving, it should be placed back in the place from which it was taken. The same principle applies when having someone else take it up before leaving. However, when departing after requesting leave, one should request leave according to the method stated previously, beginning with: “When a bhikkhu is present, the bhikkhu should be asked for leave” (Pāc. Aṭṭha. 116), and then depart.

Dutiyasenāsanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the second training rule concerning lodgings is concluded.

6. Anupakhajjasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Encroachment

“Jāna”nti [V 0.0337] vutte “anuṭṭhāpanīyo ‘aya’nti jānanto”ti ayaṃ viseso kuto labbhatīti āha “tenevassā”tiādi. Nanu padabhājanepi vuḍḍhabhāvādijānanameva vuttaṃ, na tu anuṭṭhāpanīyabhāvanti anuyogaṃ sandhāyāha “vuḍḍho hī”tiādi. Bahūpakāratanti “bhaṇḍāgārikattādibahuupakārabhāvaṃ”. Na kevalaṃ idamevāti āha “guṇavisiṭṭhatañcā”tiādi, tena bahūpakārattepi guṇavisiṭṭhattābhāve, guṇavisiṭṭhattepi bahūpakārattābhāve dātuṃ na vaṭṭatīti dasseti. “Bhaṇḍāgārikassa bahūpakārataṃ, dhammakathikādīnaṃ guṇavisiṭṭhatañca sallakkhetvā”ti (sārattha. ṭī. pācittiya 3.119-121) keci. Dhuvavāsatthāyāti niccavāsatthāya. Sammannitvāti apalokanena kammena sammannitvā. Kāmañcettha gilānassāpi saṅghoyeva anucchavikaṃ senāsanaṃ deti, gilāno pana apaloketvā saṅghena adinnasenāsanopi na pīḷetabbo anukampitabboti dassetuṃ visuṃ vutto.

When it is said, ‘knowing’ (jāna), the question arises: from where does the distinction ‘knowing that this is one who should not be displaced’ come? To address this, it is said, ‘tenevassā,’ and so on. But is it not said in the word analysis that one knows only seniority and so forth, and not the status of being non-displaceable? To address this question, it is said, ‘vuḍḍho hī,’ and so on. ‘Great helpfulness’ (bahūpakāratā) means ‘the state of being of great help, such as being a storekeeper.’ Not only this—it is further stated, ‘and distinguished qualities’ (guṇavisiṭṭhatañca), and so on, thereby showing that even with great helpfulness, if there is a lack of distinguished qualities, or even with distinguished qualities, if there is a lack of great helpfulness, it is not proper to give. Some say, “After considering the great helpfulness of a storekeeper and the distinguished qualities of Dhamma preachers, etc.” (Sāratthadīpanī, Pācittiya 3.119–121). ‘For a permanent residence’ (dhuvavāsatthāya) means for a constant residence. ‘Having been authorized’ (sammannitvā) means having been authorized by an act of proclamation. Although here the Sangha itself gives a suitable lodging even to a sick person, it is stated separately to show that a sick person, however, even in a lodging not given by the Sangha, having made a proclamation, should not be oppressed but should be treated with compassion.

Samantā diyaḍḍho hatthoti majjhe paññattaṃ mañcapīṭhaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Ekapassena ce pahonakadisā dissati, tato gahetabbaṃ. Pādadhovanapāsāṇatoti dvāre nikkhittapādadhovanapāsāṇato. Nisīdantassa vā nipajjantassa vā pācittiyanti ettha nisīdanamattena, nipajjanamatteneva vā pācittiyaṃ. Punappunaṃ karontassāti uṭṭhāyuṭṭhāya nisīdato vā nipajjato vā.

‘One and a half cubits all around’ (samantā diyaḍḍho hattho) is said with reference to a bed or bench set up in the middle. If a sufficient direction is visible on one side, it should be taken from there. ‘From the foot-washing stone’ (pādadhovanapāsāṇato) means from the foot-washing stone placed at the door. ‘A pācittiya for one who is sitting or lying down’ (nisīdantassa vā nipajjantassa vā pācittiya): here, a pācittiya is incurred by the mere act of sitting or the mere act of lying down. ‘For one who does it again and again’ (punappunaṃ karontassa) means for one who sits or lies down each time after getting up.

Saṅghike saṅghikasaññivematikapuggalikasaññīnaṃ vasena tikapācittiyaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tikadukkaṭaṃ pana puggalike saṅghikasaññivematikaaññapuggalikasaññīnaṃ vasena. Vihārassa upacāreti tassa bahi āsannappadese.

In the case of what belongs to the Sangha, a threefold pācittiya should be understood for one who perceives it as belonging to the Sangha, one who is in doubt, or one who perceives it as belonging to an individual. However, a threefold dukkaṭa offense occurs in the case of what belongs to an individual, for one who perceives it as belonging to the Sangha, one who is in doubt, or one who perceives it as belonging to another individual. ‘In the vicinity of the monastery’ (vihārassa upacāre) means in a nearby area outside it.

Anupakhajjasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning encroachment is concluded.

7. Nikkaḍḍhanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

7. Explanation of the Training Rule on Expulsion

Anekakoṭṭhakānīti [M 0.0369] anekadvārakoṭṭhakāni. “Nikkhamāti vacanaṃ sutvā attano ruciyā ce nikkhamati, anāpattī”ti (sārattha. ṭī. pācittiya 126) vadanti.

‘Having many chambers’ (anekakoṭṭhakāni) means having chambers with many doors. “Having heard the instruction to leave, if one leaves of one’s own accord, there is no offense,” (Sāratthadīpanī, Pācittiya 126) they say.

Tassa [V 0.0338] parikkhāranikkaḍḍhaneti tassa santakaṃ yaṃ kiñci pattacīvaraparissāvanadhammakaraṇamañcapīṭhabhisibibbohanādibhedaṃ antamaso rajanachallipi atthi, tassa parikkhārassa nikkaḍḍhane. Tañcāti dukkaṭaṃ parāmasati. Nikkaḍḍhāpanepi eseva nayo. Gāḷhaṃ bandhitvā ṭhapitesu pana ekāva āpatti.

‘On the expulsion of his requisites’ (tassa parikkhāranikkaḍḍhane) means on the expulsion of any of his possessions, such as bowls, robes, water strainers, water pots, beds, stools, cushions, pillows, and so forth, down to even a piece of bark for dye. ‘And that’ (tañca) refers to a dukkaṭa offense. The same principle applies to causing them to be expelled. However, if they are firmly tied together and placed, there is only one offense.

Bhaṇḍanakārakakalahakārakameva sakalasaṅghārāmato nikkaḍḍhituṃ labhati. So hi pakkhaṃ labhitvā saṅghampi bhindeyya. Alajjiādayo pana attano vasanaṭṭhānatoyeva nikkaḍḍhitabbā. Sakalasaṅghārāmato nikkaḍḍhituṃ na vaṭṭati. Tenāha “sakalasaṅghārāmatopī”tiādi.

One who causes quarrels and disputes alone may be expelled from the entire monastery of the Sangha. For if he gains a faction, he might even split the Sangha. But shameless ones and the like should be expelled only from their own dwelling places. It is not proper to expel them from the entire monastery of the Sangha. Therefore, it is said, ‘even from the entire monastery of the Sangha’ (sakalasaṅghārāmatopi), and so on.

Nikkaḍḍhanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning expulsion is concluded.

8. Vehāsakuṭisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

8. Explanation of the Training Rule on Lofty Huts

Uparivehāsakuṭiyāti uparimatale asanthatapadarāya kuṭiyā. Tenāha “upari acchannatalāyā”tiādi. Yā hi kāci upari acchannatalā dvibhūmikakuṭikā vā tibhūmikādikuṭikā vā, sā “vehāsakuṭī”ti vuccati. Idañhi vehāsakuṭilakkhaṇaṃ. Yadi evaṃ kasmā padabhājane “majjhimassa purisassa asīsaghaṭṭā”ti (pāci. 131) vuttanti āha “padabhājane panā”tiādi. Idha adhippetaṃ kuṭiṃ dassetunti imasmiṃ sikkhāpade adhippetaṃ vehāsakuṭiṃ dassetuṃ. Majjhimassa purisassāti pamāṇamajjhimassa purisassa. Sabbaheṭṭhimāhi tulāhi sīsaṃ na ghaṭṭetīti asīsaghaṭṭā. Aṅge vijjhitvāti aṭaniyo vijjhitvā. Pavesitapādakanti pavesitapādasikhaṃ. Tasmāti “bhūmatthe vā”tiādinā vuttamevatthaṃ kāraṇabhāvena paccāmasati. Yasmā āhaccapādakādīsu yathāvutto attho hoti, tasmāti vuttaṃ hoti.

‘In a lofty hut above’ (uparivehāsakuṭiyā) means in a hut on an upper floor with an un-laid plank floor. Hence it is said, ‘with an uncovered floor above’ (upari acchannatalāya), and so on. Any structure above with an uncovered floor, whether a two-storied or three-storied hut or similar, is called a ‘lofty hut’ (vehāsakuṭī). This is indeed the defining characteristic of a lofty hut. If so, why is it said in the word analysis, ‘not striking the head of a man of medium height’ (majjhimassa purisassa asīsaghaṭṭā) (Pāci. 131)? To this it is said, ‘But in the word analysis’ (padabhājane pana), and so on. ‘To show the hut intended here’ means to show the lofty hut intended in this training rule. ‘Of a man of medium height’ (majjhimassa purisassa) means of a man of average height. ‘Not striking the head’ (asīsaghaṭṭā) means that the head does not strike the very lowest beams. ‘Having pierced the limbs’ (aṅge vijjhitvā) means having pierced the pegs. ‘With an inserted foot’ (pavesitapādaka) means with the tip of the foot inserted. ‘Therefore’ (tasmā) refers back to this very meaning stated by ‘or on the ground’ (bhūmatthe vā), and so on, as the reason. This means: because in the case of a removable footrest and so forth, the meaning is as stated, therefore it is said.

Sahasāti abhibhavitvā ajjhottharitvā. Avehāsakuṭikāyāti bhūmiyaṃ katapaṇṇasālādīsu, tattha anāpatti. Na hi sakkā tattha parassa pīḷā [M 0.0370] kātuṃ. Sīsaghaṭṭāyāti yā sīsaṃ ghaṭṭā hoti, tatthāpi anāpatti. Na hi sakkā tattha heṭṭhāpāsāde anoṇatena vicarituṃ, tasmā asañcaraṇaṭṭhānattā parapīḷā na bhavissati. Uparitalaṃ vā padarasañcitanti uparimatalaṃ dāruphalakehi ghanasanthataṃ. Kiñci gaṇhāti vāti upari nāgadantakādīsu laggitaṃ cīvarādiṃ yaṃ kiñci gaṇhāti vā. Laggati vāti etthāpi eseva [V 0.0339] nayo. Paṭipakkhabhūtā āṇi paṭāṇi. Yassā dinnāya nisīdantepi pādā na nipatanti, evaṃbhūtā āṇi mañcapīṭhānaṃ pādasikhāsu dinnā hotīti attho. Tenāha “pādasīsāna”ntiādi.

‘Forcefully’ (sahasā) means having overcome and overwhelmed. ‘In a non-lofty hut’ (avehāsakuṭikāya) refers to leaf huts and so forth made on the ground; there is no offense there, for it is not possible to cause affliction to others there. ‘In one that strikes the head’ (sīsaghaṭṭāya) refers to that which strikes the head; there too there is no offense, for it is not possible to move about on the lower floor without bending; therefore, since it is not a place for moving around, affliction to others will not occur. ‘Or the upper floor is laid with planks’ (uparitalaṃ vā padarasañcitaṃ) means the upper floor is densely laid with wooden planks. ‘Or takes something’ (kiñci gaṇhāti vā) means one takes whatever robe or other item is hung above on elephant-tusk pegs and so forth. ‘Or hangs’ (laggati vā): here too the same principle applies. A counter-peg is a `paṭāṇi`. The meaning is that such a peg, when it is fixed, prevents the feet from falling even when one is sitting, and is fixed at the ends of the legs of beds and benches. Therefore, it is said, ‘of the feet and head’ (pādasīsānaṃ), and so on.

Vehāsakuṭisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on lofty huts is concluded.

9. Mahallakavihārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

9. Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning a Large Monastery

Piṭṭhasaṅghāṭassāti dvārabandhassa. Sāmantā aḍḍhateyyahattho padesoti yassa (pāci. aṭṭha. 135) vemajjhe dvāraṃ hoti, uparibhāge ca uccā bhitti, tassa tīsu disāsu sāmantā aḍḍhateyyahattho padeso. Khuddakassa pana vihārassa dvīsu disāsu. Tatrāpi yaṃ bhittiṃ vivariyamānaṃ kavāṭaṃ āhanati, sā aparipuṇṇūpacārāpi hoti. Sace pana dvārassa adhobhāgepi lepokāso atthi, tampi limpituṃ vaṭṭati. Aggaḷaṭṭhapanāyāti ettha aggaḷasaddena taṃsambandhato dvāraphalakasahitaṃ dvārabandhanaṃ adhippetaṃ. Tenāha “sakavāṭakassā”tiādi. “Niccalabhāvatthāyā”ti iminā tañca kho ṭhapanaṃ idha niccalabhāvenāti dasseti. Ko panettha adhippāyoti āha “kavāṭañhī”tiādi. Kampatīti calati. Yāva dvārakosā aggaḷaṭṭhapanāya punappunaṃ limpitabbo vā lepāpetabbo vāti aggaḷaṭṭhapanatthāya yāva dvārakosā punappunaṃ attanā limpitabbo vā, parehi lepāpetabbo vāti attho.

‘Of the door frame’ means of the door jamb. ‘A space of two and a half cubits around it’: this refers to a place where the door is in the middle of the wall and the upper part is a high wall; for such a place, there is a space of two and a half cubits around it on three sides. For a small dwelling, however, it is on two sides. Even there, the wall that the door panel strikes when being opened is also considered to have an incomplete approach. However, if there is space for plastering also below the door, it is allowable to plaster that too. Regarding ‘for the fixing of the bolt’—here, by the word ‘bolt’ is meant the door jamb together with the door panel connected to it. Hence, he says, ‘together with its door panel,’ and so on. By ‘for the purpose of stability,’ he shows that this fixing here is for the sake of stability. What is the intention here? He says, ‘Indeed, the door panel,’ and so on. ‘It shakes’ means it moves. ‘Up to the door frame, for the fixing of the bolt, it should be repeatedly plastered or caused to be plastered’ means that for the sake of fixing the bolt, up to the door frame, one must repeatedly plaster it oneself or have it plastered by others.

Nanu cāyamattho neva mātikāyaṃ, na padabhājane vutto, atha kuto daṭṭhabboti āha “tatthā”tiādi. Kiñcāpīti yadipi. Aṭṭhuppattiyanti sikkhāpadassa nidāne. Adhikāratoti anuvattanato. Ālokaṃ sandheti pidhetīti ālokasandhi. Tenāha “ālokasandhīti vātapānakavāṭakā vuccantī”ti. Tattha vātapānakavāṭakāti vātapānaphalakā. Anuññātappadesato [M 0.0371] pana aññattha punappunaṃ vilimpituṃ vā vilimpāpetuṃ vā na vaṭṭati. “Mattikāya kattabbakiccaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā puna catutthalepe dinne pācittiya”nti (sārattha. ṭī. pācittiya 3.135) keci. “Punappunaṃ lepadānassa vuttappamāṇato aññattha paṭikkhittamattaṃ ṭhapetvā pācittiyassa avuttattā dukkaṭa”nti apare.

But is this meaning not stated in the Mātikā, nor in the word analysis? So, from where should it be understood? He says, ‘Therein,’ and so on. ‘Even though’ means although. ‘In the arising of the matter’ means in the origin story of the training rule. ‘From its relevance’ means from its continuity. ‘It joins the light’ means it obstructs it; hence, ‘light-joining.’ Therefore, it is said, ‘By “light-joining” are meant window shutters.’ Therein, ‘window shutters’ means window panels. However, outside the permitted area, it is not allowable to repeatedly plaster or have it plastered. Some say, ‘After completing the work to be done with clay, if a fourth coat of plaster is applied, it is a pācittiya offense.’ Others say, ‘Since the repeated application of plaster beyond the stated measure is merely prohibited elsewhere, and a pācittiya offense is not mentioned, it is a dukkaṭa offense.’

Adhiṭṭhātabbanti saṃvidhātabbaṃ. Appahariteti ettha appasaddo “appiccho”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.252, 336; saṃ. ni. 2.148) viya abhāvatthoti āha “aharite”ti. Sālivīhiādi [V 0.0340] (sārattha. ṭī. 2.30) pubbaṇṇaṃ “purakkhataṃ sassaphala”nti katvā, tabbipariyāyato muggamāsādi aparaṇṇaṃ. Vuttanti vapitaṃ. “Tasmiṃ ṭhatvā adhiṭṭhahanto dukkaṭaṃ āpajjatī”ti iminā yasmiṃ padese samantā vuttappamāṇe paricchede pubbaṇṇādīni na santi, tattha vihāro kāretabbo. Yattha pana santi, tattha kārāpetuṃ na vaṭṭatīti dasseti. Tathevāti mukhavaṭṭiantena. Tasmiṃ ṭhātabbaṃ patantassa vihārassa apatanokāsattā, tassa bhikkhuno upari na pateyyāti adhippāyo. Yathāparicchinnassa pana okāsassa abbhantaraṃ vihārassa patantassa okāso hotīti appaharitepi tasmiṃ ṭhatvā adhiṭṭhātuṃ na labhati. Tenāha “tassa anto aharitepi ṭhātuṃ na labhatī”ti.

‘To be determined’ means to be arranged. In ‘where there is little green growth,’ the term ‘appa’ signifies absence, as in ‘of few wishes’ (appiccho) and similar contexts; hence he says ‘without green growth.’ Early grain such as rice and paddy is called ‘primary grain;’ conversely, later grain refers to mung beans, other beans, and so on. ‘Sown’ means planted. By ‘Standing there and determining, one incurs a dukkaṭa offense,’ he shows that a dwelling should be built in a place where, within the surrounding area of the stated measure, early grains and so on are not present. But where they are present, it is not allowable to have it built. ‘Similarly’ refers to the extent of the mouth-rim. One should stand in that place, the intention being that since it is a space where a falling dwelling would not land, it should not fall upon that monk. However, if there is space for the dwelling to fall within the delimited area, then one is not permitted to stand there and determine, even if it is a place without green growth. Therefore, he says, ‘Even inside that, in a place without green growth, one is not permitted to stand.’

Tato ce uttarīti tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ vā pariyāyānaṃ vā upari catutthe magge vā pariyāye vāti attho. Tenāha “maggena chādiyamāne”tiādi. Tattha maggena chādiyamāneti aparikkhipitvā ujukameva chādiyamāne. Pariyāyenāti parikkhepena. Tattha maggena chādanaṃ iṭṭhakasilāsudhāhi labbhati, pariyāyena chādanaṃ tiṇapaṇṇehīti āha “iṭṭhakasilāsudhāhī”tiādi. Tasmā yathā icchati, tathā dve magge vā dve pariyāye vā adhiṭṭhahitvā tatiyaṃ maggaṃ vā pariyāyaṃ vā “evaṃ chādehī”ti āṇāpetvā pakkamitabbaṃ. Sace na pakkamati, tuṇhībhāvena ṭhātabbaṃ. Sabbampi cetaṃ chadanaṃ chadanūpari veditabbaṃ. Uparūparichanno hi vihāro ciraṃ anovassako hotīti maññamānā evaṃ chādenti. Tiṇamuṭṭhigaṇanāyāti tiṇakaraḷagaṇanāya.

‘If it is further than that’ means above three courses or three layers, that is, on the fourth course or layer. Therefore, he says, ‘when covering with a course,’ and so on. Here, ‘when covering with a course’ means covering straight without encircling. ‘By a layer’ means by encircling. In this context, covering with a course is done with bricks, stones, or plaster, while covering with a layer is done with grass or leaves—thus he says, ‘with bricks, stones, or plaster,’ and so on. Therefore, having determined two courses or two layers as desired, one should give the instruction for the third course or layer, ‘Cover it like this,’ and then depart. If one does not depart, one should remain silent. All this covering should be understood as being upon the roofing. Believing that a dwelling covered layer upon layer will remain rainproof for a long time, they cover it thus. ‘By the count of handfuls of grass’ means by the count of bundles of grass.

Tikapācittiyanti atirekadvattipariyāye atirekasaññivematikaūnakasaññīnaṃ vasena tīṇi pācittiyāni. Setavaṇṇādikaraṇeti setavaṇṇakāḷavaṇṇagerukaparikammamālākammalatākammamakaradantakapañcapaṭikānaṃ [M 0.0372] karaṇe. Leṇaguhātiṇakuṭikādīsūti ettha leṇanti dvārabaddhaṃ. Guhāti kevalā pabbataguhā. Tiṇakuṭikā pākaṭā eva.

‘A pācittiya offense in a group of three’ means that in the case of exceeding two or three layers, there are three pācittiya offenses by way of one who perceives it as exceeding, one who is uncertain, and one who perceives it as less. ‘In the application of white color, and so on’ refers to the application of white color, black color, red ocher, decorative work, garland work, creeper work, crocodile-tooth work, and the five-fold pattern. In ‘a rock-shelter, cave, grass hut, and so on,’ herein, ‘rock-shelter’ means one that is fitted with a door. ‘Cave’ means simply a mountain cave. ‘A grass hut’ is just as is evident.

Mahallakavihārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning a large dwelling is concluded.

10. Sappāṇakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

10. The Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Water With Living Beings

Ekasmiṃ ghaṭe ekāva āpattīti ekasmiṃ udakaghaṭe ekāva āpatti. Esa nayo sabbabhājanesu[V 0.0341]. Vicchindantassāti dhāraṃ vicchindantassa. Ekekaṃ pakkhipantassāti ekekaṃ tiṇaṃ vā paṇṇaṃ vā mattikaṃ vā aññaṃ vā kaṭṭhagomayādiṃ pakkhipantassa. Pariyādānanti khayaṃ.

‘In one pot, one offense’ means that in one water pot, there is one offense. This is the principle for all vessels. ‘For one who interrupts’ means for one who interrupts the stream. ‘For one who puts in one by one’ means for one who puts in, one by one, a blade of grass, a leaf, clay, or anything else such as wood, cow dung, and so on. ‘Exhaustion’ means depletion.

“Padīpe (sārattha. ṭī. pācittiya 3.140) patitvā paṭaṅgādipāṇakā marissantī”ti jānantassāpi kusalacittena padīpujjalanaṃ viya “siñcanena pāṇakā marissantī”ti pubbabhāge jānantassāpi “idaṃ jalaṃ siñcāmī”ti siñcantassa vadhakacittaṃ na hotīti āha “vinā vadhakacetanāyā”tiādi. Evañca katvā “paṇṇattivajja”nti idampi samatthitaṃ hoti. Ticittanti kusalākusalābyākatavasena ticittaṃ. Tathā hi paṇṇattiṃ madditvā siñcantassa vā siñcāpentassa vā akusalacittena hoti, “āsanaṃ dhovissāmī”ti cittena dhovanatthaṃ siñcantassa vā siñcāpentassa vā kusalacittena hoti, paṇṇattiṃ ajānatā arahatā siñcanādikaraṇe abyākatacittena hotīti kusalākusalābyākatacittavasena ticittaṃ hoti.

Just as for one lighting a lamp with a wholesome mind, even while knowing that ‘insects such as moths will die by falling into it,’ so too, even if one knows beforehand that ‘living beings will die from the sprinkling,’ when one sprinkles with the thought, ‘I am sprinkling this water,’ there is no intention to kill. Thus it is said, ‘without the intention to kill,’ and so on. And by this, ‘an offense by designation’ is also supported. ‘Three minds’ refers to three minds by way of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate. For when one sprinkles or causes another to sprinkle, transgressing the designation, it is with an unwholesome mind. When one sprinkles or causes another to sprinkle for the purpose of washing, with the thought, ‘I will wash the seat,’ it is with a wholesome mind. When an Arahant, unaware of the designation, performs the act of sprinkling or the like, it is with an indeterminate mind. Thus, there are three minds by way of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.

Sappāṇakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning water with living beings is concluded.

Bhūtagāmavaggo dutiyo.

The Chapter on Plant Life, the Second.

3. Ovādavaggo

3. The Chapter on Admonition

1. Ovādasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Admonition

Aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgatassāti “sīlavā hotī”tiādīhi (pāci. 147) aṭṭhahi aṅgehi samannāgatassa. Anuññātāti imassa sikkhāpadassa nidāne anuññātā[M 0.0373]. “Vassasatūpasampannāyā”tiādi vakkhamānaaṭṭhagarudhammadassanaṃ. Tattha sāmīcikammanti maggasampadānabījanapānīyāpucchanādikaṃ anucchavikaṃ vattaṃ. Ādisaddena –

‘Of one endowed with eight factors’ means endowed with the eight factors beginning with ‘is virtuous,’ and so on. ‘Permitted’ refers to those permitted in the origin story of this training rule. ‘For one fully ordained for a hundred years,’ and so on, is the showing of the eight grave rules that will be described. Therein, ‘proper conduct’ refers to suitable duties such as providing requisites for a journey, asking about seeds and drinking water, and so on. By the word ‘etc.,’ –

“Na bhikkhuniyā abhikkhuke āvāse vassaṃ vasitabbaṃ, anvaddhamāsaṃ bhikkhuniyā bhikkhusaṅghato dve dhammā paccāsīsitabbā uposathapucchakañca ovādūpasaṅkamanañca, vassaṃvuṭṭhāya bhikkhuniyā ubhatosaṅghe tīhi ṭhānehi pavāretabbaṃ diṭṭhena [V 0.0342] vā sutena vā parisaṅkāya vā, garudhammaṃ ajjhāpannāya bhikkhuniyā ubhatosaṅghe pakkhamānattaṃ caritabbaṃ, dve vassāni chasu dhammesu sikkhitasikkhāya sikkhamānāya ubhatosaṅghe upasampadā pariyesitabbā, na bhikkhuniyā kenaci pariyāyena bhikkhu akkositabbo paribhāsitabbo, ajjatagge ovaṭo bhikkhunīnaṃ bhikkhūsu vacanapatho, anovaṭo bhikkhūnaṃ bhikkhunīsu vacanapatho”ti (cūḷava. 403; a. ni. 8.51) –

“A nun should not spend the Rains in a residence where there is no monk. Every half-month, a nun should expect two things from the Saṅgha of monks: to ask about the Uposatha day and to come for the exhortation. Having spent the Rains, a nun should invite pavāraṇā from both Saṅghas on three grounds: by what has been seen, by what has been heard, or by what is suspected. A nun who has transgressed a grave rule should undergo penance for half a month before both Saṅghas. A female probationer, having trained in the six rules for two years, should seek higher ordination from both Saṅghas. A nun should not in any way abuse or revile a monk. From today onward, the admonition of monks by nuns is forbidden; the admonition of nuns by monks is not forbidden.”

Ime satta dhamme saṅgaṇhāti. Garudhammeti garuke dhamme. Te hi gāravaṃ katvā bhikkhunīhi sampaṭicchitabbattā “garudhammā”ti vuccanti.

These seven qualities comprise the weighty rules. ‘Garudhamma’ means weighty rules. For they are called ‘garudhammā’ because they are to be respectfully accepted by nuns.

Aññena vā dhammenāti ṭhapetvā aṭṭha garudhamme aññena yena kenaci dhammena. Bhikkhunīsu upasampannamattaṃ vā ovadatoti bhikkhunīsu upasampannamattaṃ garudhammena ovadato vā. Bhikkhūnaṃ santike upasampannāya yathāvatthukameva. “Adhammakamme”tiādīsu bhikkhunovādasammutikammaṃ “kamma”nti veditabbanti āha “sammatassāpī”tiādi. Vagge bhikkhunisaṅghe ovadato tikapācittiyanti vagge bhikkhunisaṅghe ovadato vaggasaññivematikasamaggasaññīnaṃ vasena tīṇi pācittiyāni. Tathā vematikassa cāti adhammakamme vematikassa ca vagge bhikkhunisaṅghe ovadato tikapācittiyanti attho. Esa nayo dhammakammasaññino cāti etthāpi. Yathā ca vagge bhikkhunisaṅghe ovadato nava pācittiyāni, evaṃ adhammakamme adhammakammasaññino samagge bhikkhunisaṅghe ovadato tasmiṃ saṅghe vaggasaññivematikasamaggasaññīnaṃ vasena tikapācittiyaṃ, tathā vematikassa ca dhammakammasaññino cāti nava pācittiyāni. Tenāha “samaggepi bhikkhunisaṅghe navā”tiādi. Dhammakamme pana adhammakammasaññino vaggaṃ bhikkhunisaṅghaṃ ovadato [M 0.0374] tikadukkaṭaṃ, tathā vematikassa, dhammakammasaññino cāti nava dukkaṭāni. Samaggaṃ pana bhikkhunisaṅghaṃ ovadato aṭṭhāti sattarasa dukkaṭāni. Tenāha “sace panā”tiādi. Aññaṃ dhammanti aññaṃ suttantaṃ vā abhidhammaṃ vā. “Samaggāmhāyyā”ti vacanena hi ovādaṃ paccāsīsanti. Tasmā ṭhapetvā ovādaṃ aññaṃ dhammaṃ bhaṇantassa dukkaṭaṃ. Ovādañca aniyyātetvāti “eso bhagini ovādo”ti avatvā. Paripucchaṃ detīti tassāyeva paguṇāya garudhammapāḷiyā atthaṃ bhaṇati. Osārehīti uccārehi, kathehīti attho. Osāretīti aṭṭhagarudhammapāḷiṃ vadati. Pañhaṃ puṭṭhoti garudhammanissitaṃ vā khandhādinissitaṃ vā pañhaṃ bhikkhuniyā puṭṭho.

‘By another Dhamma’ means, apart from the eight weighty rules, by any other Dhamma. ‘Or admonishes those merely fully ordained among the nuns’ means admonishing those merely fully ordained among the nuns with the weighty rule. For one ordained in the presence of the monks, it is just as it is. In the case of ‘an unlawful act,’ etc., the act of a monk’s being authorized to admonish nuns is to be understood as ‘an act,’ as stated in ‘even of one authorized,’ etc. When admonishing a divided nuns' Saṅgha, there are three pācittiya offenses: for one perceiving a division, for one in doubt, and for one perceiving unity. Similarly, for one in doubt about an unlawful act, admonishing a divided nuns' Saṅgha results in three pācittiya offenses – this is the meaning. The same principle applies also to one perceiving a lawful act. Just as when admonishing a divided nuns' Saṅgha there are nine pācittiya offenses, so too when admonishing a united nuns' Saṅgha in an unlawful act, for one perceiving it as an unlawful act, there are three pācittiya offenses in that Saṅgha by way of perceiving division, doubt, and unity; likewise, for one in doubt and one perceiving it as a lawful act, there are nine pācittiya offenses. Hence it is said, ‘even in a united nuns' Saṅgha, nine,’ etc. However, in the case of a lawful act, when one perceiving it as unlawful admonishes a divided nuns' Saṅgha, there are three dukkaṭa offenses; similarly, for one in doubt, and one perceiving a lawful act, there are nine dukkaṭa offenses. However, when admonishing a united nuns' Saṅgha, there are eight—thus, seventeen dukkaṭa offenses. Hence it is said, ‘but if,’ etc. ‘Another Dhamma’ means another sutta or Abhidhamma. By the statement ‘we are unified, venerable sir,’ they anticipate admonishment. Therefore, apart from admonishment, speaking about another Dhamma incurs a dukkaṭa offense. ‘Without delivering the admonishment’ means without saying, ‘This, sister, is the admonishment.’ ‘Gives an explanation’ means explaining the meaning of that well-known passage on the weighty rules. ‘Osārehi’ means ‘utter,’ that is, ‘speak.’ ‘Osāreti’ means reciting the passage on the eight weighty rules. ‘Asked a question’ means being asked a question by a nun related to the weighty rules or related to the aggregates, etc.

Ovādasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Admonition is concluded.

2. Atthaṅgatasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Sunset

Ekatoupasampannanti [V 0.0343] bhikkhunisaṅghe upasampannamattaṃ. Ito parampi ca yattha yattha “ekatoupasampanna”nti vuccati, sabbattha ayameva attho daṭṭhabbo.

“Ordained on one side” means one who has received the full ordination only in the Nuns’ Saṅgha. And wherever else the term “ordained on one side” is mentioned, this same meaning should be understood.

Atthaṅgatasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Sunset is concluded.

3. Bhikkhunupassayasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Nuns’ Residences

Saṃvāsāyāti uposathādiatthaṃ. Itaranti ubhatosaṅghe upasampannaṃ.

“For communion” means for the purpose of Uposatha and so forth. “The other” refers to one fully ordained in both Saṅghas.

Bhikkhunupassayasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Nuns’ Residences is concluded.

4. Āmisasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Material Gain

Taṇhādiṭṭhīhi āmasitabbato āmisaṃ, cīvarādi, āmisameva hetu āmisahetu. Tenāha “cīvarādīnaṃ aññatarahetū”ti. Ādisaddena piṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayasakkāragarukāramānanavandanapūjanānaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Avaṇṇakāmatāyāti ayasakāmatāyeva.

“Āmisa” refers to what is to be grasped by craving and wrong views, such as robes and so forth. Material gain itself is the cause, hence “āmisahetu” (a cause of material gain). Therefore, it is said, “a cause for one or another of such things as robes.” The word “ādi” (and so forth) includes almsfood, dwelling places, medicinal requisites, honor, respect, reverence, salutation, and veneration. “Avaṇṇakāmatā” means simply the desire for dispraise.

Dhammakammetiādīsu [M 0.0375] bhikkhunovādasammutikammaṃ “kamma”nti veditabbaṃ. Tattha tikapācittiyanti dhammakamme dhammakammasaññivematikaadhammakammasaññīnaṃ vasena tīṇi pācittiyāni. Tatheva adhammakamme tikadukkaṭaṃ veditabbaṃ. Asammatanti sammatena vā saṅghena vā bhāraṃ katvā ṭhapitaṃ upasampannaṃ. Nanu ovādasammuti upasampannasseva dīyati, na sāmaṇerassāti āha “tatthā”tiādi. Sammatena vā saṅghena vā ṭhapito pana bahussuto sāmaṇero “asammato”ti veditabbo. Pakatiyā cīvarādihetu ovadantaṃ pana evaṃ bhaṇantassāti pakatiyā cīvarādihetu ovadantaṃ “esa cīvarādihetu ovadatī”ti saññāya evaṃ bhaṇantassa. “Na cīvarādihetu ovadatī”ti saññāya pana evaṃ bhaṇantassa dukkaṭaṃ. Anāmisantaratāti āmisacittābhāvo, “āmisahetu ovadissāmī”ti evaṃ pavattaajjhāsayābhāvoti attho. Cittapariyāyo hettha antarasaddo “yassantarato na santi kopā”tiādīsu (udā. 20) viya.

In matters such as a lawful act, the formal act of authorizing the admonition of nuns is to be understood as a “kamma.” Here, in the case of a lawful act, there are three pācittiya offenses: for one who perceives it as a lawful act, who is doubtful, or who perceives it as an unlawful act. Similarly, in an unlawful act, three dukkaṭa offenses should be understood. “Unappointed” refers to a fully ordained monk who has been set aside from this duty by an appointed individual or by the Saṅgha. But isn’t the authorization to admonish given only to the fully ordained, not to a novice? To this, it is said, “in that regard,” etc. However, a learned novice who has been appointed by an authorized individual or by the Saṅgha is to be understood as “unappointed.” As for one who admonishes for the usual reasons, such as for robes, etc., and speaks thus, it means for one who admonishes for the usual reasons, such as for robes, etc., and speaks thus with the perception, “He admonishes for the sake of robes, etc.” But if one speaks thus with the perception, “He does not admonish for the sake of robes, etc.,” then it is a dukkaṭa offense. “Without material motives” means the absence of a mind set on material gain—that is, the absence of the intention, “I will admonish for material gain.” Here, the term “antara” (inner) refers to the state of mind, as in the phrase, “in whom there are no inner angers,” etc.

Āmisasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Material Gain is concluded.

5. Cīvaradānasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

5. Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning the Giving of Robes

Pañcamasikkhāpadaṃ [V 0.0344] uttānatthameva.

The fifth training rule is self-explanatory.

Cīvaradānasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning the Giving of Robes is concluded.

6. Cīvarasibbanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Robe-Sewing

Sūciṃ pavesetvā pavesetvā nīharaṇeti ārāpathe ārāpathe pācittiyaṃ. “Sibbissāmī”ti pana vicārentassa, chindantassāpi dukkaṭaṃ. Satakkhattumpi vijjhitvā sakiṃ nīharantassāti sakalasūciṃ anīharanto dīghasuttappavesanatthaṃ satakkhattumpi vijjhitvā sakiṃ nīharantassa. “Sibbā”ti vuttoti sakiṃ “cīvaraṃ sibbā”ti vutto. Niṭṭhāpetīti sabbaṃ sūcikammaṃ pariyosāpeti. Tassa ārāpathe ārāpathe pācittiyanti āṇattassa sūciṃ pavesetvā pavesetvā nīharaṇe ekamekaṃ pācittiyaṃ.

Inserting and withdrawing the needle repeatedly—this is a pācittiya offense for each stitch. For one who deliberates, thinking, “I will sew,” or for one who cuts the cloth, it is a dukkaṭa offense. “Even if one pierces a hundred times but withdraws only once”—this means not withdrawing the entire needle, but piercing a hundred times and withdrawing only once for the purpose of inserting a long thread. “When told, ‘Sew’” means when told once, “Sew the robe.” “Completes” means finishing all the needlework. “For each stitch, a pācittiya offense”—this means that for each act of inserting and withdrawing the needle by one who has been instructed, each is a separate pācittiya offense.

Udāyittheranti [M 0.0376] lāḷudāyittheraṃ. Vuttalakkhaṇaṃ sibbanaṃ vā sibbāpanaṃ vāti “sūciṃ pavesetvā”tiādinā vuttalakkhaṇaṃ sibbanaṃ vā sibbāpanaṃ vā.

“The Elder Udāyī” refers to the Elder Lāḷudāyī. “Sewing or causing to sew of the stated characteristic” means sewing or causing to sew of the characteristic stated by “having inserted the needle,” and so forth.

Cīvarasibbanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Robe-Sewing is concluded.

7. Saṃvidhānasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

7. Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Agreements

Saṃvidahitvāti “ehi, asukagāmaṃ gacchāmā”ti vā “sve ahaṃ gacchāmi, tvampi āgaccheyyāsī”ti vā vatvā. Tañca kho saṃvidahanaṃ atthato saṅketakammanti āha “gamanakāle saṅketaṃ katvāti attho”ti. Akappiyabhūmiyaṃ saṃvidahantassāti antogāme, bhikkhuniupassayadvāre, rathikāya, aññesu vā catukkasiṅghāṭakahatthisālādīsu ṭhatvā saṃvidahantassa. Tenāha “tattha ṭhapetvā”tiādi. Āsannassāpīti accāsannassāpi, ratanamattantarassāpīti adhippāyo. Aññassa gāmassāti yato nikkhamati, tato aññassa gāmassa. Taṃ okkamantassāti taṃ antaragāmassa upacāraṃ okkamantassa. Sace dūraṃ gantukāmo hoti, gāmūpacāragaṇanāya okkamante okkamante purimanayeneva āpatti. Tenāha “iti gāmūpacārokkamanagaṇanāya pācittiyānī”ti. Tassa tassa pana gāmassa atikkamane anāpatti. Gāme asatīti addhayojanabbhantare gāme asati. Tasmiṃ pana gāme sati gāmantaragaṇanāyeva [V 0.0345] pācittiyāni. Addhayojanagaṇanāya pācittiyanti addhayojane addhayojane pācittiyaṃ, ekamekaṃ addhayojanaṃ atikkamantassa “idāni atikkamissāmī”ti paṭhamapāde dukkaṭaṃ, dutiyapāde pācittiyanti attho. Imasmiñhi naye atikkamane āpatti, okkamane anāpatti.

“Having agreed upon,” means saying, “Come, let us go to such-and-such village,” or “Tomorrow I will go, you should come too.” That agreement, in essence, is a matter of arrangement, as stated: “The meaning is, having made an arrangement regarding the time of going.” For one who agrees upon in an improper place—standing inside a village, at the gate of a bhikkhunī's residence, on a street, or in other places like a crossroads, elephant stables, and so on. Therefore it is said, “excluding those places,” etc. “Even if very near” means even if extremely close; the intention is, even if at a distance of only a jewel's measure. “To another village” means from where one departs, to another village. “When entering that” means when entering the boundary of that intermediate village. If one wishes to go far, by repeatedly entering the boundaries of villages, offenses arise as before. Hence it is said, “Thus, by the counting of entering village boundaries, there are pācittiya offenses.” However, when passing beyond each village, there is no offense. “When no village is present” means when no village exists within a half-yojana’s distance. But if a village is present within that, then counting intermediate villages results in pācittiya offenses. “Counting by half-yojanas results in pācittiya offenses” means for each half-yojana, a pācittiya offense. For one passing beyond each half-yojana, thinking, “Now I will pass it,” at the first step, a dukkaṭa offense; at the second step, a pācittiya offense—this is the meaning. In this case, an offense arises when passing beyond, but no offense when entering.

Visaṅketenāti (pāci. aṭṭha. 185) ettha “purebhattaṃ gamissāmā”ti vatvā pacchābhattaṃ gacchanti, “ajja vā gamissāmā”ti sve gacchanti, evaṃ kālavisaṅketeyeva anāpatti. Dvāravisaṅkete, pana maggavisaṅkete, vā satipi āpattiyeva. Āpadāsūti raṭṭhabhede cakkasamāruḷhā jānapadā pariyāyanti, evarūpāsu āpadāsu anāpatti. Cakkasamāruḷhāti ca iriyāpathacakkaṃ vā sakaṭacakkaṃ vā [M 0.0377] samāruḷhāti attho. Mātugāmasikkhāpadenāti (pāci. 413 ādayo) sappāṇakavagge sattamasikkhāpadena.

“By a change in the arrangement” (Pācittiya Aṭṭhakathā 185): Here, if one says, “We will go before the meal,” but they go after the meal, or says, “We will go today,” but they go tomorrow—in such a case of a change in the time of the arrangement, there is no offense. However, if there is a change in the arrangement regarding the door or the path, there is an offense. “In emergencies”: In times of national disorder when villagers travel mounted on wheels—in such emergencies, there is no offense. “Mounted on wheels” means mounted either on the 'wheel' of walking or a cartwheel. “By the training rule concerning a woman” (Pācittiya 413, etc.) refers to the seventh training rule in the Sappāṇaka group.

Saṃvidhānasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning arrangements is concluded.

8. Nāvābhiruhanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

8. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Embarking on a Boat

Kīḷāpurekkhāroti lokassādamittasanthavavasena kīḷāpurekkhāro. Tathevāti kīḷāvaseneva. Agāmakatīrapassenāti addhayojanabbhantare gāmānaṃ abhāvato agāmakatīrapassena. Pāḷiyaṃ “uddhaṃgāminiṃ vā adhogāminiṃ vā”ti (pāci. 186) vacanato pana vāpisamuddādīsu kīḷāpurekkhāratāyapi gacchantassa anāpatti. Tenāha “samudde pana yathāsukhaṃ gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Visaṅketenāti idhāpi kālavisaṅketeneva anāpatti, titthavisaṅketena, pana nāvāvisaṅketena vā gacchantassa āpattiyeva.

“Intent on amusement” means intent on amusement by way of the world’s delight and friendly association. “Similarly” means just for the sake of amusement. “On the shore without villages” means on the shore without villages due to the absence of villages within half a yojana. However, according to the Pāli text, “whether going upstream or downstream” (Pāc. 186), there is no offense even for one going to places like reservoirs or the sea with amusement as the primary intention. Therefore, it is said, “But at sea, it is permissible to go as one pleases.” “By a change in the arrangement”—here too, there is no offense only in the case of a change in the time of the arrangement; but for one who goes with a change in the arrangement regarding the ford or the boat, there is an offense.

Sesanti saddhiṃ samuṭṭhānādīhi avasesaṃ, keci pana “kīḷāpurekkhāro ‘saṃvidahitvā’ti (sārattha. ṭī. pācittiya 3.188) vacanato imaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ akusalacittaṃ lokavajjaṃ, tasmā sesaṃ nāma ṭhapetvā ‘paṇṇattivajjaṃ ticitta’nti idaṃ dvayaṃ avasesa”nti vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Kīḷāpurekkhāratāya hi abhiruhitvāpi gāmantarokkamane, addhayojanātikkame vā saṃvegaṃ paṭilabhitvā arahattaṃ vā sacchikareyya, niddaṃ vā okkameyya, kammaṭṭhānaṃ vā manasi karonto gaccheyya, kuto cassa akusalacittasamaṅgitā, yenidaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ akusalacittaṃ, lokavajjañca siyāti.

“The rest” means the remainder along with the origins and so forth. Some, however, say, “Because this training rule, [which is about] being intent on amusement, [is stated as] ‘having arranged beforehand’ (Sāratthadīpanī, Pācittiya 3.188), it involves an unwholesome mind and is blameworthy in the world; therefore, setting aside the term ‘the rest,’ what remains refers to ‘an offense by regulation’ and ‘the threefold mind.’” This should not be accepted. For even if one embarks with amusement as the primary intention, one might, while entering another village or exceeding half a yojana, gain a sense of spiritual urgency and realize arahantship, or fall asleep, or go while attending to a meditation subject. How then could there be association with an unwholesome mind, such that this training rule would involve an unwholesome mind and be blameworthy in the world?

Nāvābhiruhanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Embarking on a Boat is concluded.

9. Paripācitasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

9. The Explanation of the Training Rule concerning What Has Been Prepared

Paripācitanti [V 0.0346] paripākamāpāditaṃ, yathā labhati, tathā katvā ṭhapitanti vuttaṃ hoti. Tenāha “neva tassā”tiādi tassāti yo paribhuñjeyya, tassa bhikkhuno. Bhikkhussa guṇaṃ pakāsetvāti “ayyo bhāṇako, ayyo bahussuto”tiādinā (pāci. 195) guṇaṃ pakāsetvā[M 0.0378]. Piṇḍapātanti pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ aññataraṃ. Kammasādhanoyaṃ samārambhasaddoti āha “samāraddha”nti. Paṭiyāditassāti sampāditassa. Yasmā ñātakappavāritehi bhikkhussa atthāya asamāraddhopi piṇḍapāto atthato samāraddhova hoti yathāsukhaṃ harāpetabbato, tasmā “ñātakappavāritānaṃ vā santaka”nti vuttaṃ.

“Prepared” means brought to a state of readiness; it means it has been made and set aside so that he may receive it. Therefore, it is said, “not for him,” and so forth. “For him” refers to the monk who would partake of it. “Having proclaimed the monk’s virtue” means proclaiming his qualities such as, “This venerable is a reciter, this venerable is learned,” and so forth (Pācittiya 195). “Almsfood” refers to any one of the five kinds of food. This word “samārambha” (undertaking) denotes the accomplishment of an action, thus it is said, “has been undertaken.” “Of what has been prepared” means of what has been made ready. Because even almsfood not specifically undertaken for a monk by relatives or those who have made an invitation is, in effect, considered as undertaken, as it can be brought at will, therefore it is said, “or what belongs to relatives or those who have made an invitation.”

Ubhayatthāti paripācitāparipācitesu. Avaseseti bhikkhuniparipācitepi yāgukhajjakaphalāphalādike sabbattha. Nimittobhāsaparikathāviññattivasena pana avasesepi dukkaṭato na muccati.

“In both cases” refers to what has been prepared and what has not been prepared. “In the remaining cases” means in all cases, including rice gruel, hard food, fruits, and so on, even when prepared by a bhikkhunī. However, in the remaining cases, one is not exempt from a dukkaṭa offense if it is obtained through making signs, hinting, speaking indirectly, or making an intimation.

Paripācitasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule concerning What Has Been Prepared is concluded.

10. Rahonisajjasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

10. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Sitting in Private

Uparīti acelakavagge. Upanandassa catutthasikkhāpadenāti appaṭicchanne mātugāmena saddhiṃ rahonisajjasikkhāpadena (pāci. 284 ādayo). Tañhi upanandattheraṃ ārabbha paññattesu catutthabhāvato “upanandassa catutthasikkhāpada”nti vuttaṃ. Yadi ekaparicchedaṃ, atha kasmā visuṃ paññattanti āha “aṭṭhuppattivasena pana visuṃ paññatta”nti. Tattha aṭṭhuppattivasenāti atthassa uppattivasena, bhikkhuniyā eva rahonisajjāya uppattivasenāti attho. Ayaṃ hetthādhippāyo – catutthasikkhāpadavatthuto imassa sikkhāpadassa vatthuno paṭhamaṃ uppannattā ekaparicchedepi idaṃ paṭhamaṃ visuṃ paññattanti.

“Above” refers to the Acelakavagga. “By Upananda’s fourth training rule” refers to the training rule on sitting in private with a woman in an unscreened place (Pācittiya 284 and so forth). Indeed, because it is the fourth among those rules laid down concerning the Elder Upananda, it is called “Upananda’s fourth training rule.” If it is a single section, then why was it laid down separately? It is said, “But because of the arising of the occasion, it was laid down separately.” Here, “because of the arising of the occasion” means due to the arising of the matter—that is, the arising of the private sitting with a bhikkhunī. This is the underlying intention here: because the occasion for this training rule arose before the occasion for the fourth training rule, this was laid down separately first, even though they are a single section.

Rahonisajjasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Sitting in Private is concluded.

Ovādavaggo tatiyo.

The Third Chapter: On Advice

4. Bhojanavaggo

4. The Chapter on Food

1. Āvasathasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. The Explanation of the Training Rule on a Guesthouse

“Agilāno”ti [V 0.0347] ettha antamaso dvigāvutaṃ gantuṃ samattho adhippetoti āha “addhayojanampi gantuṃ samatthenā”ti. Āvasathapiṇḍoti [M 0.0379] āvasathe piṇḍo, sālādīsu anodissa yāvadatthaṃ paññattaṃ pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ aññataraṃ bhojananti attho. Tenāha “imesaṃ vā”tiādi. Tattha imesaṃ vāti imesaṃ pāsaṇḍānaṃ vā. Ettakānaṃ vāti imasmiṃ pāsaṇḍe ettakānaṃ pāsaṇḍānaṃ vā. Pāsaṇḍanti channavutividhaṃ samaṇaparibbājakādiṃ. Te hi taṇhāpāsañceva diṭṭhipāsañca ḍenti oḍḍentīti pāsaṇḍāti vuccanti. Anodissāti anuddisitvā, aparicchinditvāti attho. Sālādīsu yattha katthacīti sālārukkhamūlaabbhokāsādīsu yattha katthaci ṭhānesu. Ekadivasameva bhuñjitabboti ekadivasaṃ sakiṃyeva bhuñjitabbo, ekasmiṃ divase punappunaṃ bhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭati. Dutiyadivasato paṭṭhāyāti bhuttadivasassa dutiyadivasato paṭṭhāya. Ajjhohāre ajjhohāre pācittiyanti ālope ālope kabaḷe kabaḷe pācittiyaṃ. Nānākulehi (pāci. aṭṭha. 206) pana nānāṭṭhānesu paññattaṃ, ekasmiṃ ṭhāne ekadivasaṃ bhuñjitvā dutiyadivase aññattha bhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati, paṭipāṭiṃ pana khepetvā puna ādito paṭṭhāya bhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭati. Ekapūganānāpūgaekagāmanānāgāmesupi eseva nayo. Yopi ekakulassa vā nānākulānaṃ vā ekato paññatto taṇḍulādīnaṃ abhāvena antarantarā chijjati, sopi na bhuñjitabbo. Sace pana “na sakkoma dātu”nti upacchinditvā puna kalyāṇacitte uppanne dātuṃ ārabhanti, etaṃ puna ekadivasaṃ bhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati.

“Not sick” here means one who is capable of walking at least two gāvutas, as is intended. Thus it is said, “by one capable of walking even half a yojana.” “Lodging alms” means alms at a lodging place, that is, any one of the five kinds of food offered without specific designation in halls and so forth, according to need. Hence it is said, “or of these,” and so forth. Here, “or of these” means “or of these sectarians.” “Or of so many” means “or of so many sectarians in this sect.” “Sectarians” refers to the ninety-six kinds of ascetics, wanderers, and so forth. They are called “sectarians” because they ensnare and entrap with the snares of craving and views. “Without specific designation” means without designating or specifying. “In halls and so forth, wherever” means in places such as halls, the roots of trees, open spaces, and so forth, wherever. “Should be eaten only for one day” means it should be eaten only once on one day; it is not permissible to eat repeatedly on the same day. “Starting from the second day” means starting from the second day after the day it was eaten. “For every mouthful, a pācittiya” means a pācittiya offense for every mouthful or morsel. However, regarding what is offered in various places by various families (Pācittiya Aṭṭhakathā 206), having eaten at one place for one day, it is permissible to eat elsewhere the next day; but it is not permissible, having exhausted the sequence, to start eating again from the beginning. The same principle applies to one group or many groups, one village or many villages. Also, food that is offered collectively to one family or to many families but is interrupted from time to time due to the lack of rice and so forth, should not be eaten. But if the donors discontinue it, saying, “We are unable to give,” and then, when a good intention arises again, they start to give, this may be eaten for one more day.

Tikapācittiyanti agilāne agilānasaññivematikagilānasaññīnaṃ vasena tīṇi pācittiyāni. Gilānassa gilānasaññinoti gilānassa pana “gilāno aha”nti saññino anuvasitvā bhuñjantassa anāpatti. Sakiṃ bhuñjatīti ekadivasaṃ bhuñjati. “Gacchanto vā”ti idaṃ addhayojanavasena gahetabbaṃ, tathā “paccāgacchanto”ti (sārattha. ṭī. pācittiya 3.208) idampīti vadanti. Kenaci upaddavenāti nadipūracorabhayādinā kenaci upaddavena. Aññanti yāgukhajjakaphalāphalādibhedaṃ yaṃ kiñci aññaṃ. Anuvasitvāti puna vasitvā.

“Three pācittiyas” means there are three pācittiya offenses for a person who is not ill: when he perceives himself as not ill, when he is uncertain, and when he perceives himself as ill. “For an ill person who perceives himself as ill” means there is no offense for an ill person who, perceiving “I am ill,” eats after having stayed overnight. “Eats once” means eats for one day. “Or going” should be understood as referring to a distance of half a yojana, and they say that “or returning” (Sāratthadīpanī, Pācittiya 3.208) is also to be understood in this way. “By any danger” means by any danger such as a flood or the fear of thieves. “Other” refers to any other kind, such as rice gruel, hard food, fruits, and so on. “Having stayed overnight” means having stayed again.

Āvasathasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Lodging is concluded.

2. Gaṇabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Group Meals

Gaṇabhojaneti [M 0.0380][V 0.0348] gaṇena laddhattā gaṇassa santake bhojane. Tenāha “gaṇassa bhojane”ti. Nanu cettha “gaṇassa bhojane”ti vuccati, so ca kho gaṇo “katthaci dvīhi, katthaci tīhī”tiādinā anekadhā adhippeto, idha katihīti āha “idha cā”tiādi. Taṃ panetaṃ gaṇabhojanaṃ dvīhi pakārehi pasavati nimantanato vā viññattito vāti āha “tesaṃ nimantanato vā”tiādi. Tattha nimantanato vāti akappiyanimantanato vā. Odanādīnaṃ pañcannanti odanasattukummāsamacchamaṃsānaṃ pañcannaṃ.

Gaṇabhojana means a meal obtained by a group, belonging to a group. Therefore, it is said, “a meal for the group.” Now, when “a meal for the group” is said here, that group is understood in various ways, such as “sometimes two, sometimes three,” and so on. Here, as to how many are meant, he says, “Here, moreover…” and so on. Furthermore, this group meal arises in two ways: either through invitation or through solicitation. Thus he says, “either through their invitation…” and so on. Here, “through invitation” means through an improper invitation. “Of the five, such as rice” refers to the five: rice, parched grain meal, gruel, fish, and meat.

“Odanena nimantemi, odanaṃ me gaṇhathā”tiādinā nayena yena kenaci vevacanena vā bhāsantarena vā pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ nāmaṃ gahetvā nimantetīti sambandho. Cattāroti ekaṭṭhāne vā nānāṭṭhānesu vā ṭhite cattāro bhikkhū. Lakkhaṇavacanañcetaṃ, tasmā cattāro vā tato vā adhike bhikkhūti attho. Vevacanena vāti bhattaannādipariyāyasaddena vā. Bhāsantarena vāti andhadamiḷādibhāsantarena vā. Pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ nāmaṃ gahetvāti pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ aññatarassa nāmaṃ gahetvā. Odanena nimantemīti tumhe bhante odanena nimantemi. Ādisaddena “ākaṅkhatha oloketha adhivāsetha paṭimānetha, sattunā nimantemi, sattuṃ me gaṇhatha ākaṅkhatha oloketha adhivāsetha paṭimānethā”tiādīnaṃ (pāci. aṭṭha. 217-218) gahaṇaṃ. Ekato vāti ekattha ṭhite vā nisinne vā bhikkhū disvā “tumhe, bhante, odanena nimantemī”tiādinā evaṃ ekato nimantitā. Nānāto vā nimantitāti cattāri pariveṇāni vā vihāre vā gantvā nānāto vā nimantitā. Ekaṭṭhāne ṭhitesuyeva vā eko puttena, eko pitarāti evampi nimantitā nānātoyeva nimantitā nāma honti. Ekato gaṇhantiti aññamaññassa dvādasahatthūpacāre ṭhitā gaṇhanti.

The connection is that one invites by taking the name of one of the five kinds of food, using any synonymous term or different language, in the manner of “I invite you with rice; please accept my rice,” and so on. “Four” means four bhikkhus staying in one place or in different places. This is a descriptive term; therefore, the meaning is four bhikkhus or more. “By a synonym” means by a synonymous term such as “food” (bhatta) or “meal” (anna), and so on. “By a different language” means by a different language such as Andha or Damiḷa, and so on. “Taking the name of the five kinds of food” means taking the name of any one of the five kinds of food. “I invite you with rice” means “Venerable sirs, I invite you with rice.” The term “etc.” includes the phrases “desire, look, accept, partake,” “I invite you with parched grain meal; please accept my parched grain meal, desire, look, accept, partake,” and so on (Pācittiya Aṭṭhakathā 217–218). “Together” means, having seen bhikkhus staying or sitting in one place, they are invited together in this way with “Venerable sirs, I invite you with rice,” and so on. “Or invited separately” means having gone to four enclosures or monasteries and inviting them separately. Or even if they are staying in one place, if one is invited by a son and another by a father, they are still considered to have been invited separately. “Taking together” means they take it standing within twelve handspans of each other.

Kasmā pana nānāto bhuttepi gaṇabhojanaṃ hotīti āha “paṭiggahaṇameva hettha pamāṇa”nti. Yadi evaṃ atha kasmā pāḷiyaṃ “gaṇabhojanaṃ nāma yattha cattāro bhikkhū pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ aññatarena bhojanena nimantitā bhuñjanti, etaṃ gaṇabhojanaṃ nāmā”ti (pāci. 218) vuttaṃ? Taṃ paṭiggahaṇaniyamanatthameva[M 0.0381]. Na hi appaṭiggahitakaṃ bhikkhū bhuñjantīti “bhuñjantī”ti padaṃ paṭiggahaṇaniyamavacanaṃ hoti. Ekato vā nānāto vā viññāpetvāti cattāro bhikkhū ekato ṭhitā vā nisinnā vā upāsakaṃ disvā “amhākaṃ catunnampi bhattaṃ dehī”ti vā pāṭekkaṃ pavisitvā “mayhaṃ bhattaṃ dehi, mayhaṃ bhattaṃ dehī”ti vā ekato vā nānāto [V 0.0349] vā viññāpetvā. Tassa duvidhassāpīti yañca nimantanato laddhaṃ gaṇabhojanaṃ, yañca viññattito laddhaṃ, tassa duvidhassāpi gaṇabhojanassa. Evaṃ paṭiggahaṇeti ekato paṭiggahaṇe.

But why is it a group meal even when eaten separately? He said, “The act of receiving is the measure here.” If so, then why is it stated in the Pāli, “A group meal is when four bhikkhus, invited with any one of the five kinds of food, eat; this is called a group meal” (Pāc. 218)? That is just to establish the rule regarding receiving. For bhikkhus do not eat what has not been received; thus the word “eat” is a term that regulates receiving. “Having requested together or separately” means whether four bhikkhus, standing or sitting together, see a lay follower and say, “Give food to all four of us,” or whether they enter individually and say, “Give me food, give me food,” having requested together or separately. “Of these two kinds” refers to both kinds of group meal: that which is obtained through an invitation, and that which is obtained through a request. “In receiving thus” means in receiving together.

Pādānampi phalitattāti (pāci. aṭṭha. 217-218) antamaso pādānampi yathā mahācammassa parato maṃsaṃ dissati, evaṃ phalitattā. Na sakkā piṇḍāya caritunti vālikāya vā sakkharāya vā phuṭṭhamatte dukkhuppattito antogāme piṇḍāya carituṃ na sakkoti. Cīvare kariyamāneti sāṭakañca suttañca labhitvā cīvare kariyamāne. Yaṃ kiñci cīvare kattabbakammanti cīvaravicāraṇachindanamoghasuttāropanādi yaṃ kiñci cīvare kattabbaṃ kammaṃ, antamaso sūcivedhanampīti adhippāyo. “Addhayojanampī”tiādi avakaṃsato vuttaṃ. Yo pana dūraṃ gantukāmo, tattha vattabbameva natthi, gacchanto addhayojanabbhantare gāvutepi bhuñjituṃ labhati, gato pana ekadivasaṃ. Yadā nāvaṃ abhiruhitukāmo vā hoti āruḷho vā oruḷho vā, ayaṃ nāvābhiruhanasamayo nāmāti āha “nāvābhiruhanasamayepi eseva nayo”ti. Ayaṃ pana viseso – abhiruḷhena icchitaṭṭhānaṃ gantvāpi yāva na orohati, tāva bhuñjitabbaṃ. Cattāro bhikkhūti antimaparicchedo. Yattha pana sataṃ vā sahassaṃ vā sannipatitaṃ, tattha vattabbameva natthi. Tasmā tādise kāle “mahāsamayo”ti adhiṭṭhahitvā bhuñjitabbaṃ. Yo koci pabbajitoti sahadhammikesu vā titthiyesu vā aññataro.

'Even the feet being blistered' (Pācittiya Aṭṭhakathā 217–218) means that even the feet are blistered, just as flesh is visible on the outside of a large hide. 'It is not possible to go for alms' means that due to the arising of suffering from merely touching sand or gravel, one cannot go for alms within the village. 'While the robe is being made' refers to when the robe is being made, having obtained both the cloth and the thread. 'Whatever work is to be done on the robe' means any work to be done on the robe, such as examining the robe, cutting it, applying a temporary thread, and so on; the intention is even piercing with a needle. 'Even half a yojana' and so on are said by way of concession. For one who wishes to go far, there is no need to mention it; while going, one may eat even within half a yojana or a gāvuta, but once one has gone a full day. When one wishes to board a boat, or has boarded, or has disembarked, this is called 'the time of boarding a boat.' Thus he says, 'The same principle applies to the time of boarding a boat.' Here, however, there is a distinction: having boarded, even after reaching the desired place, one may eat until one disembarks. 'Four bhikkhus' refers to the minimum number. But where a hundred or a thousand have gathered, there is no need to mention it. Therefore, on such occasions, one should determine it to be 'a great gathering' and then eat. 'Any ascetic' means any one among co-religionists or sectarians.

Ye ca dve tayo ekato gaṇhantīti yepi akappiyanimantanaṃ sādiyitvā dve vā tayo vā ekato gaṇhanti, tesampi anāpatti. Paṇītabhojanasūpodanaviññattīhi pana āpattiyevāti vadanti, upaparikkhitabbaṃ. Niccabhattādīsūti niccabhatte salākabhatte pakkhike uposathike pāṭipadike. Tattha niccabhattanti dhuvabhattaṃ vuccati. “Niccabhattaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vadanti[M 0.0382], bahūnampi ekato gaṇhituṃ vaṭṭati. Salākabhattādīsupi eseva nayo.

'Those who take two or three together' means even those who, having approved of an improper invitation, take two or three together—for them too, there is no offense. However, they say there is an offense with regard to requesting delicious food, soup, or rice. This should be investigated. 'Regarding regular meals, etc.' refers to regular meals, ticket meals, fortnightly meals, Uposatha meals, and Pāṭipadika meals. There, 'regular meal' means a fixed meal. They say, 'Take the regular meal,' and it is allowable for many to take it together. The same principle applies to ticket meals and the others.

Gaṇabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on group meals is completed.

3. Paramparabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Consecutive Meals.

Gaṇabhojane vuttanayenevāti bhikkhuṃ upasaṅkamitvā “tumhe, bhante, odanena nimantemi, odanaṃ me gaṇhathā”tiādinā (pāci. aṭṭha. 217-218) nayena yena kenaci vevacanena vā bhāsantarena vā pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ aññatarassa nāmaṃ gahetvā nimantetīti vutteneva nayena[V 0.0350]. Nimantitassāti akappiyanimantanena nimantitassa. Avikappetvāti sammukhāsammukhavasena avikappetvā, apariccajitvāti attho. Ayañhi bhattavikappanā nāma sammukhāparammukhāpi vaṭṭati. Tenāha “yo bhikkhu pañcasu sahadhammikesū”tiādi.

‘Just as it was said in the case of communal meals,’ approaching a bhikkhu and saying, ‘Venerable sir, I invite you for rice; please accept my rice,’ and so on (Pācittiya Aṭṭhakathā 217-218), in whatever manner or with whatever different expression, by mentioning the name of any one of the five kinds of food, the invitation is made—this is the method described. ‘To one who has been invited’ means to one who has been invited by an unallowable invitation. ‘Without refusing’ means without refusing whether face to face or not face to face, that is, without relinquishing. For this refusal of food is valid whether face to face or not face to face. Therefore it is said: ‘If a bhikkhu among five fellow practitioners,’ and so on.

Aññatra nimantanabhojanavatthusminti aññatra paṭhamaṃ nimantitā hutvā aññasmiṃ nimantane bhuñjanavatthusmiṃ. Yadi tividhā anupaññatti, atha kasmā parivāre “catasso anupaññattiyo”ti vuttanti āha “parivāre panā”tiādi. Vikappanampi gahetvāti vikappanānujānanampi anupaññattisamānanti anupaññattibhāvena gahetvā. Ekasaṃsaṭṭhānīti ekasmiṃ missitāni. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti (pāci. aṭṭha. 229) – dve tīṇi kulāni nimantetvā ekasmiṃ ṭhāne nisīdāpetvā ito cito ca āharitvā bhattaṃ ākiranti, sūpabyañjanaṃ ākiranti, ekamissakaṃ hoti, ettha anāpattīti. Sace pana mūlanimantanaṃ heṭṭhā hoti, pacchimaṃ pacchimaṃ upari, taṃ uparito paṭṭhāya bhuñjantassa āpatti. Hatthaṃ pana anto pavesetvā paṭhamanimantanato ekampi kabaḷaṃ uddharitvā bhuttakālato paṭṭhāya yathā tathā vā bhuñjantassa anāpatti. Dve tīṇi nimantanāni ekato vā katvā bhuñjatīti dve tīṇi nimantanāni ekato pakkhipitvā missetvā ekaṃ katvā bhuñjatīti attho. “Sakalena gāmena vā”tiādīsu sakalena gāmena ekato hutvā nimantitasseva yattha katthaci bhuñjato anāpatti. Pūgepi eseva nayo. Nimantiyamāno vā “bhikkhaṃ gahessāmī”ti vadatīti “bhattaṃ gaṇhā”ti nimantiyamāno [M 0.0383] “na mayhaṃ tava bhattena attho, bhikkhaṃ gahessāmī”ti bhaṇati. Kiriyākiriyanti ettha bhojanaṃ kiriyaṃ, avikappanaṃ akiriyaṃ.

‘Except in the case of an invited meal’ means except in the case of having been invited first and then eating at another invitation. If there are three kinds of subsequent enactments, then why is it said in the Parivāra, ‘There are four subsequent enactments’? He says, ‘But in the Parivāra,’ and so on. ‘Even the refusal is included’ means that the authorization of refusal is also similar to a subsequent enactment, thus it is included as a subsequent enactment. ‘Mixed together’ means combined into one. This is what is meant (Pācittiya Aṭṭhakathā 229): Having invited two or three families, seating them together in one place, they bring food from here and there and serve it, they serve sauces and curries—it becomes a single mixture. In this case, there is no offense. But if the original invitation is at the bottom and the later ones are above, then eating from the top onward incurs an offense. However, if one inserts the hand inside and, after taking even a single morsel from the first invitation, from the time of having eaten, eats in any way, there is no offense. ‘Eating after combining two or three invitations’ means mixing two or three invitations together into one and then eating—this is the meaning. In the case of ‘the entire village,’ and so on, if one is invited by the whole village together, there is no offense wherever one eats. The same principle applies to a guild. ‘Or if, while being invited, one says, “I will take alms”’ means, when invited to a meal, one says, ‘I have no need of your meal; I will take alms.’ ‘Action and non-action’—here, eating is action, non-refusal is non-action.

Paramparabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning consecutive meals is concluded.

4. Kāṇamātāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Kāṇamātā.

Paheṇakatthāyāti paṇṇākāratthāya. Pātheyyatthāyāti maggaṃ gacchantānaṃ antarāmaggatthāya. Sattūti baddhasattu, abaddhasattu ca. Dvattipattapūre paṭiggahetvāti mukhavaṭṭiyā heṭṭhimalekhāya samaṃ pūre dvattipattapūre gahetvāti attho. Imassa catthassa heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva pākaṭattā tattha kattabbappakārameva dassetuṃ “etthā”tiādimāha. Sesanti tato ekapattato aññaṃ pattaṃ. Sace tayo pattapūrā gahitā dve, sace dve gahitā, ekanti vuttaṃ hoti.

‘For the sake of a gift’ means for the sake of a present. ‘For the sake of provisions’ means for the sake of supplies for those traveling on a road. ‘Flour’ refers to both bound flour and unbound flour. ‘Having received two or three bowlfuls’ means having taken two or three bowlfuls filled level with the lower line of the rim. Because the meaning of this is clear from the method explained below, he says ‘here,’ and so on, only to show the procedure to be followed there. ‘The rest’ means the other bowl(s) apart from that one. If three bowlfuls have been taken, ‘the rest’ means two; if two have been taken, it means one—this is what is said.

Gamane [V 0.0351] vā paṭippassaddheti antarāmagge upaddavaṃ disvā, anatthikatāya vā “mayaṃ idāni na pesissāma na gamissāmā”ti evaṃ gamane upacchinne dentānanti attho.

‘Or when the going has ceased’ means that when the journey is cut off in this way—having seen danger on the way or because of lack of need, thinking, ‘We will not send anyone now, nor will we go’—this is the meaning of ‘to those who give’.

Kāṇamātāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning Kāṇamātā is concluded.

5. Paṭhamapavāraṇāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the First Training Rule concerning Satisfaction.

Bhuttavāti katabhattakicco. Sāsapamattampi ajjhoharitanti evaṃ parittampi bhojanaṃ saṅkhāditvā vā asaṅkhāditvā vā gilitaṃ. Pavāritoti paṭikkhepito. Yo hi bhuñjanto parivesakena upanītaṃ bhojanaṃ anicchanto paṭikkhipati, so tena pavārito paṭikkhipito nāma hoti. Byañjanaṃ pana anādiyitvā atthamattameva dassetuṃ “katappavāraṇo katappaṭikkhepoti attho”ti vuttaṃ. Sopi ca paṭikkhepo yasmā na paṭikkhepamattena, atha kho pañcaṅgavasena. Tenassa padabhājane “asanaṃ paññāyatī”tiādi (pāci. 239) vuttaṃ.

‘He has eaten’ means his meal duty is done. ‘Has swallowed even a mustard seed’s worth’ means that even such a tiny amount of food has been swallowed, whether chewed or unchewed. ‘Pavārita’ means refused. For one who, while eating, refuses food offered by the server, not desiring it, is said to be ‘pavārita,’ refused by that act. However, without considering the literal expression, just to show the meaning, it is said, ‘He has made the declaration of sufficiency, he has made the rejection’—this is the meaning. That refusal, too, is not merely by the act of refusal, but is dependent on five factors. Therefore, in the analysis of the word, it is said: ‘Eating is understood,’ and so on (Pācittiya 239).

Bhojanaṃ [M 0.0384] paññāyatīti pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ aññataraṃ pattādīsu dissati. Tenāha “pavāraṇappahonakaṃ ce bhojana”ntiādi. Sālīti (pāci. aṭṭha. 238-239) antamaso nīvāraṃ upādāya sabbāpi sālijāti. Vīhīti sabbāpi vīhijāti. Yavagodhumesu bhedo natthi. Kaṅgūti setarattakāḷabhedā sabbāpi kaṅgujāti. Varakoti antamaso varakacorakaṃ upādāya sabbāpi setavaṇṇā varakajāti. Kudrūsakoti kāḷakodravo ceva sāmākādibhedā ca sabbāpi tiṇadhaññajāti.

‘Food is understood’ means any one of the five kinds of food is seen in bowls and the like. Hence it is said, ‘if food is suitable for the declaration of sufficiency,’ and so on. ‘Rice’ (sāli) means all kinds of rice, including even wild rice (nīvāra). ‘Paddy’ (vīhi) refers to all varieties of paddy. There is no distinction between barley and wheat. ‘Millet’ (kaṅgū) includes all kinds of millet, whether white, red, or black. ‘Varaka’ refers to all varieties of varaka grain, even including varakacoraka, all being white in color. ‘Kudrūsaka’ includes black kodrava and all other kinds of wild grains like sāmāka, etc., all being varieties of grass grains.

Nīvāravarakacorakā cettha “dhaññānulomā”ti vadanti. Yāgunti ambilayāgukhīrayāguādibhedaṃ yaṃ kiñci yāguṃ. Imināva pāyāsassāpi gahitattā “ambilapāyāsādīsu aññataraṃ pacāmāti vā”ti na vuttaṃ. Pavāraṇaṃ janetīti anatirittabhojanāpattinibandhanaṃ paṭikkhepaṃ sādheti. Sace pana odhi na paññāyati, yāgusaṅgahaṃ gacchati, pavāraṇaṃ na janeti. Puna pavāraṇaṃ janeti ghanabhāvagamanato paṭṭhāya bhojanasaṅgahitattāti adhippāyo.

Here, they call nīvāra and varakacoraka ‘grain-followers’. ‘Yāgu’ refers to any kind of gruel, such as sour gruel, milk gruel, and so on. Since this also includes rice-milk porridge, it is not said, ‘We cook one of sour rice-milk porridge, etc.’ ‘It generates a declaration of sufficiency’ means it establishes the refusal that is the basis for the offense concerning food that is not a leftover. But if the limit is not evident, it falls under the category of gruel and does not generate a declaration of sufficiency. Again, it generates a declaration of sufficiency because, from the point of becoming thick, it is included under ordinary food—this is the meaning.

Udakakañjikakhīrādīni ākiritvāti udakañceva kañjikañca khīrādīni ca ākiritvā tehi saddhiṃ amadditvā bhattamissake katvā. Tenāha “yāguṃ gaṇhathā”tiādi. Sace pana bhatte udakakañjikakhīrādīni ākiritvā madditvā “yāguṃ gaṇhathā”ti denti, pavāraṇā [V 0.0352] na hoti. Yāguyāpīti evaṃ yāgusaṅgahaṃ gatāya vā aññāya vā yāguyāpi. Suddharasako, pana rasakayāgu vā na janeti.

‘Having scattered water, rice gruel, milk, etc.’ means having scattered water, rice gruel, and milk, etc., and without kneading them together, having made a mixture with the food. Therefore, it is said, ‘Take the gruel,’ and so on. But if, having scattered water, rice gruel, milk, etc., on the food and kneaded it, they give it saying, ‘Take the gruel,’ then there is no declaration of sufficiency. ‘Even with gruel’ means whether with gruel that falls under the category of gruel or with another gruel. However, pure broth, or broth-gruel, does not generate a declaration of sufficiency.

Pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ aññataravasena vippakatabhojanabhāvassa upacchinnattā “dvepi khāditāni honti…pe… na pavāretī”ti vuttaṃ. Akappiyamaṃsaṃ (pāci. aṭṭha. 238-239), akappiyabhojanañca buddhapaṭikuṭṭhaṃ paṭikkhipato pavāraṇāya avatthutāya na pavāraṇā hotīti āha “yo panā”tiādi.
