Yañhi bhikkhuno khādituṃ vaṭṭati, taṃ eva paṭikkhipato pavāraṇā hoti. Idaṃ pana jānanto akappiyattā paṭikkhipati. Ajānantopi paṭikkhipitabbaṭṭhāne ṭhitameva paṭikkhipati nāma, tasmā na pavāreti. Sace pana akappiyamaṃsaṃ khādanto kappiyamaṃsaṃ vā bhojanaṃ vā paṭikkhipati, pavāreti. Kasmā? Vatthutāya. Yañhi tena paṭikkhittaṃ, taṃ pavāraṇāya vatthu. Yaṃ pana khādati, taṃ [M 0.0385] kiñcāpi paṭikkhipitabbaṭṭhāne ṭhitaṃ, khādiyamānaṃ pana maṃsabhāvaṃ na jahati, tasmā pavāreti. Ko pana vādo kappiyamaṃsaṃ khādato kappiyamaṃsabhojanappaṭikkhepe. Esa nayo akappiyabhojanaṃ khādato kappiyabhojanappaṭikkhepe.

Due to the cessation of the state of being unfinished food through one of the five kinds of food, it is said: ‘Even if two are eaten… he does not make a declaration of sufficiency.’ Regarding unallowable meat and unallowable food, which are disapproved by the Buddha, it is said in the passage beginning, ‘Now, whoever…,’ that for one who rejects them, there is no declaration of sufficiency, because they are not a valid basis for a declaration of sufficiency. For whatever is allowable for a bhikkhu to eat, if he rejects that, then a declaration of sufficiency is made. But here, knowing it to be unallowable, he rejects it. Even if he does not know, he still rejects what stands in the position of what should be rejected; thus he does not make a declaration of sufficiency. However, if one eats unallowable meat but rejects allowable meat or food, he does make a declaration of sufficiency. Why? Because there is a basis. Whatever he rejects is the basis for the declaration of sufficiency. But what he eats, though it stands in the position of what should be rejected, does not relinquish its nature as meat while being eaten—therefore, he makes a declaration of sufficiency. What need is there to speak of rejecting allowable meat or food while eating allowable meat? The same principle applies when eating unallowable food and rejecting allowable food.

Bhojane satīti pañcasu bhojanesu ekasmimpi bhojane sati. Aññaṃ vuttalakkhaṇaṃ bhojananti pattādigatato aññaṃ vuttalakkhaṇaṃ pañcasu bhojanesu ekampi bhojanaṃ. “Nirapekkho hotī”ti etasseva vivaraṇaṃ “yaṃ pattādīsū”tiādi. Na kevalaṃ nirapekkho vāti āha “aññatra vā”tiādi. So paṭikkhipantopi na pavāretīti tasmiṃ ce antare aññaṃ bhojanaṃ abhihaṭaṃ, taṃ so paṭikkhipantopi na pavāreti. Kasmā? Vippakatabhojanabhāvassa upacchinnattā.

‘When there is food’ means when there is even one of the five kinds of food. ‘Other food of the described characteristic’ means any one of the five kinds of food of the described characteristic, other than what is in the bowl, etc. ‘He is indifferent’ is an explanation of this very phrase, ‘whatever is in the bowl, etc.’ He says ‘or elsewhere,’ and so on, to show that it is not only that he is indifferent. ‘Even if he refuses, he does not make a declaration of sufficiency’ means that if another food is brought during that interval, even if he refuses it, he does not make a declaration of sufficiency. Why? Because the state of unfinished food has ceased.

“Upanāmetī”ti (pāci. aṭṭha. 238-239) iminā kāyābhihāraṃ dasseti. Hatthe vā ādhārake vāti ettha vā-saddo avuttavikappattho, tena “ūrūsu vā”ti vikappeti. Dūre nisinnassa daharabhikkhussa pattaṃ pesetvā “ito odanaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti vadati, gaṇhitvā pana gato tuṇhī tiṭṭhati, tampi paṭikkhipato eseva nayo. Kasmā? Bhikkhussa dūrabhāvato, dūtassa ca anabhiharaṇato. Sace pana gahetvā āgato bhikkhu “imaṃ bhattaṃ gaṇhā”ti vadati, taṃ paṭikkhipato pavāraṇā hoti. Evaṃ vuttepīti “bhattaṃ gaṇhā”ti vuttepi.

“He brings near” shows the act of physical presentation. “Either in the hand or in a receptacle”—here the word “or” expresses an unspoken alternative, thus it also implies “or on the thighs.” If one sends a bowl to a young monk sitting at a distance and says, “Take rice from here,” but after taking it, the young monk goes away while remaining silent, the same principle applies to one who refuses it. Why? Because the monk is at a distance, and the messenger does not present it. But if, after taking it, the monk comes back and says, “Take this food,” then refusing it constitutes a declaration of sufficiency. ‘Even when it is said thus’ means even when ‘Take this food’ is said.

Bhattapacchiṃ gahetvā parivisantassāti ekena hatthena bhattapacchiṃ gahetvā ekena hatthena kaṭacchuṃ [V 0.0353] gahetvā parivisantassa. Añño “ahaṃ dhāressāmī”ti gahitamattakameva karotīti añño āgantvā “ahaṃ pacchiṃ dhāressāmi, tvaṃ odanaṃ dehī”ti vatvā gahitamattakameva karoti. Abhihaṭāva hotīti parivesakeneva abhihaṭāva hoti. Idāni asati tassa dātukāmābhihāre gahaṇasamayepi paṭikkhipato na hotīti dassetuṃ “sace panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Uddhaṭeti uddhaṭe bhatte. Kaṭacchuabhihāroyeva hi tassa abhihāroti adhippāyo. Anantarassa diyyamāneti anantarassa bhikkhuno bhatte diyyamāne. Kāyavikārenāti “aṅguliṃ vā hatthaṃ vā macchikabījaniṃ vā cīvarakaṇṇaṃ vā [M 0.0386] cāleti, bhamukāya vā ākāraṃ karoti, kuddho vā oloketī”ti (pāci. aṭṭha. 238-239) evaṃ vuttena aṅgulicalanādinā kāyavikārena. “Alaṃ mā dehī”tiādinā vacīvikārenāti “ala”nti vā “na gaṇhāmī”ti vā “mā ākirā”ti vā “apagacchā”ti vā evaṃ yena kenaci vacīvikārena.

‘While serving, taking the rice basket’ means while serving, taking the rice basket with one hand and the serving spoon with the other hand. ‘Another person, saying “I will hold it,” merely does so’ means another person comes and says, ‘I will hold the basket, you give the rice,’ and merely does so. ‘It is indeed offered’ means it is indeed offered by the server. Now, to show that if there is no presentation with a desire to give on the server's part, there is no declaration of sufficiency for one who refuses even at the moment of taking, the phrase ‘but if’ and so on is stated. ‘He removes’ means when the rice has been removed. Indeed, the presentation of the spoonful is his presentation: this is the meaning. ‘When being given to the next’ means when rice is being given to the next monk. ‘By bodily gesture’ means by a bodily gesture such as moving a finger, etc., as stated in ‘moves a finger or a hand or a fly-whisk or the edge of his robe, or makes a sign with his eyebrow, or looks angrily’. ‘By verbal gesture such as “Enough, do not give”’ means by any verbal gesture such as ‘Enough,’ or ‘I will not take,’ or ‘Do not scatter,’ or ‘Go away.’

Abhihaṭe pana bhatte pavāraṇāya bhīto hatthe apanetvā punappunaṃ patte odanaṃ ākirantaṃ “ākira ākira, koṭṭetvā pūrehī”ti vadato pavāraṇā na hoti. Esa nayo bhattaṃ abhiharantaṃ bhikkhuṃ sallakkhetvā “kiṃ, āvuso, itopi kiñci gaṇhissasi, dammi te kiñcī”ti vadatopi.

But when food is offered, for one who, being afraid of the declaration of sufficiency, withdraws his hand and repeatedly says to the one scattering rice into the bowl, ‘Scatter, scatter, fill it up by pounding,’ there is no declaration of sufficiency. The same principle applies to one who, observing a monk bringing food, says, ‘Friend, will you take anything more from here? Shall I give you something?’

“Rasaṃ paṭiggaṇhathā”ti appavāraṇājanakassa nāmaṃ gahetvā vuttattā “taṃ sutvā paṭikkhipato pavāraṇā natthī”ti vuttaṃ. Maṃsarasanti ettha pana na kevalaṃ maṃsassa rasaṃ “maṃsarasa”micceva viññāyati, atha kho maṃsañca rasañca maṃsarasanti evaṃ pavāraṇājanakanāmavasenāpi. Tasmā taṃ paṭikkhipato pavāraṇāva hotīti āha “maṃsarasanti vutte pana paṭikkhipato pavāraṇā hotī”ti. Parato macchamaṃsaṃ byañjananti etthāpi eseva nayo. Yasmiṃ iriyāpathe pavāreti, taṃ avikopenteneva bhuñjitabbanti yo gacchanto (pāci. aṭṭha. 238-239) pavāreti, tena gacchanteneva bhuñjitabbaṃ. Kaddamaṃ vā udakaṃ vā patvā ṭhitena atirittaṃ kāretabbaṃ. Sace antarā nadī pūrā hoti, naditīre gumbaṃ anupariyāyantena bhuñjitabbaṃ. Atha nāvā vā setu vā atthi, taṃ abhiruhitvāpi caṅkamanteneva bhuñjitabbaṃ, gamanaṃ na upacchinditabbaṃ. Esa nayo itarairiyāpathesupi. Taṃ taṃ iriyāpathaṃ kopentena atirittaṃ kāretabbaṃ. Yo ukkuṭikova nisīditvā pavāreti, tena ukkuṭikeneva bhuñjitabbaṃ. Tassa pana heṭṭhā palālapīṭhaṃ vā kiñci vā nisīdanaṃ dātabbaṃ. Pīṭhake nisīditvā pavāritena pana āsanaṃ acāletvāva catasso disā parivattantena bhuñjituṃ labbhati. Mañce nisīditvā pavāritena ito vā etto vā saṃsarituṃ na labbhati. Sace pana saha [V 0.0354] mañcena ukkhipitvā aññatra nenti, vaṭṭati. Nipajjitvā pavāritenāpi nipanneneva bhuñjitabbaṃ. Parivattantena yena passena nipanno, tassa ṭhānaṃ nātikkametabbaṃ.

‘Accept the broth’ was said by using the name of something that does not generate a formal satisfaction (pavāraṇā); hence it was stated, ‘Upon hearing that and refusing, there is no formal satisfaction.’ Regarding ‘meat broth,’ here not only is the broth of meat understood as ‘meat broth,’ but also meat and broth together are understood as ‘meat broth,’ by way of a name that generates a formal satisfaction. Therefore, refusing it constitutes a formal satisfaction; thus it is said, ‘But when ‘meat broth’ is mentioned, refusing it constitutes a formal satisfaction.’ The same principle applies to ‘fish or meat as a side dish’ later on. One should eat without changing the posture in which one made the formal satisfaction: that is, if one made the formal satisfaction while walking (Pāci. Aṭṭha. 238–239), one should eat while continuing to walk. If one encounters mud or water, one should stop and have the food made leftover (atiritta). If a river is full along the way, one should eat while circling a thicket on the riverbank. If there is a boat or a bridge, one may board it and eat while pacing, but the walking should not be interrupted. The same principle applies to other postures as well. One who changes that particular posture should have the food made leftover. One who made the formal satisfaction while sitting in a squatting position should eat while remaining squatting. However, a straw seat or some other sitting support should be provided beneath them. If one made the formal satisfaction while sitting on a low seat, one may eat while turning to the four directions without moving the seat. If one made the formal satisfaction while sitting on a couch, one cannot shift from one place to another. But if one is lifted together with the couch and moved elsewhere, it is permissible. If one made the formal satisfaction while lying down, one should eat while remaining lying down. While turning, one should not move beyond the position of the side on which one was lying.

Alametaṃ sabbanti etaṃ sabbaṃ alaṃ pariyattaṃ, idampi te adhikaṃ, ito aññaṃ na lacchasīti adhippāyo. Yo atirittaṃ karotīti yo “alametaṃ [M 0.0387] sabba”nti atirittaṃ karoti. Paṭipakkhanayenāti “kappiyakataṃ, paṭiggahitakataṃ, uccāritakataṃ, hatthapāse kataṃ, bhuttāvinā kataṃ, bhuttāvinā pavāritena āsanā avuṭṭhitena kataṃ ‘alametaṃ sabba’nti vutta”nti (pāci. 239) imehi sattahi vinayakammākārehi yaṃ atirittaṃ kappiyaṃ kataṃ, yañca gilānātirittaṃ, tadubhayampi atirittanti evaṃ tasseva paṭipakkhanayena. Ettha ca “alametaṃ sabba”nti tikkhattuṃ vattabbaṃ, ayaṃ kira āciṇṇo. Vinayadharā pana “sakiṃ eva vattabba”nti vadanti.

‘This is enough, all’: the meaning is ‘all of this is sufficient, complete; this is extra for you, you will not get anything else beyond this.’ ‘One who makes it leftover (atiritta)’: that is, one who makes something leftover by saying, ‘This is enough, all.’ ‘By the method of opposition’: that is, by the method of opposition to that very thing, namely: ‘What is made allowable, what is received, what is uttered, what is done within arm’s reach, what is done by one who has finished eating, what is done by one who has finished eating and has been formally satisfied but has not risen from their seat when “This is enough, all” is said’ (Pāci. 239)—by these seven modes of Vinaya procedure, that which is made leftover from what is allowable, and that which is a leftover for the sick, both are considered ‘leftover’. And here, ‘This is enough, all’ should be said three times—this, it is said, is the custom. The experts in the Vinaya, however, say, ‘It should be said only once.’

Kasmā taṃ so puna kātuṃ na labhatīti āha “yañhī”tiādi. Tattha yañhi akatanti yena paṭhamaṃ kappiyaṃ kataṃ, tena yaṃ akataṃ, taṃ kātabbaṃ. Paṭhamabhājane pana kātuṃ na labbhati. Yena ca akatanti aññena bhikkhunā yena paṭhamaṃ na kataṃ, tena ca kātabbanti attho. Vuttanti sīhaḷaṭṭhakathāsu vuttaṃ. Aññasmiṃ pana bhājaneti yasmiṃ pana bhājane paṭhamaṃ kataṃ, tato aññasmiṃ patte vā kuṇḍe vā pacchiyaṃ vā yattha katthaci purato ṭhapetvā onāmitabhājane.

As to why he is not able to do it again, he says, ‘Because...’ and so on. Therein, ‘what was not done’ means: that which was not done by the one who first made it allowable should be done by him. However, it cannot be done in the first vessel. And ‘by whom it was not done’ means it should be done by another monk, by whom it was not done at first. ‘Stated’ means stated in the Sinhala commentaries. ‘In another vessel’ means in a vessel other than the one in which it was first done—be it a bowl, a pot, or a basket, or anything whatsoever—placed in front, in a vessel that has been tilted down.

Aññatra bhuñjanavatthusminti bhuttāvinā pavāritena hutvā aññatra bhuñjanavatthusmiṃ. Tikapācittiyanti anatiritte anatirittasaññivematikaatirittasaññīnaṃ vasena tīṇi pācittiyāni. Ajjhoharato ca dukkaṭanti ajjhoharato ajjhohāre ajjhohāre dukkaṭaṃ. Sace pana āmisasaṃsaṭṭhāni honti, āhāratthāyapi anāhāratthāyapi paṭiggahetvā ajjhoharantassa pācittiyameva. Tesaṃ anuññātaparibhogavasenāti yāmakālikādīnaṃ anuññātaparibhogavasena, yāmakālikaṃ pipāsāya sati pipāsacchedanatthaṃ, sattāhakālikaṃ yāvajīvikañca tena tena upasametabbake ābādhe sati tassa upasamanatthanti vuttaṃ hoti. Idampi ajjhoharaṇato kāyakammaṃ, vācāya “atirittaṃ karotha bhante”ti akārāpanena vacīkammanti āha “samuṭṭhānādīni paṭhamakathinasadisānevā”ti. Kiriyākiriyanti ettha paṭikkhipitvā bhuñjanaṃ kiriyaṃ. Atirittassa akaraṇaṃ akiriyanti veditabbaṃ.

‘Except regarding the matter of eating’: that is, having finished eating and having been formally satisfied, except regarding the matter of eating. ‘Three pācittiyas’: that is, there are three pācittiya offenses based on perception: for one who perceives it as not leftover, for one who is uncertain, and for one who perceives it as leftover. ‘And a dukkaṭa for swallowing’: that is, for each act of swallowing, there is a dukkaṭa offense. But if they are mixed with staple food, then for one who receives and swallows it, whether for the purpose of food or not for the purpose of food, there is a pācittiya offense. ‘For them, by way of permitted use’: this means by way of the permitted use of items allowed for a limited time (yāmakālika), and so on. It is said that the yāmakālika is for quenching thirst when there is thirst, and the sattāhakālika (seven-day allowance) and yāvajīvika (lifetime allowance) are for alleviating a particular ailment when it arises. This too is a bodily action due to swallowing, and a verbal action due to not having it made leftover by saying, ‘Venerable sirs, make this leftover.’ Thus it is said, ‘The origins and so on are just like those of the first Kathina rule.’ ‘Action and non-action’: here, eating after having refused is the action. Not making it leftover is to be understood as the non-action.

Paṭhamapavāraṇāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the first training rule concerning formal satisfaction is concluded.

6. Dutiyapavāraṇāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Second Training Rule Concerning Formal Satisfaction

Sutvā [M 0.0388][V 0.0355] vāti aññena vā teneva vā ārocitaṃ sutvā. “Bhuttasmiṃ pācittiya”nti (pāci. 243) vuttattā bhojanapariyosāne pācittiya”nti vuttaṃ.

‘Or having heard’: having heard it announced by another or by that same person. Because it is said, “There is a pācittiya offense for having eaten” (Pāci. 243), it is said, “there is a pācittiya offense at the conclusion of the meal.”

Dutiyapavāraṇāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the second training rule concerning formal satisfaction is concluded.

7. Vikālabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Eating at the Wrong Time

Vikāleti ettha aruṇuggamanato paṭṭhāya yāva majjhanhiko, ayaṃ buddhādīnaṃ ariyānaṃ āciṇṇasamāciṇṇo bhojanassa kālo nāma. Tadañño vikālo “vigato kālo”ti katvā. Tenāha “vigate kāle”tiādi. Ṭhitamajjhanhikopi (pāci. aṭṭha. 248-249) kālasaṅgahaṃ gacchati. Tato paṭṭhāya pana khādituṃ vā bhuñjituṃ vā na sakkā. Sahasā pivituṃ sakkā bhaveyya, kukkuccakena pana na kātabbaṃ. Kālaparicchedajānanatthañca kālatthambho yojetabbo. Kālabbhantareva bhattakiccaṃ kātabbaṃ. “Yaṃ kiñci…pe… khādanīyaṃ vā”ti iminā yaṃ tāva sakkhalimodakādi pubbaṇṇāparaṇṇamayaṃ, tattha vattabbameva natthīti dasseti. Bhojanīyaṃ nāma pañca bhojanāni.

In the phrase ‘at the wrong time,’ the time from the rising of the dawn until midday is called the time for eating, this being frequented and well-practiced by noble ones such as the Buddha. Any other time is the wrong time (vikāla), it being ‘time that has passed’ (vigato kālo). Therefore, it is said, “when the time has passed,” and so on. Even the moment of midday (Pāci. Aṭṭha. 248–249) is included in the reckoning of time. From that point on, however, it is not permissible to chew or to eat. One might be able to drink hastily, but this should not be done out of scrupulousness. And for the purpose of knowing the time limit, a time-post should be set up. The business of the meal should be done within the time limit. By the phrase “whatever… or chewable,” it shows that there is nothing even to be said regarding things such as coarse sugar sweets and so on, which are made from grains and pulses. ‘Edible food’ refers to the five kinds of staple foods.

Sati paccayeti pipāsādikāraṇe vijjamāne. Romaṭṭhakassāti romaṭṭhakassa bhikkhuno ajjhoharitvā uggiritvā mukheva ṭhapito bahi mukhadvārā viniggato bhojanassa maggā bahi niggato “romaṭṭho”ti pavuccati. Idha pana ajjhoharitvā uggiritvā mukheva ṭhapitoti adhippeto. Tenāha “na ca, bhikkhave”tiādi. Ṭhapetvā romaṭṭhakaṃ sesānaṃ āgataṃ uggāraṃ mukhe sandhāretvā gilantānaṃ āpatti. Sace pana asandhārentameva paragalaṃ gacchati, vaṭṭati.

‘When there is a condition’: this means when a cause such as thirst is present. ‘Regarding romaṭṭhaka’: for the monk Romaṭṭhaka, that which, having been swallowed and regurgitated, is kept in the mouth, has gone out from the opening of the mouth, has exited from the path of food, is called ‘romaṭṭha’ (regurgitated food). Here, however, what is intended is that which, having been swallowed and regurgitated, is kept in the mouth. Therefore, he said, “And not, monks…” and so on. Except for the case of regurgitated food, for other monks who retain in the mouth what has been brought up by regurgitation and swallow it, there is an offense. But if it goes down the throat without being retained, it is permissible.

Vikālabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning eating at the wrong time is concluded.

8. Sannidhikārakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Storing Food

“Kāro karaṇaṃ kiriyāti atthato eka”nti etena kārasaddassa bhāvatthataṃ dasseti. Sammā nidhānaṃ ṭhapanaṃ sannidhi. “Paṭiggahetvā ekarattaṃ vītināmitassetaṃ [M 0.0389] nāma”nti iminā paṭiggahetvā [V 0.0356] ekarattaṃ vītināmite imassa duddhotabhāvaṃ dasseti. Kiñcāpi yāmakālikaṃ khādanīyaṃ, bhojanīyaṃ vā na hoti, “anāpatti yāmakālikaṃ yāme nidahitvā bhuñjatī”tiādi vacanato pana tatthāpi yāmātikkame sannidhipaccayā pācittiyena bhavitabbanti “yaṃ kiñci yāvakālikaṃ vā yāmakālikaṃ vā”ti vuttaṃ. Idāni duddhotabhāvameva vibhāvetuṃ “yaṃ aṅguliyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yaṃ aṅguliyā ghaṃsantassa lekhā paññāyatīti yaṃ pattaṃ dhotaṃ aṅguliyā ghaṃsantassa patte aṅgulilekhā paññāyati, so patto duddhoto hotīti attho. Telavaṇṇapatte pana aṅgulilekhā paññāyati, sā abbohārikā. Snehoti telaṃ. Sandissatīti yāguyā upari sandissati. Tādise pattepīti paṭiggahaṇaṃ avissajjitvā sayaṃ vā aññena vā bhojanaṃ nīharitvā na sammā dhote pattepi. Punadivase bhuñjantassa pācittiyanti patte laggaṃ avijahitappaṭiggahaṇaṃ hotīti dutiyadivase bhuñjantassa pācittiyaṃ. Pariccatte pana patte punadivase bhuñjantassa anāpatti.

'Kāra,' 'karaṇa,' and 'kiriya' are one in meaning.' By this, it shows that the word 'kāra' has the sense of an action. Proper keeping or placing is 'sannidhi' (storing). By 'having received it and letting one night pass, that is its name,' it shows the state of being poorly washed for that which has been received and kept for one night. Although what is allowable for a watch is neither solid food nor soft food, since it is said, 'There is no offense if one eats what is allowable for a watch after having kept it aside for a watch,' still, if the watch passes, then due to the condition of storage, there would be an offense of expiation. Therefore, it is stated, 'whatever is allowable for the time being or allowable for a watch.' Now, to explain this very state of being poorly washed, it is said, 'that which by the finger,' and so on. Therein, 'that on which a line appears when one rubs it with a finger' means that if, when a washed bowl is rubbed with a finger, a finger-line appears on the bowl, that bowl is poorly washed—this is the meaning. But on an oil-colored bowl, a finger-line might appear; it is not to be reckoned with. 'Sneha' is oil. 'Is seen' means it is seen on top of the rice gruel. 'Even in such a bowl' means even in a bowl that is not properly washed after the food has been removed by oneself or by another, without having relinquished the acceptance. 'For one who eats on the following day, there is an offense of expiation' means that because the unrelinquished acceptance remains attached to the bowl, for one who eats on the second day, there is an offense of expiation. But when the bowl has been relinquished, there is no offense for one who eats on the following day.

Yaṃ panāti yaṃ bhojanaṃ pana. Apariccattameva hīti anapekkhavissajjanena vā anupasampannassa nirapekkhadānena vā apariccattameva. Kappiya bhojananti antamaso ekasitthamattampi kappiyabhojanaṃ. Akappiyesūti akappiyamaṃsesu. Sesesūti manussamaṃsato avasesesu hatthiassasunakhaahisīhabyagghadīpiacchataracchamaṃsesu ceva appaṭivekkhite uddissakatamaṃse ca. Pāḷiyaṃ “sattāhakālikaṃ yāvajīvikaṃ āhāratthāya paṭiggaṇhāti, āpatti dukkaṭassā”tiādinā (pāci. 255) sannihitesu sattāhakālikayāvajīvikesu purebhattampi āhāratthāya ajjhoharaṇepi dukkaṭassa vuttattā yāmakālikepi āhāratthāya ajjhoharaṇepi visuṃ dukkaṭenāpi bhavitabbanti āha “āhāratthāya ajjhoharato dukkaṭena saddhiṃ pācittiya”nti. Sabbavikappesūti “kappiyabhojanaṃ bhuñjantassā”tiādinā vuttesu sabbesu vikappesu aparampi pācittiyaṃ vaḍḍhati. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti (pāci. aṭṭha. 253) – kappiyabhojane dve pācittiyāni, manussamaṃse thullaccayena saddhiṃ dve pācittiyāni, avasesesu pana akappiyamaṃsesu dukkaṭena saddhiṃ dve pācittiyāni. Yāmakālikaṃ sati paccaye sāmisena mukhena [M 0.0390] ajjhoharato dve pācittiyāni, nirāmisena ekameva. Āhāratthāya ajjhoharato vikappadvayepi dukkaṭena saddhinti.

'Yaṃ pana' means 'whatever food.' 'Apariccattameva hi' means it is indeed not relinquished, either by giving it away without concern, or by giving it to an unordained person without any regard. 'Kappiya bhojana' means allowable food, even as little as a single mouthful. 'Akappiyesu' refers to unallowable meats. 'Sesesūti' means in the remaining cases, that is, in the meats remaining apart from human flesh—such as the flesh of elephants, horses, dogs, snakes, lions, tigers, leopards, bears, and hyenas—and in meat that was specifically prepared but not inspected. In the Pāli text (Pāc. 255), by the words 'If one accepts what is allowable for seven days or for a lifetime for the purpose of eating, there is an offense of wrongdoing,' and so on, it is stated that for stored items allowable for seven days or for a lifetime, consuming them for the purpose of eating even before the mealtime is an offense of wrongdoing; so too for what is allowable for a watch, consuming it for the purpose of eating should also separately be an offense of wrongdoing. Therefore, he said: 'For one consuming for the purpose of eating, there is an offense of expiation along with an offense of wrongdoing.' 'Sabbavikappesūti' means that in all the alternatives mentioned by 'for one eating allowable food...' and so on, another offense of expiation is added. This is what is meant (Pāc. Aṭṭha. 253): for allowable food, there are two offenses of expiation; for human flesh, two offenses of expiation along with a grave offense; for the remaining unallowable meats, two offenses of expiation along with an offense of wrongdoing. For what is allowable for a watch, when there is a reason, for one consuming it with savory food in the mouth, there are two offenses of expiation; without savory food, only one. For one consuming for the purpose of eating, in both alternatives, it is with an offense of wrongdoing.

Avasesesūti yāmakālikādito avasesesu. Pācittiyaṃ vaḍḍhatiyevāti aparampi pācittiyaṃ vaḍḍhatiyeva. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – sace vikāle ajjhoharati, pakatibhojane sannidhipaccayā [V 0.0357] ca vikālabhojanapaccayā ca dve pācittiyāni, akappiyamaṃsesu manussamaṃse thullaccayena saddhiṃ dve pācittiyāni, avasesesu dukkaṭena saddhiṃ dveti.

'Avasesesu' means in the remaining cases, apart from what is allowable for a watch and so on. 'An offense of expiation is indeed added' means that another offense of expiation is indeed added. This is what is meant: if one consumes at the wrong time, in the case of ordinary food, there are two offenses of expiation: one due to the condition of storing and one due to the condition of eating at the wrong time; in the case of unallowable meats, for human flesh, there are two offenses of expiation along with a grave offense; for the remaining cases, two along with an offense of wrongdoing.

Belaṭṭhasīso nāma jaṭilasahassassa abbhantare eko mahāthero. Tikapācittiyanti sannidhikārake sannidhikārakasaññivematikaasannidhikārakasaññīnaṃ vasena tīṇi pācittiyāni. Saṃsaṭṭhānīti saṃsaṭṭharasāni. Sambhinnarasaṃ sandhāyeva hi “tadahupaṭiggahitaṃ kāle kappatī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tenāha “tasmā”tiādi. Ettha ca asambhinnarasanti amissitarasaṃ. Idañca sītalapāyāsādinā saha laddhaṃ sappipiṇḍādikaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. “Sudhotaṃ vā”ti idaṃ pana piṇḍapātena saddhiṃ laddhaṃ takkolajātiphalādiṃ, yāguādīsu pakkhipitvā dinnasiṅgīverādikañca sandhāya vuttaṃ.

Belaṭṭhasīsa was the name of a great elder among a thousand matted-hair ascetics. 'Three offenses of expiation' means three offenses of expiation for one who stores, according to whether one perceives it as storing, is uncertain, or perceives it as not storing. 'Mixed' means with mixed flavors. Indeed, it is with reference to blended flavors that it is said, 'What was received on that day is allowable at the proper time,' and so on. Therefore, he said, 'For this reason,' and so on. And here, 'unblended flavors' means unmixed flavors. This is said with reference to things like a lump of ghee obtained along with cold rice-gruel and so on. 'Or well-washed' is said with reference to things like cubeb pepper and nutmeg obtained along with alms-food, and things like ginger given after being put into gruel and so on.

Tenāti sattāhakālikena. Tadahu paṭiggahitaṃ assāti tadahupaṭiggahitaṃ, tena tadahupaṭiggahitena. Esa nayo “dvīhapaṭiggahitenā”tiādīsupi. Tasmāti yasmā purebhattaṃ paṭiggahitampi vaṭṭati, tasmā. Paṭiggahitaṃ sattāhaṃ kappatīti vuttanti “sattāhakālikena, bhikkhave, yāvajīvikaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ sattāhaṃ kappati, sattāhātikkante na kappatī”ti (mahāva. 305) bhesajjakkhandhake vuttaṃ. Kiñcāpi mukhe ekarattaṃ na vuttaṃ, tathāpi mukhe pakkhittameva yasmā sannidhi nāma hoti, tasmā “mukhasannidhī”ti vuttaṃ.

'By that' means by what is allowable for seven days. 'Tadahupaṭiggahitaṃ' is 'tadahu paṭiggahitaṃ assā'; by that which was accepted on that day. This is the same method for 'by what is accepted for two days,' and so on. 'Therefore' means because what is accepted before the meal is also allowable, therefore. 'What is accepted is allowable for seven days' is said in the Bhesajjakkhandhaka (Mahāvagga 305): 'Monks, a lifelong provision, when it is a seven-day allowable, is allowable for seven days; after seven days have passed, it is not allowable.' Although 'one night' is not mentioned in connection with the mouth, nevertheless, since what is put in the mouth is indeed called storing, it is therefore called 'mouth-storing'.

Catasso kappiyabhūmiyoti ussāvanantikā, gonisādikā, gahapati, sammutīti catasso kappiyakuṭiyo. Tattha ussāvanantikā (mahāva. aṭṭha. 295) nāma gehe kariyamāne samparivāretvā ṭhitehi “kappiyakuṭiṃ karoma, kappiyakuṭiṃ karomā”ti vā “kappiyakuṭi kappiyakuṭī”ti vā vadantehi ṭhapitapaṭhamiṭṭhakathambhādikā saṅghassa vā ekassa bhikkhuno vā kuṭi. Yo pana ārāmo yebhuyyena vā aparikkhitto hoti, sakalopi vā[M 0.0391], so “gonisādī”ti vuccati. Gahapatīti yā ṭhapetvā bhikkhuṃ sesehi “kappiyakuṭiṃ demā”ti dinnā, tesaṃ vā santakā. Sammuti nāma kammavācāya sāvetvā katā. Kathaṃ panetāsaṃ vinicchayo jānitabboti āha “tāsaṃ vinicchayo samantapāsādikāyaṃ vutto”ti.

'Four allowable grounds' means four allowable huts: the announcement boundary, the cattle-resting place, the householder's, and the designated. Among these, the 'announcement boundary' (Mahāva. Aṭṭha. 295) is a hut for the Saṅgha or for a single bhikkhu, established by laying the first brick, pillar, etc., by those who, having gathered around while a dwelling is being built, say, 'Let us make an allowable hut, let us make an allowable hut,' or 'An allowable hut, an allowable hut.' A monastery that is mostly or entirely unenclosed is called a 'cattle-resting place.' 'Householder's' is one that is given by others, excluding a bhikkhu, saying, 'We give an allowable hut,' or one that belongs to them. 'Designated' is one made by being announced through a formal act. But how is the legal decision regarding these to be known? He said, 'Their legal decision is stated in the Samantapāsādikā.'

Sannidhikārakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning storing is concluded.

9. Paṇītabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

9. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Choice Foods.

“Paṇītabhojanānī”ti [V 0.0358] idaṃ majjhe padalopaṃ katvā niddiṭṭhanti āha “paṇītasaṃsaṭṭhānī”tiādi. Sabbopi “odako”ti vuttalakkhaṇo macchoti “maccho nāma odako vuccatī”ti (pāci. 260) evaṃ vibhaṅge vuttalakkhaṇo, sabbopi maccho eva. Yo koci udake jāto maccho nāmāti vuttaṃ hoti. Mahānāmasikkhāpadenāti –

'Choice foods' (paṇītabhojanāni)—this is indicated with the elision of a word in the middle; he says, 'mixed with choice things' (paṇītasaṃsaṭṭhāni), and so on. All fish have the characteristic of being called a 'water-dweller' (odako), as in the Vibhaṅga it is said, 'A fish is called a water-dweller' (Pāc. 260); thus, all are indeed fish. This means it is said that whatever is born in water is called a fish. By the Mahānāma training rule:

“Agilānena bhikkhunā catumāsapaccayapavāraṇā sāditabbā aññatra punapavāraṇāya aññatra niccapavāraṇāya. Tato ce uttari sādiyeyya, pācittiya”nti –

By a bhikkhu who is not ill, a four-month invitation for requisites may be consented to, except for a further invitation or a perpetual invitation. If he should consent to more than that, it is an offense of expiation.

Iminā sikkhāpadena (pāci. 306). Ettha hi saṅghavasena gilānapaccayapavāraṇāya pavāritaṭṭhāne sace tattha rattīhi vā bhesajjehi vā paricchedo kato hoti “ettikāyeva rattiyo, ettakāni vā bhesajjāni viññāpetabbānī”ti, tato rattipariyantato vā bhesajjapariyantato vā uttari nabhesajjakaraṇīyena vā bhesajjaṃ, aññabhesajjakaraṇīyena vā aññaṃ bhesajjaṃ viññāpentassa pācittiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Tasmā agilāno gilānasaññīpi hutvā pañca bhesajjāni viññāpento nabhesajjakaraṇīyena bhesajjaṃ viññāpento nāma hotīti “mahānāmasikkhāpadena kāretabbo”ti vuttaṃ.

By this training rule (Pāc. 306). Here, in a place where an invitation for requisites for the sick has been made by the Saṅgha, if a limit has been set there—either by nights or by medicines—‘Only this many nights, or only this many medicines, are to be requested,’ then for one who requests medicine beyond that limit—either beyond the limit of nights or beyond the limit of medicines—or requests medicine when there is no need for medicine, or requests one medicine when there is a need for another, a pācittiya offense is declared. Therefore, one who is not sick but, perceiving himself as sick, requests the five medicines, is called one who requests medicine when there is no need for medicine, and it is said he is to be ‘dealt with according to the Mahānāma training rule.’

Yo pana nabhesajjatthāya viññāpeti, atha kho kevalaṃ attano bhuñjanatthāya, so sūpodanaviññattiyāyeva kāretabbo. Vuttañhetaṃ samantapāsādikāyaṃ “suddhāni sappiādīni viññāpetvā bhuñjanto pācittiyaṃ nāpajjati[M 0.0392], sekhiyesu sūpodanaviññattidukkaṭaṃ āpajjatī”ti (pāci. aṭṭha. 259). Sūpodanaviññattiyā kāretabboti “na sūpaṃ vā odanaṃ vā agilāno”tiādinā (pāci. 613) sikkhāpadena kāretabbo, dukkaṭena kāretabboti vuttaṃ hoti. Imināti iminā paṇītabhojanasikkhāpadena.

Whoever asks for something not for the purpose of medicine, but simply for his own eating, should be dealt with according to the rule on requesting soup and rice. For it is said in the Samantapāsādikā: ‘One who, having requested plain ghee and so on, eats it, does not incur a pācittiya offense, but incurs a dukkaṭa offense for requesting soup and rice among the Sekhiya rules’ (Pāci. aṭṭha. 259). The phrase ‘should be dealt with according to the rule on requesting soup and rice’ means he should be dealt with according to the training rule beginning, ‘Unless one is ill, one should not ask for soup or rice’ (Pāci. 613); this means he should be dealt with by a dukkaṭa. ‘By this’ (iminā) refers to this training rule on choice foods.

“Sappibhattaṃ dehī”ti vutte kiṃ hotīti āha “sappibhattaṃ ‘dehī’ti vutte panā”tiādi. Sūpodanaviññattiyā dukkaṭameva hotīti sambandho. Kasmāti āha “yasmā”tiādi. Atha yathā “paṇītabhojanānī”ti, evaṃ “sappibhatta”nti idampi kasmā na viññāyatīti ce? Anekantikattā. Tathā hi “paṇītabhojanānī”ti vutte “paṇītasaṃsaṭṭhāni bhojanāni [V 0.0359] paṇītabhojanānī”ti ayamattho ekantato paññāyati, “sappibhatta”nti vutte pana “sappimayaṃ bhattaṃ sappibhatta”ntipi viññāyamānattā ‘sappisaṃsaṭṭhaṃ bhattaṃ sappibhatta”nti ayamattho na ekantato paññāyati. Esa nayo “navanītabhattaṃ dehī”tiādīsupi.

‘When ‘Give rice with ghee’ is said, what happens?’ He explains, ‘When ‘Give rice with ghee’ is said, then...’ The connection is that it is only a dukkaṭa for requesting soup and rice. ‘Why is that?’ He explains, ‘Because...’ Now, if it is asked, ‘Just as with ‘choice foods,’ why is ‘rice with ghee’ not understood in the same way?’ The answer is because it is ambiguous. For when ‘choice foods’ is said, the meaning ‘foods mixed with choice things’ is definitively understood. But when ‘rice with ghee’ is said, since it can also be understood as ‘rice consisting of ghee,’ the meaning ‘rice mixed with ghee’ is not definitively clear. The same principle applies to ‘Give rice with fresh butter’ and so on.

Purimanayenevāti “bhattaṃ datvā sappiṃ katvā bhuñjā”ti purimeneva nayena. Sace pana “sappinā”ti vutte kevalaṃ sesesu navanītādīsu aññatarena deti, visaṅketameva hoti. Anāpattīti visaṅketattā sabbāhiyeva āpattīhi anāpatti. “Kiñcāpi anāpatti, attano pana payogena nibbattattā na bhuñjitabba”nti vadanti. Kappiyasappināti kappiyamaṃsasappinā. Esa nayo akappiyasappināti etthāpi. Kappiyākappiyatā hi maṃsānaṃyeva, na sappiādīnaṃ. Ṭhapetvā ekaṃ manussavasātelaṃ sabbesaṃ khīradadhisappinavanītavasātelesu akappiyaṃ nāma natthi.

The phrase ‘by the former method itself’ (purimanayeneva) refers to the former method, namely, ‘having given food, prepare ghee and eat.’ But if, when ‘with ghee’ is said, one gives only one of the remaining items like fresh butter, it is merely a misunderstanding. ‘There is no offense’ (anāpatti) means there is no offense whatsoever because of the misunderstanding. Some say, ‘Even though there is no offense, it should not be eaten because it was produced through one’s own effort.’ ‘With permissible ghee’ (kappiyasappinā) means with ghee from permissible meat. The same principle applies here to ‘with impermissible ghee’ (akappiyasappinā). For permissibility or impermissibility applies only to meats, not to ghee and the like. Except for human fat-oil, there is nothing impermissible among all milk, curd, ghee, fresh butter, and fat-oils.

Paribhogepi dukkaṭameva idha anadhippetattāti adhippāyo. Sace asati akappiyasappimhi purimanayeneva akappiyanavanītādīni deti “sappiṃ katvā bhuñjā”ti, akappiyasappināva dinnaṃ hoti. Yathā ca “kappiyasappinā dehī”ti vutte akappiyasappinā deti, visaṅketaṃ, evaṃ “‘akappiyasappinā’ti vutte kappiyasappinā detī”ti etthāpi paṭipāṭiyā ekamekaṃ vitthāretvā vuccamānepi ayamevattho vattabbo siyā, so ca saṅkhepenapi sakkā viññātunti vitthāranayaṃ hitvā imināva [M 0.0393] nayena sabbapadesu vinicchayo veditabboti vuttaṃ. Ayañhettha saṅkhepattho – yena yena viññatti hoti, tasmiṃ vā tassa mūle vā laddhe taṃ taṃ laddhameva hoti. Sace pana aññaṃ pāḷiyā āgataṃ vā anāgataṃ vā deti, visaṅketanti. Nānāṭṭhāne vāti tasmiṃyeva ghare sappiṃ, itarasmiṃ navanītantiādinā nānāṭṭhāne vā.

Even in use, it is only a dukkaṭa here because it was not intended—this is the idea. If, in the absence of impermissible ghee, one gives impermissible fresh butter and so on by the former method, saying, ‘Prepare ghee and eat,’ then it is considered as given as impermissible ghee. And just as when one is told, ‘Give with permissible ghee,’ but one gives with impermissible ghee, it is a misunderstanding, so too when one is told, ‘Give with impermissible ghee,’ but one gives with permissible ghee. Even if each of these cases were explained in detail one by one, the same meaning would be stated, and this can be understood even briefly. Therefore, omitting the detailed method, it is said that the decision should be understood in all cases by this method alone. Here is the summary of the meaning: By whatever a request is made, when that thing or its basis is obtained, that very thing is considered obtained. But if one gives something else, whether mentioned in the Pāḷi text or not, it is a misunderstanding. ‘Or in different places’ (nānāṭṭhāne vā) means, for example, ghee in one house and fresh butter in another, and so on, thus in different places.

Paṇītabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Choice Foods is completed.

10. Dantaponasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

10. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Tooth-Cleaning Sticks

Kāyenāti hatthādīsu yena kenaci sarīrāvayavena, antamaso pādaṅguliyāpi gaṇhanto kāyena gaṇhāti nāmāti veditabbo. Dānepi eseva nayo. Kāyappaṭibaddhenāti pattādīsu yena kenaci sarīrasambaddhena upakaraṇena. Dānepi eseva nayo. Kaṭacchuādīsu yena kenaci upakaraṇena dinnaṃ kāyappaṭibaddhena dinnaṃyeva hoti. Aññatarenāti kāyena vā kāyappaṭibaddhena vā nissaggiyena vāti attho. Tattha nissaggiyenāti (pāci. aṭṭha. 265) kāyato ca kāyappaṭibaddhato [V 0.0360] ca mocetvā hatthapāse ṭhitassa kāye vā kāyappaṭibaddhe vā pātiyamānañhi nissaggiyena payogena dinnaṃ nāma hoti. Tassāti paṭiggahitakassa. Vuttavipallāsavasenāti vuttassa paṭipakkhavasena. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yaṃ kāyakāyappaṭibaddhanissaggiyānaṃ aññatarena diyyamāne kāyena vā kāyappaṭibaddhena vā gaṇhāti, etaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ nāmāti.

‘By the body’ means that when one takes with any limb of the body, such as the hand, even down to a toe, it is to be understood as taking by the body. The same principle applies to giving. ‘By what is bound to the body’ means by any implement connected to the body, such as a bowl. The same principle applies to giving. What is given with any implement, such as a ladle, is indeed considered as given to what is bound to the body. ‘By any one of these’ means either by the body, by what is bound to the body, or by relinquishment. Here, ‘by relinquishment’ (Pāc. Aṭṭha. 265) means that when something is released from the giver's body or from what is bound to it, and is dropped onto the body or what is bound to the body of a recipient standing within hand's reach, this is called ‘given by the act of relinquishment.’ ‘His’ refers to the recipient. ‘Due to the contrary of what was said’ means due to the opposite of what was stated. This is what is meant: when something is given by any one of these—the body, what is bound to the body, or by relinquishment—and one receives it either with the body or with what is bound to the body, this is called ‘received.’

Saṃhārimenāti thāmamajjhimena purisena saṃhārimena, iminā asaṃhārime phalake vā pāsāṇe vā paṭiggahaṇaṃ na ruhatīti dasseti. Dhāretuṃ samatthenāti sandhāretuṃ yoggena, iminā sukhumesu tintiṇikādipaṇṇesu paṭiggahaṇaṃ na ruhatīti dasseti. Atatthajātakarukkhapaṇṇenāti jātaṭṭhānato cutena paduminipaṇṇādinā, iminā pana mahantepi tatthajātake paduminipaṇṇe vā kiṃsukapaṇṇādimhi vā paṭiggahetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Na hi taṃ kāyappaṭibaddhasaṅkhaṃ gacchatīti dasseti. Yathā ca [M 0.0394] tatthajātake, evaṃ khāṇuke bandhitvā ṭhapitamañcādimhipi. Nanu paṭibaddhappaṭibaddhenāpi pattādhārādinā paṭiggaṇhantassa paṭiggahaṇaṃ ruhati, atha kasmā kāyakāyappaṭibaddhehiyeva paṭiggahaṇaṃ idha vuttaṃ, na paṭibaddhappaṭibaddhenāpīti āha “paṭibaddhappaṭibaddhaṃ nāma idha natthī”ti. Keci pana “ādhārakena paṭiggahaṇaṃ kāyappaṭibaddhappaṭibaddhena paṭiggahaṇaṃ nāma hoti, tasmā na vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti, taṃ vacanamattameva. Atthato pana sabbampi taṃ kāyappaṭibaddhameva hotīti dasseti.

‘Movable’ means movable by a person of moderate strength. By this, it is shown that receiving on an immovable plank or stone is not permissible. ‘Capable of being held’ means suitable for holding. By this, it is shown that receiving on delicate leaves like tamarind leaves is not permissible. ‘By a leaf not grown there’ refers to a lotus leaf, etc., that has been cut from its place of origin. By this, it is shown that it is not permissible to receive on even a large lotus leaf or flame-of-the-forest leaf, etc., that has grown there. For it does not count as something bound to the body. And just as with what has grown there, so too with a couch, etc., bound to a stump or placed there. One might ask: ‘Is not receiving permissible for one who receives even by something connected to what is bound to the body, such as a bowl stand? If so, why is receiving mentioned here only by the body and by what is bound to the body, and not also by what is connected to what is bound to the body?’ He replies: ‘Here, there is no such thing as what is connected to what is bound to the body.’ Some, however, say: ‘Receiving by a stand is called receiving by what is connected to what is bound to the body, and therefore it is not permissible.’ But that is merely a verbal distinction. In essence, it is shown that all such cases are still considered bound to the body.

Akallakoti gilāno. Mukhena paṭiggaṇhātīti sahatthena gahetvā paribhuñjituṃ asakkonto mukhena paṭiggaṇhāti. Abhihaṭabhājanato patitarajampi vaṭṭati abhihaṭattāti adhippāho.

‘Akalla’ means sick. ‘He receives with his mouth’ means that being unable to take and consume with his own hand, he receives with his mouth. Even dust fallen from a vessel that has been brought near is permissible because it has been brought near—this is the intention.

Tasmiṃ ṭhatvāti tādise hatthapāse ṭhatvā. Yanti yaṃ bhāraṃ. Majjhimo purisoti thāmamajjhimapuriso. Vinaye paññattaṃ dukkaṭaṃ vinayadukkaṭaṃ. Taṃ anupasampannassa datvāti piṇḍāya caritvā vihāraṃ vā āsanasālaṃ vā gantvā taṃ bhikkhaṃ anupasampannassa datvā, idañca pubbābhogassa anurūpavasena vuttaṃ. Yasmā pana taṃ “anupasampannassa dassāmī”ti cittuppādamattena taṃsantakaṃ nāma na hoti, tasmā vināpi tassa dānādiṃ paṭiggahetvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati.

'Standing there' means standing within such arm's reach. 'Yanti' means whatever burden. 'Majjhimo puriso' means a man of moderate strength. The offense of wrong-doing prescribed in the Vinaya is a Vinaya wrong-doing. 'Giving it to one not yet fully ordained' means having gone for alms, then having gone to the monastery or the assembly hall, and having given that alms-food to one not yet fully ordained. This is stated in accordance with the initial intention. However, since it does not become his property merely by the arising of the thought 'I will give this to one not yet fully ordained,' it is permissible to partake of it even without giving it to him and so forth.

Assukheḷasiṅghāṇikādīsūti ettha assu nāma akkhijalaṃ. Kheḷo nāma lālā. Siṅghāṇikāti antosīsato pūtisemhabhāvaṃ āpannaṃ matthaluṅgaṃ galitvā tālumatthakavivarena otaritvā [V 0.0361] nāsāpuṭe pūretvā ṭhitaṃ vuccati, ādisaddena muttakarīsasemhadantamalaakkhigūthakaṇṇagūthakānaṃ, sarīre uṭṭhitaloṇassa ca gahaṇaṃ. Ṭhānatoti akkhikūpādito. Antarā ce gaṇhāti, kiṃ hotīti āha “uggahitakaṃ nāma hotī”ti, duṭṭhu gahitakaṃ nāma hotīti attho. Phalininti phalavantaṃ. Tatthajātakaphalinisākhāya vāti tasmiṃ rukkhe jātāya phalinisākhāya vā. Durupaciṇṇadukkaṭanti “na kattabba”nti vāritassa katattā duṭṭhu āciṇṇaṃ caritanti durupaciṇṇaṃ, tasmiṃ dukkaṭaṃ durupaciṇṇadukkaṭañca āpajjatīti attho.

Regarding 'tears, saliva, snot, etc.': here, 'assu' means eye-fluid. 'Kheḷo' means saliva. 'Siṅghāṇikā' refers to the brain-matter that, having become a putrid phlegm-like state inside the head, flows down through the opening at the top of the palate, fills the nasal passages, and remains there. The word 'etc.' includes urine, feces, phlegm, tooth-dirt, eye-discharge, earwax, and salt that arises on the body. 'From its place' means from the eye-socket, etc. If one takes it in between, what happens? He says, 'It is called "uggahitaka," ' meaning it is badly taken. 'Phalinī' means fruitful. 'Or by a fruitful branch grown there' means or by a fruitful branch grown on that tree. 'Durupaciṇṇadukkaṭa' means that because one has done what was prohibited as 'should not be done,' it is a badly practiced conduct, hence 'durupaciṇṇa'; and in that, one incurs a wrong-doing, which is a 'durupaciṇṇadukkaṭa'—this is the meaning.

Āharīyatīti āhāro, ajjhoharitabbaṃ yaṃ kiñci, idha pana cattāri kālikāni adhippetānīti āha “yaṃ kiñcī”tiādi. Tattha aruṇuggamanato [M 0.0395] yāva ṭhitamajjhanhikā bhuñjitabbato yāva kālo assāti yāvakālikaṃ. Aruṇuggamanato yāva yāmāvasānā pipāsāya sati pipāsacchedanatthaṃ pātabbato yāmo kālo assāti yāmakālikaṃ. Yāva sattāhaṃ nidahitvā paribhuñjitabbato sattāhaṃ kālo assāti sattāhakālikaṃ. Yāvajīvampi pariharitvā paribhuñjitabbato yāva jīvaṃ etassāti yāvajīvikaṃ. Tenāha “tatthā”tiādi.

'Āharīyati' means that which is brought, hence food; anything whatsoever that should be ingested. Here, however, four time-based categories are intended, as indicated by 'whatever,' etc. Of these: 'Yāvakālika' is that for which the time is until midday, from the rising of the dawn, because it should be eaten before the sun is at its zenith. 'Yāmakālika' is that for which the time is a watch, from the rising of the dawn until the end of the watch, because it should be drunk to relieve thirst if thirst arises. 'Sattāhakālika' is that for which the time is seven days, because it can be stored away and consumed within seven days. 'Yāvajīvika' is that which one may keep even for as long as life lasts and consume, that which belongs to one as long as life lasts. Therefore, he said, 'therein,' etc.

Vanamūlapattapupphaphalādīti ettha tāva mūlaṃ nāma mūlakakhārakacaccutambakādīnaṃ tesu tesu janapadesu pakatiāhāravasena manussānaṃ khādanīyatthañceva bhojanīyatthañca pharaṇakaṃ sūpeyyapaṇṇamūlaṃ. Pattaṃ nāma mūlakakhārakacaccutambakādīnaṃ tādisaṃyeva pattaṃ. Pupphaṃ nāma mūlakakhārakādīnaṃ tādisaṃyeva pupphaṃ. Phalaṃ nāma panasalabujādīnaṃ tesu tesu janapadesu pakatiāhāravasena manussānaṃ khādanīyatthañceva bhojanīyatthañca pharaṇakaṃ phalaṃ. Ādisaddena kandamūlādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ.

Regarding 'roots, leaves, flowers, fruits, etc., from the forest': here, first, 'roots' means roots such as radish, khāraka, kacchu, tamba, etc., which in those various regions are naturally consumed by people as food for both snacks and meals, roots which are suitable for soup. 'Leaves' means leaves of radish, khāraka, kacchu, tamba, and similar plants. 'Flowers' means the flowers of radish, khāraka, etc., of the same kind. 'Fruits' means fruits such as jackfruit and breadfruit, etc., which in those various regions are naturally consumed by people as food for both snacks and meals. The word 'etc.' includes bulbous roots, etc.

Ambapānanti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 300) āmehi vā pakkehi vā ambehi katapānaṃ. Tattha āmehi karontena ambataruṇādīni bhinditvā udake pakkhipitvā ātape ādiccapākena pacitvā parissāvetvā tadahupaṭiggahitehi madhusakkarakappūrādīhi yojetvā kātabbaṃ. Evaṃ kataṃ purebhattameva kappati. Anupasampannena kataṃ labhitvā pana purebhattaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ purebhattaṃ sāmisaparibhogenāpi vaṭṭati, pacchābhattaṃ nirāmisaparibhogena yāva aruṇuggamanā vaṭṭati. Esa nayo sabbapānesu.

'Mango drink' (Mahāvagga Aṭṭhakathā 300) is a beverage made from raw or ripe mangoes. In preparing it with raw mangoes, one should crush young mangoes, place them in water, cook them in the sun by solar heat, strain them, and then mix them with honey, sugar, camphor, etc., received on that day. Such a drink, when prepared, is permissible only before the meal. However, if it is prepared by an unordained person and received before the meal, what is received before the meal is permissible even with solid food; after the meal, it is permissible without solid food until sunrise. This principle applies to all drinks.

Tesu pana jambupānanti jambuphalehi katapānaṃ. Cocapānanti aṭṭhikehi kadaliphalehi katapānaṃ. Mocapānanti anaṭṭhikehi kadaliphalehi katapānaṃ. Madhukapānanti madhukānaṃ jātirasena katapānaṃ. Taṃ pana udakasambhinnaṃ vaṭṭati, suddhaṃ na vaṭṭati. Muddikāpānanti muddikā udake madditvā ambapānaṃ viya katapānaṃ[V 0.0362]. Sālūkapānanti rattuppalanīluppalādīnaṃ sālūke madditvā katapānaṃ. Phārusakapānanti phārusakehi ambapānaṃ viya katapānaṃ. Imināva nayena vettapānādīni veditabbāni. Etāni ca pana sabbāni pānāni aggipākāni na vaṭṭanti. Tenāha “sītodakenā”tiādi. Avasesesupi [M 0.0396] anuññātaphalapattapuppharasesūti dhaññaphalapakkasākamadhukapuppharasato avasesesu “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sabbaṃ phalarasaṃ ṭhapetvā dhaññaphalarasa”ntiādinā (mahāva. 300) anuññātakesu phalapattapuppharasesupi.

Among these, 'jambu drink' is a beverage made from jambu fruits. 'Coca drink' is a beverage made from bananas with seeds. 'Moca drink' is a beverage made from bananas without seeds. 'Madhuka drink' is a beverage made from the essence of madhuka. However, that mixed with water is permissible, but pure is not permissible. 'Muddikā drink' is a beverage made by crushing muddikā in water, like mango drink. 'Sālūka drink' is a beverage made by crushing the sālūka of red and blue lotuses, etc. 'Phārusaka drink' is a beverage made with phārusaka, like mango drink. In the same way, drinks made from vetta, etc., should be understood. And all these beverages are not permissible if cooked with fire. Therefore, he said, 'with cool water,' etc. And among the remaining permitted juices of fruits, leaves, and flowers—that is, among those remaining from grain-fruit juice, cooked vegetables, and madhuka flower juice—are the permitted juices of fruits, leaves, and flowers that the Buddha allowed when he said, 'Monks, I allow all fruit juice except grain-fruit juice,' etc. (Mahāvagga 300).

Khādanīyatthanti khādanīyena kattabbakiccaṃ. Neva pharatīti na nipphādeti. Anāhārepi udake āhārasaññāyāti “āhāraṃ āhareyyā”ti padassa padabhājane (pāci. 265) vuttamatthaṃ sammā asallakkhetvā “āharīyatīti āhāro”ti anāhārepi udake āhārasaññāya kukkuccāyantānaṃ. Dantapone ca “mukhadvāraṃ āhaṭaṃ ida”nti saññāyāti mukhadvāraṃ anāhaṭampi dantaponaṃ “mukhadvāraṃ āhaṭaṃ idaṃ dantapona”nti vipallatthasaññāya kukkuccāyantānaṃ. Yathāsukhaṃ pātunti paṭiggahetvā vā appaṭiggahetvā vā yathākāmaṃ pātuṃ. Dantaponaparibhogenāti dantakaṭṭhaparibhogena, dantadhovanādināti attho, iminā tassa pana rasaṃ gilituṃ na vaṭṭatīti dasseti.

'For the purpose of edible food' means the function to be done with edible food. 'Neva pharati' means it does not accomplish. 'Perceiving food in water, which is not food' refers to those who, without properly considering the meaning stated in the word analysis of the phrase 'should bring food' (Pācittiya 265), are anxious through perceiving even water, which is not food, as food, thinking, 'It is something brought as food.' And regarding tooth-cleaning sticks, 'perceiving "this has been brought to the mouth"' refers to those who are anxious due to a distorted perception, perceiving a tooth-cleaning stick, even though it is not brought to the mouth, as 'This tooth-cleaning stick has been brought to the mouth.' 'To drink as one pleases' means to drink as one wishes, whether having received it or not. 'By the use of a tooth-cleaning stick' refers to the use of a tooth-stick, meaning tooth-cleaning, etc.; by this, it is shown that one should not swallow its taste.

Cattāri mahāvikaṭānīti gūthaṃ, muttaṃ, chārikā, mattikā (mahāva. 268) ca “āsayādivasena virūpāni jātānī”ti katvā vikaṭānīti vā apakatibhojanattā vikaṭāni “virūpāni jātānī”ti vā attho. Sati paccayeti kāraṇe sati, sappadaṭṭheti attho. Dhūmādiabbohārikābhāvoti dhūmapupphagandhadantakhayādiabbohārikābhāvo.

The four great repulsive things are feces, urine, ashes, and clay (Mahāvagga 268). They are called 'repulsive' (vikaṭa) because they are produced in a foul way due to their origin, etc., or because they are not normal food; thus, 'vikaṭa' means 'produced in a foul way'. When the condition is present: 'when the cause is present' is the meaning, as in 'when bitten by a snake'. The absence of conventional signs like smoke, etc.: this means the absence of conventional signs such as smoke, flowers, fragrance, tooth decay, etc.

Dantaponasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning the tooth-stick is concluded.

Bhojanavaggo catuttho.

The Food Section, the Fourth.

5. Acelakavaggo

5. The Section on the Naked Ascetics.

1. Acelakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. The explanation of the training rule concerning the naked ascetic.

Acelakassāti [V 0.0363] yassa kassaci pabbajjāsamāpannassa naggassa. Paribbājakassāti ṭhapetvā bhikkhuñca sāmaṇerañca avasesassa yassa kassaci pabbajjāsamāpannassa. Paribbājikāyāti ṭhapetvā bhikkhuniṃ, sikkhamānaṃ, sāmaṇeriñca avasesāya yāya kāyaci pabbajjāsamāpannāya. Ete ca sabbe aññatitthiyā veditabbā. Tenāha “etesaṃ acelakādīnaṃ aññatitthiyāna”nti.

'Acelakassa' (for a naked ascetic) means for any naked person who has undertaken the ascetic life. 'Paribbājakassa' (for a wanderer) means for anyone who has undertaken the ascetic life, excluding a monk and a novice. 'Paribbājikāya' (for a female wanderer) means for any woman who has undertaken the ascetic life, excluding a bhikkhunī, a probationer, and a female novice. All these should be understood as belonging to other sects. Therefore, it is said, 'for these naked ascetics and others, who are adherents of other sects'.

Tesanti [M 0.0397] aññatitthiyānaṃ. Bhājanaṃ nikkhipitvāti āmisabharitaṃ bhājanaṃ nikkhipitvā. Bāhirālepanti telādiṃ.

'Tesaṃ' (for them) means for other sectarians. 'Bhājanaṃ nikkhipitvā' (having put down the bowl) means having put down a bowl filled with food. 'Bāhirālepaṃ' (external application) means oil and the like.

Acelakādayo yasmā, titthiyāva matā idha;

Tasmā titthiyanāmena, tikacchedo kato tayo.

Since the naked ascetics and others are considered sectarians here, therefore, a threefold division is made with the name 'sectarian'.

Atitthiyassa naggassa, tathā titthiyaliṅgino;

Gahaṭṭhassāpi bhikkhussa, kappatīti vinicchayo.

For a naked person who is not a sectarian, and likewise for one bearing sectarian marks, and even for a monk's householder, it is allowable—this is the judgment.

Atitthiyassa cittena, titthiyassa ca liṅgino;

Sotāpannādino dātuṃ, kappatītīdha no mati.

To give to one who is a non-sectarian in mind, to one bearing the marks of a sectarian, or to a Stream-enterer and the like—herein, it is not our view that this is allowable.

Acelakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning the naked ascetic is concluded.

2. Uyyojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. The Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Dismissal

Gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vāti ettha nagarampi gāmaggahaṇeneva gahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Pavisissāmāti ettha gahetvā “gantvā”ti pāṭhaseso, asamannāhāro vā tassā itthiyā tasmiṃ gāme sannihitabhāvaṃ ajānanto vā “ehāvuso, gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā piṇḍāya pavisissāmā”ti bhikkhuṃ [V 0.0364] gahetvā gantvāti attho. Yaṃ kiñci āmisanti yāguādikaṃ yaṃ kiñci āmisaṃ. Uyyojeyyāti attano kīḷānurūpaṃ itthiṃ disvā uyyojeyya pahiṇeyya. Tenāha “mātugāmena saddhi”ntiādi. Ādisaddena vuttāvasesaṃ kāyavacīdvāravītikkamaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. “Gacchā”tiādīni vatvāti “gacchāvuso, na me tayā saddhiṃ kathā vā nisajjā vā phāsu hoti, ekakassa me kathā vā nisajjā vā phāsu hotī”ti (pāci. 275) vatvā. Etaṃ anācāramevāti etaṃ yathāvuttaṃ hasanādianācārameva. Na aññaṃ patirūpaṃ kāraṇanti ṭhapetvā vuttappakāraṃ anācāraṃ ubhinnaṃ ekato na yāpanādiṃ aññaṃ patirūpakāraṇaṃ paccayaṃ karitvā na hotīti attho. Assāti uyyojakassa. Soti yo uyyojito, so.

‘A village or a town’: here, even a city should be understood as included by the term ‘village’. ‘We will enter’: here, ‘having gone’ (gantvā) is the remaining text, or it is a case of non-connection (asamannāhāra). Or, not knowing that that woman is present in that village, taking a monk and going, saying, ‘Come, friend, let us enter the village or town for alms’—this is the meaning. ‘Whatever material thing’: this means any material thing such as gruel, etc. ‘He should dismiss’: seeing a woman suitable for his sport, he should dismiss or send her away. Hence it is said, ‘with a woman,’ etc. By the term ‘etc.,’ the remaining transgressions of the doors of body and speech are included. ‘Having said, “Go,” etc.’: this means having said, ‘Go, friend, conversation or sitting together with you is not comfortable for me; conversation or sitting alone is comfortable for me’ (Pāci. 275). ‘This is merely improper conduct’: this means merely the aforementioned improper conduct such as laughing, etc. ‘No other suitable reason’: this means that, setting aside the aforementioned type of improper conduct, it is not done for any other suitable reason or condition, such as the two not getting along together, and so forth. ‘His’: this means of the one who dismisses. ‘He’: this means the one who is dismissed.

Anupasampanneti sāmaṇere. Sova idha anupasampannoti adhippetoti vadanti. Ubhinnampīti upasampannassa vā anupasampannassa vāti dvinnampi. Kalisāsanāropaneti (pāci. aṭṭha. 277) kalīti kodho, tassa sāsanaṃ āṇaṃ kalisāsanaṃ[M 0.0398], tassāropaneti attho, “appeva nāma imināpi ubbāḷho pakkameyyā”ti kodhavasena ṭhānanisajjādīsu dosaṃ dassetvā “passatha bho imassa ṭhānaṃ nisajjaṃ ālokitaṃ vilokitaṃ, khāṇu viya tiṭṭhati, sunakho viya nisīdati, makkaṭo viya ito cito ca viloketī”ti evaṃ amanāpavacanassa bhaṇaneti vuttaṃ hoti. Suddhacittena panevaṃ bhaṇane doso natthi. Evamādīhīti ettha ādisaddena “mahagghaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ passitvā lobhadhammaṃ uppādessatī”ti uyyojeti, “mātugāmaṃ passitvā anabhiratiṃ uppādessatī”ti uyyojeti, “gilānassa vā ohiyyakassa vā vihārapālassa vā yāguṃ vā bhattaṃ vā khādanīyaṃ vā nīharā”ti uyyojeti, “na anācāraṃ ācaritukāmo sati karaṇīye uyyojetī”ti (pāci. 278) etesaṃ gahaṇaṃ.

‘Anupasampanna’ (unordained): this refers to novices. They say that here, ‘unordained’ is intended to mean the novice himself. ‘Ubhinnampi’ (for both): this means for both, whether ordained or unordained. ‘Kalisāsanāropana’ (imposing harsh discipline) (Pāci. Aṭṭha. 277): ‘kalī’ means anger; its instruction is a command, hence ‘kalisāsana’. ‘Tassāropana’ means the act of imposing it. It is said that this means uttering unpleasant words out of anger, showing fault in matters like standing, sitting, etc., saying, ‘Perhaps, being annoyed by this, he might leave,’ or ‘See, sirs, his standing, sitting, looking around—he stands like a post, sits like a dog, looks around from here and there like a monkey.’ However, if spoken with a pure mind, there is no fault. ‘Evamādīhi’ (and so forth): here, by the term ‘etc.,’ it includes cases where one dismisses another thinking, ‘He will generate a state of greed upon seeing expensive goods’; or dismisses thinking, ‘He will generate discontent upon seeing a woman’; or dismisses another to fetch gruel, food, or edibles for the sick, for one who has been left behind, or for the monastery keeper; or dismisses when there is a duty to perform, not intending to engage in improper conduct (Pāci. 278).

Uyyojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Dismissal is concluded.

3. Sabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Eating Together

“Sabhojane”ti bāhiratthasamāsoyaṃ, ubhasadde ukārassa ca lopoti āha “saha ubhohi janehī”tiādi. Tattha ubhohi janehīti jāyā ca pati cāti ubhohi janehi. Bhuñjitabbanti vā bhojanaṃ, itthī ca puriso ca, tena saha vattatīti sabhojananti āha “atha vā”tiādi. Rāgapariyuṭṭhitassāti methunādhippāyassa. Sayanigharanti sayanīyagharaṃ, vāsagehanti attho. Mahallakassāti mahallakassa sayanigharassa. Piṭṭhasaṅghāṭatoti dvārabāhato khuddakassa [V 0.0365] vāti yathā tathā vā katassa khuddakassa sayanigharassa. Vemajjhaṃ atikkamitvā nisīdeyyāti piṭṭhivaṃsaṃ atikkamitvā nisīdeyya. Khuddakaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. pācittiya 3.280) nāma sayanigharaṃ vitthārato pañcahatthappamāṇaṃ hoti, tassa ca majjhimaṭṭhānaṃ piṭṭhasaṅghāṭato aḍḍhateyyahatthappamāṇameva hoti, tasmā tādise sayanighare piṭṭhasaṅghāṭato hatthapāsaṃ vijahitvā nisinno piṭṭhivaṃsaṃ atikkamitvā nisinno nāma hoti. Evaṃ nisinno ca vemajjhaṃ atikkamitvā nisinno nāma hoti. Tena vuttaṃ pāḷiyaṃ “piṭṭhivaṃsaṃ atikkamitvā nisīdatī”ti (pāci. 281). Sacittakañcettha anupavisitvā nisīdanacittena daṭṭhabbaṃ.

‘Sabhojane’: this is an external compound. He says there is an elision of the ‘u’ sound in the word ‘ubha’, explaining it as ‘saha ubhohi janehi’ (with both persons), and so on. Here, ‘both persons’ refers to the wife and the husband—that is, both of them. Or alternatively, ‘bhojana’ means that which is to be eaten, and ‘sabhojana’ means that which occurs together with a woman and a man, as stated in ‘or alternatively,’ and so on. ‘Rāgapariyuṭṭhitassa’ refers to one overcome by lust, with the intention of sexual intercourse. ‘Sayanighara’ means a bedroom, that is, a dwelling place. ‘Mahallakassa’ refers to a large bedroom. ‘Piṭṭhasaṅghāṭato’ means from the back panel of a small bedroom made from a door-post, or of a small one constructed in some other way. ‘Vemajjaṃ atikkamitvā nisīdeyya’ means one should sit having passed beyond the ridge-pole. A ‘khuddaka’ (small) bedroom is defined as being five cubits in width, and its middle point from the back panel is only two and a half cubits. Therefore, in such a bedroom, one sitting having left an arm's length from the back panel is called one sitting having passed beyond the ridge-pole. Thus, one sitting in this way is called one sitting having passed beyond the middle. For this reason it is said in the Pāli: ‘one sits having passed beyond the ridge-pole’ (Pāci. 281). And here, ‘with intention’ should be understood as with the intention of entering and sitting.

Sabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Eating Together is concluded.

4-5. Rahopaṭicchannarahonisajjasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4-5. The Commentary on the Training Rules Concerning Sitting in Seclusion and in a Concealed Place

Catutthapañcamasikkhāpade [M 0.0399] yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ sabbaṃ aniyatadvaye vuttamevāti āha “seso kathānayo aniyatadvaye vuttanayeneva veditabbo”ti.

Whatever needs to be said concerning the fourth and fifth training rules has already been stated in the two indefinite rules. Therefore, it is said: ‘The remaining method of exposition should be understood in the same way as explained in the two indefinite rules.’

Rahopaṭicchannarahonisajjasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rules Concerning Sitting in Seclusion and in a Concealed Place is concluded.

6. Cārittasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Conduct

Antoupacārasīmāya dassanūpacāre bhikkhuṃ disvāti yattha ṭhitassa kulāni payirupāsanacittaṃ uppannaṃ, tato paṭṭhāya gacchanto antoupacārasīmāya dassanūpacāre bhikkhuṃ passe vā abhimukhe vā disvā. Pakativacanenāti yaṃ dvādasahatthabbhantare ṭhitena sotuṃ sakkā, tādisena vacanena, ito cito ca pariyesitvā ārocanakiccaṃ pana natthi. Yo hi evaṃ pariyesitabbo, so asantoyeva. Tenāha “tādisa”ntiādi. Anāpucchitvāti anārocetvā.

‘Having seen a monk within the boundary of approach and sight’: this means that, where the thought to attend upon families has arisen for one who is standing, then, going forth from there, one sees a monk within the boundary of approach and sight, whether at one's side or in front. ‘By ordinary speech’ means by such speech as can be heard by one standing within a distance of twelve cubits; but there is no need to search around here and there to inform him. For one who must be sought out in this way is indeed not present. Therefore, it is said, ‘such,’ and so on. ‘Without asking permission’ means without informing.

Antarārāmabhikkhunupassayatitthiyaseyyapaṭikkamanabhattiyagharānīti ettha antarārāmanti antogāme vihāro. Paṭikkamananti āsanasālā. Bhattiyagharanti nimantitagharaṃ vā salākabhattādidāyakānaṃ vā gharaṃ. Āpadāsūti jīvitabrahmacariyantarāyesu. Kiriyākiriyanti ettha kulesu cārittāpajjanaṃ kiriyaṃ, anāpucchanaṃ akiriyanti veditabbaṃ.

‘Within the monastery, the nuns' quarters, the heretics' lodging, the assembly hall, the meal house’—here, ‘within the monastery’ means a monastery inside the village. ‘Assembly hall’ means a sitting hall. ‘Meal house’ means either an invited house or the house of those who give alms such as ticketed food. ‘In times of danger’ means dangers to life or to the holy life. ‘Action and inaction’—here, ‘action’ should be understood as undertaking the alms-round among families, and ‘inaction’ as not asking permission.

Cārittasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Conduct is concluded.

7. Mahānāmasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Mahānāma Training Rule

Sabbañcetaṃ [V 0.0366] vatthuvasena vuttanti “agilānena bhikkhunā catumāsapaccayapavāraṇā sāditabbā aññatra punapavāraṇāya aññatra niccapavāraṇāyā”ti (pāci. 306) etaṃ sabbaṃ sikkhāpadanidānasaṅkhātassa vatthuno vasena vuttaṃ. Tattha hi mahānāmena sakkena “icchāmahaṃ, bhante, saṅghaṃ catumāsaṃ bhesajjena pavāretu”ntiādinā (pāci. 303) ussannussannena ca bhesajjena catumāsaṃ [M 0.0400] puna niccaṃ pavāraṇā katā, tasmā bhagavatā tassa vasena evaṃ vuttanti vuttaṃ hoti. Aññatra punapavāraṇāyāti yadi punapavāraṇā atthi, taṃ ṭhapetvā. Aññatra niccapavāraṇāyāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Yadi pana tāpi atthi, sāditabbāvāti adhippāyo. Tenāha “ayaṃ panettha attho”tiādi. Tatthāti tissaṃ pavāraṇāyaṃ. Bhesajjehi vā paricchedo kato hotīti “sappi tela”nti evamādinā nāmavasena vā “patthena nāḷiyā āḷhakenā”tiādinā parimāṇavasena vā “ettakāni vā bhesajjāni viññāpetabbānī”ti bhesajjehi paricchedo kato hoti. Nabhesajjakaraṇīyeti missakabhattenāpi ce yāpetuṃ sakkoti, nabhesajjakaraṇīyaṃ nāma hoti. Aññaṃ bhesajjanti sappinā pavārito telaṃ, āḷhakena pavārito doṇaṃ.

'All this is stated based on the incident' means that the entire statement 'A healthy monk should accept the four-month invitation for requisites, except for a repeated invitation or a permanent invitation' (Pāci. 306) is stated based on the incident that constitutes the origin of the training rule. For there, Mahānāma the Sakyan said, 'Venerable sir, I wish to invite the Saṅgha for four months with medicine,' and so on (Pāci. 303). And due to the abundant supply of medicine, a repeated and permanent invitation for four months was made. Therefore, it is said that the Blessed One spoke thus based on that. 'Except for a repeated invitation' means excluding it if there is a repeated invitation. The same principle applies here too for 'except for a permanent invitation.' If those also exist, then the intention is that they should be accepted. Therefore, it is said, 'But this is the meaning here,' and so on. 'There' refers to the three invitations. 'A limit is set with medicines' means that a limit is set with medicines either by name, such as 'ghee, oil,' and so on, or by measure, such as 'by the bowl, by the nāḷi, by the āḷhaka,' and so on, or by stating, 'Only this amount of medicines should be requested.' 'No need for medicine' means that even if one can sustain oneself with mixed food, it is called 'no need for medicine.' 'Other medicine' means if one was invited with ghee, then one asks for oil; if invited with an āḷhaka, then one asks for a doṇa.

Yathābhūtaṃ ācikkhitvāti “imehi tayā bhesajjehi pavāritamhā, amhākañca iminā ca iminā ca bhesajjena attho, yāsu tayā rattīsu pavāritamhā, tā rattiyo vītivattā, amhākañca bhesajjena attho”ti yathābhūtaṃ ārocetvā. Evañca viññāpetuṃ gilānova labhati, na itaro.

'Having informed truthfully' means declaring accurately: 'We were invited by you with these medicines, and we also need this and that medicine. The nights for which we were invited by you have passed, and we still need medicine.' Only the sick one can request in this way, not another.

Mahānāmasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Mahānāma training rule is concluded.

8. Uyyuttasenāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

8. Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning a Prepared Army

Caturaṅgininti hatthiassarathapattīti cattāri aṅgāni etissāti caturaṅginī, taṃ caturaṅginiṃ. “Dvādasapuriso hatthī, tipuriso asso, catupuriso ratho, cattāro purisā sarahatthā pattī”ti (pāci. 314) ayaṃ pacchimakoṭiyā caturaṅgasamannāgatā senā nāma, īdisaṃ senanti attho. Taṃ pana vijahitvāti kenaci antaritā vā ninnaṃ oruḷhā vā na dissati, idha ṭhatvāna sakkā daṭṭhunti taṃ dassanūpacāraṃ vijahitvā aññaṃ ṭhānaṃ gantvā.

The fourfold army—elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—is called "four-limbed" (caturaṅginī) because it has four limbs. "An elephant with twelve men, a horse with three men, a chariot with four men, and four men as infantry with weapons in hand" (Pāc. 314): this is an army endowed with four divisions at its minimum. Such is the meaning of "an army like this." But "having abandoned it" means having gone to another place, leaving behind that proximity for seeing, where it is not seen, being obstructed by something or having descended into a low-lying area, even though it would be possible to see it from that spot.

Senādassanavatthusminti [V 0.0367] senaṃ dassanāya gamanavatthusmiṃ. Ayameva vā pāṭho. Hatthiādīsu ekamekanti hatthiādīsu catūsu aṅgesu ekamekaṃ, antamaso [M 0.0401] ekapurisāruḷhahatthimpi ekampi sarahatthaṃ purisanti attho. Anuyyuttā nāma rājā uyyānaṃ vā nadiṃ vā gacchati, evaṃ anuyyuttā hoti. Tathārūpappaccayeti “mātulo senāya gilāno hotī”tiādike (pāci. 312) anurūpakāraṇe sati. Āpadāsūti jīvitabrahmacariyantarāyesu “ettha gato muccissāmī”ti gacchato anāpatti.

In 'the section on the reason for seeing the army' means regarding the reason for going to see the army. Or this may be the reading. 'Among elephants and so on, one by one' means among the four divisions of the army, namely elephants and so on, each one; even a single elephant mounted by one man, or a single armed man—this is the meaning. An army is called `anuyyuttā` (not engaged) when the king goes to a park or a river; in such a case, it is `anuyyuttā`. 'Under such circumstances' means in cases such as 'the maternal uncle is sick in the army' (Pāc. 312), when there is a suitable reason. 'In times of danger' means in dangers to life or the holy life, there is no offense for one who goes thinking, 'Going there, I will be freed.'

Uyyuttasenāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning a prepared army is concluded.

9. Senāvāsasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

9. Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Lodging in an Army

Paṭisenāruddhāyāti yathā sañcāro chijjati, evaṃ paṭisenāya ruddhāya senāya. Kenaci palibuddhassāti verikena vā issarena vā kenaci ruddhassa.

`Paṭisenāruddhāya` means by an army that is obstructed by an opposing army in such a way that movement is cut off. `Kenaci palibuddhassa` means obstructed by someone, such as an enemy or a lord.

Senāvāsasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning lodging in an army is concluded.

10. Uyyodhikasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning a Military Review

Sampahāraṭṭhānassāti yuddhabhūmiyā. Balassa aggaṃ jānantīti “ettakā hatthī, ettakā assā, ettakā rathā, ettakā pattī”ti (pāci. 324) balassa koṭṭhāsaṃ jānanti. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, vihāraggenā”tiādīsu (cūḷava. 318) viya koṭṭhāsattho hettha aggasaddo. Tenāha “balagaṇanaṭṭhānanti attho”ti. Senāya viyūhanti “ito hatthī hontu, ito assā hontu, ito rathā hontu, ito pattī hontū”ti (pāci. 324) senāya ṭhapanaṃ, rāsiṃ katvā ṭhapananti attho. Tenāha “senāsannivesassetaṃ nāma”nti. Dvādasapuriso hatthīti cattāro ārohakā, ekekapādarakkhakā dve dveti evaṃ dvādasapuriso hatthī. Tipuriso assoti eko ārohako, dve pādarakkhakāti evaṃ tipuriso asso. Catupuriso rathoti eko sārathi, eko yodho, dve āṇirakkhakāti evaṃ catupuriso rathoti.

'Sampahāraṭṭhāna' means the battlefield. 'They know the strength of the army' means they know the portion of the army, thinking, 'So many elephants, so many horses, so many chariots, so many foot soldiers' (Pāc. 324). Just as in phrases like 'I allow, monks, the foremost part of the dwelling' (Cūḷava. 318), the word 'agga' here has the meaning of a portion. Therefore, it is said, 'the meaning is a place for counting the army.' 'They array the army' means arranging the army, arranging them in formations, thinking, 'Let the elephants be here, the horses here, the chariots here, the foot soldiers here' (Pāc. 324). Therefore, it is said, 'this is a name for the encampment of the army.' An elephant with twelve men means four riders, and two foot-guards for each, thus an elephant with twelve men. A horse with three men means one rider and two foot-guards; thus a horse with three men. A chariot with four men means one charioteer, one warrior, and two wheel-guards; thus a chariot with four men.

Uyyodhikasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning a military review is concluded.

Acelakavaggo pañcamo.

The Fifth Chapter on the Naked Ascetics.

6. Surāpānavaggo

6. The Chapter on Intoxicating Drinks

1. Surāpānasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Intoxicating Drinks

Piṭṭhādīhi [M 0.0402][V 0.0368] kataṃ majjaṃ surāti piṭṭhapūvaodanakiṇṇasambhārehi kataṃ majjaṃ surāti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – piṭṭhasurā, pūvasurā, odanasurā, kiṇṇapakkhittā, sambhārasaṃyuttāti (pāci. 328) imāni pañca surā nāmāti. Tattha piṭṭhaṃ bhājane pakkhipitvā tajjaṃ udakaṃ datvā madditvā katā piṭṭhasurā (sārattha. ṭī. pācittiya 3.326-328). Evaṃ sesāsupi. Kiṇṇāti pana tassā surāya bījaṃ vuccati. Ye “surāmodakā”tipi vuccanti, te pakkhipitvā katā kiṇṇapakkhittā. Harītakisāsapādinānāsambhārehi saṃyojitā sambhārasaṃyuttā.

'Surā' means liquor made from flour and so on; the meaning is that liquor made from flour, cakes, rice, yeast, or other ingredients is called surā. This is stated: 'flour-surā, cake-surā, rice-surā, that mixed with yeast, and that combined with ingredients' (Pāc. 328)—these five are called surā. Here, flour-surā is made by putting flour in a container, adding suitable water, and kneading it (Sārattha. Ṭī. Pācittiya 3.326-328). The same applies to the rest. Kiṇṇa, moreover, is said to be the starter (seed) of that surā. That which is made by mixing in what are also called 'surāmodakā' is kiṇṇapakkhittā. That which is combined with various ingredients, such as harītakī and mustard seeds, is sambhārasaṃyuttā.

Pupphādīhi kato āsavo merayanti pupphaphalamadhuguḷasambhārehi kato ciraparivāsito merayanti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – pupphāsavo, phalāsavo, madhvāsavo, guḷāsavo, sambhārasaṃyuttoti pañcamerayaṃ nāmāti. Tattha madhukatālanāḷikerādi puppharaso ciraparivāsito pupphāsavo. Panasādiphalaraso phalāsavo. Muddikāraso madhvāsavo. Samantapāsādikāyaṃ pana “phalāsavo nāma muddikāphalādīni madditvā tesaṃ rasena kato. Madhvāsavo nāma muddikānaṃ jātirasena kato, makkhikāmadhunāpi karīyatīti vadantī”ti (pāci. aṭṭha. 328) vuttaṃ. Ucchuraso guḷāsavo. Harītakāmalakakaṭukabhaṇḍādinānāsambhārānaṃ raso ciraparivāsito sambhārasaṃyutto. Ettha ca surāya, merayassa ca samānepi sambhārasaṃyoge madditvā katā surā, ciraparivāsitamattena merayanti evamimesaṃ nānākaraṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Bījato paṭṭhāyāti sambhāre paṭiyādetvā cāṭiyaṃ pakkhittakālato ceva tālanāḷikerādīnaṃ puppharasassa abhinavakālato ca paṭṭhāya.

'Meraya' means a fermented drink made from flowers and so on; the meaning is that a fermented drink made from flowers, fruits, honey, molasses, or other ingredients and aged for a long time is called meraya. This is stated: 'flower-meraya, fruit-meraya, honey-meraya, molasses-meraya, and ingredient-combined meraya'—these five are called meraya. Here, flower-meraya is the juice of flowers like madhuka, tāla palm, and coconut, aged for a long time. Fruit-meraya is the juice of fruits like jackfruit. Honey-meraya is the juice of grapes. In the Samantapāsādikā, it is said: 'Fruit-meraya is made by crushing fruits like grapes and using their juice. Honey-meraya is made from the natural juice of grapes, or they say it can also be made with bee honey' (Pāc. Aṭṭha. 328). Molasses-meraya is the juice of sugarcane. Ingredient-combined meraya is the juice of various ingredients like harītakī, āmalaka, and pungent spices, aged for a long time. Here, even though surā and meraya share a combination of ingredients, surā is made by pressing or kneading, while meraya is distinguished by being simply aged—this difference should be noted. 'Starting from the seed' means from the time of preparing the ingredients and adding them to the jar, or from the fresh juice of flowers like tāla palm and coconut.

Loṇasovīrakaṃ vā suttaṃ vāti ime dve anekehi bhesajjehi abhisaṅkhatā āsavavisesā. Vāsaggāhāpanatthanti sugandhabhāvagāhāpanatthaṃ. Vatthuṃ ajānanatāya cettha acittakatā veditabbā. Akusaleneva pātabbatāya lokavajjaṃ. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ sabbaṃ paṭhamapārājikavaṇṇanāya vuttanayameva.

'Loṇasovīraka' or 'sutta'—these two are special kinds of fermented liquor prepared with various medicinal ingredients. 'For the purpose of absorbing scent' means for the purpose of absorbing the quality of fragrance. Here, since the object is not known, it should be understood as unintentional. Because it is to be drunk only with an unwholesome mind, it is a worldly fault. Whatever else should be said here is entirely in accordance with the method stated in the explanation of the first pārājika.

Surāpānasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on drinking intoxicating beverages is concluded.

2. Aṅgulipatodakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Poking with a Finger

Hasādhippāyassāti [M 0.0403][V 0.0369] khiḍḍādhippāyassa, iminā kāyasaṃsaggādhippāyaṃ paṭikkhipati.

'With the intention of laughter' means with the intention of play. By this, the intention of bodily contact is precluded.

Ettha ca bhikkhunimpi hasādhippāyena phusato bhikkhussa dukkaṭaṃ. Tathā bhikkhumpi phusantiyā bhikkhuniyāti āha “idha pana bhikkhunīpi bhikkhussa, bhikkhu ca bhikkhuniyā anupasampanno evā”ti. Kāyappaṭibaddhādīsu sabbatthāti “kāyena kāyappaṭibaddhe, kāyappaṭibaddhena kāye, kāyappaṭibaddhena kāyappaṭibaddhe, nissaggiyena kāye, nissaggiyena kāyappaṭibaddhe, nissaggiyena nissaggiye”ti (pāci. 332) sabbattha.
