By this same method, a park site, a dwelling, and a dwelling site should also be exchanged for a grove. And for a park site, whether large or small, a park, a park site, a dwelling, or a dwelling site may be exchanged.

Kathaṃ vihārena (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 321; vi. saṅga. aṭṭha. 228) vihāro parivattetabbo? Saṅghassa antogāme gehaṃ hoti, manussānaṃ vihāramajjhe pāsādo, ubhopi agghena samakā. Sace manussā tena pāsādena taṃ gehaṃ yācanti, sampaṭicchituṃ vaṭṭati. Bhikkhūnaṃ ce mahagghataraṃ gehaṃ hoti, “mahagghataraṃ amhākaṃ geha”nti vutte “kiñcāpi mahagghataraṃ pabbajitānaṃ asāruppaṃ, na sakkā tattha pabbajitehi vasituṃ, idaṃ pana sāruppaṃ, gaṇhathā”ti vadanti, evampi sampaṭicchituṃ vaṭṭati. Sace pana manussānaṃ mahagghaṃ hoti “nanu tumhākaṃ gehaṃ mahaggha”nti vattabbaṃ. “Hotu, bhante, amhākaṃ puññaṃ bhavissati, gaṇhathā”ti vutte pana sampaṭicchituṃ vaṭṭati. Evaṃ vihārena vihāro parivattetabbo. Eteneva nayena vihāravatthupi ārāmopi ārāmavatthupi vihārena parivattetabbaṃ. Vihāravatthunā ca mahagghena vā appagghena vā [M 0.0424] vihāraṃ vihāravatthuṃ ārāmaṃ ārāmavatthuṃ. Evaṃ tāva thāvarena thāvaraparivattanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

How should a dwelling be exchanged for another dwelling? (Cūḷavagga Aṭṭhakathā 321; Vinaya Saṅgaha Aṭṭhakathā 228) There is a house belonging to the Sangha within the village, and a mansion belonging to laypeople in the middle of the monastery. Both are of equal value. If the laypeople request that house in exchange for the mansion, it is permissible to accept. If the monks have a more valuable house, and when it is said, 'Our house is more valuable,' the laypeople say, 'Although it is more valuable, it is unsuitable for ascetics; ascetics cannot dwell there. But this one is suitable—take it,' even so, it is permissible to accept. However, if the laypeople's dwelling is more valuable, it should be said, 'Is not your house more valuable?' If they reply, 'Let it be, venerable sirs, it will be our merit—take it,' then it is permissible to accept. In this way, a dwelling should be exchanged for another dwelling. By this same method, a dwelling site, a grove, and a grove site may also be exchanged for a dwelling. And a dwelling site, whether more or less valuable, may be exchanged for a dwelling, a dwelling site, a grove, or a grove site. Thus, the exchange of immovable property for immovable property should be understood.

Itarena itaraparivattane pana mañcapīṭhaṃ mahantaṃ vā hotu, khuddakaṃ vā (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 321; vi. saṅga. aṭṭha. 228), antamaso caturaṅgulapādakaṃ gāmadārakehi paṃsvāgārakesu kīḷantehi katampi saṅghassa dinnakālato paṭṭhāya garubhaṇḍaṃ hoti. Sacepi rājā vā rājamahāmattādayo vā ekappahāreneva mañcasataṃ vā mañcasahassaṃ vā denti, sabbe kappiyamañcā sampaṭicchitabbā, sampaṭicchitvā vuḍḍhappaṭipāṭiyā “saṅghikaparibhogena paribhuñjathā”ti dātabbā, na puggalikaparibhogena dātabbā. Atirekamañce bhaṇḍāgārādīsu paññapetvā pattacīvaraṃ nikkhipitvā paribhuñjitumpi vaṭṭati. Bahisīmāya “saṅghassa demā”ti dinnamañco [V 0.0390] saṅghattherassa vasanaṭṭhāne dātabbo. Tattha ce bahū mañcā honti, mañcena kammaṃ natthi. Yassa vasanaṭṭhāne kammaṃ atthi, tattha “saṅghikaparibhogena paribhuñjathā”ti dātabbo, na puggalikabhogena. Mahagghena satagghanakena vā sahassagghanakena vā mañcena aññaṃ mañcasataṃ labhati, parivattetvā gahetabbaṃ. Na kevalaṃ mañcena mañcoyeva, ārāmaārāmavatthuvihāravihāravatthupīṭhabhisibibbohanānipi parivattetuṃ vaṭṭati. Eseva nayo pīṭhabhisibibbohanesupi. Varasenāsanādīnaṃ saṃrakkhaṇatthanti sace dubbhikkhaṃ hoti, bhikkhū piṇḍapātena na yāpenti, ettha rājarogacorabhayāni, aññattha gacchantānaṃ vihārā palujjanti, tālanāḷikerādike vināsenti, senāsanapaccayaṃ sandhāya yāpetuṃ sakkā hoti, evarūpe kāle varasenāsanādīnaṃ saṃrakkhaṇatthaṃ. Lāmakāni vissajjetunti lāmakaṃ lāmakaṃ vissajjetuṃ, lāmakakoṭiyā vissajjetunti adhippāyo. Vissajjetvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭatīti vissajjetvā tato laddhayāgubhattacīvarādīni paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Kāḷalohatambalohakaṃsalohavaṭṭalohānanti ettha kaṃsalohaṃ, vaṭṭalohañca kittimalohaṃ. Tīṇi hi kittimalohāni kaṃsalohaṃ, vaṭṭalohaṃ, ārakūṭanti. Tattha tiputambe missetvā kataṃ kaṃsalohaṃ, sītatambe missetvā kataṃ vaṭṭalohaṃ, rasakatambe missetvā kataṃ ārakūṭaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “kaṃsalohaṃ, vaṭṭalohañca kittimaloha”nti. Tato atirekanti tato atirekaggaṇhanako.

In the case of exchanging one thing for another, whether a bed or a bench is large or small (Cūḷavagga Aṭṭhakathā 321; Vinaya Saṅgaha Aṭṭhakathā 228), even one with four-inch legs made by village boys playing in sand-houses becomes heavy property for the Sangha from the moment it is given. Even if a king or royal ministers and so on donate a hundred or a thousand beds at once, all the allowable beds must be accepted. After accepting them, they should be distributed according to seniority with the instruction, 'Use these as communal property,' not as personal property. If there are excess beds, it is permissible to arrange them in storerooms and so on, and use them for placing one's bowl and robe. A bed given outside the boundary with the words, 'We give this to the Sangha,' should be given to the senior monk’s dwelling place. If there are many beds there and there is no use for a bed, it should be given where there is use for it with the instruction, 'Use this as communal property,' not as personal property. If by exchanging a single bed worth a hundred or a thousand one obtains a hundred other beds, they should be accepted in exchange. Not only may a bed be exchanged for a bed, but it is also permissible to exchange it for a grove, a grove site, a dwelling, a dwelling site, a bench, a mattress, or a bolster. The same principle applies to benches, mattresses, and bolsters. 'For the protection of superior lodgings, etc.': if there is a famine and monks cannot sustain themselves on almsfood, if there are dangers from kings, diseases, or thieves here, if monasteries fall into ruin when monks go elsewhere, if they destroy palm trees, coconut trees, and so on, and it is possible to sustain oneself by means of the requisites for lodgings, in such a time, it is for the protection of superior lodgings, etc. 'Inferior items should be disposed of' means that one should dispose of inferior items. The meaning is that they should be disposed of as items of the lowest grade. 'It is permissible to use after disposing of them' means it is permissible to use the gruel, rice, robes, etc., obtained from the proceeds after disposing of them. 'Black iron, copper, bronze, and vaṭṭaloha': here, bronze and vaṭṭaloha are artificial metal. There are three types of artificial metal: bronze, vaṭṭaloha, and ārakūṭa. Among these, bronze is made by mixing tin and copper, vaṭṭaloha by mixing lead and copper, and ārakūṭa by mixing zinc and copper. Hence, it is said, 'bronze and vaṭṭaloha are artificial metal.' 'Anything beyond that' means one who takes in excess.

Sarakoti [M 0.0425] majjhe makuḷaṃ dassetvā mukhavaṭṭivitthataṃ katvā piṭṭhito nāmetvā kātabbaṃ ekaṃ bhājanaṃ. “Sarāva”ntipi vadanti. Ādisaddena kañcanakādīnaṃ gihiupakaraṇānaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Tāni hi khuddakānipi garubhaṇḍāneva gihiupakaraṇattāti. Pi-saddena pageva mahantānīti dasseti. Imāni pana bhājanīyāni bhikkhūpakaraṇattāti adhippāyo. Yathā ca etāni, evaṃ kuṇḍikāpi bhājanīyā. Vakkhati hi “yathā ca mattikābhaṇḍe, evaṃ lohabhaṇḍepi kuṇḍikā bhājanīyakoṭṭhāsameva bhajatī”ti (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. dubbalasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā). Saṅghikaparibhogenāti āgantukānaṃ vuḍḍhatarānaṃ datvā paribhogena. Gihivikaṭāti gihīhi vikatā paññattā, attano vā santakakaraṇena virūpaṃ katā. Puggalikaparibhogena na vaṭṭatīti āgantukānaṃ adatvā attano santakaṃ viya gahetvā pariharitvā paribhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭati. Pipphalikoti kattari. Ārakaṇṭakaṃ sūcivedhakaṃ. Tāḷaṃ yantaṃ. Kattarayaṭṭhivedhako kattarayaṭṭhivalayaṃ. Yathā tathā ghanakataṃ lohanti lohavaṭṭi lohaguḷo lohapiṇḍi lohacakkalikanti evaṃ ghanakataṃ lohaṃ. Khīrapāsāṇamayānīti mudukakhīravaṇṇapāsāṇamayāni.

'Sarako' is a certain vessel that should be made showing a bud in the middle, with its mouth widened, and bent back from the rim. They also call it a 'sarāva.' By the word 'ādi,' the inclusion of household utensils such as golden ones is meant. For these, even if small, are heavy items because they are household utensils. By the word 'pi,' it is shown 'how much more so the large ones.' But these are divisible because they are requisites for monks; this is the intention. And just as these, so too a water pitcher is divisible. For it will be said: 'Just as with earthenware, so too with metalware, a water pitcher falls into the category of divisible items' (Kaṅkhā-aṭṭhakathā, Dubbalasikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā). 'By communal use' means by use after giving to senior visiting monks. 'Altered by laypeople' means altered or designated by laypeople, or made misshapen by one's own doing. 'It is not permissible for personal use' means it is not permissible to take it as one's own, carry it about, and use it without giving it to visiting monks. 'Pipphaliko' is a cutter. 'Ārakaṇṭakaṃ' is a needle-piercer. 'Tāḷaṃ' is a lock or mechanism. 'Kattarayaṭṭhivedhako' is the ring of the cutter-stick. 'Solid metal, in whatever way' means metal made solid, such as a metal rod, a metal ball, a metal lump, or a metal disc. 'Made of milk-stone' means made of soft, milk-colored stone.

Gihivikaṭānipi na vaṭṭanti anāmāsattā. Pi-saddena pageva saṅghikaparibhogena vā puggalikaparibhogena [V 0.0391] vāti dasseti. Senāsanaparibhogo pana sabbakappiyo. Tasmā jātarūpādimayā sabbepi senāsanaparikkhārā āmāsā. Tenāha “senāsanaparibhoge panā”tiādi.

Items altered by laypeople are also not allowable because they are not to be handled. The word 'pi' indicates 'how much more so for communal or personal use.' However, the use of lodgings is allowable in every way. Therefore, all lodging requisites made of gold and so forth are to be handled. Hence it is said, 'But in the case of the use of lodgings,' and so on.

Sesāti tato mahattarī vāsi. Yā panāti yā kudārī pana. Kudālo antamaso caturaṅgulamattopi garubhaṇḍameva. Nikhādanaṃ caturassamukhaṃ vā hotu, doṇimukhaṃ vā vaṅkaṃ vā ujukaṃ vā, antamaso sammuñjanidaṇḍakavedhanampi daṇḍabandhaṃ ce, garubhaṇḍameva. Tenāha “kudālo daṇḍabandhanikhādanaṃ vā agarubhaṇḍaṃ nāma natthī”ti. Sipāṭikā nāma khurakoso. Sikharaṃ pana daṇḍabandhanikhādanaṃ anulometīti āha “sikharampi nikhādaneneva saṅgahita”nti. Sace tampi pana adaṇḍakaṃ phalamattaṃ, bhājanīyaṃ. Upakkhareti vāsiādibhaṇḍāni.

'The rest' means a larger adze. 'Which pana' means which small axe (kudārī). A hoe (kudālo), even if only four fingers in size, is heavy property. A digging tool, whether with a square face or a trough-shaped face, whether curved or straight, and even a tool for piercing a hole for a broomstick, if it has a handle attached, is heavy property. Therefore, it is said, 'There is no such thing as a hoe or a digging tool with a handle that is not heavy property.' A 'sipāṭikā' is a razor case. 'A sikhara, however, follows the rule for a digging tool with a handle,' so it is said, 'a sikhara is also included with the digging tool.' But if even that is without a handle, just the blade, it is divisible. 'Upakkhara' means requisites, such as adzes and other tools.

Pattabandhako nāma pattassa gaṇṭhikādikārako. “Paṭimāsuvaṇṇādipattakārako”tipi vadanti. Tipucchedanakasatthaṃ, suvaṇṇacchedanakasatthaṃ, kataparikammacammacchindanakakhuddakasatthanti [M 0.0426] imāni cettha tīṇi pipphalikaṃ anulomentīti āha “ayaṃ pana viseso”tiādi. Itarānīti mahākattariādīni.

A 'pattabandhako' is one who makes the knots and so on for a bowl. They also say it means 'a maker of bowls with images, gold, and so on.' 'The knife for cutting tin, the knife for cutting gold, and the small knife for cutting prepared leather—these three here follow the rule for a cutter (pipphalika),' so it is said, 'But this is the distinction,' and so on. 'The others' means large cutters and so on.

Aḍḍhabāhuppamāṇāti (sārattha. ṭī. cūḷavagga 3.321) kapparato paṭṭhāya yāva aṃsakūṭappamāṇā, vidatthicaturaṅgulappamāṇāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tatthajātakāti saṅghikabhūmiyaṃ jātā. Ārakkhasaṃvidhānena rakkhitattā rakkhitā ca sā mañjūsādīsu pakkhittaṃ viya yathā taṃ na nassati, evaṃ gopanato gopitā cāti rakkhitagopitā. Tatthajātakāpi pana arakkhitā garubhaṇḍameva na hoti. “Saṅghakamme ca cetiyakamme ca kate”ti iminā saṅghasantakena cetiyasantakaṃ rakkhituṃ, parivattituñca vaṭṭatīti dīpeti. Suttaṃ panāti vaṭṭitañceva avaṭṭitañca suttaṃ.

Half a forearm's length means from the elbow up to the shoulder joint; this is said to be the measure of a span and four finger-widths. Born there means born on Sangha land. Because it is protected by security arrangements, it is guarded; and just as something placed in a chest or the like does not perish, so it is preserved by being looked after; thus it is 'protected and preserved.' But even if born there, if it is unprotected, it is not heavy property. By the phrase 'when Sangha business and shrine business are done,' this indicates that it is permissible to protect shrine property with Sangha property and also to exchange it. As for thread, it is both spun and unspun thread.

Aṭṭhaṅgulasūcidaṇḍamattoti antamaso dīghaso aṭṭhaṅgulamatto, pariṇāhato sīhaḷapaṇṇasūcidaṇḍamatto. Etthāti veḷubhaṇḍe. Daḍḍhaṃ gehaṃ yesaṃ teti daḍḍhagehā. Na vāretabbāti “mā gaṇhitvā gacchathā”ti na nisedhetabbā. Desantaragatena sampattavihāre saṅghikāvāse ṭhapetabbā.

A needle-case of eight finger-widths means at least eight finger-widths in length, and in circumference, the size of a Sinhalese palm-leaf needle-case. Here means in the case of bamboo goods. Those whose house is burned, they are 'the house-burned.' Should not be prevented means they should not be forbidden by saying, 'Do not take it and go.' Having gone to another region, it should be placed in a Sangha dwelling in the monastery one has reached.

Avasesañca chadanatiṇanti muñjapabbajehi avasesaṃ yaṃ kiñci chadanatiṇaṃ. Yattha pana tiṇaṃ [V 0.0392] natthi, tattha paṇṇehi chādenti (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 321). Tasmā paṇṇampi tiṇeneva saṅgahitanti āha “chadanatiṇasaṅkhepagatesū”tiādi. Aṭṭhaṅgulappamāṇopīti vitthārato aṭṭhaṅgulappamāṇo. Likhitapotthako pana garubhaṇḍaṃ na hoti.

And the remaining thatching grass means any thatching grass remaining apart from muñja grass and pabbaja grass. But where there is no grass, they thatch with leaves (Cūḷavagga Aṭṭhakathā 321). Therefore, since leaves are also included under grass, it is said, 'included in the category of thatching grass,' and so on. Even one of eight finger-widths in measure means eight finger-widths in breadth. However, a written book is not heavy property.

Veḷumhi vuttappamāṇoti “aṭṭhaṅgulasūcidaṇḍakamattopī”ti veḷubhaṇḍe vuttappamāṇo. Saṅghassa dinno vāti dārudullabhaṭṭhāne saṅghassa dinno vā. Kurundiyaṃ vuttakkamena dārubhaṇḍavinicchayaṃ vatvā idāni mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttakkamena vattuṃ “apicā”tiādimāha. Āsandikādīnīti ettha āsandikoti caturassapīṭhaṃ vuccati. “Uccakampi āsandika”nti vacanato ekatobhāgena dīghapīṭhameva hi aṭṭhaṅgulapādakaṃ vaṭṭati. Caturassāsandiko pana pamāṇātikkantopi vaṭṭhatīti veditabbo. Ādisaddena “sattaṅgo, bhaddapīṭhakaṃ, eḷakapādakapīṭhaṃ, āmalakavaṭṭakapīṭhaṃ, phalakaṃ, kocchaṃ, palālapīṭhaka”nti [M 0.0427] (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 321) ime saṅgaṇhantīti veditabbaṃ. Tenāha “antamaso”tiādi. Paṇṇehi vāti kadalipaṇṇādīhi vā. Byagghacammonaddhampi vāḷarūpaparikkhittaṃ ratanaparisibbitaṃ kocchakaṃ garubhaṇḍameva.

The stated measure in the case of bamboo means the measure stated for bamboo goods: 'even a needle-case of eight finger-widths.' Or given to the Sangha means or given to the Sangha in a place where wood is scarce. Having stated the legal decision on wooden goods according to the method stated in the Kurundī, now, to state it according to the method stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, he says, 'Moreover,' and so on. Here, regarding 'long chairs and so on,' a long chair is called a rectangular stool. According to the phrase 'even a high long chair,' only a long stool with legs of eight finger-widths is permissible on one side. But it should be understood that a rectangular long chair is permissible even if it exceeds the measure. By the word 'and so on,' it should be understood that these are included: 'the seven-limbed, the auspicious chair, the goat-footed stool, the myrobalan-shaped stool, the plank, the wicker chair, and the straw stool' (Cūḷavagga Aṭṭhakathā 321). Therefore, he says, 'at least,' and so on. Or with leaves means with banana leaves and so on. Even a wicker chair covered with a tiger's skin, surrounded by figures of wild beasts, and stitched with jewels is indeed heavy property.

Ghaṭṭanaphalakaṃ nāma yattha ṭhapetvā rajitacīvaraṃ hatthena ghaṭṭenti. Ghaṭṭanamuggaro nāma anuvātādighaṭṭanakoti vadanti. Daṇḍamuggaro nāma yena rajitacīvaraṃ pothenti. Ambaṇanti phalakehi pokkharaṇī viya kataṃ pānīyabhājanaṃ. Rajanadoṇīti pakkarajanaṃ ākiritvā ṭhapanabhājanaṃ.

A rubbing board is that on which, having placed a dyed robe, they rub it with the hand. A rubbing mallet, they say, is a tool for rubbing with the grain and so on. A staff mallet is that with which they beat the dyed robe. An ambaṇa is a water container made of planks, like a lotus pond. A dyeing trough is a container for placing the boiled dye after pouring it in.

Akappiyacammanti sīhādīnaṃ cammaṃ. “Bhūmattharaṇaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti idaṃ akappiyacammaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. “Paccattharaṇagatika”nti iminā mañcapīṭhepi attharituṃ vaṭṭatīti dīpeti. Pāvārādipaccattharaṇampi garubhaṇḍanti eke. Noti apare. Vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbaṃ. Kappiyacammānīti migādīnaṃ cammāni.

Unallowable hides are the hides of lions and so on. The statement, 'It is permissible to make a ground-covering,' is said with reference to this unallowable hide. By 'fit to be used as a covering,' it is shown that it is permissible to spread it even on beds and chairs. Some say that even coverings such as cloaks are heavy property. Others say they are not. It should be adopted after investigation. Allowable hides are the hides of deer and so on.

Sabbaṃ cakkayuttayānanti rathasakaṭādikaṃ sabbacakkayuttayānaṃ. Visaṅkharitacakkaṃ pana yānaṃ bhājanīyaṃ. Anuññātavāsi nāma yā sipāṭikāya pakkhipitvā pariharituṃ sakkāti vuttā. Muṭṭhipaṇṇanti tālapattaṃ. Tañhi muṭṭhinā gahetvā pariharantīti “muṭṭhipaṇṇa”nti vuccati. Muṭṭhipaṇṇanti chattacchadanapaṇṇamevāti keci. Araṇisahitanti araṇiyugaḷaṃ, uttarāraṇī, adharāraṇīti araṇidvayanti attho.

All wheeled vehicles means all wheeled vehicles such as chariots, carts, and so on. But a vehicle with a dismantled wheel is divisible. The allowed adze is that which, it is said, can be carried by placing it in a bag. A fist-leaf means a palm leaf. Indeed, because it is carried by grasping it in the fist, it is called a 'fist-leaf.' Some say a fist-leaf is only a leaf for an umbrella or a roof. With fire-sticks means a pair of fire-sticks—the upper fire-stick and the lower fire-stick; the meaning is two fire-sticks.

Phātikammaṃ [V 0.0393] katvāti antamaso taṃagghanakavālikāyapi thāvaraṃ vaḍḍhikammaṃ katvā. Phātikammaṃ akatvā gaṇhantena tattheva valañjetabbo. Gamanakāle saṅghike āvāse ṭhapetvā gantabbaṃ. Asatiyā gahetvā gatena pahiṇitvā dātabbo. Desantaragatena sampattavihāre saṅghikāvāse ṭhapetabbo. Etthāti mattikābhaṇḍe. Kuṇḍikāti ayokuṇḍikā ceva tambalohakuṇḍikā ca. Bhājanīyakoṭṭhāsameva bhajatīti bhājanīyapakkhameva sevati, na tu garubhaṇḍanti attho. Kañcanako pana garubhaṇḍamevāti adhippāyo. Itaranti garubhaṇḍaṃ.

Having made an improvement means having made a lasting improvement, at least with sand of that value. One who takes it without making an improvement must use it right there. At the time of departure, it should be left in a Sangha dwelling before going. If taken and gone unmindfully, it should be sent back and given. Having gone to another region, it should be placed in a Sangha dwelling in the monastery one has reached. Here means in the case of earthenware goods. A water pot means both an iron water pot and a copper water pot. It belongs only to the category of divisible articles means it pertains to the side of divisible articles, not heavy property; this is the meaning. But the intention is that a golden one is indeed heavy property. The other means heavy property.

Dubbalasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on weakening is concluded.

12. Pariṇāmanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

12. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Transference.

Dvādasame [M 0.0428] na kiñci vattabbaṃ atthi.

In the twelfth, there is nothing to be said.

Pariṇāmanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on transference is concluded.

Sahadhammikavaggo aṭṭhamo.

The Sahadhammika Chapter, the Eighth.

9. Ratanavaggo

9. The Chapter on Jewels.

1. Antepurasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. The Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning the Inner Quarters.

Anikkhantarājake aniggataratanaketi ettha “sayanighare”ti pāṭhaseso daṭṭhabboti āha “anikkhanto rājā ito”tiādi. Tattha itoti sayanigharato. Sayanighareti sayanīyaghare. Yattha rañño sayanaṃ paññattaṃ hoti, antamaso sāṇipākāraparikkhittampi, tasminti vuttaṃ hoti. Ratijananaṭṭhena ratanaṃ, hatthiādi. Idha pana itthiratanaṃ adhippetanti āha “ratanaṃ vuccati mahesī”ti.

In the phrase 'when the king has not departed, when the jewel has not been removed,' here the textual remainder 'in the sleeping chamber' should be seen; thus he says, 'the king has not departed from here,' and so on. There, 'from here' means from the sleeping chamber. In the sleeping chamber means in the sleeping quarters. Wherever the king's bed is prepared, even if it is enclosed by a hemp-cloth wall, that is what is meant. A jewel (ratana) is so called because it generates delight, such as an elephant, and so on. Here, however, the woman-jewel is intended; thus he says, 'a jewel is called the chief queen.'

Ubhosūti [V 0.0394] rājamahesīsu. Kiriyākiriyanti ettha indakhīlātikkamo kiriyaṃ, appaṭisaṃviditaṃ akiriyanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Both means the king and the chief queen. Regarding 'action and inaction,' here, crossing the threshold-post is the action, and not being announced is the inaction; this should be understood.

Antepurasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning the inner quarters is concluded.

2. Ratanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Jewels.

Muttādidasavidhanti “muttā maṇi veḷuriyo saṅkho silā pavāḷaṃ rajataṃ jātarūpaṃ lohitaṅko masāragalla”nti (pāci. 506) dasavidhaṃ ratanaṃ. Ajjhāvasatheti gehe. Tenāha “parikkhittassā”tiādi, parikkhittassa āvasathassāti attho. Āvasathoti cettha antogāme niviṭṭhagehaṃ adhippetaṃ. Ārāme niviṭṭhagehaṃ pana ajjhārāmaggahaṇeneva gahitaṃ. “Āvasathoti cettha antoārāme vā hotu, aññattha vā, attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ vuccatī”ti (sārattha. ṭī. pācittiya 3.506) keci. Sabbesampi atthāya dukkaṭamevāti attano vā tesaṃ saṅghādīnaṃ vā atthāya uggaṇhantassa vā uggaṇhāpentassa vā dukkaṭameva. Sace pana mātāpitūnaṃ santakaṃ avassaṃ paṭisāmetabbaṃ [M 0.0429] kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ hoti, attano atthāya gahetvā paṭisāmetabbanti āha “tādisaṃ panā”tiādi. Tādisanti yaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ santakaṃ avassaṃ paṭisāmetabbaṃ kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ, tādisaṃ. Chandenapi bhayenapīti vaḍḍhakiādīsu chandenapi, rājavallabhesu bhayenapi.

The ten kinds beginning with pearls means the ten kinds of jewels: 'pearl, gem, beryl, conch, crystal, coral, silver, gold, ruby, and cat's-eye' (Pācittiya 506). Resides in means in a house. Therefore he says, 'of one who is enclosed,' and so on; the meaning is, of a dwelling that is enclosed. Here, a dwelling is intended to be a house established within a village. But a house established in a monastery is included by the taking of the term 'within a monastery.' Some say, 'Here, a dwelling refers to one's own place of residence, whether it be within a monastery or elsewhere' (Sāratthaṭīkā, Pācittiya 3.506). For the benefit of all means it is a dukkaṭa offense for one who picks it up or causes it to be picked up for one's own benefit or for the benefit of them, the Sangha and so on. But if there is allowable property belonging to one's parents that must necessarily be put away, he says, 'but such as that,' and so on, meaning it should be taken and put away for one's own benefit. Such as that means such allowable property belonging to one's parents that must necessarily be put away. By desire or by fear means by desire in the case of carpenters and so on, or by fear in the case of royal favorites.

Tādise ṭhāneti mahāvihārasadisassa mahārāmassa pākāraparikkhitte pariveṇe. Saññāṇaṃ katvāti “ettakā kahāpaṇā”tiādinā rūpena vā lañchanādinimittena vā saññāṇaṃ katvā, sallakkhetvāti attho. Patirūpānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ hattheti lajjīnaṃ kukkuccakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ hatthe. Lolajātikānañhi hatthe ṭhapetuṃ na labbhati. Neva pakkamatīti neva tamhā āvāsā pakkamati. “Thāvaraṃ senāsanaṃ vā”tiādinā attano cīvarādimūlaṃ na kātabbanti (pāci. aṭṭha. 506) dasseti. Taṃ dassetvāti yaṃ thāvarasenāsanādi kataṃ, taṃ upāsaka tava santakena idaṃ nāma katanti evaṃ dassetvā. Samādapetvāti aññaṃ samādapetvā, “uddissa ariyā tiṭṭhanti, esā ariyāna yācanā”ti vuttanayena yācitvāti attho.

`Tādise ṭhāne` (in such a place) means in a precinct enclosed by walls, of a great monastery like the Mahāvihāra. Having made a sign means having made a sign by saying, 'so many coins,' and so forth, or by a mark, etc.; the meaning is having noted it. Into the hands of suitable monks means into the hands of monks who are modest and conscientious. For it is not permissible to place it in the hands of those who are of a greedy nature. `Neva pakkamati` (he does not depart) means he does not depart from that residence. By 'a permanent dwelling, or' and so forth, it is shown that one should not make it the capital for one's own robes and so forth (Pāc. Aṭṭha. 506). Having shown that means having shown what was made, such as a permanent dwelling, saying, 'Lay follower, this so-and-so was made with your property.' Having encouraged means having encouraged another, having begged in the way stated, 'The noble ones stand (in need); this is the request of the noble ones'—this is the meaning.

Anuññātaṭṭhāneti ajjhārāmaajjhāvasathe. Āmāsanti āmasitabbañceva paṭisāmetabbañca vatthādi.

`Anuññātaṭṭhāne` means in allowed places, within the monastery and within the dwelling. `Āmāsa` means cloth, etc., that should both be touched and taken care of.

Ratanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning jewels is finished.

3. Vikālagāmappavesanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Training Rule on Entering a Village at an Unsuitable Time

Cāritteti [V 0.0395] cārittasikkhāpade. Upacāranti dutiyaleḍḍupātaṃ. Aññaṃ gāmaṃ gacchantānaṃ puna āpucchanakiccaṃ natthīti ussāhaṃ appaṭippassambhetvā aññaṃ gāmaṃ gacchantānaṃ gāmasatampi hotu, puna āpucchanakiccaṃ natthīti attho. Tenāha “sace panā”tiādi. Ussāhanti gāmappavisanussāhaṃ. Antarārāmādīsu (pāci. aṭṭha. 515) na kevalaṃ anāpucchā gacchantasseva, kāyabandhanaṃ abandhitvā saṅghāṭiṃ apārupitvā gacchantassāpi anāpatti. Āpadāsūti sīho vā byaggho vā āgacchati, megho vā uṭṭheti, añño vā koci upaddavo uppajjati[M 0.0430], anāpatti. Evarūpāsu āpadāsu bahigāmato antogāmaṃ pavisituṃ vaṭṭati.

`Cāritte` (conduct) refers to the training rule on conduct. `Upacāra` means the second clod-throw distance. For those going to another village, there is no need to take leave again. The meaning is that for those going to another village, without abandoning the effort, even if it is a hundred villages, there is no need to take leave again. Therefore it is said, 'But if...' and so forth. `Ussāha` means the effort of entering a village. In places such as between monasteries (Pācittiya Aṭṭhakathā 515), not only is there no offense for one who goes without asking leave, but there is also no offense for one who goes without fastening his waist-band or without draping his outer robe. In emergencies—such as a lion or tiger approaching, a cloud arising, or any other danger occurring—there is no offense. In such emergencies, it is allowable to enter a village from outside.

Vikālagāmappavesanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on entering a village at an unsuitable time is concluded.

4. Sūcigharasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. Explanation of the Training Rule on the Needle Case

Taṃ assa atthīti (sārattha. ṭī. pācittiya 3.517) paṭhamaṃ bhinditvā pacchā desetabbattā taṃ bhedanakaṃ assa pācittiyassa atthīti.

`Taṃ assa atthīti` (Sāratthadīpanī Ṭīkā, Pācittiya 3.517) means that since it must first be broken and then confessed, that breaking pertains to that offense entailing confession.

Araṇiketi araṇidhanuke. Vidheti vedhake. Vāsijaṭeti vāsidaṇḍake ca.

`Araṇike` means in the fire-stick bow. `Vidhe` means in the piercer. And `Vāsijaṭe` means in the axe-handle.

Sūcigharasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on the needle case is concluded.

5. Mañcapīṭhasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

5. Explanation of the Training Rule on Beds and Chairs

Aṭṭhaṅgulapādakanti bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso. “Chedanakaṃ bhedanakasadisamevā”ti iminā “chedanameva chedanakaṃ, taṃ assa atthīti chedanaka”nti imamatthaṃ atidisati.

`Aṭṭhaṅgulapādaka` is a neuter gender designation for a state of being. By this, '`Chedanaka` is just like `bhedanaka`,' it extends the meaning that 'cutting itself is `chedanaka`, and that which has this (cutting) is `chedanaka`'.

Yathā pamāṇameva upari dissati, evaṃ nikhaṇitvā vāti sace pana na chinditukāmo hoti, yathā pamāṇameva upari dissati, evaṃ bhūmiyaṃ nikhaṇitvā vā. Aṭṭakaṃ vā bandhitvāti ukkhipitvā tulāsaṅghāte ṭhapetvā aṭṭaṃ katvā.

Or, having dug it in so that only the prescribed measure appears above. But if one does not wish to cut it, then having dug it into the ground so that only the prescribed measure appears above. Or 'having bound a frame' means having lifted it and placed it on a crossbeam, making a frame.

Mañcapīṭhasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on beds and chairs is concluded.

6. Tūlonaddhasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. Explanation of the Training Rule on Cotton Padding

Cimilikaṃ [V 0.0396] pattharitvā tūlaṃ pakkhipitvāti mañcapīṭhānaṃ upari cimilikaṃ pattharitvā tassa upari tūlaṃ pakkhipitvāti attho. Upari cimilikāyāti uparimabhāge cimilikāya.

`Having spread a cīmilikā and placed cotton on it` means having spread a cīmilikā over the bed or seat and placed cotton on top of it. `Upari cimilikāya` means on the upper part of the cīmilikā.

Sīsappamāṇanti [M 0.0431] (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 297; sārattha. ṭī. cūḷavagga 3.297) yattha galavāṭakato paṭṭhāya sabbasīsaṃ upadahanti, taṃ sīsappamāṇaṃ. Tañca ukkaṭṭhaparicchedato tiriyaṃ muṭṭhiratanaṃ hoti, dīghato dviratananti dassetuṃ “yassa vitthārato tīsu koṇesū”tiādimāha. Dvinnaṃ antaraṃ vidatthi caturaṅgulaṃ hotīti dvinnaṃ koṇānaṃ antaraṃ miniyamānaṃ vidatthi ceva caturaṅgulañca hoti. Majjhe muṭṭhiratananti bibbohanassa majjhaṃ tiriyato muṭṭhiratanappamāṇaṃ hoti. Ayañhi sīsappamāṇassa ukkaṭṭhaparicchedo. Tato uddhaṃ na vaṭṭati, heṭṭhā vaṭṭati. Agilānassa sīsūpadhānañca pādūpadhānañcāti dvayameva vaṭṭati. Gilānassa bibbohanāni santharitvā upari paccattharaṇaṃ datvā nipajjitumpi vaṭṭati.

`Sīsappamāṇa` (Cūḷavagga Aṭṭhakathā 297; Sāratthadīpanī Ṭīkā, Cūḷavagga 3.297) is that where, starting from the hollow of the neck, the entire head is placed; that is the measure of the head. And to show that its maximum limit is a fist-span across and two spans in length, it states, 'whose width at the three corners...' and so forth. `The distance between two is a span and four fingers` means that when the distance between two corners is measured, it is a span and four fingers. `The middle is a fist-span` means that the middle of the bolster is a fist-span across. This is indeed the maximum limit for the head-measure. Above that it is not allowed, but below that it is allowed. For one who is not ill, only two things are allowed: a head-support and a foot-support. For one who is ill, it is also allowed to lie down after spreading out bolsters and placing a top sheet.

Tūlonaddhasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on cotton padding is concluded.

7. Nisīdanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

7. Explanation of the Training Rule on Sitting Cloths

Sattamaṃ uttānameva.

The seventh (rule) is simply clear.

Nisīdanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on the sitting cloth is concluded.

8. Kaṇḍuppaṭicchādisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

8. Explanation of the Training Rule on Covering for Itches

Adhonābhiubbhajāṇumaṇḍalanti nābhiyā heṭṭhā jāṇumaṇḍalānaṃ upari. Kaṇḍupīḷakaassāvathullakacchābādhānanti ettha kaṇḍūti kacchu. Pīḷakāti lohitatuṇḍikā sukhumapīḷakā. Assāvoti arisabhagandalamadhumehānaṃ vasena asucipaggharaṇaṃ. Thullakacchābādhoti mahāpīḷakābādho vuccati.

`Adhonābhiubbhajāṇumaṇḍala` means below the navel and above the kneecaps. `Kaṇḍupīḷakaassāvathullakacchābādhāna`—here, `kaṇḍu` means scabies. `Pīḷaka` means blood-filled blisters or fine sores. `Assāva` means the oozing of impurities due to conditions like hemorrhoids, fistula, or diabetes. `Thullakacchābādha` is called a severe affliction of large boils.

Kaṇḍuppaṭicchādisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on covering for itches is concluded.

9-10. Vassikasāṭikanandasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

9-10. Explanation of the Training Rule on the Rains-bathing Cloth and Ānanda

Navamaṃ [M 0.0432][V 0.0397] dasamañca uttānameva.

The ninth and tenth (rules) are simply clear.

Vassikasāṭikanandasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on the rains-bathing cloth and Ānanda is concluded.

Ratanavaggo navamo.

The Ninth Chapter: The Chapter on Jewels.

Iti kaṅkhāvitaraṇiyā pātimokkhavaṇṇanāya

Thus ends the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī, the Explanation of the Pātimokkha.

Vinayatthamañjūsāyaṃ līnatthappakāsaniyaṃ

In the Vinayatthamañjūsā, the Līnatthappakāsanī.

Pācittiyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Pācittiya rules is concluded.

Pāṭidesanīyakaṇḍaṃ

The Chapter on Offenses Requiring Confession

1. Paṭhamapāṭidesanīyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the First Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule

Antaragharaṃ [M 0.0433][V 0.0398] paviṭṭhāyāti rathikaṃ byūhaṃ siṅghāṭakaṃ gharaṃ paviṭṭhāya. Asappāyanti saggamokkhānaṃ ahitaṃ ananukūlaṃ. Bhikkhuniyā antaraghare ṭhatvā dadamānāya vasenettha āpatti veditabbā, bhikkhussa ṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ pana appamāṇaṃ. Tenāha “antaragharaṃ paviṭṭhāyāti vacanato”tiādi. Antarārāmādīsūti antarārāmabhikkhunupassayatitthiyaseyyāpaṭikkamanesu. Rathiyābyūhasiṅghāṭakagharānanti ettha rathiyāti racchā. Byūhanti anibbijjhitvā ṭhitā gatapaccāgataracchā. Siṅghāṭakanti catukkoṇaṃ vā tikoṇaṃ vā maggasamodhānaṭṭhānaṃ. Gharanti kulagharaṃ. Yathā ca rathiyādīsu ṭhatvā dadamānāya gaṇhato āpatti, evaṃ hatthisālādīsupi daṭṭhabbaṃ.

“Having entered the house”—this refers to having entered a street, a junction, a crossroads, or a house. “Unsuitable”—meaning not beneficial or conducive to heaven and liberation. An offense is to be understood here on account of a bhikkhunī giving while standing inside a house; for a bhikkhu, however, the standing place is unlimited. Therefore it is said, “from the statement ‘having entered the house,’ and so forth.” “Inside a monastery, etc.” means inside a monastery, a bhikkhunī’s dwelling, a hermitage of sectarians, or places for lying down and returning. “Street, junction, crossroads, and house”—here, “street” means a road. “Junction” means a road where one stands without passing through, where one goes and returns. “Crossroads” means a place where paths meet, whether four-cornered or three-cornered. “House” means a family house. Just as an offense is incurred when one receives from a bhikkhunī giving while standing in a street, etc., so too should it be understood in places like an elephant stable, etc.

“Yāmakālikādīsu paṭiggahaṇepi ajjhoharaṇepi dukkaṭa”nti idaṃ āmisena asambhinnaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, sambhinne pana ekarase pāṭidesanīyameva. Ekato upasampannāyāti bhikkhunīnaṃ santike upasampannāya, bhikkhūnaṃ santike upasampannāya pana yathāvatthukameva.

“In accepting or consuming yāmakālika items, etc., it is a dukkaṭa.” This is said with reference to what is unmixed with food. But if it is mixed and of a single taste, it is only a pāṭidesanīya. “Ordained on one side” means one ordained in the presence of bhikkhunīs. For one ordained in the presence of bhikkhus, however, it is according to the case.

Ñātikāya vā dāpentiyāti sayaṃ adatvā yāya kāyaci ñātikāya dāpentiyā, aññātikāyāti attho. Upanikkhipitvā vā dadamānāyāti bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapetvā “idaṃ, ayya, tumhākaṃ dammī”ti dadamānāya. Evaṃ dinnaṃ “sādhu, bhaginī”ti sampaṭicchitvā tāya eva vā bhikkhuniyā, aññena vā kenaci paṭiggahāpetvā idaṃ bhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati.

“Or having it given by a female relative” means not giving it herself, but having it given by some female relative; the meaning is that the agent may be a non-relative. “Or giving after setting it down” means giving after placing it on the ground, saying, “Venerable, I give this to you.” It is permissible to eat what is given in this way, after accepting it with the words, “Very well, sister,” and having had it received either by that very bhikkhunī or by some other person.

Paṭhamapāṭidesanīyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the first Pāṭidesanīya training rule is concluded.

2. Dutiyapāṭidesanīyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Second Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule

Yo [V 0.0399] ca paṭiggahetvā bhuñjatīti sambandho. Attano vā bhattaṃ dāpentiyāti ettha sacepi attano bhattaṃ deti, iminā sikkhāpadena anāpattiyeva, purimasikkhāpadena āpatti. Aññesaṃ vā bhattaṃ dentiyāti ettha [M 0.0434] pana sace dāpeyya, iminā sikkhāpadena āpatti bhaveyya, dentiyā pana neva iminā, na purimena āpatti.

“And one who receives and eats”—this is the connection. “Or having one’s own food given”—here, even if one gives one’s own food, there is no offense by this training rule, but there is an offense by the previous training rule. “Or giving others’ food”—here, however, if one were to have it given, there would be an offense by this training rule. But if one were to give, there would be no offense by this rule, nor by the previous one.

Dutiyapāṭidesanīyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the second Pāṭidesanīya training rule is concluded.

3. Tatiyapāṭidesanīyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Third Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule

Laddhasekkhasammutikānīti ñattidutiyena kammena laddhasekkhasammutikāni. Yañhi kulaṃ saddhāya vaḍḍhati, bhogena hāyati, evarūpassa kulassa ñattidutiyena kammena sekkhasammutiṃ denti, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

“Those designated as learners by a motion followed by one proclamation” means those designated as learners by a motion followed by one proclamation. For a family that increases in faith but declines in wealth, to such a family they grant the designation of a learner by a motion followed by one proclamation. This is said with reference to that.

Gharato nīharitvāti gharato āsanasālaṃ vā vihāraṃ vā ānetvā. Tenāha “āsanasālādīsu vā”ti. Imassa “dentī”ti iminā sambandho. Dvāramūle vā ṭhapitaṃ dentīti dvāramūle ṭhapitaṃ pacchā sampattassa denti. Bhikkhuṃ pana disvā antogehato nīharitvā diyyamānaṃ na vaṭṭati. Niccabhattaketi niccaṃ dātabbabhattake. Salākabhatteti rukkhasāramayāya salākāya vā veḷuvilīvatālapaṇṇādimayāya paṭṭikāya vā “asukassa nāma salākabhatta”nti evaṃ akkharāni upanibandhitvā gāhāpetvā dātabbabhatte. Pakkhiketi ekasmiṃ pakkhe ekadivase dātabbabhatte. Uposathiketi uposathe dātabbabhatte. Pāṭipadiketi pāṭipadadivase dātabbabhatte.

“Having taken it out from the house” means having brought it from the house to the assembly hall or the monastery. Hence it is said, “or in the assembly hall, etc.” This is connected with the word “giving.” “Or giving what was placed at the door” means giving what was placed at the door to one who arrives afterward. But if, seeing a bhikkhu, one takes it out from inside the house and gives it, it is not allowable. “Regular meal” means a meal that should be given regularly. “Token meal” means a meal to be given by means of a wooden stick made of heartwood, or a strip made of bamboo, rattan, palm leaf, etc., having inscribed words like “This is the token meal for so-and-so,” and having had it taken. “Fortnightly meal” means a meal to be given on one day in a fortnight. “Uposatha meal” means a meal to be given on the Uposatha day. “Pāṭipada meal” means a meal to be given on the pāṭipada day.

Tatiyapāṭidesanīyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the third Pāṭidesanīya training rule is concluded.

4. Catutthapāṭidesanīyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. Explanation of the Fourth Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule

Tassa parivāraṃ katvā, aññaṃ vā tena saddhiṃ bahukampīti yāguyā paṭisaṃviditaṃ katvā “kiṃ suddhāya yāguyā dinnāya, pūvabhattādīnipi etissā yāguyā parivāraṃ katvā, dassāmā”tiādinā [V 0.0400] tassa khādanīyassa vā bhojanīyassa vā parivāraṃ katvā, aññaṃ vā yaṃ kiñci tena saddhiṃ bahukampi āharīyatu. Khādanīyanti nidassanamattaṃ “bhojanīyaṃ vā”tipi icchitabbattā. Tena saddhiṃ āharantūti tena saddhiṃ attano deyyadhammaṃ āharantu. “Yāguyā [M 0.0435] paṭisaṃviditaṃ katvā pūvaṃ vā bhattaṃ vā āharanti, etampi vaṭṭatī”ti (pāci. aṭṭha. 573) kurundiyaṃ vuttaṃ.

“Having prepared accompaniments for it, or having brought much of something else along with it”—this means having made it properly prepared with gruel, thinking, “Why give only pure gruel? Let us prepare accompaniments for this gruel, such as cakes and rice, and give them,” and so forth; thus having prepared accompaniments for that chewable food or edible food, or let them bring much of whatever else along with it. “Chewable food” is merely an example, because “or edible food” is also intended. “Let them bring it along with that” means let them bring their own gift along with that. “It is also allowable if, having made it properly prepared with gruel, they bring cakes or rice,” as stated in the Kurundiya commentary.

Paṭisaṃviditagilānāvasesakaṃ vāti paṭisaṃviditañca gilāno ca paṭisaṃviditagilānā, tesaṃ avasesakaṃ, paṭisaṃviditassa ca gilānassa ca sesakanti attho. Ekassatthāya paṭisaṃviditaṃ katvā āhaṭaṃ, tassa sesakaṃ aññassāpi paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Catunnaṃ vā pañcannaṃ vā paṭisaṃviditaṃ katvā bahūnaṃ āhaṭaṃ hoti, aññesampi dātuṃ icchanti, etampi paṭisaṃviditasesakameva, sabbesampi vaṭṭati. Atha adhikameva hoti, sannidhiṃ mocetvā ṭhapitaṃ dutiyadivasepi vaṭṭati. Gilānassāhaṭāvasesepi eseva nayo. Yaṃ pana appaṭisaṃviditameva katvā ābhataṃ, taṃ bahiārāmaṃ pesetvā paṭisaṃviditaṃ kāretvā āharāpetabbaṃ, bhikkhūhi vā gantvā antarāmagge gahetabbaṃ. Yampi vihāramajjhena gacchanto vā vanacarakādayo vā vanato āharitvā denti, purimanayeneva paṭisaṃviditaṃ kāretabbaṃ. Katthaci pana potthakesu “paṭisaṃviditaṃ katvā āhaṭaṃ vā gilānāvasesakaṃ vā”ti pāṭho dissati, so na gahetabbo. Tatthajātakameva vāti ārāme jātakameva. Mūlaphalādinti mūlaphalatacapattādiṃ aññena kappiyaṃ katvā dinnaṃ paribhuñjato anāpatti. Sace pana taṃ gāmaṃ haritvā pacitvā āharanti, na vaṭṭati. Paṭisaṃviditaṃ kāretabbaṃ.

“Or the remainder of what was properly prepared for the sick”—this means the remainder of what was properly prepared and what was for the sick. What was brought after being properly prepared for one person, the remainder of that may be consumed by others as well. When a large amount is brought after being properly prepared for four or five people, and they wish to give it to many others, this too is the remainder of what was properly prepared, and it is allowable for all. If there is even more, after releasing it from storage, it is allowable even on the second day. The same principle applies to the remainder of what was brought for the sick. But what was brought without being properly prepared should be sent outside the monastery, properly prepared, and then caused to be brought back. Or the bhikkhus may go and receive it along the way. Also, if those walking through the monastery or forest-dwellers bring something from the forest and give it, it should be properly prepared in the same way as before. However, in some texts, the reading “what was brought after being properly prepared, or the remainder of what was for the sick,” is found—this should not be accepted. “What is naturally grown in the monastery” means what is grown in the monastery itself. “Roots, fruits, etc.” means roots, fruits, bark, leaves, etc.; if made allowable by another and given, there is no offense in consuming it. But if they take it to the village, cook it, and bring it back, it is not allowable. It must be properly prepared.

Catutthapāṭidesanīyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the fourth Pāṭidesanīya training rule is concluded.

Iti kaṅkhāvitaraṇiyā pātimokkhavaṇṇanāya

Thus in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī, the commentary on the Pātimokkha,

Vinayatthamañjūsāyaṃ līnatthappakāsaniyaṃ

in the Vinayatthamañjūsā, elucidating subtle meanings,

Pāṭidesanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

the commentary on the Pāṭidesanīya rules is concluded.

Sekhiyakaṇḍaṃ

The Chapter on Training

1. Parimaṇḍalasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Training Rule on Wearing the Lower Robe Evenly

“Antaraghare”ti [M 0.0436][V 0.0401] visesetvā na vuttattā “ārāmepi antaragharepi sabbatthā”ti vuttaṃ. Ārāmepīti buddhūpaṭṭhānādikālaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Yathā “tatrime cattāro pārājikā dhammā uddesaṃ āgacchantī”tiādinā tattha tattha paricchedo kato, evametthāpi “tatrime pañcasattati sekhiyā dhammā uddesaṃ āgacchantī”ti kasmā paricchedo na katoti āha “ettha cā”tiādi. Vattakkhandhake vuttavattānipīti āgantukāvāsikagamikānumodanabhattaggapiṇḍacārikāraññasenāsanajantāgharavaccakuṭiupajjhācariyasaddhivihārikaantevāsikavattāni. Idañca nidassanamattaṃ aññesampi khandhakavattānaṃ ettheva saṅgahassa icchitabbattā. Ayañhettha adhippāyo – sekhiyaggahaṇena cettha vattakkhandhakādīsu (cūḷava. 356 ādayo) āgatavattādīnampi gahaṇaṃ. Tepi hi sikkhitabbaṭṭhena “sekhiyā”ti icchitā. Tasmā mātikāyaṃ pārājikādīnaṃ viya sekhiyānaṃ paricchedo na katoti. Na kevalaṃ vattakkhandhakādīsu (cūḷava. 356 ādayo) āgatavattādīnaṃ gahaṇatthamevāti āha “cārittavinayadassanatthañcā”ti. Etthāpi paricchedo na katoti ānetvā yojetabbaṃ. Mātikāya “dukkaṭa”nti avutte kathaṃ panettha dukkaṭanti veditabbanti āha “yo panā”tiādi.

Because 'inside a house' is not specifically mentioned, it is stated that the rule applies 'in a monastery or inside a house, everywhere.' 'In a monastery' refers to times such as attending upon the Buddha. Just as in various places divisions are made, such as 'here, these four pārājika rules come up for recitation,' so too here, why is a division not made, such as 'here, these seventy-five sekhiya rules come up for recitation?' Thus it is stated, 'and here,' and so forth. The duties mentioned in the Vattakkhandhaka are also included, such as the duties for visiting monks, resident monks, monks setting out, giving thanks, the refectory, going for alms, the wilderness, lodgings, heated rooms, latrines, and the duties toward preceptors, teachers, co-residents, and pupils. This is merely illustrative, since the inclusion of other duties from the Khandhakas here is also to be desired. The intention here is this: by the term 'sekhiya,' the duties mentioned in the Vattakkhandhaka and other places (starting with Cūḷavagga 356) are also included. For they too are to be trained in, hence they are called 'sekhiya.' Therefore, unlike the pārājika rules, etc., in the summary, no division is made for the sekhiya rules. It is not only for the sake of including the duties mentioned in the Vattakkhandhaka and other places that no division is made, but also, it is said, for showing proper conduct and discipline. Here too, it should be understood that no division is made. In the summary, 'dukkaṭa' is not mentioned, so how then is 'dukkaṭa' to be understood here? It is said, 'but whoever,' and so forth.

Aṭṭhaṅgulamattanti pakataṅgulena aṭṭhaṅgulamattaṃ. Yo pana sukkhajaṅgho vā mahāpiṇḍikamaṃso vā hoti, tassa sāruppatthāya aṭṭhaṅgulādhikampi otāretvā nivāsetuṃ vaṭṭati.

'Eight fingerbreadths in measure' means eight fingerbreadths by the standard fingerbreadth. But for one who has thin shanks or large calf-muscles, it is allowable to lower the robe more than eight fingerbreadths to wear it suitably.

Pāsantanti pāsassa antaṃ, dasāmūlanti attho.

'The end of the pāsa' means the end of the hem; the meaning is 'the base of the fringe.'

Aparimaṇḍalaṃ nivāsessāmīti “purato vā pacchato vā olambetvā nivāsessāmī”ti evaṃ [V 0.0402] asañcicca. Kiñcāpi parimaṇḍalaṃ nivāsetuṃ ajānantassa anāpatti, tathāpi nivāsanavattaṃ sādhukaṃ uggahetabbameva. Sañcicca anuggahaṇañhi anādariyaṃ siyāti āha “apica nivāsanavattaṃ uggahetabba”nti.

'I will wear the lower robe unevenly' means 'I will wear it hanging down in front or behind.' Although there is no offense for one who does so unintentionally, or for one who does not know how to wear it evenly, still, the proper way of wearing the lower robe should be well learned. For intentional non-learning would be disrespect, hence it is said, 'moreover, the proper way of wearing the lower robe should be learned.'

Parimaṇḍalasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Wearing the Lower Robe Evenly is Concluded.

2. Dutiyaparimaṇḍalasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Second Training Rule on Wearing Evenly.

Paṭikkhittaṃ [M 0.0437] gihipārutanti khuddakavatthukhandhake paṭikkhittaṃ gihipārutaṃ. Idāni “na, bhikkhave”tiādinā (cūḷava. 280-281) saṅkhepena vuttamatthameva vitthāretvā dassetuṃ “tatthā”tiādimāha. Yaṃ kiñci aññathā pārutanti sambandho. Tasmāti yasmā setapaṭapārutādi gihipārutaṃ nāma, tasmā. Setapaṭāti etasseva vivaraṇaṃ. Aḍḍhapālakanigaṇṭhāti aḍḍhaṃ pālentīti aḍḍhapālakā, aḍḍhapālakā ca te nigaṇṭhā cāti aḍḍhapālakanigaṇṭhā. Te hi upari ekameva setavatthaṃ upakacchake pavesetvā paridahanti, heṭṭhā naggāpi aḍḍhameva pālenti. Paribbājakāti gihibandhanaṃ pahāya pabbajjūpagatā. Uraṃ vivaritvāti hadayamajjhaṃ vivaritvā. Akkhitārakāmattanti akkhimattaṃ. Ārāme vāti buddhūpaṭṭhānādikālaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Antaraghare vāti antare gharāni ettha, etassāti vā “antaraghara”nti laddhanāme gāme.

'The householder's way of covering is prohibited' means the householder's way of covering that is prohibited in the Khuddakavatthukkhandhaka. Now, to explain in detail the meaning briefly stated with 'No, bhikkhus,' etc. (Cūḷavagga 280-281), he says 'in that case,' etc. The connection is 'whatever is covered otherwise.' 'Therefore' means: because a covering with a white cloth, etc., is called a householder's covering, therefore. 'White cloth' is the explanation of this. 'Half-covering Nigaṇṭhas' means: those who protect half are 'half-protectors,' and they are Nigaṇṭhas, hence 'half-covering Nigaṇṭhas.' They wear only a single white cloth, tucking it in at the side and wearing it; below, they are naked, thus protecting only half. 'Wanderers' means those who have abandoned household bonds and gone forth into the homeless life. 'Baring the chest' means opening the middle of the chest. 'The measure of the pupil of the eye' means just the measure of an eye. 'Or in the monastery' is said with reference to times like attending upon the Buddha. 'Or inside a house' means in a place 'amidst houses,' or in a village named 'Antaraghara.'

Dutiyaparimaṇḍalasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Second Training Rule on Wearing Evenly is Concluded.

3-4. Suppaṭicchannasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3-4. Explanation of the Training Rule on Being Well Covered.

Suṭṭhu paṭicchannoti jattumpi urampi avivaritvā paṭicchādetabbaṭṭhāne paṭicchādanena paṭicchanno, na sīsapāruto. Tenāha “gaṇṭhikaṃ paṭimuñcitvā”tiādi. Tattha gaṇṭhikaṃ paṭimuñcitvāti gaṇṭhikaṃ pāsake paṭimuñcitvā. Antaraghare vāti gocaragāme. Ekadivasampi vāsūpagatassa santikaṃ yathāsukhaṃ gantuṃ vaṭṭati, ko pana vādo catuppañcāhaṃ vāsamadhiṭṭhāya vasitabhikkhūnaṃ santikanti gaṇṭhipade likhitaṃ.

'Well covered' means being covered in the places that should be covered, without exposing the collarbone or chest, and not with the head covered. Hence, it is said, 'having fastened the knot,' etc. Here, 'having fastened the knot' means having fastened the knot in the loop. 'Or inside a house' means in the alms-resort village. It is allowable to approach as one pleases someone who has come to stay for even a single day, so what need be said of monks who are residing after having determined to stay for four or five days?—this is written in the section on the knot.

Vāsūpagatassāti [V 0.0403] rattivāsatthāya upagatassa rattibhāge vā divasabhāge vā kāyaṃ vivaritvā nisīdato anāpatti.

'Of one who has come to stay' means of one who has approached for the purpose of staying the night. For one sitting with the body uncovered, whether during the night or the day, there is no offense.

Suppaṭicchannasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Being Well Covered is Concluded.

5-6. Susaṃvutasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

5-6. Explanation of the Training Rule on Being Well-Restrained.

Susaṃvutoti [M 0.0438] susaṃyato. Yathā panettha susaṃvuto nāma hoti, taṃ dassetuṃ “hatthaṃ vā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

'Well-restrained' means well-controlled. To show how one is here called 'well-restrained,' it is said, 'the hand or,' and so on.

Susaṃvutasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Being Well-Restrained is Concluded.

7-8. Okkhittacakkhusikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

7-8. Explanation of the Training Rule on Downcast Eyes.

Kittakena pana okkhittacakkhu hotīti āha “yugamattaṃ bhūmibhāgaṃ pekkhamāno”ti. Yugayuttako hi danto ājāneyyo yugamattaṃ pekkhati, purato catuhatthappamāṇaṃ bhūmibhāgaṃ, imināpi ettakaṃ pekkhantena gantabbaṃ. Yo anādariyaṃ paṭicca taṃ taṃ disābhāgaṃ pāsādaṃ kūṭāgāraṃ vīthiṃ olokento gacchati, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Hatthiassādiparissayābhāvanti parissayanaṭṭhena, abhibhavanaṭṭhena, viheṭhanaṭṭhena vā parissayo, hatthiassādiyeva parissayo hatthiassādiparissayo, tassābhāvaṃ, hatthiassādi upaddavābhāvanti attho. “Yathā ca ekasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhatvā, evaṃ gacchantopi parissayābhāvaṃ oloketuṃ labhatiyeva, tathā gāme pūja”nti (sārattha. ṭī. pācittiya 3.582) vadanti.

But to what extent is one 'with downcast eyes'? It is said: 'Looking at a yoke’s length of ground.' For a tamed thoroughbred horse yoked to a yoke looks a yoke’s length ahead—a portion of ground measuring four cubits in front; one should also walk while looking that same distance. One who, out of disrespect, looks around at various directions, palaces, gabled mansions, or streets while walking commits an offense of wrong-doing. 'The absence of danger from elephants, horses, and so on'—'danger' is in the sense of harassment, oppression, or injury; 'danger from elephants, horses, and so on' is the danger that is elephants, horses, etc.; 'its absence' means the absence of harm from elephants, horses, and so on. They say: 'Just as when standing in one place, so also while walking, one is certainly permitted to look for any absence of danger; likewise for veneration in the village' (Sāratthaṭīkā, Pācittiya 3.582).

Okkhittacakkhusikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Downcast Eyes is Concluded.

9-10. Ukkhittakāyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

9-10. Explanation of the Training Rule on Hitching Up the Robe.

Antoindakhīlato paṭṭhāyāti parikkhittassa gāmassa antoummārato paṭṭhāya, aparikkhittassa pana dutiyaleḍḍupātato paṭṭhāya na evaṃ gantabbaṃ.

'Starting from within the city-post' means, for a fortified village, starting from the inner threshold; but for an unfortified one, starting from the place where a second clod would fall. One should not walk in this manner.

Ukkhittakāyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Hitching Up the Robe is Concluded.

11-12. Ujjagghikasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

11-12. Explanation of the Training Rule on Loud Laughter.

Hasanīyasmiṃ [V 0.0404] vatthusminti nimittatthe bhummaṃ, hasitabbavatthukāraṇāti attho.

'On a laughable matter'—the locative case here is used in the sense of cause; the meaning is 'for the reason of a laughable matter.'

Ujjagghikasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Loud Laughter is Concluded.

13-14. Uccasaddasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

13-14. Explanation of the Training Rule on Loud Noise.

Kittāvatā [M 0.0439] appasaddo hotīti āha “ayaṃ panetthā”tiādi. Saddameva suṇātīti aparibyattakkharaṃ saddamattameva suṇāti. Tenāha “kathaṃ na vavatthapetī”ti.

'To what extent is one of low sound?' He says, 'But here, this…' and so on. 'One hears only the sound' means one hears merely the sound with indistinct syllables. Therefore, it is said: 'How does one not ascertain it?'

Uccasaddasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Loud Noise is Concluded.

15-20. Kāyappacālakādisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

15-20. Explanation of the Training Rules on Swaying the Body, and so on.

“Kāyādīni paggahetvā”ti etasseva vivaraṇaṃ “niccalāni ujukāni ṭhapetvā”ti gantabbañceva nisīditabbañcāti samena iriyāpathena gantabbañceva nisīditabbañca. Kāyappacālakādiyuttaṃ chakkaṃ.

'Holding up the body, and so on' is explained by 'one should walk and sit keeping them still and straight.' One should both walk and sit with a balanced posture. This is the set of six rules connected with swaying the body, and so on.

Kāyappacālakādisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rules on Swaying the Body, and so on, is Concluded.

26. Pallatthikasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

26. Explanation of the Training Rule on Sitting Cross-legged.

Dussapallatthikāyāti ettha āyogapallatthikāpi dussapallatthikāyeva.

Regarding “with legs crossed with a cloth”—here, even “with legs crossed with a strap” is considered “with legs crossed with a cloth.”

Pallatthikasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on sitting cross-legged is concluded.

Chabbīsatisāruppasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the twenty-six Sāruppa training rules is concluded.

27. Sakkaccapaṭiggahaṇasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

27. Explanation of the Training Rule on Receiving Attentively.

Satiṃ [V 0.0405] upaṭṭhāpetvāti chaḍḍetukāmo viya ahutvā piṇḍapāte satiṃ upaṭṭhāpetvā, “piṇḍapātaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti satiṃ upaṭṭhāpetvā.

“Having established mindfulness” means: not being like one who wishes to throw it away, one establishes mindfulness on the almsfood; one establishes mindfulness with the thought, “I will receive almsfood.”

Sakkaccapaṭiggahaṇasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on receiving attentively is concluded.

28. Pattasaññīpaṭiggahaṇasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

28. Explanation of the Training Rule on Receiving with Perception of the Bowl.

Upanibaddhasaññī [M 0.0440] hutvāti piṇḍapātaṃ dente anādariyaṃ paṭicca tahaṃ tahaṃ anoloketvā patte ābhogasaññī hutvā.

“Having become one with perception fixed upon it” means, when almsfood is being given, not looking here and there out of disrespect, but having one's perception directed to the bowl.

Pattasaññīpaṭiggahaṇasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on receiving with perception of the bowl is concluded.

29. Samasūpakapaṭiggahaṇasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

29. Explanation of the Training Rule on Receiving an Equal Portion of Curry.

Samasūpakanti pamāṇayuttaṃ sūpavantaṃ katvā, bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso cāyaṃ. Byañjanaṃ pana anādiyitvā atthamattameva dassetuṃ “samasūpako nāmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sabbāpi sūpeyyabyañjanavikatīti oloṇisākasūpeyyamacchamaṃsarasādikā sabbāpi sūpeyyabyañjanavikati.

“With equal curry” means making it laden with curry to an appropriate measure; this is a neuter noun indicating a state of being. But without taking the relish into account, only the meaning is to be shown; hence, it is said, “named ‘with equal curry’,” and so on. All varieties of curry and relish—that is, all varieties of curry and relish such as salted water, greens, soup, fish, meat, and juices—are included.

Samasūpakapaṭiggahaṇasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on receiving an equal portion of curry is concluded.

30-32. Samatittikādisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

30–32. Explanation of the Training Rules Beginning with ‘Level with the Brim’.

Samatittikanti bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso, samatittikaṃ katvāti attho. Evamaññesupi īdisesu ṭhānesu attho daṭṭhabbo. Samapuṇṇanti (sārattha. ṭī. pācittiya 3.605) pattassa antomukhavaṭṭilekhāsamapuṇṇaṃ. Samabharitanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Tañca kho adhiṭṭhānupagapattasseva, netarassa. Tenāha “adhiṭṭhānupagapattassā”tiādi. Racitanti kataṃ, pakkhittaṃ pūritanti attho. Yaṃ kiñci yāvakālikanti yāgubhattaphalāphalādiṃ yaṃ kiñci āmisajātikaṃ. Yattha katthacīti adhiṭṭhānupago vā hotu, anadhiṭṭhānupago vā yattha katthaci patte[V 0.0406]. Thūpīkatānīti thūpaṃ viya katāni, adhiṭṭhānupagassa pattassa antomukhavaṭṭilekhaṃ atikkamitvā katānīti attho. Idañca “yāmakālikādīnī”ti imassa vasena vuttaṃ, “yāvakālika”nti imassa pana vasena vacanabyattayaṃ katvā “thūpīkatampi vaṭṭatī”ti yojetabbaṃ. Pi-saddena athūpīkatāni vaṭṭantīti ettha kathāva natthīti dasseti. Heṭṭhā orohatīti samantā okāsasabbhāvato cāliyamānaṃ heṭṭhā bhassati[M 0.0441]. Takkolavaṭaṃsakādayoti ettha matthake ṭhapitatakkolameva vaṭaṃsakasadisattā takkolavaṭaṃsakaṃ. Ādisaddena pupphavaṭaṃsakakaṭukaphalādivaṭaṃsakānaṃ (pāci. aṭṭha. 605) gahaṇaṃ, na taṃ thūpīkataṃ nāma hoti pāṭekkaṃ bhājanattā paṇṇādīnaṃ.

“Level with the brim” is a neuter verbal noun, meaning “having made it level.” The meaning should be understood in the same way in other similar instances. “Completely full” (Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā, Pācittiya 3.605) means completely full up to the inner circular rim of the bowl. “Completely filled”: the same method applies here as well. And that applies only to a bowl that has been designated, not to another. Therefore, it is said, “of a bowl that has been designated,” and so on. “Arranged” means made, put in, filled. “Anything allowable until noon” means any kind of food, such as rice-gruel, cooked rice, fruit, and so on. “In any” means in any bowl, whether it is one that has been designated or one that has not been designated. “Mounded” means made like a mound, that is, made exceeding the inner circular rim of a designated bowl. And this is said with reference to “things allowable for a watch, and so on.” But with reference to “things allowable until noon,” a distinction should be made in the wording and it should be connected by saying “even that which is mounded is allowable.” The word “pi” shows that there is no question that those which are not mounded are allowable. “It goes down” means, being shaken because of the availability of space all around, it falls down. “Takkola-crest, etc.”: Here, a takkola berry placed on top is like a crest-ornament, hence it is a “takkola-crest”. The word “etc.” includes flower-crests, bitter-fruit-crests, and so on (Pācittiya Aṭṭhakathā 605). But these are not considered “mounded” because leaves and so on are individual containers.

Samatittikādisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rules beginning with ‘Level with the Brim’ is concluded.

33-34. Sapadānasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

33–34. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Walking Sequentially for Alms.

Sapadānanti (sārattha. ṭī. pācittiya 3.608) ettha dānaṃ vuccati avakhaṇḍanaṃ, apetaṃ dānato apadānaṃ, anavakhaṇḍanti attho, saha apadānena sapadānaṃ, avakhaṇḍanavirahitaṃ, anupaṭipāṭiyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tenāha “tattha tattha odhiṃ akatvā anupaṭipāṭiyā”ti.

Regarding `sapadāna` (Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā, Pācittiya 3.608): here `dāna` is called ‘breaking’; `apadāna` is ‘apart from breaking,’ meaning ‘unbroken.’ `Sapadāna` is ‘with `apadāna`,’ ‘without breaking.’ This means ‘sequentially.’ Therefore it is said: “without making a limit here and there, sequentially.”

Sapadānasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Walking Sequentially for Alms is concluded.

36. Odanappaṭicchādanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

36. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Covering Rice.

Māghātasamayādīsūti ettha yasmiṃ samaye “pāṇo na hantabbo”ti rājāno bheriṃ carāpenti, ayaṃ māghātasamayo nāma. Byañjanaṃ paṭicchādetvā dentīti byañjanaṃ channaṃ katvā denti.

Regarding ‘at the time of non-killing, etc.’: here, the time when kings have a drum beaten proclaiming, “No living being should be killed,” is called the ‘time of non-killing.’ ‘They give, having concealed the relish’ means they give, having made the relish covered.

Odanappaṭicchādanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Covering Rice is concluded.

37. Sūpodanaviññattisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

37. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Asking for Curry and Rice.

Ekādasameti sūpodanaviññattiyaṃ. Ettha pana yassa mukhe pakkhipitvā vippaṭisāre uppanne [V 0.0407] puna uggiritukāmassāpi sace sahasā pavisati, ayaṃ asañcicca paribhuñjati nāma. Yo pana viññattampi aviññattampi ekasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhitaṃ sahasā anupadhāretvā gahetvā bhuñjati, ayaṃ asatiyā bhuñjati nāma.

The eleventh is the rule on asking for curry and rice. Here, if, after placing food in one’s mouth, regret arises, and though one wishes to spit it out again, it hastily goes down, this is called 'consuming unintentionally'. If, however, one takes and eats food that is in one place—whether requested or not requested—hastily and without considering it, this is called 'eating unmindfully'.

Sūpodanaviññattisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Asking for Curry and Rice is concluded.

38. Ujjhānasaññīsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

38. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Perception of Fault-Finding.

Ujjhāyati [M 0.0442] etenāti ujjhānaṃ, cittaṃ, tasmiṃ saññā ujjhānasaññāti āha “ujjhānasaññī”tiādi. Olokentassāti paresaṃ pattaṃ olokentassa.

`Ujjhāyati etenāti ujjhānaṃ` means ‘that by which one finds fault,’ that is, the mind. `Tasmiṃ saññā ujjhānasaññā` means ‘the perception of that is the perception of fault-finding’; hence it is said `ujjhānasaññī` (one who perceives fault-finding), and so on. `Olokentassa` means ‘of one who looks at others’ bowls.’

Ujjhānasaññīsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Perception of Fault-Finding is concluded.

39. Kabaḷasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

39. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Morsels.

“Mayūraṇḍaṃ atimahanta”nti vacanato mayūraṇḍappamāṇopi kabaḷo na vaṭṭati. Keci pana “mayūraṇḍato mahantova na vaṭṭati, na mayūraṇḍappamāṇo”tipi vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Kukkuṭaṇḍaṃ atikhuddakanti etthāpi eseva nayo, gilānassa pana atikhuddakaṃ kabaḷaṃ karotopi anāpatti.

According to the statement, “A peacock’s egg is extremely large,” even a morsel the size of a peacock’s egg is not permitted. Some, however, say, “Only what is larger than a peacock’s egg is not permitted, not what is the size of a peacock’s egg.” That should not be accepted. As for “a hen’s egg is extremely small,” the same principle applies here; but for a sick person, even making a very small morsel is not an offense.

Kabaḷasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Morsels is concluded.

41-42. Anāhaṭasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

41–42. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Not Inserting the Hand

Sakalaṃ hatthanti sakalā aṅguliyo. Hatthasaddo cettha tadekadesesu aṅgulīsu daṭṭhabbo “hatthamuddā”tiādīsu viya. Evañca katvā sabbaggahaṇaṃ samatthitaṃ hoti. Aññathā sakalaṃ hatthaṃ mukhe pavesetumasakkuṇeyyattā sabbaggahaṇamasamatthitameva siyā. Samudāye pavattassa ca vohārassa avayavepi pavattanato ekaṅgulimpi tato ekadesampi mukhe pakkhipituṃ na vaṭṭati.

`Sakalaṃ hatthaṃ` (the entire hand) means all the fingers. Here, the word `hattha` (hand) should be understood as referring to its parts, the fingers, just as in phrases like `hatthamuddā` (hand gesture) and so on. And by taking it thus, the inclusion of 'entire' is justified. Otherwise, since it is impossible to put the entire hand into the mouth, the inclusion of 'entire' would be unjustified. And because a term that applies to a whole also applies to its parts, it is not allowable to put even a single finger, or even a part of one, into the mouth.

Anāhaṭasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Not Inserting the Hand is concluded.

43. Sakabaḷasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

43. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Speaking with a Mouthful

Tattake [V 0.0408] sati vaṭṭatīti tattake mukhamhi sati kathetuṃ vaṭṭati.

`Tattake sati vaṭṭati` means that when there is that much in the mouth, it is allowable to speak.

Sakabaḷasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Speaking with a Mouthful is concluded.

50-51. Capucapukārakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

50–51. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Making Chomping Sounds

“Capu [M 0.0443] capū”ti evaṃ saddaṃ katvāti “capu capū”ti evaṃ anukaraṇasaddaṃ katvā. “Pañcavīsatimepi eseva nayo”ti iminā “surusurukārakanti ‘surū surū’ti evaṃ saddaṃ katvā”ti imamatthamatidisati.

`‘Capu capū’ti evaṃ saddaṃ katvā` means making an onomatopoeic sound like “capu capu.” By the phrase `pañcavīsatimepi eseva nayo` (the same method applies also in the twenty-fifth), this meaning is extended to `surusurukārakaṃ` (making a slurping sound), meaning “making a sound like ‘suru suru’.”

Capucapukārakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Making Chomping Sounds is concluded.

Tiṃsabhojanappaṭisaṃyuttasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Thirty Training Rules Connected with Food is concluded.

57. Chattapāṇisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

57. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning a Person with an Umbrella in Hand

Yaṃ kiñci chattanti setacchattakilañjacchattapaṇṇacchattesu yaṃ kiñci chattaṃ. Yampi tatthajātakadaṇḍakena kataṃ ekapaṇṇacchattaṃ hoti, tampi chattameva. Yattha katthaci sarīrāvayaveti aṃsaūruādike yattha katthaci sarīrāvayaveti.

`Yaṃ kiñci chattaṃ` (any kind of umbrella) refers to any umbrella among white umbrellas, bamboo-strip umbrellas, or leaf umbrellas. Even a single-leaf umbrella made with a stick that grew there is also an umbrella. `Yattha katthaci sarīrāvayave` (on any part of the body) means on any part of the body whatsoever, such as the shoulder, thigh, and so on.

Chattapāṇisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning a Person with an Umbrella in Hand is concluded.

60. Āvudhapāṇisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

60. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning a Person with a Weapon in Hand

Sabbāpi dhanuvikatīti cāpakodaṇḍādibhedā sabbāpi dhanuvikati. Cāpoti (sārattha. ṭī. pācittiya 3.637) majjhe vaṅkā kājadaṇḍasadisā dhanuvikati. Kodaṇḍoti vaṭṭaladaṇḍā dhanuvikati. Paṭimukkanti pavesitaṃ laggitaṃ. Yāva na gaṇhātīti yāva hatthena na gaṇhāti, ayameva vā pāṭho. Tāva vaṭṭatīti tāva dhammaṃ desetuṃ vaṭṭati.

`Sabbāpi dhanuvikati` (all kinds of bows) means all variations of bows, with types such as the `cāpa` and the `kodaṇḍa`. `Cāpa` (Sāratthaṭīkā, Pācittiya 3.637) refers to a type of bow curved in the middle, like a carrying-pole. `Kodaṇḍa` refers to a type of bow with a rounded staff. `Paṭimukka` means inserted or attached. `Yāva na gaṇhāti` means 'as long as one does not take it with the hand'; or this is the reading. `Tāva vaṭṭati` means 'for that long it is allowable'; that is, it is allowable to teach the Dhamma.

Āvudhapāṇisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning a Person with a Weapon in Hand is concluded.

61-62. Pādukasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

61-62. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Footwear

Kevalaṃ [V 0.0409] akkantassāti kevalaṃ pādukaṃ akkamitvā ṭhitassa. Paṭimukkassāti paṭimuñcitvā ṭhitassa. Tenāha “pavesetvā ṭhānavasenā”ti.

`Kevalaṃ akkantassa` means 'of one who is standing having merely stepped on a sandal'. `Paṭimukkassa` means 'of one who is standing having put it on'. Therefore, it is said, 'by way of standing having inserted the foot'.

Pādukasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Footwear is concluded.

63. Yānasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

63. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Vehicles

Yānagatassāti [M 0.0444] “yānaṃ nāma vayhaṃ, ratho, sakaṭaṃ, sandhamānikā, sivikā, pāṭaṅkī”ti (pāci. 640, 1187) vuttaṃ yānaṃ upādāya antamaso hatthasaṅghāṭamhi gatassa. Tenāha “sacepi dvīhi janehī”tiādi. Vayhādiketi ettha vayhanti upari maṇḍapasadisaṃ padaracchadanaṃ, sabbapāliguṇṭhimaṃ vā chādetvā kataṃ sakaṭavisesaṃ “vayha”nti vadanti. Ādisaddena rathādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ.

`Yānagatassa` refers to one who has gone in a vehicle, taking 'vehicle' to mean what is stated as: 'a vehicle, namely, a `vayha`, a chariot, a cart, a `sandhamānikā`, a palanquin, a litter' (Pācittiya 640, 1187), down to one who has gone on an elephant's back-cloth. Therefore, it is said, 'even if by two people,' and so on. Here, in the phrase `vayhādike`, `vayha` is said to be a special kind of cart made by covering it above with a roof of planks like a pavilion, or by completely enveloping it with a cloth. By the word `ādi`, chariots and so on are included.

Yānasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Vehicles is concluded.

75. Udakeuccārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

75. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Discharging Excrement in Water

Pakiṇṇakanti vomissakanayaṃ. Sacittakanti (sārattha. ṭī. pācittiya 3.576) vatthuvijānanacittena, paṇṇattivijānanacittena ca sacittakaṃ. “Anādariyaṃ paṭiccā”ti (pāci. 654) vuttattā yasmā anādariyavaseneva āpajjitabbato idaṃ sabbaṃ kevalaṃ akusalameva, tañca pakatiyā vajjaṃ, sañcicca vītikkamanañca domanassikasseva hoti, tasmā “lokavajjaṃ akusalacittaṃ dukkhavedana”nti vuttaṃ. Sesesupi eseva nayo.

`Pakiṇṇaka` means the method of what is mixed. `Sacittaka` means with a mind that knows the object and with a mind that knows the concept (Sāratthaṭīkā, Pācittiya 3.576). Because it is said, 'on account of disrespect' (Pācittiya 654), and since this is entirely unwholesome, being an offense to be incurred only through disrespect, and it is blameworthy by nature, and an intentional transgression is indeed accompanied by displeasure, therefore it is said, 'worldly blame, unwholesome consciousness, painful feeling.' The same method applies to the remaining cases as well.

Ekūnavīsatidhammadesanāpaṭisaṃyuttasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Nineteen Training Rules Connected with the Exposition of the Dhamma is concluded.

Iti kaṅkhāvitaraṇiyā pātimokkhavaṇṇanāya

Thus in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī, the commentary on the Pātimokkha,

Vinayatthamañjūsāyaṃ līnatthappakāsaniyaṃ

in the Vinayatthamañjūsā, the Līnatthappakāsanī,

Sekhiyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

the Commentary on the Sekhiya Rules is concluded.

Adhikaraṇasamathavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Settlement of Legal Issues

Gaṇanaparicchedoti [V 0.0410] saṅkhyāparicchedo. Adhikarīyanti etthāti adhikaraṇāni. Ke adhikarīyanti? Samathā. Kathaṃ adhikarīyanti? Samanavasena. Tasmā te tesaṃ samanavasena pavattantīti āha “adhikaraṇāni samentī”tiādi. Uppannānaṃ uppannānanti uṭṭhitānaṃ uṭṭhitānaṃ. Kiñcāpi [M 0.0445] adhikaraṇaṭṭhena ekavidhaṃ, tathāpi vatthuvasena nānā hotīti “adhikaraṇāna”nti bahuvacanaṃ kataṃ. Idāni tassa nānāttaṃ dassetvā vivarituṃ “vivādādhikaraṇa”ntiādimāha. Vivādoyeva adhikaraṇaṃ vivādādhikaraṇaṃ. Esa nayo sesesupi. Samathatthanti samanatthaṃ.

'Gaṇanapariccheda' means defining the count. 'Adhikarīyanti' means 'these are settled here,' hence 'legal questions' (adhikaraṇāni). What are settled? The means of settlement. How are they settled? By way of reconciliation. Therefore, because they proceed for them by way of reconciliation, it is said, 'the legal questions are settled,' and so forth. 'Uppannānaṃ uppannānaṃ' means 'of those that have arisen, of those that have arisen.' Although it is of one kind in terms of being a legal question, yet it is diverse in terms of its object; therefore, the plural 'adhikaraṇānaṃ' is used. Now, to show its diversity and to explain it, he says 'vivādādhikaraṇa' and so forth. A dispute itself is a 'vivādādhikaraṇa.' The same method applies to the rest. 'Samathattha' means 'for the purpose of settlement.'

Adhikaraṇassa sammukhā vinayanato sammukhāvinayo. Dabbamallaputtattherasadisassa sativepullappattassa khīṇāsavasseva dātabbo vinayo sativinayo. Sammūḷhassa gaggabhikkhusadisassa ummattakassa dātabbo vinayo amūḷhavinayo. Paṭiññātena karaṇabhūtena karaṇaṃ paṭiññātakaraṇaṃ. Atha vā paṭiññāte āpannabhāvādike karaṇaṃ kiriyā, “āyatiṃ saṃvareyyāsī”ti parivāsadānādivasena ca pavattaṃ vacīkammaṃ paṭiññātakaraṇaṃ. Yassā kiriyāya dhammavādino bahutarā, esā yebhuyyasikā nāma. Yo pāpussannatāya pāpiyo, puggalo, tassa upavāḷabhikkhusadisassa kattabbato tassapāpiyasikā, aluttasamāsoyaṃ. Tiṇavatthārakasadisattā tiṇavatthārako. Yathā (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 212) hi gūthaṃ vā muttaṃ vā ghaṭṭiyamānaṃ duggandhatāya bādhati, tiṇehi avattharitvā suppaṭicchāditassa panassa gandho na bādhati, evameva yaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ mūlānumūlaṃ gantvā vūpasamiyamānaṃ kakkhaḷattāya vāḷattāya bhedāya saṃvattati, taṃ iminā kammena vūpasantaṃ gūthaṃ viya tiṇavatthārakena paṭicchannaṃ suvūpasantaṃ hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “tiṇavatthārakasadisattā tiṇavatthārako”ti.

Because a legal question is settled face-to-face, it is called 'face-to-face resolution' (sammukhāvinaya). The resolution to be given to one like the Elder Dabbamallaputta, who has attained the fullness of mindfulness and is an arahant, is called 'resolution through mindfulness' (sativinaya). The resolution to be given to one who is confused and insane, like the monk Gagga, is called 'resolution on account of insanity' (amūḷhavinaya). An act done by means of acknowledgment is called 'resolution by acknowledgment' (paṭiññātakaraṇa). Alternatively, an act performed regarding one who has acknowledged an offense or the like—such as granting probation or other verbal procedures that proceed with the statement, 'You should restrain yourself in the future'—is called 'resolution by acknowledgment.' That procedure in which those who speak according to the Dhamma are in the majority is called 'resolution by majority' (yebhuyyasikā). The 'resolution for one who is worse' (tassapāpiyasikā) is to be done for a person who is worse due to an abundance of evil, like the monk Upavāḷa; this is an unelided compound. It is called 'covering with grass' (tiṇavatthāraka) because it resembles covering with grass. For just as (Cūḷavagga Aṭṭhakathā 212) feces or urine, when stirred, cause distress due to their foul smell, but when covered with grass and well concealed, their odor no longer causes distress—so too, a legal question that, when pursued to its roots and settled, leads to harshness, ferocity, and schism, becomes well-settled when resolved by this act, like feces covered with a covering of grass. Therefore, it is said, 'Because it resembles covering with grass, it is called "covering with grass" (tiṇavatthārako).'

Tatrāti tesu sattasu adhikaraṇasamathesu. “Aṭṭhārasahi vatthūhī”ti lakkhaṇavacanametaṃ “yadi me byādhikā bhaveyyuṃ, dātabbamidamosadha”ntiādinā (saṃ. ni. ṭī. 2.3.39-42) viya. Tasmā tesu aññatarena vivadantā aṭṭhārasahi vatthūhi vivadantīti vuccati. Vivādoti vipaccanīkavādo. Upavadanāti akkoso. Codanāti anuyogo. Dveti thullaccayadubbhāsitāpattiyo [V 0.0411] dve. Catunnaṃ kammānaṃ karaṇanti catunnaṃ kammānaṃ antare yassa kassaci kammassa karaṇaṃ.

'Tatra' (therein) refers to these seven means of settling legal questions. 'By eighteen grounds' is a descriptive term, like in the phrase, 'If they were to become ill, this medicine should be given,' and so forth (Saṃyutta Nikāya Ṭīkā 2.3.39-42). Therefore, those who dispute by any one of these are said to dispute by eighteen grounds. 'Vivāda' means opposing speech. 'Upavadana' means abuse. 'Codanā' means investigation. 'Two' refers to the two offenses: a grave offense and wrong speech. 'The performance of the four acts' means the performance of any one among the four acts.

Evaṃ adhikaraṇāni dassetvā idāni tesu idaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ ettakehi samathehi sammatīti dassetuṃ “tatthā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yasmiṃ vihāre uppannaṃ[M 0.0446], tasmiṃyeva vā sammatīti sambandho. Evaṃ sesesupi.
